The ARGO Glossary

A.E.F.American Expeditionary Forces, the American army sent to Europe in World War I. Duffey claims that before joining the army in 1917 he drove ambulances with Hemingway in Italy and E. E. Cummings in France. The narrator doubts even his brief presence in an American army camp and suggests that he borrowed some of these experiences from Sebastian Hilton, while allowing that he lived borrowed scenes fully [MTM B2:72].

MTM B2:72

A.M.Loy Larkin, in a letter to Finnegan from Cambeltown, New South Wales, dated Thursday, February 11, 1943, set a rendezvous time of 7:45 A.M. for the next day, acknowledging Finnegan might find it decadent to wake so early [A:27].

A:27

Aansen, SwedeOne of the resident regulars at the Old Wooden Ship, in the town where Finnegan first met Seaworthy, the Devil, and Anastasia [D:215-216]. Aansen belongs to a group of five men called Swede, none of whom is Swedish: their origins are Norse, Danish, Icelandic, German, and Orcadian. The passage does not assign a particular origin to Aansen [D:217].

D:215-216; D:217

AaronFormer owner of the marbles in Phoebe Anne Ankerson’s suitcase, which Finnegan steals. Her label says Aaron is too old for them and that they are to be given to Harold Michael; some are agates [D:171-172].

D:171-172

Aaron, AvrilOne of the women living at the Old Wooden Ship who are called “salt water widows,” most of them married to seamen [D:221].

D:221

Aaron, Casper StoneOne of the Princes of the Ekklesia at the conclave in Babylonia Bagascia. First called in Conrad Stone Hackenschmidt’s armed roll call, he votes for the straw man, speaking surlily as though under compulsion [MB:566–567].

MB:566–567

Ab SalomName by which Teresa Piccone Stranahan identifies Absalom Stein when she recounts the company’s earlier lives aboard the Argo. She calls him Ab-Salom, the Father of Peace, and says that he was a ship’s chandler and provisioner on the Euxine who joined the voyage to look after his investments [MTM B7:233-234]. See Stein, Absalom.

MTM B7:233-234

Abbott, Catherine StoneOne of the Princes of the Ekklesia at the conclave in Babylonia Bagascia. Called after Casper Stone Aaron in Conrad Stone Hackenschmidt’s armed roll call, she votes for the straw man [MB:566–567].

MB:566–567

Abd Aliah of the SeaAbd-Aliah of the Sea, former owner of the Argo and father of a famously beautiful daughter with a tail. He sold the ship to Sindbad of El-Basrah [MTM B13:404].

MTM B13:404

Abdo, AdrianActor playing the title role in Goat Boy at the Castle Theatre when Casey, acting on a bet, walks uninvited onto the stage. Casey reads seven names from a Greater Chicago telephone directory and provokes an ecstatic ovation; afterward nobody remembers why the crowd reacted so strongly [PG:543].

PG:543

Abdo, JamesJames Gate Abdo, one of the Princes of the Ekklesia at the Last Conclave in Babylonia Bagascia [MB:561] [MB:566-567]. He votes “Ego eligo effigiem” for the straw-man after Conrad Stone Hackenschmidt orders that response while covering the assembled Princes with a Browning Automatic Rifle. Six dissenters vote for Joseph Cardinal Hedayat and are killed; the straw-man is elected and burned [MB:567-568]. Abdo’s vote belongs to this coerced ceremony intended to terminate the Church [MB:567-568].

MB:561; MB:566-567; MB:567-568

Abomination of DesolationProphetic phrase that Mr. X applies to 'the world that God so loved, becoming trivial and narrow.' In his letter to Absalom Stein, X predicts that they will see this desolation and immediately rebukes Stein for having read Teilhard without laughing [A:265] [A:266].

A:265; A:266

Absalom (Son of King David)Biblical son of King David. His supposed appearance in Finnegan’s discussion of dynastic succession remains unverified; the passage previously cited concerns Absalom Stein [MTM B5:169].

MTM B5:169

AbsintheIngredient in the “Green Ladies” drunk in the Quarter during the appearance of the Royal Pop People. Margaret Stone describes the drink to Mary Virginia as “like Peppermint Schnapps, except with absinthe instead of the schnapps” [MTM B11:309].

MTM B11:309

Absolute MinimumFinnegan's reserve against going completely broke. His last hundred-dollar bill is Miguel; reaching that reserve tells him he must find work. Earlier bills included Jose-Ramires, Hernandez, Aloysius, and Gottfried von Guggenheim [D:19]. The narrator calls this the economic law of the cushion and the absolute minimum [D:20].

D:19; D:20

Academy (U.S. Military)The United States Military Academy at West Point, to which Private Gregory says he gained an appointment about a year after deserting and changing his identity in 1907. After more than a century as a sergeant, he passed for a man of twenty, cultivated political patrons, and entered the Academy. He was later commissioned and became an army historian and archivist [A:77] [A:78].

A:77; A:78

AcastusAcastus of Iolcus, who with his unnamed wife subjects Peleus to what Melchisedech Duffey calls a “badger-game.” In his commentary in “Promontory Goats,” Duffey identifies Peleus as Casey’s primordial Argo role [PG:534-535]. Hilary Hilton and Mary Jean occupy the corresponding positions in Casey’s twentieth-century life, though Duffey says their game is played in reverse. He suggests that Casey may have sought death at Hilary’s hands and received a more painful derision instead. Duffey admits that he does not know what either Hilton wanted from Casey and wonders whether the original game was also reversed [PG:536].

PG:534-535; PG:536

Acme Pump CompanyWords cast on iron pump handles, among the household inscriptions Duffey remembers from his childhood. He gathers these particulars through close observation and by appropriating other people’s memories [MTM B1:16-17].

MTM B1:16-17

Acme Royal Top, TheEarlier erroneous heading, which inserted Royal into the carriage’s name. See Acme Top, The.
Acme Top, TheHorse-drawn carriage named “The Acme Top” in a Royal Pop Historian’s account of the memories preserved in a Decatur Street flagstone. He lists it with the Acme Open, the Southern Beauty, and other old vehicles during a nostalgic address at Duffey’s place [MTM B11:329].

MTM B11:329

AcornsFood eaten by Gautier, the goat-man, and his goats during their wandering life in New Jersey. The narrator associates this part of Gautier's diet with his old-world stock [A:196] [A:197].

A:196; A:197

ActionFinnegan’s term for what his paintings of the thirteen murdered cardinals portray. When Biloxi Brannagan exclaims over their passion, Finnegan contrasts acting with passively undergoing and insists that action does not require exterior motion. The exchange takes place aboard the Argo, where the paintings cover the bulkheads of the Bread and Wine Room [MTM B13:452-453]. His explanation breaks off after “Action is...” when Brannagan interrupts him [MTM B13:453].

MTM B13:452-453; MTM B13:453

ActiumSite of the naval battle of 31 BC. In the history spoken by the talking oak in its wheel, the Argo had been the Anthony Ship at Actium and had been shamed there [MTM B13:404].

MTM B13:404

AdamFinnegan's counterpart 'in a variant account' of creation. In the opening scene Finnegan is the first man, drinking the first beer; when he raises his eyes from his drink, the Garden is gone and he is in the World. Both he and Adam are said to be 'a little more than half Italian and a little more than half Irish' [A:1].

A:1

AdelphosWord X says Anastasia used for Finnegan. He explains it as meaning cousin as well as brother in Old Greek, and takes it as evidence of their kinship through the ancestor he identifies as the Devil [D:279].

D:279

AdenMarket in Biloxi Brannagan’s stories where a shrewd trader can supposedly make a fortune in Circassian slave-girl futures. Finnegan is willing to credit this part of his account [D:206].

D:206

Admiror audiensDuffey's Latin reply to Mr. X's description of the nested black, gray, and brown boxes. Duffey gives his own loose translation, 'I am surprised to hear it,' then asks whether he has seen the box before. Mr. X says he has brought it from Chicago after stealing it from Casey [A:136].

A:136

Adrian the DutchmanOne of the figures aboard the Navicula Petri in Henry's dream, named beside Hildebrand among apostles and figures from the history of the Church [A:44] [A:45]. The epithet probably identifies Pope Adrian VI, Adriaan Florensz of Utrecht, whose pontificate lasted from 1522 to 1523. This is an identification inferred from the epithet; the passage does not give his papal number.

A:44; A:45

Adriatic SeaSea on which Ragusa lies. Duffey tells a New Orleans hull dealer that the Argo’s keel was laid at Ragusa and its timbers came from the Dinaric Alps; he qualifies the whole encounter as symbolically rather than ordinarily accurate [MTM B13:412].

MTM B13:412

AdversariesFormidable opponents of the Argonauts, including the Evil Prince, the Purple Prince, the Mocking Prince, and the Laughing Prince. The narrator credits them with mystery, personality, and courage, and allows that they sometimes defeat and kill great Ship Masters. The Laughing Prince of Tartary may be the strongest and trickiest; reports call him the Prince of the Third Way, claimed by neither God nor the Devil [MTM B13:437].

MTM B13:437

AdversaryThe Devil as opponent of Duffey and the fiefdoms of Invisible Neustria [MTM B8:245-246]. The group is said to have known him before his thousand-year imprisonment [MTM B7:236]. In Cleo Mahoney’s account of the sixth possible future, the Adversary and the Patriarch are the only persons left in the world, and the Adversary presses him to sign a covenant that would unmake everyone else [MTM B10:294] [MTM B10:296].

MTM B8:245-246; MTM B7:236; MTM B10:294; MTM B10:296

AeetesKing of Colchis and father of Medea in Greek myth. Rosemary Riorden tells Finnegan in Sydney that he will be loved by Aeetes’ daughter in several forms, including Rosemary herself, as part of his renewed Argonautic story [A:88-89].

A:88-89

Aegean SeaSea whose islands enter Finnegan’s account of creation: a shattered electrum cup becomes the islands, and the first five-island group comprises Andros, Tinos, Paros, Amargos, and Naxos [A:35]. Anastasia locates the mermaids’ original home in the Cyclades, with an early extension to the Dodecanese and Kos; the survivors have largely retreated to Naxos and nearby rocks [D:35-36]. Naxos is her own home, and she claims descent from its fishtail people [D:115].

A:35; D:35-36; D:115

Aerie (geographical)High refuge to which Sergeant Santee climbs for the night in Don Lewis’s account of Willy Jones Island. Casper takes an opposite crest, while Lewis remains in the valley with Yokipoki’s body [D:46].

D:46

Aerie (poetic)Symbol of a bright, solitary, high home mentioned in Hans Schultz's unwritten poem ("Bright is my Aerie. / Aloft and alone.") [A:210].

A:210

AesonFather of Jason in Greek myth. Rosemary Riorden tells Finnegan that he is the son of “Aeson a demiurge,” although he believes his father’s name was Giulio and regards him as a slob. She makes this identification while explaining his Argonautic life in Sydney [A:88-89].

A:88-89

AffidavitDocument declaring the Aussies superior to the Yanks at drinking and everything else, with obscenities spelled out. Tom Shire inspires it and an unnamed “scribe of genius” writes it. Finnegan, drunk and believing he is signing a roster for beer chits, signs without reading. The narrator says an Aussie non-commissioned officers’ club still keeps it after Shire and Freddy Castle have passed beyond its members’ memory [A:13].

A:13

Afghan borderSetting of military actions in Biloxi Brannagan’s stories. Finnegan does not know enough about these actions, Australian irregulars, or service in the Empire’s forces to test Brannagan’s account [D:206].

D:206

AfricaContinent on the Brunhilde’s route from Port of Spain to Freetown, Sierra Leone [D:85]. The African Hump is associated with inward, deathlike dreams; Finnegan experiences apprehension on the crossing [D:80] [D:90]. In Freetown Joseph, a Haussa diamond smuggler, calls his people “the Jews of Africa” and proposes a partnership; Brannagan later recognizes Finnegan’s diamond as Sierra Leonean [D:93-94] [D:207]. Don Barnaby explicitly says that Madame Le Mourcheor’s Old Original Juju Joy Pills are made in New Orleans, not Africa [D:249].

D:85; D:80; D:90; D:93-94; D:207; D:249

African HumpDestination in the chapter-six epigraph’s imagined geography of sea-dreams: sailors traveling from Port of Spain are said to suffer dreams of deathlike introspection. The epigraph is attributed to Ian McIfreann’s Psychologia Nugarum [D:80-81]. Its image recurs as apprehension enters Finnegan’s dreams [D:90].

D:80-81; D:90

African-ExtravaganzaDuffey’s derisive name for claims of extreme human antiquity in the African fossil evidence discussed with a Pattenite. He calls the claims fraudulent and likens the “African Extravaganza” to a pop-rock hymn, yet accepts evidence from elsewhere for a human antiquity greater than the Fundamentalers allow [MTM B9:282-283].

MTM B9:282-283

AfrikaansLanguage Joseph knows, unlike “proper Dutch,” which he says he still needs to learn for his diamond business. He makes the distinction while describing his linguistic qualifications to Finnegan [D:94].

D:94

AgadirPort in the Brunhilde’s itinerary after Arrecife on Lanzarote and Ifni, and before Magadar, Safti, Mazagan, Casablanca, and Rabat [D:101].

D:101

Agape (Love)Hot purple flower in the image of underground New Orleans sunshine bursting through broken pavement. With Philos and Eros, Agape gives the decade’s warmth the form of flowering love; the narrator calls it the theme flower of the hundred-and-twenty-month late summertime shared by Duffey and Letitia [MTM B7:211].

MTM B7:211

Age of giantsPatrick Stranahan’s name for the period of spiritual greatness he believes has just ended in the Church, giving way to an “age of pygmies” [A:109-110].

A:109-110

Age of pygmiesPatrick Stranahan’s name for the diminished age he believes is beginning in the Church after its “age of giants.” He calls the arrival of the common Hell and attacks secular liberalism in the Church; Father McGuigan protests that he has gone too far [A:109-110].

A:109-110

AgeingAge is unstable across the cycle. Private Gregory says he never seems to age and changes identities to conceal his longevity; an army doctor’s interest forces another escape [A:77-78]. Finnegan recalls a young hobo who became forty years older overnight, while Saxon Seaworthy appears to age forty years in three seconds at the sight of Papa Devil [D:14] [D:22]. In Don Lewis’s Big House story, the inhabitants remain unaged by killing and consuming visitors; without a visitor for a year they age one year [D:48]. Members of the other recension are said to deepen rather than age [D:161-162]. Duffey looks younger than he did twenty years earlier [MTM B8:261-262], and Stein later describes his progressive rejuvenation, which Duffey had thought no one had mentioned aloud [MTM B11:317].

A:77-78; D:14; D:22; D:48; D:161-162; MTM B8:261-262; MTM B11:317

Agency, Royal Imperial Dominion DetectiveEmployer of Shamus McGregor (Marie Monaghan's uncle 'Shaw'), who worked as a night watchman for the agency [A:28].

A:28

Aghri DaghName that Zabotski says the mountain bore before an Armenian king renamed it Ararat. His account questions whether the king correctly identified the biblical mountain. The gloss “Mountain” in the passage belongs to Ararat, not to Aghri Dagh [MTM B9:280-281].

MTM B9:280-281

AhrimanThe evil spirit of Zoroastrian tradition. In the epigraph attributed to Arpad Arutinov’s The Back-Door of History, “the children of Ahriman” return like primordial monsters or frightening mutations. The passage places them among its claims about overlapping species, mingled spirit and flesh, and demonic possession [D:26].

D:26

AionJung’s work invoked in the Postscript for the Ego, Self, Shadow, Anima, and Animus. Lafferty counts these as five persons within the human person and uses the account to introduce his claim that inner multiplicity can sometimes become physically visible [PS:477].

PS:477

AirMedium from which Finnegan says he learned Doppio di Pinne's name: “I read it in the air.” He also knows that Dopey was killed; Joe Cross asks whether he read that in the air too [D:63]. A fuller counterpart appears in The Elliptical Grave, where the Pioneer Reventlo Expedition in Calabria seeks human origins and mutations by excavating earth, haunted air, and the higher noosphere. Joseph Abramswell invents air excavation, startling hidden presences into activity and using detection and amplification equipment. The air yields human and animal ghosts, particularly recent ones, and still more ghost plants; reconstructed trees supply landscape history. Joseph calls haunted air “recording air”: its records repeatedly lose clarity and need amplification. He admits that he does not understand their survival in the wind, but describes immaterial pens and baffles and anomalously cohesive clumps. Joseph and Dorothy Blue-Ice also extract the outlines of grumpus fish. Jeffery Wind instead leads the uncertain work of excavating the noosphere, chiefly from a tethered balloon. Cecelia Calca infers a thirty-meter limit for haunted-air ghosts from her own inability to rise higher. She identifies the Invisible Man, whom Jeffery meets in his balloon, as a more tenuous ghost, but the narrator questions that classification. Later, Jeffery experiments with recycling air, and Anabella conjectures that their cocoons are made of air. The book also shows a Phoenix leaking air in Fritz Otto's projected film and gives a verse about shoveling air. (The Elliptical Grave, PDF pp. 26, 42-44, 47, 50, 56, 73, 79, 85).

D:63

AkroreiaOne of the three Oreads whom Finnegan meets in dreams on the mountain at Naxos, with Anemotrephes and Oreibates. They call Anastasia their sister, warn Finnegan to flee after the coming night’s events, and forbid him to join their climb. When he recognizes their kinship with the teras, Akroreia sadly asks how he knew; Oreibates calls it their “destitution and destruction.” The sisters push Finnegan from the dream-mountain [D:136-139].

D:136-139

Al-Raschid, HarounAbbasid caliph who ruled from 786 to 809. Anastasia uses his reign as a marker in her mermaid history, saying that mermaids had reached the Persian Gulf by his time [D:35]. In Lafferty's Sindbad, the Thirteenth Voyage, Harun al-Rashid is a recurring Golden Boy or Boy-Caliph, associated with Baghdad Mirage, masks, magic, and cruel practical jokes. Reports of his deaths and rebirths conflict in chronology. Redcrown Charnel, his father in a previous Kentauron Mikron life, receives a coded message announcing his rebirth on Gaea-Earth. Harun appears about eleven, though described as fifty in his present life. Citizen Heifritz says he ruled for three days twenty-seven years earlier, in Moslem year 164, before his sons Al-Amin and Mamun made him Caliph-Emeritus. The current action also has him install Al-Amin as caliph. These are the novel's accounts, not historical chronology. Harun builds towers by magic; Mamun calls him the chief creator of the present Baghdad Mirage, and Essindibad's ship suggests that he could have begun its creation before birth. Legends link his strong hands to Hercules-like snake strangling and to killing his own twin. He can escape recognition, although his many masks also paradoxically leave him recognizable to everyone. John Thunderson resembles him, calls him a friend, reports his boyish “Ifrit treble,” and receives a promise of a vizierate contingent on Harun remaining caliph. Harun claims invisibility and friendship with devils, with a foot in Earth, heaven, and hell. His delightful aura later turns to revulsion when his mask falls. Spy Alexander describes him as a potentially good creature of God who actually serves evil as Satan's recurrent pawn. Harun collects Christian blood for Al-Amin's installation, mocks and repudiates Al-Amin, calls Mamun his only son, and seeks Al-Amin's corpse for further jokes. He wears green clown motley and a dog mask in Dog Country, where victims protest his permanent transformation of humans into dogs. Harun himself insists that a caliph's bones are holy. Near the Fountain of Life-Bubbles, a murdered man's widow pours a dog-attracting essence over him, and savage dogs kill him. In his final seconds he receives two surrogate ninety-year dogs' lives. The Dog Magician extracts his still-living, transparent heart and gives it to Scheherazade, identified as his widow as well as Al-Amin's. Its apparent goldfish identifies itself as a bottled, miniaturized golden whale; Scheherazade has it installed beside her own heart. The Dog Magician thinks this is Harun's seventh and last life, and explains his bodies as contraptions inhabited by devils. He and the Dog Surgeon later record the death and burial in the Royal Archives. (Sindbad, the Thirteenth Voyage, PDF pp. 10-11, 16, 20, 27, 34-36, 38-40, 46, 66, 70, 73, 117, 120, 128, 133, 136, 138-142).

D:35

AlabamaOne of three possible settings, with Louisiana and Mississippi, for the rural scenes in the first chamber of Elroy Redheart’s four-chambered heart artwork. Its fields, working people, and young dancers also contain the disturbing scene of the dead Jill of Hearts [MTM B7:221].

MTM B7:221

AlaricGothic leader of about AD 395-410, named by Mr. X among kings and heroes whose followers await their awakening from enchanted sleep. X uses their legends as a comparison for the Devil's imprisonment [MTM B6:204-205]. Alaric is central to Lafferty's The Fall of Rome. That book places his birth in 376, as a Roman and a member of the Balthi, while qualifying the tradition of his birth on Peuce island and its fulfillment of a Gothic prophecy. His father's name Alareidar comes from a doubtful source; his father dies in a horse accident, and his mother's fate has conflicting accounts. Raised by male tutors and his older cousin Stairnon, later his wife and formative oracle, Alaric grows into a “boy giant” with a powerful capacity for learning. Athaulf, Sarus, and Singerich are his close kindred, though their precise family relationships remain uncertain. Their affinities diverge: Athaulf remains Gothic, Sarus commits himself to Rome, and Singerich becomes Greek. Alaric attends the Imperial School, hears Theodosius and Stilicho, and recognizes in Stilicho the equal who will be his ally, enemy, and eventual friend. He excels at transporting armies and aspires to become Master General, while Stairnon insists on his Gothic kingship. The book follows his command in the costly battle of Frigidus in 394; his approach to, negotiations with, and withdrawal from Constantinople in 395; his appointment as Master General of Illyricum and elevation as Gothic king in 397; and his Italian campaign beginning late in 401 and ending in defeat in 403. He then sincerely pledges himself to the Empire and helps maintain its eastern peace until 408. Secretly summoned to the Italian border by the generals' council, especially Sarus, he is drawn into the conflict after Stilicho's murder. The narrative places his first siege of Rome in 409, acknowledges uncertainty over siege details, and subsequently has him secure Attalus's elevation as emperor. Negotiations at Ravenna collapse after Sarus attacks under a truce. Under pressure from Stairnon, Athaulf, and the Gothic elders, Alaric abandons his Roman allegiance before taking Rome in 410. The narrator calls this a werewolf-like change: the Empire has become a cruel joke to Alaric, and he would replace it. The ensuing events enter an explicitly legendary register. A tempest destroys the Goths' fleet; Alaric dies of fever three months after taking Rome; and his burial beneath the diverted River Busento is a legend whose literal truth the narrator doubts. (The Fall of Rome, PDF pp. 32-35, 38, 40, 51, 60, 62, 101, 114, 120, 143-144, 176-177, 221, 232, 246, 251, 272, 278, 287, 300, 302, 304-305, 308-310).

MTM B6:204-205

Alaric's SwordRelic listed among the Argo Masters' recoveries [MTM B13:422]. In The Fall of Rome, a related Alaric sword is a broken-hafted, nearly rusted-through blade brought from Shade Island, a Gothic cemetery in the Danube. In Alaric's reported encounter, a towering ancestral figure who speaks with the authority of the dead gives him the sword and says that no other man can wield it. Useless in battle, it becomes an impressive talisman and recognized symbol of authority, held by Alaric when the Goths raise him as king. The narrator preserves uncertainty: Stairnon and Athaulf might have contrived the encounter, and the old Goths either recognized the sword's signs or came to believe that they did. (The Fall of Rome, PDF pp. 99, 101-104).

MTM B13:422

Alarm (Clock)Hans Schultz’s alarm clock, pictured as a chrome-colored dragon with an “ivory grin.” It gives a clattering roar until he throttles it; when he releases the lever it can only go “tunkle tunkle” [A:16-17].

A:16-17

Alarm (Mind-Alarm)Nonphysical alarm that Charlotte Garfield believes she triggered while robbing a walk-in vault containing Aga Gonof’s stash. She claims a small share of the stash is hers [MTM B3:84] [MTM B3:86]. The alarm detects her temporary name Mullens but not her appearance [MTM B3:93]. After Gloria and Manolo are murdered, Letitia says the killers acquired the Mullens name and hotel from this alarm but never knew their target was a little girl or midget [MTM B3:97].

MTM B3:84; MTM B3:86; MTM B3:93; MTM B3:97

AlbaniansPeople whom others claim are related to the Transylvanians, according to Countess Margaret. She lists them with Slavs, Greeks, Armenians, and Goths, then rejects all these proposed origins while asserting Transylvanian separateness [MTM B8:255].

MTM B8:255

Albertus Magnus (Albert the Great) (c. 1200--1280)German Dominican, bishop, philosopher, and natural investigator; teacher of Thomas Aquinas and commentator on Aristotle. His studies included zoology in De animalibus, and the breadth of his learning earned him the title Doctor universalis. He was canonized and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1931. John William Schultz insists that fourth-graders should already have mastered the catechism and should be studying Aquinas and Albert [A:208-209].

A:208-209

Albion of the White CliffsBritain or England under an ancient literary name. In Henry Salvatore’s dream, Albion of the White Cliffs is one of the shattered masts of the Navicula Petri, alongside Moscovy and Gaul. The dream’s account describes Albion’s apostasy as foretold in the Apocalypse [A:44-45].

A:44-45

AlcoholRecurring element of the characters’ social life and Finnegan’s dependence. While cleaning bars and washing dishes he drinks during breaks and in the evenings [D:19]. The narrator later calls him the most addicted of the four friends on Basse-Terre, though Johnny Duckwalk can drink more [D:236]. At the Old Wooden Ship, John Indelecio and John Jereboam bear the nicknames Little Alcohol and Big Alcohol [D:215].

D:19; D:236; D:215

AlcoveStorage nook Duffey builds for the hundred bushels of barley bought to supply the Big Pot. The barley fills the alcove six feet deep [A:133].

A:133

Alexander the GreatHistorical ruler used as a chronological marker in Anastasia’s account of mermaids. She says that they had reached the Red Sea by his time, though how they arrived is unknown [D:34-35].

D:34-35

AlexandrianEarlier heading that misspelled the proposed vehicle model. See Ford Alexandrine.
AliBoy in Don Lewis’s Big House tale. Its inhabitants stay young by killing visitors and eating their organs. Ali brings two ta’a nuts, plants one before entering, and keeps the other in his pocket, which prevents the household from killing him. He snaps his fingers to bring morning; the planted nut has become a tree with a branch at his window, and he climbs down to escape. The household consequently ages a year [D:48-49].

D:48-49

AliceTown named by Demetrio among the places he visited in his youth, in his account of having traveled throughout the world and the United States [D:58].

D:58

AlkiesCaptain Guiterrez’s term for the Dirty Fivers as heavy drinkers. At the Buffalo Bar he calls them “a bunch of Alkies,” including himself when he is with them [A:66].

A:66

AllentownTown on the Pittsburgh bus route described to Finnegan. The bus goes through Allentown and Reading rather than Philadelphia [D:170].

D:170

Alligator CallsAnimal-call instruments Giulio Solli whittles from tupelo-gum for Finnegan to blow while they drift through the Cajun swamps. The set calls alligators, panthers, devil-fish, swamp boas, hairy men, and white sharks; Finnegan says he never knew what would answer from the water or trees [MTM B5:174].

MTM B5:174

Alligator Tail SoupAlligator-tail stew mixed into Duffey’s barley soup among the changing ingredients of the Big Pot [A:134].

A:134

AlmondsFood Finnegan eats while wandering Tangier during the hunt that ends in Don Lewis’s death [D:103-105]. Almond also appears among the skin-color comparisons applied to the island women pursued by Don Barnaby and Johnny Duckwalk [D:236].

D:103-105; D:236

Aloysia, LinusLinus Aloysia, one of Duffey’s musical friends during the Chicago years. He is named in a group spanning opera, ragtime, Chicago hot music, and string bands, with composers, players, and stagers among them; the passage does not assign an individual specialty to him [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

Aloysius (Currency)One of the hundred-dollar bills Finnegan has named and kept as the reserve at the bottom of an adventure. Aloysius is listed among the predecessors of Miguel [D:19].

D:19

Aloysius McGivern Basket WeaverRegular patron at the Old Wooden Ship tavern; receives a stipend from his affluent ("red-dog rich") family to stay away and avoid causing them embarrassment, with the condition that they won't return him to a sanitarium [D:225]; known for complaining about being compelled into basket weaving ("'The Devil finds work for idle hands to do,' they say... Why the devil don't they put the Devil to basket weaving...?") [D:225]; one of the diverse group of fifty regulars at the tavern [D:216].

D:225; D:216

Aloysius, BrotherUnverified identification. The supplied citations do not establish a Brother Aloysius, his alleged mathematical blessing, his clothing, his journey to Rome, or his connection with Finnegan.
Aloysius, LinusEarlier heading that misspelled the musician’s surname. See Aloysia, Linus.
Alpha (Plan)Earlier phase of Casey Szymansky’s plan to become world leader. He tells Letitia that Alpha will become past history when he mounts the white horse and begins Beta, first taking Chicago, then America, then the world [MTM B4:117].

MTM B4:117

Alpha CentauriOne of the stars whose right ascension Hans learns to calculate under Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni. The Professor treats such calculations as only the childhood of astronomy [A:211] [A:214].

A:211; A:214

AlpineOne of the racial categories, alongside Mediterranean, that the narrator says anthropologists impose on the Cajuns. The passage mocks these classifications and insists on the Cajuns as a people apart [A:123].

A:123

Altar stoneConsecrated stone used as a portable altar for Mass. In Ignacio’s story, the eighth-century Benedictine Joseph of Maintz packs one into the chamber he fires to the moon, with bread, wine, grape cuttings, and wheat for continued celebration of Mass. His books include the Missal, Scriptures, writings of Augustine and Jerome, and Pliny’s Natural History [A:271]. The stone belongs to the tradition of consecrated altars containing saints’ relics; Aquinas explains the stone altar as signifying Christ and his stone tomb.

A:271

Alternate realityThe alternative present that the closing directions in More Than Melchisedech ask the reader to approach from another side. Enniscorthy Sweeny compares an event to a solid object viewed from past, present, alternative present, and future: no view is to cancel the others [MTM B13:467]. “Great Day in the Morning” offers a different disturbance of shared reality when Duffy sees other people pass through walls that still bruise and bloody him; he wonders whether his own subjectivity is at fault [GD:498].

MTM B13:467; GD:498

AmargosAmargos is the form in Archipelago; Amorgos is used in The Devil Is Dead. See Amorgos.
Amateur DrunksFinnegan’s name for the drinkers who “blossom at receptions.” At Vincent and Theresa’s wedding reception in May 1946, he says he becomes an amateur himself for the occasion, “for sheer love of it,” then performs his familiar antics among the guests [A:95] [A:113].

A:95; A:113

AmazonsMythical warrior women; featured in Casey Szymansky's second erotic dream world fantasy, alongside female gladiators, Cretan girl bull-fighters, and circus girl acrobats [A:157].

A:157

Ambulance DriverWartime occupation Duffey claims to have held with Hemingway in Italy and Cummings in France before joining the American army. The narrator questions Duffey’s service and suggests he may have borrowed experiences from Sebastian Hilton, whom the account identifies as an ambulance driver in both countries [MTM B2:72].

MTM B2:72

AmericaDestination reached by St. Brandon in the Argo’s legendary history [MTM B13:404], and by some of Anastasia Grandmother’s emigrant granddaughters [D:125]. Anastasia’s mermaid account denies New World varieties [D:35]. Finnegan tells Brannagan that he has known beer served in pitchers only as an Australian custom [D:199]. Widow Waldo is said to have been Miss America [MTM B9:275].

MTM B13:404; D:125; D:35; D:199; MTM B9:275

American (Nationality)Nationality of Santee, Casper, and Lorrigan, the three soldiers in Don Lewis’s account of the disappearance on Willy Jones Island [D:44]. In Tangier it is Don Lewis, not Finnegan, whose Spanish sounds like an American imitating an Arab; Lewis also offers five hundred dollars American for a hiding place [D:107]. Manuel is separately described as South American [D:145].

D:44; D:107; D:145

American BalzacTitle Casey imagines earning in his fourth dream world, the literary one. He will write ten thousand words daily and become so great that Balzac will eventually be called the French Szymansky [A:157-158].

A:157-158

American Blood and Thunder (Old)The sensational Western and crime romances that survive in the Harlow House library after Gautier’s goats have eaten the books they are allowed. The narrator lists “Old Wild West,” “Train Robber,” “Buffalo Hunter and Indian Scalper,” and “Bank Robber and Brigand” as descriptions of the surviving reading matter. Gautier, the goat-man, loves these books in both paper and hard covers [A:196-198].

A:196-198

American Colonel (elderly)Missing elderly officer whose fingerprints match those of the apparently twenty-year-old Australian Private Gregory. Gregory offers the discovery as the reason the authorities detained and questioned him after his latest change of identity [A:78-79].

A:78-79

American counterpartUnnamed American counterpart of the Australian brigadier whom a raiding party embarrasses during the Tania episode. Unaware of the scheme, he demands an explanation and then goes through the jungle seeking someone to blame [A:54]. The later account attributes a further layer of the trick to Stein [A:55].

A:54; A:55

American FigZabotski’s name for the sycamore he compares to Bryan Blackstone. He curses Blackstone’s tree to wither so that it will await its owner on the blessed shore, but expressly denies that he can command a man to die [MTM B9:270].

MTM B9:270

American HistorySubject that John William Schultz would have children read through on the second night of his five-evening preparatory curriculum before serious education begins [A:209]. In Duffey’s first high-school year, American History is one of the subjects at which Sebastian Hilton leads the class [MTM B1:25].

A:209; MTM B1:25

American JournalismField that Casey says Stein, Gabrielovitch, and Duffey have disgraced in his Crock attack on the newly launched Bark. He denounces their politics and qualifications in an extended polemic against the rival Catholic magazine [A:128-130].

A:128-130

American MediterraneanCasey’s name for the Great Lakes in his high-school notebook. He praises their shores and hinterland over the European Mediterranean and makes Chicago the center of the world [A:166].

A:166

American style cabaretCabaret that Falo and Nauti are building on Luzon after the war. They declare it open when Vincent and Finnegan arrive, using a large box as a table and two smaller boxes as chairs while construction continues [A:63-64].

A:63-64

American Values ('Reaffirmation of')Rehabilitation class Casey must attend three times weekly after four weeks in the stockade and demotion from sergeant. Its teacher is Stein the Red, whose influence Casey resents [A:50].

A:50

AmnesiaFinnegan describes memory loss when moving between his upper and lower lives; Seaworthy answers that all their kind indulge in amnesia [D:11]. Finnegan claims its advantages when refusing to recognize Papa-D [D:15], while Anastasia challenges him with “Which will it be, amnesia or me?” [D:16]. The narrator recalls the gaps in his Green Islands identity and his personification of Amnesia as an old companion [D:50] [D:75]. Duffey’s Sea of the Seven Lost Years connects by a hidden strait with the Sea of Amnesia [MTM B13:406]. A counterpart in Fourth Mansions concerns Freddy Foley's disputed memory and identity during confinement in “the Bug.” Doctor Decker says that he was found wandering and amnesiac, identified as Julius Smith, and needs to recover his past as part of his cure. Foley denies that Smith is his name and accuses the authorities of hiding him under it. Richard Bencher reports that the official record instead says Foley insisted that he was Julius Smith and did not know or remember Fred Foley. Foley calls the record wrong and alleges “dirty work.” (Fourth Mansions, PDF pp. 161, 183, 186-187).

D:11; D:15; D:16; D:50; D:75; MTM B13:406

Amnesia's WoodsImage for Finnegan’s gaps in memory. As he wonders whether he belongs to the “other human race,” the narrative recalls his passage through Amnesia’s woods and his meeting with Amnesia in the clearing [D:50].

D:50

Amoral HypnosisDon Barnaby’s name for the condition induced by Madame Le Mourcheor’s Joy Pill, in which sleep becomes temporary death, then a transported and detached existence. He claims to move among distant places and many lives within the garden where he took the pill [D:250-251].

D:250-251

AmoralityThe Laughing Prince’s supposed freedom from moral allegiance. The narrator first calls total amorality impossible, then describes the Prince’s closed world of television images and hallucinations as the first massive instance of it. The desert and figures in which Duffey is murdered are called amoral, though his death in that unreal scene is real [MTM B13:438] [MTM B13:441-442].

MTM B13:438; MTM B13:441-442

AmorgosIsland named in Finnegan’s account of the original Aegean five-island group [A:35]. In Anastasia’s mermaid history, surviving mermaids inhabit Naxos and the rocks between it and Amorgos [D:35-36].

A:35; D:35-36

AmosProphet quoted in the narrator’s introduction to Casey’s problem of evil: “Shall there be evil in a city which the Lord hath not done?” The wording comes from Amos 3:6 and is presented as a puzzle before Casey declares evil the only problem in the world [A:154].

A:154

AmoySick parakeet visiting Ward Fourteen, whose stories Ignatius Ti expands from a few words of Tagalog-Parakeet. In Ti’s account, Amoy was once a red-winged blackbird trained by thieves, then a jewel thief in Karachi. After marrying an uncommon magpie of the common species, he withheld a blue diamond intended for her. His master Ali ben Taife, also called Lord Peter Petrof, County von Vinger, Sinhor Dedos, and Mr. Fingers, cut his throat to recover it. Amoy died and became a fish before becoming a parakeet [A:79-81]. A sadistic medico poisons him, and an official order calls for his death. He continues visiting friends, tries to be cheerful despite genuine persecution, and may be the ward’s best-balanced resident [A:81-82]. He later dies in terrible agony [A:88].

A:79-81; A:81-82; A:88

Amphora of rumQuantity of rum Finnegan and Anastasia take past a cigar factory to the ruins and old walls above an unnamed harbor. The narrator places the episode possibly at Paraiso, Campeche, or another stop; it is not the later visit to Naxos [D:67-68].

D:67-68

AmraphelOne of the Three Slant-Faced Men whom Duffey recognizes by names printed in the comic strip Flame Man. The narrative identifies Amraphel as king of Shinar or Upper Babylonia and groups him with Arioch and Thadal as opposite kings or anti-magi without magic. It further identifies them as followers of Chodorlahomor, king of Elam, while noting that this detail is absent from the strip [MTM B7:227-228].

MTM B7:227-228

Amusement park ridesAmusement parks are among the crowded places Herman Hercules says he needs for his well-being. His list includes arenas, opera houses, circuses, fairs, music halls, and other places that remain alive with people [MB:585].

MB:585

Amyl acetateOne of Askandanakandrian’s seven “sovereigns,” the small set of substances he says can rehabilitate distressed merchandise ranging from fish to furniture [A:257]. Amyl acetates have a banana-like odor and are associated with the commercial name banana oil.

A:257

AnachronismTerm Finnegan mistakenly applies to the redundancy he hears in “saltcellar.” When Doll questions “anachronism,” he corrects himself to “that other thing” meaning saying the same thing twice, then derives cellar from saliere and sal [D:189]. Duffey calls the arrival of his own cremated ashes while he is still alive an anachronism; Dotty replies that Duffey himself is one [MTM B6:203].

D:189; MTM B6:203

AnamnesisRecollection, the principal function Teresa Piccone attributes to the Argo talismans. She describes them as gold filigree laid over pieces of the Talking Oak Dordogne, with gold from the Great Fleece. Their function is less to create the companions than to awaken them and restore their remembering, enabling them to recognize one another after renewed birth and sleep. Their reunion prefigures the Resurrection [MTM B5:178-179].

MTM B5:178-179

Anas PaludosaDuck species named by Biloxi Brannagan in his account of handling diamonds larger than ducks’ eggs. When Finnegan suggests the ducks must be small, Brannagan answers that they are large for their kind [D:207].

D:207

AnastasiaName Finnegan interprets as “the resurrection” when Anastasia Demetriades restores his respectability with an electric shaver and tends his wounds [D:16]. On Naxos, she and her grandmother share the name: Anastasia Gyiagyia is the grandmother, and Anastasia Engone is the visiting granddaughter, Demetriades herself [D:125-126].

D:16; D:125-126

Anastasia DemetriadesSee Demetriades, Anastasia, the name she gives Finnegan when he asks who she is [D:16].

D:16

Anastasia EngoneAnastasia Demetriades under the designation “Anastasia Engone,” glossed as granddaughter during her visit to Anastasia Gyiagyia on Naxos [D:125-126]. She is the granddaughter who jokes that the morning when Prometheus brought fire was cold [D:127].

D:125-126; D:127

Anastasia Grandmother (Gyiagyia)Anastasia Demetriades' grandmother on the mountain road of Naxos. Black-haired and black-eyed, she immediately recognizes her granddaughter but pretends otherwise as a game. She speaks only Romaic and lives alone in a diminished house with fire-damaged rooms boarded off. Though poor, she remains vital and pretty, and was once prettier than her granddaughter [D:125-126]. She cooks the kid Finnegan and Anastasia buy and prepare. At dinner, she jokes that her granddaughter was too little to remember the morning of Prometheus [D:126-127]. She calls Finnegan one of the violent ones of the other blood, says that she shares it, and that her granddaughter has a little of it [D:128].

D:125-126; D:126-127; D:128

AnatoliaOrigin of the Seabach when it approaches the blind side of Naxos with six men aboard [D:135]. Earlier, Finnegan includes Anatolia among the directions from which Anastasia's awaited boat might come; she declines his help watching [D:131]. Turkish Anatolia is also the source of the turbaned, laughing marble Christ in Duffey's collection [MTM B3:104].

D:135; D:131; MTM B3:104

Ancient WorldThe books' varied accounts of prehistory, classical antiquity and the medieval centuries, often given by speakers with conflicting histories. Captain Sammy Guiterrez calls the West old and the East young, dismissing Chinese and Irish claims as “toy history” [A:66]. Zabotski speculates that a thousand years of supposed dark ages might have originated in a sick boy's chronicle in 1348 [MTM B9:281-282]. A Pattenite challenges the Olduvai evidence, and Duffey calls it fraudulent while accepting other evidence for human antiquity beyond the Pattenite's allowance [MTM B9:282-283]. Zabotski describes the Pristine World as real, essential and intuitively inhabited. It occupies the ordinary Molasses World's space differently, excludes duplicated and invalid persons and situations, and lets him live years within an ordinary day or two [MTM B9:277] [MTM B9:279]. The Royal Pop Historians claim new ways of recovering history from stone patinas and transparencies, maintain that they were present at ancient events, and announce the obliteration of history's former subject matter [MTM B11:323-325]. Duffey examines their goatskin proclamation with violet light and finds older writing beneath it, including a Fourth Gospel with marginal pagona shorthand [MTM B11:326-327]. Hugh de Turenne announces the Black Sea's obliteration at Himself's command, partly to erase the memory of his imprisonment and undermine Colchis and the Fleece [MTM B11:336]. Cyrus Roundhead reduces Rome to an Etruscan neighborhood, calls the Etruscans a pop people, and says the Macedonians invented heroic Greece, Athens and its romances. He describes Jerusalem as a failed modern property venture and asserts that most Jews were and remain in Babylon. These are the Royal Pop revisionists' assertions within the conflict, not a settled history shared by all the characters [MTM B11:337]. Other accounts supply different foundations. Behind Duffey's twentieth-century childhoods stands his more real life of thousands of years as the Boy King, with dromedary-hide tents, flocks, pastures and silver rivers [MTM B1:17]. The opening applies the phrase “without father, without mother” to Duffey with explicit uncertainty about its fit [MTM B1:6]. His childhood also includes invisible giants commanded to ring a bell [MTM B1:15]. Ignacio Ti's story places Joseph of Maintz, Bishop Turpin and Charlemagne in an eighth-century “noon-time of the World”; Joseph takes Augustine's writings, among other books, to the moon [A:271]. An epigraph attributed to G. K. Chesterton's The Everlasting Man presents the Creator's personal appearance in the Roman Empire as a unique claim [MTM B5:176]. Absalom Stein's notes call 946-1946 the Devil's imprisonment and the empire of Neustria or Christendom [MTM B6:185]. Henri Salvatore's unsent letter says Otto I first bolted the door at Aachen in 946 and transferred the prisoner that year to the Crimean Chersonese [MTM B5:180]. X's account calls the peninsula Tauric or Euxine Chersonese, dates the transfer 946 or 947, and says its names Phylake and Carcer meant Prison for more than a thousand years before the actual imprisonment [MTM B6:204]. Henri is identified as the former Euphemus, later Emperor Henry of Neustria and now emperor of Invisible Neustria [MTM B8:245]. Ancient geography also enters poems, journeys and arguments. Hans imagines a southern voyage farther than Ulysses went and beyond Ophir, to which the men of Solomon and Hiram made their three-year voyage [A:16]. Finnegan calls the Aegean the original Pentanesia, naming Andros, Tinos, Paros and Amargos, with Hans supplying Naxos. In the same island reverie Finn invokes Strabo's sense of islands, St. Paul and Xavier's greater archipelagos [A:35]. The Argo's later history includes carrying St. Paul [MTM B13:404]. The Fin-Iason poem proposes climbing Sinai to recover what Moses forgot and asks whether the burning bush is at Hebron or Hest [A:171]. Its next page separates Argonauts mired in Friesian bogs from the conjecture that Illyrian fleets vanished in Illyrian fogs [A:172]. Casey's notebook records claims that the Romanies founded and named Rome and that Hinnegan's Milesians were in Ireland before the Flood [A:164-165]. San Simeon's forgotten ancient name is Babylon, and its rulers are the mad Balbo dynasty [MB:558]. Rosemary Riorden tells Finn that he and his friends began in Illyria: he is the son of the demiurge Aeson although he believes his father to be Giulio, and his companions include Orpheus, Peleus, Euphemus and Meleager. She forecasts his later company with the Dioscuri and the love of Aeetes' daughter in several forms, including her own, and says he will find the Fleece without knowing what he has found [A:89]. Teresa's later catalogue names Finnegan as Iason, Hans as Orpheus and subsequently Faust, Vincent as Meleager, Henry as Euphemus, Casey as Peleus, Dotty as Medea, Marie as Eurydice, Mary Virginia as Laonome, herself as Atalanta, Mary Catherine as Antigone and Stein as Ab-Salom. She calls their Colchis voyage the prototype of quests, says they passed the Devil's future Chersonese prison, and insists that they still hide the Golden Fleece from him [MTM B7:234]. Duffey's commentary traces Casey from Peleus through Kasmir Gorshok and Prince Casimir to his modern identity. His Peleus is Achilles' father and the victim of Acastus of Iolcus and his wife's badger game [PG:534-536]. Dotty says the Argo voyages continue as the company's other life [MTM B5:180]. The ship's logs make the finding of the Fleece of Colchis one of its early triumphs, though other quests were equally or more important [MTM B13:421]. Gorshok later makes the fleshless Duffey a mask, scarf and gauntlets from the Fleece's combings [MTM B13:443]. Patrick Stranahan's ancient standards include Livy as history and the advice to read Augustine once in youth [A:109]. He polemically compares contemporary opponents to Sadducees who reject resurrection [A:110]. He calls St. Patrick Roman rather than Irish, his own wife Monica returned, Dante a rimester and Petrarch a sonnet writer, and prefers the anonymity he associates with better medieval artists [A:111]. Patricia Solli calls her father Giulio literally antediluvian and reports that an important man called him the Monster Forgotten [A:174-175]. Duffey recognizes Finnegan as the son of the Monster Giulio, whom he himself knew [MTM B5:174]. In an uncertain ocean dream, Marie calls herself Demeter and Persephone and explains a Demeter-Pontos grouping as a precursor of the pietà form [D:91-92]. Finn's story of Galen's lunar measurements uses a giant goat-sucker passing behind the moon [D:132]. A chapter epigraph attributed in the novel to Galen describes daemons begetting Tityroi or Satyroi and renewing their race, including a night's procreation with thirteen women at Calchedon. The narrator follows it by asking about Galen's teacher Satyrus and the source of his information [D:160-161]. Ewaglouwshkoul, the Neanderthal Eve, is awakened from the ice by the magus Duffey. She guesses she was her tribe's last woman, but allows that males and other bands may have survived; she says her people invented ships and seamen [MTM B13:399-401]. The Laughing Prince of Tartary claims enmity with both God and the Devil, although reports question his independence. Duffey eventually recognizes him as the Giggling Prince [MTM B13:437-438] [MTM B13:441]. An unlabeled speaker in “Promontory Goats” recalls Justinian's skull giving judgments to chieftains through a snake emerging from its right eye-socket for yes and left for no, then uses the image to disown the judgments his own body may make after death [PG:545]. Teresa explains the talismans as Argo gold filigree over Talking Oak Dordogne, with the gold derived from the Fleece. Their work is Anamnesis or Recollection, awakening the company to recognition, and their reunion prefigures Resurrection [MTM B5:178-179]. Henri describes Paradise and the completed quest as an already possessed foundation from which the world must be rebuilt [MTM B5:179-180]. The Devil Is Dead locates the Terrestrial Paradise in the Antilles [D:234]; its narrator connects the Haggada's wormy forbidden fruit with a possible hint in Augustine [D:264]. Angela's father exploits the Caribbean's true and false passages in his Master Map and half-map trade [D:260-261].

Andaman SeaSea included in the catalogue of waters sailed by the Argo and remembered by Melchisedech Duffey [MTM B13:406].

MTM B13:406

AndrosIsland Finnegan names in the Aegean Pentanesia, the original five-island cluster in his account of archipelago origins. He also names Tinos, Paros, and Amargos; Hans supplies the forgotten fifth name, Naxos [A:35].

A:35

Anegada PassageOne of the seven true passages through the Antilles in Angela Cosquin's account of her father's treasure-map trade. She contrasts these with seven false or shoal passages, where a logical ship ought to have gone down [D:260].

D:260

AnemotrephesOne of the three Oreads Finnegan encounters in his Naxos mountain dreams, with Akroreia and Oreibates. They call Anastasia their sister and warn him to leave after the coming night's events [D:137]. Anemotrephes denies being a teras, while her sisters' answers concede the affinity; Anastasia later confirms that they share it a little. The three push Finnegan off the dream mountain [D:139].

D:137; D:139

Angela CosquinBarmaid and factotum at Joseph Chastaigne's establishment on Basse-Terre, called the Imperial or Royal Bar and nicknamed Sloppy Joe's [D:235] [D:258] [D:266]. Angela is beautiful in an old island fashion, dazzlingly dressed, musical and talkative; her ancestry includes French, Carib, English, noble and enslaved forebears. She can carry two hundred pounds on her head and launch a six-man boat alone [D:259]. She says that her stories are true, unlike those of the four topers. Her father was a skilled cartographer and antiquarian whose decorative maps developed into a trade in fabricated pirate treasure maps and supporting papers; Angela retains some for sale [D:259-261]. She denies the nearby St. Marc and Sangre del Cristo wrecks, but the narrator reveals that she knows them well and dives among their real treasure. After attracting suspicion by spending old coins and wearing diamonds, she returns her loot and deposits her own money in a submerged copper box marked “Angela Cosquin sa Caisse.” Every month Johnny Duckwalk steals the sovereign she has just added [D:262-263]. Her seven accurate maps of Finnegan's hidden stashes, marked S X S and robado por C F, alarm him; he infers that she has read his mind, and she says she will keep the maps as a memory. She is the first to call him Count Finnegan [D:263]. She deplores Barnaby's and Le Marin's departures and predicts that those who leave never return [D:265-266]. She offers Finnegan two ships full of gold and everything else if he stays. They promise to protect the poor, and he sits on her strong knees to say goodbye. He never returns [D:268].

D:235; D:258; D:266; D:259; D:259-261; D:262-263; D:263; D:265-266; D:268

AngelsLazarus Reilly offers newcomers lodging, credit and loans at the Old Wooden Ship lest he slight an angel in disguise. The narrator identifies Soft-Talk Susie Kutz as the only actual angel among the regulars; her favorable reports help the tavern prosper [D:216]. In the debate about the Ark, Fundamentalers ask whether angels guard it in the Armenian mountains. Zabotski says that angels guard things beyond human reach, including wooden castles even if they are not the Ark [MTM B9:280-281].

D:216; MTM B9:280-281

AngerSeaworthy's response to the Texas beer served after his and Finnegan's awakening: “There should be a punishment to fit the crime” [D:12]. The narrator also describes Papa Devil as often on the edge of anger, making him someone to fear [D:87].

D:12; D:87

Angry League For Style In The Universe, The Unbelievers'The Unbelievers' Angry League For Style In The Universe, whose members hate The Resurrection of Count Finnegan although none has seen it [MB:554]. At the close of How Many Miles to Babylon, the League condemns the happy ending and its supposed lack of true style, calling it “shameful corn” [MB:598-599].

MB:554; MB:598-599

AnimaIn Jung's terminology, the feminine aspect of the male psyche. The Postscript names Anima and Animus as opposing twins alongside Ego, Self and Shadow in its account of Jung's Aion, using this plurality to discuss the several persons within a person [PS:477].

PS:477

Animal FormFinnegan tells the Capuchin that an old animal is taking him over, linking this to his new memories of the Devil's kindred and different blood [D:119]. Later the narrator describes him as feral, a living gargoyle and an ape-cat while he climbs buildings, attacks a man and escapes with Seaworthy's treasure. The passage says he becomes a man again after the escape, while leaving the precise nature of the transformation elusive [D:162] [D:164-165]. A local legend calls the climber an ape or monstrous man [D:162]. Joe Cross compares Dopey's scream to that of a terrified animal [D:64], and Doll repeats someone else's description of Finnegan as a hooked-nosed ape during a night of rough amusement [D:173].

D:119; D:162; D:164-165; D:64; D:173

AnimalityQuality whose denigration Finnegan challenges in his visionary account of the older people. He calls them brothers of the great animals and asks how animality became “a dirty thing” [D:212-213]. Duffey uses the word adversely in a different context, listing animality among the degradations the Devil will bring and have mistaken for holy poverty [MTM B6:194].

D:212-213; MTM B6:194

Animated MarvelsDuffey's extraordinary company of talismanic creations, called Animated Marvels, magnificent animations and splendid animations. At the Rounders' Club they have “Unreality Fringes,” a smokey halo, yet are real; their extravagant conversations cannot later be recalled [MTM B5:158-161]. Duffey says he literally helped form twelve people in his present life, with an additional uncounted creation and others of mixed status, while conceding that he did not do everything [MTM B5:151]. The talismans are described as small engraved flat gold sticks distributed during his hidden years, including one for Giulio's unborn child; Letitia's rib-shaped talisman makes her a bonus outside the twelve [MTM B4:120-121] [MTM B3:90] [MTM B3:93]. Duffey had begun giving talismans away as a child [MTM B1:18]. He says that he put more than ordinary Teras blood into his creations [MTM B5:170]. Dotty's letter gives another account: through Finnegan they share a Teras intellectual stratum between conscious and unconscious thought, an elusive power expressed in his paintings and their conversations [MTM B6:189]. Their origin remains contested. Marie Monaghan Schultz says Duffey collected their forgotten souls, gave them settings and sparkle, and displayed them, rather than making them; she invokes his Razzle Daz comic strip [MTM B5:159]. Stein's Diminishing Theory alternates groups making Melchisedechs and Melchisedechs making groups, each somewhat smaller than its predecessor [MTM B4:121]. In his notebook Stein believes on one day that the company and Duffey's earlier acquaintances made Duffey; on other days he believes Duffey evoked them from clay. They love him despite his unlovely qualities [MTM B10:304]. Teresa describes talismans of Argo gold filigree and Talking Oak Dordogne, their principal work being recollection and awakening rather than creation; reunion prefigures Resurrection [MTM B5:178-179]. Patrick Plunket likewise distinguishes Duffey's animated clays and quick-earths from the reality they became, and says he only woke them [MTM B12:390-391]. The dung, blood and lightning in the Muck of Animation produce a later dozen, which Duffey calls better than his first dozen [MTM B12:394]. The formal list names Finnegan/John Solli, son of Monster Giulio; Hans/John Schultz; Henri Salvatore; Vincent Stranahan; Casey Szymansky; Dotty Yekouris; Mary Monaghan Schultz; Mary Virginia Schaeffer; Teresa Piccone; Absalom Stein; and Mr. X. Although called twelve, the enumeration supplies eleven names [MTM B5:161-162]. Mary Catherine Carruthers is already recognized as one of the creations in the preceding scene [MTM B5:158]. Teresa later supplies the Argonaut identities: Finnegan is Iason/Jason; Hans Orpheus and later Faust; Henry Euphemus; Vincent Meleager; Casey Peleus; Dotty Medea; Marie Eurydice; Mary Virginia Laonome; Teresa Atalanta; Mary Catherine Antigone; and Stein Ab-Salom. She withholds Margaret Stone's identity and does not identify X [MTM B7:234]. Duffey calls Finnegan the original Finn McCool and places his Marvels in the intersecting Argo Legend and Finnegan Cycle [MTM B5:169]. He also describes Casey as the medieval Prince Casimir and his own twentieth-century creation [PG:536]. The Countess is said to be someone's animation, but whose remains unclear [MTM B7:215]. Henri describes their condition as Quest Completed, Fleece found and Grail Abundant, with rebuilding the world still to do [MTM B5:179-180]. The narrative says the Splendid Animations have sailed, are sailing and will continue to sail on Argo [MTM B10:300]. Most are Argo Masters, probably nearly as old as Duffey, forming an interdependent living corporation; Teresa's role is probably animating, while Duffey's is creative. Brannagan belongs to this larger circle [MTM B13:446]. Their Land, also called the Archipelago or Greater Archipelago, is a scattered recuperative island concentrated in Chicago, St. Louis and New Orleans. It offers the ship water, provisions, healing and virtues; the temporal relations remain uncorrelated [MTM B13:448]. Related groups should be distinguished. Cyrus Roundhead's Royal Pop company resembles Duffey's creations but goes further in a treacherous direction; its presence produces the Geometry of Shining Space [MTM B11:321]. Its young performers supply the Horse Opera's splendor before the slaughter [MTM B11:333]. Roundhead's claim that the final persons have no human chromosomes, blood, hormones or mental processes describes his own group and recruits [MTM B11:350]. The shining bodies that move through matter and apparently time belong to the Casey Machine's broader description of the splendid moment [CM:511]. The Devil is Dead offers parallels through the other human race, Non-people, Teras, double blood and Other Flesh [D:50] [D:121] [D:139] [D:209] [D:237] [D:285]; its attributed Overlark passage connects Neanderthal inheritance with imagination and ghostliness [D:270-272]. These parallels do not establish that every such figure is one of Duffey's twelve. Papa Devil I and II are grandchildren of the Devil through Ifreann; Doll resists X's account of primordial control and insists that people can act against it [D:278-279] [D:285] [D:292]. Herman, his primary Cardinal Erculo, and the remembered Saul are other long-lived figures, without being identified there as Duffey's creations [MB:584-585].
