AnimosityEfram Gate Gratz's declared attitude at the Last Conclave, where the leaders of the institution now called the Crowd assemble to dismantle it. He proclaims “total animosity” and vows to bury Peter and prevent the institution's return [MB:561].

MB:561

AnimusIn Jung's terminology, the masculine aspect of the female psyche. The Postscript names Animus and Anima as opposing twins alongside Ego, Self and Shadow in its account of Jung's Aion, using this plurality to discuss the several persons within a person [PS:477].

PS:477

AnneRadio broadcaster for the Japanese from Java during the Pacific war. Her intimate voice, homesickness-inducing songs and understanding of the soldiers give her an advantage that Stein's Anopheles Network cannot match in some respects. She signs off, “This is your best enemy, Anne, Good Night” [A:46].

A:46

AnninaSister of Dominic Vinobianco, whom Casey records thinking about constantly in his notebook at St. Bonaventure's boarding school [A:161-162] [A:166]. She is later named Annina Vinobianco among the girls he goes out with [A:168].

A:161-162; A:166; A:168

Annunciation Church of Sydney, AustraliaChurch where John Gottfried Schultz (Hans) and Marie Anna Monaghan marry on Monday, February 15, 1943. Because Hans lacks army permission, the marriage is to remain secret for a while; twenty or thirty attendees are all Marie's relatives [A:31].

A:31

Anopheles NetworkSmall G.I. radio station Stein establishes as part of his Special Service duties during the Pacific war. It occupies one of his two pyramidal tents. Casey writes squibs for its broadcasts, which also feature comic sponsors, records, volunteer speakers and jokes read by Stein [A:46].

A:46

AntagonistPapa Devil warns that their clever antagonist may turn the Naxos trap into a double ambush [D:123]. Finnegan later believes he has killed his principal prey at the Pirate Hotel, but Seaworthy’s sour laugh shows that he has escaped again [D:231]. In the town of the final rendezvous Finnegan senses his old antagonist’s presence. The left-footed tracker is also there, with his employer; the tracker is not simply another name for the antagonist [D:275].

D:123; D:231; D:275

AntarcticaCasey’s fifth imaginary world, that of the explorer, requires a cartographic error that makes Earth fifty percent larger and melon-shaped. In it Antarctica is an ice ring around a southern sea and sunny continent, probably Atlantis after continental dispersal. Casey imagines taking modern techniques there and bringing its Higher Ethic home [A:158].

A:158

Antebellum periodA period before a war. In the account of superimposed Brunhilde voyages, X says that some incidents attributed to Finnegan in the first decade of the “second antebellum period” actually happened to Giulio Solli in the decade before World War I, and that Finnegan remembers them filially. The commentator immediately cautions that X cannot be depended upon [MTM B6:187].

MTM B6:187

Antecedent WorldsNine discarded but still animated and populated worlds in a fancy Mary Virginia Schaeffer records in her Duffey Book. She explicitly says that the idea of divine false starts has no authority in Scripture or revelation, though legends support it. Our world is the tenth and might itself be discarded. She speculates that Duffey has wandered in from one of the earlier worlds, whose different conditions explain his circular continuity and lack of parents [MTM B10:291-292].

MTM B10:291-292

AntediluvianPatti Solli’s description of her father Giulio, whose antiquity embarrasses her. She insists that she means the word literally: he was “from before the beginning,” and Finnegan and she look a little that way too [A:174].

A:174

Anthony (Saint)Saint invoked when the narrator compares the beautiful, treacherous women in Casey’s second imaginary world to St. Anthony’s temptations [A:157], an allusion to Anthony the Abbot’s legendary struggle. An Anthony also appears beside Francis among the saints aboard the Navicula Petri in Henry’s dream, though that passage does not specify which Anthony [A:45].

A:157; A:45

Anthony ShipFormer name of Argo at Actium, where the ship was shamed, according to the history told by the talking oak in its wheel [MTM B13:404].

MTM B13:404

Anthropomorphic Colts (Strong Experience of)Phrase that rises half-consciously in Duffey’s mind during the Great Day upheaval. As façades and whole buildings topple, the noisy, airish activity outside seems like a clattering experience of anthropomorphic colts. Duffey then exclaims over the phrase itself [MTM B11:311].

MTM B11:311

Anti-ChristusTitle Casey publicly claims as Casey of the Zodiac [MTM B12:382]. Mary Catherine says that his followers hail the Antichrist role as the highest human status, while she is unsure how fully Casey believes it himself [MTM B12:377]. Hilary Hilton equates him with Rolo Danovitz, the Antichrist of a quasi-fictional cycle [MTM B12:378]. Casey’s projection of his face and voice over television programs has helped make him known as Anti-Christus [MTM B12:380]. Teresa quotes a latter-day prophecy that ghostly Duffey will carry Prince Casimir on Argo to the coast nearest Armageddon, where he will reign for a while as Anti-Christ [MTM B12:388]. Finnegan likewise foretells Argo’s transport of Antichrist to Megiddo, while Duffey and the other Masters seek to prevent his coming aboard [MTM B13:453-454]. Duffey’s later commentary allows that Casey may instead be one of the false, premature antichrists [PG:535].

MTM B12:382; MTM B12:377; MTM B12:378; MTM B12:380; MTM B12:388; MTM B13:453-454; PG:535

Anti-Corn-Law LeagueBritish organization founded in 1839 to campaign for repeal of the Corn Laws, which were repealed in 1846. Its encyclopedia article runs into the defective ANTICHRIST entry that gives Casey’s birth details: after “His manifestation as the Antichrist was,” the text switches to the League’s founding and purpose [PG:528-529].

PG:528-529

Anti-PrizeThe Sword and Scabbard of Saint Sécaire, a peril to the world that Argo’s Masters want to lose rather than recover. They lose it three times; on the last occasion they weld sword to scabbard with molten fillers and bury it deep in the Nine Mile Depth. Four hundred years later Cyril and Cyrus Dimbeau accidentally recover it while taking bathysphere core samples [MTM B13:422].

MTM B13:422

AntichristEschatological role claimed by Casey, who calls himself Casey of the Zodiac, the Anti-Christus [MTM B12:382]. Finnegan foretells Argo carrying Antichrist to the Plains of Megiddo [MTM B13:453]; Duffey’s commentary nevertheless leaves open whether Casey is the final Antichrist or a premature, false one [PG:535].

MTM B12:382; MTM B13:453; PG:535

ANTICHRIST (encyclopedia entry)Defective entry in about one percent of copies of the A-C volume of a cheap Chicago encyclopedia, reported by Silas and Maud Whiterice. It identifies the Antichrist as Kasmir (Casey) W. Szymansky, born in Chicago on October 7, 1921, to pawnbroker and antique dealer Gabriel Szymansky and Miriam Lessing, then runs into the Anti-Corn-Law League article. The commentators call it a hoax, wonder whether Casey or his printery colleagues inserted it, and confirm the biographical particulars [PG:528-529].

PG:528-529

AntillesIsland region in which the narrator locates the Terrestrial Paradise at precisely sixteen degrees north and sixty-one degrees, forty-four minutes, forty-two seconds west [D:234]. The following scene identifies the setting as Basse-Terre [D:235-236]. Angela Cosquin describes her father’s maps of seven true and seven false passages through the Antilles [D:260]. The narrator also uses the region to measure Johnny Duckwalk’s drinking: fewer than a dozen men in all the Antilles can outdrink him [D:236].

D:234; D:235-236; D:260; D:236

Antipodal GhostFinnegan’s phrase for Mr. X after a disguised-voice telephone warning that he must flee. Asked by Brannagan who called, Finnegan says “My antipodal ghost” and explains that they are alike but a world apart [D:209].

D:209

AntipodesThe far southern world in Hans’s thoughts about Australia, a place beyond the voyages of Ulysses and the men of Solomon and Hiram, to which old legends are relegated and where griffins and dragons seem naturally at home [A:16]. Theresa Piccone teasingly asks Vincent for a fuller account of “the Rover Boys at the Antipodes” in her letter [A:49].

A:16; A:49

AntiquarianOne of Angela Cosquin’s father’s occupations, alongside cartography. His skill with old scripts, seals, inks, papers, parchment and documents helps him make convincing maps and supporting records for an increasingly fraudulent treasure-map trade [D:259-261].

D:259-261

Antique DealerGabriel Szymansky’s occupation on the rich-street side of his business. His two shops face different streets and connect through a passage beneath the alley: antique dealer to the rich, pawnbroker to the poor. He prospers but lets Casey think him poor [A:160].

A:160

AnvilsObjects among the household “iron words” Duffey remembers and appropriates from other minds. The anvils bear the names S.R. & Co. or Peter Wright [MTM B1:17].

MTM B1:17

Apathy (Goat)One of the goats that understands Finnegan, named with Hermione, Cecille and Diocletian as the smartest of Gautier’s flock [A:199-200]. Gautier and his goats now live year-round in New Jersey and frequent the Barrens [A:196-197].

A:199-200; A:196-197

ApeOne of the animal semblances assigned to Tityroi or Satyrs in the chapter epigraph attributed to Galen [D:160-161]. Finnegan becomes a feral climber, living gargoyle and ape-cat during the Pirate Hotel raid; the narration says he could not have performed the escape as a man and becomes a man again afterward. The climber also gives rise to a local ape or monstrous-man legend [D:162] [D:164-165]. Doll later echoes someone else’s description of him as a hooked-nosed ape [D:173]. A related treatment appears in Lafferty’s Serpent’s Egg. Its Axel’s Apes, also called Smithy, Golden and Blue-Eyed Apes, are the Unfallen People of Second Eden in Ethiopia. Their gargoyle faces connect them with the novel’s legends of cathedral builders; adult height averages just over two meters, and a later passage raises a possible affinity with the old Titans. Ansel Grindstone interprets their human chromosome count as proof that they are men. A separate speaker reports that the boy Axel’s X-rays show a human skeleton beneath his fleshy hump, face and feet. The explicit human/ape/mechanical-hybrid speculation chiefly concerns the Dolophonoi-Assassins, with all three species proposed as their possible components. The Apes are extraordinary smiths, stoneworkers and mathematicians, and speak slowly and thoughtfully. They possess bi-location or trans-location, exceptional strength, animal and bird communication, and the ability to smell and appraise metal deposits as far as two hundred kilometers away. The experimental child Axel’s intelligence is off the scale. The group appears somewhat childish to humans and computers, enjoys meditation, puzzles and animal stories, and has a weakness for wine, including the mushroom wine of its underground taverns. The narrator says the Apes are afraid of nothing and incapable of anger. Their refusal to give testimony is specifically a refusal to testify about human origins, not a general refusal of self-description. The novel’s legends connect the Unfallen People with an Ape Bridge, which Axel Grindstone believes should be called the Angel Bridge, and with teaching smithcraft to the Romanies. Ansel proposes that God has not yet fully activated them. Their discovery by the human Axel Grindstone leads raiders to Second Eden. The reigning sleepy one calls the raiders unwitting divine agents and directs the Apes to go with them. Five hundred are taken away and sold to zoos and institutions; the newborn Axel goes to the Lynn-Randal experiment in America. About a hundred of the dispersed Apes are consumed by lightning within five minutes, which the narrator says is God taking them to himself. The infant’s father, Alpha, follows, gathers companions from American zoos and founds Apes’ Alley in limestone caverns near the experiment. The community has shops, smithies, a mint, clubs, a silent-film theater and meditation halls, with old gas wells supplying light and power. Alpha and Satrap Saint Ledger are close friends. Inneall says that her own circulating blood is partly human and partly Axel’s, secretly taken from the two boys while they slept. The caverns are eventually closed, and a giant hand extinguishes the holy fire as a voice imposes three nights and days of Holy Sleep. The expected worldwide awakening is to begin when Axel wakes at midnight cockcrow, but he is stabbed in the throat in the instant before he can awaken the others. His friends place him in an ocean-floor cenotaph. Sebastian Lazar later suggests treating him and the other murdered children as Leaders Asleep who may return. The sea-louse epilog calls their condition an undead coma and says neither the Apes nor the Whales were promised succession to humanity, while also boasting of its own ability to outdo Inneall’s lies. (Serpent's Egg, PDF pp. 13, 17, 21-23, 25, 27-32, 52, 54-61, 77-78, 152-153, 157-158, 171, 176).

D:160-161; D:162; D:164-165; D:173

Ape-catNarratorial name for the form Finnegan takes when climbing, attacking and escaping the Pirate Hotel. The passage says that as a man he could not have done it; only as the ape-cat could he accomplish the raid, and afterward he becomes a man again [D:164-165].

D:164-165

APO OceansHumorous name for the waters separating Casey’s overseas army service from home, using APO, Army Post Office. At a Crock stockholders’ meeting a stranger presents a new signed proxy from Casey, still “across the APO Oceans”; it supersedes the earlier proxy Casey gave Duffey before going overseas [MTM B4:144].

MTM B4:144

ApocalypseThe Book of Revelation, named in the account of Henry Salvatore’s Navicula Petri dream. Among the shattered masts is Albion of the White Cliffs, whose apostasy the narration says is foretold in the Apocalypse [A:45].

A:45

ApocryphalStatus of some Finnegan adventures that the narrator says cannot be separated from the canonical accounts. His travels invite questions about simultaneous worlds and people; his friends remember different versions, and both Finnegan and X are unreliable tellers [A:187].

A:187

ApolloGreek god of music and prophecy, one of the identities assigned to Hans Schultz alongside Dr. Faustus and Aquinas Redevivus [A:39]. Hans’s dream of climbing an iron ladder toward the sun culminates in the statement that he was Apollo [A:62]. The narrator later again calls Hans Faust and Apollo while describing Casey’s place among the Dirty Five; it says Casey comes close to Hans in compassion [A:169].

A:39; A:62; A:169

Apollonius of Rhodes (c. 3rd century BC)Hellenistic Greek poet of the third century BCE, author of the Argonautica, a four-book epic in hexameters about Jason and the Argonauts’ expedition for the Golden Fleece. His learned Alexandrian poem draws on Homeric epic and other earlier accounts of the voyage. Ancient biographical traditions associate him with Rhodes and the headship of the Alexandrian Library, though the details and chronology of his career are uncertain.
ApopkaOne of the Florida towns through which Finnegan, Doll and X drive in the evenings, along with Orlando, Kissimee, Pine Castle and sometimes Daytona, passing through citrus and scrub [D:183].

D:183

ApostasyRenunciation of religious faith, represented in Henry’s Navicula Petri dream by a shattered mast named Albion of the White Cliffs. The narration says Albion’s apostasy is foretold in the Apocalypse [A:45].

A:45

ApostateThe narrator’s description of W., one of four initialled figures whose episodes affect the Pelican and Bark circle. W. and Y. are omitted from the chronicle for reasons of space, and the narrator says little has been missed by omitting W. [A:132].

A:132

Apostle to the greater ArchipelagosFinnegan’s title for Francis Xavier in his meditation on ocean islands as constellations that prefigure the skies [A:35]. Xavier was a Jesuit missionary whose work extended from India through the Maluku islands to Japan.

A:35

ApostlesChrist’s apostles, present among the saintly crew of Henry’s Navicula Petri dream [A:45]. Salvation Sally imagines the Apostles accepting rest and kindness from flippant unbelievers, as she has received from Hans and Marie [A:8]. In a letter, Show Boat repeats Papa Piccone’s Italian legend of an unnamed tippling apostle, perhaps Thomas, Bartholomew or Jude, who finishes wine left in cups and wineskins but nevertheless converts tens of thousands [A:262]. Dotty calls Jude the patron of printers and little magazines; Finnegan supplies his association with impossible causes [A:115].

A:45; A:8; A:262; A:115

Apostolo, EvelynMember of Duffey’s bookish and literary North Chicago circle, listed with Tony Apostolo. The narrator calls 1925-1935 its golden age, followed by an electrum age of mixed gold and silver lasting until about 1946 [MTM B3:98].

MTM B3:98

Apostolo, TonyReporter among Duffey’s literary Chicago friends [MTM B3:98]. Tony’s extravagant partisan opinions are frequently opposed by Rollo McSorley. He challenges the story that the Depression began with the 1929 stock-market crash, appealing to his own work for the International News Service at the time [MTM B4:122]. He bets one hundred dollars against Rollo that Duffey can move a mule by magic, points out nearby street-department mules, and calls a photographer to record the test; Rollo and Elena O’Higgins call their own photographers [MTM B4:129-130].

MTM B3:98; MTM B4:122; MTM B4:129-130

Apostolus Potator Incognitus, SanctusShow Boat’s Latin title for the unknown drinking apostle of Papa Piccone’s Italian legend, approximately “Holy Apostle, Unknown Drinker.” In her letter to Dotty she says she prays to him, using Sanctus Apostolus Potator Incognitus, while defending Finnegan despite his failings [A:262].

A:262

Apparition (Feast of the)Marie Monaghan’s name for the feast on the day she becomes engaged to Hans. She calls it the second Thursday in February [A:28]; the marriage date places this in 1943, making the engagement February11 [A:31].

A:28; A:31

Apparition (Ghostly manifestation)Papa Devil’s silent arrival on ruined walls is likened to a spook; the narrator leaves the port uncertain, perhaps Paraiso or Campeche [D:67-70]. In a later possible future, Casey appears as the Apparition, Man of Mystery and Antichristus aboard Argo, his glory made of tampered-with light [MTM B13:462].

D:67-70; MTM B13:462

ApparitionsOne of the phenomena Royce Rollins attributes to his supposed Neanderthal aliens in The Return of the Neanderthal: The Alien Within. The chapter epigraph presents this through Charles O. A. Harrington’s hostile review in Science for Today, which reports Rollins’s claim that apparitions, fetches, second sight and related manifestations are normal aspects of the species [D:240-242].

D:240-242

Apple ButterOne of the foods Duffey buys when provisioning his first St. Louis establishment, later Rounders’: a five-gallon jar, alongside pigs’ feet, spiced sausage, cheese, bread, potatoes and drink [MTM B2:41].

MTM B2:41

Aquilae congregabunt dumque In nostram memoriam quotiescumqueLatin couplet announced as the company’s motto in the poem opening Stranahan’s chapter: “Aquilae congregabunt dumque / In nostram memoriam quotiescumque” [A:91]. It associates gathering eagles with remembrance. Henry’s dream ship bears the different, related inscription Ubicumque fuerit corpus illic congregabuntur et aquilas, which the narration calls an echo of the Dirty Five’s high motto [A:44]. The imagery recalls the Gospel’s gathering eagles, while the remembrance language suggests the Latin Eucharistic formula.

A:91; A:44

Aquinas in a T ShirtFinnegan’s caption for Hans Schultz among the Seven Pillars of Righteousness in his illustrated masthead for the Bark [A:121-122]. It combines Hans’s Thomistic identity with an ordinary T-shirt.

A:121-122

Aquinas Redevivus“Aquinas revived,” one of the learned identities assigned to Hans Schultz alongside Apollo and Dr. Faustus in the account of the Dirty Five’s earlier lives [A:39].

A:39

Aquinas, ThomasDominican philosopher and theologian, born about 1225 and died 1274, author of the Summa Theologiae and Summa Contra Gentiles. His theology brings Aristotelian reasoning into conversation with Christian revelation; the Summa Theologiae includes the Five Ways concerning God’s existence and extensive treatments of ethics, law and sacraments. Canonized in 1323 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1567, he has been repeatedly commended by the Church as a model of theological and philosophical inquiry. In the novels, the Answer incorporates material from Aquinas alongside Augustine and Pope Benedict [MTM B4:114]. John William Schultz urges that Aquinas and Albert be taught to fourth-graders [A:208-209]. The narrator’s notes on time quote Thomas’s distinction between eternity as an instantaneous whole and time as the measure of change [MTM B13:468-469]. The chapter epigraph attributed to Carmody Overlark calls him the angelic ox and imagines his massive back-brain [D:271-272]. Another epigraph attributes to his Summa Contra Gentiles a defense of divine knowledge of singulars [D:43].

MTM B4:114; A:208-209; MTM B13:468-469; D:271-272; D:43

ArabicLanguage Joseph says he learned while working as a caravan boy, alongside several others [D:94]. Finnegan has studied an O’Leary book of colloquial Arabic during the Atlantic crossing, but people in Tangier, especially Arabs, cannot recognize the language when he speaks it [D:104].

D:94; D:104

ArabsAmong the people Finnegan encounters in Tangier. They fail to understand his book-learned Arabic, but a little Arab boy shares his finger-count game, pledges lifelong friendship and organizes runners to keep him informed [D:104].

D:104

ArachniaEarlier heading misread the word arachnid. See Arachnid.
ArachnidDuring his display of miscellaneous learning in Orlando’s Marine Room, Finnegan asks Doll how many legs an arachnid has [D:190].

D:190

Arafura SeaSea between Australia and New Guinea, included with the Timor and Savu seas in the catalogue of waters sailed by Argo and remembered by Duffey [MTM B13:406].

MTM B13:406

AraghOne of the names the Malay boy gives his canoe, glossing it as “the direction,” alongside Aral and Bumi. These names lead Finnegan to recognize the canoe as Argo [A:89].

A:89

AralName the Malay boy gives his canoe, glossed as “hindrance.” He also names it Bumi and Aragh, and Finnegan recognizes the Ship Argo in it [A:89].

A:89

Aransas PassOne of Brunhilde’s nightly coastal ports, listed after Port O’Conner and before Corpus; the ship next anchors off Padre Island for a beach party and fish fry [D:34].

D:34

Ararat (Mt.)Mountain in eastern Turkey traditionally associated with Noah’s Ark. A Cummings-clan Fundamentaler treats belief in the Ark’s survival, snowbound and guarded by angels in Armenia, as a test of faith. Zabotski accepts angelic guardians but questions the identification of the biblical country and mountain; Duffey thinks the wooden remains may be castles [MTM B9:280-281]. Zabotski later calls the structures on Ararat discarded models and his own flood-going contraption the original [MTM B9:287]. Askandanakandrian identifies Mt. Ararat in his “own Armenia” as the present secluded center of the other blood [A:258].

MTM B9:280-281; MTM B9:287; A:258

ArbuthnotOne of the aliases X lists for Gregory McColum Papadiabolous, the Irish Papadiabolous II. His other surnames include Noonan, Flaherty, Christy, Clarenden, Cobbett, Malory and Ingraham; both he and his Asiatic twin use variants of John with Gregory [D:285]. The name may allude to John Arbuthnot (1667-1735), the Scottish physician and literary friend of Jonathan Swift and Alexander Pope.

D:285

ArcaSpanish word for a chest. In Angela Cosquin’s account, her father marks his fabricated land-treasure maps with a baul or arca beneath crossed pickaxe and shovel. Brands such as T, K and BP suggest Teach, Kidd and Bartolomo Portuguese to credulous buyers [D:259-260].

D:259-260

ArcadesPassageways among the shops and bars on the street floor of Sydney’s Plaza, where Finnegan and his companions gather [A:3]. Arcades are also among the amenities of the newly appearing Bayougoula Park in New Orleans [MTM B11:331-332].

A:3; MTM B11:331-332

ArcadiaGreek region idealized in pastoral literature. Don Barnaby says Madame Le Mourcheor uses honey from bees in the meadows around Megapolis in “Arcady” for her Juju Joy Pills [D:248-249].

D:248-249

Arcadian motifAn old pattern of pastoral symbolism Duffey thinks he recognizes in the landscape of the Presence. Patrick Plunket corrects his habit of treating it as contrived art: it is real, and their ascent is of the invisible, interior mountain [MTM B12:390].

MTM B12:390

Archangel StatuesThree spread-winged archangels on the south front of St. Malachy’s Church in Chicago. Duffey sees the stone as quivering with wings; each side of the church also bears nine large-winged angels [MTM B3:87].

MTM B3:87

ArchbishopChurch official to whom Bascom Bagby reports supposed heresies in New Orleans parishes during a visit [MTM B7:227]. Henry Salvatore visits a bishop and an archbishop while arranging entry into the seminary in Louisiana [A:124-125].

MTM B7:227; A:124-125

ArchipelagoScattered homeland of the Animated Marvels, also called the Greater Archipelago, with much of its population in Chicago, St. Louis and New Orleans. It supplies Argo with provisions, healing and virtues; many of its people are Argo Masters, though their relations across time and place remain incompletely understood [MTM B13:448]. The poem opening Stranahan’s chapter describes the Fivers themselves as islands in a weird Archipelago, discovering valleys and skerries in sky-lands [A:91]. Finnegan tells creation stories of island groups formed from a broken electrum cup, a shattered bronze bowl and a mat torn by sea turtles; Hans observes that archipelago originally meant a great sea rather than its islands [A:35-36].

MTM B13:448; A:91; A:35-36

Archipelago (The Greater)Another name for the Land of the Animated Marvels, the scattered recuperative island whose people chiefly live in Chicago, St. Louis and New Orleans and provide for Argo [MTM B13:448]. Finnegan also calls Francis Xavier the Apostle to the greater Archipelagos, imagining ocean islands as constellations that prefigure the skies [A:35].

MTM B13:448; A:35

ArchipelagoesIsland groups whose origins Finnegan describes through creation legends: an electrum cup broken into the Aegean islands, a bronze bowl shattered into the long islands off Malaya, and a woven mat torn by sea turtles into the green islands, with Guinea retaining its stitched center. He says each began as a five-island cluster or pentanesia, and calls Xavier the Apostle to the greater Archipelagos [A:35].

A:35

Architects of all the new realmsX’s description of the influential notables who gather in Crimea to adore the released Devil and receive their status in the new order. His account includes clergy, political advisers, intellectuals and artists [MTM B6:204-205]. The narrative dates the release to the last Saturday of May 1946, while also questioning whether such releases recur [MTM B5:184].

MTM B6:204-205; MTM B5:184

Archive, LeonardOne of three hospitable men living by a Louisiana swamp landing, with Oliver Greenflag and Harry A. “Honeybucket” Kincaid. He welcomes Duffey and Brannagan and promises anything the travelers need [MTM B13:416-417]. Archive explains that varying voltages, frequencies and electrodes lets them collect fish, animals, plants, chemicals, minerals, salts, alcohols, petroleums and sugars from water. Selective polarization and differences of potential provide power, and he says they have given these techniques to the world [MTM B13:418]. He claims frequency modulation and broadcasting can also draw feelings, weather, notions, ideas, emotions and people. After Honeybucket summons three young women, Archive asks them whether they want anything beyond the pleasure of the men’s company [MTM B13:419].

MTM B13:416-417; MTM B13:418; MTM B13:419

ArchivistArmy-history occupation in which Private Gregory says he spent years after admission to the U.S. Military Academy and his eventual commission. He sought obscurity but became a leading expert and teacher, drawing on his centuries of personal experience [A:77-78].

A:77-78

ArdorPassion, especially sexual passion, in Hillary Hilton’s joke that cold snow acting on Casey’s ardor produced a lasting coolness toward him. Hilton tells Finnegan that he caught Casey with Mary Jean, dragged him naked from bed into the snowy road, and left him there [A:251-252].

A:251-252

“Arena del Mar”One of the nine projected volumes into which Endymeon Ellenbogen says he has classified his poetry. The poems are uncollected and unpublished, though he recites them readily [A:237].

A:237

ArgoThe ancient Quest Ship around which the company’s overlapping lives and legends gather. The Dirty Five are identified as Iason/Finnegan, Orpheus/Hans, Meleager/Vincent, Peleus/Casey and Euphemus/Henry [A:38-39]. Teresa’s later account adds Hans’s Faust identity, Marie/Eurydice, Dotty/Medea, Mary Virginia/Laonome, Teresa/Atalanta, Mary Catherine/Antigone and Stein/Ab-Salom. She calls their voyage older than Greek myth, invokes Homer as witness to their antiquity, and says their quest was the prototype of all quests; they sailed to Colchis and still possess the Golden Fleece [MTM B7:233-234]. Casey calls the Five’s transport Argo “for this night at least” near the Talaud Islands [A:63], and the poem opening Stranahan’s chapter recalls sailing the ship anciently called Argo [A:91]. Its identities include the Navicula Petri or Peter Ship, which Henry dreams as a galleon-like vessel of pennants, saints and shattered masts, then recognizes as the Argo whose quest has been sanctified [A:44-46]. Henry’s dream supplies the name and Finnegan’s storm-battered masthead for the magazine Bark, also spelled Barque [A:121] [A:128]; Hans likewise calls the remembered ship the Bark [MTM B5:178]. The talking oak in its wheel recounts appearances as the Anthony Ship at Actium, the flagship of Abd-Aliah of the Sea and then Sindbad’s ship; as St. Brandon’s Land of Behest, the Salle du Roi of Robert of Namur, Willy Jones’s Flying Serpent and Dana Coscuin’s Catherine. It has carried St. Paul, Godfrey of the Gate, Mark Twain and Judas, and has repeatedly come into infidel ownership [MTM B13:404-405]. As Brunhilde it belongs to Saxon Seaworthy and carries Finnegan among dangerous associates [D:21] [D:30]; Seaworthy is identified with Sindbad when commissioning the lounge paintings [D:59]. X calls Finnegan’s disputed ship Delay, World or Argo, while the narrator questions both its registration and the reliability of the voyage’s accounts, including Seaworthy’s threat to have Finnegan killed [A:187]. Argo is a Hope Ship and, in its primary sense, a show boat. It goes where other ships cannot, carries dangerous passengers and cargo, opens dark lands and ports, breaks conspiracies, and brings joy, grace and entertainment [MTM B13:400] [MTM B13:405]. It is above all a Quest Ship: the Golden Fleece is an early triumph, and its later recoveries include the Holy Cross. The Sword and Scabbard of Saint Sécaire are an anti-prize that its Masters have repeatedly tried to lose; the most recent discovery is made by the Dimbeau brothers against the Masters’ wishes [MTM B13:421-422]. In another account it delivers the Peter-Bell to the mooring rock north of San Simeon [MB:577-578]. Duffey and Brannagan also root out future evils before they can flow into the present; their most complete successes erase the evils so thoroughly that the achievements cannot be remembered [MTM B13:416] [MTM B13:420-421]. It knows seas, islands, shores and promontories, including migrating islands and seas. An old log even claims a voyage on the moon’s Mare Nectaris [MTM B13:405-406]. The Sea of the Seven Lost Years has scattered shores and channels amid other waters; Duffey’s years on it are not consecutive [MTM B13:406]. The ship also sails outside the cosmos and within minds and persons [MTM B13:437]. It ordinarily moves smoothly and rapidly against wind and waves [MTM B13:402]. A voyage is a cycle or dynasty of adventures, interrupted by hiatus, mutation or a death of the ship, not simply one trip between ports. Argo Twelve is already active when Duffey names his balloon, and the later adventure cycle is called the climactic Fourteenth Voyage [MTM B2:64] [MTM B13:410-412]. Duffey describes its log as a dating clock covering nine thousand past years and sixty-seven future years, with some later futures recorded in a different, elusive ledger. The talking oak can announce an artifact’s date, though it sometimes gives geographical bearings instead [MTM B13:411]. Argo’s dimensions and fittings vary: she has as many masts as a voyage needs, sometimes funnels and engines, innumerable decks and unfamiliar rooms, animal stalls, unknown families, shops and cottage industries, yet can fit a small boat slip. Some suppose the present vessel is only the boat of a greater Ship. It retains the talking-oak wheel, Noah’s broken molar in a plank, the Special Dove’s cote, grist mills, log books and a lantern that shines around headlands and corners [MTM B13:403-404]. Duffey recounts rediscovering her as an old hull in New Orleans, built at Ragusa of Dinaric oak with unusual spring and able to regain her fittings by remembering them; the account is expressly called symbolically rather than ordinarily accurate [MTM B13:412]. She can be frozen solid in blue ice and released for sailing [MTM B13:398-402]. A later account shows constant emergency repairs and poor ordinary seaworthiness, while declaring that she cannot sink forever [MB:590]. The Masters form an interdependent society, including Duffey, Brannagan, Casey, Finnegan, Henry and others of the Animated Marvels [MTM B13:446]. Melchisedech is an extraordinary pilot [MTM B13:402]; X is admitted as a servitor with half shares, rather than a full Master [MTM B13:434-435]. The mechanical, ghostlike seamen are materialized residues or place tokens of absent travelers; arriving Masters don their own effigies. Effigies of respected companions also exist, and Casey mars those of Finnegan and two companions. The ship carries more coffins than there are Masters [MTM B13:415-416] [MTM B13:449-450]. After Duffey’s killing, his bones are laid in one; God comes aboard and tells him that his duties do not require flesh. Gorshok supplies the golden mask, scarf and gauntlets with which Duffey resumes sailing [MTM B13:443-444]. Other passengers include the rescued Neo-Neanderthal Eva and the returning Monsignor X, who brings the flayed skin attributed to Cardinal Artemis [MTM B13:400-407] [MTM B13:451-452]. Coryphaena fish play a salute when a present or future Pope rides aboard [MTM B13:450-451]. The Sindbad Lounge contains Finnegan’s oceanic paintings, made in his youth when the ship was Brunhilde [MTM B13:404]; their commission and prophetic grave scenes are recounted in the earlier cruise [D:59-61] [D:85-86]. The Bread and Wine Room hosts meaningful gatherings and later bears his thirteen Deaths of the Cardinals paintings directly on its bulkheads [MTM B13:403] [MTM B13:452]. The chart room preserves moral instruction even during evil ownership [MTM B13:437]. The scattered Land of the Animated Marvels, or Greater Archipelago, is a recuperative island for Argo, supplying water, provisions, healing and virtues, although its relation to the ship across time and place remains unresolved [MTM B13:448]. Teresa identifies the birth talismans as pieces of Argo’s gold filigree over talking oak, their gold from the Fleece and their function anamnesis or recollection; Hans describes the people as stranded on a mundane shore awaiting their return [MTM B5:178-179]. Finnegan foretells that Argo will carry Antichrist to Megiddo [MTM B13:453]. Duffey, Brannagan and Gorshok nevertheless try to prevent the mysterious passenger’s entry, seeking detectives’ advice and installing alarms, firedrakes and Gunboat Smith as guards [MTM B13:454-458]. An entourage, altered sea, magnetic wind and growing disturbance surround the ship; the winds now carry her instead of opposing her [MTM B13:459-460]. Her mirrors shatter into cubistic reflections, and the Man of Mystery emerges from below decks as Peleus, Gorshok, Prince Casimir, Casey and Antichristus. Argo lands him at Habonim by the Plains of Megiddo [MTM B13:461-462]. These events are increasingly marked as a probable but unsettled future. The ship disappears while Duffey, Brannagan and Gunboat fade out of that world; rediscovering her becomes their next task, and the whole coming of Antichrist subsequently recedes with the scene [MTM B13:451] [MTM B13:460] [MTM B13:463] [MTM B13:468]. The Brunhilde itinerary includes Freeport, Palacios, Port O’Conner, Aransas Pass and Corpus, then an anchorage off Padre Island [D:34]; Port Isabel and Brownsville [D:55]; Mexican coastal anchorages, with one episode uncertainly placed at Paraiso or Campeche [D:59] [D:67]; Campeche, Progreso, Cozumel, Ciudad Chetumal, Belize, Puerto Barrios, La Ceiba, Trujillo, Cabo Gracias a Dios, Blue Fields, Limon and San Cristobal [D:81]; Portobello, Manana, Cartagena, Santa Maria, Willemsted, Caracas, Cumana and Port of Spain [D:85]; Cayenne, Belem, Sao Luis, Camocim, Fortaleza and Natal [D:86]; Freetown [D:89]; Bissau, Bathurst, Dakar, St. Louis, Memrhar, Port Etienne, Villa Cisneros, Las Palmas and Grand Canary [D:96]; Arrecife on Lanzarote, Ifni, Agadir, Magadar, Safti, Mazagan, Casablanca, Rabat and Tangier [D:101]; Palermo, Messina, Zakinthos and Naxos [D:114-115]. Argo’s later or differently ordered journeys include Biloxi [MTM B13:408] and Habonim [MTM B13:462].

Argo Company (Teresa's account)Teresa Piccone Stranahan’s account of the old company awakened by Duffey. She says he assembled and awakened them rather than created them, causing them to be born again to oppose the newly loosed Devil. She explicitly denies that they were the first crew, pilots or voyagers, although they sailed on the first ship, the Argo, identified with the Ark, and added its sails and rudder [MTM B7:233-234]. Her identifications are Finnegan as Iason, later Jason; Hans as Orpheus and later Faust; Henry as Euphemus; Vincent as Meleager; Casey as Peleus; Dotty as Medea; Marie as Eurydice; Mary Virginia as Laonome; Teresa herself as Atalanta; and Mary Catherine as Antigone. Duffey is the original Melchisedech, but his Argonaut name was something else. Stein is Ab-Salom, Father of Peace, a Euxine ship’s chandler who joined to protect his investments. Teresa says Henry learned to walk on water from his ocean-father, rejects Dotty’s evil reputation, and substitutes Marie’s journey to Australia and motherhood of its peoples for Eurydice’s descent to the underworld. Gabrielovitch, Zabotski and Salvation Sally may belong to an older company; Teresa does not know about X, and knows Margaret’s company but refuses to disclose it [MTM B7:234].

MTM B7:233-234; MTM B7:234

Argo TwelveDuffey’s first name for his custom-made, hydrogen-filled silk-bag balloon during his early St. Louis years, the period beginning in 1915 [MTM B2:38] [MTM B2:63-64]. He takes friends including Bagby, Mary Louise, Charley Murray and Beth Keegan on ascents. A powerful misty visitor tells him Argo Twelve is already active, so he renames the balloon Argo Twelve and Half [MTM B2:64].

MTM B2:38; MTM B2:63-64; MTM B2:64

Argo Twelve and HalfDuffey’s revised name for his balloon after a misty person of great power tells him the actual Argo Twelve is currently active and its name unavailable. The visitor permits the balloon sometimes to serve as a pinnace or ship’s boat for Argo’s Twelfth Voyage [MTM B2:64]. The same page also calls it Argo Twelve and a Half.

MTM B2:64

ArgonautsThe people of Argo, including its interdependent society of Masters such as Duffey, Brannagan and Casey [MTM B13:446] [MTM B13:454]. The narrator portrays them as commando experts against evil, able to distinguish right from wrong apart from a short interlude at Wien, with guidance preserved in the chart room even during evil ownership of the ship [MTM B13:437]. In his Notes on the Finnegan Cycle, Absalom Stein says that everyone must first have existed in legend before living in life [MB:549-550].

MTM B13:446; MTM B13:454; MTM B13:437; MB:549-550

AriadneDaughter of King Minos of Crete in Greek myth, associated with her abandonment by Theseus on Naxos. The novel calls Naxos the home of Ariadne and white wine, as well as the home of Anastasia Demetriades [D:115].

D:115

AriochOne of the Three Slant-Faced Men whose names Duffey finds in Flame Man, with Amraphel and Thadal. The narration identifies him as king of Ellasar, Pontus or Lower Babylonia and describes the three as crooked kings or anti-magi who have no magic [MTM B7:227].

MTM B7:227

Aristotle (384--322 BC)Greek philosopher (384-322 BCE), student of Plato, tutor of Alexander and founder of the Lyceum in Athens. His works range across logic, ethics, politics, biology and metaphysics; his systematic treatment of inference helped establish logic as a discipline. The Nicomachean Ethics and Politics examine human flourishing and political life. Known to medieval scholars as the Philosopher, he profoundly influenced later philosophy and Christian theology. Casey’s school notebook mocks an attributed statement about lynx urine and signets [A:162] [A:165]. The narrator of The Devil Is Dead treats the Unities of Aristotle, alongside Plutarch’s Heroics, as conventions from which Finnegan’s shadow life is freed [D:161].

A:162; A:165; D:161

Ark (Noah's)Noah’s biblical vessel. In Casey’s school notebook, Hinnegan claims the Milesians were in Ireland before the Flood; Casey retorts that knowledge of this would require Noah to have taken two Irishmen aboard the Ark [A:162] [A:164-165]. Fundamentalers ask Zabotski and Duffey whether the Ark survives in Armenia under angelic guard. Their debate distinguishes belief in the Ark from the disputed identification of Ararat and from Duffey’s suggestion that the wooden remains were castles [MTM B9:280-281].

A:162; A:164-165; MTM B9:280-281

Ark-advocateParticipant in the Fundamentalers’ discussion who insists that one wooden structure in Ararat’s snow is the true Ark. He says people have entered it and brought objects back as proof [MTM B9:283].

MTM B9:283

Armageddon (Plains of Megiddo)In Finnegan’s prophecy, the destination to which Argo will carry the Antichrist for the last battle [MTM B13:453]. The culminating voyage reaches the seaport of Habonim, said to serve the Plains of Megiddo; the emerging Antichrist recognizes Casey as Prince Casimir [MTM B13:462]. These events belong to a shimmering possible future, and that future recedes again [MTM B13:451] [MTM B13:463] [MTM B13:468].

MTM B13:453; MTM B13:462; MTM B13:451; MTM B13:463; MTM B13:468

ArmeniaCountry and older regional name invoked in the debate about the Ark. A Fundamentaler locates the Ark in Armenia’s high mountains, while Zabotski questions whether the present place names identify the biblical country and mountain correctly [MTM B9:280-281]. Askandan calls Mount Ararat in his “own Armenia” the secluded center of the other blood [A:258]. These are the speakers’ identifications; Mount Ararat lies in modern Turkey, not in the present Republic of Armenia.

MTM B9:280-281; A:258

ArmenianEthnic designation applied to Askandanakandrian, or Asking Dan, the ancient comic dealer in distressed or “nervous” merchandise, associated with Chicago [A:256-258]. Margaret Stone is described as his niece and as embodying many ethnic lineages at once [MTM B7:212].

A:256-258; MTM B7:212

Armstrong'sName on cheese presses in the catalogue of household inscriptions remembered and appropriated by Melchisedech Duffey. Many of these “iron words” are stolen from other people’s minds; the surrounding memories range across Iowa, St. Louis and Boston [MTM B1:17].

MTM B1:17

ArrachtIrish word meaning a spectre or monster. In the account of the Dirty Five’s earlier lives, Finnegan is called Dionysus or Ulysses but also a Terras or Arracht [A:39].

A:39

ArrecifePort city on Lanzarote in the Canary Islands. Brunhilde calls there after Grand Canary and before Ifni, on the African coast [D:96] [D:101].

D:96; D:101

ArsonCasey jokingly offers arson and mayhem as pleasanter topics than Absalom Stein [A:67]. Henry’s subsequent “No arson, no mayhem” praises Sammy’s successful confidence trick after the boy obtains money and whisky; it is a comment on that performance, not a general account of the Dirty Five’s conduct [A:68].

A:67; A:68

Art Bijou (Duffey's Walk-In)Duffey’s New Orleans art business, established in the Pelican Press building after his move south in May 1946. The building also contains his pawn shop and the press’s common workroom [MTM B5:184] [MTM B6:190]. The related establishment includes a second-hand book and antique business; the press premises initially have cots and a cook stove for living quarters [A:116] [A:143]. Letitia’s affectionate catalogue joins the Art Bijou, bookstore, pawn shop, press, institute and soup kitchen [MTM B7:211]. Duffey conceives the Bijou as a flexible fortress defending the arts, while his creative stasis allows him to move back and forth through the years [MTM B6:199]. The painting The Resurrection of Count Finnegan arrives around the middle of the 1950s [MB:550]. Stein views it [MB:551]; Hilary Hilton buys it for twenty thousand dollars but leaves it hanging in the Bijou, visiting it at least annually [MB:553]. It remains on the walls for at least thirty years [MB:554]. Duffey also contemplates his own ashes on a table in the Bijou [MTM B1:6].

MTM B5:184; MTM B6:190; A:116; A:143; MTM B7:211; MTM B6:199; MB:550; MB:551; MB:553; MB:554; MTM B1:6

Art DealerProfession represented by buyers seeking Finnegan’s pictures [A:182]. A reputable dealer gives Finnegan van Ghi a standing commission for as many pictures as he can paint [A:191]. Duffey sees art dealing, together with pawnbroking, as his own vocation and a means of rebuilding the world [MTM B6:199].

A:182; A:191; MTM B6:199

Art-and-Elegance ShopLily Koch’s Chicago shop, where Duffey encounters Lily and her sister Letitia. Lily identifies Letitia as her partner in the establishment [MTM B3:90-91].

MTM B3:90-91

Artaguette ParkPark beside Sarkis Popotov’s residence in the changed New Orleans landscape. Margaret reports that Sarkis had lived beside buildings for forty years but can no longer remember what they were; now Artaguette Park occupies the neighboring space. The others tell him it will soon seem familiar [MTM B11:309].

MTM B11:309

Artemis (Diana)Greek goddess of the hunt, identified with the Roman Diana, whose imagery also associates her with the moon. The chapter “DIANA ARTEMIS” places Finnegan and Anastasia on Naxos [D:130]. By moonlight, Anastasia’s head resembles Diana’s [D:132]. The narrator specifies the light-bringing Artemis, comparing her head with a painted-marble image at Messene in Asclepius’s sanctuary, said to have been seen by Pausanias, and with a little cypress-wood Artemis on a temple step at Delos [D:133].

D:130; D:132; D:133

Artemis, Carlos CardinalCarlos Cardinal Artemis of Santa Cruz, one of the thirteen Cardinals pursued by John Mogul’s Track and Total. His designated double is Gilberto Levine y O’Brien of Rio [MB:579]. After Cardinal Ti’s death, Mogul’s next predicted killing is Artemis’s flaying [MB:583]. The account describes an arranged accident in Portugal: a cork-cutting machine, which the Cardinal has come to bless, strips off his skin; he dies shortly afterward [MB:591]. The identity of the victim and surviving double remains uncertain. Gilberto has copied Artemis’s natural skin markings with tattoos, adding personal marks. Monsignor X shows Duffey a purportedly cardinal’s skin aboard Argo, but neither can determine whose skin it is [MTM B13:451-452]. Separately, Finnegan has radiation-imprinted a masterwork on the inside of Artemis’s skin while he was alive and unaware. The account asks whether this picture is now inside the trophy skin cherished by Mogul or inside the living Gilberto’s skin [MB:591].

MB:579; MB:583; MB:591; MTM B13:451-452

Arthur (King)Legendary British king. X includes Arthur among figures such as Barbarossa, Alaric, Brian Boru and the Cid who await awakening or release from an enchanted trance-sleep [MTM B6:204-205].

MTM B6:204-205

ArtilleryIn Casey’s ninth proposed world, a workers’ revolution uses artillery in streets and parks to overthrow skyscrapers and factory smokestacks [A:160].

A:160

ArtistFinnegan is explicitly identified as a painter [D:37], and paints the voyages of Sindbad on Brunhilde’s barroom panels [D:59] [D:62]. Demetrio, the cantina proprietor, is himself an artist who makes Finnegan a belt and gives each of the two girls a silver ring [D:59]. Angela Cosquin’s father is praised as an exquisite artist and meticulous mapmaker [D:259]. X has also worked as a stage magician and Escape Artist under the name Great X-Capo [D:276].

D:37; D:59; D:62; D:259; D:276

Artist's tieTie, accompanied by a beret, that Duffey wears “for the trade” after opening a second-hand bookstore, art and antique shop, and hock-shop in New Orleans [A:143].

A:143

Artistic DegradationOne of the seven heads of the modern enemy named by Bascom Bagby [MTM B5:169].

MTM B5:169

Arutinov, ArpadName credited as the author of The Back-Door of History in the epigraph to the second chapter of The Devil Is Dead. The passage attacks abstraction and describes the intermingling of human and inhuman blood [D:26].

D:26

Ascend into the cityDuffey’s command to Finnegan after joining him in the burial cave: “Ascend into the city. There are doings that only you can do.” Their surrounding exchange combines lament, biblical prayer and calls to rise and act [MTM B12:374-375].

MTM B12:374-375

AscendereItalian verb meaning to ascend or go up, sung by Finnegan in the fragment beginning “Vecchia zimarra senti” [A:31]. The song is Colline’s farewell to his coat in Puccini’s La Bohème. Finnegan sings during the Australian Bay Hotel picnic: because the hotel forbids a lawn bonfire, the company gathers around a plate of burning charcoal [A:29-31].

A:31; A:29-31

AsclepiusGreek god of medicine and healing. The narrator compares Anastasia’s head with an image of Diana Artemis said to have been seen by Pausanias in Asclepius’s sanctuary at Messene: a little statue of painted marble with a natural expression [D:133].

D:133

AshesDuffey’s ashes exist alongside his surviving bones. After the slant-faced killers strip his flesh, the slack-faced men burn the flesh and viscera and place the ashes in a cigar canister formerly owned by a King of Spain. X takes custody, intending to return them to a living Duffey [MTM B13:442]. X shows them to Duffey in another encounter [MTM B6:203], and they stand on his table in the New Orleans Art Bijou [MTM B1:6]. They flame when Teresa touches them [MTM B7:233]. Their coexistence with Duffey alive exemplifies his disrupted sequence of death and life [MTM B13:445]. Fresh human ashes are also used for the test at the Decatur Street Opera House. They burn human hands and distinguish the participants by the resulting flames; these ashes are not identified as Duffey’s [MTM B11:347-348].

MTM B13:442; MTM B6:203; MTM B1:6; MTM B7:233; MTM B13:445; MTM B11:347-348

AsiaThe continental setting invoked when X calls Smyrna-born Papadiabolous I Asiatic [D:285]. Smyrna is modern İzmir on the Anatolian peninsula in Turkey. In Seaworthy’s dream of an Indian city, a wheel repeatedly falls from a cart carrying corpses; he calls this a defect of small Asian carts [D:72]. Duffey’s familiarity with Asian deserts helps him recognize that the Laughing Prince’s amoral desert is artificial [MTM B13:439].

AsiaticX’s description of Papadiabolous I, Gregory McIfreann, who was born in Smyrna. His twin, Papadiabolous II, was born in Cork and is called an Irishman. The distinction in this account turns on their different birthplaces, not an independently established difference in ancestry [D:285].

D:285

Asimov, IsaacScience-fiction writer and biochemist (1920-1992). The first chapter’s epigraph is credited to Asimov and imagines a groomed, well-dressed Neanderthal passing unnoticed on Fifth Avenue [D:9]. It introduces the question of ancient identities beneath ordinary appearances. During Finnegan’s transport about the other blood, Asimov is named with Mendel, Morgan, Galton and Painter in a rhetorical challenge about primordial ancestors reappearing after a thousand generations [D:214].

AskandanakandrianAskandan, or Asking Dan, the ancient comic Armenian dealer in distressed merchandise in Chicago and uncle of Margaret Stone [MTM B7:212]. He joins Finnegan and Hilary Hilton at dinner, bargaining over green fish sticks and unusable soap base. His habitual “I was just asking,” together with his name, explains the nickname [A:256]. He describes himself as a specialist in rehabilitating nervous merchandise and weevily grain, then tells Finnegan that a man he has crossed will have him followed and murdered [A:257]. After Finnegan names that man, Askandan says he knows him and knows about the other blood, whose secluded center he locates at Mount Ararat. He affirms that Finnegan is a Teras and has a soul. The narrator calls him a reader of souls and master of dialects and roles [A:258]. He joins Finnegan’s plot against Casey. When Casey finds himself naked on the road, Asking Dan offers a zoot suit, pointed shoes and an enormous hat, finally selling them on a promise of payment the next morning. Finnegan has bought the old suit for nine dollars to supply the stunt [A:258-261].

MTM B7:212; A:256; A:257; A:258; A:258-261

Asking DanNickname of Askandanakandrian, the little old dealer in distressed merchandise. It comes from his habitual “I was just asking” and the sound of his name [A:256]. He supplies the naked Casey with a zoot suit, pointed shoes and a large hat on credit [A:259-261]. See Askandanakandrian.

Aspects (1)In the passage attributed to Bascom Bagby’s Letters After I Am Dead, beings or manifestations inhabiting Iron Meadows. Bagby says that some aspects of the Argo Legend occupy one such meadow, unknown to either Duffey or God [MTM B5:177].

Aspects (2)Alternative persons or manifestations of a self. Doctor Saul Rafelson’s notes propose that Duffey’s other selves may be projections, captured independent people, or living images split off from him. Rafelson speculates that Duffey’s twelve independent creations express twelve aspects of him and explicitly distinguishes them from his shadows [MTM B4:146-147]. On Naxos, after Finnegan confesses his fear of the animal or other kindred within him, the Capuchin absolves his present person “in all its aspects” [D:119-120].

AssDonkey, in Joe’s comparison of Dopey’s second scream to that of an ass seized by a lion. Joe is recounting Dopey’s disappearance after Papa Devil entered the cabin [D:64].

They brandish knives and claim that their jealous Djinn is the only nocturnal Real Presence. Margaret answers with sweet talk and a claim that New Orleans is a truce city. She doubts whether such a sect exists: the three local Arabs attend Tulane and may merely be teasing her. She fears the Slant-Faced Men much more [MTM B7:225].

Niccolo Crotolus says he takes his first name from this Florentine “father,” whom he resembles in mind, and invokes the discussion of a prince’s faithfulness. He applies the distinction between appearing faithful and actually obeying to his employer’s contradictory instructions about a killing [A:279]. The passage echoes chapter XVIII of The Prince.

AtalantaSwift-footed huntress of Greek mythology. Teresa Piccone names Atalanta as one of her identities while recounting the ancient Argo company, adding that it is only a small part of who she is [MTM B7:234].

The source is the encyclical Divini Redemptoris, dated 19 March 1937, whose third paragraph identifies bolshevistic and atheistic Communism in these terms.

Atlantic OceanOcean crossed eastward by Brunhilde from Natal, Brazil, on January 18 to Freetown, Sierra Leone, on January 26. The narrator calls westward travel easier; Papa Devil enlarges this into a story of ancient Atlantic crossings whose eastward returns were almost impossible [D:89]. Anastasia’s account of mermaids denies that true mermaids live in the Atlantic, distinguishing northern sea-cows from them [D:34-35]. During the Atlantic crossing, Finnegan’s uncertain waking dream with Marie concerns immortality and her identification with Demeter and Persephone. Although they should be aboard ship in mid-ocean, the scene places them on a jungle beach [D:91-92].

He explains that he worked below in the engine room and passed free time with drink and old comic magazines, uncertain whether he had actually circumnavigated the globe [A:145].

A different auditorium, at Ursuline Academy, is the venue for Seven Roads, announced at the Ghost Coffee Shop and later shown in performance with Duffey playing his own role [MTM B10:293] [MTM B12:366].

Later club members are too young to have known Shire and Freddy Castle but still cherish the affidavit [A:11-13].

Aussie PrivateThe young Australian identity adopted by Private Gregory after escaping his long American officer career. In 1907 he had abandoned his century-long sergeancy, made himself about twenty, and obtained an appointment to the U.S. Military Academy. Investigators matched this young private’s fingerprints to those of the vanished elderly American colonel and kept him under observation [A:78-79].

B. Flat, BennyName Dotty gives successively to several suitors associated with the Jazz Magazine. The narrator explains their differing descriptions by the fact that they are different young men, all nice and swinging [MTM B7:212].

Babel, Tower ofBiblical tower whose language division Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni accepts literally. He describes the event to Hans as a catastrophic umlaut shift with vowel breaking and the shattering of sonants, applying philological terminology to the birth of dialects [A:213].

Babylonia SanctaHoly Babylon, the name John Giwa gives the newly risen Mooring-Stone land, formerly Babylonia Oceania or Oceanic Babylon. Its emergence combines volcanic activity with an effusion of grace in the account, and the conclave there elects Finnegan Pope [MB:597].

Back-BrainIn the epigraph attributed to Carmody Overlark’s Studies in the Imagination, an enlarged basal region of the skull associated with unconscious and subliminal activity, psychical phenomena, parapsychology and ghostliness. Overlark claims that the Neanderthal back-brain was six times the modern size and invokes Plato’s broad head, Homer’s bust and Aquinas’s massive back-brain as later examples [D:270-271]. His speculative lineage also includes Grimaldi and Aurignacian types and connects this anatomy with imagination [D:272].

Charlotte Mullens recalls that her mother Gloria involved her, while still a child, in such schemes against male callers, fetching witnesses and threatening imprisonment to extract payment [MTM B3:87]. In Past Graduate, Duffey says that Acastus of Iolcus used a badger game against Peleus and discusses Hilary and Mary Jean’s attempted reverse badger game against Casey. He suggests that the old Acastus incident may itself have been the reverse variety [PG:535-536].

Bagby, BascomDuffey’s St. Louis friend and business associate, later his brother-in-law through marriage to Mary Louise [MTM B2:62] [MTM B2:73]. A cabinetmaker with a shop next to Duffey’s premises, Bagby proposes that they work together [MTM B2:46]. He also fights professionally and introduces Duffey to boxing managers [MTM B2:50]. He is a humorously rough-looking man with beetling brows and belly, a “baroque” or flawed pearl, and a slob whose shanty mind contains the accumulated life of whole nations [MTM B2:43] [MTM B2:61-62]. He frequents Chestnut Street fleshpots and fights brutally, at times leaving others or himself for dead. His violent political, economic and religious opinions include condemnation of most local clergy as Judas Priests; he attends Mass across town at St. Malachy’s, which he considers nearest to the true faith [MTM B2:62-63]. He composes and whistles the Gadarene Swine Song [MTM B2:48]. Duffey calls him his dark object, uncleansed stables and another part of himself [MTM B2:73] [MTM B5:155]. His weekly letters offer Duffey intelligence and compassion, even during Duffey’s seven hidden years [MTM B4:145]. After Duffey and Letitia attend his St. Louis funeral, letters continue arriving every Monday for many years, by a means the narrative leaves mysterious [MTM B8:237]. Later letters discuss life outside ordinary time and give Duffey advice from beyond death [MTM B8:248] [MTM B10:302].

MTM B2:62; MTM B2:73; MTM B2:46; MTM B2:50; MTM B2:43; MTM B2:61-62; MTM B2:62-63; MTM B2:48; MTM B5:155; MTM B4:145; MTM B8:237; MTM B8:248; MTM B10:302

Bagby, Mary Louise (Byrne)Duffey’s sister, almost certainly his stepsister, two years older than he is [MTM B2:54]. She bears the surname Byrne from the kindred or supposed kindred who raised her. Red-haired and blue-eyed, with large strong hands and swinging shoulders, she is described as his anima made animate and the flame-red part of his soul. The narrative calls her intelligent, proud, friendly and ghostly, and associates her strength with the royal bovine or sacred cow of chthonic goddesses [MTM B2:55]. Duffey has appropriated much of her St. Louis experience into his own childhood [MTM B1:16] [MTM B2:54]. She says that her own attributes and talismans arrange coincidences, including his meeting with Bagby and the old horse barn, and that she created Beth Keegan, though creating persons is less easy for her than for Duffey [MTM B2:61]. She likes Bagby despite his failings and eventually marries him [MTM B2:63] [MTM B2:73]. After Letitia’s death she flies from St. Louis to the wake in New Orleans [MTM B8:254]. In Duffey’s final St. Louis visit she is called Dame Bagby, weighty and ponderous but still merry. She is present at his death and anticipates their reunion [MTM B12:384-385] [MTM B12:388].

MTM B2:54; MTM B2:55; MTM B1:16; MTM B2:61; MTM B2:63; MTM B2:73; MTM B8:254; MTM B12:384-385; MTM B12:388

Bagby, Mary Louise (née Byrne)Earlier heading treated Byrne as a demonstrated birth surname, although the novel says it came from those who raised her. See Bagby, Mary Louise (Byrne).
BaghdadCity in Iraq. The epigraph attributed to Moisha El-Gazma calls Bassorah the port of Baghdad and questions whether Bassorah could have been a port or even a town [D:53]. In the narrator’s account of Hans Schultz’s encounter with Cosmopolis, New York exceeds the combined imaginative promise of Baghdad, Paris, Heidelberg and Lyonesse [A:224]. The Bassorah epigraph also opens Sindbad, the Thirteenth Voyage, whose Baghdad is an elaborate, internally conflicting magical city. In Sindbad, Baghdad is a mirage or cloud city built in a single night, its name meaning the Last City Built by Magic in Old Kentauron. Essindibad’s account places it on the east bank of the Tigris, the seventh city on a site previously occupied by Babel, Gade, Babylon, Burj Aqarquf, Seleucia and Cispon. Its thousand gates lead to a thousand suburbs, each with a fair, circus and trade bazaar; a hundred suburbs have slave markets, and each has numerous theatres and nightclubs. Central Baghdad reserves such large communal entertainments to its Grand Bazaar, Grand Fair and Grand Circus. Its roof-gardens, salons and musical clubs coexist with high-altitude dives and subterranean meeting places in cellars, cisterns and sewers, which Harun is rumored to frequent. Its citizens are said to love novelties. Much of the city’s original magic has become substantial, though breaks in its surfaces expose depths and even blue sky below. Trams and taxis are anachronistic survivals, and a partly credible railroad runs almost to Constantinople; the citizen who describes it doubts the Boy-Caliph’s complete belief in his own creation. An inserted Kerney quotation describes square brick-and-bitumen walls with twenty-five brass gates per side, parenthetically suggesting two hundred and fifty instead; an adjacent Arabian Nights quotation evokes the City of Brass. The narrator describes bedrock under Baghdad and an artificial electrum sky, which Al-Amin later removes. Mamun, however, says that its stones and splendor are illusions: beneath Lady Narkos’s narcotic enchantment lie mud, poor bricks, wattle, oversized mud palaces and sand-and-pebble roads continually sinking into mud. Harun, in Mamun’s account, is its principal maker of illusion. Named places include Blacksmith Street, Cork and Bottle Street, the botanical gardens and their weeping olive groves, the High Place of the Hanging Gibbets, the Royal Archives, the hundred-door main treasury and the Fountain of Life-Bubbles. The bubbles can give a condemned person a full and pleasant ninety-year life in ten seconds, and uneasy observers call them Devil’s Gifts. Scheherazade calls Baghdad a weak place in Gaea-Earth, where the imprisoned devils of other worlds can emerge through thin earth or rivers. She regards its magic as black and tainted; Blue Moon disagrees about the taint. Lady Narkos inhabits narcotic cookies, smoke and powders, while size-changing Ifrits move through the city. Rival spies dispute the nature and location of the gates of hell, including the supposed main underground gates near Baghdad. Dragons carry swallowed demons out of confinement, accounting in the Spy-Bird’s report for their fire-breathing, and deliver them to spacecraft. Harun defends these devils as his friends in the Three Worlds; his delightful aura briefly reverses into horror. He also claims that the citizens he transformed into dogs can never be changed back. Citizen Heifritz says that Harun’s sons moved the capital to Merv and left Baghdad an innocuous ornament housing their Caliph-Emeritus father. The novel calls its present Moslem Year 191 and Christian Year 813, the Year of Three Caliphs. Al-Amin’s brief reign brings public works, irrigation and navigation projects, musicians’ guild recognition, a performing-arts institution, slave-freeing laws, public distribution of treasury wealth and removal of the artificial sky. His sanitation programme targets foul sewers and a stranded whale whose odor reaches Baghdad. Mamun succeeds after killing him in their duel and bears the Mark of Cain at his throat. He defends the continuing need for Narkos’s illusions, orders the construction of spacecraft to pursue the escaping devils, and welcomes the prospect of their occupying themselves in Carouse Town east of Baghdad. Scheherazade’s account of that town mixes events already happening with her anticipated fiction. She later imprisons Mamun in a bottle; their negotiated arrangement allows time for rule, marriage, entertainment and soldierly carousing, leaving three hours of daily confinement. This negotiated account differs from Mamun’s opening claim that he leaves his cell for only one hour a day. (Sindbad, the Thirteenth Voyage, PDF pp. 5, 10, 22-25, 27, 29, 56, 65, 76-78, 84-89, 112, 116-117, 120, 126-128, 132-133, 136, 138, 142-148).

BaitLure for fish. Oliver Greenflag explains that the bait for Puff Fish is a frequency and that frequency itself would have to be altered to make the fish unavailable [MTM B13:418-419]. Honeybucket Kincaid operates the apparatus that can attract them [MTM B13:420].
