Bait BoxMetaphor for Sebastian Hilton’s repertoire of calculated come-ons that lure bullies into attacking him. His apparent weakness, tears and simpering conceal his ability to defeat them [MTM B1:22].

MTM B1:22

Bait BucketDuffey’s metaphor for the frequency that attracts Puff Fish. He enters the Main Frequency Modulator while Biloxi prevents interference, then declares that he has abolished the frequency in past, present and future. He insists that the apparatus still works perfectly; it is the possibility of attracting Puff Fish that he has destroyed [MTM B13:420].

MTM B13:420

Bait HouseThe pleasant, shady building where Finnegan and Doll Delancy drink beer after fishing in Florida. It is long and low, with whitewashed rafters and water moving beneath and sometimes through its floor planks. Photographs of unnamed notable anglers and their catches form a comic caste hierarchy on its walls. There a man from Minneapolis tells Finnegan that a left-footed man has been asking for him [D:182].

D:182

BakeliteSynthetic resin named in Casey’s high-school notebook XVI, which says that it is made from “formaldehide and gum arabic” [A:163]. That is the notebook’s formulation; Bakelite is actually a phenol-formaldehyde resin.

A:163

Balbo VII, GaetanEarlier heading shortened the printed name Gaetano to Gaetan. See Balbo VII, Gaetano.
Balbo VII, GaetanoThe heir expected to become San Simeon’s Mad King Gaetano VII. In the Balbo dynasty a prince leaves home at nineteen and returns at thirty-nine as Mad King, allowing his father to become Mad King Emeritus and his grandfather to die. Gaetano VII instead becomes a high churchman at thirty-nine and does not return. His father must continue as Mad King and his grandfather cannot obtain the relief of death [MB:558-559].

MB:558-559

BaliEarlier heading obscured the fact that the cited voyage catalogue names a sea. See Bali Sea.
Bali SeaThe Bali Sea, included in the catalogue of seas sailed by the Argo [MTM B13:406].

MTM B13:406

Balinese Room, TheHistoric Galveston nightclub on a pier. Dutch Duquesne boasts of earning a hundred dollars a night in tips as a waiter at the Balinese Room, or possibly another swank place at the end of a pier. Mary, who works the clubs, exposes him as a kitchen boy who cleans fish and opens oysters [D:221].

D:221

BalkansRegion of southeastern Europe, printed “Balkins” in Casey’s editorial attack on The Bark. He accuses the magazine of supporting clerical-reactionary elements in Poland, Hungary and the Balkans [A:130].

A:130

Bally AlleyPlace where Finnegan proposes a midnight stroll, only for Herman Hercules to warn that their enemies are there too. Hercules recommends the concealed harbor express, a route under buildings and through sewers, cisterns and piers, to reach the Argo [MB:587].

MB:587

BalmOintment the Devil reportedly uses on the galls left by his neck, wrist and ankle shackles. In Zabotski’s radio news, the newly released Devil buys ten kilograms of balm from a nearby pharmacy [MTM B6:191].

MTM B6:191

BaltimoreCity where Joe Cross once worked in a raw bar [D:40]. Finnegan and Doll Delancy check the heavy suitcase through to Baltimore by bus, but leave the bus at Philadelphia, cross town by taxi and complete their own journey by train [D:171-172]. Separately, Charlotte Mullens says that she saw the Devil at the Royal Rogues and Graceful Swindlers Convention in Baltimore [MTM B7:217].

D:40; D:171-172; MTM B7:217

Baltimore busBus boarded by Doll Delancy and Finnegan in Newark, with the heavy suitcase checked through to Baltimore. They leave the bus at Philadelphia and continue to Baltimore by train, leaving the luggage to complete the bus journey [D:169] [D:171-172].

D:169; D:171-172

Balzac, Honoré deFrench novelist whom Casey Szymansky intends to surpass as the American Balzac, making Balzac in turn the French Szymansky [A:158]. Gautier the goat-man reads Les Contes Drolatiques to his goats and says that Balzac appeals to goats and to the goat in man [A:198].

A:158; A:198

Bam (palm wine)Palm wine drunk by Finnegan and Joseph, the Haussa boy, in Freetown; the available edition prints its name as “barn.” Finnegan becomes drunk, while Joseph remains unaffected. Joseph proposes moving on to gin and then discussing business [D:93]. Their subsequent conversation leads to the diamond-smuggling arrangement [D:94-95].

D:93; D:94-95

Banana NoseFinnegan’s conspicuous nose, described as banana-shaped when he first studies his reflection [A:1] and as a bugle nose in his comic-mask face [A:6]. In the painting of his future Count persona, the same banana nose has acquired nobility and distinction [MTM B12:368].

A:1; A:6; MTM B12:368

Banana-nosed bratDotty Yekouris’s name for Finnegan as she watches him join Vincent, Hans and Casey after their difficult conversation. Her affection is mixed with frustration at his failure to understand what she offers him [A:93].

A:93

Bananas onlyThe only food Falo and Nauti can offer Finnegan and Vincent at their newly opened cabaret. They charge a peso a dozen because they have no change, although the bananas cost them nothing. Boxes serve as table and chairs, with chunks of wood providing additional seats [A:64-65].

A:64-65

Bandicoot Enterprises LimitedCompany whose president is Bandicoot Blackstone. In the accelerating family succession, he says that he will remain chairman of the various boards while his son John, as First Executive, runs the businesses [MTM B9:287-288].

MTM B9:287-288

BanditsThe supposed thieves of a bottle of Finnegan’s rum while he sleeps near the buffalo’s capital. The narrator offers bandits as the explanation only because the alternative would be to believe that the buffalo stole it [A:206].

A:206

BandolierPart of Casey’s elaborate military costume for his planned appearance as the Leader. He is belted and bandoliered in a scarlet tunic and shako when Letitia intercepts him [MTM B4:117].

MTM B4:117

BandsMusical ensembles include the three bands playing military and inspirational music for the Leader’s promised appearance in Henry Horner Park [MTM B4:116-117], and the Rounders’ String Band, in which Duffey takes over the banjo [MTM B2:51-52]. String, horn and flute bands also appear in the narrator’s catalogue of popular arts damaged by the new degradation of culture [MTM B6:207].

MTM B4:116-117; MTM B2:51-52; MTM B6:207

Bands (Rubber)Rubber bands binding the paper in Finnegan’s chrysus suitcase. The thirty-six thousand pieces are packed in bundles of one hundred, arranged three bundles by six and stacked twenty bundles deep [D:166].

D:166

Bang-headsThe sophisticated headaches suggested by the drinks depicted in the third room of Elroy Redheart’s miniature artwork. Glinty hints evoke the drinks, while hot artificial colors and cheap plastic figures express the artificial sins and feverish opulence of the scenes [MTM B7:223].

MTM B7:223

BanjoInstrument Duffey takes up in the Rounders’ String Band and continues playing throughout his life [MTM B2:51-52]. He carries a banjo and straw hat to the Duffeys’ puppet shows, using local mice as living performers and ending the show with tunes [MTM B4:134]. When asked whether a banjo suits his role as a Patriarch, he offers to play his recorder flute instead [MTM B9:266].

MTM B2:51-52; MTM B4:134; MTM B9:266

BankFinancial institution invoked in several episodes. Saxon Seaworthy proposes finding a bank after he and Finnegan recover enough over drinks, promising to buy Finn shoes when he has funds [D:10]; he later cites his bank balance as evidence of his philosophical success [D:82]. Finnegan makes a close-out bank call before leaving his New York portraitist career [A:193]. Hans visits banks among his business errands [A:97], and Adrian Hilton is identified as a banker [MTM B4:123]. Duffey must discover the location and number of the bank’s safety-deposit box so that Charlotte can recover the Gonof stash [MTM B3:84-86]. Mike Melchiades tells Duffey that, after his wife leaves, he empties their joint account and refuses her a withdrawal despite knowing that she supplied much of the money [MTM B4:142-143].

D:10; D:82; A:193; A:97; MTM B4:123; MTM B3:84-86; MTM B4:142-143

Bank BuildingBuilding containing the safety-deposit box, described as a walk-in, holding the Gonof stash sought by Charlotte Mullens. Duffey first recovers the key’s form and later the bank and box details during the episode Charlotte calls a psychosomatic trance [MTM B3:84-86].

MTM B3:84-86

Bank Robber and BrigandOne of the adventure subjects listed among Gautier’s surviving books at Harlow House. His goats have eaten much of the library, leaving the old American “Blood and Thunder” romances he loves [A:198].

A:198

BannerPennants and flags on the Navicula Petri in Henry’s dream. Their mottoes include In hoc signo vincet (printed “Ih hoc signo vincet”); Finnegan’s unfinished Nisi esses sollicitus, scratched out and replaced with “If you can’t be careful, be good”; Ubicumque fuerit corpus illic congregabuntur et aquilas; and the sequence Tu es Petrus, Portae inferi non prevalebunt, tibi dabo claves regni. Their devices include a Lamb, Greek Cross, Fish, Six-Pointed Star, Woman, Serpent and Crescent Moon [A:44-45].

A:44-45

Bannon, TerryOne of the Forty Scribbling Seamen who succeed Terry Cork in supplying The Plimsoll Line for The Bark and work for the Seaman’s Paper during their intervals ashore. The other named Terrys are Anderson, Jamil and Renier; the collective name also belongs to a song composed by Dotty [MTM B7:213].

MTM B7:213

BantryTown in County Cork, Ireland, where Finnegan says he once spent a day and a half unloading cargo. He offers this brief visit as a rebuttal when Doll says that he has never been in Ireland [D:192].

D:192

BaptismThe sacramental rite and several less literal uses of its language. Finnegan teases Theresa that the baptismal salt flamed against her brimstone nature and that the font cracked; she replies that any of a dozen witches could have cracked it [A:108]. In their uncertain alternate life, Theresa remembers baptizing Chiara, Rafaello and Theresa Anna in a known parish church; Archipelago explicitly calls them her children by Finnegan, distinct from her children by Vincent [A:203-204]. A later More Than Melchisedech passage gives the same three names to Theresa and Vincent’s younger children [MTM B12:385]. X says that Katie Noonan’s son was baptized Columkill and received the surname Gregorovitch through his adoptive father [D:279]. The talking oak in the Argo’s wheel claims to have been baptized in the spirit and to be speaking in tongues [MTM B13:460].

A:108; A:203-204; MTM B12:385; D:279; MTM B13:460

BaptistJohn the Baptist appears among the sacred figures aboard the Navicula Petri in Henry’s dream, alongside the Apostles, Stephen, Paul, Linus, Clement and Cletus [A:45]. Separately, George Koran’s account of the Majesty’s speaking itinerary includes a Baptist audience in Waco [MTM B8:244].

A:45; MTM B8:244

Baptist's HeadRelic included among the Argo Masters’ discoveries: John the Baptist’s head remains in good flesh, with uncut, growing hair and beard each more than a hundred feet long [MTM B13:421-422].

MTM B13:421-422

BarDrinking establishments recur throughout the narratives. Finnegan and Seaworthy wait outside a bar opposite a graveyard, then enter for beer [D:10] [D:12]. Anastasia works at the adjoining club and later tends the tiny four-stool bar on the Brunhilde [D:13] [D:16] [D:22]. The Cadillac Bar is dingy outside but rich within and favored by Texans [D:58]; Finnegan’s friends nickname a clean Antillean establishment Sloppy Joe’s although its actual name is uncertain between Imperial Bar and Royal [D:235]. Finnegan has frequented New Orleans oyster bars [D:40], meets Francine in a Chicago bar [A:181], and provokes near-riots with his dog-housebreaking product in Buffalo taverns [A:189-190]. The Dirty Five drink with Captain Guiterrez at the Buffalo Bar [A:66]. Duffey’s youthful enterprise includes a whisky bar operated by John Rattigan [MTM B1:27], and his later Rounders’ premises also sell whisky [MTM B2:44]. Kate’s Neanderthal Bar in Biloxi interests Eva as a place to meet her own people [MTM B13:407]. In Trinali’s poem, the Brimstone Combo plays at a saloon on Beelzebub and Hell-Raiser Streets near Iniquity Square [A:235].

D:10; D:12; D:13; D:16; D:22; D:58; D:235; D:40; A:181; A:189-190; A:66; MTM B1:27; MTM B2:44; MTM B13:407; A:235

BAR (Browning Automatic Rifle)Browning Automatic Rifle. Conrad Stone Hackenschmidt uses a BAR to coerce the Conclave into voting for a straw-man and kills Stockton Stone Crocker when he votes for Cardinal Hedayat instead [MB:567]. BAR fire is heard during the Naxos violence, and the boy guiding Finnegan warns that the men aboard the Brunhilde have such weapons and could shoot his head off if he approaches [D:143-145].

MB:567; D:143-145

Bar-boysThe Cadillac Bar staff, dressed in white jackets among chrome and crystal furnishings. Most of the customers there are Texans [D:58].

D:58

Bar-flyOne of the kinds of acquaintances Finnegan recruits, along with show-girls, to populate his Manhattan art exhibition as Gregory van Ghi. He coaches them in arty remarks so that the show will appear well attended [A:191].

A:191

Barataria BayLouisiana coastal bay where the young Henry Salvatore spends weeks trapping muskrats. The novel prints the name Baratarria Bay [A:124].

A:124

BarbaraSaint Barbara, appearing with Catherine as a pair of sea-urchin-like figures aboard the Navicula Petri in Henry’s dream [A:45]. In her traditional martyr legend, her wealthy pagan father Dioscorus confines her in a tower; she rejects marriage, receives Christian baptism, refuses to abandon her faith under torture and is beheaded by her father, who is then killed by lightning. The tradition also recounts miraculous aid during her suffering. Venerated among the Fourteen Holy Helpers, she is invoked against lightning and sudden death and as patron of artillerymen, miners and others exposed to explosive danger. Her art commonly includes a tower, sometimes with three windows, and her customary feast is December 4. Her life lacks secure early historical documentation, though veneration is attested from the seventh century. Her feast was removed from the General Roman Calendar in 1969, while devotion to her continued.

A:45

BarbariansTrinali Peterson’s derisive name for people who dine under electric light. Her insistence on candlelight also masks the fact that her own electricity has been cut off for nonpayment [A:228]. The More Than Melchisedech narrator uses a separate comic ethnic contrast at the wedding, describing distinguished Irish and Italian guests together with a sprinkling of people of barbarian races [MTM B5:183].

A:228; MTM B5:183

BarbarossaFrederick I, the Holy Roman Emperor. Mr. X includes Barbarossa among the leaders supposedly sleeping in enchantment or imprisonment while their subjects await their return [MTM B6:204-205]. Duffey claims to have attended Kings’ Conclaves with him, Solomon, Saul, Ptolemy, Chandragupta, Nebuchadnezzar, Hsien, Stephen of Hungary and Conrad the Second [MTM B5:166].

MTM B6:204-205; MTM B5:166

Barbary ApeOne of the waterfront establishments in Melchisedech’s catalogue of memories aboard the Argo. It is listed near the Fanged Fish, Octopus Joe’s, the Sulu Ritz and other places of maritime hospitality [MTM B13:407].

MTM B13:407

Barbary FlamesFlames in which the speaker proposes to scorch himself in the travel poem opening Finnegan’s chapter: “And get myself scorched in the Barbary flames” [A:171-172].

A:171-172

BarbudaIsland Ignacio calls good for nothing in this world. In his account it belongs to a group of five Leeward islands including St. Kitts, prompting Finnegan’s theory that each five-island group has a rogue island. Finnegan, not Ignacio, responds “Barbuda, my brother!” [A:272].

A:272

Barbuda IslandSee Barbuda: the island Ignacio identifies as the useless member of his five-island Leeward group [A:272].

A:272

BargeA Pattenite Fundamentaler’s name for Noah’s vessel while comparing his faction’s chronology with Zabotski’s Pristine History of the World. He places its flotation and the Floodtide Catastrophes about 2800 BC, while noting that Zabotski does not quite call it Noah’s barge [MTM B9:278]. Barges also carry paper in the H and H H Magazine editor’s promised continuation of the Zabotski-house account [MTM B9:288]. Finnegan says he has worked on river barge-trains [A:99].

MTM B9:278; MTM B9:288; A:99

BargirlAnastasia Demetriades, who seeks the bartender’s berth and then opens the bar aboard the Brunhilde [D:16] [D:22]. An unnamed bargirl serves Finnegan and Seaworthy Texas beer at the first bar they enter; it is the only beer cold enough to be available, although Seaworthy dislikes it [D:12].

D:16; D:22; D:12

Bark, TheJournal printed by the Pelican Press in New Orleans as the fellowship’s work of rebuilding the world. Paid printing subsidizes a publication intended to reach roughly twenty-five thousand people who influence public opinion [A:118]. Henry proposes the name from his dream of an endangered boat, and Finnegan draws that boat for the masthead. Its Seven Pillars of Righteousness are Henry, Duffey, Stein, Dotty, Hans, Gabrielovitch, and Finnegan [A:121–122]. Casey attacks the journal and its personnel in The Crock, including a complaint about the ship’s rigging [A:128–131].

Dotty and Mary Virginia largely run the journal after Mary leaves her father’s trucking firm; Duffey contributes to both it and the separate Investigator [A:143]. After Dotty disappears, Letitia becomes editor, loses some paying print accounts, and keeps The Bark going with private funds [MTM B8:238–239]. In “Great Day in the Morning” it is scheduled for Thursday or whenever it appears, and Duffey’s earlier article has anticipated the disastrous new condition [GD:490] [GD:492–493].

A:118; A:121–122; A:128–131; A:143; MTM B8:238–239; GD:490; GD:492–493

Barkers' MalletHochstapler’s own small mallet or gavel, used by the Wool-Hat to kill him over less than three hundred dollars. The killer says he meant only to strike him and receives a year and a day. Hochstapler is Betty’s father [A:217].

A:217

BarleyGrain Duffey buys for the Big Pot: a hundred bushels, filling a storage alcove six feet deep [A:133]. The opening creation conceit says barley and hops were made on the third day, so beer is already available [A:1]; Toohey’s, Tooth’s and K.B. Lager are named on the next page [A:2].

A:133; A:1; A:2

Barley and hopsBeer ingredients already available in Archipelago’s opening creation conceit because, the narrator says, barley and hops were made on the third day [A:1].

A:1

Barley soupSoup served from Duffey’s Big Pot, which he intends to keep boiling forever and which the narrator says has already boiled for at least a quarter-century. He begins with water and barley and offers bowls to the poor at a cent apiece [A:133]. Additions include donated salt and onions, rough fish, seasonal produce from Henry’s Cajun cousins, X’s dead horse, an occasional bony old cow, game, alligator-tail stew, potatoes, greens, turnips, nine kinds of fish, leeks and garlic. Finnegan and Dotty once contribute seventy pounds of honey from four bee trees; Regal brewery supplies a keg of beer weekly. The operation reaches about three hundred meals daily, with someone on duty around the clock [A:134].

A:133; A:134

BarmYeast foam from fermenting malt liquor. Mr. X tells Doll that, after Finnegan’s crisis and a briefing, their instructions will work in him like a barrel of barm, and they will meet him again the following year. The fighting binge follows this prediction [D:190-191].

D:190-191

BarmaidDotty Yekouris worked as a barmaid before the war, with Finnegan as her customer [A:96]; Casey’s hostile editorial calls her the Beautiful Barmaid and ridicules the supposed limits of her drink repertoire [A:129]. Anastasia Demetriades becomes bargirl aboard the Brunhilde [D:16] [D:22], while an unnamed bargirl serves Finnegan and Seaworthy Texas beer in the opening bar [D:12]. Soft-Talk Susie Kutz tends the Old Wooden Ship’s bar and is, the narrator says, its sole actual angel unaware, submitting kindly exaggerated reports to the Lord [D:216].

A:96; A:129; D:16; D:22; D:12; D:216

BarnFinnegan and Howland stay in an abandoned barn during their northward travels; Howland chants his five-gophers song as they lie in a hay loft [A:179]. Duffey buys a rickety horse barn or livery stable on Walnut Street in St. Louis [MTM B2:40], provides beds, food, drink and horseshoe pitching there, and eventually develops it into the Rounders’ Club [MTM B2:47] [MTM B2:49]. Giulio receives hospitality and a talisman there [MTM B2:42-43] [MTM B2:47]. In Finnegan’s playful account of Greek astronomy, a barn is one imagined measure of the sun’s or moon’s size [D:132].

A:179; MTM B2:40; MTM B2:47; MTM B2:49; MTM B2:42-43; D:132

Barn Owl (Giant)Finnegan’s comparison for the buffalo seen from the front in their ancestral city. He comically insists on a precise species distinction, though no listener is present. The narrator tentatively locates the ancestral city in Frio County [A:205-206].

A:205-206

Barnaby, Don (Duke of Moule)One of Finnegan’s three companions in the Basse-Terre terrestrial Paradise, with Charles Le Marin and Johnny Duckwalk [D:233-236]. Duke of Moule is only his nickname. He and Duckwalk chase the island girls while Finnegan and Le Marin do so less enthusiastically [D:236]. His arrival seems to Finnegan like a third presence gradually coalescing around him and Le Marin, but the narrator calls this an impression [D:258-259]. He reminds Finnegan of another Don, apparently Don Lewis, yet is larger, rougher and fearless; Finnegan regards him as a lecher, a fugitive for homicide and a genuine poet who might have ghostly extensions [D:249]. He tells the extravagant story of Madame Le Mourcheor’s Juju Joy Pills and the many lives he experiences in her garden [D:248-252]. A voice other than his twice speaks from his hammock while his even breathing continues: first asking Finnegan to repay Anastasia fifty dollars, then pleading for rescue after three years dead in the sand [D:238] [D:256]. He slips into memories of the Brunhilde and Manuel, then denies that he was there [D:253] [D:265]. Restless, he leaves Paradise promising to return; Angela says he will not, and reports his claim that he has not been the other Don for several years [D:265].

D:233-236; D:236; D:258-259; D:249; D:248-252; D:238; D:256; D:253; D:265

Barnacle (Holy)The Holy Barnacle and the Pearl Beyond Price, one of the announced topics of the Society for Creative History, also called the Royal Pop Historians. Margaret Stone reports the program and decides to attend lest the group discard something she wants to preserve [MTM B11:307].

MTM B11:307

Barnacle Remover (Dr. Stein's)Dr. Stein’s Barnacle Remover, one of the drinks Absalom Stein mixes at the Bay Hotel picnic with gin and ice. His other inventions are the Flying Steinmetz, Steinheim Stinger, Stein Zombie, Stein Collins, Ein-Stein and Stein Julip [A:29-30].

A:29-30

BarnaclesImage of accreted material obscuring history in the Royal Pop Historians’ opening speech. The speaker claims that misplaced times and incidents can be recovered from barrows or from beneath the cement of barnacles, freed from their incrustations and revised as events still happening in the present [MTM B11:323-324].

MTM B11:323-324

BarnardOne of the twenty Stone boys whom Margaret Stone identifies as first cousins in four families, all living within three blocks of Duffey’s former Chicago bookstore [MTM B4:112].

MTM B4:112

BarneyCommercial fisherman and resident regular at the Old Wooden Ship [D:215-216]. He, Shrimp Boat Gordon and Tom inspect the sea and sky and smell the air each morning, each asking what the others think; more often than not they declare the day unsuitable for fishing and remain to drink [D:220].

D:215-216; D:220

BaronTitle Finnegan assigns to Gottfried von Guggenheim, one of the named hundred-dollar bills he keeps as the financial cushion beneath his adventures. The sequence also includes Aloysius, Hernandez, Jose-Ramires and the current Miguel [D:19-20].

D:19-20

BaroqueDescription of Bascom Bagby as a flawed pearl, combining extraordinary mental depth and scope with slovenliness and turbulent habits [MTM B2:62]. In the transformed world, Cyrus Roundhead says that the people of the thunder dimension woke to consciousness when the world was already in its baroque phase [MTM B11:350].

MTM B2:62; MTM B11:350

BarracadedThe source’s spelling of barricaded in Trinali Peterson’s account of resisting eviction. She had burned her stock of driftwood after the heat was cut off; while barricaded inside, she received food from Lupido in a basket lowered from her window [A:229].

A:229

BarracksTom Shire and Freddy Castle’s military quarters, with a wet canteen. Their elaborate hoax makes Finnegan and Vincent believe Americans are barred: they disguise the two in winter tunics and digger hats, cut Vincent’s hair, rehearse an Australian accent and take them over back fences. At the canteen, orderly sergeant Bushmaster recognizes and welcomes them, nearly spoiling the joke [A:10-12].

A:10-12

Barracuda Bar (Biddy's)Biddy’s Barracuda Bar, one of the waterfront establishments in Melchisedech’s catalogue of memories aboard the Argo, alongside the Fanged Fish, Salty Dog’s Shack-Up House and many others [MTM B13:407].

MTM B13:407

Barrel HouseA kind of drinking establishment in the narrator’s account of New Orleans nightlife continuing into daylight: a party can go straight from Breakfast at Brennan’s to a barrel house or night club and find entertainment [MTM B7:219].

MTM B7:219

Barrels of WineThree barrels, with additional jugs, that Papa Piccone plans to provide for Vincent and Theresa’s wedding reception. Maurine tells Monica that he refuses to let people remember a shortage two thousand years later, as at Cana [A:105].

A:105

BarrensPart of the wild New Jersey back country where Finnegan meets Gautier the goat-man. The narrator describes low mountains, high seas, hard sands, soft rocks and unusually isolated inhabitants [A:193-194]. Gautier and his goats often occupy the abandoned Harlow House; although many Barrens shacks are haunted, the narrator explicitly leaves that house’s haunting uncertain, and Finnegan never visits it [A:196-197].

A:193-194; A:196-197

BarrierFinnegan’s name for the division he feels between himself and humanity, despite the affection of his friends; he says he touched his father only briefly and years after his father’s death [D:90]. Duffey encounters a barrier to a valid future on the normal track of time [MTM B10:290]. On Dumaine Street he later meets the sign “The Future Begins Right Here,” solid to him though others pass through it; calling on his giants and his qualified lordship of time, he breaks through the barrier and figurative breakers into clear water, jumping a year ahead while the world also advances [MTM B12:358].

D:90; MTM B10:290; MTM B12:358

BarroomThe Brunhilde’s small bar, where Anastasia serves drinks until Papa Devil orders it closed [D:22]. Seaworthy commissions Finnegan to paint its panels with the Voyages of Sindbad [D:59-60]. Anastasia becomes the dead wife of the fourth voyage and Marie the wife of the seventh; Papa Devil is proposed as the man-eating ogre and William Gerecke as the Old Man of the Sea [D:61-62]. Unable to draw Papa Devil’s apparent face convincingly, Finnegan discovers that it is a living mask and paints the concealed face; the picture later matches the face of the dead man whom the others cannot identify [D:62-63]. After remembering the burial, he paints the buried man’s face together with another [D:77]. The later explanation distinguishes the dead Papadiabolous painted atop another corpse from a separate dead figure with the current Papa Devil’s true face; their meanings are understood by different observers [D:85-86].

D:22; D:59-60; D:61-62; D:62-63; D:77; D:85-86

BartenderSee Barmaid, for Dotty Yekouris, Anastasia Demetriades, the unnamed woman serving Texas beer, and Soft-Talk Susie Kutz [A:96] [D:12] [D:16] [D:22] [D:216].

A:96; D:12; D:16; D:22; D:216

BartholomewOne of three possible names, with Thomas and Jude, for the tippling Apostle in the old Italian legend Show Boat says her father remembers imperfectly. The Apostle finishes leftover wine, bottles of wine are found changed to water, and he nevertheless converts tens of thousands. Show Boat uses the tale to defend Finnegan in a letter to Dotty [A:262].

A:262

BartolomoBartolomo Portuguese, one of the old pirates whom Angela Cosquin says customers might imagine behind initials on her father’s fabricated treasure maps. BP on a depicted treasure chest suggests his name, as T suggests Teach and K suggests Kidd [D:259-260].

D:259-260

Basal bulgeFeature of the Neanderthal-type head in the chapter-eighteen epigraph attributed to Carmody Overlark’s Studies in the Imagination. The epigraph links a large back-brain with ghostliness and imagination [D:270-272].

D:270-272

BaselineSebastian Hilton’s image for the danger of being with Duffey: the three slant-faced pursuers can use the two targets as a baseline and triangulate on them. He says two of their rare kind together register too strongly on the hunters’ receptors, yet insists that they will continue to associate despite the danger [MTM B1:36].

MTM B1:36

BashfulnessMr. X’s stated reason for staying away from his wife in Milano. A promised week’s absence first becomes three weeks; fear of her irony delays him further, events send him abroad, and his youthful shyness returns so strongly that he fears he can never face her again, though he loves her and hears that she waits faithfully [A:140-141].

A:140-141

BasicReduced enlisted status held by Casey Szymansky and Hans Schultz. After four weeks in the stockade, Casey attends rehabilitation classes three times a week and works as a basic during the rest of his time [A:50]. Hans loses his sergeant’s rank for marrying without permission; the later account explicitly calls him a basic in the battery where he had been staff sergeant [A:50] [A:58].

A:50; A:58

BasilOne of Henry Salvatore’s older cousins who follow his lead, with Sebastian, Fabian and Adrian; Peter, a younger cousin, also follows him [A:123].

A:123

Basin StreetNickname of George Becaud, an Old Wooden Ship regular [D:216]. An orchestral bull-fiddle player, he knows Shot Gun Schaeffer’s story and uses his large instrument case to pretend he is a professional killer owed the five thousand dollars Schaeffer received by mistake [D:223].

D:216; D:223

BasketTrinali Peterson lowers a basket from her window so Lupido can supply food while she is barricaded against eviction. She compares herself with St. Paul, then clarifies that Paul escaped in a basket [A:229], as in Acts 9:25. Hillary Hilton separately expands the eggs-in-several-baskets metaphor into his trading philosophy: eggs and baskets may be rotated, sold or given away with one another [A:255].

A:229; A:255

Basket WeaverNickname of Aloysius McGivern, a resident regular at the Old Wooden Ship [D:216]. His wealthy family pays him to remain there peacefully without embarrassing them and promises not to send him to a sanitarium again. He especially resents the compulsory basket weaving there and asks why the Devil, concerned with idle hands, is not made to do it himself [D:225].

D:216; D:225

BasqueLanguage Casey Szymansky speaks intuitively with a shepherd on a mountaintop in a night dream, although he has never seen or heard it. Such dreams realize his ambition to know all languages [A:159].

A:159

Bassa AccompanimentEarlier heading altered the printed phrase basso accompanamento. See Basso accompanamento.
Basse-TerreThe Basse-Terre of Finnegan’s terrestrial Paradise in the Antilles, distinguished by the narrator from Basseterre on St. Kitts, which Finnegan originally meant to visit. The narrative gives precise coordinates while Finnegan himself remains confused about the names [D:234-235]. His friends’ Sloppy Joe’s is actually named either the Imperial Bar or the Royal [D:235]. The narrator’s requirements for paradise include French-speaking Black islanders and English-speaking Frenchmen [D:237]. Finnegan later learns that a leftfooted man has hired a local friend to kill him; he pays more for protection, supplies clothes that turn up on a murdered lookalike, and begins rationalizing his departure [D:267]. In Archipelago he cites Basse Terre among the pleasure resorts he has sacrificed to help Casey [A:252].

D:234-235; D:235; D:237; D:267; A:252

BasseterreCapital on St. Kitts, the Basseterre Finnegan meant to reach before arriving instead at the other Basse-Terre [D:235]. In Angela Cosquin’s account of her father’s treasure-map business, the passage between Basseterre and Nevis is one of seven false or shoal passages where wrecks accumulated, or would have if ships had followed his imaginative logic [D:260].

D:235; D:260

Basso accompanamentoGiulio the Monster’s howled bass part in Hi, Ho! The Gadarene Swine! Sebastian, Countess Margaret, Letitia and Melchisedech sing the ballad in four voices; Giulio cannot sing and howls along [MTM B3:107].

MTM B3:107

BassorahPort of Sindbad’s stories. The Moisha El-Gazma epigraph calls it Baghdad’s folkloric port, then contradicts ordinary geography by describing a scorched rock slab in mud shallows and imagining it as an ancient launch pad for space fleets [D:53]. In the Argo’s history as told by the talking oak, Abd-Aliah of the Sea sells the ship to Sindbad of El-Basrah; much later it becomes the Brunhilde, whose Sindbad Lounge Finnegan paints [MTM B13:404]. Marie says Seaworthy has sailed from more Bassorahs than Sindbad would understand, as she imagines herself his final-voyage wife [D:61-62].

D:53; MTM B13:404; D:61-62

BastosTagalog word for rude or impolite, used in Amoy’s angry protest “Hindi bastos. Pinakamabuti” when Ti calls the magpie he loved common. Ti freely renders the protest as a denial that she was common and calls her an uncommon member of the common species [A:80]. Hindi is the Tagalog negative, meaning no or not; pinakamabuti means best.

A:80

BatBat wings carry the deformed counterparts of the bright arts from the Devil’s reopened pit in the narrator’s account; Duffey repeats the image while describing the Company of One Thousand and its corruption of the world [MTM B6:207-208]. A separate baseball bat appears in Vincent’s Theory of the Uncreated Creation: newly created batters could already be in slumps without having seen a bat [A:57].

MTM B6:207-208; A:57

BatangasPhilippine place from which an uncle of one of the cabaret girls is expected to bring a piano on Saturday, if he can obtain a cart. Nauti then identifies herself as the player, saying Falo lacks the talent [A:64-65]. Batangas names both a province and its capital city; the dialogue does not specify which is meant.

A:64-65

BathService advertised by Duffey at his new St. Louis establishment [MTM B2:41]. He heats water for Giulio in a horse trough, and Giulio removes his clothes and scapulars and bathes with relief [MTM B2:42-43]. Finnegan takes a bath after renting a room on the morning of his encounter with Seaworthy [D:17].

MTM B2:41; MTM B2:42-43; D:17

BathildesOne of the women’s names assigned to the bottles drunk by Finnegan and his three friends in Paradise. In the day’s alphabetical progression, Bathildes follows Agatha and precedes Clotilda [D:243].

D:243

BathurstWest African port, now Banjul in The Gambia, visited by the Brunhilde after Bissau and before Dakar as it moves north from February 1 [D:96].

D:96

BathysphereSubmersible used by the French brothers Cyril and Cyrus Dimbeau at Nine Mile Depth. Their hundred-meter seabed cores strike the Sword and Scabbard of Saint Sécaire, which they bring into the vessel with grapples and raise to their attending boat [MTM B13:422]. After the brothers begin drawing the sword, Duffey and Brannagan reseal it, drop it back to its former hiding place and cast a Forgetfulness Mesh. They leave the bathysphere party sampling ocean fleas at middle depths, unable to remember the sword [MTM B13:423-424].

MTM B13:422; MTM B13:423-424

BattersBaseball players already in slumps despite never having seen a bat, one of Vincent’s examples of an apparent past created with the world in his Theory of the Uncreated Creation [A:57].

A:57

Battling SikiBoxer whom Finnegan names, with Harry Wills, when describing his own style after his fighting binge. Finnegan says he fights somewhat like Siki [D:192].

D:192

BaulTreasure-chest emblem, also called an arca, drawn below a crossed pickaxe and shovel on the maps fabricated by Angela Cosquin’s father. Initials such as T, K or BP suggest old pirates [D:259-260]. Angela’s separate seven maps of Finnegan’s buried stashes use the maleta, or suitcase, instead of the baul [D:263].

D:259-260; D:263

BavariaProfessor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni’s approximate birthplace: the narrator places his birth around 1860 in Bavaria, but allows a slightly different place and time [A:211].

A:211

Bavarian ClubSt. Louis drinking and singing club visited by Duffey and Bagby on the first night of Duffey’s new business. Costumed young women give patrons rides on their backs, and Duffey befriends Helen [MTM B2:47]. Later outings identify her as Helen Platner [MTM B2:58].

MTM B2:47; MTM B2:58

BaxterBaxter Blackstone, Bryan Blackstone’s young son, nicknamed Bandicoot by the neighborhood boys. He begs Zabotski not to kill his father and fears the family will starve if he dies [MTM B9:271].

MTM B9:271

Bay HotelSite of the group picnic where a double table is placed on the terrace, the company plays softball on the lawn, swims, drinks Stein’s invented gin mixtures and eats large seafood platters. The party includes Hans and Marie, Finnegan, Loy, Tom Shire, Freddy Castle, Virginia, Dorothy and Stein; Casey refuses to attend with Stein and leaves with one of the new girls [A:29-30].

A:29-30

Bay RumNickname of Benny Boerum, one of the resident regulars at the Old Wooden Ship [D:216]. The narrator groups him with Raviola and Saddle Sore as unkempt and uncouth, supposedly falling below the other residents’ standards [D:224].

D:216; D:224

Bayougoula ParkPark suddenly present beside Duffey’s buildings in the transformed New Orleans of the Fifth Contingency. It replaces buildings Zabotski half-remembers owning, although Stein finds records giving the park a history of more than a century [MTM B11:331]. Zabotski continues to suspect he owns its land [MTM B11:333]. After Duffey returns from that contingency, the park is gone and some of Zabotski’s buildings stand there again [MTM B12:356].

MTM B11:331; MTM B11:333; MTM B12:356

Bazaar (Parish)Parish bazaaring, included among the everyday popular arts that the narrator says lose their style and vitality after the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207-208].

MTM B6:207-208

Beacon ClubOne of the remembered waterfront establishments in Melchisedech’s catalogue aboard the Argo [MTM B13:407].

MTM B13:407

BeakThe Pelican magazine is figured as a bony bird with an empty beak, surviving on scant nourishment [A:132]. In the seventh future outlined by Cleo Mahoney, an ominous bird carries in its beak the pennant “Whatever can go wrong will go wrong” [MTM B10:296-297]. Buzzards’ sharp beaks tear at Duffey in his post-fall suffering [MTM B12:393].

A:132; MTM B10:296-297; MTM B12:393

BeansOne of San Simeon’s crops, contrasted with the gold that accounts for its exceptional wealth [MB:558]. In Adrian Hilton’s banking analogy, a comic-strip detective stops people eating poisoned beans by shooting them; Adrian compares that destructive rescue with the bank moratorium [MTM B4:123].

MB:558; MTM B4:123

Beanstalk (Giant of the)The Giant of the Beanstalk, one of Henry Salvatore’s mythic identities in the narrator’s catalogue, alongside Friar Tuck and Pantegruel [A:39].

A:39

BearMabel, the trained bear who walks with Hans and Betty Hochstapler and assists their comic hypnosis act, acting as an audience volunteer and imitating animals [A:216] [A:219]. Elena Angelino claims a bear great-grandfather, and Professor Kirol says he knew the ancestral couple and confirms her story [A:218]. Eva is released from the ice wearing a blond female cave-bear skin [MTM B13:399]; the crew later kills cave bears for grease to soften frozen lines and for a replacement cloak [MTM B13:402]. In his transport concerning the older people, Finnegan calls them kin to the cave bear and other great animals [D:212-213].

A:216; A:219; A:218; MTM B13:399; MTM B13:402; D:212-213

BeardDuffey’s full, pointed beard is part of Casey’s description of him [A:42], and accompanies his arrival from Chicago [A:97]. As a young proprietor he has a growing red or sorrel beard [MTM B2:41]; later the narrative contrasts his red beard with Bagby’s black whiskers [MTM B2:61], and in New Orleans he keeps it white and bright for his art-dealing persona [A:143]. Giulio’s beard hosts possums in the comic Gadarene Swine ballad [MTM B3:107]. The Baptist’s preserved head has a still-growing beard exceeding a hundred feet [MTM B13:422]. Gautier’s resemblance to an aged Pan includes a dirty-white beard and gray tangled hair [A:194]. Joe Cross’s youthful face is encircled by a red beard on the voyage [D:100].

A:42; A:97; MTM B2:41; MTM B2:61; A:143; MTM B3:107; MTM B13:422; A:194; D:100

BearingsLatitude-and-longitude coordinates that the Argo’s talking oak sometimes gives when asked to date an artifact, even when they appear unrelated to the object [MTM B13:411]. Lost bearings also describe the Argonauts’ temporary confusion on waking from their hectic lives [MTM B13:398]. The narrator gives the terrestrial Paradise’s location as 61° 44′ 42″ W, 16° N [D:234].

MTM B13:411; MTM B13:398; D:234

BeastAnimal and bestial imagery includes the lions and leopards eating Nimrod Flesh Plant at Zabotski Flats [MTM B12:362], Papa Devil’s claim that he was once a tiger and will regain his stripes [D:122], and Finnegan, Vincent and Stein as the metaphorical hyenas sabotaging Show Boat’s preaching [MTM B7:231-232]. The white shark waiting for Finnegan above his underwater cave is a preternatural sea predator [MB:555]. In “Promontory Goats,” the Sonnet to Pained Victory invokes beasts and scapegoats carrying burdens [PG:529]; later, human celebrants stage the saying about wild beasts devouring entrails in holy places [MB:565].

MTM B12:362; D:122; MTM B7:231-232; MB:555; PG:529; MB:565

Beatific VisionIn Catholic theology, the direct vision of God in heavenly glory. Professor Kirol compares Heaven to a tapestry whose face is the Beatific Vision, while embodied observers see only its tangled reverse; he tells Hans that they already inhabit the spiritual universe without yet perceiving it fully [A:214]. The account of Hell in “Promontory Goats” imagines portions possessing natural happiness while lacking the happiness of the Beatific Vision [PG:532].

A:214; PG:532

BeatitudesHappiness associated with the terrestrial Paradise, though the narrator warns that snakes remain and eventually drive the friends out [D:235]. The fourth contingency for Duffey, the Argo’s Fourteenth Voyage within the Seven Lost or Golden Years, concerns ongoing beatitudes and the promise of Final Beatitude, with the completed quest’s great moment abiding [MTM B10:300].

D:235; MTM B10:300

Beautiful Barmaid (Dotty the)Casey’s epithet for Dotty Yekouris in his hostile editorial about the Pelican Press group. He professes affection for her beauty while belittling her skills as barmaid and journalist and regretting her investment in the venture [A:129].

A:129

Becaud, George (Basin Street)George Becaud, called Basin Street, is a regular at the Old Wooden Ship [D:216]. He plays bull fiddle in an orchestra and carries it in a large case. Knowing Shot Gun Schaeffer’s story about a mistaken five-thousand-dollar payment, he pretends the case holds an 800-gauge shotgun that could decapitate a bull elephant, then claims the money was meant for one of his own jobs. He repeats the intimidating joke nightly, sending Schaeffer scurrying upstairs to lock himself in; the narrator emphasizes Becaud’s sinister appearance and Schaeffer’s terror [D:223-224].

D:216; D:223-224

BedDuffey buys three cheap iron beds and mattresses when fitting out his St. Louis establishment [MTM B2:40-41]. Finnegan seldom sleeps in beds, although he does sleep in his rented room after meeting Seaworthy [D:18-19]. Marie Courtois lies across a hotel bed in catalepsy [D:112], and X speaks from bed while Finnegan sits by the window [D:157]. Aboard the Brunhilde, Finnegan shares a cabin with Don Lewis and Joe Cross [D:31]; an envelope hidden above a balk can be seen from his bunk [D:50]. Joe says Dopey previously occupied that bunk and describes the frightening circumstances of his disappearance [D:63-64]; Finnegan later feels Dopey’s presence there [D:78]. Casey’s school furnishings include a black-blanketed bed [A:161], while Finnegan sets up a cot behind the print shop during his stay with Casey [A:183].

MTM B2:40-41; D:18-19; D:112; D:157; D:31; D:50; D:63-64; D:78; A:161; A:183

Bed PanIn Ignatius Ti’s warning against turning one’s back on a corpse, a falling bed pan is one of the accidents a frightened ward boy may attribute to the dead man [A:85-86].

A:85-86

Bee TreeHoney source raided by Finnegan and Dotty, who bring seventy pounds from four bee trees to sweeten Duffey’s soup [A:134]. Gautier the goat-man taps a score of bee trees along his route every year [A:197].

A:134; A:197

Beebee TownOne of seven Iowa communities said to dispute the honor of being Duffey’s birthplace, within the account of one of his possible childhoods [MTM B1:7].

MTM B1:7

BeefServed in many varieties at the Harvesters’ Dinner in Chicago’s Colony Club [MTM B3:94]. Zabotski also has two heavy steers barbecued whole for Duffey’s supposed four-thousandth birthday party [MTM B8:257-258].

MTM B3:94; MTM B8:257-258

BeerThe Sydney beers Toohey’s, Tooth’s and K. B. Lager remind Finnegan of Paradise [A:2]. Beer drives the wet-canteen hoax played on Finnegan and Vincent [A:11-14], followed by Hans Schultz’s victorious contest with Joe Bushmaster [A:15-23]. Patrick Stranahan’s recommended four brews are American, Danish, Bohemian and Guiness [A:110]. Gautier makes corn beer [A:196], while the Regal brewery sends Duffey a weekly keg for his soup [A:134]. Finnegan orders two glasses when he believes he has met his father again [A:244]. With Seaworthy he drinks Texas beer because nothing else is cold [D:12]; he drinks between bar-cleaning jobs [D:19] and with Doll at the bait house [D:182]. Biloxi Brannagan drinks beer from a pitcher in his kitchen garden [D:199], where Finnegan finds his long retirement spent drinking and watching ships [D:201].

A:2; A:11-14; A:15-23; A:110; A:196; A:134; A:244; D:12; D:19; D:182; D:199; D:201

Beer ChitSupposed authorization to buy beer at the Australian wet canteen. As part of Tom Shire and Freddy Castle’s hoax, Sergeant Bushmaster tells Finnegan to sign for beer chits; the document actually insults American drinking prowess. The bartender explains that no chit is required, only sixpence [A:13-14].

A:13-14

Beer GardenFinnegan’s mistaken identification of Biloxi Brannagan’s private kitchen garden. Seeking cover from pursuers, he vaults its fence and joins Brannagan at a table; Gertrude serves a pitcher of beer before correcting his assumption that the place is open for business [D:198-199]. Brannagan later claims to have spent thirty-five years sitting by the sea, ten in an old chair and twenty-five in its replacement [D:204].

D:198-199; D:204

Beetles (Sexton)Sexton beetles in an as-yet-unlocated Paean passage, described in the original glossary as consuming dead flesh so that it cannot remain to remember. The supplied Archipelago edition does not contain the cited poem.
Beetling BellyBascom Bagby’s conspicuous belly, paired with his beetling brows when he arrives for a shave and haircut at young Duffey’s establishment [MTM B2:43].

MTM B2:43

Beetling BrowsBascom Bagby’s projecting brows, paired with his beetling belly at his first visit to Duffey’s establishment [MTM B2:43].

MTM B2:43

BellsYoung Melchisedech summons a giant hand to help ring a church bell [MTM B1:14-15]; Bagby suggests a service bell linking Duffey’s shop with his own cabinet work [MTM B2:46]. Tower bells toll in Casey’s imagined Fortress Major [A:157]. Naxos has animal, boat, buoy and farmyard dinner bells [D:131]. Off San Simeon, the Sea-Bell, Martyr-Bell and Peter-Bell summon a hidden assembly despite official efforts to silence them [MB:560]. Hackenschmidt orders all bells broken and melted lest they awaken the supposedly dead Church [MB:568]. The novel’s prophecy attributed to Nostradamus calls Finnegan the Pope of Bells and Bay [MB:598].

MTM B1:14-15; MTM B2:46; A:157; D:131; MB:560; MB:568; MB:598

BEMs (Bug-Eyed Monsters)Bug-eyed monsters, a pulp science-fiction term. Bagby says the Slant-Faced Men receive the same comic treatment as BEMs and HLPs in pulp-magazine letter columns, although he and the others know the Slant-Faced Men are real and dangerous [MTM B7:225].

MTM B7:225

Bench (Park)The park-bench sleeper device, one of four basic practical-joke formulas for the dog-housebreaking product Finnegan sells in Buffalo. Its variant is the bus-waiter trap [A:189-190].

A:189-190

BenedictineReligious affiliation of Joseph of Maintz in Ignacio’s story of an eighth-century priest who shoots himself to the moon to escape worldly temptations without committing suicide. Ignacio attributes the tale to Turpin of Rheims and professes belief in it [A:271].

A:271

BenedictionChurch service at which Casey served one winter evening before seeing rich parishioners enter the monsignor’s study. The meeting actually concerned fundraising, but Casey imagined a higher religion reserved for the wealthy. This fed the esoteric dream-world whose library he had begun with material from a magazine advertisement [A:158-159].

A:158-159

BeneficientOne side of the opposition Papa Devil gives Finnegan when asked to explain the plot: monsters and men, Policia y Ladrones, the Beneficient and the Maleficent [D:120].

D:120

Benevolent Shark at MauleWaterfront establishment at Maule remembered in Melchisedech’s catalogue aboard the Argo, alongside the Fanged Fish at Ogopo and other seafaring haunts [MTM B13:407].

MTM B13:407

BenignityDon Barnaby’s “bedamned benignity” during his experience with Madame Le Mourcheor’s Juju Joy Pill. Pitying the supposedly miserable John Sourwine, or Sour John, he tries to bring him across the street for a pill so that they can share the pleasure [D:249-251].

D:249-251

Benning, MartinSoldier in Ward Fourteen whom the Sergeant considers sound except on a few points [A:75]. Benning demands proof of Green’s theory that God sustains the universe from moment to moment; George Buckram, rather than Benning, then asks whether Green is God [A:76]. Benning leaves the ward after a few weeks, before the Sergeant’s departure [A:88].

A:75; A:76; A:88

BeraB-flat trumpet player in the Brimstone Combo in Trinali’s poem about the old saloon at Beelzebub and Hell-Raiser Streets [A:235]. His name echoes Bera, king of Sodom in Genesis 14:2; the combo’s other names also adapt names of kings and places from that chapter.

A:235

BeretPart of Duffey’s art-dealer appearance in New Orleans: he keeps a bright white beard and adds an artist’s tie and beret while running his second-hand book, art and antique shops [A:143].

A:143

Bergen (Swede)One of five men called Swede at the Old Wooden Ship, although the group consists of a Norwegian, a Dane, an Icelander, a German and an Orkneyman, with no Swede among them [D:215] [D:217]. Unlike his seafaring companions, Bergen has sailed only once and was so seasick that he vowed never to leave land again. His wife also refuses to sail after childhood seasickness. For twenty years each has written asking the other to cross the Atlantic; the narrator says they will remain apart unless someone builds a bridge [D:217].

D:215; D:217

Bering SeaOne of the seas named in the catalogue of the Argo’s voyages and Melchisedech’s maritime memories [MTM B13:406].

MTM B13:406

BerlitzLanguage manuals on Duffey’s shelves, available to Casey in his pursuit of every language. The list also includes Thimms, Hugos, Marlboroughs, Cortina, Langenscheidt and Metoula [A:159].

A:159

Berny CacciatoreSee Cacciatore, Berny.
Berry JellyOne of Gautier the goat-man’s homemade provisions, alongside berry wine, corn beer and potato whisky [A:196-197].

A:196-197

Berry WineDrink made by Gautier the goat-man alongside his berry jelly, corn beer and other provisions [A:196].

A:196

Best enemyAnne’s affectionate phrase in her sign-off from the Japanese radio station in Java. Her intimate voice and homesick songs give her broadcasts an appeal that Stein’s Anopheles Network cannot match [A:46].

A:46

BetelgeuseOne of the stars whose right ascension Hans learns to calculate for a given date while studying with Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni [A:214].

A:214

Beth KeeganSee Keegan, Beth.
Betrayal of GiottoGiotto painting cited by Van Ghi in Finnegan’s story about accidentally painting a devil. Van Ghi claims that the same sinister figure recurs in the backgrounds of the Betrayal and other artworks, and tells Finnegan he has drawn the Joker instead of the Queen [D:255].

D:255

Better Life LeagueOrganization that recognizes Zabotski as an Entrance Person, although he thinks little of the organization. Duffey’s account nevertheless says its classification of Zabotski is correct [MTM B9:268].

MTM B9:268

BevoAnheuser-Busch’s non-alcoholic near beer. In the novel it is sold with snacks and sweets by vendors at the Chicago park gathering where ten-year-old Casey’s planned appearance as the Leader is thwarted by Letitia [MTM B4:118].

MTM B4:118

BibleBiblical quotations frame several episodes: Genesis 14:18 on Melchisedech’s bread and wine opens Book Two [MTM B2:38], and Hebrews 7:9-10 on Levi paying tithes through Abraham opens Book Seven [MTM B7:210]. Genesis 6:4 supplies the giants epigraph [D:212], and excerpts from Numbers 13-14 introduce Angela Cosquin’s chapter [D:258]. Duffey’s expectation that he has no end invokes scriptural Melchisedech [MTM B10:290], recalling Hebrews 7:3. A Bible is among the books supplied in Casey’s schoolroom, although its translation is unspecified [A:161-162]. The cited passages do not establish that all these Bibles and quotations are Douay-Rheims; some wording differs from that translation.

MTM B2:38; MTM B7:210; D:212; D:258; MTM B10:290; A:161-162

Bible (Douay-Rheims)Earlier heading assigned the Douay-Rheims translation to passages and a school Bible whose translation is not established. See Bible.
Bicycle ridingOne of the popular arts said to lose its style and vitality in the widespread degradation following the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207].

MTM B6:207

Biddy's Barracuda BarWaterfront establishment in Duffey’s catalogue of maritime memories aboard the Argo [MTM B13:407].

MTM B13:407

Bierceian IronyFinnegan’s phrase for an ironic ending in the manner of Ambrose Bierce. In his supposed life after death, he questions why his existence should follow a human literary pattern of Wordsworthian beginning, Baconian middle and Bierceian end; he insists that he has reached something, but not the end [D:237].

D:237

Big BirdThe giant huracan or hurricane bird said to nest in San Simeon’s limestone crags. The narrative offers alternative accounts of one repeatedly flying bird or several newly hatched birds, and says its twisting flights tear away pieces of the country that form at least thirteen Antillean islands [MB:557-558].

MB:557-558

Big BoyUnlocated expression attributed in the original glossary to Josephine McSorely’s Underground Eagle material. The cited Casey Machine page does not contain it.
Big Fat-HeadOne of the familiar valley names Don Lewis lists when recounting how three American soldiers became lost on Willy Jones Island after pursuing and killing Yokipoki. Big Fat-Head is paired with Little Fat-Head; the valley where they are stranded is one they do not recognize [D:44-46].

D:44-46

Big HouseHouse on Willy Jones Island in one of Don Lewis’s supposedly happy island stories. Its inhabitants kill first-night visitors and make broth from their organs to preserve their own youth; a year without a visitor makes everyone a year older [D:48]. Ali carries one protective ta’a nut and plants another before entering. When the inhabitants come to kill him, he brings morning by snapping his fingers, finds the planted nut grown into a tree reaching his window, and climbs down to escape. That year the household ages [D:48-49].

D:48; D:48-49

Big PotZabotski’s huge glass-lined experimental crock, given to Duffey [A:132]. Duffey sets the thousand-gallon vessel over gas burners and establishes his continuing barley-soup service [A:133]. BirdsThe narrative gives Black Papua an extravagant abundance of birds among its caves and cliffs [A:36]. Melchisedech can turn stones into birds [MTM B1:18]. Hillary Hilton includes tropical birds among the distressed merchandise he trades [A:254-255]. In Finnegan’s painting, an apparent smaller bird is really a bird-cry written in a speech balloon; its message predicts the meat to come into Duffey’s pot [MTM B6:196]. A rowdy bird carries the ominous pennant in Cleo’s seventh contingency [MTM B10:297]. Trinali’s poem calls the birds over the Dead Sea Devil Birds [A:235-236], while the frozen world around the Argo contains motionless birds suspended in the air [MTM B13:398].

Henri’s letter names the Crimean peninsula as the prison site [MTM B5:180], while Stein dates the imprisonment and release to 946-1946 [MTM B6:185]. In the Royal Pop history, Margaret announces the sea’s obliteration [MTM B11:308], Zabotski asks about its disasters [MTM B11:333], and Hugh de Turenne explains the destruction as an attack on the Devil’s former prison and Colchis’s support for the Argo and Fleece [MTM B11:336]. Duffey’s account of finding the Argo says that a Black Sea-built hull would have been cedar; her actual oak is from the Dinaric Alps and her keel was laid at Ragusa [MTM B13:412]. The ship’s mysterious bell-bearer later supplies Black Sea ship-biscuit to the people at the Mooring-Stone [MB:578].

BlackbirdsWith crows, birds that come from the nearby woods to Trinali’s driftwood graveyard and taunt the seabirds [A:233]. Finnegan’s scattered shipmates in Tangier are compared to a flock of blackbirds while he tries to watch them on the day of the hunt [D:103].

Blackstone, BandicootBaxter Blackstone, Bryan’s son, nicknamed Bandicoot by the neighborhood boys. At five he begs Zabotski not to kill his father and fears having to work in the mines or starve [MTM B9:271]. On what Duffey experiences as the next morning, Bandicoot is starting high school, the dead sycamore has long been removed, and Bryan complains of the withers of middle age; a neighbor says eight years have passed [MTM B9:276]. The surrounding satirical clippings attack deliberately lowered literacy and pornography in teaching, ideological standards for judging wars, dehumanization and murder of opponents, selective recognition of Christ in others, and a priests’ senate leader’s claims of supremacy over diocesan authorities [MTM B8:251-252].

BloodBodily blood, ancestry and violent imagery recur throughout the cycle. Finnegan wakes in a dump with his own dried blood in his hair [A:177], while the Captain metaphorically smells blood as he breaks the amnesiac Sergeant [A:74]. Sebastian Hilton sheds other boys’ blood in calculated fights [MTM B1:23]; Melchisedech keeps jars of blood, and Charles Hart says he once did likewise [MTM B1:18]. The Brunhilde’s peculiar people are described as full of old black blood [D:50]. Anastasia Grandmother claims the other blood for herself and a little for her granddaughter [D:128]. Papa Devil places himself, Anastasia and Finnegan among the Non-people and calls Dopey a seaman of strange blood [D:121]. Brannagan says he and Finnegan each have a little double blood, in differing recensions [D:209-210]; Finnegan later calls all four Paradise friends people of double blood [D:237]. Casey calls the Dirty Five brothers who are not blood relatives [A:154]. X’s genealogy makes the earlier Ifreann a son of the Devil [D:278], and attributes the Devil’s dark power to Papadiabolous I [D:286]. Duffey explains the Pelican’s Christ symbolism through the traditional belief that it feeds its young with its blood [A:121]. After Dopey vanishes, Papa Devil dismisses the remaining dribble as bug blood [D:64]. Don Lewis’s body has only a trickle at the mouth [D:110], and the dead Bloke’s hat is bloodied [D:147]. Finnegan escapes through broken glass with cuts to face and hands [D:165-166]. Marie boasts of the pleasure of blood on her hands [D:92], and Patrick Stranahan’s crossroads image has fresh, old and placental blood running down its signpost [MTM B5:164].

BlueOther uses include the sky-blue Mediterranean scenes Finnegan paints [D:114], the blue mountain and haze on Naxos [D:127], the blue-dream sea of Paradise [D:233], and the blue deep water beyond green shallows [D:37]. Blue Fields is a port of call [D:81]. Blue-birds appear in the verse about Li Tai Po [A:222], and Mary Catherine serves blue cheese [A:247]. BobResident regular at the Old Wooden Ship [D:215–216]. With Russ and Charleyhorse Heckel, he seeks out men willing to buy drinks for everyone and steers them to the tavern. The three also rob customers outside after they have finished spending but still have money [D:220].

Boerum, Benny (Bay Rum)Benny Boerum, nicknamed Bay Rum, is one of the resident regulars at the Old Wooden Ship [D:216]. The narrator groups him with Raviola and Saddle Sore as unkempt and uncouth exceptions to the establishment’s supposedly high standards [D:224].

D:216; D:224

Boethius (c. 480--524/525 AD)Roman philosopher, Christian theologian and senator, apparently intended by the printed “Boëthus” in the narrator’s list of people with seven hidden years, beside Caesar, Diocletian, Carl the Great, Wellington, Lincoln, Sam Houston, George Barrow and Hans Schultz [MTM B2:72]. The proposed seven-year parallel belongs to the novel’s account of Duffey’s missing years. Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison before his execution. Its prose-and-verse dialogue with personified Philosophy draws on ancient philosophy and became influential in medieval thought; its relationship to Christianity is debated, since it makes no explicit Christian appeal. His Latin translations and commentaries transmitted Aristotelian logic, and his mathematical writings supplied material for the quadrivium of arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and music. Dates are approximate: standard accounts often give about 480 to 524, while other scholarship argues for about 475-477 to 526. The short notes on time in More Than Melchisedech also attribute to Boethius the distinction between the flowing instant that produces time and the abiding instant that produces eternity [MTM B13:469].

MTM B2:72; MTM B13:469

Bogovitch, I.N.C.G.P.Inscription on the old gravestone that Finnegan shows Doll and X in the cemetery across from the club [D:275-277]. X interprets Bogovitch as “son of God,” a euphemism for Chortovitch, “son of the Devil,” and reconstructs the earlier occupant’s name as Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch Papadiabolous Chortovitch [D:277-278]. This is the old Ifreann, father of the two later Papadiabolous brothers, not simply another name for Papadiabolous I [D:285-286]. The grave is also Gregory McIfreann’s, the son whom X calls Papadiabolous I [D:284-285]. Finnegan’s earlier burial account explains the shared grave: he and Seaworthy place a new corpse above the bones of an older occupant [D:76].

BogsPart of the wild New Jersey country through which Finnegan wanders before meeting Gautier the goat-man. The description begins with bogs and bog-men, then names the Barrens, mountains, and sea [A:193-194].

BohemianA Bohemian brew is one of the four beers Patrick Stranahan considers sufficient, with an American, a Danish and Guinness [A:110]. Bohemian is also one strain of the Angelino clan, whose members are described as predominantly Italian and German, with Mexican and Irish Tinker ancestry too [A:218]. In the account of the artistic and political patrons who might support Finnegan, he can be a Bohemian with Bohemians as readily as a drinker among drinkers [A:184].

The later passage inconsistently calls Lloyd, previously paired with Cardinal Lloyd Spencer, the double of the dead Ti [MB:579] [MB:594].

BolognaFinnegan’s comparison for an inside-out tiger, a huge mass of bologna encased in its own intestinal membrane. He says it would resemble Papa Devil, who replies that he is speaking of himself and intends to become a tiger again [D:122].

Bolshevestic and Atheistic CommunismThe danger named in an epigraph attributed to Pius XI’s Atheistic Communism, which sets modern revolution within the continuing struggle between good and evil after the Fall [MTM B5:177]. The passage comes from sections 2-3 of the 1937 encyclical Divini Redemptoris; the novel’s “Bolshevestic” differs from the official English “bolshevistic.”

MTM B5:177

Bonaventure's (St.)Casey’s boarding high school, forty miles from his home; he lives in St. Martin’s Hall [A:161]. Its school paper, The Towers, is dominated by Gregory Hall, while the St. Martin’s boys produce the manuscript rival Chambers. Their individually drawn chamber-pot mastheads parody Gregory’s towers. This rivalry supplies the earlier model for Casey’s later Crock magazines [A:167].

A:161; A:167

BondThe restraints Don Lewis ties around the wrists and ankles of the dead Yokipoki before burying him. Awakened by noises, Don imagines the corpse cutting its bonds with the buried butcher knife; the disturbance and apparent attack prove to be rats [D:46-47].

D:46-47

BoneHans’s joking argument contrasts supposedly scarce ancient fingers with commonly found jawbones, brainpans and pelvises [A:4-5]. Finnegan feels terror melt his bones at Papa Devil’s presence [D:15], and feels an electric shock from Anastasia’s bones [D:20]. He identifies shapes by touch among the older remains in the grave where he and Seaworthy bury a new corpse [D:76]. X says the Papadiabolous brothers have indistinguishable skeletons and facial bones despite their differing fleshed appearances [D:286]. Duffey’s killers strip his bones and separately burn his flesh to ashes. X and Casey recover both, and the bones are placed aboard the Argo. God subsequently confirms that Duffey may continue as a Master without flesh [MTM B13:442-443].

Bone-Bleached WorldThe exclamation of an imagined future professor who recognizes an Australian femur found in Turkestan thirty thousand years later. The narrator uses the fancy to exaggerate Tom Shire and Freddy Castle’s unmistakably Australian appearance [A:5].

Bone-mealOne of the products John Mogul says his murder business makes from victims’ bodies when practicable, alongside soap and essential oils. He describes himself as a knacker and euthanasiast, and specifies bone-meal for farmers [MB:573].

BonesHans, not Finnegan, jokes that prehistoric fingers are harder to find than jawbones, brainpans and pelvises [A:4-5]. Trinali imagines the driftwood shore as an elephants’ graveyard, with larger pieces becoming the bones of mammoths, behemoths and Leviathan; these are images for timber, not excavated animal remains [A:232]. Finnegan feels Anastasia’s bones like an electric shock [D:20], handles an older skeleton while digging the grave for the first Papa Devil [D:76], and later hears X explain that the Papadiabolous twins have the same skeletal and facial-bone structure [D:286]. X brings living Duffey his own future ashes in an urn [MTM B6:203]. In the later account of their recovery, X and Casey identify Duffey’s bones and ashes separately; X keeps the ashes, and both men carry the bones to the Argo [MTM B13:442-443].

BonfireIn Ignacio’s account of Joseph of Maintz, the eighth-century priest fires himself to the moon and promises a bonfire every full moon as proof that he still lives; the fires continue for ninety years [A:271]. At the Bay Hotel picnic the management forbids a lawn bonfire, so a waitress lights charcoal briquettes on a broad trencher-plate for the party’s singing [A:29-31].

Booby-hatchPrivate Gregory’s disparaging name for the army psychiatric ward in which he is already confined. He fears years of observation after authorities link his young Australian identity to the fingerprints and papers of a vanished elderly American colonel [A:79].

BoogerOne of the Teras types Duffey lists with Gargoyles, Neanderthals, Vagaries and Variants. He says everyone has some variant blood and that he put more than usual into his own creations [MTM B5:169-170].

In New Orleans Duffey again runs a secondhand bookstore, together with art, antique and pawn businesses [A:143].

“Books Abroad”A section of the Crock written by Polly Polyglot, the pen name of Mary Frances Rattigan [A:41].

BoondocksMarie’s term for the extreme backcountry where her uncle Shakes Pearson supposedly writes tobacco-contest verses on bark with oak-ball juice because paper is unavailable [A:25]. BootsDon Lewis removes Yokipoki’s boots before burial so that the dead man may rest comfortably [D:46]. Borg (Surname)One of the Angelino clan’s family names, listed with Obermeyer, Viskochil, Trevino and Larrigan [A:218].

He later often claims to come from Boston [MTM B1:7] [MTM B1:9]. PFC Timothy Lorrigan is from Boston [D:44], as is Emmet Collins, Cardinal Merry’s double [MB:579]. Casey says infiltrates come from Boston to heckle Duffey at communion breakfasts [A:42-43]. Finnegan’s puzzlement at being called a Yankee includes his lack of the supposed Bostonian speech affliction [A:273].

BottleFinnegan credits Italians with inventing the bottle and the fork for extracting olives; Vincent prefers an Irish claim [A:5]. Before the Brunhilde sails, Finnegan figuratively hides in a bottle to escape a real threat to his life [D:27]. Empty beer bottles become gasoline lamps in the army camp [A:39]. Other bottles hold Black Label at the Buffalo Bar [A:66], or the Canadian whisky Duffey carries to Chicago during Prohibition [MTM B3:77]. On Naxos, Finnegan and Anastasia buy a wineskin and propose leaving it in a forked bush on the mountain [D:126]. Finnegan later takes gin uphill as protection against forebodings, carries the bottle through the disaster and Anastasia’s death, and cannot bring himself to discard it [D:130] [D:148]. In Paradise, fifty cents buys a bottle [D:235]. The four friends name successive bottles Agatha, Bathildes, Clotilda, Delphina, Etheldreda, Faustina, Georgina and Hildegarde, eventually opening Idabel before sleeping [D:243] [D:256]. Ignatius Ti says a falling pill bottle near a corpse can make a frightened attendant blame the dead man [A:85-86]. Show Boat’s story of an unidentified tippling Apostle describes wine bottles mysteriously replaced with water [A:262]. An epigraph credited to Belloc’s “Heroic Poem in Praise of Wine” imagines bottling God the Father in a flask [MTM B5:176].

A:5; D:27; A:39; A:66; MTM B3:77; D:126; D:130; D:148; D:235; D:243; D:256; A:85-86; A:262; MTM B5:176

BouldersHenry and Casey sit on two boulders after swimming in a waterfall pool in the New Guinea jungle, continuing their conversation about Duffey [A:42].

Boule, DanDaniel Jean Boule, also spelled Boulle, is named as the double of Henri Cardinal Salvatore of New Orleans. Henri quotes a prophetic account in which this double travels up the Mexican coast by tramp steamer after the Cardinal’s death; Henri instead proposes to survive and travel as the double of his dead cousin Dan [MTM B12:387-388]. The Mooring-Stone narrative names Boulle among the thirteen doubles and describes that steamer journey to the conclave [MB:579] [MB:592-593] [MB:596].

BoundaryFinnegan describes his personal boundaries as indefinite when Dopey’s face persists in his shaving mirror [D:188]. Elsewhere he laments a barrier between himself and human beings despite their friendship and love [D:90]. In the Great Day Contingency, the abolition of boundaries threatens individuality itself and results in the obliteration of persons [MTM B10:298].

Bounty HuntersAfter killing the thirteen principal Cardinals in hiding, Track and Total offers bounties for their surviving doubles. The shadow-men converge on the waters around Mooring-Stone, where hunters operate on land and sea [MB:589-590]. The hunters try to close their trap after the Argo and other vessels enter, but changing shoals wreck their attack [MB:595].

BowEach diner on Zabotski’s ark has a small bow and arrows for attacking the dangerous creatures in the slumgullion. One child has trained midget octopuses to shoot back, with lethal poisoned arrows of their own [MTM B12:364-365]. In the epigraph credited to Hiram Hunt’s The Death of the Species, the taut bow represents a balance between competing elements of humanity; destroying either wood or string destroys the whole [D:283-284].

BowneeOne of Gautier’s seven youngest goat kids, listed with Luin, Mairt, Keadin, Ordin, Haoine and Sahirn. The goat-man gives this group hebdomadal, or weekly, names; Luin is subsequently glossed as Monday [A:194-195].

A:194-195

BoxBoxes serve as objects, receptacles and metaphors across the cycle. The roadhouse music box plays “Seems Like Old Times” and “It’s a Great Big World” [A:99]. Falo and Nauti furnish their new cabaret with one large box as a table and two small ones as chairs [A:64]; Captain Sammy borrows a shoeshine box without its owners noticing, earns money and returns it [A:67]. Askandan keeps his foul, sticky soap base in a boxcar [A:256]. Childhood Duffey knows which households keep box-elder or elm in their wood boxes [MTM B1:17]. Sebastian Hilton’s bait box is figurative, his collection of tricks for provoking bullies into fights [MTM B1:22]. X brings Duffey nested black, gray and brown boxes. The brown one holds the Crock’s infiltrate cards, which X admits stealing; Duffey introduces an apparently real version of X’s old disappearing-red-box trick, then replaces it with roses [MTM B6:201-203]. X also brings the cigar container or urn holding Duffey’s own ashes [MTM B6:185] [MTM B6:203]. The safety-deposit box sought by Charlotte and Duffey is the Chicago stash associated with Aga Gonof, and Charlotte later calls it a walk-in [MTM B3:84-86]. Duffey notices the theft of his box of war medals during the coming-leader affair [MTM B4:115-116]. The bony Duffey regains flesh and a working voice box on voyages that fall earlier than his death [MTM B13:444]. Stein has requested burial in a plain pine box with a lighted cigar [GD:493]. Mail is supposedly waiting for Finnegan in a call box [D:267]. Advertisements in the Crock give box numbers for ordering consecrated hosts or stolen dead bodies [PG:524] [PG:546]. Angela Cosquin has a copper cash box inscribed “Angela Cosquin sa Caisse” and keeps it with the sunken treasure ships, adding a saved sovereign each month [D:262].

Box CarFreight car holding Asking Dan’s eighty-three thousand pounds of unscented soap base. The substance becomes sticky and foul-smelling when wet; Hillary Hilton offers twenty cents per hundred pounds, but Dan refuses to sell [A:256].

Box-elder woodOne household’s firewood, contrasted with another’s elm, in the account of young Duffey’s extraordinarily detailed awareness of other homes. The narrator says such knowledge combines observation and memory with theft from other minds [MTM B1:17].
