BoxerThe Stranahans are a sporting family of amateur boxers, and old boxers are among Patrick’s visitors [A:103-104]. Finnegan has boxed and habitually carried his left low to draw fire [D:172]. His extravagant fighting reminiscences include Harry Greb, Joe Gans and Tom Sharky, followed by comparisons with Harry Wills and Battling Siki [D:191-192]. Bascom Bagby fights professional bouts, and introduces young Duffey to a preliminary contest with Dandy Dan Dillard [MTM B2:50]. Berny Cacciatore is a boxing and sports historian among the Royal Pop Historians [MTM B11:322].

A:103-104; D:172; D:191-192; MTM B2:50; MTM B11:322

Boy (Anastasia's cousin)Anastasia’s young cousin on Naxos. He intercepts the noisy Finnegan descending the mountain after the shooting, tells him Anastasia has instructed him to hide, and warns that hunters mean to kill him [D:144]. He reports the armed men, the dead in the streets, and the danger to Finnegan, the big man and the South American; he later identifies his relationship to Anastasia, says she is dead, and describes the sunken smaller boat and Manuel’s search for Papa Devil [D:145-146].

D:144; D:145-146

Boy (Malayan)The unnamed Malayan boy who guides the Sergeant, Finnegan, through the shifting journey after his ward experience. He says the Sergeant has spent long enough in the Green Islands and must grow up, brings him to Sydney, and directs him to the Plaza Hotel while he visits the Malayan and Indonesian Club [A:88]. Later, back in the islands, they travel by canoe. The boy supplies the names Aral, Bumi and Aragh, which the Sergeant takes to mean the Argo; they dive into extraordinarily wet water by the coral reefs [A:89].

A:88; A:89

Boy King, TheMelchisedech Duffey’s primordial childhood identity. The narrator calls the Boy King’s thousands of years the solid basis of Duffey’s other lives, and his tents, flocks, rivers and groves more real than the landscapes of his later childhood [MTM B1:17]. The golden-handed king feeds visitors with bread and wine, summons visible and invisible giants to release waters or overthrow rival kings, helps physicians cure the sick, and turns stones into birds. Usually concealed by an “urchin disguise,” he distributes replenishing talismans that confer gifts and help create the Duffey Nation [MTM B1:18]. As an eight-year-old he commands a giant to ring a church bell [MTM B1:15]. His later displays include golden sparks and gold coins [MTM B2:38] [MTM B5:167]. In a dream he calls himself the Boy King or Boy Magician and makes clay Paradise Birds; their destruction leads Beth to interpret the dream as doubt in his powers and creations [MTM B2:67].

MTM B1:17; MTM B1:18; MTM B1:15; MTM B2:38; MTM B5:167; MTM B2:67

Boy MagicianDuffey’s name for himself, alongside Boy King, in a dream he relates to Beth. He makes clay birds, turns them to living gold and sends them flying as Paradise Birds. When rough men shoot them down, they fall as clay pigeons. Beth interprets the dream as doubt in his powers and creations [MTM B2:67].

MTM B2:67

Brace of steinsA pair of beer steins, in the mock Australian request Tom Shire coaches Finnegan to use at the wet canteen: “Hoy soy, dyg, me moit and oi need a broice of stoins.” It forms part of the attempt to pass as Australians [A:12].

A:12

BraceletsGolden bracelets and jangles in Finnegan’s song for Elena, whose sound he compares to the Tambuls of Spain as she tends his battered face [A:274].

A:274

BrainBrain and mind imagery ranges from anatomy to psychic power and damaged identity. Hans’s comic argument about ancient forks cites surviving jawbones, brain pans and pelvises rather than fingers [A:5]. An epigraph credited to Carmody Overlark’s Studies in the Imagination contrasts the modern forebrain with a supposedly greater Neanderthal back-brain, associates the latter with unconscious and ghostly powers, and adduces Plato, Homer and Aquinas among its examples [D:270-272]. The narrator’s fantastic account of Papua similarly makes other peoples dependent on the Papuans’ bottomless unconscious [A:37]. Sulem distinguishes the tujuan, or personal directions, supposedly located under a brain lobe, in the liver or in the diaphragm, from the semangat, or soul; he places both in the diaphragm himself [A:60]. In Don Lewis’s Big House tale, the inhabitants consume visitors’ brains and other organs [D:48]. Duffey enters Lily Koch’s mind, where she recognizes him and invites a reciprocal intimacy of minds [MTM B1:29]. Newton Prescott may require brain surgery if writing and burning his journal fails to free him from compulsive memories [CM:503]. Stein explains his supposed soul exchange with Casey as a trade of interior goblins, kabouters, that share their former owners’ secrets [PG:537-538]. In the Great Day, Stein’s once plentiful brains have metaphorically evaporated [GD:493]. Finnegan’s resurrected brain retains his old identity despite the new assignment and modified identity he receives [MB:554]. Duffey’s returning life appears to him as life in the past, an effect of the Argo’s ambiguous relation to time [MTM B13:445]. Hillary Hilton deals figuratively in distressed brains [A:255]. Seaworthy’s shovel spills part of the first Papa Devil’s brain [D:75]. Finnegan resumes using his human brain after the ape-cat escape [D:165], and describes his own indefinite boundaries after seeing Dopey in his mirror [D:188]. Brannagan calls the world’s selective idiocy an epidemic spread by a man-sized germ [D:202].

Brain DamageBiloxi Brannagan’s diagnosis of the world’s selective idiocy. He describes a recurring infection carried by a man-sized germ and calls the parasite “the alien within” [D:202-203].

BramblesThe brambles on the sheer Naxos mountainside through which Finnegan makes his hazardous descent, and the bushes he bursts through while fleeing downhill after the shots [D:141] [D:144].

BranchThe Frio is named as a river branch in Finnegan’s confused account of his travels [A:202]. In Don Lewis’s tale a ta’a nut tree grows a branch to Ali’s window and enables his escape from the Big House [D:49]; old gnarled branches are among the features of the Naxos mountaintop [D:132]. Margaret Stone uses branch for the Stein side of the family [MTM B4:112], while Charlotte Garfield says she and Duffey belong to closely related branches of the old people [MTM B8:260]. The child hero proposes a forked peach branch for reading an object’s history, and Duffey has such a red-peach dowser’s stick [MTM B11:326]. In their shared prayer Duffey responds to Finnegan’s shaken-earth verse with “Heal its branches, for it quakes” [MTM B12:375].

A:202; D:49; D:132; MTM B4:112; MTM B8:260; MTM B11:326; MTM B12:375

Brannagan, GertrudeBiloxi Brannagan’s hospitable wife. Finnegan meets her at their Biloxi house, mistaking the private kitchen garden for a beer garden, and she adopts him on sight [D:199-200]. A full-built, dark, slightly Frenchy woman of forty-five, give or take fifteen years, she is described as a fortress and “Living Gothic” [D:200]. She supplies rice ribby, huckleberry and greenberry wine, perry, pecan pancakes, roast pork and turtle chowder [D:208], and arranges the transfer of Finnegan’s impounded car in exchange for her nearly worthless one [D:209]. Finnegan kisses her goodbye once, then four or five times more [D:210]. Duffey recalls her expansive kisses to both himself and Biloxi [MTM B13:410].

BrassMetal used for the bright stops and frets of the Coryphaena fishes’ shell horns [MTM B13:450], and for the stop-keys and filigree of Duffey’s handmade recorder [MTM B6:190]. Brass is also part of the figurative alloy of Betty Hochstapler’s heart, along with vanadium steel, phosphor bronze and a warmer glowing metal [A:216]. Duffey initially mistakes the nail holding the Royal Pop Historians’ parchment for brass or bronze; it is copper-iron, of old Macedonian workmanship [MTM B11:313].

BraveFinnegan speaks “bravely” when making his rehearsed request for brews to Sergeant Bushmaster [A:13]. The Old Wooden Ship’s fifty regulars are called a brave company [D:216]. BrazilBrazil is the western end of the Atlantic crossing discussed aboard the Brunhilde. After sailing from Natal to Freetown, the narrator says a ship should go from Africa to Brazil, where westward drift assists it; Papadiabolous claims many earlier peoples made that westward passage and that returning was much harder [D:89]. X includes Brazil among countries where Irish teachers could give English an Irish accent [D:279]. It is also the surname of Cicero Brazil among Duffey’s Chicago acquaintances [MTM B3:99].

D:89; D:279; MTM B3:99

Brazil, CiceroOne of the college and university people in Duffey’s Chicago circle during its golden age [MTM B3:99].

BreadBread and wine introduce Melchisedech in the Genesis 14:18 epigraph to Book Two [MTM B2:38]. Young Duffey stocks ten loaves of black bread for his new establishment [MTM B2:41]. Among his Seven Christs is a wheat-and-rye Danish bread head, baked and varnished, which the narrator connects with Corpus Christi loaves [MTM B3:103]. In Ignacio’s moon-voyage story Father Joseph packs bread and wine, wheat and grape cuttings for celebrating Mass [A:271]. The Bohemes eat tough fish with old bread from Lupido’s, and Trinali claims she could feed a multitude [A:234]. Finnegan unloads bread and other provisions at Anastasia’s grandmother’s house [D:126]. Duffey orders pond-scum bread at the extraordinary marine restaurant [MTM B13:417]. Gautier, by contrast, does not bother with bread but boils wheat and eats it with milk and honey [A:197].

MTM B2:38; MTM B2:41; MTM B3:103; A:271; A:234; D:126; MTM B13:417; A:197

Its name recalls the bread and wine of the Melchisedech epigraph [MTM B2:38]. Duffey also has an earlier small Bread and Wine Room at his St. Louis establishment, where he dines with friends [MTM B2:58].

MTM B13:403; MTM B13:422; MTM B2:38; MTM B2:58

BreathingFinnegan hears Marie Courtois’s ecstatic breathing through her hotel-room door before finding her in a cataleptic rapture [D:112]. In the island hammocks, a voice from the sleeping Don Barnaby asks Finnegan to repay Anastasia fifty dollars, and later says it has been dead in the sand for three years; Barnaby’s vigorous, regular breathing is uninterrupted on both occasions [D:238] [D:256]. On the Argo all breathing stops immediately before the Great One appears, then resumes at a different pace [MTM B13:461-462].

BreezeA breeze and a bloom are among the narrator’s comic requirements for an earthly paradise [D:237]. At the bar Finnegan and his companions call Sloppy Joe’s, a light blue breeze ruffles golden air [D:235]. In New Orleans the new breeze of the coming Splendor carries putridity and the smell of change [MTM B11:313]; after the Opera House killings, it blows beneath a jeweled sky, described as new and unlegacied [MTM B11:351].

Brendon, Saint (Brendan the Navigator)Brendan the Navigator, the sixth-century Irish abbot associated with legendary Atlantic voyages. The Chapter Nine epigraph in The Devil Is Dead attributes an account of unredeemable, long-lived species to “Saint Brendon, Trachtas” [D:130]. The title means a treatise, rather than voyages. The Argo’s talking-oak history identifies its Land of Behest phase with St. Brandon’s voyage from Ireland to America, the great fish Jascoyne and the transport of Judas [MTM B13:404]. Biloxi Brannagan identifies himself as an Argo Master by producing a red-gold coin bearing a Celtic cross, a coracle and the name “Naomh Brandon” [MTM B13:425]. These are the cycle’s transformations of the Brendan tradition, not proof of a historical voyage to America.

D:130; MTM B13:404; MTM B13:425

Brewery horsesEdward Ranwick’s disparaging comparison for the sturdy girls of the Bavarian Club. The narrator rejects it, calling them powerful but trim; Helen Platner is one of the girls with whom Duffey is friendly [MTM B2:58].

MTM B2:58

BrewsFinnegan asks Sergeant Bushmaster for a “clutch of brews” while trying to pass as an Australian [A:13]. Patrick Stranahan’s compressed philosophy allows four brews: an American, a Danish, a Bohemian and Guinness [A:110].

A:13; A:110

BrhzhlozhThe intuitive music-writing machine credited with the Bear Ballet at the Decatur Street Opera House. Mary Virginia says Brhzhlozh is only a machine, and Cyrus Roundhead agrees; he explains that the splendid people rejected even keeping a few unmutated humans as composers [MTM B11:349-350]. The machine’s music accompanies the cruel spectacle of bears, net wielders and human victims.

MTM B11:349-350

BrideTheresa Piccone, Show Boat, is Vincent Stranahan’s bride; Finnegan sits on her lap at their wedding reception [A:113]. The earlier Bride and Bridegroom remark in the Lotus Eaters belongs to Marie Monaghan’s engagement celebration with Hans Schultz [A:28-29].

A:113; A:28-29

BridegroomVincent Stranahan is the bridegroom at his wedding to Theresa Piccone, Show Boat [A:113]. In the earlier Lotus Eaters scene, Marie Monaghan speaks of Bride and Bridegroom while celebrating her engagement to Hans Schultz [A:28-29].

A:113; A:28-29

BridgeDuffey emerges from the Sea of Lost Years onto the Mississippi shore below Eads Bridge in St. Louis [MTM B13:465]. In Chicago he identifies himself with the Pont du Sable Traffic Trestle, whose supposedly ornamental support is knocked out; its loss carries weight for him [MTM B3:104-105]. Theresa compares the performer Maria Tornabuoni’s overhang to a Renaissance bridge [A:49], while Hillary Hilton buys an actual bridge in Grundy County with Finnegan accompanying him [A:254]. Hugh Stranahan’s friends play bridge, the card game [A:104]. In Finnegan’s uncertain dream-conversation with Marie Courtois, crossing a bridge figures death and immortality; Marie insists it has only one shore, a belief Finnegan later recalls as she dies [D:91-92] [D:157]. Another dream-bridge takes him from the Naxos mountaintop to a higher, internally lit, translucent mountain, where he pursues the Oreads [D:138].

MTM B13:465; MTM B3:104-105; A:49; A:254; A:104; D:91-92; D:157; D:138

Bridge-playingHugh Stranahan’s bridge-playing friends form one of the many circles of visitors to Patrick and Monica’s house [A:104].

A:104

BrigOne of the vessels in Terry Cork’s comic verse about Dotty: her face launches tugs, tramps, a brig, a coracle and the Bark [MTM B7:214].

MTM B7:214

BrigadierThe unnamed Australian brigadier falsely implicated in the Tania hoax. The conspirators tell Stein that the officer has smuggled a woman onto the island for sexual purposes; Tania is actually Tommy Trouncer in costume [A:51]. Casey urges Stein to enlist officers for a raid and a charge of moral turpitude. The brigadier first thinks an unauthorized woman must be punished, then becomes furious on learning that he is the accused [A:53-54]. Stein’s general access to unusual colonels and brigadiers is mentioned earlier [A:19].

A:51; A:53-54; A:19

BrigandBrigands belong to the Old American Blood and Thunder adventure material Gautier loves in the Harlow House library, alongside train robbers, buffalo hunters, Indian scalpers and bank robbers [A:198].

A:198

Bright SpotDotty’s name for the few remaining sources of good in a world filling with spiritual trash: she says they are mostly themselves, and Duffey agrees that the world still contains many good people. Bagby’s death immediately follows this exchange [MTM B7:236].

MTM B7:236

Brilliant young man with a stutter, TheThe unnamed brilliant man whom the Argo Masters encounter at Weinsburg on the Nechar River. His mind is compared to a burning sphere, and his frustrated fury makes him a dangerous overturner. Duffey says “Ephphatha,” opening his lips and tongue and curing his stutter [MTM B13:430]. The man objects that he never asked for the cure: frustration supplies the anger needed for his destructive mission. Duffey refuses to restore it and leaves with Brannagan. Casey lingers, and the narrator pointedly asks why anyone would give the man his stutter back [MTM B13:431].

MTM B13:430; MTM B13:431

BrimstoneSulfur, associated with diabolic fire. Finnegan tells Theresa Piccone that her baptismal salt flamed on contact with real brimstone and that the font cracked; she answers his witchcraft teasing in kind [A:108]. Brimstone is among the boiling materials used to seal Saint Sécaire’s sword inside its scabbard [MTM B13:422]. Doll’s “Diabolique” calls for salting the buried Devil with sulphur [D:293].

A:108; MTM B13:422; D:293

Brimstone ComboThe band in Trinali’s poem about an old saloon by Beelzebub and Hell-Raiser Streets near Iniquity Square. Birsha plays diatonic harp, Shinar a nine-stringed kithara, Bera a B-flat trumpet, Zoar drums, and Schemember a ram’s horn. The Seven Just Men visit nightly for toddies [A:235]. The names adapt Genesis 14: Bera, Birsha and Shemeber are kings, whereas Shinar is a land and Zoar a city.

A:235

Briquettes (Charcoal)Charcoal briquettes in a two-foot trencher-plate supplied and lit by the hotel waitress when a lawn bonfire is forbidden. The picnic party sits around the small fire singing childhood camp songs [A:30-31].

A:30-31

Brisbane, GilbertOne of the artists whose work Duffey sells and whose creative ideas contribute to the Rebuilding Thesis. He appears in the roster with Rita Tinder and Crystal O’Boyle [MTM B6:198-199].

MTM B6:198-199

BritishSeaworthy claims that a Hindu belief in India as Purgatory has been interpreted as a criticism of life under British rule [D:72]. The Naxos raiders carry Enfield rifles of old British issue [D:136]. The narrator distinguishes the British Basseterre from the French Basse-Terre while stressing Finnegan’s confusion about which island he has reached [D:235].

D:72; D:136; D:235

Brokebolt, Paul CardinalPaul Cardinal Brokenbolt of Freemantle, Australia, whose double is Cecil Octavian of England [MB:579]. The name is printed Brokebolt in the “Deaths of the Cardinals” painting list [MTM B13:452]. He is among the thirteen primaries killed in the Track and Total campaign; his burial stone recalls the Lord walking by the Sea of Galilee and seeing two brothers [MB:588-589].

MB:579; MTM B13:452; MB:588-589

Brokenbolt, Cecil OctavianEarlier heading attached the primary’s surname to his double. See Octavian, Cecil (of England).
BroodA collective word for offspring or creations. X says the perversity in Katie Noonan’s family brood cannot, in his view, be explained by the kind man who adopted Ifreann [D:279]. In the talisman discussion, Duffey is credited with a brood of beautiful, bumptious people whose creation is compared with biological parenthood [MTM B5:165].

D:279; MTM B5:165

BrookFinnegan and Howland wade several brooks or creeks flowing west or southwest during their early northward wanderings toward Chicago [A:178-179].

A:178-179

Brooms (Family)One of the four so-called families, alongside the Darts, Oakleys and Leakys, attacked by a Pattenite in the debate with Duffey. The speaker claims their fossil discoveries support one another circularly and that rift faults invalidate the evidence’s original location [MTM B9:282-283]. The name likely alludes to Robert Broom, the South African palaeontologist associated with important hominin finds. The family grouping and attack are the speaker’s polemic.

MTM B9:282-283

BrotherhoodThe Dirty Five form a mystic brotherhood, compared with the secret societies of the Papuan men around them; its members are Henry, Hans, Vincent, Casey and Finnegan [A:38-39]. The word is used ironically for the psychiatric professionals who cannot appreciate Howell’s humor [A:82-83]. In the Argo episode, the unrecognized Casey Gorshok warns Duffey and Brannagan that failure to recognize a fellow Master could break the Brotherhood [MTM B13:425-426].

A:38-39; A:82-83; MTM B13:425-426

Brown BoxThe Crock’s archive of cards on infiltrators, brought by X from Chicago inside a gray box nested in a black one. Duffey recognizes the archive as the Crock’s property, and X admits stealing it [MTM B6:201-203]. Most cards are in Duffey’s hand; others are by X and fellow contributors. X adds an unnaturally large orange-red card that nevertheless fits inside the small box [MTM B6:203].

MTM B6:201-203; MTM B6:203

Brown Stone Statues of SjahrirThe brown stone statues in Brannagan’s extraordinary stories, said to be people petrified upright by Seti darts dipped in quick-acting juices. Finnegan is willing to accept this, alongside tales of trading Circassian slave-girl futures at Aden and of Prester John in Madagascar, while remaining uncertain how far to trust Brannagan [D:206].

D:206

Brown, Father (Code Name)One of the expert advisers summoned by the Argo Masters, under a name borrowed from G. K. Chesterton’s priest-detective. The narrative allows that such advisers may be fictional persons or actual persons under disguises [MTM B13:455]. Father Brown warns that the hardest intruder to exclude is already inside, then recommends a trusted English bulldog to detect the familiar turning strange and wrong. Duffey accordingly brings Gunboat Smith aboard [MTM B13:457-458].

MTM B13:455; MTM B13:457-458

Browne's PreludeThe music whose first eight bars Finnegan plays softly on his harmonica while urging X to continue the graveyard history [D:285]. The group is at the shared grave of Ifreann and Gregory McIfreann, whom X identifies as Papadiabolous I [D:284-285].

D:285; D:284-285

BrownieA helpful supernatural being, traditionally an elf that works at night. Charley Murray asks whether brownies make Duffey’s otherwise impossible magic props. The narrator calls the term vague but potentially apt for the very large helpers involved, then identifies them as ebony faber-giants working under Duffey’s orders [MTM B1:21].

MTM B1:21

BrownsvilleThe port visited by the Brunhilde the day after Port Isabel. Seaworthy has associates at each stop [D:55].

D:55

Brubaker, GeorgeThe Newark resident whose unlocked car Finnegan takes while fleeing New York with Doll Delancy. From the car’s papers Finn supplies Doll with the identity Mrs. George Brubaker and says he may briefly have to be George himself [D:167-168]. After returning the car to Brubaker’s house, Finn leaves a note signed Roving Magistrate Number Sixteen, admonishing him for leaving it unlocked and ordering him to Room 101 of the Epimetheos Building. Finn does not know whether that building exists [D:169]. He later guesses that the borrowed glasses he wears also belong to Brubaker [D:170].

D:167-168; D:169; D:170

Brubaker, Mrs. GeorgeThe identity Finnegan assigns Doll Delancy while she drives George Brubaker’s stolen car from New York toward its owner’s Newark address [D:167-168]. Half asleep, Finn believes they are stopped and hears her tell a questioner with a flashlight that she is Mrs. George Brubaker and is driving home [D:169].

D:167-168; D:169

BrunhildeSaxon X. Seaworthy’s ship, formerly a millionaire’s steam yacht and now a diesel vessel. The narrator calls her a rakish, welcoming old ship despite the killers and cutthroats she carries [D:21] [D:55]. Captain Orestes Gonof commands a crew including Harry Scott, Don Lewis, Joe Cross, Art Emery and Chris McAbney; Finnegan is also carried as a crewman, under John Solli [D:30] [D:39]. Anastasia Demetriades opens the ship’s small bar [D:22]. Manuel first appears as a stowaway and self-described spy; Papa Devil obtains papers that make him a crew member [D:54-55] [D:59]. Finnegan decorates the bar with Sindbad-voyage panels and works out the living face concealed beneath Papa Devil’s assumed appearance [D:59] [D:62]. Anastasia calls the Brunhilde a plague ship that infects wherever it touches [D:69]. Finnegan, rather than Anastasia explicitly speaking of herself, comes to understand that the water-witch’s true form resembles the ship [D:31]. Joe Cross reports Dopey’s screams and unexplained disappearance from a cabin after Papa Devil enters [D:64]; Papa later leaves open whether he or Finnegan killed Dopey, or whether the double was absorbed into Finn [D:121-122]. Don Lewis is murdered by Marie Courtois ashore at Tangier, and Finnegan buries him in sand [D:110-114]. Later Finn says Marie is dying aboard after Joe Cross shot her during the Naxos battle [D:157]. The coastwise voyage calls at Freeport, Palacios, Port O’Conner, Aransas Pass, Corpus and Padre Island, then Port Isabel and Brownsville [D:34] [D:55]. It continues down Mexico and Central America through Campeche, Progreso, Cozumel, Ciudad Chetumal, Belize, Puerto Barrios, La Ceiba, Trujillo, Cabo Gracias a Dios, Blue Fields, Limon and San Cristobal [D:81]. South American stops include Cayenne, Belem, Sao Luis, Camocim, Fortaleza and Natal [D:86]. Leaving Natal on January 18, the ship reaches Freetown on January 26 [D:89], then goes by Bissau, Bathurst, Dakar, St. Louis, Memrhar, Port Etienne, Villa Cisneros and Las Palmas to the Grand Canary [D:96]. It proceeds through Arrecife on Lanzarote, Ifni, Agadir, Magadar, Safti, Mazagan, Casablanca, Rabat and Tangier [D:101], and onward through Palermo, Messina and Zakinthos to Naxos [D:114-115]. The Argo’s later history explicitly recalls the Brunhilde as a name the ship bore under evil owners, with Finnegan’s paintings still in the Sindbad Lounge [MTM B13:404]. Stein’s notes pose further questions about its place in the sequence of Argo and Barque and the overlap of Finnegan’s experience with Giulio’s [MB:549-550]. Those notes say Finn did not die in the early cabin encounter, while recording his hazy memory of Papa Devil bending over to kill him before his first boarding [MB:548].

D:21; D:55; D:30; D:39; D:22; D:54-55; D:59; D:62; D:69; D:31; D:64; D:121-122; D:110-114; D:157; D:34; D:81; D:86; D:89; D:96; D:101; D:114-115; MTM B13:404; MB:549-550; MB:548

BrunissendeThe heroine named in the Occitan romance Jaufre and Brunissende. Hans meets a poor scholar asking for a quarter to buy it; Hans funds the purchase but buys Les Cents Novelles Nouvelles for himself, and the two read together in a New York park [A:224]. The medieval Jaufre, the sole surviving Arthurian romance in Occitan, follows its knight through combats and courtly trials toward union with Brunissende, lady of Montbrun. Their courtship and eventual marriage combine the Arthurian quest with the culture of southern French romance. Its treatment of chivalry includes comic and critical elements as well as idealized love.

A:224

BrushBrush and bushes provide cover and uncertain boundaries. Finnegan and Anastasia walk through dunes and brush at Padre Island [D:34] [D:38]; at a stop uncertainly identified as Paraiso, Campeche or another port, luxuriant growth over the old walls shelters lizards, snakes and birds [D:67-68]. At Tangier, Finn follows his companions into the weeds and sparse shanties [D:104], then buries Don Lewis in cleaner sand beneath aromatic bushes [D:110]. On Naxos, wine is left in a bush fork [D:126], Oreads emerge from bushes in Finn’s dream [D:137], and Finn and Manuel hide in a thicket after the battle [D:148]. Duffey deliberately chooses thorn hedges in the Delectable Place and discovers a dangerous-looking mechanical lever in the thicket despite Patrick’s warning [MTM B12:391]. The suit-selling Old Dan emerges from bushes, appearing to the naked young customer as perhaps a man or a gnome [A:259]. Ghosts haunt the Barrens and brush in Gautier’s account [A:197], and Elena Musquiz finds the exhausted Finnegan in scrub brush after his buffalo vigil [A:206].

D:34; D:38; D:67-68; D:104; D:110; D:126; D:137; D:148; MTM B12:391; A:259; A:197; A:206

Buffalo (American Bison)The old buffalo bulls of an ancestral city, believed to lie in Frio County just above the fork of two creeks. Finnegan recognizes their distinctive smell and real dung but sees through them, as they seem to see through him, in the altered vision associated with his drinking and life-travel [A:205]. Most of the herd has gone north for summer, leaving sore-footed elders to guard the Capital. Finn sleeps within their circle and feels kinship with their ancient remnant stock; the next morning Elena Musquiz rescues him from the scrub [A:206].

A:205; A:206

Buffalo BarThe bar on Luzon where the Dirty Five drink with their friend Captain Guiterrez, nicknamed Sammy, a young-looking Tagalog officer [A:63] [A:66].

A:63; A:66

Buffalo Hunter and Indian ScalperOne of the adventure subjects listed among Gautier’s old American “Blood and Thunder” romances, the books left after his goats have thinned the Harlow House library [A:198].

BuffoonAccording to Hans, Stein understood and helped devise the practical joke played on him, enjoying the part of the buffoon [A:55]. After shooting Stockton Stone Crocker, Hackenschmidt says Sic simper zannionibus, glossed in the text as “thus ever to buffoons or zanies” [MB:567].

BugFinnegan tells the Muses who visit him in a dream, “Go away, girls, you bug me” [A:181]. In Joe Cross’s account of Dopey’s disappearance, Papa Devil dismisses the blood in the cabin as “Bug blood, I guess” [D:64].

BuggerDon Lewis calls the apparent Japanese soldier whom his patrol pursues “the little bugger” [D:44]. In his account of confronting Castleman, Le Marin substitutes “You’re a bugger and a Turk” for the words he actually used [D:245-246].

BuggernosedDoll Delancy calls Finnegan and X “loop-eared, buggernosed bums” while challenging their dismissal of ordinary people’s power to save themselves [D:291-292].

BuggyBuggies appear in the comic account of Cajun antiquity [A:124] and among Duffey’s private vehicles for outings with Mary Louise and Beth [MTM B2:58]. The Royal Pop History catalogue includes Johnson’s Jump-Seat Buggy [MTM B11:329]. An old horse that pulled a buggy around the French Quarter becomes the first large animal put into the Pot [MTM B6:196]. Tommy Katt calls his vehicle a “buggy” when he helps the wounded Finnegan escape [D:232].

A:124; MTM B2:58; MTM B11:329; MTM B6:196; D:232

Bugle NoseFinnegan’s face is described as a comic mask with a bugle nose [A:6]. Papa Devil calls attention to it [D:23], Anastasia calls Finnegan “buglenosed” [D:24], and Dopey’s writing asks why “bugle nose” is not dead [D:78]. Dotty’s related phrase is “banana-nosed brat” [A:93].

A:6; D:23; D:24; D:78; A:93

BuildingBuildings include the Plaza and its many bars [A:3] [A:88]; the Cat Castle, Patrick Stranahan’s family home [A:102]; the warehouse and loft adjoining the New Orleans print shop, fitted out for a library, institute, auditorium, and living quarters [A:126]; the Federal Buildings where Finnegan might obtain mural commissions [A:184]; and the abandoned Harlow House, sometimes occupied by the goat-man and his goats [A:197]. In The Devil Is Dead, Don Lewis seeks protection at the consulate and at a paid hiding place in Tangier [D:106-108]. Finnegan climbs six stories up a Gothic hotel [D:162], invents an appointment at the possibly nonexistent Epimetheos Building [D:169], drinks at the shady bait house [D:182], and attacks the Pirate Hotel [D:231]. The Old Wooden Ship is a four-story, unpainted, pungent building on a garlic block, with a raked-shell sidewalk, many doors, interior and exterior stairs, loose slat shutters, and a swaying, creaking motion [D:215]. Zabotski’s boat palace on Pristine Cove is called the Big Red Barn [MTM B10:290].

Bulfinch's MythologyThe mythology book from which Duffey says he knows the Argo, when Teresa asks whether he remembers sailing on the ship [MTM B12:386].

MTM B12:386

BullFinnegan is compared to a yearling bull [A:1], and Count Finnegan in the painting retains the strength and speed of a yearling bullock [MTM B12:368] [MB:551]. Mary Louise is figured as the royal bovine or sacred cow [MTM B2:55]. Casey’s imagined women include Cretan girl bull-fighters [A:157], and his school notebook defines a Free Martin as a sterile heifer born twin to a bull calf [A:164]. The Cretan Bull Drama at the Decatur Street Opera House combines athletic displays with the killing of human victims [MTM B11:349]. Bull snakes occur at the Nursery and in the lore of Chosky Bottoms [A:208] [D:274]. Basin Street Becaud plays a bull fiddle and pretends its case holds a shotgun capable of decapitating a bull elephant [D:223]. The bull-sinew bowstring figures the tension between the elements composing humanity [D:283].

Bull snakesSnakes among the wildlife along Hans’s mile-long running route through the Nursery [A:208]. Eighteen-foot bull snakes are also part of the lore of Chosky Bottoms [D:274].

Bull-fighters (Cretan Girl)Women in Casey Szymansky’s second imaginary world, an erotic fantasy populated by figures from history and legend [A:157].

Bulldog (English)Father Brown recommends an English bulldog to detect the moment when something familiar becomes strange and wrong, as protection against the Man of Mystery. Duffey chooses Gunboat Smith, whom he trusts despite Kasmir Gorshok’s objections [MTM B13:458].

Bulldog CourageCourage attributed to Joe Bushmaster’s forebears by his supporters during the drinking contest. Finnegan jokes that some of those forebears were bulldogs [A:23].

BumFinnegan tells Hillary Hilton that the Shaman diagnosed him as a “natural born bum,” and Hilton agrees [A:255]. Giulio Solli, Finnegan’s father, is called a poor bum and is recalled as a dock worker [A:244]. BumiOne of the names of the canoe in the Malayan boy’s account, glossed by him as “of the world.” Its other names are Aral and Aragh, and the Sergeant recognizes it as the Argo [A:89].

BurglarsJohn (Little Alcohol) Indelecio and John (Big Alcohol) Jereboam, among the Old Wooden Ship’s characters, work as burglars: Little Alcohol climbs to high windows, while Big Alcohol handles drilling and prying [D:218]. Burglary (Upper-story)Finnegan has recently committed several upper-story burglaries to obtain evidence, rather than money, before he perches like a living gargoyle on a Gothic hotel [D:162].

BurialFinnegan helps Saxon Seaworthy bury Papadiabolous I in an already occupied grave [D:75-76] [D:84] [D:153]. X later identifies the older occupant as their father, called Ifreann, buried in 1930 [D:285] [D:288]; the stone is inscribed I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch [D:277]. The ground has split since the second burial [D:293]. Finnegan buries Don Lewis in clean sand near Tangier [D:110-111], recalling Don’s account of burying Yokipoki in mud [D:46]. Anastasia receives a lavish funeral, which X thinks Seaworthy arranged [D:157].

BurlesquePapa Piccone defends the Star and Garter’s shows as burlesque in the original sense, despite threats to close the theatre unless it drops the designation [A:48]. Finnegan’s cigar-store Indian carvings also have a touch of burlesque [A:183], and Anastasia can appear as a “burlesque of the pretty” [D:20]. Piccone’s account of Oscar Oliver Omygosh turns on the failure of a stage caricature when its original appears in person [MTM B5:168]. Burlesque is also among the popular arts described as being systematically degraded [MTM B6:207]. These uses connect theatrical entertainment with comic distortion.

Burton, Sir Richard Francis (1821--1890)English explorer, soldier, linguist, diplomat, and translator (1821-1890). The introduction to The Devil Is Dead invokes “Old Burton” and his warning that subscribers should keep their copies of the Nights under lock and key [D:7]. His Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, privately published under the Kama Shastra Society imprint from 1885, is unexpurgated, uses deliberately archaic language, and carries extensive notes on customs and sexuality. It also draws heavily on John Payne’s earlier English translation. Burton’s other publishing ventures included the Kama Sutra and The Perfumed Garden. He visited Mecca in disguise in 1853, explored East Africa with John Hanning Speke, and held consular appointments including Fernando Po, Damascus, and Trieste. He died in Trieste.

D:7

BushX tells Absalom Stein that he has seen the burning bush and must wander forty years in the desert [A:265-266]. Other settings include the scrub brush where Elena Musquiz rescues Finnegan [A:206], the haunted brush near the Harlow House [A:197], and the bushes from which the suit-selling, gnome-like stranger emerges [A:259]. Finnegan and Anastasia walk through dunes and brush [D:38]; on Naxos they leave wine in the fork of a bush [D:126], Oreads emerge from bushes in Finnegan’s dream [D:137], and Finnegan and Manuel later hide in a thicket [D:148]. Aromatic bushes cover the place Finnegan chooses for Don Lewis’s grave [D:110]. Duffey deliberately leaves the green way to enter thorn hedges in the Delectable Place [MTM B12:391-392]. See Brush.

A:265-266; A:206; A:197; A:259; D:38; D:126; D:137; D:148; D:110; MTM B12:391-392

Bushmaster, JoeAustralian sergeant on orderly duty at the wet canteen, described as larger and fiercer-looking than a gorilla [A:12]. He joins the joke played on Finnegan and Vincent, including the fictitious beer-chit requirement [A:13-14], but stops the torment because he dislikes seeing innocents suffer [A:14]. Calling himself the world’s heavyweight drinking champion, he agrees to face Hans Schultz [A:15]; Jimmy Hansen advertises him as the “Lion of the South” [A:19]. His confidence gives way to worry and panic as Hans drinks steadily ahead of him [A:20-21]. He finally fails to finish a glass after four hours and twenty minutes [A:23].

A:12; A:13-14; A:14; A:15; A:19; A:20-21; A:23

Busker (Street)Finnegan plays the concertina in bars and streets during the Ignacio and Elena episode. Ignacio thinks it undignified for a Yankee to play in the streets. Elena accompanies the instrument she sold him, and later Finnegan refuses to play for rude visitors [A:272-273]. The passage describes street performance but does not establish that busking was his youthful occupation.

A:272-273

BustThe Ambrosian bust of Homer appears in the chapter-opening discussion of supposedly Neanderthal features and capacities [D:270-271].

D:270-271

BusterUnverified term. The earlier glossary attributes “Buster” to Casey and Seaworthy as a name for Finnegan; neither claimed use has been located.
BusybodyUnverified attribution. No supporting passage has been located for Casey calling Duffey a busybody because of his interference.
ButcherIn Don Lewis’s story, Yokipoki has a double-edged butcher knife, which Don uses while digging his grave [D:46]. Don imagines that the dead man is cutting his bonds and attacking him with it, then discovers rats at the body [D:47]. A butcher also buys Homer Hochheimer’s purple cow in Marie’s anecdote [A:24].

D:46; D:47; A:24

ButlerSurname of Buttercup Butler, the perennial senior who serves as room captain in Casey’s chamber at St. Bonaventure’s [A:161-162]. See Butler, Buttercup.

A:161-162

Butler, ButtercupPerennial senior and room captain in Casey Szymansky’s six-boy chamber at St. Bonaventure’s. Smallest of the boys, he looks like an owl, has some wit, and gives little help with lessons [A:161-162].

A:161-162

ButterflyX’s conspicuous eight-toned car is called a “butterfly.” He argues that its very conspicuousness will confound pursuers, then admits Doll is right that he simply fell in love with it [D:179-180]. Butterflies gather at the old wood graveyard [A:233]. Gloria Mullens calls her supposedly dead husband a grasshopper and a butterfly, describing his improvident character rather than a literal transformation [MTM B3:79].

D:179-180; A:233; MTM B3:79

BuzzardsBuzzards attack Duffey with “knifie beaks” after he falls into the dung heap [MTM B12:392-393]. Casey’s attack on the Bark remarks that “even buzzards sometimes gag,” referring to Finnegan’s departure [A:128-129]. Zabotski compares the strange episode hanging over the town to a fancy-Dan buzzard with peacock feathers [MTM B11:306-307].

MTM B12:392-393; A:128-129; MTM B11:306-307

Byrne, Mary LouiseSee Bagby, Mary Louise (Byrne).
Byzantine Empire/styleUnverified composite entry. The earlier glossary connects Byzantine history and iconoclasm with Professor Kirol and compares Anastasia’s story to a Byzantine puzzle. Supporting passages for these connections have not been located.
CabalaThe Jewish mystical tradition also called Kabbalah. The novels use “cabalistic” more loosely for mysterious signs: Finnegan invents meaningless markings on a lead weight [D:164], and teasingly tells Theresa that witches have marks on their fingernails which appear on Fridays [A:107-108]. These passages do not identify particular symbols from Jewish mysticism.

D:164; A:107-108

Cabalistic MarkingsMeaningless signs invented by Finnegan and marked on the lead weight he uses to break a window during his attack on the meeting in the Gothic hotel [D:162-164].

D:162-164

CabbageOne of the foods served at the Colony Club’s Harvesters’ Dinner, alongside kale and sauerkraut [MTM B3:94].

MTM B3:94

CabbyJoe Sorrell, who drives Finnegan and Anastasia across to the bay side to visit the Brunhilde [D:21].

D:21

CabinFinnegan shares a cabin on the Brunhilde with Don Lewis and Joe Cross [D:31]. In Joe’s account, Papa Devil enters while Dopey is alone in the bunk; Joe hears two screams, then a third cut short. When he enters, only Papa Devil and a little blood remain, although Dopey could not have escaped [D:64]. Finnegan later senses Dopey’s dead presence there [D:78].

D:31; D:64; D:78

Cabinet headAn unnamed minister imagined as losing sleep over Seaworthy and Papa Devil’s conspicuous company while they dine on the Grand Canary [D:99-100].

D:99-100

Cabinet MakerOne of Duffey’s natural crafts, alongside carpentry and joinery [MTM B1:21]. Bagby also has a cabinet shop adjoining Duffey’s premises; both buildings are made of fine walnut [MTM B2:46].

MTM B1:21; MTM B2:46

Cable exercisesPart of Hans Schultz’s physical training, drawn from mail-order muscle builders as he strives to match his father John William’s strength [A:208].

CablesThe giant spider’s web in Hans’s climbing dream has cable-like threads eight inches thick [A:61]. Duffey climbs through hidden cables and struts above a stage to investigate the Majesty [MTM B8:240]. In the Great Day’s disordered streets, severed electrical feeders leave wires dangling and sparking above a dead child [GD:488].

A:61; MTM B8:240; GD:488

Cabo Gracias a DiosCape on the Caribbean coast at the Honduras-Nicaragua boundary. Cabo Gracias a Dios appears among the Brunhilde’s stops, after Trujillo and before Blue Fields [D:81].

D:81

Cabo RojoOne of the seven false or shoal passages through the Antilles in Angela Cosquin’s account of her father’s shipwreck maps. Her list also names Jardines Banks, Vieques, St. Barthelemy, the Basseterre-Nevis passage, the Basse-Terre-Marie Galante passage, and the Grenadines [D:259-260].

D:259-260

CabriolarOne of the Spanish “goatish verbs” offered by Gautier in his discussion of Finnegan’s “cut capers” pun; it names the capering side of the joke, paired with capar [A:196] [A:199].

A:196; A:199

CabronSpanish for a male goat, given as cabron by Gautier in his explanation of Finnegan’s goat pun [A:196] [A:199]. The usual Spanish spelling is cabrón.

A:196; A:199

Cacciatore, BernyWriter for the Sporting News Sheet and companion of Gabrielovitch and Bulo Belonki on their early-morning rounds of the bars [A:126]. He tells the Pelican group that Finnegan boxed before the war under the name Solli and was good at it, a fact even Dotty had not known [A:127]. He is later described as the finest historian of boxing and other sports [MTM B11:322].

A:126; A:127; MTM B11:322

Cactus kingdomThe noon-day devils’ offer to Finnegan in the heat of the chaparral. He sees that their promised kingdom is only the cactus country already available to him [A:205].

A:205

Cadensus, CatherineDescribed as the prettiest girl staying at the Old Wooden Ship. She goes about with Vivian Gilligan, Ouida Garrard, and Mercedes Morrero; the four draw admiring attention in the bar. Finnegan comes increasingly often to see Catherine, although he stays to look at Mercedes [D:224].

D:224

CadesBiblical Kadesh, named in Melchisedech’s psalm exchange with Finnegan: “The Lord shakes the desert of Cades” [MTM B12:375]. The passage corresponds to Psalm 29:8, numbered Psalm 28:8 in the Douay-Rheims Bible.

MTM B12:375

CaiOne of the places where summer is eternal in the verse opening the Finnegan chapter of Archipelago [A:171].

A:171

CainSon of Adam and Eve, introduced before his brother Abel in Genesis 4. During his Transport, Finnegan asks whether Cain belonged to his own older people and links the question to the facial mark or protuberance “like another nose” [D:212-213].

D:212-213

CajunThe south-Louisiana people whose history includes the settlement of Acadian exiles. Henry Salvatore is explicitly identified as Cajun [A:123]. His cousins send seasonal produce for Duffey’s soup by intercoastal-canal boatmen [A:134]. Ouida Garrard is also Cajun [D:224], and Cajun French is one ingredient of Finnegan’s speech [A:6]. A Cajun riverman receives the talisman from which Henri Salvatore is said to originate [MTM B5:152]; “Henri” is pronounced “Onree” in the Cajun fashion [MTM B6:195]. In “Great Day in the Morning,” Duffy supposes that drunken Cajuns must have assembled the disorderly newspaper [GD:486].

A:123; A:134; D:224; A:6; MTM B5:152; MTM B6:195; GD:486

Cajun FrenchOne of the elements of Finnegan’s mixed New Orleans dialect. The narrator describes it as a “shapeless drift of Cajun French come to town” [A:6].

A:6

CakeFinnegan and Doll have coffee and cakes at the station before leaving Newark [D:169-170]. Doll also brings cakes to the graveyard picnic; when X calls them devil’s food, she corrects him that they are gingerbread [D:277] [D:284]. The Widow Waldo brings freshly made cakes with coffee [MTM B6:196]. Duffey’s first talisman goes to an Italian pushcart seller of little cakes when Duffey is no more than three [MTM B1:18]. Lily orders a sixty-four-inch-square cake, about three feet high and nine hundred pounds, for the birthday she declares Duffey’s four-thousandth [MTM B8:257]. In the Majesty’s speech, hatred is “both the cake and the frosting on the cake” [MTM B8:242].

D:169-170; D:277; D:284; MTM B6:196; MTM B1:18; MTM B8:257; MTM B8:242

CalfFinnegan’s psalm prayer makes Lebanon skip like a calf [MTM B12:375], corresponding to Psalm 29:6. Casey’s notebook defines a Free Martin as a sterile heifer born twin to a bull calf [A:164]. Dotty compares Finnegan to a wandering calf her family eventually butchered [A:95-96]. Loy writes that her father killed the fatted calf for his returning prodigal daughter [A:27].

MTM B12:375; A:164; A:95-96; A:27

CaliforniaThe location of an unpublished Man from Uncle manuscript mentioned by Rick Norwood in the publisher’s back matter to Archipelago [A:285]. The name also occurs in California Street [MTM B1:25], California Fruit chewing gum [MTM B1:26], and California Bucking Rolls [MTM B2:45-46]. These names alone do not place Duffey’s school or establish where the products were made.

A:285; MTM B1:25; MTM B1:26; MTM B2:45-46

California Bucking RollsOne explanation offered for the padded leather straps found in Duffey’s former livery stable: fittings that can be added to an ordinary saddle to make it suitable for breaking horses [MTM B2:45-46].

California Fruit Chewing GumOne of the goods sold during the boys’ secret nighttime sales at school, alongside drinks, sweets, and pigs’ feet [MTM B1:25-26].

MTM B1:25-26

California StreetStreet named in the account of Duffey and his friends returning to school after ten at night. The narrator immediately qualifies it as whatever street, in whatever town, provided the scene that year [MTM B1:25].

MTM B1:25

Call boxThe supposed place where unforwarded letters await Finnegan, one of the reasons he offers himself for leaving Paradise [D:267].

D:267

CallagyOne of the leaders who try to rally the old-line people against the Royal Pop People, alongside Fitzherbert, Chastellain, Faucher, Panebianco, Cassady, and Loubet. The leaders either join the new people or perish, but the text does not specify which fate belongs to Callagy [MTM B11:335].

Calumet, AliceOne of the pleasant, competent, interesting, but “slippery” people in Duffey’s Chicago circle, printed as “Alive Calumet” in that list [MTM B3:100]. With Olivia Hallahan, Shirley Israel, and Josephine McSorley, Alice hisses at Demetrio Glauch when he rejects their entertainment and leaves [MTM B4:127].

MTM B3:100; MTM B4:127

Calumet, JohnMember of Duffey’s Chicago circle, listed with Alice Calumet among its “slippery” people [MTM B3:100] [MTM B4:127]. He stays at the supper after Demetrio Glauch leaves; the Calumets belong to the group that later seeks to keep Duffey close and use his magic [MTM B4:127] [MTM B4:137].

MTM B3:100; MTM B4:127; MTM B4:137

CalumetsJohn and Alice Calumet belong to the social circle that seeks to keep Duffey close and exploit his supposed magic, while promoting the reputation of salons allegedly superior to his [MTM B4:127] [MTM B4:137].

Calvados, Dry GulchEarlier heading that reversed letters in the surname. See Cavaldos, Dry Gulch.
CambeltownNew South Wales location named in the heading of Loy Larkin’s letter to Finnegan, dated Thursday, February 11, 1943 [A:27].

A:27

CamelHoneybucket owns a camel left over from an unsuccessful amusement-park ride; it eats weeds behind the Old Wooden Ship. He claims to have twenty milk camels and a plankton-feed business, with camels the first animals willing to eat the feed, but the narrator explains that he has never tried the scheme or even seen plankton [D:219]. Camel-hair tents belong to Duffey’s remote childhood memories, and his Boy King realm includes silk from camel, ass, ewe, and gazelle [MTM B1:6] [MTM B1:17]. Piccone calls camels natural burlesques that cannot be burlesqued further [MTM B5:167].

D:219; MTM B1:6; MTM B1:17; MTM B5:167

CampecheA stop on the Brunhilde’s voyage down the Mexican coast [D:81]. Campeche, Paraiso, or another stop may be the setting of The Unaccountable Corpse, and either may also be where Don Lewis had a seaman knifed and left behind to divert suspicion from himself [D:67] [D:105]. In the geography of San Simeon, Campeche is one of five more powerful neighboring countries to which San Simeon pays gold tribute [MB:559].

D:81; D:67; D:105; MB:559

Campeche BankThe Campeche Banks mark the far reach of the intermittent and sometimes ghostly shoal waters north of San Simeon, more than a hundred kilometers from its north coast [MB:559]. After two bells arrive at the mooring rock, the people install about a hundred more along the coast and shoals as far as “Campche Bank” and Perez Island [MB:577-578].

MB:559; MB:577-578

Campfire songsChildhood songs sung by the picnic party at the Bay Hotel around a charcoal-filled trencher: “Clementine,” “Ivan Scravinski Scravar,” “Red Wing,” “Casey Jones,” “Camp Town Race Track,” “Rye Whisky,” “Trail of the Lonesome Pine,” “I Wonder Who’s Kissing Her Now,” “Frankie and Johnny,” “Stardust,” “Waltzing Matilda,” and “There’s a Long Long Trail A-Winding” [A:29-31].

A:29-31

CanaSite of the wedding at which Jesus turns water into wine in John 2:1-11. Maurine tells Mamma Monica that Papa Piccone is supplying three barrels and additional jugs for the reception because he refuses to be remembered for running out of wine as the hosts at Cana were [A:105].

A:105

CanadaSource of the liquor that, in Charlotte Mullens’s account, Aga Gonof’s boats bring to Chicago, Detroit, and Cleveland [MTM B3:83-84].

CanalHenry’s cousins send produce from Cajun country for Duffey’s soup by the intercoastal-canal boatmen [A:134]. In a separate anatomical usage, “linkage patterns of Volkman canals” appear among the purported tests establishing Duffey’s great age in an excerpt from The Eighteenth Book of Strange Encounters [MTM B8:250].

A:134; MTM B8:250

Canary (bird)Hans’s stage command makes Mabel the bear imitate a canary by squealing and flapping her legs like wings [A:219]. Le Marin compares the disappearance of the Sarcophagus crew to a cat reporting an empty canary cage, with the incriminating signs still visible, suggesting that the predator’s own account reveals the answer [D:245].

A:219; D:245

Canary (Grand)Island where the Brunhilde party stops for two days [D:96]. At its luxurious night restaurant, Papa Devil dons a monocle and resembles Count von Baummenbauch; other distinguished diners stare at Seaworthy’s party [D:99-100]. Finnegan’s brandy drinking there is recalled in Archipelago [A:188]. Absalom Stein later says he watched the party dine there in “death-like glitter” but could not cross the room to them [MB:549-550]. Don Lewis tells Finnegan that the world is on fire and that they have been lighting the fuses [D:99].

D:96; D:99-100; A:188; MB:549-550; D:99

CandlelightLupido favors candlelight in his cafe and gives Trinali his candle stubs; she also steals the long candles [A:228]. Duffey’s formal balloon dinner is held by candlelight high above the city in the “late-ish darkness” [MTM B2:65].

A:228; MTM B2:65

CandlesCandlelight or kerosene lamps illuminate Duffey’s school-store sales from ten-thirty to midnight and help Charley Murray’s magic tricks [MTM B1:26]. In Finnegan’s night-dune imaginary, people have candle-lit pumpkin heads [D:50]. Trinali uses candles after her electricity is cut off, receiving stubs and stealing longer candles from Lupido’s cafe [A:228]. Four thousand candles are lit on the cake for Duffey’s birthday [MTM B8:257]. Duffey blows out the candles at the end of his balloon dinner before descending [MTM B2:65-66].

MTM B1:26; D:50; A:228; MTM B8:257; MTM B2:65-66

CandySold nightly with sandwiches in Duffey’s school store, whose larger stock includes drinks and pigs’ feet [MTM B1:26]. In Elroy Redheart’s miniature art tableau, an opened candy box beside a dead girl contains her removed heart as an oversized red chocolate; a Jill of Hearts card is pinned beside the scene [MTM B7:221].

MTM B1:26; MTM B7:221

Canned Goods (Doubtful)Uncertain merchandise used by Hillary Hilton as a comparison in discussing distressed stock. He would rather deal in distressed cigars than doubtful canned goods; distressed eggs are worse still [A:253].

A:253

CannibalFinnegan’s response to Hans’s hints about unfamiliar meat invokes the cannibal story he attributes to Melville and calls partly phony [A:58]. Hans objects that “cannibal” is too common and says that initiates use “necrophagists”; the exchange leaves the nature of their meal uncertain [A:59].

A:58; A:59

Cannibal Duffey's Irish RestaurantGarish sign painted on the Big Pot by three medical-student jazzers, tightly enough to remain bright almost forever. The same men are suspected of planting the human bones they fish out of the stew; the sign is generally taken in good humor [MTM B6:197].

MTM B6:197

CannibalismOne of the activities an unnamed mother predicts people will seek out through the Casey Machine. Rejecting her daughter’s hope that users will choose the best of others’ lives, she expects scandal, cruelty, and knowledge useful for personal ruin [CM:505].

CM:505

Cannon, OrvilleSee Howland, Orville Cannon.
CanoeVessel from which the Sergeant and the Malayan boy dive among the islands. The boy names it Aral, Bumi, and Aragh, glossing these as “hindrance,” “of the world,” and “the direction”; the Sergeant then recognizes it as the Ship Argo [A:89].

A:89

CanonicalUsed for the established account of Finnegan’s adventures, which the narrator says cannot be separated from their apocrypha [A:187]. Duffey’s possible deaths in different times prompt the question whether there is a canonical impediment to dying twice [MTM B12:361]. The narrative’s “canonical ratio” is one corrupt priest in twelve, one devil-serving nun in twelve, and one lay participant in the abomination in twelve [MTM B8:245].

A:187; MTM B12:361; MTM B8:245

Cant (Riming)Rhyming patter invoked in Finnegan’s “Antipodal Ode to Loy Larkin”: “And cut your teeth on riming cant” [A:32].

A:32

CantinaDrinking place on the corner near the Mogul’s quarters, from which several of his guards return after a late drink, according to X [MB:573].

MB:573

Cap (Hat)Finnegan wears an oversized digger hat while pretending to be Australian and later regrets giving it up [A:13] [A:15]. Sammy leaves his cap on a table while Finnegan prepares to distract him [A:67]. In Bagby’s image of the seven-headed enemy, one head wears a red stocking cap [MTM B5:169].

A:13; A:15; A:67; MTM B5:169

Cape (Clothing)Duffey imagines Absalom Stein in a purple cape with scarlet lining, although Stein actually wears an unfigured sports shirt [MTM B5:161]. Monsignor X returns secretly to the Argo in red robes and a red-piped cape [MTM B13:451]. At the graveyard meeting, X wears his old magician’s cloak, full of pockets and concealed drops, from his career as X-Capo [D:276].

MTM B5:161; MTM B13:451; D:276

Cape (Geographical)Coastal headland. The Cape of Delgan appears in a travel poem as a place where gold lies unclaimed on the ground [A:172]. “The Horn” appears in Finnegan’s joke about Hans and Marie swimming by the long route when the canal would be shorter [A:30].

A:172; A:30

Cape buffaloComparison for Henry Salvatore’s strength during his years as a merchant seaman: his apparent fat is deceptive, and he has never been beaten in a fight [A:124].

A:124

CapellaUnverified reference. The earlier glossary identifies Capella as a star by which Gomez sails, but the cited passage does not establish this.
CapersDancing and playing tricks, in Finnegan’s explanation of his joke about Castrador-Capros, who “cut capers.” He offers fare delle capriole and castrare becchi as the two senses, while the goat-man criticizes the pun’s language [A:199].

A:199

Capital (Buffalo)The buffalo herd’s center, guarded in high summer by old bulls while the rest of the herd has moved hundreds of miles north. Finnegan sleeps within their circle [A:206].

A:206

Capital (City)New York is Patrick Stranahan’s “Capital (as it were)” in his list of gracious American cities [A:110]. Separately, X’s newly purchased car bears a D.C. plate [D:177].

A:110; D:177

Capital (Financial)Casey mistakes his prosperous father Gabriel Szymansky for a poor man because Gabriel bargains tightly and is stingy; Gabriel runs adjoining antique and pawn shops [A:160]. Casey later inherits money from his father’s estate, spends much of it, keeps careful accounts, and never runs out [A:168].

A:160; A:168

Capital (Goat)Earlier mislabel for the buffalo herd’s capital. See Capital (Buffalo) [A:206].

A:206

CapitalismUnverified attribution. No passage has been located for the earlier glossary’s claim that Papadiabolous practices State Capitalism.
Capo, X- (alias)X-Capo, Mr. X’s former stage name as a magician and escape artist. His many-pocketed cloak at the graveyard is the same one he used in that career [D:276]. See Great X-Capo, The.

D:276

CapoteUnverified entry. The earlier glossary combines a cape or cloak with a person called El Capote, but neither intended source reference has been established.
CapricornZodiac sign singled out by an absurd new traffic signal during the Great Day: “Capricorns should not cross any streets today.” Another signal permanently forbids Leos to cross [GD:488].

GD:488

CaptainSeveral figures bear the title. Captain Guiterrez, nicknamed Sammy, is a youthful-looking Tagalog friend of the Dirty Fivers; he borrows a shoeshine box without its owners’ knowledge to earn more drinking money, and joins the singing and night in the horse pasture [A:66-69]. Orestes Gonof is the “forgotten captain” of the Brunhilde, imagined as an ancient Phoenician at the Grand Canary dinner [D:100]. An unnamed army captain cruelly interrogates the amnesiac Sergeant until he breaks; the Sergeant then promises to find and torment him in Hell [A:73-74]. The haberdasher is acting captain and pilot of the Seabach [D:135], and the fleshless Melchisedech is pilot and captain aboard the Argo [MB:591-592].

A:66-69; D:100; A:73-74; D:135; MB:591-592

Captain Cook (Bar)Pub visited by the four Dirty Fivers, Marie, Tom, and Freddy after Hans defeats Bushmaster in the drinking contest. Their crawl continues to Blarney’s, the Dutchman’s, and the Commodore before they take Hans home to bed [A:23].

A:23

Captain JusticeOne of three comic strips in which Dotty Yekouris has seen the Slant-Faced Men, alongside Flame Man and The White Avenger. Dotty says she could find them comic if she did not know they were real; Margaret Stone stresses that they actually kill people [MTM B7:225].

MTM B7:225

Capuchin priest, TheYoung Greek Capuchin whom Finnegan finds on Naxos on Passion Sunday to hear his confession before Mass. Finnegan initially assumes he is Italian; the priest speaks Italian but reproaches Solli for not knowing better Greek [D:118-119]. When Finnegan describes another person or kindred within him and doubts that he is human, the priest accepts that such another kindred exists and assumes salvation is available to it. He absolves Finnegan’s present person “in all its aspects” [D:119-120].

D:118-119; D:119-120

Caravan boyOne of Joseph’s former occupations. He tells Finnegan that his caravan journeys taught him Arabic and French [D:93-94].

D:93-94

CarbineA short, light rifle. The narrator describes Nick the Rattle’s weapon during the beach shooting as “greater than a carbine and less than a rifle” [A:282].

A:282

Carbon balancesOne of the apparent records of the earth’s age in Vincent’s speculation that the universe might have been created ten minutes ago. Carbon balances, partly exhausted atomic clocks, and ancient sediments would then have been created with it [A:56].

A:56

Carbon FourteenGertrude Brannagan’s comparison for the phrase “Argo Fourteen,” which sounds to her like a cosmic dating method such as Carbon Fourteen. Duffey replies that the Argo really is a dating clock, with logs extending far into the past and partly into the future [MTM B13:410-411].

MTM B13:410-411

Card sharpsArt (One Shot) Yodel and Art (Two Shot) Welch, unsuccessful card sharps and tricksters at the Old Wooden Ship who are repeatedly beaten by more skillful sharpies [D:221]. The earlier resident list gives the first name as Ant (One Shot) Yoder [D:216].

D:221; D:216

Card-carrying CommunistCasey’s accusation against Absalom Stein in the Crock attack on the Bark: he calls Stein a card-carrying Communist under the name Hugo Stone [A:128-129].

Cardigan-Pembroke, LloydWelsh pig butcher of Tywyn listed as the double of David Cardinal Lloyd Spencer of Cardiff [MB:579]. CardinalA prince of the Church. Manuel is described as a man accustomed to dining with cardinals and ministers of state [D:100]. In X's account of the Devil's release from imprisonment in the Crimea, Catholic cardinals are disproportionately represented among the spectators; several prostrate themselves before the Devil [MTM B6:205-206].

In Book Thirteen, X brings Duffey a flayed skin said to be Cardinal Artemis's. Its markings cannot securely distinguish Artemis from his double, Gilberto [MTM B13:451-452]. Finnegan paints thirteen executions or murders in the Deaths of the Cardinals series on the bulkheads of the Argo's Bread and Wine Room; Salvatore, one of the subjects, is an Argo Master [MTM B13:452]. Finnegan subsequently says that the thirteen supposed doubles include one surviving holy man, whose presence preserves the line [MTM B13:453].

In How Many Miles to Babylon, John Mogul's Track and Total hunts the thirteen cardinals and their doubles [MB:578-580]. The list names Hedayat, Brokenbolt, Ti, Merry, Leviathan, Artemis, Lloyd Spencer, Salvatore, Gregorio, Doki, Gabrailovitch, Erculo, and Runosake; some names differ in spelling or form from the Book Thirteen list. Roughly five hundred abdicated cardinals are also still alive. Mogul solicits methods of murder through a public contest, to which the hunted cardinals and their doubles themselves contribute [MB:579-580].

Casey MachineAn “Achronological Eaves-Dropping Machine,” encountered in coin parlors, tea rooms, and bars, through which users gain access to other people’s lives and thoughts. Newton Prescott recounts its history in a journal intended to treat his compulsion to forget it [CM:503-504]. Josephine McSorely’s account traces its origin to a gathering that performs its own Particular Judgment; Casey supplies the impulse of invasive curiosity but denies the machine’s existence and tries to withdraw his contribution [CM:506-507]. Prescott credits Casey, his own electronics, and the promoters together. He gives the devices charges collected after clinical death and, for added effect, dead people’s eyes [CM:507-509].

The machine develops within the wider Casey Condition. According to Prescott, everyone can read the minds, bodies, memories, and unconscious lives of the living, the dead, and the unborn, because all time is simultaneously accessible. The physical machines become unnecessary, though their trade remains profitable [CM:510-512]. The initial demand is largely for sexual exposure, slander, and blackmailing knowledge. But others find that fuller knowledge increases their love for people. Their appeal to grace and good will disputes Prescott’s assumption that degradation must prevail [CM:505] [CM:511-512].

The Condition occupies an abiding moment which, Prescott says, can remain eternal although people enter and leave it. Anticipating collective forgetfulness, he arranges perpetual federal payments and has a memory capsule implanted in his brain [CM:512-513]. The mania is forgotten; its emotional and historical contents are said to enter the earth’s forces. Prescott has the capsule removed and can no longer understand most of his own journal, though the money continues to arrive [CM:514-515].

The Addenda complicate this account. Prescott identifies himself as a ghostly fragment of Casey’s personality, moving through time as Casey’s eyes and ears. He describes a subscription device that hooks wealthy listeners and claims that Casey transfers his guilt to him. These are Prescott’s assertions, including his suspicion that the transfer has deceived God [CM:515-516].

Catherine (Saint)Saint seen beside Barbara aboard the Navicula Petri in Henry’s dream; both look like sea-urchins. The passage names her only Catherine, so identification with Alexandria or Siena remains uncertain [A:44-45]. Catherine of Siena lived in 1347-1380. The martyr legend belongs instead to Catherine of Alexandria: a learned noblewoman traditionally placed in the early fourth century, who defends Christianity before the emperor’s philosophers and converts them, survives the miraculous breaking of the wheel intended for her execution, and is beheaded. Traditions also associate her with the conversion of the empress and with the Fourteen Holy Helpers. Her book and wheel mark her learning and martyrdom; she is commemorated on November 25 in Catholic and Greek usage. The details of her life are historically uncertain, and her Roman-calendar observance, removed in 1969, was restored in 2002 as an optional memorial.

A:44-45

Catherine, TheName of the Argo when Dana Coscuin takes her around the Horn [MTM B13:405]. In Half a Sky, the ship is first La Catalina, encountered repeatedly at Guayaquil. Before buying her, Dana places a splinter of his murdered wife Catherine Dembinska’s skull aboard, joining ship and bride in a ghostly marriage. Valiente Tirana supplies the additional money for purchase and refitting. Dana outfits her with nine brass cannon, a crew including Damisa and Serafino, blue and green sails, and a ghost-green hull; her new name is painted Catherine Dembinska. Sailing against the Humboldt current, she is haunted by the stowaway Ifreann Chortovitch, whose malign influence, theft, and murder provoke an unsuccessful search and a priest’s prayers at Tocopillo. Following a wise woman’s advice, Dana baits Ifreann into the hold; Dana, Damisa, Serafino, and Osborne eventually throw him overboard. Later the crew remember incompatible mundane versions of these events. The near-invisible Catherine breaks the sea-siege of Valparaiso, destroying the revolutionary gunships and altering history and memory. On the voyage around the Horn she damages Ifreann’s pursuing ironclad Brami Piekielne, the Gates of Hell, and escapes to repair at Bahia Blanca. In early 1854 she reaches Basse-Terre. During the earthquake, Angelene, briefly the messenger who orders Dana to Carloforte, then tells him to bury the ship at the shoal called the Grave of Catarina Dama Binación. Dana describes the ship as his wife’s body during her purgatorial stay. With Jack Galopade he deliberately floods her; Catherine’s spirit departs as the ship explodes, and the vessel is destroyed in the encounter with Ifreann’s ship. (Half a Sky, PDF pp. 102, 105-108, 110-111, 116, 120, 122-124, 134, 138-139, 146, 151-153, 184, 198-199, 201-203).

Catholic Center Party of AmericaDuffey’s political party, of which Casey says he is the sole member: “He is the Party.” Casey, d’Allesandro, Mary Frances, and Demetrio Glauch are prospective recruits rather than enrolled members [A:42].

Catholic ChurchThe Church is central to the characters’ religious and political disputes. Casey describes Duffey’s one-man Catholic Center Party and his index of supposed infiltrators in Catholic lay groups [A:42-43]. Henry fears a Secular-Liberal Religion working from inside the Church but containing no Catholic element [A:125]. Casey attacks the Bark’s claim to be a Catholic publication, emphasizing its lack of ecclesiastical sanction [A:128]. Duffey visits Chicago’s stone, angel-covered St. Malachy’s, whose ruddy turrets catch the morning sun [MTM B3:87-88]. X’s family story invokes the parish records of St. Elmo near Krakow and says landed Catholic families employed Irish governesses for religious teaching and manners [D:279]. In X’s account of the Devil’s release, Catholic clergy are among the gathered notables and some cardinals worship the released Devil [MTM B6:204-206]. Duffey also reports X’s unreliable claim that Finnegan was secretly made a papal count [MTM B12:367]. The Peter-Bell is said to have belonged to one of Rome’s many St. Peter’s churches [MB:578]; later Finnegan is elected and crowned Pope Finnegan I in the Argo conclave [MB:597].

Catholic PublicationDescription claimed by the Bark and challenged by Casey, who calls it neo-Centrist and anti-Communist and says it has no ecclesiastical sanction [A:128].

CattleCattle boats are among the vessels on which Henry sails [A:124]; Tommy Cow-Town Borger and Jake-Leg Lewis are similarly called salt-water cowboys because their work is on cattle boats [D:222]. Trinali imagines a piece of driftwood as a former tree shading Georgia cattle [A:233], and Demetrio lists cattlemen among his bar’s customers [D:58]. Cattle graze among the strange fruits at Zabotski Flats [MTM B12:363]. Honeybucket claims cattle can be induced to eat plankton, though the narrator says he has never tried his scheme [D:219]. A Sudanese Christ statue carries a cattle herder’s crooked rod [MTM B3:104]. Mary Louise is described as a royal bovine or sacred cow [MTM B2:55]. The Pyramid Lord calls monkeys, humans, alligators, and whales his people’s cattle, a claim of dominion rather than an inventory of domestic animals [MB:593]. Cow bells sound around the Naxos landing [D:131]. In Anastasia’s mermaid account, the creatures the Norse called mermaids are instead sea-cows [D:34-35].

CaucasianRacial category invoked in the narrator’s comic complaint that anthropologists classify Cajuns under broad types, then as Alpine or Mediterranean, rather than recognizing them as a distinct people. The passage proceeds into deliberately impossible claims about Cajun blood, heads, language, and antiquity [A:123-124].

Cauldron (Pit or)Image of extinction in Absalom Stein’s account of forgotten people. He fears that people hanging by their fingernails at the rim of oblivion will fall into a pit or cauldron and cease ever to have existed unless someone remembers them [MTM B11:315].

MTM B11:315

Cauliflowers (Prince of the)“Prince of the Cauliflowers,” title given to Bello Belonki of the Sporting News among Dotty’s journalistic circle [MTM B7:213].

CausewayRoad by which Finnegan rides a produce truck onto the island and into the city for his final confrontation. He senses his antagonist there and considers it likely that his old ship is in port [D:275].

Cavaldos, Dry GulchFrequent visitor to the Old Wooden Ship, called “Dry Gulch Cavaldos” in the text, who comes in twenty times a day. He is distinguished from the fifty regulars who live there [D:216].

CaveGautier and his goats winter in a cave [A:194]; caves also run like spongework through the hollow cliffs of Black Papua [A:36-37]. In Finnegan’s primordial transport, caves are places of ancestral worship and of refuge after defeat [D:213-214]. Anastasia says mermaids live in water-level caves on rocky islands [D:34-35]. Finnegan dreams of sitting with an old teras in a cave or at the foot of a cliff [D:140], while Don Barnaby claims to visit caves in the middle of the earth during his joy-pill experience [D:251]. Finnegan’s sea-burial cave on the Marianao Coast is depicted in The Resurrection of Count Finnegan and is later visited by Duffey [MTM B12:371-374] [MB:550-551]. The cave or room beneath Mooring-Rock, reached from the well shaft, becomes the Room of the Conclave [MB:577] [MB:596]. Casey also uses an echo cave as a metaphor for political slogans amplified by apparently independent voices [A:185-186].

A:194; A:36-37; D:213-214; D:34-35; D:140; D:251; MTM B12:371-374; MB:550-551; MB:577; MB:596; A:185-186

Cave BearPrehistoric bear, Ursus spelaeus. During his primordial transport, Finnegan speaks of his people’s brotherhood with the cave bear, giant stag, bison, and woolly rhinoceros [D:213]. Eva emerges from the ice wrapped in the blond skin of a female cave-bear [MTM B13:399-400].

D:213; MTM B13:399-400

Cave Bear (Female)Animal whose blond skin wraps Eva when Duffey and his simian helpers free her from the ice [MTM B13:399-400]. See Cave Bear.

CavendishFamily name under which Charlotte and the Mullens household are known as show people at Chicago’s Colony Club. Manolo is excepted because he is apparently a newly acquired son [MTM B3:93].

Cavern SpiritsBeings included with demiurges, angelics, pure intellects, and monsters in the narrator’s comparison: the extraordinary conversations of Duffey’s splendid animations, like theirs, cannot be recalled afterward [MTM B5:160-161].

MTM B5:160-161

Caverns (Vast)Vast caverns of the Papuans’ “under-persons,” the unconscious in which the narrator says all other peoples and lands subsist. The Kiriwinans understand that their existence depends on being maintained there [A:37].

CayeneEarlier heading omitted a letter from the port’s name. See Cayenne.
CayenneCayenne, the French Guianan port visited by the Brunhilde before Belem, Sao Luis, Camocim, Fortaleza, and Natal on the outward voyage [D:86].

D:86

CaymanIsland destination named with Kingston and Moule in the opening voyage stanza of Finnegan’s chapter [A:171].

CC624Star designation in the list of positions Hans learns to calculate under the Professor’s instruction [A:214]. The supplied page prints “CC624”; it does not identify the star further.

CecilName Le Marin says a Nigerian acquaintance gave his moustache, in the joke arising from Hildegarde Katt’s description of her husband Tommy [D:229].

CedarWood Duffey says would have been used for the Argo had she been built in a Black Sea port at that remote date. In his account she was instead built at Ragusa from Dinaric oak; he qualifies the account as symbolically rather than ordinarily accurate [MTM B13:412].

CeilingBagby’s and Duffey’s adjoining St. Louis buildings have walnut ceilings as well as walnut walls, rafters, and other woodwork [MTM B2:46]. A noose hangs from the ceiling of the vacant fourth room in Elroy Redheart’s heart artwork [MTM B7:224]. Finnegan recalls drifting through the Cajun swamps with Giulio under a ceiling of fronds only three feet above their flatboat [MTM B5:174].

MTM B2:46; MTM B7:224; MTM B5:174

Celeste, Marie“Marie Celeste,” Johnny Duckwalk’s name for the derelict-ship story he accuses Le Marin of recycling. Le Marin insists on the form “Mary Celeste” and denies the resemblance [D:246].
