Cell (attic)Little closet or cell off the main attic room in the large town house where Duffey lives with pretended kindred. It contains the peaked fourth-floor Prisoner John Window, from which he sees the three slant-faced boys [MTM B1:12].

MTM B1:12

CelliniBenvenuto Cellini (1500-1571), Florentine goldsmith, sculptor, and autobiographer. Papa Piccone names him with Buonorroti and Sancho in answer to Patrick Stranahan’s dismissal of later artists; Patrick replies that such craftsmen were good but should have remained anonymous [A:111]. Cellini’s works include the bronze Perseus with the Head of Medusa in Florence and the gold Saliera made for Francis I. His Autobiography, composed late in his life and partly dictated, offers a vivid, self-dramatizing account of Renaissance craftsmanship, patronage, quarrels, and his own exploits.

A:111

Celluloid CuffsCuffs or gauntlets Lily Koch snaps on as her merchant’s trademark at her Saturday art sales. After the noon closing and departure of the customers, she unsnaps them until the next sale [MTM B1:28-29].

MTM B1:28-29

CenacleThe Upper Room associated with the Last Supper. The Argo’s recovered Lord’s Table is said to have come from the Cenaculum in Jerusalem and to rest in her Bread and Wine Room [MTM B13:422]. “Cenacle” also names the supper room at Randal’s where Duffey’s party watches the television over-picture of Casey [MTM B12:380].

MTM B13:422; MTM B12:380

Cenotaphs (Cretan)Cretan tomb-monuments from which, the narrator says, statuettes of Anastasia have been excavated. The claim accompanies her resemblance to a ship’s carved figurehead and the question of what she really is [D:32].

D:32

CentaurCentaurus, partly visible and labeled at the right edge of the celestial ship illustration on the cover of the supplied More Than Melchisedech PDF [MTM:1].

MTM:1

CentristPolitical position Casey attributes to Duffey, sole member of the Catholic Center Party of America [A:42]. Henry Salvatore, in conversation with his father, declares “We are the Centrists” and says they stand in the middle and build the world around themselves [A:125].

A:42; A:125

Centrists (Neo-)Term in Casey’s hostile description of the Bark as a neo-Centrist Catholic publication; he questions whether its hyphenated label has any meaning [A:128]. Stein had proposed the long title Neo-Centrist Review of Evolvate Socio-Geopolitical Motifs in a Disintegrating World for the magazine [A:121].

A:128; A:121

CenturiesHistorical periods repeatedly mixed with uncertain memories, symbolic history, and long lives. The Capuchin dates Sicilian Naxos to the seventh century before Christ [D:119]; Casey’s Kasmir Gorshok identity is placed in the ninth century [A:39]; Anastasia says Norse sea-cows were taken as mermaids as late as the tenth [D:35]. Lawrence tells Henry that he cannot restore the thirteenth century, only the sixteenth [A:125]. Scanlon assigns different colors to sixteenth- and eighteenth-century seas [A:234], and Angela’s father imitates sixteenth-, seventeenth-, and eighteenth-century handwriting on his treasure maps [D:260]. The postscript describes Ellis’s Mermaid Series as a revival of seventeenth-century drama [PS:476]. X is described as a mid-nineteenth-century north Italian type [MTM B6:200], and his family account discusses Irish governesses and obscure people of a century earlier [D:279-280]. Duffey remembers three overlapping twentieth-century childhoods [MTM B1:6] and later interprets the Presence through twentieth-century Jungian imagery, which Plunket rebukes as mistaking reality for art [MTM B12:390]. The young Casey invents a Blue Book for 2001 [A:157]. Private Gregory, not Duffey, recalls centuries at sea [A:77]. The narrator pictures Pan as old for twenty-odd centuries [A:194]; Marie Courtois has a beauty forbidden for centuries [D:37]. A passage attributed to Galen says Daemons must return each century to renew their descendants [D:160-161]. Finnegan blames centuries of altered sky-color on smoke [D:127]. The Argo has logbooks of voyages lasting centuries and extraordinarily long-lived pilots [MTM B13:405]; X’s history makes the Devil’s imprisonment similarly span centuries [MTM B6:204-205]. Beth Keegan’s theatrical walk is extravagantly compared with something unseen for thirty centuries, since Tarshish fell [MTM B2:57].

Cephalic IndexTerm in Casey’s school notebook: he says one adds three to the skull index to obtain the cephalic index, then jokes that there are more living roundheads than dead ones and threatens an unnamed living example [A:162-163].

CepheidsPulsating variable stars. Professor Kirol places the noonday devil among the Cepheids in his account of time, space, and eternity [A:215].

Ceram SeaIndonesian sea, also called the Seram Sea, between Seram and northwestern New Guinea. It is among the many seas sailed by the Argo and remembered by Melchisedech [MTM B13:406].

Cerebral AthleticismProfessor Kirol’s term for rapid calculation, large additions, squaring, extracting roots, and prodigious memory. He distinguishes these feats from thought, while insisting that a developed memory is an indispensable tool for a thinking person [A:212].

A:212

Ceremonies, TheRitual proceedings of the Conclave at Babylonia Bagascia. After offerings to the assembled cults, Conrad Stone Hackenschmidt conducts the roll call and coerced election of a straw-man, which Monsignor X burns. The delegates then make their avowals and denials [MB:565-568].

MB:565-568

CeremonyIn Finnegan’s story, a Jesuit gives his Devil painting a short-form exorcism, while saying that it is unnecessary to waste ceremony on the Devil [D:255]. The kindred’s farewell to fifteen-year-old Duffey after he finishes high school is a hand-washing ceremony, concluded with a gift of one hundred dollars [MTM B2:38]. Howland ceremoniously uncorks and replaces Finnegan’s bottle while posing as his valet for Casey [A:182]. The Conclave at Babylonia Bagascia has its own offerings, straw-man election and burning, and avowals and denials [MB:565-568].

D:255; MTM B2:38; A:182; MB:565-568

CertaintyFinnegan asserts that Papa Devil is dead finally, after the deaths of the original and the surrogate [D:150]. He recalls Anastasia’s promise that they will be together again, first professing certainty and then doubting that his own people possess that promise [D:149]. Seaworthy keeps Finnegan as confirmation of his sanity after the man he believes he killed appears alive; X later explains the confusion as a substitution of twins [D:86] [D:289]. A passage attributed to Belloc lists public certainty among the communal supports lost through the Reformation’s isolation of the soul [MTM B5:176]. Finnegan’s conviction that he is the only person in the world persists [A:205]; elsewhere the narrator jokes that certainty of hostile intent develops when someone repeatedly shoots at you [D:197].

Cerulean saltcellarOne of Finnegan’s extravagant self-descriptions during his St. Patrick’s Day logorrhea. He calls himself a perfectly spherical “saitcaster,” the grandfather of the saltshakers, and the cerulean saltcellar [D:189].

Chaff-cupTerm equated with “glume” in Casey’s school notebook, beside the observation that the beard of wheat is called the awn [A:164].

ChainAsking Dan says Casey’s new zoot suit needs a jangle chain, which he promises to supply later [A:261]. Truck drivers carry lengths of chain as weapons in Casey’s imagined revolution [A:160]. Finnegan wears Heliogabalus on a neck chain with his Miraculous Medal [A:61]. Zabotski pulls a boat-whistle chain as his ark floats away [MTM B9:287]. A fictional murder-contest proposal describes an exponentially spreading chain reaction of animals driven to attack one victim [MB:580-581].

ChainsLengths of chain arm the truck drivers in Casey’s imagined revolution [A:160]. Asking Dan promises Casey a jangle chain to complete his zoot-suit outfit [A:261]. See Chain.

ChairThree huge easy chairs fill much of the Brunhilde’s small bar [D:22]. Finnegan and Anastasia watch the town from a giant’s chair, an eight-foot-wide dished and backed slab among old ruins; the stop may be Paraiso or Campeche [D:67-70]. Finnegan drinks all night in a chair by X’s window [D:157], and slumps in an easy chair while entertaining Casey with lies and Howland’s valet routine [A:182]. Patrick Stranahan shoots his pistol from an easy chair [A:104]; each boy in St. Martin’s six-boy rooms has his own chair [A:161]. Bagby offers Duffey a barber chair [MTM B2:43]. Shot Gun Schaeffer barricades his door with a chair to escape Basin Street’s intimidation [D:223]. At the Voltaire Festival, Voltaire is awakened and seated to watch the spectacle [MB:563]. Casey descends from his Curile Chair in the Zodiac to attend Duffey’s party [MTM B12:383]. Gertrude says Biloxi has occupied the same chair for thirty years [MTM B13:409]; in his own earlier account he gives twenty-five years in that chair and ten in its predecessor [D:204].

Anastasia imagines that the waves write Chaldee on the sand; Finnegan claims that all clairvoyants can read it and that its message frightens him [D:38]. Ignatius Cardinal Ti’s grave bears the words “My chalice indeed you shall drink” [MB:588-589]. ChamberSt. Martin’s Hall at St. Bonaventure’s has six-boy chambers, which give The Chambers its name and chamber-pot masthead [A:167]. In Ignacio’s tale, Joseph of Maintz fashions a spherical passenger chamber for his moon rocket [A:271]. Finnegan’s comic letter imagines a gas-chamber sentence had he demanded a jury [A:264]. His story of an analyst’s dissection leads to a chamber where the scattered remains glow with a possible diffused essence, complicating the analyst’s conclusion that the man was merely an empty jug wrapped in primordial straw [MTM B5:181-182]. Elroy Redheart’s ceramic heart has four dog-house-sized chambers filled with miniature scenes [MTM B7:221]. A sea-cave burial crypt appears in The Resurrection of Count Finnegan [MB:550].

Chambers, The (school paper)Manuscript paper produced by boys in St. Martin’s Hall at St. Bonaventure’s. Audifax O’Hanlon draws each masthead individually as a row of chamber pots whose silhouette imitates the towers on Gregory Hall’s Towers. The name comes from St. Martin’s six-boy rooms [A:167].

In Don Barnaby’s joy-pill story, he marries a chameleon-like woman whose names and appearances vary while he recognizes her as the same person [D:250].

ChamonixPlace named by Finnegan with St. Zermatto and Guebwiller in his argument about prehistoric rock paintings. He says supposed butterfly images are actually speech-and-song balloons in an original complex language. Duffey challenges him and calls the painters Neanderthals [MTM B6:193].

ChampionJoe Bushmaster, the Lion of the South, holds the heavyweight beer-drinking championship until Hans Schultz, the Milwaukee Seidel, defeats him [A:17] [A:19] [A:23]. The narrator jokes that a woman in a contestant’s corner once brought down a former champion [A:19]. Johnny Duckwalk is an old champion drinker whom fewer than a hundred men in the world can outdrink [D:236]. Casey’s childhood record books make his imagined sporting self the greatest running back, gaining sixteen and a fraction yards per carry [A:156-157]. Herman Hercules, not Finnegan, says he was the ninety-nine-pound wrestling champion for many years [MB:585].

ChanceFinnegan doubts Hans’s chances against Bushmaster, although Hans confidently agrees to bet [A:17]. Dotty’s hopes for a life with Finnegan are described as still having every chance even as the narrator suggests their failure [A:93-94]. Colonel Laycheck offers Casey a chance to retreat from challenging Stein [A:47]. The amnesiac sergeant asks for a chance to regain reliable memory of his name [A:71-74]. Duffey says he gave Casey’s father a talisman in a chance encounter [MTM B5:151]. Don Lewis briefly thinks he may escape because he has accounted for every man on the Brunhilde; an unexpected killer immediately destroys that hope [D:109]. Finnegan calls to the graveyard dead because he wants to give them a chance to rise [D:284]. Stein hopes to save forgotten people by remembering their faces [MTM B11:315-316]. The seventh contingency of the girls’ play promises the beatific vision with only one chance in a hundred billion of failure, then introduces a contrary omen [MTM B10:296-297].

ChangelingIn folklore, a fairy child substituted for a stolen human child. The narrator calls Finnegan a changeling of the other or double blood [A:39]. Patricia Solli says that, despite their shared childhood, he seems a changeling to her [A:175]; The Devil Is Dead repeats her speech [D:18-19]. Seaworthy speaks of changelings like himself and Finnegan coming late to understanding their nature [D:11].

A:39; A:175; D:18-19; D:11

Channel (Irish)New Orleans neighborhood from which Patricia Solli says her family came, distinguishing it from the French Quarter [A:175].

Channel (Shipping)The Brunhilde reaches the channel as its voyage begins; its lurch accompanies the narrator’s turning wheel of fortune [D:28]. In Zabotski’s flood story, a reporter describes the flooded channel outside his house, humorously called Dumaine Street, as sufficient to carry an ocean-going ship away in a good rain [MTM B9:289].

D:28; MTM B9:289

Channels of communicationSignals and communication arrangements X proposes before he, Doll, and Finnegan scatter and later meet beside Ifreann’s grave. X offers to arrange the plan, though he says they will also know the time and place intuitively [D:186].

ChantHowland chants his five-gophers jingle to a hoedown tune while he and Finnegan lie in a hayloft [A:179]. Beth Keegan, now Beth Erlenbaum, greets Duffey’s St. Louis visit with a chant beginning “Kerowl, kerowl!” [MTM B5:154].

A:179; MTM B5:154

ChaosAskandanakandrian says nervous-merchandise dealers try to bring confusion out of chaos, because less complexity invites competition and more is intolerable [A:256-257]. The narrator of Promantia posits a dozen false chaoses before true chaos, a dozen false creations before real creation, and twenty false falls before the falls of angels and humanity [PG:530].

A:256-257; PG:530

ChaparralTexas brush country where Finnegan spends about 105 hours, from Tuesday evening until Sunday morning, somewhere in Medina or Frio County, probably northeast of the Frio branch. The interval includes delirium, noonday devils, and portions of the twelve-year life he shares with Theresa in another, perhaps valid, existence [A:202-205].

A:202-205

Chapel (Our Lady of the Dolphins)Chapel of Christian mermaids on a small island between Patmos and Lipsos, according to Anastasia’s account of mermaid history. She places the community in the second century and says the chapel still stands in poor condition [D:35-36].

Character DefectFinnegan’s explanation to Doll for his behavior: he has a character defect and is a slob. The exchange follows his suggestion that they fight a few rounds without trying for a knockout, and Doll’s reply that she always fights for one [D:193].

CharismaShow Boat jokingly claims special charisma as the source of her knowledge that the serpent of Eden is the many-armed hydra still active in the world [A:263]. Charisma is also among the fashionable words embellishing the Devil’s public speech, concealing no change in its underlying message [MTM B8:243].

CharityMarie tells Sally that charity is a Latin word for love [A:9]. Duffey’s charity is imperfect but has gained some ground from his natural state [MTM B4:110]. Deeds of kindness and charity join the Law and worship of God among the three requirements for preserving the world [MTM B7:228]. Art as Charity belongs to the synthesis Duffey seeks and recognizes in Teresa [MTM B7:229]. It is Duffey whose charity prevents his phoning Casey at a quarter past three in the morning about the stolen box; X urges the immediate call [A:137].

A:9; MTM B4:110; MTM B7:228; MTM B7:229; A:137

CharlemagneCharles or Carl the Great (birth year disputed, traditionally 742 or 747/748; died 814), king of the Franks from 768 and Lombards from 774, crowned emperor by Pope Leo III in 800. His Carolingian empire covered much of western and central Europe, with Aachen a major seat of rule, and revived western Roman imperial authority. His government used royal envoys, the missi dominici, to supervise justice and promoted legal and monetary reform, including new weights and coinage. His patronage of scholars such as Alcuin supported schools, Latin learning, the copying of classical works, Carolingian minuscule, and church and liturgical reform. These political and cultural legacies underlie the later epithet Father of Europe; the designation Holy Roman Emperor is retrospective. In Ignacio’s tale, Archbishop Turpin, a peer of Charlemagne, records Joseph of Maintz’s journey to the moon [A:271]. The Iron Crown of Charlemagne is among the treasures recovered by the Argo [MTM B13:422].

A:271; MTM B13:422

Charles (Uncle)Charles Salvatore, one of Henry Salvatore’s closest uncles, named with Alphonse, Fulgence, George, and Matthew [A:122].

A:122

Charnel houseOne destination on the blood-covered crossroads sign in Patrick Stranahan’s ominous account of the postwar world, alongside nowhere, easy house, and crossbar hotel [MTM B5:164].

Charon's (boat)Papadiabolous II’s image of death as the alternative to escaping Naxos in his own boat. He tells Finnegan and Anastasia that none of the three will return to the Brunhilde: they will leave in his vessel or Charon’s. His boat is the Seabach, pronounced Shouakh and also called the Hawk [D:121-122].

In a separate scene concerning the Brunhilde, X asks Finnegan what tracings he made in its chart room as part of an interrogation that exposes Finnegan’s failure to gather the evidence X expects [D:188-189].

Charter (carnival acts)To hire or engage performers: Professor Kirol sometimes charters acts and forms combinations when assembling his carnival [A:215].

Chase, TheThe pursuit in a saying Endymeon attributes to the Arabs: days spent in the chase do not count against the length of life. He uses this analogy to claim that translation does not exhaust an author’s allotted creative talent [A:237].

ChasmBottomless fissure in Duffey’s central apocalyptic dream, swallowing towns and people, especially the young. His magic fails to arrest it, but he crosses to the other side and says a veil now separates him from others. The giants’ hands he summons appear severed and manacled, then become a child’s mittens joined by their drawstring. Beth interprets the dream as his coming seven-year absence [MTM B2:68-69].

Chastaigne, JosephProprietor of the Imperial Bar or Royal on Basse-Terre, jokingly called Sloppy Joe’s by Finnegan and his three companions. The place is fastidious, green-fronted, breezy, and scented with rum and lime; the narrator likens its faint tinkling to both ice in a glass and the music of the spheres [D:235]. After Finnegan’s companions leave, Chastaigne sees the same restlessness in him and predicts that he too will leave within a month, on the next boat. He and Angela Cosquin are Finnegan’s remaining close friends there [D:266].

ChastellainOne of the named would-be leaders of the non-splendid, old-line humans resisting the Royal Pop transformation. Their leadership fails as some join the splendid people and others die disintegrating into trash; Chastellain’s individual fate is not specified [MTM B11:335].

ChastityVirtue praised in a passage attributed to St. Francis de Sales as the lily among virtues and as integrity opposed to corruption. The narrator connects chastity of mind with the highest intelligence and says Duffey sometimes fails in practice but never redefines corruption as virtue [MTM B1:27]. Duffey condemns a war on chastity alongside wars on poverty and obedience [MTM B6:193]. In Promantia’s account of Casey’s past lives, Prince Casimir’s lifelong vow of chastity frustrates his father’s succession plans [PG:536].

MTM B1:27; MTM B6:193; PG:536

Chattering (little idiot)Corporal Robert Casper’s instruction in Don Lewis’s patrol story: keep the apparently Japanese soldier talking while Casper gets behind him. The fugitive repeatedly eludes their attempts to surround him [D:44-45].

D:44-45

Cheap-Shot Artist, The (also Old Clootie)The Devil as the Cheap-Shot Artist and father of all cheap-shot artists. X identifies him as the power behind Finnegan and Dotty’s reported deaths [MTM B8:238]. Soon afterward Duffey encounters him as the Majesty at a meeting of the New Catholic Press Guild and calls him Old Clootie [MTM B8:239-243]. Entering the Devil’s mind, Duffey hears him glory in cheap shots, hatred, slander, destruction, and the negation of creation [MTM B8:242]. Clootie is a Scots name associated with the Devil. Duffey later uses it to unsettle the adversary in their struggle over his creative powers [MTM B10:303-304].

MTM B8:238; MTM B8:239-243; MTM B8:242; MTM B10:303-304

CheckbookGertrude Brannagan proposes to fetch her checkbook to help Eva obtain Kate’s Neanderthal after the men’s magically manufactured money proves impractical [MTM B13:415]. Sebastian Hilton pays Lily Koch a hundred dollars in cash for a statuette because he has left his checkbook at school [MTM B1:28-29].

MTM B13:415; MTM B1:28-29

CheekFinnegan reports having a Z cut into his cheek after his jukebox quarrel [A:264]. Duffey lightly nicks Bagby’s cheek while shaving him, to keep his new acquaintance from getting too far ahead in their verbal contest [MTM B2:45].

A:264; MTM B2:45

CheeseDuffey eats cheese with black bread and beer at the Dublin [MTM B2:39], then buys ten pounds as stock for his own establishment [MTM B2:41]. Mary Catherine serves blue cheese to Finnegan [A:247], and Letitia includes cheese in the meal she sets out for Giulio [MTM B3:106]. The Harvesters’ Dinner at the Colony Club also includes cheeses [MTM B3:94]. “Cheese Factory” is among the words on milk-can covers that young Duffey remembers or obtains from other minds [MTM B1:17]. Gautier eats a pound of cheese daily and makes two pounds to barter [A:196]. Honeybucket calls his proposed plankton-and-livestock venture the Ancient Syrian Cheese Company, although the narrator reveals that he has not tried the plan and does not know what plankton looks like [D:219].

MTM B2:39; MTM B2:41; A:247; MTM B3:106; MTM B3:94; MTM B1:17; A:196; D:219

Cheese FactoryWords on milk-can covers among the iron-lettered household inscriptions that young Duffey knows by observation or by borrowing other people’s memories [MTM B1:17].

MTM B1:17

Chef (from Martinique)Unnamed chef from Martinique at Howland Jerome Howland’s luxurious Club Royal in Chicago [A:246].

A:246

Chef (High)Olga Sanchez’s unnamed husband, described as a beautiful Mexican man, who becomes high chef of the Rounders’ Club main dining room [MTM B2:74].

MTM B2:74

Chemical UnbalanceOne of the possible explanations Elena lists while asking Finnegan why he drinks. He answers her whole series with nine yesses and a no, then attributes his drinking to its pleasure and his excess to an evil streak; he does not identify which proposed reason he rejects [A:274].

A:274

ChemicalsAmong the materials Leonard Archive says the settlement can selectively draw from water through varied electrical voltages, frequencies, and electrode arrangements. His list also includes fish, crustaceans, animals, plants, minerals, salts, alcohols, petroleum, and sugars. Honeybucket Kincaid demonstrates the equipment while preparing the visitors’ meal [MTM B13:417-418].

MTM B13:417-418

ChemistZabotski’s former occupation. He is a retired chemist and experimenter who supplies Duffey with the large glass-lined distillation pot that becomes the communal soup crock [A:132-133] [MTM B6:195]. The later description calls him a smelly man in a smelly trade, then specifies that his offensiveness is to the eye rather than the nose [MTM B11:306].

A:132-133; MTM B6:195; MTM B11:306

Cherry bombSimile for the heart bursting as Duffey wrestles Morpheus, panics at extinction, and collapses toward the single-celled remnant of their diminishing world [GD:500].

GD:500

ChersonName X says the Goths used for the Crimean peninsula, the Tauric or Euxine Chersonese, in his account of the Devil’s imprisonment [MTM B6:204]. See Chersonese (Euxine/Tauric).

MTM B6:204

Chersonese (Euxine/Tauric)Crimean peninsula in the accounts of the Devil’s thousand-year imprisonment. X calls it the Tauric or Euxine Chersonese and says Christians brought the prisoner from Aachen in 946 or 947, delivered him first to Muslim authorities, and then to devil-worshipping guards. In his account it was divided between Kiev and Tmutarakan and had been called the Prison, Phylake or Carcer, long before this confinement [MTM B6:204-205]. Henri’s account dates the transfer from Aachen to 946 [MTM B5:180]. Teresa says the ancient Argo sailed past the Devil’s preordained prison on its way to Colchis [MTM B7:234].

MTM B6:204-205; MTM B5:180; MTM B7:234

ChestPatrick Stranahan, not Henry, has the chest and shoulders of a heavyweight wrestler [A:102]. The thunder colt tears open the chest of Deutero-Finnegan, the Finnegan effigy, in the Opera House spectacle [MTM B11:351]. Duffey sees the Devil’s tetragrammaton cut into Sebastian Hilton’s chest in a transport, but on examining the body finds plague sores forming the same design, not knife wounds [MTM B7:226]. In the container sense, Papa Devil brings an ice chest to the Padre Island beach party [D:34] [D:40]; treasure chests marked with suggestive pirates’ initials feature on Angela’s father’s forged maps [D:259-260].

A:102; MTM B11:351; MTM B7:226; D:34; D:40; D:259-260

ChestnutColor of Dotty’s memorable hair [A:105-106], and one of the color terms used for the women Johnny Duckwalk and Don Barnaby pursue on Basse-Terre [D:236]. Chestnut Street names the St. Louis district of fleshpots frequented by Bagby [MTM B2:62].

A:105-106; D:236; MTM B2:62

Chestnut StreetSt. Louis street whose fleshpots Bagby frequents. The same portrait describes his brawling throughout the city [MTM B2:62].

MTM B2:62

Chewing TobaccoProduct advertised by the company sponsoring the limerick contest in Marie’s Shakes Pearson story. Her uncle repeatedly begins tobacco verses on bark, only to abandon them for whisky and find them eaten by squirrels when he returns [A:25].

A:25

ChiangChiang Kai-shek, the Chinese Nationalist leader. In his polemic against the Bark, Casey condemns its support for Chiang and calls him discredited and possibly the most evil man alive [A:130].

A:130

ChiaraOne of the three children, with Rafaello and Theresa Anna, whom Theresa remembers from her twelve-year other life with Finnegan. She has Masses said for them while uncertain whether that life was a dream; the narrator explicitly distinguishes these children from those she has with Vincent [A:203-204]. A later account names Chiara, Rafaello, and Theresa Anna as Vincent and Teresa Stranahan’s three younger children, born many years after their older ones [MTM B12:385].

A:203-204; MTM B12:385

ChicagoMajor home and working city for Duffey and his circle. One account includes Chicago among the cities where he lived with kindred between five and twelve; his 1925 return is a night-train journey from Omaha [MTM B1:7] [MTM B3:77]. He joins Gabriel Szymansky’s business, adding books and art to its paired antique and pawn shops [MTM B3:81-82]. North Chicago’s golden age lasts from 1925 to 1935, followed by an electrum age to about 1946; its circle includes the Kochs, Hiltons, Szymanskys, artists such as Groben, and the young Carruthers, Rattigan, and Stones [MTM B3:98-99]. The city is the setting of the Leader’s appearance and the portfolio blackmail against Duffey [MTM B4:116] [MTM B4:139]. The Crock belongs to this Chicago world, which also lies behind Duffey’s warning about Hugo Stone and Stein [A:40-41]. Finnegan plans to visit Casey there [A:120], receives Chicago friends’ mail at Palermo [D:114-115], and returns to the city during his later human-life interval [D:272]. Duffey leaves Chicago for St. Louis in 1946 and does not return from that trip [MTM B5:149]; later he and X do visit Chicago by traveling backward in time after their Cuban search for Finnegan [MTM B12:376]. Margaret Stone recalls her Chicago childhood through her father’s unread Cook County history [MTM B11:308].

MTM B1:7; MTM B3:77; MTM B3:81-82; MTM B3:98-99; MTM B4:116; MTM B4:139; A:40-41; A:120; D:114-115; D:272; MTM B5:149; MTM B12:376; MTM B11:308

Chicago Herald and ExaminerNewspaper publishing Elena O’Higgins’s modest November 14 report on the mule transported thirty feet through the air beneath the Pont du Sable Traffic Trestle. Its photograph shows the airborne mule without giant hands, and its witnesses disagree about the means of transport [MTM B4:132].

MTM B4:132

Chicago style jazzJazz style favored in the Crock’s short survey of new recordings [A:41].

A:41

Chicago TribuneNewspaper publishing Tony Apostolo’s November 14 report on the transported mule. It includes accounts from numerous witnesses and all three photographs exchanged among the reporters, including the image showing giant hands. The witnesses offer conflicting explanations, though most describe giant hands lifting the mule [MTM B4:132-133].

MTM B4:132-133

Chicago-Hot JazzMusic Rollo McSorley says can still be heard only on Fleshpot Row. The narrator mocks his musical judgment, concedes some truth to the location claim, and describes the row’s version as emphasizing the style’s faults [MTM B4:126].

MTM B4:126

ChicleCrop grown in the fictional country San Simeon, listed with henequen among the industries that do not account for its exceptional wealth, which lies in its possession of gold [MB:558].

Child-Hero, TheOne of the Royal Pop People whom Duffey meets in New Orleans. Although his designation sounds like a type, the narrator insists that he and the other named figures are unique, enduring persons [MTM B11:322]. He disparages Duffey’s historical apparatus and questions the reality of the classical past [MTM B11:326-327]. In the new morning park he affirms its reality, identifies his people as newly awakened children of the thunder and mountain, and justifies the destruction of those judged insufficiently splendid [MTM B11:331-334]. Salvation Sally reports that she and the Child Hero clear a building’s third floor of its inhabitants [MTM B11:338]. He joins the dinner at Girardeau’s and then performs in the Cretan Bull Drama at the Decatur Street Opera House, where Zabotski is killed [MTM B11:344] [MTM B11:349].

MTM B11:322; MTM B11:326-327; MTM B11:331-334; MTM B11:338; MTM B11:344; MTM B11:349

Childhood (in deep fimbul-winter)Finnegan’s image of his people’s primordial life in the deep fimbul-winter. In his ancestral outcry, he says they invented the inventions of childhood and asks how they have since been cast as monsters [D:213].

D:213

Childhood of astronomyThe narrator’s name for the elementary knowledge Hans gains by learning to calculate the positions of familiar stars. The Professor’s theories about the universe follow this practical lesson [A:214].

A:214

Childhood of the soulThe Professor’s term for the present limits of human perception. He argues that sight reveals only the reverse of Heaven’s tapestry: people already inhabit the spiritual universe and eternity, but cannot yet perceive them fully [A:214].

A:214

Childrens' Gin FundMock charitable fund to which Dotty says Marie should give her money instead of paying Salvation Sally’s passage to America. The suggestion appears in Dotty’s comic letter complaining about Sally’s arrival [A:147].

A:147

China LobbyPolitical alignment Casey attributes to the Bark in his hostile review. He calls the magazine straight China Lobby and attacks its support for Chiang and opposition to the Communist movement in China [A:130].

A:130

China ShopMary Louise’s comparison for Bagby’s eagerness to buy anything, after he pays a thousand dollars for Elroy Redheart’s chambered-heart artwork: a kid in a China Shop [MTM B7:224].

China StraitsStraits traversed by the returning voyagers after skirting the d’Entrecasteau Islands and Trobriands in Archipelago [A:36]. Biloxi Brannagan has not only sailed through them but dived there for old wrecks [D:203].

Chinese girl (Angela Ching)See Ching, Angela.
Chinese periodHans’s name for the phase in which Chinese ballads and Heine’s influence mingle with a Rhineland sadness, German roofs, Chinese houses, river junks, and love. His unpublished Li Tai Po ballad introduces the account [A:221-223].

Chinese styleThe manner in which Hans proposes to decorate his flat. Jimmy suggests rugs on the walls and a red-and-black color scheme [A:229].

Ching-Ling Charley's Doss HouseOne of the fictitious sponsors advertised on Stein’s G.I. radio station, the Anopheles Network, housed in one of his two tents. The spoof promises genteel surroundings and an atmosphere one can cut with a knife [A:46].

Ching, AngelaSlim Chinese girl among Duffey’s ladies who gather at his Rounders’ Club in St. Louis and kiss him goodbye before his departure [MTM B2:70].

ChiodoItalian for nail, used in Theresa’s saying to Finnegan that a chiodo in the heart never killed. She speaks of loving Finnegan while expecting happiness with Vincent [A:107].

A:107

ChipmunksOne of Finnegan’s first guesses about the small animals around him as he wakes before dawn. He gradually recognizes rats, his own dried blood, and the foul dump in which he has slept [A:177].

A:177

ChithDestination beyond mountains in the voyage poem opening Finnegan’s chapter, whose subtitle identifies him with Iason and the Other People: he will go over the mountains to Chith [A:171].

A:171

ChivKnife word that Casey’s notebook identifies as Romani, using the term Gypsy in its list of language facts [A:164].

ChlorosGreek color word for a pale or yellowish green. Hans considers and rejects it as a description of Marie’s green eyes, reasoning that nobody would have eyes of that shade [A:24].

A:24

ChocolateAmong the provisions Finnegan unloads at Anastasia Grandmother’s house on Naxos [D:126]. Casey includes a chocolate soldier among the eminent figures who echo the propagandists’ chosen language [A:185-186]. Chocolate is also one of the color terms for the Basse-Terre women pursued by Don Barnaby and Johnny Duckwalk [D:236]. In Elroy Redheart’s chambered-heart artwork, a dead girl’s own red chocolate heart lies among the candies beside her, removed from her opened breast [MTM B7:221].

D:126; A:185-186; D:236; MTM B7:221

Chocolate SoldierOne of the ostensibly independent eminent figures who echo the phrases of Casey’s propagandists. Casey lists him with a physicist, wit, widow, educator, and statesman [A:185-186].

A:185-186

ChodorlahomorKing of Elam or Susiana, described in Duffey’s narrative as ruler of a Devildom east of the Tigris and leader of the three crooked kings Amraphel, Arioch, and Thadal. Duffey recognizes those three names in the Flame Man comic strip as the Slant-Faced Men, the magicless anti-magi; their allegiance to Chodorlahomor is supplied outside the strip. Duffey remembers blessing Abraham after his victory over the four kings [MTM B7:227-228].

MTM B7:227-228

Chok-chok-chok-kachoomOne of the animal sounds in the immense rhapsody heard the night before Zabotski, Wife Waldo, children, and animals depart in his giant ark-like contraption [MTM B9:285].

ChortDevil-name in Zabotski’s account of Slavic folk-comic tales and the Devil’s release from an underground prison [MTM B6:191]. In X’s family history, Chortovitch means son of the Devil and has been euphemized on a gravestone to Bogovitch, son of God [D:277].

MTM B6:191; D:277

Chortovitch, Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch PapadiabolousThe elder Devil whose history X reconstructs from the neglected grave marked I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch, which Finnegan locates. X interprets Bogovitch as a euphemism for Chortovitch, son of the Devil [D:276-278]. In his account the man is born near Krakow in 1830 to the Irish governess Katie Noonan, is baptized Columkill, and receives Gregorovitch from his adopter Gregory. X believes the father was literally the Devil, as the parish record reportedly says, while admitting the alternative that Gregory fathered him; Katie affectionately calls him Ifreann [D:278-279]. X describes him as a murderer, participant in the Paris Commune, disciple of Kropotkin, and old-line communist who sires twins at seventy, simultaneously but to different mothers on different continents and in different centuries [D:280-281]. X says a document conferring dangerous power is buried with the father [D:290].

D:276-278; D:278-279; D:280-281; D:290

ChorusRefrain or collective voice: the cicadas surrounding Finnegan and Anastasia on the Naxos mountaintop [D:132]; the Gadarene Swine Song sung by Sebastian, Countess Margaret, Letitia, and Duffey, with Giulio Solli howling its basso accompaniment [MTM B3:107]; and the short counter-ode preceding Duffey’s curtain speech in Cleo Mahoney’s play [MTM B10:297].

D:132; MTM B3:107; MTM B10:297

Chosen (the)The privileged company invoked by the poem opening Stranahan’s chapter, whose speaker chooses the life of the Fiver, grappling ghosts and cozening coneys with his companions [A:91].

A:91

Chosky Bottoms, TheElusive local bottoms discussed by Finnegan and his country friends after a night with coon dogs. They disagree whether they have just been there; Old Pop Potter treats the name as a general spook place always beyond the next ridge. Its legends include a man-killing panther, swamp ghost, masked riders, a Northern Platoon lost in quicksand, ancestral coons and fish, Bloody Mulligans, and eighteen-foot bull snakes. Finnegan compares its elusive character with the St. Kitts he hopes to find, rather than placing the bottoms near that island [D:273-274].

D:273-274

Christ-heads (Danish-bread)The Danish-bread Christ is one of the Seven Christs Duffey brings back from his lost years: a head shaped from mixed wheat and rye dough, baked and varnished. The narrator says such heads are baked in parts of Denmark for Corpus Christi, and marvels at this particular example’s artistic power and preservation [MTM B3:103].

MTM B3:103

Christian ChineseDescription of Ignatius Ti, the ward boy who translates the parakeet Amoy’s stories. His family has lived in the islands for centuries [A:79].

A:79

Christian mermaidsMermaids who, according to Anastasia’s account, lived on a small island between Patmos and Lipsos in the second century. Their chapel of Our Lady of the Dolphins still survives in poor condition [D:34-35].

D:34-35

ChristmasOne of the four annual occasions on which Finnegan writes to Dotty while in the army [A:176]. Mary Catherine’s Irish whisky has remained unopened since Christmas when she brings it out for Finnegan [A:249]. The Brunhilde party spends eight or nine days at Port of Spain over Christmas and New Year’s [D:85]. Duffey remembers spending a Christmas vacation at Sebastian Hilton’s wealthy Chicago home [MTM B3:81].

A:176; A:249; D:85; MTM B3:81

Christopher (brother of Henry)One of Henry Francis Salvatore’s brothers, alongside Eustace, Hilaire, Joseph, Louis, Mark, and Simeon [A:122].

A:122

Christopher (Saint)Earlier heading that treated an island name as an account of the saint. See St. Kitts (St. Christopher).
Christopher Columbus (c. 1451--1506)Italian navigator (1451-1506) whose four Spanish-sponsored Atlantic voyages began in 1492 as a search for a westward route to Asia. His Caribbean landfalls inaugurated sustained European contact and colonization, with extensive transfers of organisms, goods, and people known as the Columbian Exchange. His colonial government and the enslavement of Indigenous people belong to the contested legacy of those voyages. In The Devil Is Dead, discovery by Columbus is one of the narrator’s playful requirements for an island paradise [D:237]; Ignacio similarly calls St. Christopher holy as a Columbus landfall [A:272].

D:237; A:272

Chromatic BeautyBeauty coupled with the continuity of evil in Casey’s childhood theory of personalized temptations. His erotic imaginary world contains treacherous, beautiful women from history and legend, compared with St. Anthony’s temptations [A:157].

A:157

ChromePart of the rich interior of the outwardly dingy Cadillac Bar, where white-jacketed bar-boys preside amid chrome and crystal [D:58]. In Elroy Redheart’s chambered-heart artwork, chrome babes, cars, and domiciles furnish the affluent half of the second red room [MTM B7:222].

D:58; MTM B7:222

Chrome babesFigures among the brash, affluent scenes in the second red room of Elroy Redheart’s chambered-heart artwork, alongside chrome cars and chrome domiciles [MTM B7:222].

MTM B7:222

ChromosomesIn the turbaned speaker’s account of the Royal Pop Historians’ techniques, an ancestral cicada had two more chromosomes and, coincidentally, two more notes in its song than modern descendants. He claims both the old song and the missing chromosomes can be recovered, the latter duplicated by advanced techniques [MTM B11:323-325].

MTM B11:323-325

Chronicker, S.J., Thomas J.Jesuit contributor to the Crock, whose article in the issue described in Archipelago is on Diabolism in the World Today [A:41]. Listed as Thomas Chroniker S.J. among the ecclesial or vineyard people of Duffey’s Chicago golden age [MTM B3:99], and as Thos. J. Chronicker, S.J. among the magazine’s contributors during Duffey’s wartime editorship [MTM B4:138].

A:41; MTM B3:99; MTM B4:138

Chrysostom (Papadiabolous I alias)Alias of Gregory McIfreann Papadiabolous, the Asiatic twin or Papadiabolous I born in Smyrna, according to X. His other names include Sanditen, Protagoras, and Hochstruwelpieter-Goltz. X distinguishes him from the Irish twin Gregory McColum, Papadiabolous II, whose aliases include Noonan and Flaherty [D:285].

D:285

Chrysostom (Saint)St. John Chrysostom, whom Finnegan tentatively names, with Jerome as an alternative, when discussing Le Marin’s theory of an island Terrestrial Paradise. Finnegan thinks such authorities sought Paradise in the Near East, not in Le Marin’s Antilles [D:234].

D:234

Chthonic GoddessesThe goddesses invoked in the portrait of Mary Louise Byrne’s strength and bovine quality. The narrator presents her as the royal bovine or sacred cow through which such goddesses pass, as well as an embodied part of Duffey’s own soul [MTM B2:55].

MTM B2:55

Church (building/institution)Both a religious institution and a place of worship. Sally calls churches traps in her argument with Hans and Marie [A:8]. Particular buildings include Sydney’s Annunciation Church, where Hans and Marie marry [A:31]; the unnamed small Naxos church where Finnegan receives confession and attends Mass [D:119-120]; and the unnamed church opposite his encounter with Tommy Katt [D:232]. Duffey visits the winged stone church of St. Malachy in Chicago while seeking his future wife [MTM B3:87-88]. Teresa’s and the Stranahans’ shared parish hosts her wedding to Vincent [MTM B5:183]; in her memories of another life or dream she also knows the church where her children with Finnegan were baptized [A:204]. X locates Ifreann Columkill’s baptismal record, naming the Devil as his father, at St. Elmo’s near Krakow [D:279]. A priest from St. Katherine’s blesses the communal pot [A:133] [MTM B6:195]. St. Michael’s is being unstructured on the Great Day [GD:496], while Elena describes St. Cristina’s Chicago parish using Casey’s substituted music for special liturgy [PG:525]. In How Many Miles to Babylon, Hackenschmidt declares the Thing dead after a ritual destroying the Ekklesia’s straw-man Peter [MB:568].

A:8; A:31; D:119-120; D:232; MTM B3:87-88; MTM B5:183; A:204; D:279; A:133; MTM B6:195; GD:496; PG:525; MB:568

Church of St. ElmoParish nearest Krakow in X’s reconstructed family history. He says its record names the Devil as father of Katie Noonan’s child, who is baptized Columkill [D:279].

D:279

Church of St. KatherineChurch supplying the priest whom Duffey brings to bless the great communal soup pot [A:133] [MTM B6:195].

A:133; MTM B6:195

Church of St. MalachyChicago stone church two blocks north of Duffey’s hotel, with three spread-winged archangels on its south front and nine large angels on each east and west side. Its ruddy, winged turrets catch the morning sun while Duffey searches the arriving worshippers for his moth, his future wife [MTM B3:87-88]. Letitia makes arrangements there for their wedding [MTM B3:92]; they visit it while preparing their home and marriage [MTM B3:96], and the subsequent account confirms that they marry [MTM B3:98].

MTM B3:87-88; MTM B3:92; MTM B3:96; MTM B3:98

Church of St. MichaelChurch being dismantled through faith in the Great Day episode. After leaving the Pelican, Duffey visits its damaged stone Michael at what was the entrance; the statue says that the living water has gone and that no Mass or even morning remains [GD:496].

Church of St. PhilomenaEarlier heading that misclassified the school as a church. See St. Philomena's.
Church of the Annunciation (Sydney)Sydney church where John Gottfried Schultz, called Hans, marries Marie Anna Monaghan on Monday, February 15, 1943. Hans lacks army permission, so the wedding is temporarily secret and none of their friends attends; twenty or thirty of Marie’s relatives are present [A:31].

A:31

Churchy peopleThe ecclesial or vineyard members of Duffey’s Chicago golden-age circle: Thomas Chroniker S.J.; Tim and Gale Tuthill; Sister Mary Cornelia (Sullivan) Foster and Alma Ruch; Dan and Nan Donovan; Sister Mary Aurora (Rittenhouse); Martin and Katherine Redwine; Frantz and Elaine St. Clair. The narrator says these vineyard workers keep the world turning [MTM B3:99].

ChurnHousehold vessel bearing the iron-lettered names Sturgis, Curtis Improved, or Star Barrel in Duffey’s remembered or mind-borrowed childhood observations [MTM B1:17]. The narrator later compares the ten-year-old Casey, after his attempted debut as world Leader, to a churn in which butter of a particular flavor is forming [MTM B4:118].

MTM B1:17; MTM B4:118

Churning CreekDescriptive phrase, not a stated place-name, for the creek Henry and Casey climb up to before swimming in a deep hole below a waterfall [A:42].

A:42

CicadasInsects whose chorus surrounds Finnegan and Anastasia on the moonlit Naxos mountaintop while their donkey grazes below [D:132]. A turbaned Royal Pop Historians speaker claims that an ancestral cicada had two additional chromosomes and, coincidentally, two extra notes in its song, both accessible to their reconstruction techniques [MTM B11:324-325].

D:132; MTM B11:324-325

Cid, TheOne of the enchanted or trance-sleeping leaders X lists, with Barbarossa, Alaric, Brian Boru, and Arthur, whose subjects await their awakening or release. X contrasts their sleep with the Devil’s wakefulness in prison [MTM B6:204-205].

MTM B6:204-205

CigarA recurrent character prop. Stein smokes while typing beneath his publisher’s placard [A:120]; in the Great Day episode he wishes to be buried with a lit cigar and claims his lengthening stogie is made of faith-tobacco [GD:493-494]. Le Marin includes a still-smoking cigar in the standard derelict-ship story he applies to the Sarcophagus [D:243]. The dead hack from the Seabach has a mauled cigar in his mouth [D:135] [D:147]. Hillary Hilton trades in distressed cigars [A:253]. After buying his St. Louis premises, Duffey smokes half a cigar and later gives it to Giulio [MTM B2:40] [MTM B2:42]; he accidentally knocks Charley Murray’s cigar from the balloon before releasing its hydrogen [MTM B2:66]. X smokes one of the Mogul’s cigars while awaiting him in his apartment [MB:570].

CincinnatiOne of the gracious American cities Patrick Stranahan recommends knowing [A:110]. In Finnegan’s confused rhapsody of places and times, some of the bars he seems to be visiting are, he thinks, really in Cincinnati [A:200].

CindersWhat remains of Chicago in Casey’s ninth imaginary world, a revolutionary fantasy in which workers topple buildings and start a fire greater than the original Chicago fire [A:160].

CircleA grouping of companions or a pattern of association. The soldiers pass their last bottle around a circle in the grass [A:69]; Patrick Stranahan’s household welcomes Monica’s and the daughters’ many social circles [A:104]. The account How Many Miles to Babylon is attributed to a member of Finnegan’s old outer circle [MTM B12:368], while Charlotte says Casey’s Antichrist title carries little prestige with the real inner-circle people [MTM B12:379]. Bagby’s letters after death describe circles differentiated by intensity and transfiguration rather than by inner and outer position [MTM B8:248-249]. Stein notes the stir caused by the Devil’s release in esoteric circles, while varying his opinion of whether that released figure is the Devil or a decoy [MTM B10:291].

In the performing sense, X says he played the circuits as the Great X-Capo [A:137]. Duffey visits his circuit of midwestern cities for a year or more after the missing years, starting and selling three businesses [MTM B3:77]. Anastasia says Seaworthy and his company make circuits to check their apparatus and men in different towns, calling the business deep and murderous [D:39].

CircusA source of images and performances: circus girl acrobats populate Casey’s erotic dream world [A:157]; Professor Kirol has performed in European and American circuses [A:215-216]; and Marie Courtois’s strength and excitement are compared with a circus woman and a circus [D:37]. Monica calls Finnegan’s behavior with Mary Schaeffer either a scandal or a circus [A:105]. Circuses also figure among the popular arts the narrator says are deliberately degraded after the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207].

MTM B2:41; MTM B2:42

Cisterns, DeepAncestral depths invoked in Finnegan’s litany about his primordial people. His question about the earth’s deep cisterns stands between questions about making blood from elemental materials and remembering childhood’s blue ice [D:213].

Citadel of sanityFinnegan’s description of the Brannagans’ hospitable home. His thanksgiving for this refuge follows praise of Gertrude’s extravagant cooking and the joke that her southern kitchen has escaped fried chicken and cornbread [D:208].

CitizenA political or civic identity: X says Ifreann claimed Krakow citizenship throughout his life, although he left below citizenship age [D:280]. Carmelo’s travel papers make Duffey the Irish Free State citizen Mike Duffey for the Cuban journey [MTM B12:369]. Widow Waldo reports that the state inspector relies on pressure from neighbors and fellow citizens against the part of Zabotski’s structure on his own lot [MTM B9:274]. An excerpt attributed to Leo XIII’s The Condition of Labor speaks of industrious, modest men winning their fellow citizens’ sympathy [MTM B5:176].

D:280; MTM B12:369; MTM B9:274; MTM B5:176

City CommissionMunicipal body to which a reporter says Zabotski complained about flooding on Dumaine Street, severe enough to float an ocean-going ship past his house. Zabotski concedes that the remark sounds like his own and that sufficient rain could carry his giant contraption to Lake Borgne [MTM B9:289].

MTM B9:289

City HallChicago municipal building visited by Duffey and Letitia while preparing their home and marriage, in a round of visits also including St. Malachy’s, an insurer, a bank, and a lawyer [MTM B3:96].

MTM B3:96

Civil litigationOne of the popular arts the narrator includes in the sweeping loss of style and class following the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207].

MTM B6:207

Civil War, AmericanAmerican conflict of 1861-1865, beginning with the bombardment of Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861. Lee’s April 9, 1865 surrender at Appomattox was a decisive ending, though other Confederate surrenders followed. The novel associates Prisoner John’s twenty-year captivity in an attic cell with Civil War days [MTM B1:13]. Private Gregory says he lost his papers during the war and used that loss to reduce his recorded age [A:77].

MTM B1:13; A:77

Civilized personTrinali’s joking name for herself when she insists that only barbarians dine by electric light. Her electricity has been cut off for nonpayment, so she brings candles and would rather nobody else use electricity either [A:228].

A:228

Claim checkTicket X steals from Doll’s bag while she shops, enabling him to retrieve the suitcase of money from its locker. He substitutes the matching suitcase packed with banded newspaper pieces and lays a trail for the pursuers to find that decoy [D:178].

D:178

Clancys (Family)One of the families an older relative names among Duffey’s kin in an account of his childhood among Iowa farms and towns and several cities. Duffey disputes the genealogy, suggesting that she remembers his twin instead [MTM B1:7-8].

MTM B1:7-8

Clang-for-service bellBell Bagby proposes for Duffey’s establishment, so customers can call him back while he works in Bagby’s adjoining cabinet shop. A boarded doorway between the buildings can be reopened for that arrangement [MTM B2:46].

MTM B2:46

ClarencePlace whose beaches appear with those of Mona and Baile in the projected voyage of the poem opening Finnegan’s chapter [A:171].

A:171

Clarence (Sulphur-Bottom Sullivan)Baptismal name of Sulphur-Bottom Sullivan, and the only name his parents used for him. The narrator calls the nickname’s origin remarkable but declines to tell it [D:217].

ClarendenAlias X assigns to Gregory McColum Papadiabolous, the Irish twin or Papadiabolous II. His other listed names are Noonan, Flaherty, Christy, Cobbett, Malory, Ingraham, and Arbuthnot [D:285].

D:285

ClarityLucidity that can be revealing or deceptive. Finnegan calls his conviction that he is the world’s only person full clarity during his chaparral ordeal [A:205]; after burying Don Lewis, a little clarity makes him recognize that Papa Devil was not the killer [D:112]. Hans asks Marie to turn his incoherent but revealing insights into clarity [MTM B6:186]. The magus recovers his identity as Melchisedech as his clarity increases [MTM B13:402], yet the poisoned spring later makes him see unreal things with deceptive clarity before he gains the special perception of dying [MTM B13:441]. “To Trinali with Clarity” is a projected ode-title in Trinali’s fantasy of a significant early death [A:232].

A:205; D:112; MTM B6:186; MTM B13:402; MTM B13:441; A:232

Claxton, JohnArtist whose slate-slab paintings Duffey adds to his New Orleans art-dealing stock [MTM B6:199].

MTM B6:199

CleavageRock property mentioned in Casey’s notebook claim that rocks can be left- or right-handed according to their formation and type of cleavage [A:164].

A:164

ClementClement of Rome, recognizable among Linus and Cletus aboard the sacred ship in Henry’s vision [A:45]. One of the Apostolic Fathers and traditionally the fourth bishop of Rome, he led the Roman church in the late first century; chronological lists variously give about 88-97 or 92-99. Early church tradition connects him with the Apostles, and one tradition makes Peter his consecrator. His First Letter to the Corinthians, usually placed around 96, seeks to resolve a dispute within that church and is a very early Christian witness to communal unity and order. Later tradition relates his exile and martyrdom by drowning with an anchor; these are hagiographical reports rather than securely established biographical details. His Roman Catholic feast is November 23.

A:45

Clement (Hal)Author of Left of Africa, listed as number 1 in Manuscript Press’s Lost Manuscripts series in the publisher’s notice at the end of this edition of Archipelago; Archipelago itself is number 2 [A:286].

A:286

CleopatraOne of the exalted names Hilary Hilton says reincarnation claimants choose. He uses the analogy to ridicule Casey’s claim of exchanging souls with the Devil; he does not say Casey claims to have been Cleopatra [PG:531].

PG:531

Cleveland BaysHorses drawing Sebastian Hilton’s hired carriage for the school dance, praised by the narrator as unsurpassed in style. The liveried driver, post-boy’s horn, and circuitous ride with the girls briefly relieve the boys’ dread of formal pairing [MTM B1:32].

MTM B1:32

Cliff peoplePeople Hans reaches by climbing the apparently inaccessible cliffs of the island. He eats with them and learns their language; their food includes taro, goop, cuscus or coconut possum, birds, and meat whose peculiar taste prompts his teasing hints of cannibalism [A:58]. Finnegan is afraid to meet them, and the narrator explains that they look exactly like him: great noses, chinlessness, a deceptive shambling gait, and sudden speed and strength. Whatever remnant they represent, Finnegan belongs to it too [A:59].

A:58; A:59

ClimaxA culmination whose possibility the narratives repeatedly question. The noises at Yokipoki’s grave build to a climax before Finnegan discovers the rats [D:47]. Doll demands a climax to the conflict with the older people, but X insists their method is endless gnawing and undermining, not climaxes [D:292]. Finnegan’s response to Dotty resembles the culmination of longing and also sheer terror [A:92]; even the final shooting is denied the name of crisis because it changes nobody’s attitude [A:282]. Other uses include the jungle raid’s climax [A:54], Endymeon’s search for a climactic line for his fourth stanza [A:238], the ironic description of America’s entry into the world war as a climax of political unease [MTM B4:138], and the Thunder Colt Game as the opera’s climax piece [MTM B11:350].

D:47; D:292; A:92; A:282; A:54; A:238; MTM B4:138; MTM B11:350

ClimbingA recurrent practical skill and dream action. Jungle roots can serve as ladders [A:36], and Hans climbs cliffs to reach the cliff people [A:58]; his ascents through arrows and pistol fire, up an immense iron ladder, and into a giant spider’s web are explicitly dreams [A:61]. At school Rattigan climbs like a monkey, Sebastian like a squirrel, Duffey competently with giant hands available for support, and Charley Murray in terror [MTM B1:25]. Duffey also escapes his attic by a vine-covered rope [MTM B1:13] and, drawing on his rigging experience, climbs above the stage to inspect the Majesty’s apparent height [MTM B8:240]. Finnegan scales six stories of a Gothic hotel using its ornamentation; his recent upper-story burglaries have sought evidence rather than profit [D:162]. Little Alcohol handles climbing and high windows for his burglary partnership [D:218].

A:36; A:58; A:61; MTM B1:25; MTM B1:13; MTM B8:240; D:162; D:218

ClioGreek Muse of History. In Finnegan’s dream she carries a trumpet and clepsydra, joining the other muses in an investiture he resists because accepting it means lifelong work [A:181]. The narrator later quotes a prediction attributed to Nostradamus in which the new Pope redirects Clio’s road, applying it to Pope Finnegan I [MB:598].

A:181; MB:598

Clock (Argo as dating)One of the Argo’s functions according to Duffey. An artifact touched to the talking oak in its wheel elicits its year of origin in the appropriate era and annals. When confused, the wood instead calls out coordinates that may have no relation to the object. The log also records the last nine thousand years and the next sixty-seven, though interpreting it requires interior illumination and later futures belong to another log [MTM B13:411].

MTM B13:411

Clootie, OldScots name for the Devil, associated with cloven hooves. Duffey uses its familiar, belittling tone toward the Majesty while exploring the giant’s trashy mind at the New Catholic Press Guild assembly [MTM B8:239-243]. He uses it again while accusing the devil confronting him in the closed place of being unable to create; that figure alternates between claiming authority and speaking as an agent for a client [MTM B10:303].

MTM B8:239-243; MTM B10:303

ClothesGarments repeatedly used to mark role and identity. The well-fitted clothes of the opening Asimov epigraph disguise a hypothetical Neanderthal, while Seaworthy first appears shabby [D:9]. Finnegan buys a satchel, clothes and shoes with Seaworthy’s money [D:17], and later looks like a Montenegran prince in evening dress [D:100]. For the swim to Paros, he and Manuel tow their clothes and shoes in leather sacks tied to floats [D:151]. On Basse-Terre he gives old clothes to a friend without understanding the plan; a similar-looking seaman is then found murdered in them [D:267]. Other appearances include the Bavarian Club girls’ peasant costumes [MTM B2:47], Elena’s refusal to undress while playing concertina [A:273], the hired Cuban sleeper’s work clothes beside his nude body [MTM B12:373], and old travel clothes beside Count Finnegan in his painting [MB:551]. On the Great Day, clothed Duffey is treated as conspicuous and improper to look at [GD:496].

ClotildaThird of the women’s names assigned to the four companions’ daily bottles in Paradise, after Agatha and Bathildes. On the unusually heavy drinking night described, they have continued through Clotilda, Delphina, Etheldreda, Faustina and Georgina to Hildegarde [D:243].

D:243

CloudburstSudden storm announced by Bandicoot as it arrives. Its flood carries Zabotski’s ark, its human passengers and its animals along the street toward Lake Borgne [MTM B9:287].

MTM B9:287

Cloudy MountainsMountains in New Guinea whose peaks Biloxi Brannagan has climbed and whose streams and dips he has panned for gold, part of the catalogue showing his travels exceeding Finnegan’s [D:203].

ClownA recurring comic role, image and insult. Howland plays at being Finnegan’s valet [A:182]; the Seabach’s black crewman has clownish moments beneath his undersized pearl-gray derby [D:135]; and X arrives looking both happy and wistful [A:136] [MTM B6:200]. The Fleshpot Row comedian’s tortured face forms a clown’s flesh mask [MTM B4:127], while nightclub comedian Otto Glotglutz is reduced to tears by Hiram III’s retort [MB:564]. Trinali makes clown figures from cork and raffia [A:228], and Finnegan’s verse dismisses Omar as a clown [A:276]. Finnegan applies the insult to Don Barnaby while wondering whether he is the other man he remembers [D:249], and sees through X’s performance as a comical drunk [D:174]. The narrator finally calls Pope Finnegan I a big-nosed clown as well as a wanderer and master artist [MB:598].

A:182; D:135; A:136; MTM B6:200; MTM B4:127; MB:564; A:228; A:276; D:249; D:174; MB:598

ClubSocial, professional and entertainment associations recur throughout the books. Duffey’s Rounders’ Club combines restaurant, bar, residence, transport hire and games, with automatic Steeplechase Club membership for patrons [MTM B2:49]; he joins, or in another version founds, the World-Wide Argonauts Argo Balloon Club [MTM B2:63]. The Sydney Plaza houses seamen’s and other clubs [A:3], Stein lectures to service clubs [A:19], a Malayan boy names an Indonesian Club [A:88], and Maurine jokingly calls her family’s men the Rod and Gun Club [A:103]. The Pelican has an unofficial Glee Club [MTM B7:226]; Mary Catherine belongs to three book clubs [A:249]; and Kirol works in nightclub entertainment [A:216]. Finnegan drinks with Seaworthy and meets Papa Devil in a club [D:13-15], takes Doll to a supper club [D:173], and later seeks X and Doll in the club opposite the graveyard [D:275]. Named establishments include the Bavarian Club [MTM B2:47], Chicago’s Colony Club [MTM B3:93], and the Beacon Club in Duffey’s waterfront catalogue [MTM B13:407]. Charlotte calls the circle of extraordinary acquaintances her Prodigious Peoples’ Club [MTM B8:260].

MTM B2:49; MTM B2:63; A:3; A:19; A:88; A:103; MTM B7:226; A:249; A:216; D:13-15; D:173; D:275; MTM B2:47; MTM B3:93; MTM B13:407; MTM B8:260

Club RoyalHowland Jerome Howland’s plush establishment, catering to patrons whose hard childhoods have fostered an appetite for conspicuous luxury. It serves Danish beer and Hungarian Tokay, employs a chef from Martinique, and has an orchestra playing old classic jazz [A:246].

Finnegan also lists coal among fuels whose different hazes obscure the sky’s true color [D:127]. Charcoal briquettes, a distinct fuel, appear during the soldiers’ island routine [A:31].

MB:560

CobberAustralian informal term for a friend. Finnegan uses it in his exaggerated imitation of an Australian while trying to pass as an Aussie in the drinking-club episode [A:13].

A:13

CobbettWilliam Cobbett (1763-1835), the radical journalist and historical writer whose works Patrick Stranahan places with Livy as a sufficient reading of history [A:109]. Separately, Cobbett is one of the aliases X lists for Gregory McColum Papadiabolous, the Irish twin or Papadiabolous II [D:285].

CobblesPaving stones. The warning that even the cobbles have ears belongs to the joke about disguising the visiting Americans as Australians [A:11]. At the Royal Pop History meeting, the turbaned speaker claims ironstone cobbles succeeded slates and shales in Decatur Street’s layered record [MTM B11:329]. Near the Naxos landing, six dead men, including the Seabach crew and Joe Cross, lie on wet cobbles [D:147].

A:11; MTM B11:329; D:147

Cocktail PartiesPart of Casey’s offered career for Finnegan as a celebrated proletarian painter: wealthy patrons, cocktail parties and house visits in exchange for occasional manifestos [A:183-184].

A:183-184

CoconutImage of the world as something Finnegan means to crack open, with or without Seaworthy’s help [D:18-19]. In Count Finnegan’s commentary, a Lever Brothers coconut plantation supplies a punning measure of Casey’s nuttiness [PG:544].

D:18-19; PG:544

Coconut PossumAnimal heard squawking above Henry and Casey as they descend through the jungle [A:44]. Coconut possum is also among the meats Hans eats with the cliff people [A:58].

A:44; A:58

CodeSecret notation or a rule of conduct. The Seabach’s log includes cryptic numerical jottings [D:135]; X claims he can break any code in the papers Finnegan might have examined [D:188], asks a telephone contact about a missing code book, and supplies whistle signals for his companions [D:184]. Count Finnegan and Cardinal Hedayat receive coded assignments in the eschatological drama [MB:554], while coded bells communicate with dolphins and porpoises [MB:575]. Charlotte says Casey violates the confidence man’s code by exploiting the helpless [MTM B12:379]. In Casey’s political attack on the Bark, free elections are called unguided elections in code [A:130]; Trinali’s code forbids deliberately planning the picturesque early death she imagines [A:232].

D:135; D:188; D:184; MB:554; MB:575; MTM B12:379; A:130; A:232

Coffee House (by the harbor)Harborside coffee house visited by Hans Schultz and Marie Monaghan after the day’s outings. They linger over coffee laced with brandy, talking about peoples, religion and marriage [A:7].

A:7

Coffee House (Ghost)The Ghost Coffee Shop, a New Orleans café run by Anthony Ghost, whose father came from the Netherlands. Its customers include dock workers, seamen, night people and schoolchildren, among them the Ursuline students discussing Seven Roads with Duffey [MTM B10:293]. A preceding account of literal ghosts gathering for one hour before and after dawn is explicitly retracted by the narrator, except for the existence of Count Finnegan’s painting of ghostly customers [MTM B10:292].

MTM B10:293; MTM B10:292

Coffee making and consumptionA frequent accompaniment to conversation and ordinary hospitality. Hans and Marie linger over brandy-laced coffee while Hans credits Clement VIII with giving the drink Christian sanction [A:7]. Finnegan, Anastasia, Marie, Papa Devil and Joe Cross have coffee ashore at a small establishment [D:67], and Doll includes it in the graveyard picnic [D:284]. Duffey discusses Seven Roads with the schoolgirls at the Ghost Coffee Shop [MTM B10:293]. Coffee becomes uncanny when Charlotte serves it without cups on the Great Day [GD:484], while the still-warm coffee on the supposedly derelict Sarcophagus belongs to Castleman’s false report as related by Le Marin [D:245]. A man Don Lewis asks for help dismisses five hundred dollars as insufficient coffee money [D:108]. Coffee bushes belong to Duffey’s remembered domain as the Boy King [MTM B1:17], and coffee making is included among the everyday arts said to be degraded after the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207].

A:7; D:67; D:284; MTM B10:293; GD:484; D:245; D:108; MTM B1:17; MTM B6:207

CoffinContainer for death, survival and jokes about both. Le Marin says the Sarcophagus was coffin-shaped [D:244]. Finnegan reports burying Papa Devil without a coffin on top of another man [D:153]. The Argo carries more coffins than would be needed for all its Masters [MTM B13:449]; Duffey’s stripped bones rest in one until God tells him to resume his work [MTM B13:443]. Zabotski supplies an unused coffin for Letitia, who had admired its class [MTM B8:253]. Show Boat jokingly hopes Dotty’s funeral will be their next reunion and says Dotty should look pretty in a coffin [A:262-263]. Trinali’s ode about herself in her coffin is buried with her [A:240].

D:244; D:153; MTM B13:449; MTM B13:443; MTM B8:253; A:262-263; A:240

CognomenFinnegan’s word for the name by which he introduces himself to Seaworthy while unable to remember his proper name [D:11]. X later describes the many names accumulated by the Papadiabolous twins [D:285].

CognoscentiOne of X’s overlapping names for the floating intellectual world, together with intelligentsia and gnostics. He says this group was disproportionately represented among the invited witnesses at the Devil’s release [MTM B6:205].

CoilThe snake coiled in Justinian’s skull in a “Promontory Goats” monologue supplies the image for judgments attributed to a snake rather than to the dead speaker himself [PG:545]. The Sidewinder, Nick, is likewise described as coiling laterally and striking as he falls wounded in the final shooting [A:282].

Coin parlorOne of the Kasmir Street businesses where, according to Newton Prescott, every coin parlor once had at least one Casey Machine, an achronological eavesdropping device [CM:503].

Coin-bendingStrongman feat in Hans Schultz’s carnival repertoire. The account says it requires angry determination and disregard for pain, comparing it with bending horseshoes and specially tempered steel bars [A:219].

ColchisBlack Sea kingdom associated with the Argonauts’ quest for the Golden Fleece. The Argo sails under its flag [MTM B12:386], and its logs record the finding of the Fleece as a major early triumph [MTM B13:421]. Combings from that Fleece furnish Duffey’s golden mask, scarf and gauntlets after his reduction to bones [MTM B13:443]. In the Royal Pop Historians’ account, destroying the Black Sea is intended both to erase the Devil’s prison and to weaken Colchis as a base of the Argo forces [MTM B11:336-337].

MTM B12:386; MTM B13:421; MTM B13:443; MTM B11:336-337

Colfax, JennyOne of the theatrical friends in Duffey and Letitia’s Chicago circle, named together with Duke Colfax [MTM B3:99].
