Collagen contractilityOne item in the elaborate physiological list used by The Eighteenth Book of Strange Encounters to claim that Duffey is more than four thousand years old, despite the apparent fifty-five-year age of his body. The fictional report groups it with Howship’s lacunar frequency, thrombocyte-shaped remnants and other tests, then quotes Duffey’s explanation that a person may be older than his body [MTM B8:250].

MTM B8:250

Collins, Emmet (Emma)Emma Collins, a young woman, celebrated impersonator and protégée of X, who appears as Emmet Collins of Boston, the double of Cardinal Merry of Cork [MB:579] [MB:598]. She talks her way past the bounty-men by pretending to inspect their operation for Track and Total [MB:595-596]. Her extraordinary laughter after Pope Finnegan laments the lack of women’s roles exposes the disguise, and John Giwa demands X’s explanation [MB:597-598].

MB:579; MB:598; MB:595-596; MB:597-598

ColmarAlsatian city in modern France where Duffey experiences a restaurant scene borrowed from Sebastian Hilton’s memory shortly before his thirteenth birthday. He eats soupe aux grenouilles and Tournedos au Poivre Vert at the Rotisserie Schillinger; the narrator only conjectures that he is staying at the Hotel du Champ de Mars. The account notes that Colmar was not formally French at that remembered time, though it calls the place France [MTM B1:35].

MTM B1:35

ColonialA historical style and a form of collective life. Angela says her father could imitate the old handwriting of Englishmen, Spaniards, Frenchmen and Colonials on his forged maps [D:260]. Brannagan orders a volvox colonial as fruit in the future settlement [MTM B13:418]. A separate grotesque catalogue of proposed murders imagines rapidly spreading colonial microbes [MB:581].

D:260; MTM B13:418; MB:581

Colony Club, TheChicago club whose sunlit rooms, gaming, loaded sideboards, abundant beef dinners and Canadian whisky embody its splendid vulgarity and fast money [MTM B3:93]. Duffey visits with Lily and Letitia Koch; the Mullens group, except the newly arrived Manolo, is known there as the Cavendishes. Charlotte describes her stolen fortune and the mind-alarm that has exposed the disposable Mullens name [MTM B3:93]. Sebastian joins the Harvesters’ Dinner and discusses Duffey’s coming marriage; the Girl Countess later plays bridge with Charlotte, Gloria and Lily [MTM B3:94-95].

MTM B3:93; MTM B3:94-95

ColorA pervasive means of describing bodies, atmosphere and art. Anastasia’s olive complexion shifts between green and gold, and her eyes between black and purple [D:32]; Marie’s coloring is vividly red-blond [D:57], Seaworthy recovers his granite color after turning ashen [D:15], and Papa Devil has a ghoulish purple hue [D:30]. Angela appears in dazzling color [D:259]. Finnegan explains differences in sky color through fuel smoke [D:127], while X’s eight-toned car surrounds him with a seeming rainbow [D:178-179]. Duffey has sorrel hair and fire-blue eyes [MTM B1:6]; Beth Keegan has black hair and ivory skin [MTM B2:56]; and the frozen woman’s veins, eyelids and flesh between the toes are sky blue [MTM B13:398]. The Finnegan effigy’s destruction releases scarlet, crimson, sulphur, saffron and flame-colored blood, converging on garish orange [MTM B11:351].

D:32; D:57; D:15; D:30; D:259; D:127; D:178-179; MTM B1:6; MTM B2:56; MTM B13:398; MTM B11:351

ColumkillBaptismal name of Katie Noonan’s son, called Ifreann by his mother and given the patronym Gregorovitch after Gregory, his adoptive father. X reports that the parish register lists the Devil as father and favors that explanation, while acknowledging Gregory as another possibility [D:279].

D:279

Combat Books (Special)Books from which Sebastian Hilton knows fighting tricks. He uses them while theatrically provoking and humiliating larger schoolboys, casting them as bullies before the witnesses [MTM B1:23].

MTM B1:23

Combat BuffalosAmphibious armed vehicles in the war-invasion half of Elroy Redheart’s second red room, emerging from landing craft with combat alligators amid artificial thunder and lightning [MTM B7:222].

MTM B7:222

Combings, GoldenThreads taken from the Great Golden Fleece of Colchis and made by Casey Gorshok into a mask, scarf and gauntlets for Duffey’s exposed bones. They enable his continued appearance as an Argo Master after God instructs him to resume service despite being dead [MTM B13:443].

MTM B13:443

ComboA small performing ensemble. Examples include Duffey’s Rounders’ String Band [MTM B2:52], the Monumental Jazz musicians at Good Guy’s [MTM B7:220], and the combo that plays The King Shall Ride and the Gadarene Swine Song during Duffey’s reunion with his creations at Rounders’ [MTM B5:158]. Kirol forms combos as part of his changing carnival arrangements [A:215]. The Brimstone Combo belongs to Trinali’s poem about a saloon in the imagined groves of Gomorrah [A:235].

MTM B2:52; MTM B7:220; MTM B5:158; A:215; A:235

ComedianSee Clown.
ComedyA mode ranging from comic entertainment to the shape of human and sacred events. X compares Finnegan’s narrow escapes from his pursuers to an old comedy [D:177]. Musical comedy, nightclub comedy and two-reel comedy making figure among the popular arts said to be trashed after the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207-209]. Showboat regards Duffey as her maker and scenarist in the human comedy [MTM B5:181]. Goldfarb’s Alley is the family television comedy interrupted by Duffey’s projected confrontation with Casey [MTM B12:380]. Pope Finnegan calls the conclave an Eschatological Comedy, joking that its sole defect is the absence of women’s roles, immediately before Emma Collins’s disguise is exposed [MB:597-598].

D:177; MTM B6:207-209; MTM B5:181; MTM B12:380; MB:597-598

Comic BooksAlternative to a newspaper proposed by the young newspaper worker whom Duffey confronts on the Great Day. Since everything is new, the worker argues, there can be no news; old comic-book reruns may replace the paper [GD:487].

GD:487

Comic MagazinesFinnegan recalls reading an abundant collection of old comic magazines, with a bottle for company, while off duty from an engine-room job on an unnamed ship. He expected an Atlantic port but disembarked in San Francisco [A:145]. Beth Keegan also draws much of her playful dialogue from comic magazines rather than plays [MTM B2:60].

A:145; MTM B2:60

Comic MaskFinnegan’s description of his face after identifying himself with the boy in the lost-face story. He says he has a comic mask for a face, a monicker for a name and only a shadow’s shadow, expressing his sense of being a changeling without a secure identity [A:56].

A:56

Comic MonstersBagby’s description of the Slant-Faced Men’s treatment in pulp-magazine letter departments, where they are made into comic monsters like BEMs and HLPs. Dotty identifies three comic strips using them; she would find them funny if she did not know they were real [MTM B7:225].

MTM B7:225

CommissionA sales fee, an artistic order or a public body. Duffey and Rattigan sell fellow pupils’ goods on commission, largely as an accommodation [MTM B1:26]. Trinali earns five dollars in rent credit for finding Hans as a tenant [A:227], while Finnegan receives a dealer’s standing order for all the Orange Period paintings he can produce [A:191]. Honeybucket faces the Corporation Commission over his proposed stock issue [D:218]. A reporter asks Zabotski about his complaint to the City Commission concerning street flooding [MTM B9:289].

MTM B1:26; A:227; A:191; D:218; MTM B9:289

Commission SalesmanFinnegan’s first white-collar employment, selling a dog-housebreaking preparation door to door in Buffalo. He initially sells only two or three bottles a day, earning seventy-five cents per bottle, while McGregor supplies exhausting demonstrations [A:189]. He becomes successful by marketing the preparation to practical jokers, selling three thousand bottles in a week before retiring from the business [A:190].

A:189; A:190

CommitteeCollective machinery for social action, sometimes satirical. The Moral Sanctions Committee for the Removal of Eye-Sores and Abominations confronts Zabotski about his growing structure [MTM B9:276-277]. The Union Sheet’s fellows seem to appear only in committees [MTM B7:213]. Manuel instead calls himself a committee of one, charged with infiltrating the apparatus that makes devils, because he trusts only his own incorruptibility [D:56].

MTM B9:276-277; MTM B7:213; D:56

Commodore (Bar)Sydney drinking place visited while Hans rapidly trains for the beer contest, and revisited on the celebratory pub crawl after he defeats Bushmaster [A:18] [A:23].

A:18; A:23

Common Law (Obscure bit)Finnegan’s claimed legal justification for temporarily appropriating George Brubaker’s car: the Lien of Extreme Need. He invokes it after the girl driving him realizes the car may not be his [D:168].

D:168

Common SenseThe narrator’s joking explanation for Stein’s quick mastery of the Dominion Rules for beer-drinking contests: little in them supposedly falls outside common law and common sense [A:19].

A:19

Communications ShackThe Sarcophagus’s radio shack, seized first when the replacement dock rats take over the ship in Le Marin’s account. Finnegan makes it an analogy for the world’s takeover, saying its communications shack was also captured first [D:244].

D:244

CommunismAtheistic Communism is one of the seven contemporary heads Bagby assigns to the old enemy [MTM B5:169]. In Show Boat’s letter, Vincent argues that their circle talks too much about Communism while neglecting the secular-liberal threat [A:263]. Casey’s editorial attacks the Bark for identifying China’s supposedly progressive forces with Western Communism [A:130].

MTM B5:169; A:263; A:130

CommunistPolitical label with unstable personal associations. Casey calls Stein, under the name Hugo Stone, a card-carrying Communist [A:129]. More Than Melchisedech preserves conflicting accounts of whether Stein and Hugo are the same person; Casey says he heard of Stein’s Chicago Communist identity but knew him only later in the army [MTM B4:112]. X describes Ifreann as an old-line Communist and gives the movement a fiercely hostile characterization [D:281]. Duffey’s Hungarian tavern-sign Christ comes from the brief Communist period of Béla Kun, but the picture itself shows a hearty Christ drinking beer, not Christ identified as a Communist [MTM B3:103].

A:129; MTM B4:112; D:281; MTM B3:103

Communist ThingHenry’s father Lawrence calls Communism one shell in the old Antagonist’s shell game and warns that it may be a diversion. Henry answers that, among the many holes admitting water to the boat, it is presently one of the largest [A:125-126].

A:125-126

Community BuildingsCity-park buildings among the venues for Duffey and Letitia’s children’s puppet shows. Their other sites include fire stations, lodge halls, children’s homes, hospitals, libraries, auditoriums and schools; Letitia makes and manipulates the puppets and supplies their voices [MTM B4:133].

MTM B4:133

CompanionA fellow participant whose identity may itself be uncertain. Vincent is Finnegan’s companion at the opening of Archipelago [A:1]. Teresa describes taking an Oread’s part with two other Oreads, and Finnegan’s ghostly participation in her marriage to Vincent [MTM B6:188]. Papa Devil calls Dopey Finnegan’s fetch or double [D:121]; a leftfooted killer and an unnamed companion follow Finnegan after his departure [D:193]. On the Argo, the newly recognized old companion of Duffey and Brannagan is Kasmir Gorshok [MTM B13:426]. The ship carries effigies of respected companions as well as Masters [MTM B13:449]. Count Finnegan arrives with Gilberto Levine and O’Brien and Herman Hercules; the text leaves open whether these are doubles of dead cardinals or the cardinals disguised as their own doubles [MTM B13:450-453].

A:1; MTM B6:188; D:121; D:193; MTM B13:426; MTM B13:449; MTM B13:450-453

CompanyA group of associates or a business concern. The Devil is Dead announces Papadiabolous and his company [D:6], and the Brunhilde’s company includes the Devil [D:31]. The Old Wooden Ship’s resident community is called the Company of Fifty [D:215-216] [D:225]; Duffey names the Devil’s invited adherents the Company of One Thousand [MTM B6:208]. Artists contribute to Duffey and his company’s rebuilding project [MTM B6:199]. Commercial examples include the Acme and Rock Island names on remembered pump handles [MTM B1:17], the chewing-tobacco firm in Marie’s Shakes Pearson anecdote [A:25], Duffey and Letitia’s insurer [MTM B3:96], and the consortium buying Duffey’s school businesses [MTM B2:38]. Honeybucket calls his untried plankton enterprise the Ancient Syrian Cheese Company [D:218-219]. The edition’s copyright page also calls its publisher a Hachette UK company [D:296].

D:6; D:31; D:215-216; D:225; MTM B6:208; MTM B6:199; MTM B1:17; A:25; MTM B3:96; MTM B2:38; D:218-219; D:296

Company of Fifty, TheThe resident regulars of the Old Wooden Ship, whose roster ought to number fifty although the narrator admits forgetting one. They include McGivern, four women called Dotty, the five so-called Swedes and many other individual characters. Frequent visitors such as Finnegan, Le Marin and Dry Gulch Cavaldos are explicitly distinguished from these residents [D:215-216]. Finnegan immerses himself in the company for reassurance in the reality of humanity; the account admits that Susie Kutz’s favorable reports color its portrayal [D:225].

D:215-216; D:225

Company of One ThousandDuffey’s name for the permitted witnesses to the Devil’s release near Yalta, whom he regards as adherents transformed by the encounter [MTM B6:208]. X says exactly one thousand people held permits and that his own, issued under an old assumed identity, was number 982 [MTM B6:204-205].

MTM B6:208; MTM B6:204-205

CompassThe Argo’s compass needle bends toward something below decks as the hidden Man of Mystery’s presence asserts itself; an effigy seaman attributes the distortion to personal magnetism [MTM B13:461]. After the Antichrist reaches the Plains of Megiddo, every compass needle in the world points there as the world’s new center [MTM B13:462].

MTM B13:461; MTM B13:462

CompassionConcern for another’s suffering, sometimes ambiguous or perilously excessive. Seaworthy professes it for Finnegan’s bleeding feet [D:11], and Manuel claims Marie has it for him [D:56]. Charley Murray feels it for the larger boys Sebastian intends to defeat [MTM B1:22]. Papa Piccone’s compassionate acceptance of a mouse instead of a dinosaur may be directed toward the mouse or toward embarrassed Duffey [MTM B5:170]. Casey nearly equals Hans in compassion but conceals it better [A:169]; the “Promontory Goats” introduction suspects his extreme compassion, especially the wish to redeem the Devil, has become sinful [PG:518]. Kasmir Gorshok’s pity for body lice motivates the creation of artificial people as hosts [PG:535]. A modest coffee place is called compassionate [D:67], while the speculative Goat Contingency leads its perpetual debt-payers toward the hell named The End of Compassion [MTM B10:299].

D:11; D:56; MTM B1:22; MTM B5:170; A:169; PG:518; PG:535; D:67; MTM B10:299

CompulsionAn overriding urge. Finnegan leaves Dotty under a compulsion to seek without finding [A:176]. Duffey feels compelled to find his future wife in Chicago before knowing who she is [MTM B3:82]; the sought moth is finally identified with Letitia [MTM B3:80] [MTM B3:90]. Cleo’s explanation of the Goat Contingency describes compulsively trading the worthy for the worthless [MTM B10:295]; Casey’s pursuit of the Devil’s redemption is already an obsession in his schooldays [PG:518].

A:176; MTM B3:82; MTM B3:80; MTM B3:90; MTM B10:295; PG:518

ComputerA device invoked in Duffey’s proposed test of Cardinal Artemis’s flayed skin against the marked skin of the sleeping Gilberto. He suggests flaying the sleeper and running both skins through their computer; the passage does not show the proposal carried out. X and Duffey remain uncertain which man is the original and which the double [MTM B13:451-452].

MTM B13:451-452

Con manA swindler or trickster. Henry toasts Sammy as a con man after Sammy borrows the distracted shoeshine boys’ box to earn whisky money, with Finnegan supplying the musical distraction [A:67-68]. Angela’s father supplies confidence men with fabricated treasure maps and matching half-maps designed for elaborate swindles [D:260-261].

A:67-68; D:260-261

ConceitVanity or an imagined construction. Amoy the parakeet is conceited enough to call himself beautiful despite the narrator’s contrary judgment [A:79]. Finnegan attributes conceit to the fugue in his letter about music’s unkindness [A:263]. Elwin Elkheart dismisses the Argo and divine interventions as Duffey’s conceits [MTM B13:402]. Anastasia reports that Marie regards the category of lady as a bourgeois conceit, while insisting on her own claim to it [D:33].

A:79; A:263; MTM B13:402; D:33

ConcentrationDuffey’s intense mental concentration, or prayer, before seven exhausted mice arrive to perform in the puppet show at Gurdon S. Hubbard Elementary School. The teacher opens the doors and Letitia plays banjo during the wait [MTM B4:136].

MTM B4:136

ConcertinaInstrument Finnegan plays in bars and streets, provoking Ignacio’s objection to his lack of dignity [A:272]. Theresa says playing it has spread her fingers, along with her work with puppets and tricks [A:108].

A:272; A:108

ConchShell whose intricate shape supplies a comparison for Trinali’s chosen driftwood, destined to become a carved lamp [A:233]. In Count Finnegan’s commentary, the shape of a conch can move Casey to tears, illustrating the sensitivity that remains alongside his dangerous commitments [PG:544].

A:233; PG:544

ConchesCreatures in Bayougoula Park’s suddenly present fountain, alongside turtles, frogs, whistling blue fish, carp, oysters and dangerous alligators [MTM B11:331].

MTM B11:331

ConclaveAn assembly, royal, personal or ecclesiastical. Duffey claims attendance at Kings’ Conclaves with Solomon, Saul, Ptolemy, Chandragupta, Nebuchadnezzar, Hsien, Barbarossa, Stephen of Hungary and Conrad II [MTM B5:166]. He suspects his talismanic creations of arranging their St. Louis gathering independently of him [MTM B5:150-152]. Cardinal Henri reads a prophetic reference to the future conclave and rejects its assumption that he will already be dead, proposing to attend as his double’s double [MTM B12:387-388]. In More Than Melchisedech’s later events, the supposed Last Conclave at Babylonia Bagascia assembles to dismantle the Ekklesia, with Monsignor X as servitor [MB:561] [MB:566] [MB:569]. X later serves the thirteen at Mooring-Stone, where the ostensibly surviving doubles include true cardinals and elect Pope Finnegan I [MB:596-598].

MTM B5:166; MTM B5:150-152; MTM B12:387-388; MB:561; MB:566; MB:569; MB:596-598

ConcordiaConcordia, one of the institutions where Duffey takes courses during the summer of 1915, alongside St. Louis University, Washington University, a pharmacy school, and a music school. The novel does not give its full institutional name [MTM B2:49].

MTM B2:49

Concordia UniversityEarlier heading supplied University, which the novel does not give. See Concordia.
Concrete (Ready-mix)Tim Stranahan’s ready-mix business, in which he offers Finnegan a job. Dotty jokes that the work may consist of modeling concrete overcoats, prompting Finnegan to doubt Tim’s fondness for him [A:100].

A:100

CondensorsDevices in which Newton Prescott claims to have trapped more than two hundred postmortem electrical discharges, each occurring about thirty minutes after clinical death. In Josephine McSorely’s purported report, he proposes using one charge in every Casey Machine and interprets part of the data as coming from beyond death [CM:507].

CM:507

ConfederateThe ringleader boy’s supposed helper in finding the Sleeping Man’s cave on the Marianao Coast. He demands two additional gold pieces from Duffey for this confederate, then returns with a cave containing a plainly recent Cuban stand-in instead of Finnegan [MTM B12:373].

MTM B12:373

ConferenceA private consultation or a formal political meeting. Finnegan, Vincent, Tom and Freddy withdraw to confer when Bushmaster nearly spoils the Australian-disguise hoax [A:12]. Sammy and Finnegan confer before their shoeshine con [A:67]. In X’s account of the Devil’s imprisonment, the principals of the Yalta Conference consult the prisoner daily or hourly [MTM B6:204].

A:12; A:67; MTM B6:204

ConfessionFinnegan confesses his drinking, sins and fear of an alien kindred within him to the Capuchin on Naxos; the priest first rejects ordinary blame-shifting, then accepts the possibility of another kindred and grants absolution [D:119]. Duffey tells his blackmailer that the genuinely guilty acts in the compromising photographs have already been confessed and absolved [MTM B4:140]. Charlotte, anticipating danger in her current theft, tells Duffey she needs confession for exploiting widows and orphans, carnality and badger games before they enter St. Malachy’s [MTM B3:87].

D:119; MTM B4:140; MTM B3:87

Confidence and gamine friendsDuffey and Letitia’s Chicago associates described as the better grade of confidence people: Charlotte Garfield, Gideon Sedgewick, Mary Regina Toast, Ralph Kirby, Ira and Rebecca Spain, Victor Ryan, Homer and Evangeline Durban, and Fred and Helen Batavia [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

Confidence peopleSwindlers represented among the roughly five hundred confidence people and thieves attending the Royal Rogues’ and Graceful Swindlers’ Ninth Annual Convention and Confidence-Men’s Congress at the Royal Orleans Hotel. Charlotte attends as a visitor [MTM B7:216]. Anastasia tells Manuel that spies and confidence men ordinarily pass themselves off as traveling salesmen [D:55].

MTM B7:216; D:55

Confirmation NameAccording to Casey, Melchisedech is Duffey’s confirmation name, taken when he was confirmed at forty; his given name in that account is Michael [A:42].

A:42

Confraternity of the RibbersThe community of practical jokers to whom Finnegan endears himself with his Buffalo dog-preparation trick, even while he and McGregor are banned from taverns. Their enthusiasm leads him to sell the product as a joke device [A:190].

A:190

ConfusionUncertainty about identity, memory and events. The apparently simple facts of Finnegan’s life are said to contain amazing confusion, as others remember them differently [A:174]. Finnegan recalls burying Papadiabolous through a mental blind, while X questions how that dead man could have sailed again [D:153]. Zabotski’s Moral Sanction visitors remember both yesterday and eight years ago as the time of their earlier complaint [MTM B9:277]. The changed New Orleans morning contains a pleasant confusion of new arrivals and an unpleasant confusion of displaced creatures [MTM B11:314]. Askandan defines his trade as bringing confusion out of chaos, between excessive simplicity and intolerable disorder [A:257].

A:174; D:153; MTM B9:277; MTM B11:314; A:257

Conger, HerbertOne of the sporty people in Duffey and Letitia’s Chicago circle [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

Conglomerate of driftwoodThe mass of cast-up wood on the rough shore that Trinali calls the Elephants’ Graveyard. Her imagery makes its largest pieces the bones of mammoths, behemoths and Leviathan [A:232].

A:232

CongressA public or professional assembly. Bagby proposes that the U.S. Congress imitate Teras councils by including living and dead members [MTM B5:165]. Charlotte attends a Confidence-Men’s Congress in New Orleans [MTM B7:216], and George Koran lists the Student Repudiation Congress among the Majesty’s engagements [MTM B8:243]. A team from the Consenting Adults’ World Congress participates in the grotesque consumption of Paul XI’s remains during the Voltaire Festival [MB:565].

MTM B5:165; MTM B7:216; MTM B8:243; MB:565

CongruenceA fitting together of events or patterns. Duffey anticipates a seemingly impossible convergence of his creations [MTM B5:150-151] and tells a distressed woman, whom he sends back toward reconciliation, not to wonder too much about the congruence of events [MTM B4:144]. In “Promontory Goats,” molecular congruencies figure among the physical traces a speaker believes invading spirits can read in the brain, while the mind itself remains inaccessible [PG:539].

MTM B5:150-151; MTM B4:144; PG:539

Conjurer's trickImage for Anastasia’s extraordinary presence as she cleans and shaves Finnegan at the bar. Reality seems too pale a word for someone both fleshly and translucent; the narration calls her a conjurer’s trick, but not a cheap one [D:13].

D:13

Conner, MikeGolfer named with Peggy Conner among Duffey and Letitia’s Chicago sporty friends [MTM B3:99]. Both later attend Hilary Hilton’s gathering for Duffey [MTM B12:383].

MTM B3:99; MTM B12:383

Conner, PeggyOne of Duffey’s Chicago friends, named with Mike Conner among the golfers [MTM B3:99]. She and Mike also attend Hilary Hilton’s later party [MTM B12:383]. See also Munster, Peggy.

MTM B3:99; MTM B12:383

ConsanguinityBlood kinship linking the goat-man’s seven youngest kids, three sets of twins and one single birth from four young sister goats. Their affection and family relationship accompany their shared ambition to climb the fallen sycamore [A:194].

A:194

ConscienceMoral unease or restraint. Finnegan’s troubled conscience accompanies the dreams in which he resists the muses [A:181]. The purported Underground Eagle report says Casey repeatedly washes his hands and conscience of the Casey Machine affair, while another participant predicts he will nevertheless buy one [CM:507]. Johnny Duckwalk, seemingly without conscience, is unexpectedly seized by repentance and resolves to confess his theft [D:264]. Hans Schultz creates a consensus of conscience in an unnamed field of business where it had almost vanished [MTM B8:247].

A:181; CM:507; D:264; MTM B8:247

ConsensusShared judgment or participation, which the books repeatedly distinguish from secure truth. Letitia calls apparently objective reality a consensus of private projections [MTM B3:96]; Zabotski’s neighbors unanimously find him quarrelsome, while the narrator insists they are all mistaken [MTM B9:269]. Hans creates a consensus of conscience in business [MTM B8:247]. X says the Liberal Consensus is prominent at the Devil’s release [MTM B6:205], and the later world’s consensus hatreds surround Hiram III after he refuses to abolish his nation [MB:563]. “Promontory Goats” describes groups in Hell choosing increasingly cruel shared tortures [PG:532-533]. Finnegan’s resurrection painting produces agreement among his friends that he is alive [MB:550]. Brannagan says withdrawing from the shimmering future can help break the consensus that makes it likely [MTM B13:470].

MTM B3:96; MTM B9:269; MTM B8:247; MTM B6:205; MB:563; PG:532-533; MB:550; MTM B13:470

Consenting Adults' World CongressGroup whose winning team of fifty devours Paul XI’s entrails in a basilica after they have been used to strangle Hiram III during the Voltaire Festival [MB:565].

MB:565

Conservatism (universe is inherently)In a recurring vision, a great mathematician explains that the universe is inherently conservative: complete alterations occur only at intervals and require grave reason. His lecture connects a new alteration to the appearance of a chicken-hearted devil [PG:542].

PG:542

ConsignmentA shipment of goods awaiting realization or sale. Joseph the Haussa diamond smuggler seeks a trustworthy partner and says realizing on a consignment can take years [D:94]. Hillary Hilton’s distressed-goods ventures include spoiled bananas and consignments of wormy sesame seed [A:254]. Eva uses the word figuratively for the tall stories she must prepare if she takes over the Neanderthal [MTM B13:408].

D:94; A:254; MTM B13:408

Consort, PassionateMary Louise Byrne’s description of herself in relation to Duffey. She calls herself both his sister “in some respect” and his passionate consort, while referring to another shared life that they keep below the threshold [MTM B2:60].

MTM B2:60

ConsortiumA group acting together. Duffey sells his boarding-school businesses to a consortium of other boys [MTM B2:38]. Beth Keegan and a consortium of friends contrive her dazzling voice, walk and theatrical persona; the narration extends this performance into the imagery of an invented woman or living statue [MTM B2:57].

MTM B2:38; MTM B2:57

ConspiraciesSecret plots that, in Papa Devil’s account, succeed partly by persuading people that no conspiracies exist [D:87]. The Loosed Devil repeats this instruction to his followers [MTM B8:242]. X describes pursuing the Conspiracy despite ridicule and reports a disputed encounter with the Devil [A:139-140]; Dotty mocks the investigators’ credulity when they accept a clipping announcing X’s death [A:141]. Breaking up secret plots and conspiracies is among the Argo’s purposes [MTM B13:405].

D:87; MTM B8:242; A:139-140; A:141; MTM B13:405

Conspiracy, TheThe hostile movement X says he pursues beyond its apparent defeat [A:139]. In his account, Ifreann joined it when its evil was still undiluted by nonsense or Slavic imperialism [D:281]. By the later graveyard encounter, X says Seaworthy’s group has declined to its fringes, though it can still obtain funds [D:289].

A:139; D:281; D:289

Conspirators, AlienX’s designation for the group containing the original Papadiabolous, whom he calls its biggest member. He describes the group as well financed and unusually free to act, with Seaworthy as executive officer [D:155].

D:155

Constant GnawingX’s description of the long struggle of the “other people”: gradual undercutting and inflaming rather than a final climax. Doll disputes his prediction and insists that the conflict must be brought to an end [D:292].

D:292

Constantine, SaintConstantine the Great, Roman emperor from 306 to 337 and the first Christian emperor, recognized as a saint in the Eastern Church. Henry recognizes Constantine among the figures aboard the Navicula Petri in his dream [A:45]. With Licinius he issued the Edict of Milan in 313, granting religious liberty. He summoned the Council of Nicaea in 325, which affirmed the Son’s full divinity, and founded the new imperial capital Constantinople on the site of Byzantium, dedicated in 330.

A:45

Constellations of the OceansFinnegan’s poetic description of ocean islands as constellations that prefigure the skies, spoken to Hans while reflecting on Xavier and the great archipelagos [A:35].

A:35

ConstitutionThe American constitutional document whose authority the Bark supports. In Casey’s hostile Crock editorial, the magazine is criticized for placing undue value on a document he regards as worthy but transitory, parts of which might survive in future constitutions [A:128] [A:130].

A:128; A:130

ConstitutionalistCasey’s label for the Bark’s domestic political position in his hostile Crock editorial, where he criticizes its attachment to the Constitution [A:128] [A:130].

A:128; A:130

Construction JobA building project on which Finnegan spends a week with Hans in a shack, probably in the summer of 1950. Hans’s off-hours recollections supply much of the account of his early life [A:207].

A:207

ContactA connection through which people exchange information or gain access. Manuel hopes Marie may become his contact in his investigation of the devils [D:56]. Papa says Don Lewis contacted him from a distance but did not recognize him on arrival [D:120]. X cites contacts who reported Papadiabolous I’s surprise, after death, at learning he had a twin [D:286]. Finnegan parks outside a police station because X says this will make pursuers pause to develop contacts inside [D:198]. X later makes contact with John Mogul of Track and Total [MB:570]. The word also describes Duffey and Bagby’s many affinities [MTM B5:154], and the glancing contact of Casey and Stein from which the Kasmir-Stein combination sparks [MTM B5:183].

D:56; D:120; D:286; D:198; MB:570; MTM B5:154; MTM B5:183

ContadinoItalian for a farmer or peasant. The term describes Giulio Solli when Finnegan realizes that Mary McCracken must have loved the old man to have married him [A:245].

A:245

Containment PolicyCasey’s proposed way of holding the Thing in check. He questions whether containment can work, but doubts it can be defeated in any other way; he contrasts this patient struggle with Henry’s attempt to settle everything in one stroke [A:155].

A:155

ContemplationDuffey’s examination of the urn containing his own ashes while he eats and drinks with X at his New Orleans art shop [MTM B1:6].

MTM B1:6

Contes Drolatiques, LesBalzac’s French stories, a favorite of Gautier the goat-man, who reads them aloud to his goats. He calls the book filthy and Gothic, doubts whether he should read it to the young goats, but says Balzac appeals to goats and to the goat in man [A:196] [A:198].

A:196; A:198

ContextThe frame in which an identity or event makes sense. Finnegan’s shipboard dreams ask whether his discontinuous lives and the “other human race” can belong to one person [D:91]; letters from old friends seem addressed to another Finnegan in another context [D:115], and his memory of bending over Papa Devil seems detached from its context [D:83]. Father McGuigan accuses Patrick Stranahan of using a false context and unlawful metaphor when he discusses creating people; Duffey answers that his own creations are literal [MTM B5:166]. Duffey’s commentary examines Casey in Argo, medieval, secular and eschatological contexts [PG:534-535]. Rebeka discusses transformation activators in dreams [MTM B10:294]; the Seven Lost Years provide the context of the Argo’s fourteenth voyage and Duffey’s anomalous returns to ordinary life [MTM B10:300] [MTM B13:445]. Stein’s later account similarly places Finnegan between several worlds [MB:548-549].

D:91; D:115; D:83; MTM B5:166; PG:534-535; MTM B10:294; MTM B10:300; MTM B13:445; MB:548-549

Continent, SouthernThe sunny land beyond an Antarctic ice ring in Casey’s fifth imaginary world. His fantasy requires a larger, melon-shaped earth; he imagines the southern continent as a possible Atlantis, to which he would carry modern techniques and from which he would bring back the Higher Ethic [A:158].

A:158

Continental ShelfUndersea location of the Green Castles in Trinali’s fanciful account of a piece of driftwood’s travels [A:232-233].

A:232-233

ContingencyA possible or conditionally realized world. Rafelson describes Duffey’s contingent creations approaching a fulfillment that could make them real retrospectively [MTM B4:146-147]; Patrick Stranahan describes talismanic creation through equations with as many as thirty billion interdependent integers [MTM B5:165-166]. Seven prominent alternatives are presented for Duffey: the Great Day’s dissolution of boundaries; the doubtful Goat Contingency involving Casey’s attempted soul trade and cosmic debt; the Petrine spy story; the Argo’s fourteenth voyage; the Thunder Colt world presentation; confrontation with the Loosed Devil; and a garden encounter with God [MTM B10:298-301]. These alternatives are not all mutually exclusive, and the Argo voyage is said to be certain. Cleo’s theatrical forecast of the seventh contingency introduces a rowdy bird carrying a warning that anything that can go wrong will [MTM B10:296-297]. Stein’s account of Finnegan likewise involves several worlds and disputed deaths [MB:548-549].

MTM B4:146-147; MTM B5:165-166; MTM B10:298-301; MTM B10:296-297; MB:548-549

ContingentIn Casey’s discussion with Duffey, contingent philosophy includes problems Casey says can be expressed only mathematically. Duffey disagrees, maintaining that every problem can be stated in straightforward words [MTM B5:150].

MTM B5:150

Continuous-Flow Federal FundingOne of the continuing subsidies Newton Prescott seeks for the Casey Machine. Alongside Counter-Flow and Impacted Entertainment Area funding, he argues for public payments because pay-per-use machines favor the rich. He obtains guarantees in perpetuity and funding for his own group to provide perpetual care for each machine site as a shrine [CM:503] [CM:512-513].

CM:503; CM:512-513

ContractA formal agreement, ranging from Duffey’s purchase of a St. Louis horse barn, with contract, bill of sale and deed [MTM B2:40], to the murder contracts against thirteen cardinals. The Final Conclave gives Track and Total the job [MB:569]. Its head John Mogul has distributed the targets among separate contractors; X asks for the entire job, but Mogul offers successive assignments conditional on performance, followed by proposed verbal agreements [MB:571-573].

MTM B2:40; MB:569; MB:571-573

Contradiction, Principle of Non-The philosophical principle which an epigraph attributed to Ignace Wolff says is thwarted by bodies; the same passage declares bodies to negate the principle of sufficient reason. It is credited to Gedanken von Leibern [D:67].

D:67

ContraptionZabotski’s enormous construction, intruding from his property onto his neighbors’ land [MTM B9:270-271]. Widow Waldo identifies its overlapping prototypes as ship, castle, anti-time machine and the old woman’s shoe [MTM B9:275]. It carries Waldo, children and animals away in the cloudburst, reaching Lake Borgne [MTM B9:287], and is later called a floating boat palace [MTM B10:290]. The watertight boat reappears when Duffey returns from the Fifth Contingency [MTM B12:356].

MTM B9:270-271; MTM B9:275; MTM B9:287; MTM B10:290; MTM B12:356

ConventionA professional gathering, as in the Royal Rogues’ and Graceful Swindlers’ Ninth Annual Convention and Confidence-Men’s Congress, attended by Charlotte at the Royal Orleans Hotel [MTM B7:216], or the Society for Creative History’s New Orleans meeting [MTM B11:307]. The word also denotes the conventions of ordinary life: after his first death, Finnegan feels freed from the narrative constraints described as Aristotle’s Unities and Plutarch’s Heroics [D:161].

MTM B7:216; MTM B11:307; D:161

Conversation of ordinanceThe gunfire Finnegan hears while still descending the hill on Naxos: rifles, BARs, fifty-caliber machine guns, and a heavier report that might be a forty-five-millimeter weapon. Not knowing what is happening below makes this “conversation” maddening [D:143-144].

D:143-144

Coogan, KesterArtist whose work Duffey offers for sale early in his New Orleans enterprise, among the artists whose ideas contribute to his rebuilding project [MTM B6:199].

MTM B6:199

Coon DogsHunting dogs with which Finnegan and his country friends have spent the night before their early-morning conversation about his coming graveyard meeting [D:273].

D:273

Coon HuntingOne of the popular arts of everyday life said to lose its class and style in the massive degradation of the arts following the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207].

MTM B6:207

CoonsRaccoons among the creatures around Hans’s childhood nursery grounds [A:208]. In Finnegan’s account of the elusive Chosky Bottoms, the grandfather of all big coons belongs to that legendary place. After a hunt, Finnegan has shot a boar coon estimated at sixty pounds and boasts it would be small where he comes from; his companions reject the boast [D:274].

A:208; D:274

Cooperative, TheA term in the Crock article title “The Consumer, the Cooperative, and the Coefficient of Cost Constancy,” identified as written in Duffey’s style among the magazine’s largely Duffey-written contents [A:41].

A:41

CopenhagenOne end of the range of ports in which Henry Salvatore is said to have sampled the vices of a merchant seaman, “from Copenhagen to Aruba” [A:124].

A:124

Copper Box (Angela Cosquin sa Caisse)Angela’s personal savings box, inscribed “Angela Cosquin sa Caisse,” meaning Angela Cosquin, her cash box. After returning salvaged treasure to the St. Marc and San gre del Cristo wrecks, she places her own money in this copper box and hides it beside the hoard. She subsequently adds one saved gold sovereign each month [D:262].

D:262

Copper-iron nailThe large, sharp nail of old Macedonian workmanship fastening the Royal Pop People’s parchment notice to Duffey’s door. He initially thinks it brass or bronze, then identifies it as copper-iron [MTM B11:312-313].

MTM B11:312-313

Coq BleuOne of the nightspots visited by Hans and his bohemian friends during the evening that ends with the group dispersing at dawn [A:239].

A:239

CoracleA small rounded boat. A coracle appears on one side of the red-gold coin Biloxi Brannagan produces to identify himself aboard the Argo; the other side bears the Celtic Cross of Christ, and the coin carries the name Naomh Brandon [MTM B13:425].

MTM B13:425

Coracle BoatSee Coracle.
CoralReef-forming material produced by hard corals’ calcium-carbonate skeletons. Hans describes islands passed on the journey to Luzon as coral and limestone [A:62]. Finnegan’s Sergeant goes out from coral reefs with the Malayan boy before their underwater journey [A:89]. Coral beaches form the invasion setting in the second chamber of Elroy Redheart’s art construction, with combat buffalos, alligators and other amphibious vehicles emerging from landing craft [MTM B7:221-222].

A:62; A:89; MTM B7:221-222

Coral SeaOne of the seas included in the catalogue of the Argo’s voyages, remembered by Melchisedech as seas he too has sailed [MTM B13:406].

MTM B13:406

CordA string fastens Phoebe Anne Ankerson’s ownership tag just inside the handle of the suitcase stolen by Finnegan and Doll [D:172]. Dangling cords also accompany the brain removed in Finnegan’s tale of an analyst who dissects a person without locating his essence [MTM B5:181-182].

D:172; MTM B5:181-182

Coriander SeedsSeeds Amoy is said to have stolen during his previous life as a blackbird, after millet and rice and before his work for jewel thieves, in Ignatius Ti’s expansive translation of the bird’s story [A:80].

A:80

Cork (Material)Material Trinali uses with bottles and raffia to make dolls, marionette figures, Mexicans, donkeys, clowns and prizefighters [A:228]. She dyes corks eight standard colors in a dishpan, building her stock while making the dishes taste strange [A:229]. A bottle cork also ends her wine poem as an image of the difficulty of keeping the god imprisoned in the bottle [A:231-232].

A:228; A:229; A:231-232

Cork (Terrance Cardinal Merry of)Cardinal of Cork named Terrence Cardinal Merry in the list of John Mogul’s targets and their doubles. His listed double is Emmet Collins of Boston [MB:579], later revealed as the young woman and impersonator Emma Collins, a protégée of X [MB:598].

MB:579; MB:598

Cork-cutting MachineMachine in Portugal that is set running after Cardinal Artemis blesses it, seizes him and removes his skin in one piece; the victim dies almost immediately. The account leaves unresolved the related confusion between Artemis and his double Gilberto, and between their skins [MB:591].

MB:591

Cork, IrelandIrish city in which Loy says there is a Duffey’s tavern [A:2], and one of the places Marie has considered looking for a husband [A:7]. X identifies Cork as the birthplace of Gregory McColum, Papadiabolous II, contrasting him with his Smyrna-born twin Gregory McIfreann, Papadiabolous I [D:285].

A:2; A:7; D:285

Cork, TerrySeaman and journalist, one of the Forty Scribbling Seamen celebrated in Dotty’s song. He writes “The Plimsoll Line” for the Bark and about half the Seaman’s Paper during his stays of a few months in town. Other Terrys, including Anderson, Jamil, Renier and Bannon, take over when he leaves [MTM B7:213].

MTM B7:213

Corn BeerDrink made by Gautier the goat-man, alongside berry wine and potato whisky [A:196-197].

A:196-197

“Corn Country Cantos”One of the nine projected volumes into which Endymeon Ellenbogen says he has classified his still uncollected and unpublished poems [A:237].

A:237

Corn-dog makingOne of the minor arts said to lose class and style during the degradation of everyday life associated with the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207-208].

Cornelia, Sister Mary FosterEarlier heading misplaced the given and family names and omitted Sullivan. See Foster, Sister Mary Cornelia (Sullivan).
Corpse (Unaccountable)The male body Seaworthy cannot dispose of in his dream of an Indian city. Attempts to bury it, abandon it in the gutter or push it through windows fail; it finally grapples with him and asks who will bury him [D:72-73]. Finnegan subsequently recognizes a real burial behind the dream and recalls helping Seaworthy dig the grave after Seaworthy struck the still-moving victim with a shovel [D:74-75].

Corpus Christi DayFeast for which, according to the novel, Christ-head loaves are baked in parts of Denmark. Duffey’s Danish-bread Christ, made of wheat and rye flour, baked and varnished, is one of the extraordinary Christs in his collection [MTM B3:103].

MTM B3:103

CorpusculizationOne of the jargon-like words spoken by the satirical holy figure of the demiurge Teilhard during the Great Day service, with McLuhan and McGonigal beside him and the Unfaithful Assembled responding [GD:497].

Corriander SeedsCorriander is the spelling printed in the novel. See Coriander Seeds.
CorridorPassages whose doors Duffey orders opened at Hubbard Elementary School so mice can reach the puppet show; the teacher has the doors opened [MTM B4:135-136]. Metaphorical gusty corridors also describe the Gadarene Swine Song as Bagby plays it on a horn at Good Guy’s [MTM B7:220].

CorruptionThe opposite of integrity in the chastity passage introducing Duffey’s schoolboy circle. Duffey sometimes suffers corruption but never redefines it as a virtue [MTM B1:27]. He later warns Casey that infiltrators intend to corrupt the Crock [A:40]. Finnegan considers a corpse as a possible dream symbol of violation or corruption before recognizing its literal referent [D:74]. Showboat recognizes coordinated crowd corruption through the three-spot device [MTM B7:231]. In the Resurrection painting, Finnegan’s flesh undergoes corruption and transfiguration simultaneously [MB:551].

MTM B1:27; A:40; D:74; MTM B7:231; MB:551

CortinaName associated with the language-learning manuals on Duffey’s shelves, which help Casey pursue his ambition to learn all languages [A:159]. Cortina published self-study language courses, including Spanish in Twenty Lessons.

Coryphaena Fish (dolphin fish)Horn-playing fish that raise their heads above the waves after Finnegan, Gilberto and Herman Hercules board the Argo. Their shell horns have bright brass stops and frets; the music signals that a present or future pope is aboard [MTM B13:450-451]. When the three disembark at the Ringing Rocks, the fish remain beside that shore [MTM B13:453]. Coryphaena is also the zoological name of the dolphinfish genus, given supernatural behavior here.

MTM B13:450-451; MTM B13:453

Coscuin, DanaVoyager who takes the Argo around the Horn while the ship bears the name Catherine [MTM B13:405].

MTM B13:405

Cosenza (or Consenza)Cosenza is a city in Calabria. The claimed connection making it Papa Devil’s place of origin remains unverified. The cited scene concerns Anastasia’s burial and Marie’s dying [D:157]; X’s later account gives Smyrna and Cork as the birthplaces of the two Papadiabolous figures [D:285].

D:157; D:285

Cosmic BalancingUnverified headword for the proposed idea that a good creature requires an evil counterpart. The supplied passage is Private Gregory’s account of changing identities and his long military service, and does not state this theory [A:77].

A:77

Cosmic EntityUnverified designation supposedly applied by X to Papadiabolous. The supplied passage instead presents Finnegan confronting Papa Devil over Don Lewis’s body and contains no such description by X [D:111].

D:111

Cosmic shiftUnverified phrase allegedly describing Casey’s role as a point man. The supplied passage concerns the Argo company’s failed recognition of X, and does not contain Casey’s alleged claim or Brannagan’s dismissal in favor of paganism [MTM B13:434].

MTM B13:434

CosmosThe universe, figured as the web in which the suns are caught in the possible confrontation between Duffey and the Devil [MTM B10:301]. Green claims to demonstrate its dependence on him by dimming Ward Fourteen’s lights, while Gregory points out that the compressor explains the effect [A:76]. Rafelson speaks of human relations to the exocosmos in his account of Duffey [MTM B4:148]. In the Great Day ending, Morpheus claims the whole cosmos was the dream of a single-celled creature and is collapsing back into that origin [GD:500]. The Promantia’s related image is of ships and oceans of middle space [D:6].

MTM B10:301; A:76; MTM B4:148; GD:500; D:6

Cosquin, AngelaBarmaid and factotum of Finnegan’s island Paradise, employed by Joseph Chastaigne at the Imperial Bar, or whatever its name may be [D:258-259] [D:266]. Angela is vividly dressed, musical, talkative and remarkably strong: she carries two hundred pounds on her head and can launch a six-man boat alone. Her ancestry includes French, Carib and English forebears, noblemen and slaves [D:259]. Her father, a cartographer and antiquarian, becomes a maker of convincing false treasure maps for confidence men [D:259-261]. The nearby St. Marc and San gre del Cristo wrecks are real, despite her denial; she dives to their treasure, returns what she has brought up when its use attracts suspicion, and hides her own savings beside it in an inscribed copper box, adding a sovereign monthly [D:262]. Johnny Duckwalk secretly steals each added sovereign [D:263]. Angela herself draws accurate maps of Finnegan’s seven land-buried stashes, marked S X S and robado por C F, and refuses to sell them. She first calls him Count Finnegan [D:263]. When he leaves, she offers him the wrecks’ gold, embraces him, and joins his pledge to protect the poor; he promises to return but never does [D:268]. Archipelago recalls Angela and the wrecks [A:188], and Finnegan later recognizes Elena as both herself and Angela [A:278].

D:258-259; D:266; D:259; D:259-261; D:262; D:263; D:268; A:188; A:278

Costerman's Whaler's InnCosterman’s Whalers’ Inn, one of the waterfront establishments recalled in Melchisedech’s catalogue of maritime places aboard the Argo [MTM B13:407].

MTM B13:407

Cotillion dancingOne of the lively arts of ordinary life said to lose class and style during the degradation following the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207].

MTM B6:207

Count FinneganFinnegan’s title, first given him by Angela Cosquin in her account of the seven hidden treasures [D:263] and used at their farewell [D:268]. He describes his scrimshaw pieces as recognizable to seamen as Count Finnegan’s work [MTM B5:173]. Duffey says X reports that Finnegan was secretly named a papal count, while acknowledging X’s unreliability [MTM B12:367]. A Latin scroll identifies the risen figure in Finnegan’s Resurrection painting as the Papal Count [MB:551]. He is the central figure of the Petrine spy-story contingency [MTM B10:300] and the listed double of Joseph Cardinal Hedayat [MB:579].

D:263; D:268; MTM B5:173; MTM B12:367; MB:551; MTM B10:300; MB:579

Count of Monte CristoOne of the compelling French tales Gautier the goat-man reads to his goats during winter evenings, alongside Tartarin of Tarascon and Gil Blas [A:198].

A:198

Count von VingerEarlier heading normalized the source’s printed County to Count. See County von Vinger.
Counterfeit CreatureThe false replacements in Le Marin’s story of the Sarcophagus: dock rats are signed on in place of vanished seamen and look exactly like them. Le Marin says he too was replaced, yet continues the tale in the first person. Finnegan compares the takeover to a world in which every person has been supplanted [D:244].

D:244

Counterpart FundsPayments of Current and Future Contingency kinds sought by Newton Prescott to offset the Casey Machine’s greater availability to rich users than to poor ones. He reports obtaining continuing guarantees [CM:513].

CM:513

Countess (Girl Countess), TheSebastian Hilton’s companion, introduced to Duffey at the Colony Club as the Girl Countess. Duffey recognizes her from his earlier reading of Sebastian’s mind. She is playing bridge as Lily Koch’s partner against Charlotte and Gloria Mullens [MTM B3:95]. See Countess Margaret, The (Margaret Hochfelsen).

MTM B3:95

Countess Margaret, The (Margaret Hochfelsen)Margaret Hochfelsen, the “ever-young countess,” is Sebastian Hilton’s companion and a friend of Duffey and Letitia in their Chicago golden age [MTM B3:98]. When Sebastian introduces the Girl Countess, Duffey recognizes her from his earlier reading of Sebastian’s mind [MTM B3:95]. Letitia claims to have projected her into the Chicago scene; the narrator later calls her an Animation without settling who made her [MTM B3:96] [MTM B7:215].

She identifies Giulio as a Teras and promises to help the son who has inherited his difficult nature [MTM B3:107]. She and Sebastian marry after decades together; he is killed a month later [MTM B7:216].

After Letitia’s funeral in New Orleans, the Countess invites Duffey to marry her and live in Transylvania. She claims that nineteen long generations of her family are still alive and that enormous wolves serve and protect them. Duffey repeatedly challenges her stories; he postpones her proposal for fifty years, and she promises to ask again [MTM B8:254-256].

The later narrative links her with the Royal Pop People through its warning that she will become one of them and grow younger [MTM B12:383]. This shifting identity should be distinguished from the role of the Countess played by Becky Stein in Seven Roads [MTM B12:352].

MTM B3:98; MTM B3:95; MTM B3:96; MTM B7:215; MTM B3:107; MTM B7:216; MTM B8:254-256; MTM B12:383; MTM B12:352

County von VingerAlias, printed “County von Vinger,” of Ali ben Taife, also called Lord Peter Petrof and, in Rio, Sinhor Dedos or Mr. Fingers. In Ignatius Ti’s account, this thief-master kills Amoy when the bird refuses to surrender a swallowed blue diamond [A:81].

A:81

CourageBushmaster’s backers praise his bulldog courage during the losing beer contest, prompting Finnegan’s joke about his forebears [A:23]. X calls pursuit of the supposedly defeated Conspiracy the most courageous act, yet admits he cannot face his ironic wife after his long absence [A:139-141]. Duffey retains strong personal courage despite his other failings [MTM B4:110]. Le Marin, emboldened when he encounters Castleman in a bar, then leaves the dangerous man alone rather than let courage carry him too far [D:245-246].

A:23; A:139-141; MTM B4:110; D:245-246

Courier fontsUnverified claim that Casey preferred Courier type for the Crock. The supplied page concerns Duffey’s encounter with a distressed woman and the magazine’s stockholders, with no typeface preference stated [MTM B4:144].

MTM B4:144

Courtois, Marie (aka the Golden Ogress)Seaworthy’s seagoing secretary on the Brunhilde. Finnegan first remembers her as the Golden Ogress who collected his information for the ship’s register; her beauty and aura of power make the transaction feel like a mortgage on his soul [D:32]. Golden-skinned, red-haired, exceptionally strong and about a foot taller than the small Anastasia, she revels in her physical power on the beach and in the surf [D:33] [D:37]. Anastasia denounces her as evil, calls her brainless and skylla in their quarrelling, and accuses her of madness; Marie answers with political diagnoses of Anastasia. Despite this, the cabin-mates are described as good friends whose feud sharpens their wits [D:33] [D:69-70]. In a possibly waking ocean dream Marie identifies herself with Demeter and Persephone and claims earthly reincarnation is the only immortality; Finnegan rejects her claim [D:91-92]. She kills Don Lewis by throttling him and breaking his neck, then describes the act with ecstatic delight. Finnegan and Joe Cross plan retaliation, but Papa Devil intervenes [D:110-113]. Manuel says she insisted on Anastasia’s killing [D:148]. Finnegan later reports that Marie shot Anastasia and was herself shot by Joe, who was then shot in turn. He perceives her dying aboard the Brunhilde, enjoying it and expecting a favored place beyond death [D:157].

D:32; D:33; D:37; D:69-70; D:91-92; D:110-113; D:148; D:157

Courtship (Romantic)One of the popular arts said to lose class and style in the degradation of everyday life following the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207].

MTM B6:207

CovenantA binding pact, appearing in opposed forms. In the sixth contingency the Adversary presses Duffey to accept a fatally defective covenant; the dramatic forecast warns that acceptance would unmake everyone [MTM B10:296] [MTM B10:301]. Finnegan later describes the saving Covenant as an intrusion that has changed time, space and the form of everything, and that the killers seek to extinguish [MB:587]. An ancestral dolphin knows this Pact and accepts that it was made with humans rather than dolphins, although hostile humans will try to nullify it [MB:594].

MTM B10:296; MTM B10:301; MB:587; MB:594

CovenanterUnverified epithet allegedly applied to Henry by Papa Devil. The cited page concerns Aunt Gertrude’s cooking and X’s coded telephone call to Finnegan, and does not contain that exchange [D:208].

D:208

CovenantersUnverified designation supposedly applied to sour members of the Brunhilde crew. The supplied passage is Finnegan and Seaworthy’s conversation on the sidewalk before their voyage, and contains no such designation [D:11].

Cow (Sacred)Image applied to Mary Louise Byrne: her strength and bovine quality are described as royal and sacred, a phase through which the narrative says all chthonic goddesses pass [MTM B2:55].

MTM B2:55

Cow County RoundupUnverified title of a supposed rodeo publication to which a friend of Gregory contributes. The supplied passage is Gregory’s account of his non-aging and military service, and contains no such publication or contributor [A:77].

Coward (self-described)Don Lewis’s evasive self-characterization in his story of the three vanished soldiers: one was a coward, and he will not identify which was himself [D:44]. His later slip identifies him with the reluctant PFC Lorrigan, who hung back from the killing [D:45]. The narrator says he has twice proclaimed his cowardice, while stressing the dangerous resistance and covert communications he has organized aboard the Brunhilde [D:105].

D:44; D:45; D:105

CowboysTommy Cow-Town Borger and Jake-Leg Lewis, the salt-water cowboys who ride cattle boats rather than horses. As live cattle shipments become rare, they spend long intervals between voyages, still wearing boots, spurs, chaps and gauntlets [D:222].

D:222

Cowboys (Mexican)Unverified entry. The earlier glossary gives Vaqueros and cites Archipelago, page 176. That page concerns Finnegan and Dotty, and no supporting Mexican-cowboy passage has been located in the supplied texts.
Cowles Buggy Whip, TheOne of the whips recalled by the turbaned Royal Pop historian while giving a Decatur Street flagstone a voice for its memories of horse traffic [MTM B11:329].

MTM B11:329

CowsAnimals in the phrase heard during Duffey’s dream, “the years that the cows have eaten.” Beth Keegan associates it with seven sheaves of grain and expects a seven-year absence [MTM B2:68-69]. The imagery suggests a blend of Pharaoh’s cows and grain in Genesis 41:26-27 with the consumed years of Joel 2:25. A “honey old cow” sometimes supplies Duffey’s soup kitchen [A:134]; cowbells mingle with sheep bells during Finnegan and Anastasia’s Naxos vigil [D:131].

MTM B2:68-69; A:134; D:131

Crab cootiesParasites among the creatures attacking Duffey in the dung heap after he turns the forbidden handle and falls from the Presence’s green meadows. He finally recognizes that the Presence remains with him even there [MTM B12:392-393].

MTM B12:392-393

CrabbingOne of the lively arts of everyday life said to lose class and style in the massive degradation following the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207].

MTM B6:207

CrackA sound, opening or fracture used in several scenes. Papa Devil’s threat over Don Lewis’s grave bursts like thunder [D:110]; Le Marin asks Finnegan to crack another bottle [D:243]. Finnegan jokingly says Theresa’s baptism cracked the font, and she counters that any of several witches might have done it [A:108]. Bagby likens Duffey to a sidewalk crack treated as a fetish mark by fates and principalities [MTM B10:302]. The nearly closed door between Finnegan and Dotty figures their dwindling relationship [A:106-107]. Casey imagines Henry aging into a priest whose thunder has cracks, a prospect Finnegan rejects [A:155]. A crack in Eva’s ice pillar frees her jaw to speak [MTM B13:399].

X’s claimed eyewitness account names the Tauric and Euxine Chersonese and alleges that the Yalta Conference principals consulted the imprisoned Devil [MTM B6:204].

Crock (3) (old butter-crock)Nostalgic object in Endymeon Ellenbogen’s catalogue of kinds of popular songs he writes, alongside remembered mothers and bee trees [A:237-238].

Crock (4) (Casey the)Casey the Crock is Kasmir Gorshok, Casey Szymansky’s medieval manifestation as a ninth-century scholar and necromancer; his Argonaut identity is Peleus [A:39] [PG:534-535]. Archipelago’s Chapter Six is titled “Casey the Crock, or the Losing of Peleus” [A:151].

Crock (5) (pottery)The pot image behind the Crock magazine’s name: its cover carries d’Allesandro’s elaborate engraving of an old chamber pot, below a black Gothic title [A:40-41]. The connection is a visual pun; the passage does not state a separate etymology for the magazine’s name.

A:40-41

Crock, TheCasey Szymansky’s magazine, published in successive college versions and later on the small press in Duffey’s Chicago bookstore [MTM B4:119]. Duffey runs it after Casey joins the army in 1942, attracting talented contributors and resisting the peculiar people’s efforts to take it over [MTM B4:138]. In Archipelago, his letter describes blackmail, assault and a warning about Casey’s stock; Casey identifies Stein as the threatened infiltrator [A:39-40]. In More Than Melchisedech, a group gains control through a new proxy from Casey. About a year later Casey returns, confirms the changed orientation, resumes the editorship and permanently excludes Duffey [MTM B4:144-145]. Casey associates his change with a soul exchange, which Stein later describes as an exchange of their older souls [MTM B4:145] [MTM B5:169]. Duffey’s admirers remember the earlier Crock as an intelligent, humorous cult sheet [MTM B5:158]. The Archipelago issue is a twenty-page tabloid with d’Allesandro’s chamber-pot engraving, a black Gothic title and the subscript Formerly the C of S [A:40-41]. Its contents include Schrade’s sonnet, Ethyl Ellenberger’s ode, Demetrio Glauch’s ballad, and articles by Thos. J. Chronicker, S.J., Christopher Tompkinson and Tom (Big Bear) Rogers. Mary Frances Rattigan writes “Books Abroad” as Polly Polyglot. Duffey supplies most of the issue; “Moles at the Grass Roots,” Fables in Fabianism, and The Consumer, the Cooperative, and the Coefficient of Cost Constancy are described as being in his style. Regular sections include “Urbe et Orbe,” “Judgement Day” reviews, recording notes favoring Chicago jazz, and a pro-and-con letters forum. Four Groben woodcuts and On the John musings with a shadowed Thinker drawing complete the description [A:41]. After the Bark appears, Casey uses the Crock to attack its editors and aims; the publications address the same influential readership [A:128-130]. Later Show Boat reports that Casey’s creditors have taken his press and building but cannot use the Crock’s name, and that he is again at odds with the group [A:262-263].

MTM B4:119; MTM B4:138; A:39-40; MTM B4:144-145; MTM B4:145; MTM B5:169; MTM B5:158; A:40-41; A:41; A:128-130; A:262-263

CrockedDrunk: Theresa warns Finnegan against getting crocked before supper [A:108], while Elena later deplores his habitual drunkenness [A:274]. Trinali and Jimmy are crocked within an hour of drinking with Hans [A:226]. Duffey retains his small-scale magic whether crocked or uncrocked [MTM B5:170]. Finnegan also calls himself the Irish crock during his St. Patrick’s celebrations [D:189].

Cromwell, Oliver (1599--1658)Oliver Cromwell (1599-1658), Parliamentary commander in the British Civil Wars and Lord Protector of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1653 until his death. His military victories and Puritan reforms were followed by a constitutionally powerful executive and broader toleration of many Protestant faiths; his Irish campaign included the massacres at Drogheda and Wexford. The glossary’s literary connection remains unverified: the supplied pages concern Papa Piccone’s Oscar Oliver Omygosh story and the Argo’s visit to Oliver Greenflag and his companions [MTM B5:167-168] [MTM B13:417-418].

Seaworthy’s cronies visit offices in foreign ports [D:103] and wait with the old netman aboard the Brunhilde during the Naxos ambush, experienced fighters despite their inconspicuousness [D:136]. X later asks what Finnegan learned from Seaworthy and his cronies [D:188]. Elsewhere, Patrick Stranahan’s visitors include K.C.s and cronies [A:104], and Finnegan’s port-town friends report his heavy drinking before the Brunhilde sails [D:27].

Cross, JoeBrunhilde crewman, cabin-mate of Finnegan and Don Lewis, and initially one of the narrator’s good people: compromised but a true prince. He has burr-short red hair and later a red beard around his youthful face [D:30-31] [D:100]. At the beach he breaks water and whistles at Finnegan and Anastasia like a comic fish [D:38]. Experience in a Baltimore raw bar equips him to help prepare the seafood supper [D:40]. During the Mexican landing he accompanies Manuel, Papa Devil, Finnegan and the women but remains with the oar boat [D:57]. Don’s covert arrangements bring Joe aboard as part of a loose resistance [D:105], yet Joe’s closeness to Marie makes Don doubt him [D:106]. In Tangier on the day Don is killed, the usually friendly Joe is armed and hostile to Finnegan [D:101-102]. After discovering Marie’s guilt, Finnegan trusts Joe again; they set out to kill her, but Papa Devil disarms Joe and stops them [D:113]. Joe is later found dead on the Naxos landing with Papa Devil and five olive-shirted raiders [D:147]. Manuel says Joe tried to play both sides, opposed Anastasia’s killing, and was murdered aboard ship before his body was dragged ashore [D:148]. Finnegan later reports the shooting sequence: Marie killed Anastasia, Joe shot Marie, and Joe was himself shot [D:157].

CubaSetting of Finnegan's last encounter with Dotty and Niccolo in Archipelago. At the opening of the final chapter he mistakes Havana for a transformed New Orleans; the telephone booth contains a Havana directory [A:269]. Dotty travels there after receiving a lawyer's letter, and she and Niccolo exchange shots on the beach, wounding Finnegan as well as one another [A:277] [A:281-282].

In More Than Melchisedech, Dotty's departure to meet Finnegan is recalled with Cuba given as a possible destination [MTM B8:237]. The Petrine Spy Story contingency locates their deaths on the Marianao Coast and treats those deaths as part of a larger masquerade [MTM B10:300]. Duffey later travels to Havana with Carmelo Mendoza, whom he discovers to be X, to investigate Finnegan's disappearance; Horace Pie joins them [MTM B12:367] [MTM B12:371]. They find the sea cave shown in The Resurrection of Count Finnegan. Duffey enters its previous day and meets Finnegan there [MTM B12:374].

CupFinnegan’s island-creation story makes the Aegean islands fragments of a smashed electrum cup [A:35]. Marie Courtois first finds Finnegan “in his cups”; Mrs. Mullens supplies paper cups for drinking Duffey’s whisky [D:32] [MTM B3:78]. On the Great Day, Duffy discovers that Charlotte’s customers, including himself, are drinking coffee without cups [GD:484].

Dali, SalvadorSalvador Dalí (1904-1989), Spanish surrealist painter. Duffey recognizes landscapes by Dalí, Doré, and Hieronymus Bosch within the Devil’s mind [MTM B8:241]. Clarence Schrade later says that Casey’s drawings burlesque the hellscapes of Dalí, Doré, Bosch, and Finnegan [PG:522]. Dalí studied at the San Fernando Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Madrid and was finally expelled in 1926. His paintings combine precise technique with dream imagery, as in The Persistence of Memory (1931). Influenced by Freud, he developed the paranoiac-critical method to explore unstable perceptions and double images. He also worked in sculpture, film, and writing, collaborating with Luis Buñuel and Alfred Hitchcock, and developed photographic projects with Philippe Halsman. The surrealists attempted to expel him in 1934; the Gala-Salvador Dalí Foundation dates his expulsion to 1939. He lived in the United States during the Second World War and returned to Spain in 1948. King Juan Carlos I made him Marquis of Dalí de Púbol in 1982. After Gala’s death in 1982 he moved to Púbol. Following a fire there in 1984, he moved to the Galatea Tower in Figueres, where he remained until his death.

DeathA recurrent, often non-final condition in the Argo narratives. The Promantia says that dying is not always serious the first time and introduces people unwilling to stay dead [D:6]. Private Gregory describes successive lives, while his fellow patient the sergeant claims to live several simultaneously [A:79]; Duffey remembers three childhoods occupying the same years [MTM B1:6]. In the psychiatric ward, Green, who identifies himself as God, says that the universe depends on God's momentary attention and would vanish if He nodded; Gregory points out that Green's demonstration coincides with the compressor dimming the lights [A:76]. The postscript calls Argo's apparent endings a continuing surge of multiplicities, rather than actual endings [PS:479]. Ignatius Ti explains midnight as the hour when people choose to die in company and a hole opens in the veil through which old ghosts can return. His account includes hospital pranks with supposed corpses, his people's practice of seating corpses at wakes and burials, and a murdered husband who returns to his wife's bed. The narration then lets loose ghosts into the ward [A:85-87]. An epigraph attributed to Ignace Wolff makes bodies the obstacle to non-contradiction and sufficient reason [D:67]. Seaworthy's dream expresses the embarrassment and inescapable stickiness of possessing a corpse [D:72]. Papa Devil's living disguise and dead face are different: Finnegan paints the concealed face before others see it on the corpse [D:63] [D:86] [D:146]. Duffey's dying is a prolonged sequence. Cardinal Salvatore speaks of his friends' worn-out mortal coils and of Duffey's departure to a greater thing [MTM B12:385]. His seizure and sudden leave-taking occur among friends [MTM B12:388]. His garden vision is explicitly an anteroom, with the last second still unfinished [MTM B12:389]. After he turns the forbidden handle, he falls into a dung heap, crying that he is falling forever; as much as fifty seconds of his last moment may still remain. He eventually recognizes God's presence in the torment and whirlwind too [MTM B12:392-393]. Earlier he tells X that remaining within two weeks of death deepens his piety [MTM B12:376]. In “The Casey Machine,” a pastor tells a sinner that everyone will know everything, with edification and joy for the saved and fiery regret for the damned. Whether complete knowledge follows particular or general judgment is uncertain, but eternity has no time differential [CM:504]. The printed quotation attributed to the Baltimore Catechism describes the just rising glorious and immortal, shining like the sun, swift as thought, able to penetrate matter, beautiful, painless and changeless, while the damned also rise to eternal punishment. The narrator's fascination with undead, dead and resurrected bodies develops alongside the Casey Condition [CM:511]. Bagby's letters describe a purgatorial life free of the tyrannies of hours and places: hard but not torturous work, ample leisure, no sleep, stronger passions disciplined again and again, and refining relationships with kindred, aliens, angels and the damned. His letters expressly question whether any damnation is irrevocable. Particularity and knowledge grow; Earth-hours are appointments for contemplating Earth. He criticizes neglected mathematical, economic and theological fields, describes thatched huts and circles of increasing intensity, and distinguishes contentment from a growing, kinetic, mustard-seed happiness [MTM B8:248-249]. Cardinal Salvatore locates him on Purgatory's north slope [MTM B12:384]. The Ghost Coffee Shop initially appears as a refuge for spirits purging the horror of haunting, but the narrator immediately retracts this account, except for Finnegan's picture, and identifies Anthony Ghost's ordinary coffee shop [MTM B10:292-293]. Hell receives several qualified accounts. In “Promontory Goats,” it was once pleasant and isolated, and some parts still provide natural happiness without the Beatific Vision. Most inhabitants join groups whose consensual pleasures become ever more extreme torture. They can withdraw but choose the pleasure of tormenting others even at the cost of their own agony. The same passage calls substitution for such souls irrational yet a greater sacrifice [PG:532-533]. The sinner Lorenzo, rather than an authoritative narrator, welcomes endless wallowing and gloating despite his pastor's warning [CM:504-505]. Clarence Schrade describes Casey's drawing of the Iron Meadows of Hell [PG:522-523], while the prose following Casey's poem identifies the troll beneath the bridge as the Devil [PG:523]. Finnegan associates the dying Marie Courtois with Persephone's recurrent visits to Hell [D:157]. Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni says that Heaven, Hell and Purgatory are already here, the visible universe being the reverse of Heaven's tapestry [A:211] [A:214]. Duffey's claim that Heaven contains traitors, sycophants and socialists belongs to his comic argument about salvation and jazz [A:117]. The Terrestrial Paradise is offered as an attainable earthly place, with exact coordinates in the Antilles [D:6] [D:234]; Archipelago also says Finnegan knew its location [A:188]. Duffey's apparent inability to end coexists with his deaths. The narrative and Stein's notes distinguish his ending from an end to his existence and fear disintegration into several strands [MTM B10:290-291]. His own ashes sit before him in an old royal urn [MTM B1:6]. One account says he is killed, stripped of flesh and cremated at Our'yev [MTM B13:436]; the fuller account has the slant-faced killers strip his flesh in the amoral desert, followed by slack-faced burners, before his bones and ashes appear in Gur'yev. His spirit lingers, and X takes custody of the ashes in a cigar canister formerly belonging to the King of Spain [MTM B13:442]. After three days in an Argo coffin, his bones answer God and resume duty as Pilot and Master [MTM B13:443]. He sails as a merry skeleton, yet can regain his former flesh in adventures falling earlier than the Laughing Prince episode, while the ashes persist [MTM B13:444]. Pseudo-Melchisedech subsequently tells him that he has lived the lost years seven times and died seven deaths; three led to Hell and four did not [MTM B13:465]. Finnegan's death quest is named through his fleece, thanato rather than mallion. Stein's account juxtaposes reports of his deaths in the Philippines, on the Brunhilde, at Tangier, Naxos, Galveston and the Marianao Coast with evidence of survival and Finnegan's differing recollections [MB:548]. A seaman resembling him is actually killed in his discarded clothes [D:267]. He remembers Papa Devil killing him during one of several incompatible first encounters [D:83]. After Anastasia's death he says he is dead too; X answers that he has undergone such a death and continued on a lesser level [D:156]. The narrator calls this Finnegan's first death and subsequent existence a shadow life [D:158]; Finnegan later finds entertainment in this life after death in Paradise [D:237]. Doll's poem predicts that he will soon be dead as the Devil [D:294]. Finnegan's belief that X had died is a separate matter: X admits fabricating and circulating the obituary as a joke [D:152-153]. Accounts of Casey also remain plural. X writes that he was dead and lives again [A:266]. Tony Apostolo reports his belief that he is the world's scapegoat [PG:525-526]; Hilary Hilton reads a divine sign making him the instrument of many people's salvation and damnation [PG:531-532]. John Schultz believes Casey died to escape his overwhelming followers, then reports the stolen body and the resurrection plaque beside the open grave [PG:541-543]. Bagby places Casey with him in Purgatory and denies that he is in Hell, while admitting the slight possibility that his visitor is a pseudo or effigy [PG:546]. Stein attributes Casey's wish to substitute for a damned soul largely to genuine compassion and describes their supposed soul exchange as a trade of kabouters [PG:537-538]. The original Papadiabolous is killed by Seaworthy and buried with Finnegan's help on top of an earlier occupant [D:75-76]. Seaworthy believes the man has returned, but Finnegan knows that the new Papadiabolous is another person [D:83-85]. X identifies the surrogate as the Irish policeman Noonan or Flaherty [D:154-155]. His death at Naxos reveals his true face; Finnegan then declares both the original and surrogate finally dead, a claim about these men rather than the extinction of every Devil [D:146] [D:150]. Anastasia is shot and falls from the breakwater [D:147]. Finnegan identifies Marie as her killer and Joe Cross as Marie's subsequent shooter; X thinks Seaworthy arranged Anastasia's lavish funeral [D:157]. Don Lewis bears the mark of death, is hunted through Tangier and killed by Marie, whose strength breaks his neck; Finnegan buries him in clean sand [D:100] [D:105-113]. Deaths of worlds and institutions extend the motif. The Great Day contingency unstructures things and obliterates boundaries and persons [MTM B10:298-299]. Its closing dream belongs to Duffey and Morpheus, not the grieving Finnegan: waking and sleeping become impossible, the cosmos diminishes, and a single creature swallows itself before Morpheus calls the apparent end a beginning [GD:500-501]. Cleo's fifth future includes replacement of humanity and slaughter [MTM B10:296]. Hugh de Turenne reports the Black Sea's obliteration and the intended erasure of its memory [MTM B11:336]. Mary Virginia reports Dominican preachers predicting the world's end that week [MTM B11:310]. Hackenschmidt declares the Ekklesia dead, orders the bells destroyed lest they awaken it, and commissions the killing of the thirteen absent princes [MB:568-569]. John Mogul's suggestion that dead men cast no shadows is explicitly contradicted by the narrator: history and the surviving doubles refute it [MB:588]. The grave marked I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch becomes the watched rendezvous of Finnegan, X and Doll [D:275-277]. It contains the earlier remains and Papadiabolous; Doll drops her poem through the ground's recurrent split to the bottom [D:76] [D:293-294]. Niccolo Crotolo explains two kinds of assassination contract: the piccola vendetta kills a victim possibly in grace, while the more expensive grande aims at death in a state of damnation. He says Finnegan's employer finally specified only the piccola [A:279-280].
