DecadenceA condition of decline invoked in contrasting settings. X reports representatives of the decadent and goatish arts at the Devil's release in the Crimea [MTM B6:205]. Le Marin calls the Old Wooden Ship's people decadent, fragmented and episodical; Finnegan nevertheless chooses their humanity over the strong patterns of his former companions [D:215].

MTM B6:205; D:215

Decatur StreetStreet in the changing New Orleans of the Royal Pop episode. The narrator says it now exists where Magazine Street, or perhaps Peters Street, had been, although residents do not remember it; the Decatur Street Opera House likewise has newly acquired its apparent history [MTM B11:346]. A turbaned speaker claims that an old flagstone has survived successive road surfaces and remembers horses, carriages, streetcars, automobiles, and every two-legged and four-legged walker [MTM B11:329-330]. Its remembered whips include the Cowles Buggy Whip, Jacksonville Drover, S.R. and Co's Australian, Western Mule Skinner, Milford Quirt, Hodson's Superior Horse Whip, San Antonio, Fancy, Never-Break Dog Whip and Elko, accompanied by wagoners' curses, rattling whipple trees and chains [MTM B11:329]. The opera house gives its name to the Thunder Colt Complex, or Presentation of the World [MTM B10:300].

MTM B11:346; MTM B11:329-330; MTM B11:329; MTM B10:300

Decatur Street Opera HouseOpera house in New Orleans whose advertisement appears in Teresa Showboat Piccone Stranahan's edition of Show-Bill. Dotty says it does not exist; Teresa calls this its first appearance and explains that it supplies a needed place for eschatological dramas [MTM B7:230]. It gives its name to the Thunder Colt Complex, the Presentation of the World [MTM B10:300]. Later it stands as a memorable old opera house despite residents' inability to remember it [MTM B11:346]. Its curtain is destroyed by lightning and simultaneous thunder instead of rising, an effect unique in the town. The Cretan Bull Drama is accompanied by the Bull Waltz [MTM B11:349]. The Fire-Drake Frolic follows, with Fritz's Fandango in Three Flames; the climax is the Thunder Colt Game, orchestrated to Thunder Torus music [MTM B11:350].

MTM B7:230; MTM B10:300; MTM B11:346; MTM B11:349; MTM B11:350

DeerDeer hunting is among the lively arts said to have been corrupted after the Devil's release [MTM B6:207]. Finnegan recalls that other fathers made swamp-deer calls for their sons, whereas Giulio made calls for panthers, alligators and stranger creatures [MTM B5:174]. The goat-man kills a deer once a year [A:197]. In his transport concerning his people's ancestry, Finnegan calls the giant stag one of their animal brothers [D:212-213]. Brannagan includes Deer Island among the islands visible from his chair [D:204].

MTM B6:207; MTM B5:174; A:197; D:212-213; D:204

Deer IslandIsland off Biloxi, Mississippi; one of four islands Brannagan says he can see from his chair [D:204].

D:204

Delancy, DollDolores Delancy, called Doll; Finnegan’s companion after the Brunhilde voyage [D:171]. He meets her in New York during his flight with Seaworthy’s money. She says she is locked out, freezing, and starving, and denies that she is hustling. He makes her drive a stolen car to Newark under the name Mrs. George Brubaker [D:166-169]. She helps him manage the suitcase and evade pursuit on the journey to Baltimore [D:169-172]. She has a broad face and bright gray eyes, and the narrator compares her placidity to a sleeping volcano. She says she has walked out of an unbearable former life [D:173]. She welcomes X into their company, calling him “the cutest little man,” and travels south with him and Finnegan [D:174] [D:178]. She receives a share of the stolen money; in the Florida lake country the three discuss their identities and plot Seaworthy’s murder [D:180]. She catches fish by hand, goes drinking with Finnegan, and repeatedly tries to tell the two men her story, but neither listens [D:181-184]. X suspects that her hearing is poor [D:185-186]. When they separate, she leaves in the little Road Runner [D:193]. At their later graveyard meeting, Doll hears X’s account of the Devil’s family [D:275-279]. Against X and Finnegan, she insists that ordinary people can help save the world, that the conflict must have a climax, and that she has long been engaged in saving the world herself. She also questions whether her first meeting with Finnegan was accidental [D:290-292]. She drops her poem Diabolique into the split in the grave [D:293]. In More Than Melchisedech, Dotty Yekouris reports X’s identification of Doll with herself and describes Doll as resembling her “with the brains knocked out.” This is a reported identification across Finnegan’s worlds [MTM B6:188-189].

DemeterGreek goddess of agriculture. In one of Finnegan's uncertain waking dreams, Marie Courtois says she is both Demeter and Demeter's daughter Persephone, returning from Hell to Earth in her own reincarnation [D:91]. Marie also links the pietà form and the thirteenth Station of the Cross to a supposed earlier group of Demeter and Pontos on the Aventine [D:92].

D:91; D:92

Demetriades, AnastasiaBarmaid at the club visited by Finnegan and Seaworthy, and later aboard the Brunhilde. She washes and shaves Finnegan, tells him they have met before, and prompts his exclamation “Anastasia, the resurrection!” [D:13] [D:16] [D:22]. Small and wiry, with a changing appearance, she has an olive and gold complexion sometimes touched with sea-green; her eyes appear black or purple [D:20] [D:32]. Her speech reaches Finnegan’s mind before its sound begins [D:20]. The narrative calls her a water-witch and associates her true form with the ship [D:31]. She is of a mermaid family of Naxos, though the Demetriades have produced no fishtail for six generations. A powerful swimmer, she supplies the account of mermaid appearance, habitation, history, and decline; the account describes mermaids as close-cropped and boyish, and Anastasia herself is boyish in figure [D:34-37]. She and Marie Courtois share a cabin, feud, and remain friends despite Anastasia’s jealousy. Anastasia calls Marie “skylla” and puts “crotin oil” in her martini; Finnegan calls Anastasia “Little Miss Resurrection” [D:33]. Her jealousy intensifies when Finnegan admires Marie at the Padre Island beach party [D:34] [D:37-38]. Anastasia notices the waves’ apparent writing but explicitly says she cannot read Chaldee; Finnegan claims that he can [D:38]. She identifies Papadiabolous as Papa Devil and says he seems nicer than on an earlier visit [D:23-24]. She brings Finnegan’s luggage aboard for the departure [D:27]. Walking inland with him on Padre Island, she suspects Don Lewis is one kind of spy and herself another, and warns that Seaworthy and the Devil own the ship’s people [D:38-40]. Later she calls the Brunhilde a plague ship, admits she deliberately joined its dangerous business, and calls Finnegan her brother [D:69-70]. Finnegan paints her dead as the wife of Sindbad’s fourth voyage, having first seen her death in his imagination [D:61-62]. On Naxos she visits her grandmother with Finnegan and takes him to a mountain vigil, bringing a reflecting lantern with which she intends to signal a boat [D:124-127] [D:131]. When he wakes before dawn, she has gone [D:140-141]. He subsequently sees her body laid on a sofa, still smiling; she has been shot once and pulled dead from the water below the breakwater. An Orthodox priest has given her the last rites and asks about her Roman rosary, which Finnegan says he gave her [D:147]. Finnegan later says Marie shot her, and X thinks Seaworthy arranged her lavish funeral [D:157]. Finnegan recalls her promise that they will be together again, then doubts whether his people have that promise [D:149]. A voice coming from the sleeping Don Barnaby says it owed Anastasia fifty dollars when it died; the narration specifies that the voice is not Barnaby’s [D:238].

DemetrioProprietor of a fly-specked Mexican bar visited by Finnegan, Marie Courtois and Anastasia after they leave the Cadillac Bar [D:57-58]. A gray-headed old bandit, he claims wide worldly experience through travel to Alice, Eagle Pass, Uvalde, Beeville, San Angelo, Weiniar and Port Isabel, and work milking goats, keeping bees and in a pickle factory. His lined face resembles both an old Roman and an old Aztec, like a face on a coin [D:58]. Finnegan makes a fine portrait in ink on a poster; the following page calls it Demetrio's own head hanging behind the bar, although the portrait sentence itself names Manuel [D:58-59]. Demetrio gives Finnegan a belt and each girl a silver ring, all his own handiwork [D:59].

He rejects Fleshpot Row and is mocked by the women at supper; Duffey's initial refusal to leave with him creates lasting doubt between them [MTM B4:126-127]. He is present when Morris Poor challenges Duffey's sanity and magical powers at Duffey's place [MTM B4:128]. He contributes to The Crock, appearing in a contributor list alongside Hermione Groben [MTM B4:138]; an issue described in Archipelago contains his ballad, without a supplied title [A:41]. His signed introduction frames the assessment and collection of Casey's work in “Promontory Goats” [PG:519]. In a later commentary he says Casey's associates stole the body and recalls a Crock advertisement offering dead bodies for special rites [PG:546].

The narrator allows as one authentic perspective that God creates through demiurges, giants and magi, without making that the sole account of creation [MTM B3:76-77]. Rosemary Riorden tells Finnegan that his father is Aeson, a demiurge, although he knows him as Giulio [A:89]. DesertThe desert of Cades appears in Melchisedech's line during his exchange of psalm-prayers with Finnegan [MTM B12:374-375]. In Tartary, Duffey encounters an imperfect, hallucinatory desert superimposed on industrial and agricultural country, with unnatural heat, intense thirst, misplaced plants and rocks, and badly realized skeletons [MTM B13:439]. The amoral desert then fades and his remains appear at Gur'yev [MTM B13:440-442]. The opening poem of the Finnegan chapter in Archipelago places a burning desert at Yenbo and Lith [A:171].

Devil (Papadiabolous II; Gregory McColum Papadiabolous; Noonan; Flaherty; Christy; Clarenden; Cobbett; Malory; Ingraham; John Gregory; N; the Irish cop; The Tiger)Gregory McColum Papadiabolous, the Irish son in X's genealogy, born in Cork to the same father as Gregory McIfreann, Papadiabolous I. X calls them twins while specifying different mothers and birthplaces. His aliases include Noonan, Flaherty, Christy, Clarenden, Cobbett, Malory, Ingraham and Arbuthnot; John Gregory can designate either brother [D:285]. X knows him as N, the undercover Irish cop [D:287]. He is a large and powerful man, comparatively good, whose earlier work as gentleman burglar, contrabandist, swindler and forger equips him for police work. The brothers share build, coloring and skull structure, but their natural fleshed faces differ [D:285-286]. He assumes his murdered brother's place the next morning and carries the impersonation through the voyage [D:288-289]. The frightening presence in the club is already this apparent return from death [D:15]; later Finnegan challenges the mask and asks how he can deceive long-standing associates so completely [D:87-88]. Papa answers questions with evasions, calling himself lamb-like when accused of killing Dopey [D:89]. He initially suspects Finnegan of Don Lewis's murder, but recognizes that Finnegan lacks the necessary strength [D:110-111]. At Naxos he is shot repeatedly and bludgeoned, his pockets emptied or cut out and his shoes removed. Finnegan recognizes the true face [D:146]. X identifies that face as Noonan or Flaherty and calls him an extraordinary mimic and a valuable ally [D:154-155]. X later attributes the killing to Seaworthy, who failed to recognize the unmasked man as his shipboard Papa Devil [D:289].

Dillard, Dandy Dan DillardPrizefighter who faces Duffey in the third preliminary bout on a Monday night bill, a four-round contest [MTM B2:50]. Duffey experiences it as an unmerciful beating equivalent to four hours of Hell, yet learns that he won the first three rounds widely and was well ahead in the fourth. The fight is stopped because Dillard is out on his feet and in danger, while Duffey is unmarked; Duffey's memory of being beaten then fades. Dillard is left a livid hulk. The experience draws Duffey into boxing, particularly promotion, which he takes up within six months [MTM B2:51].

When Cyrus draws it an inch and ten assistants fall into deep sleep, Cyril urges him to draw it completely, despite Duffey’s warning that this would end the world [MTM B13:423]. Dimbeau, CyrusFrench scientist who, with his brother Cyril, recovers the Sword and Scabbard of Saint Sécaire from beneath the seabed at the Nine Mile Depth [MTM B13:422]. DionysusGreek god of wine and ecstatic intoxication, one of the mythological identities assigned to Finnegan alongside Ulysses and the Terras or Arracht identity [A:39]. Dirty Five, TheMystic brotherhood of Henry F. Salvatore, also Euphemus; John G. Schultz, Hans or Orpheus; Vincent J. Stranahan, Meleager; Kasmir W. Szymansky, Casey or Peleus; and John A. Solli, Finnegan or Iason. The narration gives them earlier lives and multiple mythological identities, describes their shared knowledge and ambitions, and says amnesia separates them from earlier greatness [A:38-39]. Henry is the fifth member and the fat Frenchman who refuses the Australian furlough; Casey is called the fourth [A:18] [A:38]. Casey's interest in languages leads to his acceptance by John Schultz and entry into the group [A:159]. Loy's letter asks for the Dirty Fiver whom she and Margaret have not met, meaning Casey [A:27]. Casey later tells Finnegan private dreams he would not tell the others [A:161]. Hans, Henry and Finnegan solemnly shake hands after their companions fall asleep, as though forming a mystic trio within the Five [A:69]. It is Dotty who enjoys her introduction to the order during the St. Louis visit [A:176]. A banner in Henry's dream echoes the group's high motto, Ubicumque fuerit corpus illic congregabuntur et aquilas, concerning the eagles gathering at the body [A:44]. The poem opening Vincent's chapter remembers their sea-kingdom and sailing the ship anciently called Argo [A:91]. Finnegan later belongs with Le Marin, Don Barnaby and Johnny Duckwalk to a dark counterpart of the Dirty Five [A:188]. In More Than Melchisedech, Duffey describes his wider set of Animated Marvels as involving both human and Teras elements [MTM B5:169-170].

Don JuanFigure in Hans Schultz's account of dark doubles. He says Don Juan arranged for a shoddy double to suffer Hell in his place, but was himself the shoddy double of a more elegant sinner and was trapped into suffering for that man [MTM B6:186].

Don LewisCrewman aboard the Brunhilde, sharing quarters with Finnegan and Joe Cross; dark, handsome and called the ship's most handsome man [D:30-31]. His campfire story strongly identifies him with PFC Timothy Lorrigan of Boston, although he initially withholds which of three missing soldiers he was and then tries to retract his revealing first-person slip [D:44-45]. He tells how he buried the man he calls Yokipoki, mistook rats disturbing the body for a return from death, and subsequently became a furtive man under another name [D:43-48]. The narrative calls him a coward playing a daring game: he secretly organizes resistance aboard the ship, helps bring in Joe Cross, Manuel, Anastasia and Finnegan, and helps arrange the apparent resurrection of the Devil without understanding every part of it [D:105]. He is hunted through Tangier and killed by Marie Courtois, whose strength enables her to throttle him and break his neck. Finnegan finds the robbed body at the bottom of the tell and buries it in clean sand under creepers [D:105-113]. Don Barnaby, a different later companion, disconcertingly seems to carry some of Don Lewis's memories [D:265].

Doppio di Pinne (Dopey the Seaman; Finnegan's fetch)Seaman known as Dopey, intended to replace Finnegan by assuming his papers and person after Finnegan's death, but apparently killed instead [D:51]. He occupies Finnegan's bunk for the preceding two days [D:63]. Joe Cross reports Papa Devil entering the cabin, Dopey's screams ending abruptly, and the room then containing only Papa and a small dribble of blood, with no possible exit for Dopey [D:64]. Finnegan and Dopey resemble one another in size, shape and coloring, especially when seen sideways [D:65]. Dopey's writings express both ambition and fear that he, rather than Finnegan, will be trapped and killed; Finnegan continues to feel his invisible presence in the bunk [D:78]. Papa Devil calls him Finnegan's double or fetch but denies killing him, even suggesting that Finnegan may be Dopey [D:89]. Papa later says that Dopey shares the strange blood, is a sometime killer, and was summoned by Seaworthy to kill Papadiabolous; Seaworthy mistook Finnegan for him. Papa leaves open whether he or Finnegan killed Dopey, or whether the fetch was absorbed into Finnegan [D:121-122]. Finnegan subsequently shaves Dopey's face in his mirror; the dazed face says it is not dead [D:187]. Patricia also tells Dotty that Dopey is her brother and the same person as Finnegan, who sometimes became Doppio in childhood [A:174]. Finnegan later thinks of his fetch as having died in his place, either aboard the Brunhilde at Papadiabolous's hands or later on Galveston Island in Seaworthy's trap [A:278].

She explains their function as awakening and recollection, restoring the company to knowledge of themselves and one another [MTM B5:178-179]. When the Masters pretend not to recognize X, he asks them to consult the talking oak in the wheel, confident that the ship will know him [MTM B13:434].

DorothyRed-headed town girl present with Virginia at the picnic held at the Bay Hotel [A:29].

DottyNickname of Dorothy Mary Yekouris, Finnegan's beloved from New Orleans [A:92] [A:95]. She is also addressed as Dot by Patricia, Finnegan's sister, in the passage excerpted as an epigraph in The Devil Is Dead [A:174-175] [D:18-19]. She works with Duffey on the Pelican Press papers and The Bark [MTM B7:212] [MTM B7:215].

A:92; A:95; A:174-175; D:18-19; MTM B7:212; MTM B7:215

Doucet, ThereseCasting director of Seven Roads, the girls' play about the Patriarch Melchisedech's seven possible futures. She accepts Duffey for the role when he offers to play Melchisedech; Cleo Mahoney supplies the script as its playwright [MTM B9:265]. Therese is among the Ursuline Academy girls whom Duffey meets at the Ghost Coffee Shop before the planned performance in the school auditorium [MTM B10:293].

MTM B9:265; MTM B10:293

Drexel, MonicaSometimes Charley Murray's girl, one of the two Monicas at Duffey's farewell supper at Meinkmuellers. The other is Charley's sister Monica Murray. Duffey confuses them because their names and appearances are alike, apparently giving a talisman first to the wrong Monica before the other recognizes it as hers [MTM B2:69]. A girl called Monica also accompanies Charley at Beth Keegan's balloon dinner party [MTM B2:65].

MTM B2:69; MTM B2:65

Duckhunter, CrissieGeorge Duckhunter's wife in “The Casey Machine.” She calls the machines unspeakably vile and wants George and Newton Prescott to stop dealing with them even if they return [CM:503]. Distressed by their continuing wealth, she wishes they could shut off the money and become poor and honest; George replies that they were never either [CM:504].

CM:503; CM:504

Duckhunter, GeorgeCrissie Duckhunter's husband and an associate of Newton Prescott in “The Casey Machine.” He calls the machines gold mines and argues that if their vileness cannot be stopped, money can at least be made from it [CM:503]. He says that he and Crissie were never poor or honest, that he cannot shut off the continuing millions, and that they are being paid as guardians of some kind. He cannot clearly remember the circumstances and believes Crissie and Prescott suffer the same gaps [CM:504].

CM:503; CM:504

Duckwalk, Johnny (aka Doekvalk)Johnny Duckwalk, whose ship's papers spell the name Doekvalk. He is one of the four companions in Basse-Terre Paradise with Finnegan, Le Marin and Don Barnaby, and a champion drinker [D:236]. The narrator calls him a prince of a fellow and excuses his daytime sleep by his activity at night [D:238]. He accuses Le Marin of passing off a counterfeit Marie Celeste story [D:246]. He also has a mean streak: each month he steals the gold sovereign Angela Cosquin has just deposited underwater, leaving the other treasure alone [D:263]. His subsequent sickness of repentance makes him leave Paradise to confess a previously unnoticed appropriation of money and serve an expected six to ten years. He later writes from prison urging the others to leave the island [D:264-265]. The confessed offence is not identified as his thefts from Angela. He belongs with Finnegan, Le Marin and Don Barnaby to the dark counterpart of the Dirty Five [A:188].

D:236; D:238; D:246; D:263; D:264-265; A:188

Duffey, Letitia (Koch)Melchisedech Duffey's wife, Lily Koch's younger sister and the daughter of August and Elinore Koch [MTM B3:92] [MTM B3:98]. Duffey recognizes his sought-for joyful moth, tinea letitia, in her. She is Lily's partner at Koch's Galleries, retaining her half-interest after marriage; she has already anticipated their home and made its arrangements before Duffey recognizes her [MTM B3:91-92]. Charlotte calls her partly Duffey's creation through the rib-shaped talisman, a bonus outside his twelve prime creations [MTM B3:93]. Letitia also claims creative power herself, telling Lily that she projected the Countess into Chicago and treating reality as subjective projections [MTM B3:96]. She has abundant hair between blonde, scarlet and walnut, a ruddy complexion, a high-comedy look, sea-green-to-blue eyes and a full-bodied build; she is taller than Duffey [MTM B3:92]. Her fine scanning eye and haunting voice make her reading compelling, and her recorded time-and-temperature advertisements move listeners [MTM B4:114]. Her prescience helps her understand the Mullens murders and Charlotte's escape [MTM B3:97-98]. She and Duffey are central figures and, in a sense, co-creators of the North Chicago golden age [MTM B3:98]. The narrator says that they design their neighborhood, events, life scenarios and people, and calls Letitia one of Duffey’s creations, with an even stronger gift for creating people and their surroundings [MTM B3:100]. In New Orleans she arrives with their best possessions and enough cash to sustain their work [MTM B6:198]. The narrator describes her later beauty as proto-legendary, her welcome and affection illuminating the establishments [MTM B7:211]. After Dotty's disappearance she edits The Bark, maintaining it from private funds while other Pelican Press accounts decline [MTM B8:238-239]. Her sudden death leaves Duffey distraught; after protesting to a burning bush, he grudgingly accepts its explanation [MTM B8:253]. Though the death had been foreknown for years, its suddenness overwhelms him [MTM B8:254].

MTM B3:92; MTM B3:98; MTM B3:91-92; MTM B3:93; MTM B3:96; MTM B4:114; MTM B3:97-98; MTM B3:100; MTM B6:198; MTM B7:211; MTM B8:238-239; MTM B8:253; MTM B8:254

Duffey, Melchisedech

Identity and appearance. Magus, art dealer, writer and one of the Masters of the Argo. He identifies himself as the Boy King and King of Salem [MTM B1:15] [MTM B5:166] [MTM B13:402]. He has sorrel hair, fire-blue eyes, a solid but not oversized body, and a mouth that may begin grinning before his eyes. He habitually bangs his hands together and addresses people and even his own clay creatures with promises of immediate action [MTM B1:6]. He begins growing a beard at fifteen to look older [MTM B2:38]; in New Orleans he keeps it white and bright and wears an artist’s tie and beret for his trade [A:143]. His voice is Boston Irish with a touch of stage Yiddish. Archipelago calls him a patriarch without seed, a prophet without honor and a high-sounding brawler whose apparently universal knowledge is shared by others in the company [A:97]. The later narrator describes his uncertain age, wilfulness and spaciousness, and the unexplained restraints upon him [MTM B11:312]. His names include Michael, according to a relative whose account he disputes; Mikey; Melky; Mike Duffey on his seaman’s papers; and Melchisedech Himself [MTM B1:7] [MTM B1:9] [MTM B1:30] [MTM B12:369] [MTM B13:402]. Casey gives another modern account: Michael is his given name, and Melchisedech his confirmation name, received when confirmed at forty [A:42]. In the postscript Duffey signs himself the fifty-ninth King of Salem and says that he has always known of fifty-eight predecessors [PS:478]. He also passes through cycles of renewed youth; Stein accuses him of whitening his hair and beard to conceal their return to black [MTM B11:317-319].

Childhoods and kindred. Duffey remembers simultaneous twentieth-century childhoods in Iowa, St. Louis and Boston, behind which stands an older, continuing life as the Boy King [MTM B1:6-7] [MTM B1:15-18]. Seven Iowa places dispute his birthplace: Minden, Underwood, Beebee Town, Neola, Crescent, Avoca and Union Township. A relative says that his mother died when he was five, that he lived with kindred until twelve, and that he then entered boarding schools. These kindred include the Duffeys, Kellys, Byrnes, McGuires, Crooks, Bagbys, Haleys, Healeys, Haydens, Kanes, Whites, Hughes, Kennedys, Thompsons and Clancys. Duffey disputes both this genealogy and the name Michael, claiming to have been born without parents when already five years old [MTM B1:7-8]. One proposed explanation of the overlapping childhoods is his appropriation of his brother’s and sister’s experiences. The St. Louis childhood is associated particularly with the sister’s life, and an analyst concludes that Duffey was himself a girl during part of his childhood [MTM B1:15-16]. These explanations do not cancel the narrative’s account of the ancient Boy King, whose tents, flocks, gardens and powers are presented as more substantial than his modern surroundings [MTM B1:17-18].

Schooling and formation. Sent to boarding school at twelve, he spends four high-school years in more than one institution. The uncertain locations include Creighton, Loras, Rockhurst and a boys’ school near St. Louis University; the narrator says that at least two of these places are involved [MTM B1:20] [MTM B1:24]. Charley Murray, John Rattigan and Sebastian Hilton are his principal companions. A skilled carpenter, machinist and maker of molds and patterns, he makes Murray’s conjuring props, using his giants when ordinary tools cannot suffice [MTM B1:21-23]. He trades with Rattigan and appropriates his business judgment, Murray’s good nature and honesty, and Sebastian’s intelligence and taste [MTM B1:25-26]. An older priest accepts his account of being a magus and warns him against pride. Lily Koch’s art sales, and his reading of her mind and Sebastian’s, establish his lifelong vocation as an art expert [MTM B1:28-29].

Powers and their limits. His gifts include producing gold, entering other minds, moving within time, commanding invisible giants and forming persons through talismans; the last is initially called his greatest gift [MTM B1:5]. He appropriates the perceptions and memories of other children, sometimes knowing households he has never visited [MTM B1:16-17]. At Lake Manawa he believes that good divers return from the water as evil replacements; his mental effort to keep one underwater ends in a drowning, described as his first killing [MTM B1:8-9]. As Boy King he can remain invisible beneath an urchin disguise, summon giants, heal and animate birds [MTM B1:18]. His gold appears as sparks or coins as well as bars and engraved objects [MTM B1:5] [MTM B2:38-39]. His first major loss is the facility for making money, which never fully returns. This coincides with damage to the Pont du Sable Traffic Trestle, a bridge whose failing supports become an image of his own losses; he nevertheless retains substantial wealth [MTM B4:109-110]. The gifts can diminish, be forgotten or fail to achieve what he expects. His encounter with the art giants teaches him that he will more often recognize great art than make it [MTM B2:54]. His prescience and his belief that he causes persons to exist are closely connected; he later loses the effective bestowal of talismans for a period of his life [MTM B4:120]. In another episode he returns to yesterday to meet Finnegan in the burial cave [MTM B12:374].

St. Louis. At fifteen, on the last day of May 1915, Duffey sets out on his own after selling his school businesses [MTM B2:38]. He establishes the Rounders’ Club, with food, drink, lodging, transport, music, games and imported goods, and studies at several institutions while finding more hours of activity than an ordinary day permits [MTM B2:49]. Charley Murray becomes half-owner and his business partner [MTM B2:53]. Duffey boxes, wins seven of his first nine fights, and turns to promoting fights; he also becomes the band’s banjo player [MTM B2:50-54]. Bascom Bagby is his friend, business associate and quasi-brother. Mary Louise says that Bagby shares their person; Duffey later calls him his dark object [MTM B2:61-62] [MTM B2:73]. Mary Louise Byrne is Duffey’s sister or stepsister, and their relationship includes an erotic attachment. She introduces Beth Keegan as a substitute beloved [MTM B2:54-56]. When Duffey returns from his lost years, Mary Louise has married Bagby [MTM B2:73]. Duffey joins, or in another version founds, the World-Wide Argonauts Argo Balloon Club. His balloon becomes the Argo Twelve and a Half after a powerful visitor explains that the actual twelfth voyage is still active and the balloon may serve as its pinnace. Bagby later reports ghostly excursions in it, which Duffey accepts [MTM B2:63-64] [MTM B2:66].

Marriage, Chicago and performance. A compelling moth-call brings Duffey from Omaha to Chicago in 1925. Charlotte Garfield, an adult confidence woman with a child’s appearance, helps him find the woman who will become his wife; he uses his mind-reading powers to assist her search for Aga Gonof’s hidden stash [MTM B3:77-80] [MTM B3:84] [MTM B3:88-89]. Duffey marries Letitia Koch, Lily Koch’s sister, whose formation involved the special rib-shaped talisman he had given Lily in their schooldays [MTM B1:29-30] [MTM B3:90-93]. Their rooms and shops become the heart of a near-north-side Chicago golden age. They design its people, settings and events together, with Letitia said to possess the gift even more strongly [MTM B3:100]. His Priceless Item Room houses seven representations of Christ collected and sent home during the lost years, joined by an eighth brought by August Koch [MTM B3:103-104]. Duffey and Letitia give puppet shows: Letitia works made puppets, while Duffey calls out local mice and directs them as costumed actors, accompanying the performances with his banjo [MTM B4:133-134]. His supposedly last public magic act, dated November 13, 1935, is the transport of a mule through the air; witnesses and photographs offer conflicting accounts of the giant hands involved [MTM B4:127-132]. Dr. Morris Poor challenges his powers and calls him insane [MTM B4:128]. Dr. Saul Rafelson analyzes him without declaring him cured. Rafelson’s catalogue includes divine or golden childhood, mastery of giants, kingship, successive and parallel lives, inner monsters and shadows, the power to confer life, and the belief that the world depends on him. The doctor nevertheless acknowledges extraordinary facts about Duffey and the persons said to be his creations [MTM B4:146-147].

Casey and the Crock. Duffey is a part-time partner of Casey’s father and a principal influence on Casey’s education. Casey learns more from his bookshelves than at school, and learns Yiddish, Hebrew and Irish from him. Before entering the army, Casey moves his college Crock to a little press in the back room of Duffey’s bookstore [A:156] [A:159] [A:167-168]. The narrator calls Duffey closer to Casey than Casey’s father, though he seems to shrug off Casey’s later hostile editorial [A:131]. Duffey edits the Crock while Casey serves in the army; after its takeover and Casey’s return he is excluded from it [MTM B4:138] [MTM B4:145]. The attempted takeover exposes compromising photographs of his conduct with adult women and with girls from the age of eight or ten. He disputes some appearances, calls one photograph an entrapment, and says that guilty acts have been confessed and absolved; he refuses the blackmailers’ demand for control [MTM B4:139-141]. In his wartime letter to Casey he reports that the pressure temporarily drove his wife away and left him with a broken nose and right hand, and warns Casey against gambling any stock [A:40]. The Chicago double Mike Melchiades, whose marriage suffers from acts he denies committing, insists that Duffey is only his spinoff. Duffey suspects that this may be true, and helps the double’s wife return to him while knowing that Letitia is leaving their own home for a time [MTM B4:141-144]. Casey describes Duffey as the sole member of the Catholic Center Party of America, a Centrist who favors small government and opposes what he sees as collectivist infiltration; his index lists several thousand alleged infiltrators in Catholic lay groups [A:42-43]. He writes most of the issue described in Archipelago, including material identifiable as his in “Moles at the Grass Roots,” “Fables in Fabianism” and “The Consumer, the Cooperative, and the Coefficient of Cost Constancy.” That issue also contains the “Urbe et Orbe” notes, the “Judgement Day” review section, recording reviews favoring Chicago jazz and a readers’ letter forum [A:41]. His Razzle Daz comic strip uses Finnegan, Hans and Show Boat among its models [MTM B5:159]. Casey’s Answer is printed on Duffey’s press, but Duffey is initially unaware of its authorship and publication [MTM B4:113-118].

New Orleans, commerce and charity. He comes to New Orleans to put Henry’s ideas into practice. Commercial printing is to support the crusading journal, with work on it continuing after the paid working day. Mrs. Duffey sells their Chicago home and household goods and brings eighteen hundred of his books; the narrator says that he commits all he has [A:117-119]. In New Orleans Duffey helps establish the Pelican Press to publish the Bark, operates the Walk-In Art Bijou and a pawnshop, and makes and plays recorder flutes [MTM B6:190] [MTM B6:199] [MTM B7:211]. With Stein and Gabrielovitch he starts the Investigator; he writes for both journals and sells books, antiques and works by the Studios and Pirates’ Alley painters. His safe holds cash, valuable art, including authentic Van Ghis, and the Infiltrates file [A:143]. He supplies the cards on which X adds information to that file [A:137]. A poem in The Devil Is Dead is attributed to Melchisedech Duffy’s The Alien Awakens [D:197]. He insists upon a flophouse and turns Zabotski’s thousand-gallon crock into a soup service, installing gas burners, obtaining a blessing from St. Katherine’s and raising money for barley; Dotty pays the gas and water bills. Archipelago gives an initial cost of one cent a bowl, eventually about three hundred meals daily with continuous staffing, and a retrospective duration of at least a quarter-century [A:126] [A:132-134]. More Than Melchisedech instead describes growth from six recipients to about six hundred after a week and then several thousand. Medical students’ apparent planting of human bones gives the pot its name, Cannibal Duffey’s Irish Restaurant [MTM B6:197]. About the mid-1950s his Bijou receives The Resurrection of Count Finnegan, with Finnegan and Joseph Hedayat pictured decades ahead and looking identical. He sells it to Hilary Hilton for twenty thousand dollars and continues displaying it at Hilton’s request [MB:550-554].

The talismanic company. Duffey maintains that he literally helped form twelve persons, with others outside or partly within that count [MTM B5:150-151]. Henri Salvatore summons him to St. Louis for the last Saturday in May, promising the assignment for the rest of his life. There he encounters the brilliant company whose members know his Crock more readily than his kingship [MTM B5:152] [MTM B5:157-158]. The list announced as twelve names Finnegan (John Solli), Hans (John) Schultz, Henri Salvatore, Vincent Stranahan, Casey Szymansky, Dotty Yekouris, Mary Monaghan Schultz, Mary Virginia Schaeffer, Teresa Piccone, Absalom Stein and Mr. X: eleven names. Mary Catherine Carruthers is separately identified as another of the creations [MTM B5:158] [MTM B5:161-162]. Finnegan and Teresa are its two central creations [MTM B5:157] [MTM B5:162]; the narrator distinguishes Finnegan as the greatest from Teresa as the finest [MTM B5:182]. Duffey says he put unusual amounts of Teras blood into his people; Finnegan’s claim to be hollow troubles him [MTM B5:170-172].

Creation, awakening and faith. The talismans are associated with the Argo’s gold filigree, the Talking Oak and the Golden Fleece [MTM B5:178]. Marie says that Duffey collects the companions and gives them settings and sparkle rather than making them; he disputes her account [MTM B5:159]. Teresa tells Duffey that he awakened the company rather than created it, calling its members back into bodies to oppose the released Devil [MTM B7:233-234]. Stein sometimes reverses the dependence entirely, proposing that they made Duffey into the magus who thinks he made them [MTM B10:304]. The Argo Masters are also described as an interdependent society whose members act upon one another [MTM B13:446]. Duffey nevertheless insists to the Devil that he can perform primary creation [MTM B10:303]. His artistic work includes perhaps ten thousand figures in clay and baked bread dough [MTM B7:228-229]. In his commentary on Casey he recalls Peleus as a good, brave companion on the Argo, and offers another explanation of his twentieth-century Animations: they serve much the same purpose as Gorshok’s artificial hosts for body lice. His creatures doubt the account, and he says he has forgotten any other purpose [PG:534-536]. A separately unlabelled passage among Casey’s collected writings proposes that Duffey’s talismans implanted the remembered ancient lives as educational devices [PG:545]. He seeks to join art, law, divine worship, kindness and charity in daily life [MTM B7:228-229]. He rejects ordinary mediocrity while insisting upon humility [A:143]. His subordination to Henry is nevertheless described as a punishment for pride: he must serve one of his own satellites [MTM B8:245]. X calls him a “toy patriarch,” fitted for crusading rather than secret work, who must find one greater than Melchisedech [A:265-266].

The Seven Lost Years. Duffey disappears for seven years and returns in 1923, wandering among his old cities before returning to St. Louis. Eleven primary talisman children are born during his absence [MTM B2:71-74]. His claims of wartime army and ambulance service are uncertain; the narrator suggests that some experiences may have been taken from Sebastian Hilton, while witnesses also recall Duffey working with an organization named ARGO [MTM B2:72-73]. The Argo travels behind this interval, but its seven years need not follow consecutively in ordinary time [MTM B2:71] [MTM B13:406]. Absalom Stein's account places his death in Neustria and says that X later returns his ashes in a Spanish king’s old receptacle [MTM B6:185]. Duffey can keep these ashes beside him while alive in New Orleans [MTM B1:6]. His account of his ancient life explicitly rejects reincarnation, though he allows that his bodily history may include successive bodies or the renovation of one body [MTM B8:250]. He later remembers his modern lifetime as a sixty-year leave from the Holy Ship, beginning with his landing in 1923; he hopes to repeat it, while Cardinal Henri warns that repeated returns delay his arrival at the other shore [MTM B12:387].

Contingencies and rival explanations. Stein considers both identification with the biblical Melchisedech and an unusual sharing of the ancient king’s memories; he also calls Duffey the man who does not have an ending. Mary Virginia conjectures that Duffey comes from a discarded creation. These are the speakers’ proposed explanations [MTM B10:291-292]. The same Stein passage alternately treats the released Devil as a minor decoy and as the Devil himself [MTM B10:291]. Seven principal contingencies confront Duffey when his life overruns the present and fractures [MTM B10:298-301]. He refuses to represent mankind in his meeting with the Devil, rejects the Devil’s demand for his services and faces the claimed mortgage upon his soul and body [MTM B10:301-303]. The seventh contingency presents an encounter with the invisible God and a possibility of personal disaster [MTM B10:301].

Bereavement and continuing bonds. Bagby’s weekly letters continue for many years after his funeral, describing an existence outside ordinary time; Duffey rereads and savors them throughout each week [MTM B8:237] [MTM B8:248-249]. When Letitia dies suddenly, Duffey first refuses to accept it, then speaks privately with a burning Elephant Ear bush and grudgingly accepts the divine will [MTM B8:253-254]. Countess Margaret proposes marriage and a long life in Transylvania, and Lily offers marriage and renewed companionship. He postpones the Countess’s offer and tells Lily that he needs everyone [MTM B8:254-257].

Later journeys and trials. In his account for House and Home Happenings, Duffey describes studying time with Zabotski and visiting the Pristine World for three or five years, returning in two days [MTM B9:267] [MTM B9:272-273] [MTM B9:284]. Duffey answers the ritual summons of the Royal Pop People, written on parchment in squid ink and nailed to his door [MTM B11:311-313]. In the fifth contingency he is seduced by the splendid people, abandons suffering friends, and only belatedly tears himself free by reversing his movement through time. Bagby condemns his pride and cowardice and demands that he recover his strength in the wilderness [MTM B12:353] [MTM B12:356-357]. After returning from the fifth contingency he fears that he has damaged time and discovers that Margaret Stone’s death has entered his own world [MTM B12:354]. In the crash year Mary Virginia takes him for a ghost; his withdrawal returns that year to the future [MTM B12:361]. He contributes magic to the intermission of the girls’ play and later travels with Carmelo Mendoza. Horace Pie's reference to Mr. Eggs alerts him that the disguised companion is X, though he subsequently claims that he always knows his own handiwork [MTM B12:366] [MTM B12:369-372]. At Hilary Hilton’s farewell party he compels Casey’s presence by projecting Adam Scanlon’s portrait of his head onto television [MTM B12:380-383]. At the end of Book Twelve, he turns the forbidden handle, falls from the green country with shattered bones into a dung heap, where vermin, dung rats, buzzards and blood snakes attack him, and discovers that God remains present in the tempest [MTM B12:392-393]. From the dung, broken objects and his own blood he joyfully begins making another company of Animated Marvels, aided by lightning. He chooses to sail again while keeping this work as his eventual delight; the last minute of his life is still unfinished [MTM B12:394-395].

Death and the Argo. The three slant-faced attackers have stalked him since he was about six; a kit-fox helps him survive a childhood knifing. After the Crock assault he kills one of them, but their number is repeatedly restored [MTM B1:12] [MTM B1:19-20] [MTM B5:150] [MTM B7:225-227]. He identifies his priesthood with an obscure oriental rite that permits marriage [MTM B13:413-414]. As an Argo Master, Duffey cures a brilliant young man’s stutter at Weinsburg on the Nechar [MTM B13:430]. Three slant-faced killers strip the flesh from his bones and kill him; three slack-faced attendants burn the stripped flesh, sinew and viscera. His bones and ashes appear in Gur’yev, where X and Kasmir Gorshok recover them. X keeps the ashes, and the bones are taken aboard the Argo [MTM B13:442-443]. God tells him that his duties do not require a fleshed body. Casey makes a golden mask, scarf and gauntlets from the Fleece, and Duffey resumes his work as pilot [MTM B13:443-444]. When he moves into earlier portions of his life, he has flesh again while the ashes remain: the text calls this the Ambiguity of the Flesh. His Chicago and New Orleans lives consequently take on the character of incursions into the past [MTM B13:444-446]. With Brannagan and Gorshok he also tries to prevent the Antichrist from boarding the ship, holding that harmful prophecies must be resisted [MTM B13:454]. In the shimmering future their resistance fails: Casey appears as the Antichristus, the ship takes him to Habonim, and Duffey, Brannagan and Gunboat Smith remain undeceived but strongly affected. They fade out of that future without knowing whether another attempt is possible; Duffey has regained flesh [MTM B13:461-463]. His “Promontory Goats” commentary likewise foresees disputing Casey yet giving him passage against his will. He says that he has returned from the future and beyond death but is forbidden to disclose more [PG:537]. In How Many Miles to Babylon, the fleshless, golden-masked pilot carries Finnegan, Gilberto Levine-and-O’Brien and Herman Hercules toward Mooring-Stone, and later addresses the conclave that elects Finnegan pope [MB:589-590] [MB:597].

Returns and the appended story. At twenty-three Duffey comes ashore from the Sea of Lost Years and meets a young double who tells him he has lived the lost years seven times and died seven different deaths, three ending in damnation. Duffey suggests that God employs magi to explore possible endings; the double disputes this and, after Duffey has left, admits uncertainty about whether he serves God or the Devil [MTM B13:465-466]. Another return places Duffey in St. Louis in 1923, where the child Teresa offers to give him a valid birth in the future, believing that one demonstrably real life will establish the reality of the others [MTM B13:470-473]. In the appended “Great Day in the Morning,” spelled Duffy, he encounters a world losing its containers and distinctions. Its catastrophe enacts the conditions of his own bitterly comic Bark article from a year before. Horrified that the world has taken the joke seriously, he appeals to laughter and considers another article to undo the result [GD:491-493]. He insists upon a substantial universe, talks with the damaged statue of St. Michael, and wrestles with Morpheus as they shrink into a self-swallowing single cell. Morpheus calls this a return to the beginning; the final verses then enact obliteration [GD:481-501]. Lafferty’s postscript describes these apparent endings as cross-sections of continuing lives on multiple tracks [PS:479-480]. Finnegan also names him among the friends of his normal life in The Devil Is Dead [D:90].
