Dugan, DelbertName into which John Rattigan is said to turn for a year or so during Duffey's boarding-school years, as Sebastian Hilton turns into Martin Troyat, preserving the group of four boys. Duffey and Charley Murray remain together throughout; Sebastian returns for the final year after attending school in Europe [MTM B1:24].

MTM B1:24

Duke and Jenny ColfaxTheatrical people listed together among Duffey's North Chicago golden-age friends [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

Duke ColfaxTheatrical person listed with Jenny Colfax among Duffey's North Chicago golden-age friends [MTM B3:99]. See also Duke and Jenny Colfax.

MTM B3:99

Duke of Moule, The (Don Barnaby)Don Barnaby, duke by nickname, one of Finnegan's three companions in the Basse-Terre Paradise with Charles Le Marin and Johnny Duckwalk [D:236]. A voice unlike his own comes from him while he sleeps, asking Finnegan to repay Anastasia fifty dollars owed at death [D:238]. He tells the company a story beginning with the varieties of joy pills [D:248]. After Duckwalk leaves, Barnaby also departs, promising to return, though Angela doubts him. He seems to carry Don Lewis's memories while being someone else; Angela reports his claim that he has not been that other Don for several years [D:265]. He belongs to the dark counterpart of the Dirty Five [A:188].

D:236; D:238; D:248; D:265; A:188

Dürer, Albrecht (1471--1528)German Renaissance painter, printmaker and theorist whose work brought Northern European detail into dialogue with Italian concerns for proportion and perspective. His Apocalypse is a woodcut series; Melencolia I is an engraving. His theoretical publications treat measurement and geometry, fortification and human proportion. Patrick Stranahan includes Dürer with Watteau and Hogarth in his deliberately restricted list of painters worth owning, saying that one minor original and a dozen good copies are enough for an honest man's budget [A:109].

A:109

Dutch DuquesneA snapping-turtle-looking member of the Old Wooden Ship circle. He says he makes a hundred dollars nightly in tips as a waiter at the Balinese Room or another fashionable pier establishment, then loses the money at games. Mary, who works at the clubs, says he is actually a kitchen boy cleaning fish and shucking oysters, receives no tips and never has or loses more than five dollars [D:221].

D:221

Dutch Eckel (Little)See Eckel, Little Dutch [D:221] [MTM B13:458].

D:221; MTM B13:458

DutchmanName used for Hans Schultz by Marie Monaghan when he quotes verse [A:9]. James or Jimmy Fitzjames also calls him Dutch and Dutchman, beginning with a request for a quarter to buy a book in New York [A:224-225].

A:9; A:224-225

EabhraiochAddress used by Duffey to Zabotski during their bantering exchange in what Duffey calls the holy language: "Have a care, Eabhraioch" [MTM B11:320]. It apparently represents Irish Eabhrach, a Hebrew or Jew, though the novel's spelling differs from that dictionary form.

MTM B11:320

Eads bridge (St. Louis)Bridge across the Mississippi at St. Louis. Duffey, in what the narrator calls his fifth or sixth youth, walks from the river shore below it onto a low boat that is the Argo in disguise [MTM B2:71]. His eventual return from the Sea of Lost Years brings him to a pier below the bridge in 1923 [MTM B13:470], where the fishing boy identifies himself as ten-year-old Philip Stranahan [MTM B13:471]. The bridge marks both embarkation and return in Duffey's changing chronology.

MTM B2:71; MTM B13:470; MTM B13:471

EarthWorld whose history and workings receive several competing accounts. In Duffey's account of Zabotski and the Fundamentalers, Zabotski's shortened Pristine History resembles their chronology [MTM B9:278-280]. Zabotski says the Pristine and Everyday-or-Molasses worlds occupy the same space, but the Pristine World proceeds faster and excludes duplicate or non-valid people and situations [MTM B9:279]. Newton Prescott, speaking for an electronic community of minds, claims that earthly magnetism binds Earth to something beyond the solar system and contains buried memories and mysteries [CM:510]. Absalom Stein's notes date the Devil's release from his Crimean dungeon to 1946, ending a supposed thousand-year good era [MTM B6:185]. Hans Schultz invokes Coriolis as the great Earth force while explaining the direction of Australian horse races [A:4].

MTM B9:278-280; MTM B9:279; CM:510; MTM B6:185; A:4

Earth CreatureTeresa Piccone Stranahan's earthly aspect: the narrator imagines green moss growing in the corners of her eyes because she is an Earth Creature. The same passage gives her star-sparkle all over because she is also a Heavenly creature [MTM B5:180].

MTM B5:180

Earth HoursAppointments outside time described in one of Bascom Bagby's Letters After I Am Dead. During them the dead contemplate Earth and review its happenings with greater maturity and attention to particulars [MTM B8:248-249].

MTM B8:248-249

Earthly oneThe Terrestrial Paradise to which Finnegan and his friends travel, distinguished from the Heavenly Paradise. Its surviving snakes foreshadow their expulsion; the place is identified with Basse-Terre [D:234-235].

D:234-235

EastDirection taken by the Argo when its sea begins to change: unusually, it runs eastward with the wind and waves [MTM B13:459]. Other uses place Chodorlahomor's Elam or Susiana east of the Tigris [MTM B7:228], describe the Ohio River joining the Mississippi from the east [MTM B2:65], and locate the recovery of Duffey's bones and ashes at Gur'yev, called the East Mouth of the Ural [MTM B13:442].

MTM B13:459; MTM B7:228; MTM B2:65; MTM B13:442

East (the)See East for directional uses, including the Ohio River's approach to the Mississippi [MTM B2:65]. For X's account of the Devil's Crimean prison, see Euxine Chersonese [MTM B6:204].

MTM B2:65; MTM B6:204

East China SeaSea off eastern China, west of Japan's Kyushu and Ryukyu islands. It is among the many seas the narrator says Duffey and the Argo have sailed [MTM B13:406].

MTM B13:406

East Coast (Adriatic)Eastern Adriatic shore associated with Illyria. In a letter to Marie, Hans remembers the Argo sailing westward from Illyria repeatedly, though sometimes the Hadriaticus has no far shore and sometimes its western shore is not Italy [MTM B6:186].

MTM B6:186

East Mouth of the River UralLocation assigned to Our'yev in a summary that says Duffey was killed there, stripped of his flesh and cremated [MTM B13:436]. The fuller account places the killing and burning in the Prince's amoral desert. When that setting fades, the bones and smoking flesh-ashes appear in a street in Gur'yev at the East Mouth of the Ural, where X and Kasmir Gorshok identify them. The ashes are in a cigar canister once owned by the King of Spain; X takes custody of them [MTM B13:442].

MTM B13:436; MTM B13:442

EasterChristian feast celebrating Christ's resurrection. X makes his peace with the Church each Easter, only to become agnostic again by midsummer and atheist by autumn [A:138]. On Passion Sunday at Naxos, Finnegan seeks confession as part of making his Easter Duty [D:118-119].

A:138; D:118-119

Easter DutyCatholic obligation of annual Communion, ordinarily fulfilled during the Easter season, associated with the separate obligation of yearly confession. Finnegan explicitly wants to make his Easter Duty on Passion Sunday at Naxos. His inadequate Greek makes finding a confessor difficult, but a Greek Capuchin who speaks Italian hears him [D:118-119].

D:118-119

Eating and DrinkingOrdinary activities made exceptional for Finnegan and Anastasia Demetriades by their setting outside her grandmother's little farmhouse, on a blue mountain slope of Naxos [D:124-127].

D:124-127

Eckel, Little DutchEngineer at a Texas City refinery and a regular resident of the Old Wooden Ship [D:216], in Galveston, Texas [MTM B13:458]. He stays because its people housed him when he was poor. Called the prince of the place, he spends more money there than any other patron [D:221].

D:216; MTM B13:458; D:221

EcstaticsPeople whom the narrator, alongside several saints, credits with brief bilocation. Their few minutes of being in two places at once are contrasted with the twelve-year difficulty posed by Finnegan's and Theresa's overlapping histories [A:202].

A:202

Ectocarpus (Hashed) CollinsCocktail requested by Duffey from Honeybucket Kincaid, along with pond-scum bread and sea-lice soup [MTM B13:417]. Kincaid's apparatus uses frequencies to gather organisms and substances from water; it collects ectocarpus and alcohol for the drinks [MTM B13:418]. The name refers to Ectocarpus, a genus of filamentous brown algae.

MTM B13:417; MTM B13:418

EdenGarden of the first human pair in Genesis 2-3. The narrator's worm-in-the-apple discussion invokes Eden and original sin [D:264]. The Basse-Terre Paradise is also called Eden when Don Barnaby becomes restless and leaves it [D:265].

D:264; D:265

Edgewater, BerniceOne of the money-and-commerce people, or simply rich people, in Duffey's North Chicago golden-age circle. She is listed with Julian Edgewater [MTM B3:100].

MTM B3:100

Edgewater, JulianOne of the money-and-commerce people, or simply rich people, in Duffey's North Chicago golden-age circle. He is listed with Bernice Edgewater [MTM B3:100].

MTM B3:100

Edith SummerfieldMember of St. Louis high society and, with Cyrus Summerfield, a commentator on it for both the Globe and the Post Dispatch. The young couple are full of glitter, and Edith is described as a sort of cousin to Beth Keegan. They attend Beth's formal dinner in Duffey's balloon gondola two miles high [MTM B2:65] and give the event elegant treatment in the press [MTM B2:66].

MTM B2:65; MTM B2:66

EditorRole taken by Duffey when Casey joins the army in April 1942 and leaves The Crock in his care [MTM B4:138]. Dotty Yekouris edits The Bark [MTM B7:213], which she runs with Duffey, Absalom Stein and Mary Virginia Schaeffer [MTM B7:215]. Letitia Duffey becomes its new editor after the disappearances from their circle [MTM B8:238].

MTM B4:138; MTM B7:213; MTM B7:215; MTM B8:238

Edward Cardinal LeviathanCardinal of Edinburgh named among John Mogul's contracted targets [MB:571]. His double or shadow-man is Douglas McAfee of London [MB:579].

MB:571; MB:579

Edward RanwickArt-school acquaintance of Duffey in St. Louis, one of the young men who accompanies him, Mary Louise Byrne and Beth Keegan on outings. At the Bavarian Club he compares the sturdy blond girls to brewery horses. His own work attracts some attention at the art school, but Duffey calls it skinny art and finds something lacking [MTM B2:58].

MTM B2:58

EffigyRepresentation that can take a person's place. The Argo's effigies work as seamen while their Masters are absent; a returning Master dons his effigy, and the Argonauts' creative alterations to absent companions' effigies help form their personalities [MTM B13:449]. In the forced Ekklesia election, the Straw-Man is elected Cap-Stone and then burned, producing red smoke, bloody rain and a stream of blood [MB:567-568]. X distinguishes the Devil's former effigy flesh from the real flesh released from imprisonment [MTM B6:205]. In Letitia's scrapbook, an unidentified speaker calls political opponents effigies to justify even their literal killing [MTM B8:251-252].

MTM B13:449; MB:567-568; MTM B6:205; MTM B8:251-252

Effigy SeamenWorking substitutes for absent Argo Masters. Duffey initially considers three monkey-like or wraithlike seamen of his own shaping, but there are many more aboard [MTM B13:402-403] [MTM B13:405]. They are subsequently explained as materialized, programmed memories or place tokens left by the old crewmen, including Duffey and Biloxi Brannagan, to preserve their places and perform useful work [MTM B13:415-416]. Returning Masters don their effigies, and the Argonauts' alterations to absent companions' effigies help build their personalities [MTM B13:449].

MTM B13:402-403; MTM B13:405; MTM B13:415-416; MTM B13:449

EframOne of the twenty Stone boys in four families of first cousins living near Duffey's Chicago bookstore, and Myron's twin. Margaret Stone says she is their first cousin once removed and Absalom Stein their second cousin. In her account, Hugo is a joke name used by several boys, most often the twins together, whom Duffey mistakes for one fast-moving child; she denies that Absalom visited the shop. Duffey insists instead that Hugo was Absalom, a person he himself made [MTM B4:112].

MTM B4:112

EggContainer or image of emergence in several episodes. The children at Widow Waldo's orphanage say their green-clay animals come from green-clay eggs and can have life breathed into them [MTM B9:285]. In the Thunder Colt Game, a colt still within its egg is fed a human victim; lightning breaks the egg and awakens consciousness, followed by thunder awakening its thunder dimension. Cyrus Roundhead calls the colt's awakening a symbol of the Royal Pop People's own emergence into consciousness [MTM B11:350]. In an earlier comic image, the tangled account of Duffey's borrowed girlhood quacks, lays an addled egg and expires under an analyst's scrutiny [MTM B1:16]; Mary Louise Byrne is later identified as his sister-person [MTM B2:55].

MTM B9:285; MTM B11:350; MTM B1:16; MTM B2:55

EgoOne of the terms the More Than Melchisedech Postscript draws from C. G. Jung's Aion, alongside Self, Shadow, Anima and Animus. The Postscript counts these as five persons within a person and extends the idea into physically visible multiplicity [PS:477].

PS:477

EgyptAncient kingdom invoked by Duffey when he calls himself and Mary Louise a royal family. He says Egypt's kings married their sisters, while adding that he has never been sure Mary Louise is his real sister [MTM B2:55].

MTM B2:55

Eighteenth Book of Strange Encounters, ThePurported source of a mock medical report arguing that New Orleans art dealer Melchisedech Duffey is more than four thousand years old. Its impressive list of indices and tests is said to give that age consistently, although his nonessential body material seems only fifty-five years old. Duffey suggests either that he has carried his essential pattern through several bodies or that one body has been repeatedly renovated, and rejects the label reincarnation. The extract is attributed to the editors of the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Books of Strange Encounters [MTM B8:250].

MTM B8:250

EkklesiaThe Assembly or Crowd, the ancient ecclesiastical institution whose termination is declared at the supposedly last Conclave in Babylonia Bagascia. Its Princes, styled Gates or Stones, intend to dismantle it [MB:561-562]. Paul the Eleventh, its Cap-Stone, has been decapitated before the Conclave, and the destruction of his still-speaking head is treated as the institution's end [MB:562-563]. The coerced election and burning of a Straw-Man Cap-Stone is meant to complete that suppression [MB:567-568]. The story nevertheless culminates in another conclave at Mooring Rock and the election of Pope Finnegan the First [MB:597-598].

MB:561-562; MB:562-563; MB:567-568; MB:597-598

El QudsArabic name for Jerusalem, meaning the holy place. In Cyrus Roundhead's revision of history, El Quds is instead one of several ruined cities near an abortive Turkish real-estate project supposedly named Jerusalem; he denies that a real Jerusalem ever existed [MTM B11:337].

MTM B11:337

El-Nahr, Kantara fokWriter whom X credits with the eight-thousand-page novel El-Kamar. According to X, Kantara fok El-Nahr begins the tenth page from its end with the declaration that he will begin his story; X says the writer is a slow starter, not a humorist, and adopts the same declaration for his own account [D:284].

D:284

Elagabalus (Heliogabalus)Roman emperor, born Varius Avitus Bassianus around 203-204 and ruling from 218 to 222. A young priest of the Syrian deity Elagabal, he promoted that cult at Rome, became notorious in hostile accounts of his religious and personal conduct, and was killed by the Praetorian Guard. In Archipelago, Finnegan names Sulem's reptilian protective figure Heliogabalus, baptizes it, and wears it beside his Miraculous Medal, joking that he has made the old Roman a Christian [A:61].

A:61

ElamKingdom called Elam or Susiana, a Devildom east of the Tigris, in the account identifying the Three Slant-Faced Men. Their ruler is Chodorlahomor; the three crooked kings Amraphel, Arioch and Thadal are his followers [MTM B7:227-228]. Duffey recalls Abraham opposing the four kings with 318 men and himself blessing Abraham [MTM B7:228].

MTM B7:227-228; MTM B7:228

ElectrumAlloy of gold and silver, occurring naturally and also made artificially. The mixture supplies the image for Duffey's North Chicago electrum age, following the pure golden years of 1925-1935 and lasting until about 1946 [MTM B3:98]. Finnegan also tells a creation legend in which a broken electrum cup becomes the white, gold and silver islands of the Aegean [A:35].

MTM B3:98; A:35

Electrum ageThe mixed gold-and-silver phase of Duffey and Letitia's North Chicago golden age, running from the end of the pure gold years in 1935 until about 1946. It has some minor disasters, unlike the preceding 1925-1935 golden period [MTM B3:98].

MTM B3:98

Eleemosynary Institutions (State Inspector of)State official who writes and telephones Widow Waldo about Zabotski's large structure. Waldo tells Zabotski it must be removed from the grounds of the Golden Childrens Home and Haven Orphanage; the part on his own lot may be beyond the state's power to remove, though neighbors are pressing him about it [MTM B9:274].

MTM B9:274

Elegant Riverboat DeckGames area at Duffey's Rounders' Club in St. Louis. The club's advertisement names the deck and lists racquets, whist, poker and horseshoes; it also offers tuxedos for hire [MTM B2:49]. A picture of Severed Giant Hands hangs above the doorway leading to the deck [MTM B5:156].

MTM B2:49; MTM B5:156

Elena (Girl who wrote to Dotty Yekouris)Girl who, with the lawyer Ignacio, writes to Dotty Yekouris that Finnegan is coming apart and invites her to join him, possibly in Cuba [MTM B8:237-238]. In Archipelago Elena sells Finnegan his concertina, accompanies him, and summons Ignacio after a fight [A:273]. She tends Finnegan's injuries and translates his songs of loneliness into a letter to Dotty or Dorotea [A:274-276]. Looking over his drawings, Finnegan later recognizes Elena as both herself and Angela Cosquin [A:278].

MTM B8:237-238; A:273; A:274-276; A:278

Elena O'HigginsJournalist and member of Duffey's North Chicago bookish circle [MTM B3:98], among the women he loves [MTM B4:111]. She calls a photographer to witness the mule-moving challenge [MTM B4:130] and writes the measured Chicago Herald and Examiner report on November 14, following the feat of November 13, 1935. Her report acknowledges conflicting testimony; its photograph shows the airborne mule without visible giant hands [MTM B4:127] [MTM B4:132]. She attends Duffey's later party with Casey [MTM B12:383]. Her commentary on Casey objects to his sale of consecrated hosts and recounts his destruction and replacement of sacred organ music [PG:524-525].

MTM B3:98; MTM B4:111; MTM B4:130; MTM B4:127; MTM B4:132; MTM B12:383; PG:524-525

Elkheart, Elwin K.Secretary-General of WSMA, an affiliate of WSMAASRTFM. In a quoted skeptical statement, he refuses belief in either Divine Intervention or a ship sailing under its patent, and calls the Argo and such interventions conceits of Duffey the mountebank [MTM B13:402].

MTM B13:402

ElkoWhip named in the turbaned speaker's nostalgic catalogue at the Royal Pop gathering. He imagines a Decatur Street stone remembering its sound along with the Cowles Buggy Whip, Jacksonville Drover and other whips of the carriage era [MTM B11:329].

MTM B11:329

EllasarKingdom of Arioch in the novel's identification of the Three Slant-Faced Men with three crooked kings. The narration gives Ellasar, Pontus or Lower Babylonia as alternative designations [MTM B7:227].

MTM B7:227

Ellenberger, EthylOne of the young girls who begins visiting Duffey's Chicago bookstore at eight or nine. She and Mary Frances Rattigan usually come together; Duffey wrestles with them on the old black sofa, in an episode whose assurances of hearty fun are qualified by the narrator's warnings [MTM B4:111]. Ethyl contributes to The Crock [MTM B4:138], including an ode in the issue described in Archipelago [A:41]. At Duffey's later party she attends with her husband John Ryan [MTM B12:383].

MTM B4:111; MTM B4:138; A:41; MTM B12:383

Ellenbogen, Elmer Eggleton / EndymeonThe character says he legally changed his former first name Elmer. See Ellenbogen, Endymeon.
Ellenbogen, EndymeonEndymeon Ellenbogen, a member of Hans Schultz's New York Bohemian circle, introduced at Lupido's as a genius [A:236]. His former name is Elmer Eggleton Ellenbogen; he says he legally changed his first name and spent much of his inheritance subsidizing three published novels, Dawn Country, Shenandoah Saga and The Man from Minneapolis. His unpublished poems are planned as nine collections, including “Sonnets and Succotash.” He claims translations of the Greek Anthology, the Spanish Golden Book, Horace and Petrarch, and plans the Elder Edda once he learns Icelandic, maintaining that translation does not diminish one's creative gift [A:237]. He earns small sums writing popular songs and playing piano; Sally and Helen are types of songs in his catalogue, rather than identified song titles [A:238]. He also tells of carving a marble group of nereids too large to remove through his room's doors or windows, then cutting it up and distributing the figures. The previous sculptor left a book on teleportation [A:239].

A:236; A:237; A:238; A:239

Ellis, HavelockEnglish physician, writer and early sex researcher (1859-1939), known for Studies in the Psychology of Sex, including his work with John Addington Symonds on homosexuality, and for advocacy of sex education and women's rights. In the More Than Melchisedech Postscript he matters especially as the proponent of what it calls the Law of Intellectual Constancy: the idea that apparently ordinary people possess powers comparable to celebrated geniuses [PS:476]. The Postscript treats this as a basis for its account of universal genius and overflowing, multiple personality [PS:477].

PS:476; PS:477

Elmer Eggleton EllenbogenFormer full name of Endymeon Ellenbogen. He introduces himself as Elmer Eggleton Ellenbogen, then explains that he legally changed his first name [A:236-237]. See Ellenbogen, Elmer Eggleton / Endymeon.

A:236-237

Elysian Field AvenueElysian Field Avenue, one of the New Orleans streets through which ghosts supposedly slip after a night's haunting. The narrator immediately retracts this account as a lie, except for Finnegan's painting of the ghosts in the bar; the next page gives the ordinary history of Anthony Ghost's coffee shop [MTM B10:292-293].

MTM B10:292-293

Embulking pelletsImaginary murder device discussed in the Murder Contest associated with John Mogul's killings: pellets placed in food supposedly make the victim grow exponentially until exploding [MB:582-583].

MB:582-583

Emery paper (Blue)Abrasive paper used as the image for Patrick Stranahan's rough face, which is likened to blue emery paper [A:102].

A:102

Emery, ArtCrewman of the Brunhilde, hostile to Finnegan after his joke on Art's name and prettiness. At the ship's bar gathering, Art goes to inform on the company [D:22]. He is listed among the five crewmen [D:30] and grouped by the narrator with Harry Scott and Chris McAbney as the wrong sort of people; this later passage assigns the first day's informing to Chris [D:31]. Anastasia calls Art the Devil's former catamount, now rejected [D:68]. Much later Finnegan sees him on a street corner and knocks him flat in sudden hatred, learning that the Brunhilde has reached port [D:230].

D:22; D:30; D:31; D:68; D:230

Emily (Henry Salvatore's aunt)Emily is one of Henry Francis Salvatore’s two aunts in the neighborhood of his Morgan City family; the other is Marietta [A:122-123].

A:122-123

EmperorImperial title used in several different contexts. A proud former fire horse, dressed for the appearance of the leader in Henry Horner Park, holds its head like a Roman Emperor. The same episode describes a German Blue Max among missing decorations as bearing the old Emperor Maximilian's seal [MTM B4:116]. Finnegan is shriven on the feast of St. Henry Emperor while preparing for a possible death [A:277].

MTM B4:116; A:277

Emperor Henry (of Neustria)Imperial identity of Henri Salvatore, once the Argonaut Euphemus, later Emperor Henry of Neustria, and now ruler of Invisible Neustria. After the Devil's release, his small personal fiefdoms are set against the Devil and avert or postpone the world's destruction for decades; Duffey is made subordinate to this creation of his own [MTM B8:245]. Mary Virginia Schaeffer was his betrothed before he gave her up for God [MTM B7:214]. The name Neustria recalls the western kingdom of the Franks, transformed here into an invisible realm.

MTM B8:245; MTM B7:214

Empire (Roman)Historical setting invoked in the passage attributed to G. K. Chesterton's The Everlasting Man: the Creator's entry into the ordinary life of the Roman Empire is presented as the startling uniqueness of the Incarnation [MTM B5:176]. Herman Hercules also remembers Rome in the imperial centuries as one of the crowded cities whose spectacles drew long-lived people like himself [MB:585].

MTM B5:176; MB:585

Enac (sons of)Biblical giants, the sons of Anak or Enac, reported by the scouts in Canaan. The Numbers epigraph to the Angela Cosquin chapter combines the sight of these giants with the people's fearful weeping and the counter-exhortation that the inhabitants can be eaten like bread [D:258].

D:258

End of Compassion, TheName of the lower, more painful hell in the Goat Contingency contemplated by Duffey: compassionate scapegoats such as Casey would bear the world's accumulated debts forever after trading away everything. The narration calls this a very doubtful possible outcome, while leaving Casey's attempted soul-trade with the Devil uncertain [MTM B10:299].

MTM B10:299

End of TimeA problem raised by Duffey’s approaching end and his identification with the biblical Melchisedech, who has “neither beginning of days nor end of life” in the passage heading Book Six [MTM B6:185]. Duffey takes the Ursuline girls’ seven-arrowed sign to signify either his own death or the end of time itself. Cleo Mahoney’s play asks what becomes of a man who cannot end when his life or the world reaches its end [MTM B9:264] [MTM B9:265]. At the beginning of Book Ten, the narrator distinguishes Duffey’s impending ending from the possible end of the world. Duffey can no longer enter a valid future along the normal track. The passage connects this obstruction with the Seven Lost Years and his distrust of the seven futures offered him [MTM B10:290].

MTM B6:185; MTM B9:264; MTM B9:265; MTM B10:290

EndodermIn biology, the innermost embryonic germ layer. The narrative instead uses the word for the inside of Cardinal Artemis's skin, where Finnegan secretly imprints a great painting by radiation. After the Cardinal's flaying, Finnegan is uncertain whether the painted skin belongs to the trophy held by Mogul or is being worn by the double Gilberto Levine-and-O'Brien [MB:591].

MB:591

EngineerUnnamed professional who tells Duffey that the support knocked out from the Pont du Sable Traffic Trestle is ornamental, not weight-bearing [MTM B3:104-105]. The narrator adds that it had carried weight for Duffey himself, preserving the bridge's personal significance [MTM B3:105].

MTM B3:104-105; MTM B3:105

EnglandCountry named in the Argo's remembered history: King Richard of England recaptures the ship from the Saracens, and Robert of Namur later sails it as the Salle du Roi for another English king [MTM B13:404]. Cecil Octavian, double of Cardinal Brokenbolt, is from England [MB:579]. The English Bulldog chosen to help guard the Argo is Gunboat Smith, recruited at the Old Wooden Ship in Galveston, Texas [MTM B13:458].

MTM B13:404; MB:579; MTM B13:458

EnglishNationality or ancestry in Ralph Rolfe's English paternal descent [MTM B13:427], and a breed designation in the English Bulldog Gunboat Smith, recruited to protect the Argo [MTM B13:458]. In the Martyr-Bell's story, English raiders attack Ste. Genevieve in 1594 [MB:576]. The codenamed Father Brown also invokes Old English when explaining that drench could mean drown [MTM B13:457].

MTM B13:427; MTM B13:458; MB:576; MTM B13:457

EnglishmanEnglish raiders are the persecutors in the Martyr-Bell's origin story. In 1594 they murder thirty-nine Christians on Ste. Genevieve who refuse to renounce their faith; their ship, the Lord Cramner, is then wrecked and its crew drowned. Cannon recovered from it are made into the bell, which rings for four hundred years whenever Englishmen or other enemies of the faith approach [MB:576].

MB:576

Enniscorthy and Mary SweenyMusical friends in Duffey's North Chicago golden-age circle. The musical group ranges across opera, ragtime, Chicago-hot music and string bands, and includes composers, players and stagers [MTM B3:99]. The later party list names Enniscorthy and Mary Margaret Sweeny [MTM B12:383].

MTM B3:99; MTM B12:383

Enniscorthy SweenyMusical friend of Duffey's Chicago circle [MTM B3:99], also called Ennis and described as ruddy-faced and a near-genius. After an apparent ending of More Than Melchisedech, the narrative quotes his comparison of an event to a box viewed from four sides: past, present, alternative present and future. Each perspective belongs to the event and should be retained when another view appears; the quotation introduces the turn toward an alternate ending [MTM B13:467].

MTM B3:99; MTM B13:467

Entrance PersonDesignation the Better Life League gives Zabotski. In his written account, Duffey affirms that the League is right about this: Zabotski is a strong and peculiar Entrance Person, although Zabotski himself thinks little of the League [MTM B9:268].

MTM B9:268

EntrepreneurRole exemplified by Duffey's interconnected businesses. He buys and refits a St. Louis livery stable as a residence, shop, lodging house, bar and entertainment establishment [MTM B2:40-41], developed into Rounders' Club [MTM B2:49]. He also promotes his own boxing bills [MTM B2:51]. In New Orleans his Walk-In Art Bijou [MTM B1:6] and pawn shop share the building where he helps found and fit out the Pelican Press to publish The Bark and other work. The narrative connects this practical labor with rebuilding the world [MTM B6:190].

MTM B2:40-41; MTM B2:49; MTM B2:51; MTM B1:6; MTM B6:190

EnvyOne element in Stein's overflowing look at the company, mixed with amusement, compassion, contempt and proprietorship [A:30]. Finnegan is also described as the envy of men on the street while walking with Anastasia and Marie Courtois [D:57-58]. Lily Koch jokingly envies those whose way of life lets them commit murders [MTM B3:97].

A:30; D:57-58; MTM B3:97

EphphathaAramaic command meaning be opened, spoken by Jesus in Mark 7:34. Duffey uses it to release the stutter of a brilliant but unnamed young man at Weinsburg on the Nechar [MTM B13:430]. The man protests that frustration fuels the destructive work he wants to accomplish; Duffey refuses to restore the impediment. Casey lingers behind, and the narration raises the possibility of someone giving the stutter back without confirming that it happens [MTM B13:431].

MTM B13:430; MTM B13:431

Ephrata (Chicago)Biblical-sounding designation attached to Mary Catherine Carruthers in the list of Duffey's Animated Marvels: "But Thou, Chicago Ephrata, out of Thee shall come" [MTM B5:183]. It adapts Micah 5:2's prophecy of a ruler coming from Bethlehem Ephrata, substituting Chicago and leaving the sentence unfinished.

MTM B5:183

EpicHeroic literary form invoked in three different registers. A pre-pre-Homeric epic passage appears among the underlayers of the old goatskin parchment Duffey examines [MTM B11:327]. Finnegan's order of a hundred oysters prompts the question of which epic hero ate such a meal [MTM B5:172], followed by Duffey's recollection of Fingal or Finn McCool eating oysters larger than wagon wheels [MTM B5:173-174]. Marie also calls her uncle Shakes Pearson's repeatedly interrupted tobacco-contest limericks an epic, as squirrels eat the bark he writes on [A:25-26].

MTM B11:327; MTM B5:172; MTM B5:173-174; A:25-26

EpirusAncient region on the northwestern side of the Greek world. Cyrus Roundhead incorporates it into his invented geography of Greece as one of five concentric rings around Hellas, alongside Aetolia, Thessaly, Macedonia and Thrace [MTM B11:337].

MTM B11:337

Episodes of the ArgoLafferty collection listed as a 1990 title in the bibliography at the front of The Devil Is Dead [D:4]. Published by United Mythologies Press, the chapbook contains Argo material, including part of the conclusion of the More Than Melchisedech sequence.

D:4

Epistle (Third, to the Kids in St. Louis)Writing attributed to Margaret Stone, excerpted among the documents surrounding the St. Louis gathering. Margaret describes her extraordinary body heat, private flight and command over tempests, then contrasts her weak hands with the responsibility for caring for the world for one hour out of every twenty-four [MTM B5:177-178].

MTM B5:177-178

Erculo, Martino CardinalCardinal of Milan, paired with the double Herman Hercules in the list of the thirteen cardinals pursued by John Mogul [MB:579]. Hercules calls Erculo his primary, though later narration leaves uncertain whether the supposed double might be the Cardinal in disguise [MB:584] [MB:588].

MB:579; MB:584; MB:588

ErosGreek word for love, especially passionate or sexual love. Eros is one of the metaphorical flowers, with Philos and Agape, bursting through New Orleans's broken pavement in the underground sunshine. The flowers are red, yellow and purple; the passage specifically assigns hot purple to Agape [MTM B7:211].

MTM B7:211

ErrorIn the passage attributed to E. I. Watkin's The Catholic Center, Catholicism's exclusion of religious error follows from its claim to include the whole of religious truth [MTM B5:177]. Mary Virginia Schaeffer uses a different image in her Duffey Book: nine supposedly discarded but still living worlds would be anthologies of errors, failures and imperfect conceptions. She presents this as a fancy based on legends, not scriptural authority, and wonders whether Duffey came from one of them [MTM B10:291-292].

MTM B5:177; MTM B10:291-292

EuphemusHenri Salvatore's Argonaut identity. Henri himself asks whether he was Euphemus for nothing when Teresa summons him to explain the company's past [MTM B7:232]. Teresa identifies Henry as Euphemus and says that his ocean-father taught him to walk on water, though he seldom does so now [MTM B7:234].

MTM B7:232; MTM B7:234

Euxine ChersoneseName that X says the Romans used for the peninsula otherwise called the Tauric Chersonese, Krym, or Crimea. In his account the Devil was imprisoned there in 946 or 947 [MTM B6:204]. Stein's notes give the dungeon's millennium as 946-1946 and date the Devil's release to 1946 [MTM B6:185].

MTM B6:204; MTM B6:185

EvilCasey calls the Problem of Evil the only problem in the world and doubts that any of his companions' ways of confronting it will work [A:154]. Demetrio Glauch describes his particular lifelong obsession as the possible final redemption of the Devil [PG:518-519]. Evil also appears in the displaced spirits after the neighborhood's destruction [MTM B11:314], the former owners of the Brunhilde [MTM B13:404], and the Argonauts' continuing struggle, complicated by the Laughing Prince's claimed Third Way [MTM B13:437]. Duffey calls the cured stutterer an evil genius turned good or complacent [MTM B13:431]. Bagby's posthumous letter, by contrast, denies that passions themselves are evil, comparing ungoverned passions to unbroken horses [MTM B8:248]. Duffey's meeting with the Loosed Devil belongs to the sixth proposed contingency of the world [MTM B10:301-302].

A:154; PG:518-519; MTM B11:314; MTM B13:404; MTM B13:437; MTM B13:431; MTM B8:248; MTM B10:301-302

Evil EyeAn unconfirmed attribution of a malevolent gaze to Casey Szymansky.
Evil PrinceOne of the princely adversaries named with the Purple Prince, Mocking Prince, and Laughing Prince. The narrative stresses the adversaries' courage, force of personality, and ability to defeat or kill Argo Masters; it singles out the Laughing Prince of Tartary as possibly the strongest and trickiest [MTM B13:437].

MTM B13:437

Evil SpiritEvil spirits are among the displaced beings haunting the sites of the neighborhood's destruction, deprived of their places and forms [MTM B11:314]. During the effort to bar the Man of Mystery from the Argo, the expert called Professor Van Dusen warns that blind spirits can enter through blind fireplaces and then assume almost any form; he recommends guarding each fireplace with a firedrake [MTM B13:455-456].

MTM B11:314; MTM B13:455-456

Ewaglouwshkoul (Eva)The woman Duffey and the Argo’s crew release from the ice after forty thousand years. She identifies herself as Ewaglouwshkoul; Duffey calls her Little Eva, and she accepts “Neanderthal Eve” as a possible nickname. She says she is not the first woman of her tribe but perhaps the last, and hopes to find surviving men of her own people and have children [MTM B13:399-401]. The narration later calls her a Neo-Neanderthal [MTM B13:407]. She asks to be taken to Biloxi, where Duffey is already bound, and plans to acquire a waterfront establishment to meet seamen of her blood. Her father ran the Old Stone Ship in her ancient world [MTM B13:401]. She wants to buy Kate’s Neanderthal Bar and rename it Eva’s Neanderthal Bar [MTM B13:407]. When she needs a $14,000 down payment, Duffey produces gold pieces and Brannagan produces banknotes with identical serial numbers. Gertrude offers to fetch her checkbook and arrange matters [MTM B13:414-415].

MTM B13:399-401; MTM B13:407; MTM B13:414-415

EweOne of the animals supplying the Boy King Melchisedech's milk. The account first calls the product of camel, ass, ewe, gazelle, cow, and Indian buffalo his silk, then explains that it was milk in actuality [MTM B1:17-18].

MTM B1:17-18

ExocosmosThe surrounding world with which Zabotski has what Duffey calls non-mutual arrangements. The immediate example is the Better Life League, which recognizes Zabotski as an Entrance Person although Zabotski thinks little of the League [MTM B9:268].

MTM B9:268

ExorcismA religious rite seeking liberation from demonic power. In Finnegan's account of painting a devil, Father Le Faye, S.J., performs a short exorcism and orders the painting burned and its ashes swept away [D:254-255].

D:254-255

ExorcistFather Le Faye, S.J., is described as an exorcist of some fame in Finnegan's account. He arrives without being summoned, recognizes the devil in Finnegan's painting, performs a short exorcism, and directs that the picture be burned [D:254-255].

D:254-255

ExoticOne of the exuberant adjectives applied to Dotty Yekouris in a description borrowed from a nursery plant catalogue, which the narrator still judges inadequate to her [MTM B7:213].

MTM B7:213

ExpeditionA Cummings-clan member of the Fundamentalers tells Zabotski that his group has three expeditions searching the mountains of Armenia for Noah's Ark. Zabotski claims that the true High Armenia cannot be securely identified with the modern country or the mountain now called Ararat [MTM B9:280].

MTM B9:280

ExperienceCasey's erotic experiences in the second of his twelve imaginary worlds, begun before he was eight. They involve women from history and legend, including queens, nymphs, amazons, gladiators, bullfighters, and acrobats, and lead to his theory of personalized temptations [A:156-157].

A:156-157

ExperimentIn Elena O'Higgins's commentary, Casey is criticized for publishing an advertisement in the Crock offering supposedly genuine consecrated hosts for a dollar each, postpaid, for fun, experiment, or special rites. The advertisement claims that a defrocked priest supplies them and that prodigies sometimes occur; Elena says it ran in at least three issues but does not know the response [PG:524].

PG:524

ExpertDuffey becomes an art expert by ransacking the minds of Sebastian Hilton, Lily Koch, and adult customers at Lily's sales [MTM B1:29]. As a stamp and postmark expert and dealer, he examines the otherwhere stamps on Bagby's extraordinary letters [MTM B7:219]. Later the Argo Masters consult experts in detection to prevent the Man of Mystery from boarding; some are fictional, some are real persons behind disguises, and the names Philo Vance, Father Brown, Doctor Thorndyke, Max Carrados, and Professor Van Dusen may be code names [MTM B13:454-455].

MTM B1:29; MTM B7:219; MTM B13:454-455

ExplanationDuffey seeks to understand the seven-arrowed sign and the school play that appear to predict his possible endings. He consults Stein, who jokes, and then seeks the absent Zabotski [MTM B9:264-266]. Zabotski explains the extraordinary fertility of his Lake Borgne flats as God's blessing on a just man chosen for a special role [MTM B12:362].

MTM B9:264-266; MTM B12:362

ExplorerCasey's role in his fifth imaginary world. He supposes that the Earth is half again as large as generally believed, with elongated poles and an Antarctic ring of ice surrounding a sunny southern continent, probably a migrated Atlantis. As its explorer he would carry modern techniques there and bring a Higher Ethic back [A:158].

A:158

ExtinctionMelchisedech's panic while wrestling Morpheus as the dreamed cosmos contracts toward a single surviving cell; the narrator distinguishes it from the lesser fear of damnation [GD:500]. Earlier, Stein fears that forgotten people will pass into oblivion, becoming people who never existed, unless someone remembers them; he imagines them bawling against extinction [MTM B11:315].

GD:500; MTM B11:315

ExtradigitalismHaving extra digits, or polydactyly. John Mogul has five fingers and one thumb on each hand, a condition said to be common in his family. He raises all twelve digits to indicate that twelve men remain under his killing contracts [MB:574].

MB:574

ExtravaganzaThe show Duffey, Letitia, and Lily see at Morgenstein's Comedy Music Box on Randolph Street, after supper at Lily's. On leaving, they hear the news of the Mullens double murder [MTM B3:97].

MTM B3:97

EyeDuffey has fire-blue eyes [MTM B1:6]; Letitia's are described as between sea-green and Melchisedech blue [MTM B3:92]. The woman whom Duffey releases from the ice has blue eyes and identifies herself as Ewaglouwshkoul, Little Eva or the Neanderthal Eve [MTM B13:399-400]. In his later bony form Melchisedech has no eyes, although some faculty of sensing remains and is impeded by his golden mask [MTM B13:444].

MTM B1:6; MTM B3:92; MTM B13:399-400; MTM B13:444

Eye-SoresThe Moral Sanctions Committee for the Removal of Eye-Sores and Abominations objects to Zabotski's ever-growing backyard construction. Its spokeswoman complains that eight years have passed since his supposed promise to act; Zabotski replies that he promised not to act and that people fail to listen closely [MTM B9:276].

MTM B9:276

EyebrowsBascom Bagby has beetling brows when he first visits Duffey's premises for a shave and haircut [MTM B2:43]. Each of Patrick Stranahan's eyebrows is said to contain more hair than most men have on their heads [A:102].

MTM B2:43; A:102

EyelidsThe eyes of the head-only image of Casey Szymansky are sewn open, forcing it to look despite its refusal. Duffey animates the image from Adam Scanlon's hostile painting and projects it into the Goldfarb's Alley comedy broadcast, where four giants carry the head and the spectacle terrifies performers and viewers [MTM B12:381].

MTM B12:381

EzekielHebrew prophet active in the early sixth century BC. The novel calls Blessed Ezekiel a very early Argo Master and invokes his promise of opened graves and return to the land, from Ezekiel 37:12, while considering futures that must yield up past and present [MTM B13:447].

MTM B13:447

Face, Finnegan'sEarlier heading named only Finnegan although the verified catalogue also treats the faces of other characters. See Faces.
FacesFinnegan's first reflected face has a banana nose, restless cheek and temple muscles, a moving mouth, and reddened eyes [A:1]. His apparent grace gives way at close range to a gargoyle's comic mask and bugle nose [A:6]; washing cannot remove the grotesqueness of his face [D:13]. At Las Palmas he looks like a Montenegran prince, noble of nose [D:100]. On Naxos his gargoyle head contrasts with Anastasia's Diana-like head [D:133]. The later painting of Count Finnegan gives the banana nose nobility and distinction, while preserving humor, pain, and torture in the eyes [MB:551]. Joe Cross finds Finnegan disturbingly like Dopey when glimpsed from the side, though less alike face-on [D:65]. While shaving, Finnegan sees and shaves Dopey's distinct face in the mirror; after he smashes the glass, Dopey remains visible in a fragment, his eyes closed in torturous sleep [D:187-188]. Other faces form a related catalogue. Saxon Seaworthy's lined, granite face has a depth that the word dull cannot encompass [D:11]. It turns ashen and ancient when Papa Devil arrives, then regains its controlled expression [D:15]; it is tired granite during Don Lewis's story [D:43] and stony-faced during Seaworthy's own dream account [D:72]. Papa Devil has a purplish complexion and a reddish fringe around his nearly bald head [D:23], becoming more ghoulish after an admitted killing [D:30]. Finnegan discovers that the purple pumpkin-like head conceals another face and paints what lies beneath [D:62-63]. He paints this face again in a death scene [D:86], challenges Papa Devil about his living mask [D:88], and later recognizes the slain man on Naxos by that reconstructed face [D:146]. His sketch enables X to identify the impersonator as an Irish policeman called Noonan or Flaherty [D:154]. Earlier, Papa Devil speaks through a distorted face while threatening to bury Finnegan beside Don Lewis [D:111]. Anastasia appears transparent, translucent, and transcendent [D:13]; her face is comical in direct view but beautiful in memory or anticipation, with an olive complexion shifting between green and gold [D:32]. Finnegan praises her green complexion while she is seasick [D:28]. Her head is compared with statues of Diana Artemis at Messene and Delos [D:133]. Marie Courtois's beauty is described through her golden coloring, red-gold hair, strength, and stately form [D:37]. Don Lewis has a fevered handsomeness [D:100] and later tries unsuccessfully to hide his identity beneath a hood [D:102]. Demetrio's lined face recalls both an old Roman and an Aztec, like a face on an ancient coin; the following account of Finnegan's ink portrait on the back of a poster calls the sitter Manuel [D:58]. On the same page the street-food seller who joins Finnegan's joke has a face like laughing leather [D:58]. The old teras in Finnegan's sleep has a face of gloomy granite [D:140]. The man from whom Don Lewis seeks concealment twists his face in apparent spasm, then reveals that he is laughing at the small payment offered [D:107-108]. Brannagan has the clear eyes and powerful forearms of an old seaman [MTM B13:409]. In Don Lewis's story the man later called Yokipoki, probably not his real name, first appears as a ragged little man [D:44] [D:46].

FaggotsBundles of sticks used as fuel. On Naxos, Finnegan includes them among the fuels whose smoke, he says, gives different lands and islands their distinctive skies; he imagines electric, solar, or atomic heat restoring an older sky color [D:127].

D:127

FaloOne of the two girls building an American-style cabaret in the jungle on Luzon when Vincent and Finnegan arrive [A:63-64]. Falo and Nauti offer Four Feathers and Five Roses whisky; Falo brings water and firmly refuses Vincent's attempt to take her by the waist [A:64]. The cabaret has bananas to eat. Falo repeatedly wins Robber Cassino because she has used the same old cards since childhood and knows them all [A:65]. Both girls say goodbye one time, explaining that goodbye all the time would mean their guests were never coming back [A:66].

A:63-64; A:64; A:65; A:66

FalsarioSpanish for forger or counterfeiter. Finnegan supplies the word when Papa Devil, ostensibly seeking a notary on the Mexican side of the port, cannot make his actual need understood. They are promptly directed to a forger, where Papa Devil and Manuel dismiss Finnegan and the two women [D:57].

D:57

Falsetto ChorusAn unconfirmed chorus associated in the earlier glossary with a plaint and the phrase Triumphant grew a taint.
FamilyThe novels give family histories alongside more uncertain kinships and claims of shared or magically created personality. Patrick J. Stranahan, a successful attorney, and Monica Murry Stranahan have four sons, Philip, Hugh, Timothy Navisius, and Vincent J., and two daughters, Norma and Maurine [A:94]. The Koch family comprises August and Elinore and their daughters Lily and Letitia, who marries Duffey [MTM B3:98]. Letitia's hair mingles blonde, scarlet, and walnut tones; she is ruddy, full-bodied, and comical in expression, with eyes between sea-green and Melchisedech blue. She is younger than Lily and taller than Duffey [MTM B3:92]. Mary Virginia Schaeffer belongs to the family owning Red Dog Motor Freight, which serves Galveston, Houston, Morgan City, New Orleans, Baton Rouge, Shreveport, Port Arthur, Orange, and Beaumont [MTM B6:198]. Lawrence Salvatore and Mary Genevieve Hebert are parents of Henry Francis, Christopher, Eustace, Hilaire, Joseph, Louis, Mark, Simeon, Angela, Lucy, and Rita. Nearby uncles include Alphonse, Charles, Fulgence, George, and Matthew Salvatore, and Anthony, Edward, Gregory, Julien, and Nicole Hebert; nearby aunts are Emily and Marietta [A:122-123]. Henry is the fat, mean, precociously learned boy whom Lawrence finds already educated early in his thirteenth year [A:123]; his Argonaut identity is Euphemus [A:38]. Mary Louise Byrne is called Duffey's sister and, with some uncertainty, his stepsister [MTM B2:54-55]. Their erotic attachment is described through patriarchal sister-wife imagery, while Mary Louise is also presented as an exteriorized part of Duffey's personality [MTM B2:55-56]. She later marries Bascom Bagby, making him Duffey's brother-in-law [MTM B5:155]. Bagby is also taken for Duffey's brother and described as part of their shared person. His black hair and whiskers and swarthy skin contrast with Duffey's coloring, while their large hands, swinging shoulders, and stride resemble one another [MTM B2:61]. Duffey's wife in Chicago is Letitia [MTM B3:98]. The Angelino clan is described as mainly Italian and German, with Bohemian, Mexican, Irish Tinker, and Romany ancestry. Elena Angelino, who works with trained bears, insists that her great-grandfather was a bear; the Professor says that he knew him and agrees [A:218]. Giulio Solli and Mary McCracken are Finnegan's parents [A:244-245]. The military roll gives his name as John A. Solli [A:71]. His brother Giacomo, called Jake, drives taxis, and his sister Patricia is an acrobatic dancer. Patricia also calls Doppio di Pinne her brother and the same person as Finnegan, while admitting that the family never understood the alternation [A:174]. Finnegan's later meeting with the shabby, sorrowful Giulio takes place after his father's death and ends in a recognition of paternal love [A:244-245]. Anastasia Demetriades has two uncles who run a restaurant, where she has worked as cashier [D:40]. She and Finnegan visit the family farm on Naxos, where her grandmother Anastasia, called Gyiagyia, remains after hardship has emptied the household [D:124-126]. In X's account, Katie Noonan bears Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch near Krakow in 1830. X believes his father to be the Devil and cites the parish register, while acknowledging but rejecting Gregory, Katie's employer and the child's adoptive father, as a possible biological father [D:278-279]. Ifreann later fathers the twins Gregory McIfreann, Papadiabolous I, born in Smyrna, and Gregory McColum, Papadiabolous II, born in Cork, to different mothers at the turn of the century [D:281] [D:285]. X explains that names in this family move among parents, children, and grandchildren, with Papadiabolous and Chortovitch recurring as auxiliary names [D:278].
