Fancy, TheOne of the whips named by a speaker at the Royal Pop gathering while describing the memories preserved in a Decatur Street stone. It appears alongside the Milford Quirt, San Antonio, Never-Break Dog Whip, and Elko in a nostalgic catalogue of vanished street traffic [MTM B11:329].

MTM B11:329

Fandango in Three FlamesFritz's music accompanying the Fire-Drake Frolic during the opera presentation, in which further human victims are killed [MTM B11:350].

MTM B11:350

Fanged Fish, The (bar)Waterfront establishment at Ogopo in Duffey's catalogue of remembered ports and drinking places, named with the Benevolent Shark at Maule [MTM B13:407].

MTM B13:407

Fare delle caprioleItalian phrase for performing capers or leaps. Finnegan uses it while explaining a goat joke: to cut capers can mean dancing and playing tricks, while his other gloss, castrare becchi, makes it mean castrating he-goats. The goat-man criticizes the pun and discusses related French and Spanish forms [A:199].

A:199

FarerA traveler in Vincent Stranahan's poem written on the back of an insurance policy: a Farer will find a Theresa. The poem turns from roaming to life in the town on the river [A:92].

A:92

FarmerFarmers appear in Hans Schultz's comic hypnotism act, where fat farmers become bathing beauties [A:219], and in Howland's jingle, where a farmer ploughs up the five gophers' house [A:179]. Marie Monahan's story about her uncle Shakes Pearson includes a proposed limerick about an old tobacco-growing farmer; the farmer is a figure in the verse, while Shakes is the trembling, whisky-drinking author [A:25].

A:219; A:179; A:25

Farmer's Canopy-Top Surrey, theEarlier heading changed the source’s plural possessive Farmers’ to singular Farmer’s. See Farmers’ Canopy-Top Surrey.
Farmer's Daughter, The (club)One of the places on Chicago's Fleshpot Row that Shirley Israel recommends to Duffey as the haunts of all the real people. Her list includes Herm's, Curley Q, Seven Steps Down, Blow Brass, and Dung Heap [MTM B4:126].

MTM B4:126

Farmers’ Canopy-Top SurreyHorse vehicle in the nostalgic catalogue recited by the Royal Pop lecturer who describes the memories of a Decatur Street stone. The Farmers' Canopy-Top Surrey is listed with the Fulton Road Cart, Imperial Carriage, and other vehicles that once passed over the stone [MTM B11:329].

MTM B11:329

FarmhouseA farmhouse on the uphill road to Anastasia's grandmother on Naxos. Finnegan, Anastasia, and their donkey receive water at its well; the woman invites them to sit with Kathisate, but they have no time to stay [D:124]. The donkey is named Papapaleologus [D:125].

D:124; D:125

Farrell, FatherFather Walter Farrell, co-author with Martin J. Healy of My Way of Life, the Summa Simplified for Everyone. A passage credited to Farrel and Healy in the novel's collection of documents concerns the choices of heaven and hell made from moment to moment [MTM B5:177]. In the later part of Archipelago, Finnegan reads Father Farrell's books on the Summa and St. John of the Cross while attending Mass and preparing for possible death [A:277].

MTM B5:177; A:277

FascistAn accusation used by several speakers. In Letitia's scrapbook Father Blevins calls his bishop a clerical-fascist and denies his right to have views [MTM B8:251]. Rollo McSorley spits the word at Tony Apostolo when they bet on Duffey's power to move a mule [MTM B4:129]. Marie Courtois attributes neo-fascistic indoctrination to Anastasia [D:33]. Casey's Crock attack calls Gabrielovitch a poisoner of the Fascist persuasion [A:129], and Casey tells Stein to denounce the Australian brigadier as a fascist fink [A:54]. Finnegan reports being called fascist, fink, scab, and fruit by the music patrons whom he has provoked with a silent jukebox record [A:264].

MTM B8:251; MTM B4:129; D:33; A:129; A:54; A:264

Fascist FinkThe accusation Casey tells Stein to make against the Australian brigadier, during the scheme exploiting Stein's mistaken belief that Tania, the stage persona of lance corporal Tommy Trouncer, is a woman whom the brigadier has brought onto the island [A:51-53]. Casey urges Stein to say that the brigadier had him beaten for his views and that a raid will expose moral turpitude. The raid produces an international military scandal and damages Stein and his American officer allies [A:54].

A:51-53; A:54

Father (Duffey's)Duffey denies having a father when Bagby says that he believes he knew him [MTM B2:43]. The opening account applies the biblical description of Melchisedech as without father, mother, or genealogy to Duffey, while acknowledging confusion over how those specifications fit him [MTM B1:6].

MTM B2:43; MTM B1:6

Father (Finnegan's)Giulio Solli, the Monster, who calls himself a Teras. He tells Duffey that he held Duffey's talisman to his wife's belly and placed it in the hands of his Italian son at birth [MTM B3:107]; the talisman had been given to Giulio in St. Louis [MTM B4:120]. Duffey identifies Finnegan as Giulio's son and says Giulio has been dead for at least ten years, while Bagby insists that he has recently met him [MTM B5:165]. In Archipelago, Finnegan meets his shabby, sorrowful father after death and takes him for beer near the station. Giulio has a scraggly moustache, root-like hands, and a deepening silence. Finnegan attacks him as a failed dockworker and old peasant, then recognizes, when Giulio weeps and leaves, that his father loved the family and did everything he could [A:244-245]. The Devil Is Dead returns to this encounter and Finnegan's realization that Giulio belonged to a monstrous apparatus and died as the Monster Forgotten [D:228-229].

MTM B3:107; MTM B4:120; MTM B5:165; A:244-245; D:228-229

Father (Henri Salvatore's)Lawrence Salvatore, father of Henry Francis Salvatore [A:122]. Tired of disputes with Henry's teachers, he examines the boy and discovers that he is already educated; this happens early in Henry's thirteenth year [A:123]. After the war, Lawrence questions his son's haste to enter seminary and discusses Henry's fear for the Church [A:124-125].

A:122; A:123; A:124-125

Father (Theresa Piccone's)Gaetano Piccone, called Papa Piccone, father of Theresa Antoinette Piccone and proprietor of the Star and Garter Theatre [A:94] [MTM B5:163]. He is flamboyant, enjoys gambling, and flourishes hundred-dollar bills [A:95]. He claims to have accidentally made his unsuccessful burlesque character Oliver Oscar Omygosh into a real man; Bagby remembers the man but disputes Papa's claim to have created him [MTM B5:167-168]. Teresa is Beth Keegan's goddaughter [MTM B5:162]. Patrick Stranahan has represented Papa in disputes; the two become friends and argumentative companions, drinking whisky at the Stranahans' and wine at the Piccones'. Papa secretly burlesques Patrick onstage as Hallohan J. O'Hoolihan [A:104]. Before Theresa's wedding, Monica reports Papa's plan to replace the organist with accordion playing in the aisles, which Maurine calls a joke. Maurine instead anticipates his bringing three barrels of wine and jugs to the reception so that, unlike the hosts at Cana, he will not be remembered for running out [A:105].

A:94; MTM B5:163; A:95; MTM B5:167-168; MTM B5:162; A:104; A:105

Father BaumgartnerPriest involved in Hans Schultz's schooling at St. Joseph's in St. Gallen, Wisconsin [A:207-208]. John William Schultz quarrels with him over the elementary curriculum and demands Greek, Aquinas, and Albert for the children. Father Baumgartner replies that Hans is only nine, that he himself does not know Greek, and that English literacy should come first [A:208-209].

A:207-208; A:208-209

Father of LiesThe Devil, whose reputation makes X unsure how to interpret his statements about which people belong to his party [A:139]. In the account of the Fiefdoms' struggle, the claim that morals have entirely disappeared is named as one of the Father of Lies' falsehoods; the narrator insists that morality continues to resist assault [MTM B8:246].

A:139; MTM B8:246

Father TimeThe personification of time, conventionally an old man with a scythe. The goat-man resembles Father Time because he carries a scythe, but he uses it practically to cut wild grass and store winter fodder for his goats [A:194]. His name is Gautier [A:196].

A:194; A:196

Fatted CalfIn her letter to Finnegan, Loy Larkin says that Papa neglected her garden but killed the fatted calf for his returning prodigal daughter [A:27]. The phrase adapts the celebration of the returning son in Luke 15:23-24.

A:27

Faulte des BoemesThe fault or heresy of the Bohemians, from Villon's “Ballade des menus propos.” Marie Monaghan quotes the line in the novel's spelling, "Je congois le faulte des Boemes," in an in-person fashion. Salvation Sally claims the gift of tongues, interprets the phrase as the heresy of Bohemia, and asks who the heretics really are [A:8]. The glossary to Pierre Jannet's edition of Villon identifies the allusion with the followers of Jan Hus and Jerome of Prague.

A:8

FaustLegendary figure who bargains away his soul to the Devil. Hans Schultz is identified with Dr. Faustus, Apollo, and Aquinas Redevivus [A:39], and later described as simultaneously Faust and Apollo [A:169]. In Teresa Piccone's account of the Argonauts, Hans is Orpheus and is manifested at a later time as Faust [MTM B7:234]. Private Gregory uses Faust's moment of decision as the model for his theory of possessed men: an obscure beginning, a hiatus and bargain, then power and acclaim won by the devils within them [A:84].

A:39; A:169; MTM B7:234; A:84

FaustinaThe sixth in the sequence of ladies' names given to the daily bottles shared by Finnegan, Charles Le Marin, Don Barnaby, and Johnny Duckwalk in their Basse-Terre paradise [D:235-236]. Faustina follows Etheldreda and precedes Georgina; on this unusually heavy drinking day the Four reach Hildegarde, the eighth bottle [D:243].

D:235-236; D:243

Feast of the ApparitionThe feast Marie Monaghan names when announcing her engagement to Hans Schultz at the Lotus Eaters in Sydney. She calls the day the second Thursday of February and says she will never forget it [A:27-28]. In the story's 1943 chronology this is February 11, matching the feast of Our Lady of Lourdes, which commemorates the first apparition there.

A:27-28

February 11, 1943Date of Loy Larkin's letter to Finnegan from Cambeltown, New South Wales, inviting him and his friends to meet her and Margaret the following morning [A:27].

A:27

February 15, 1943Wedding date of John Gottfried Schultz, called Hans, and Marie Anna Monaghan at Annunciation Church in Sydney, Australia. Hans has no army permission to marry, so the wedding is kept secret for a while; the twenty or thirty guests are all Marie's relatives [A:31].

A:31

February 18th, 1943Date Hans Schultz and the other boys returning from the Australian furlough report to the Troop Movement Office and are sent back to New Guinea [A:31]. Henry Salvatore had refused that furlough and had stayed behind [A:38].

A:31; A:38

Federal AgrandisementCasey Szymansky's explanation of the subject of Duffey's political analogies. Duffey objects that liberals who once wanted minimal government now want maximal government, a Leviathan that consumes the other whales [A:42].

A:42

Federal Buildings (New)Potential sites for Finnegan's murals in Casey's proposal for gaining money and commissions through liberal political patronage. Party sanction would bring commissions worth thousands of dollars, including work in new federal buildings [A:183-184].

A:183-184

Federal Funding (Continuous-Flow)Federal support obtained by Newton Prescott for the Casey Machine. Arguing that paid access favors the rich, he seeks Continuous-Flow Funding, Compensatory Counter-Flow Payments, and Impacted Entertainment Area Funding. He also secures shrine status for each machine's site, with Perpetual Care paid through Perpetual Guardian Payments to his own group; several forms of payment are guaranteed in perpetuity [CM:503] [CM:513]. His underlying concern is to preserve something of the machine against anticipated forgetting [CM:512-513].

CM:503; CM:513; CM:512-513

FetchA double or wraith. Duffey has shadows, fetches, and doubles, described as often fleshed, or at least believed by him to be so [MTM B4:141]. The Postscript describes the Irish hero-giant Fingal accompanied by nine black-cloaked doubles while he wears white [PS:478]. Doppio di Pinne, called Dopey, is Finnegan's double. Papadiabolous II questions whether Dopey ever lived and whether Finnegan killed him [D:89]. He later says that Dopey was a seaman and sometime killer of the strange blood, whom Seaworthy summoned to kill Papadiabolous, but remains unsure how close the duality was [D:121]. He offers the further possibility that Dopey disappeared and was absorbed into Finnegan [D:122]. Archipelago calls Dopey Finnegan's fetch who died in his place, either in the Brunhilde's cabin at Papadiabolous's hands or later in Seaworthy's Galveston trap [A:278]. The fictional review of Royce Rollins's The Return of the Neanderthal: The Alien Within attributes to Rollins the theory that doubles and fetches are ordinary manifestations of his interior aliens [D:240-242].

MTM B4:141; PS:478; D:89; D:121; D:122; A:278; D:240-242

FetishA term associated with marks, symbolic objects, and rituals. Seaworthy bears a scar or tattoo inside his left wrist and claims to see the same mark beneath Finnegan's skin [D:10]. Finnegan perceives another, less literal mark in Seaworthy, indicating to him that the man has killed [D:16-17]. After the Naxos shooting, Finnegan's wrist seems to star like cracked glass and bleed beneath the skin before becoming the mark [D:145]. X later calls it the sign of the octopus; Finnegan dates it to the shooting and wonders whether he too belongs to the alien flesh, a category X still questions [D:156]. Bagby calls Duffey a fetish mark that fates and principalities touch or avoid in choosing their courses [MTM B10:302]. Rebeka Stein calls the absurd or incongruous device that triggers a dreamlike transformation a fetish transformation activator, exemplified by the potholes leading to alternate futures in Cleo Mahoney's play [MTM B10:293-294]. At the Final Conclave, Stone Hackenschmidt calls burning the Straw-Man Cap-Stone a fetish-ritual that has got out of hand when it produces enormous quantities of blood [MB:568].

D:10; D:16-17; D:145; D:156; MTM B10:302; MTM B10:293-294; MB:568

Fetish markBagby's description of Duffey in a letter: like a sidewalk crack or roadside post, he is something that fates and principalities touch or avoid and perhaps use to determine their courses. Bagby insists that being such a fetish is not lowly, since even the grand powers cannot ignore him [MTM B10:302].

MTM B10:302

Fetish transformation activatorRebeka Stein's name for the usually ridiculous or incongruous object that activates a transformation in a dream or detached experience. She praises the potholes in Cleo Mahoney's Seven Roads: stepping into one would bring Duffey into one of seven alternate scenes or futures, sometimes without his noticing the transition [MTM B10:293-294].

MTM B10:293-294

Fetish-ritualStone Hackenschmidt's name for burning the Straw-Man Cap-Stone at the Final Conclave. The effigy, soaked in a lamb's blood, produces red smoke, blood-red rain, and a flood far beyond what ten thousand lambs could supply; Hackenschmidt remarks that the fetish-ritual has got out of hand [MB:568].

MB:568

Fiddlers' GreensDuffey's name for the green places of amusement he hopes suit their green years. He asks whether the clubs are Fiddlers' Greens or Thelemes; Shirley Israel dismisses those as old-fashioned beside the fashionable establishments of Fleshpot Row [MTM B4:126].

MTM B4:126

Field, ElysianEarlier inverted heading omitted Avenue; the source uses singular Field. See Elysian Field Avenue.
Fiery FurnaceThe ordeal of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in Daniel 3. In his longer, unsent letter to Duffey, Henri Salvatore credits Margaret Stone with reminding them to remain aflame, then adds the nightly self-examination question, "Did I spend sufficient time in the Fiery Furnace today?" [MTM B5:179-180].

MTM B5:179-180

Fifth Avenue (New York)Manhattan street invoked in the opening epigraph attributed to Asimov: a shaved, neatly dressed Neanderthal could probably walk along New York's Fifth Avenue without attracting much notice [D:9].

D:9

Fifth HeavenHeavenly sphere used in Trinali Peterson's wine-glass poem. The half-globe of crystal resembles the transparent sphere of Fifth Heaven; its fragile stem supports that heaven's dome, and the wine holds the mystery of death and resurrection [A:231].

A:231

Fifty (Company of)The resident regulars of the Old Wooden Ship tavern. The narrator lists forty-nine names and cries that one has been forgotten from the company of fifty [D:215-216]. Finnegan immerses himself in their company to recover assurance of humanity's reality [D:225]. The forgotten regular, Hildegarde Katt, is remembered in the following chapter [D:229].

D:215-216; D:225; D:229

FigsFruit in the Boy King Duffey's groves, described as more real than Iowa's apple trees or Missouri's plum and peach trees [MTM B1:17]. Zabotski calls the sycamore the American Fig and uses it as a disparaging comparison for Bryan Blackstone [MTM B9:270]. The description of Naxos includes figs alongside olives, lemons, grapes, and honey [D:125]. In Ti's account of Amoy's earlier life as a bird working for thieves, Amoy steals figs and olives after progressing through millet, rice, coriander, and dates [A:80].

MTM B1:17; MTM B9:270; D:125; A:80

FiguresRepresentations, puppets, and persons treated as constructed figures. In Elroy Redheart's third red room, most figures are cheap Hong Kong plastic castings resembling Cracker Jack prizes; their arranged scenes depict feverish wealth, a hectic man, and a beautiful young woman [MTM B7:223]. The woman is shown giggling and sticking pins into the heart she holds in her hands [MTM B7:224]. Charlotte Mullens says she chooses empty, pliable flesh-and-blood people, usually actors, and makes them compliant figures and extensions of her aura. Duffey wonders whether her sister and son are projections or ventriloquist's figures; Charlotte insists that her method contains nothing beyond nature [MTM B3:83]. Other figures include the laughing, turbaned Christ from Turkish Anatolia, described as carved a thousand years earlier and freshly repainted within fifty years [MTM B3:104]; Teilhard's demiurgic apparition on St. Michael's altar, with McLuhan and McGonigal beside him [GD:497]; and Casey as a cult figure whom Mary Catherine Carruthers says earns more than thirty thousand dollars a week [MTM B12:377]. Theresa Piccone writes that she works a ventriloquist's figures and that dummies prefer that name [A:49]. Trinali Peterson makes figures from discarded bottles, corks, and raffia, including Dresden figures, marionettes, Mexicans, donkeys, clowns, and prize-fighters [A:228].

MTM B7:223; MTM B7:224; MTM B3:83; MTM B3:104; GD:497; MTM B12:377; A:49; A:228

FilicudiOne of the Aeolian Islands off Sicily. In Anastasia's account of mermaid history, medieval mermaids lived off Sicily, especially around Salina and Filicudi [D:34-35].

D:34-35

Final BeatitudeThe strong promise associated with the Fourteenth Voyage of the Argo, the fourth of the seven contingent futures. This voyage concerns ongoing beatitudes, the completed quest, and the enduring finding of the Golden Fleece; unlike the other contingencies, it is said to be certain to happen [MTM B10:300].

MTM B10:300

Final ConclaveThe declared last assembly of the Ekklesia, or Crowd, held in Babylonia Bagascia to confirm the institution's dismantling [MB:561-563]. Paul XI, the Cap-Stone, is decapitated the day before it opens; the final evening's entertainment is the Voltaire Festival [MB:562-565]. Monsignor X serves the assembly. Hackenschmidt threatens to kill him for failing to anticipate a demand for a submachine gun, but X denies that he will be killed and produces a BAR instead [MB:566-567].

MB:561-563; MB:562-565; MB:566-567

Fingal the HeroIrish hero-giant invoked when Duffey meets Finnegan. Duffey recalls Fingal, or Finn McCool in another version, eating a hundred oysters each larger than a wagon wheel, and wonders whether the young man is an incognito hero or giant [MTM B5:173-174]. The Postscript describes Fingal in white sheep-wool attended by nine doubles in black sheep-wool [PS:478].

MTM B5:173-174; PS:478

Finn McCoolFionn mac Cumhaill, legendary leader of the Fianna, whose adventures are set in a third-century heroic age. Duffey calls Finnegan the original Finn McCool [MTM B5:169], and recalls the hero, also named Fingal in another version, eating a hundred oysters larger than wagon wheels [MTM B5:173-174]. Absalom Stein's notes report that Lafferty rejects a Joycean derivation of Finnegan and associates him with earlier Irish legend, implying identities with Finn McCool, Fingal, and Cú Chulainn [MB:549-550].

MTM B5:169; MTM B5:173-174; MB:549-550

Finnegan (John A. Solli)Giovanni, or John, A. Solli, called Finnegan, born June 1, 1919, in New Orleans to Giulio Solli and Mary McCracken; his brother is Giacomo and his sister Patricia [A:173] [MTM B3:76]. Vincent explains Finnegan as his nickname [A:2]. Beyond the birth and family facts, the narrator warns that accounts of his life disagree [A:174-175]. Finnegan is dark and lean, with a long banana nose, restless facial muscles, and a mouth continually in motion [A:1]. His movement suggests extraordinary grace, strength, and speed, while his face is a gargoyle's comic mask and his speech an unmatched mixture of New Orleans, waterfront Irish, Italian, and Cajun elements [A:6]. He is a painter, seaman, and wanderer [A:175] [D:114], a former steeplejack and accomplished burglar who conducts upper-story break-ins to obtain evidence [D:162], and a former boxer [D:172-173]. He works a nine-hour shift on the New Orleans docks before moving into the Pelican Press print shop [A:116]. He also markets smuggled diamonds for Joseph, whom he meets in Freetown, sending him drafts over the following years [D:93-95]. He belongs to the Dirty Five with Vincent Stranahan, Hans Schultz, Henry Salvatore, and Casey Szymansky, brought together in the army [A:38-39] [MTM B5:171]. He is Iason in their Argonaut identities [A:39]. In Duffey's account of his twelve talismanic creations, Finnegan is the central creation and the salt of their lives [MTM B5:161] [MTM B5:174]. Giulio, who calls himself a Teras, describes giving Duffey's talisman to his son at birth [MTM B3:107]. Finnegan repeatedly experiences amnesia when passing between his upper and lower lives, sometimes losing months of memory and even his name [D:11-12] [D:18] [D:50]. He wonders what connects his successive returns from oblivion and whether he belongs to another human race [D:91]. His sense of alienness alternates with recognition of kinship, especially with Anastasia [D:20]. At confession he describes memories of belonging to the Devil's kindred and an old animal rising within him; the priest absolves his whole person, in all its aspects [D:119-120]. Anastasia's grandmother places him among the violent people of the other blood [D:128]; Anastasia calls both herself and him teras and says they try to make amends [D:139]. Papadiabolous II includes the three of them among the Non-people [D:121]. These identities do not settle all the competing accounts of Finnegan's existence. His clairvoyance includes perceiving Seaworthy's killer's mark, claiming to read the waves' Chaldee writing, and reading the concealed contents of Dopey's letter [D:16-17] [D:38] [D:50-51]. He reconstructs and paints Papadiabolous II's true face before seeing it exposed in death [D:63]. He speaks effective Spanish and Italian and can imitate almost any voice [D:57] [D:114]. He uses a knife in his attack on Gerecke and is an excellent rifle shot [D:164-165] [D:197]. Finnegan paints the Brunhilde's barroom with scenes of Sindbad's voyages, including the ship's people as the dead; he tells Anastasia that when he paints them dead, they are dead [D:59] [D:61]. He works on a large Yellow Period painting while helping Duffey establish the Pelican Press in New Orleans [MTM B6:190]. In Manhattan, under the name Gregory van Ghi, he successfully sells Orange Period paintings and obtains a standing dealer's commission [A:191]. His account of studying under Van Ghi in Florence is challenged by Patricia, who says Van Ghi is an invented name; the narrator of his Florence devil-painting tale also denies its stated circumstances [A:175] [D:252-256]. The painting The Resurrection of Count Finnegan arrives at Duffey's New Orleans gallery after reports of Finnegan's death. It shows a much older Finnegan rising from a sea cave and repairing his decayed flesh; his banana nose has gained nobility, while his humor, pain, and physical energy remain recognizable [MB:550-551]. Its other half depicts Joseph Cardinal Hedayat of Antioch, aged into an appearance identical to the pictured Finnegan, though the two men do not yet look identical in ordinary life [MB:552]. Hilton purchases the painting for twenty thousand dollars and leaves it displayed in Duffey's gallery [MB:553]. Later, Finnegan paints the thirteen Deaths of the Cardinals on the Argo's Bread and Wine Room bulkheads. The narrator celebrates their power while raising the problem of whether Hedayat, his accomplished painter-double, could have made them [MTM B13:452]. Finnegan sails on the Brunhilde as a crewman and shares a cabin with Don Lewis and Joe Cross, both counted among his friends [D:27] [D:30-31]. He resists claims that Seaworthy and the Devil own him [D:40]. He has helped Seaworthy bury the man whom X later identifies as Papadiabolous I, Gregory McIfreann [D:75-76] [D:153] [D:285]. The apparently resurrected Papa frightens him, but he needles and challenges him [D:22] [D:30]. He later understands that the Papa he knows is a replacement and ally: X identifies the dead man's face as the Irish policeman Noonan or Flaherty, and subsequently explains that he is Gregory McColum, Papadiabolous II [D:113] [D:154] [D:285-286]. Anastasia is his beloved companion and declares herself his sister in a sense he does not yet understand [D:20] [D:69]. Finnegan is initially drawn to Marie Courtois's beauty and strength [D:37], but recoils from her ecstatic admission of killing Don Lewis. He and Joe Cross attempt to return and kill her, until Papa intervenes [D:112-113]. Finnegan buries Don Lewis in the sand near Tangier [D:110-112] [A:188]. At Naxos he rushes down the mountain after hearing gunfire, only to find Papadiabolous II and Anastasia already dead [D:140-147]. He escapes into hiding with Manuel [D:148-149]. With Mr. X, an acquaintance from both his lives, he tries to understand what happened [D:152-154]. Anastasia's loss becomes his first death in the narrative's figurative sense, and he dedicates the remaining shadow of his life to robbing and killing Seaworthy [D:156-158]. In New York he climbs into the conspirators' meeting, kills Gerecke while intending to kill Seaworthy, and steals their immensely valuable suitcase [D:162-166]. He escapes with Doll Delancy, who becomes his companion; Mr. X subsequently joins them in Baltimore and takes charge of their protection [D:167] [D:171-174] [D:177]. Finnegan later immerses himself in the Old Wooden Ship's Company of Fifty to recover assurance of humanity's reality [D:225]. Before leaving that town, he attacks the Pirate Hotel, kills two guards and another person, but hears Seaworthy's laugh behind him [D:231]. He reaches the Basse-Terre paradise with Le Marin, Don Barnaby, and Johnny Duckwalk [D:233-236]. Eventually he returns for a watched graveyard rendezvous with Doll and X, calling Seaworthy his odd uncle as he approaches their final confrontation [D:275-276]. Finnegan's deaths remain disputed. Stein records incompatible accounts of his death or survival in the Philippines, the Brunhilde, Tangier, Naxos, Galveston, and the Marianao Coast near Havana, and believes he is still alive [MB:548-550]. In Cuba he is called the Sleeping Man; witnesses disagree about whether he has already left his sea-cave tomb [MTM B12:370-372]. He later appears on the Argo, where he and Biloxi Brannagan exchange banter and where he is explicitly named as Hedayat's double; Herman Hercules is the double of Erculo [MTM B13:453]. The list of pursued doubles confirms those pairings [MB:579]. At the conclave on the Mooring-Rock, at least one of the supposed doubles is believed to be a surviving true cardinal, preserving the succession [MB:596]. Finnegan abstains while the other twelve vote for him, and X crowns him Pope Finnegan the First [MB:597]. The closing words about the day the Devil is dead belong to Doll's poem Diabolique, which also foretells Finnegan's approaching death [D:293-294].

Finnegan CycleBody of legend studied by Absalom Stein, who says he has not determined its exact relation to the Argo legend [MTM B6:188]. His uncertainty is repeated as the opening epigraph of “How Many Miles to Babylon” [MB:550].

MTM B6:188; MB:550

Finnegan DiamondsDiamonds marketed by Finnegan through his partnership with Joseph the Haussa. He leaves Freetown with a sack of stones and sends Joseph drafts as he sells them over the following years [D:94-95]. Hillary Hilton says he has handled Finnegan diamonds [A:255]. Duffey later tells the Devil that he already wears them and that all Finnegan’s friends do likewise [MTM B10:303].

D:94-95; A:255; MTM B10:303

Finnegan O'Hannigan McGillicuddyName Finnegan gives Howland Jerome Howland during his wanderings. When Howland doubts it, Finnegan admits that he has just invented most of it, though everyone calls him Finnegan [A:178].

A:178

Finnegan ProductionFinnegan's proposed intervention to have Hillary Hilton reclaim his wife Mary Jean and displace Casey Szymansky, giving the friends another chance to straighten Casey out [A:252]. Finnegan promises that his part in the production will be funny and require a couple of gadgets [A:253].

A:252; A:253

Finnegan VisitationTeresa Piccone Stranahan’s phrase in a private letter for an experience of Finnegan’s ghostly presence. She says he inhabits his friends, and reports that Stein mistook his first such experience, on Passion Sunday afternoon in 1948, for a visitation at Finnegan’s death [MTM B6:188].

MTM B6:188

Finnerty, VincentMember of the rich money-and-commerce circle around Duffey and Letitia during Chicago's golden age [MTM B3:100]. He is one of the people described as mentalists about money who foresee the 1929 financial collapse [MTM B4:110].

MTM B3:100; MTM B4:110

FireFire appears as practical heat, destructive force, and sacred sign. Finnegan tells of an open fire in the north woods beside which a young hobo aged overnight [D:14]. Papa Devil builds a beach campfire after the Padre Island meal; its flickering light later picks out the cliffs of Seaworthy's granite-like face [D:34] [D:40] [D:48]. Finnegan and Howland make a pit fire to cook rabbits [A:178], while the Australian picnic party sings around charcoal briquettes in a large plate supplied by a hotel girl [A:31]. Hans says he painted carnival pictures of Zippo the Fire-Eater [A:230]. Finnegan tells Doll that his kind set people on fire when they dislike them [D:182], and later broods on burning cities and the possibility of hellfire consuming the earth [D:256]. After his attack on Gerecke, he escapes down iron fire-ladders [D:165]. A noble white horse intended for Casey's Leader rally had been bought from a fire department giving up its horses [MTM B4:117]. Henri Salvatore's letter credits Margaret Stone with the injunction to remain aflame [MTM B5:179-180]. At the Opera House, Margaret produces holy-ghost fire about her tongue, ignites human ashes in her mouth, and pours orange flame over herself without apparent burning [MTM B11:348]. The Fire-Drake Frolic kills further human victims to Fritz's Fandango in Three Flames [MTM B11:350]. After Duffey is killed, three slack-faced men burn his flesh, sinews, and viscera into perpetually hot ashes, leaving his bones separate [MTM B13:442]. The Straw-Man Cap-Stone is burned in the stove at the Final Conclave, producing extraordinary blood and red smoke [MB:568].

D:14; D:34; D:40; D:48; A:178; A:31; A:230; D:182; D:256; D:165; MTM B4:117; MTM B5:179-180; MTM B11:348; MTM B11:350; MTM B13:442; MB:568

Fire Drake Frolic, TheA sequence in the Decatur Street Opera House's blood entertainment, in which further human victims are killed to the accompaniment of Fritz's Fandango in Three Flames [MTM B11:350].

MTM B11:350

Fire DrakesSee Firedrakes.
Fire-Eater (Zippo the)Zippo the Fire-Eater, a carnival performer whose picture Hans Schultz includes among the many act pictures he says he painted for carnivals [A:230].

A:230

FiredrakesFabulous creatures appearing among the discarded remnants of the old world. Margaret Stone reports that a half-man, half-fire-drake bites a woman; when examined, it is only rubber, though the woman is diagnosed with infectious draconitis [MTM B11:309]. The Pop Historians' safari also attacks a building in which human remnants, morphic dragons, and papier-mâché fire-lizards have barricaded themselves [MTM B11:338]. Kasmir Gorshok says he can summon firedrakes to the Argo. The Professor recommends a firedrake at each fireplace, since blind spirits may enter through such neglected openings, to help exclude the Man of Mystery [MTM B13:456]. After the security arrangements are made, the firedrakes patrol constantly [MTM B13:458].

MTM B11:309; MTM B11:338; MTM B13:456; MTM B13:458

FirenzeFlorence, Italy, the setting of Finnegan's story about studying painting under Van Ghi [D:252]. In his tale, he paints a devil whom Father Le Faye recognizes and exorcises, and whom Van Ghi calls an old repeater appearing in many works of art; both advise burning the picture [D:253-255]. The narrator then says Finnegan did paint a devil, but not under the circumstances he has just described [D:256].

D:252; D:253-255; D:256

Firm, TheThe Stranahan family law firm, proposed as a place where Vincent could learn law alongside extension courses instead of attending college [A:103]. His father Patrick is a successful attorney [A:94].

A:103; A:94

First Day (Creation)The creation imagery of Archipelago's opening: the fresh morning evokes the making of the world, while beer is available because barley and hops have already been made on the third day. Finnegan, cast as the first man, drinks the first beer [A:1].

A:1

First Day (Finnegan)First day of Finnegan's fighting binge, when he says he won thirteen consecutive fights before losing one [D:191-192]. He separately describes the railroad man who broke his nose and disproved his boast that he could take two punches to give one; the passage does not identify that man as the opponent in the first loss [D:192].

D:191-192; D:192

First Death of FinneganThe death named by the narrator after Anastasia’s killing and Finnegan’s vow to devote his remaining “shadow life” to hunting Seaworthy [D:157-158]. The narrator distinguishes it from a later physical death on another island, while saying that this first death has a finality of its own [D:158]. The following chapter describes the shadow life as freeing Finnegan from the unities and the heroic conventions [D:161]. Doll later recalls his saying that their adventures are what he does after he is dead [D:173].

D:157-158; D:158; D:161; D:173

First ExecutiveTitle under which Bandicoot Blackstone says his son John will run the family businesses while Bandicoot remains chairman of their boards. This succession is discussed while Bryan Blackstone is dying and expected not to survive the day [MTM B9:288].

MTM B9:288

First Peter 5, 8-9Biblical exhortation to vigilance against the Devil, pictured as a prowling lion, and to resistance in faith. A version of its opening appears among More Than Melchisedech's collected documents, pointedly credited to "Dotty O'Toole. Sonnet" [MTM B5:175].

MTM B5:175

First Speaker, TheThe first lecturer at the Royal Pop Historians' sessions in Duffey's buildings. He speaks in a voice compared to a thunder colt's and defines the present as the all-embracing moment [MTM B11:323]. His gaudy turban carries a sparkling gem or eye that makes his visible face seem false. He presents history as everything in that moment, subject to the historians' continuing reconstruction and revision [MTM B11:324].

MTM B11:323; MTM B11:324

FirsterTerm associated with Peter in the earlier glossary’s account of the “Paean.” The earlier glossary cites the opening “Paean” of Archipelago, page ix. That preliminary page is absent from the supplied copy, so the reading remains unverified.
FishFish furnish meals, marvelous sea life, and figurative language. Rough fish are continually added to the Big Pot [MTM B6:196]. In futuristic Louisiana, Honeybucket Kincaid's tuned electrodes gather nine-pound alligator gar and fourteen-pound Blooper Fish for Biloxi and Duffey's meal [MTM B13:416-417]. Whistling blue fish occupy Bayougoula Park's uncanny fountain [MTM B11:331]. Duffey worries that Casey Gorshok's devil-fish mascot will recover the last scrap of the dangerous logic paper [MTM B13:430]. The Fanged Fish is a remembered waterfront establishment at Ogopo [MTM B13:407]. The Argo knows migrating seas that travel with their fish [MTM B13:405]; its talking oak recalls St. Brandon's encounter with the great fish Jascoyne [MTM B13:404]. Coryphaena Fish rise above the waves blowing shell horns after Finnegan and his companions board, a salute associated with a present or future pope aboard the Argo [MTM B13:450-451]. Sea creatures are said to enjoy the sunken bells of ships and cities [MB:575]. Henri Salvatore says some Argo mariners have fishy flesh [MTM B12:386]. Mary Louise calls Bagby's inexplicable letters as fishy as the Gascinade River [MTM B7:219]. Eva fears that paying for her bar with old fifty-dollar gold pieces will look fishy [MTM B13:414]. In his commentary on Casey, Finnegan calls him fishy as the Grand Banks and says he attracts weak-fish opinions [PG:543-544].

MTM B6:196; MTM B13:416-417; MTM B11:331; MTM B13:430; MTM B13:407; MTM B13:405; MTM B13:404; MTM B13:450-451; MB:575; MTM B12:386; MTM B7:219; MTM B13:414; PG:543-544

Fish MarketMaurine Stranahan's teasing name for her family's Club Room, where mounted fish and gun cases display the male Stranahans' sporting interests. She also calls the men the Rod and Gun Club and says her live-bait fishing shows up their fly fishing [A:103].

A:103

Fish SpearsTwo- and three-tined implements that Hans Schultz cites while disputing the saying that fingers were made before forks. He distinguishes ancient fish spears from untined stabbers used as eating forks; his claim that utensils predate fingers is part of the conversation's conceit [A:4].

A:4

Fishtail peopleThe mermaid people from whom Anastasia Demetriades claims descent on Naxos [D:115]. In her account the fishtail is disappearing: most surviving mermaids are now two-footed, and her own family has produced no fishtail for six generations [D:36].

D:115; D:36

FishyMary Louise Bagby's description of the unexplained correspondence between Bagby and Duffey: "as fishy as the Gascinade River." She objects that Bagby never writes letters; he answers that these belong to another context outside daily time [MTM B7:219].

MTM B7:219

Fitzjames, JamesYoung scholar Hans Schultz meets among New York's secondhand bookshops. Fitzjames begs a quarter for Jaufre and Brunissende; Hans buys him the book, follows him to a park to read, and shares giant bagels and a quart of beer [A:224]. Fitzjames says he sleeps in friends' hallways and on their sofas, calls himself his circle's most intelligent and least charming member, and describes the group as the new leaven [A:225]. He remarks that fish and old bread are the food of poverty [A:234]. He and Hans are the only Romans at Trinali Peterson's burial and find the service inadequate [A:240].

A:224; A:225; A:234; A:240

Five Dollar Gold PieceGold coin Duffey produces by snapping his fingers and gives to Gretchen Sisler beside a park [MTM B2:38-39]. Later he rubs his hands together and pours seven United States five-dollar gold pieces onto a library table. Patrick Stranahan observes that they were minted about ten years earlier and suggests that Duffey could have carried them beforehand; Duffey insists that he performs magic rather than tricks [MTM B5:167].

MTM B2:38-39; MTM B5:167

Five Foot ShelfAbsalom Stein's five-foot shelf of old humor magazines, from which he reads jokes on the Anopheles Network, his G.I. radio station [A:46].

A:46

Five RosesOne of the mild whiskies offered at Falo and Nauti's newly opening jungle cabaret on Luzon. Finnegan and Vincent are its first customers, and Falo brings water to accompany the Five Roses [A:63-64].

A:63-64

Flagship of Abd-AliahAn identity of the Argo in the history told by the talking oak in its wheel. After serving as the Anthony Ship at Actium, it becomes Abd-Aliah of the Sea's flagship and carries his beautiful daughter, who has a tail. Abd-Aliah later sells it to Sindbad of El-Basrah [MTM B13:404].

MTM B13:404

FlahertyAlias of Gregory McColum Papadiabolous II, the Irish cop who also uses Noonan and takes his brother Papadiabolous I's place [D:285] [D:289]. X recognizes him from Finnegan's sketch as the valuable ally killed on the Naxos landing [D:154]. Finnegan has already found his shot and bludgeoned body there [D:146].

D:285; D:289; D:154; D:146

Flame Man (comic strip)Comic strip in which Dotty Yekouris says the Slant-Faced Men have appeared [MTM B7:225]. Duffey later finds their names, Amraphel, Arioch, and Thadal, given almost casually in the strip, where the three are depicted as stooges [MTM B7:227].

MTM B7:225; MTM B7:227

Flap-jackingOne of the minor popular arts listed among the lively practices of daily life that are endangered, degraded, or disappear during the massive trashing of the arts after the Devil's release [MTM B6:207-208].

MTM B6:207-208

Flash girlFashionable female companion in Casey Szymansky's tenth imagined world, the world of money, prestige, and social standing. He wants a flash car and a flash girl, choosing whichever of Evelyn, Mary Jean, or Mary Carruthers grows up prettiest [A:160].

A:160

FlatAn editorial description of Finnegan's living quarters in the old print shop taken over for the Pelican Press: cots and a cook stove stand at the back of a cluttered shop-like building [A:116]. The separate phrase "fell flat" describes Duffey stumbling over Crissie Cristofero's future sign on Dumaine Street [MTM B12:358].

A:116; MTM B12:358

Flats, JackassOne of the regions named in Don Lewis's tale of three American soldiers lost on Willy Jones Island after Santee and Casper kill the elusive man called Yokipoki. Despite its name, Jackass Flats is the most precipitous country the narrator has seen [D:44-46].

D:44-46

Flaying of Cardinal ArtemisOne of the thirteen paintings in the Deaths of the Cardinals series on the Argo's Bread and Wine Room bulkheads, showing Cardinal Artemis's execution. It is singled out among the surpassing works attributed to Count Finnegan, although the narrator also raises the possibility of his painter-double Cardinal Hedayat [MTM B13:452].

MTM B13:452

Fleece ItselfThe Great Golden Fleece of Colchis, whose combings Casey Gorshok makes into a golden mask, neck scarf, and gauntlets for the fleshless Melchisedech Duffey [MTM B13:443]. Despite their sacred material and their maker's mastery, the garments sometimes impair Duffey's sensing, touch, and impulses [MTM B13:444].

MTM B13:443; MTM B13:444

Fleece, GoldenThe Golden Fleece of Colchis, object of Jason and the Argonauts' quest. Stranahan's poem recalls the friends sailing the ancient Argo in pursuit of golden cargo [A:91], and Rosemary tells the Sergeant that he will find the fleece without recognizing his success [A:89]. The Argo's logs record the fleece's discovery as a brilliant early triumph [MTM B13:421]. Its finding abides forever in the Fourteenth Voyage's "Quest Accomplished" motif [MTM B10:300]. Threads combed from it protect a magus on an icy cliff from freezing, falling, and death [MTM B13:397-399]; later Casey makes its golden fabric into Duffey's mask, scarf, and gauntlets [MTM B13:443].

A:91; A:89; MTM B13:421; MTM B10:300; MTM B13:397-399; MTM B13:443

Flesh Weed EaterAn agency of destruction named by the child hero among the Royal Pop People. Even the flesh weed eater cannot dispose of certain bright, strong, crookedly talented human weeds; those must be destroyed by thunder colts [MTM B11:334-335].

MTM B11:334-335

Flesh WeedsThe child hero's contemptuous term for the human remnants whom the Royal Pop People are eager to eliminate while determining who qualifies as a thunder person [MTM B11:334].

MTM B11:334

Fleshpot RowChicago entertainment row including Herm's, Curley Q, Seven Steps Down, Blow Brass, The Farmer's Daughter, and Dung Heap, frequented by Duffey and his circle. Rollo McSorley recommends it as the remaining home of Chicago-Hot Jazz, while the narrator confirms the music but condemns its worst tendencies. Letitia and Demetrio object to the establishments' atmosphere [MTM B4:125-126].

MTM B4:125-126

FleshpotsPlaces of indulgence: Bagby frequents the fleshpots of Chestnut Street [MTM B2:62]. Rollo and Josephine McSorley urge Duffey toward gaudy establishments on Randolph Street, defending fleshpots if they serve Irish stew; Letitia finds their atmosphere stifling [MTM B4:125].

MTM B2:62; MTM B4:125

FliesDuffey pictures a few perceptive people as flies who notice when the molasses trapping them hardens into amber, while most recognize only that something is wrong [MTM B9:268]. In his commentary on Casey's possible eschatological role, he calls premature antichrists flies buzzing about the Lord of the Flies [PG:534-535].

MTM B9:268; PG:534-535

FlintskinInsult aimed at Duffey by the leader of three young men after Duffey knocks them down. The speaker couples "old flintskin" with "old muleskin" and "old camelskin," continuing the Great Day encounter's imagery of old skins that must be discarded [GD:482-483].

GD:482-483

Floating palacesHillary Hilton's description of three garbage scows that he says he has refurbished and sold to an Arabian Gulf potentate [A:255].

A:255

Floating restaurantUnidentified restaurant supposedly associated with John Mogul; the proposed reference at Archipelago, page 122, does not establish this establishment or ownership.
FloodThe biblical deluge of Genesis 6-9. In Casey's school notes, Hinnegan places the Milesians in Ireland before it, prompting Casey's joke about Noah carrying two Irishmen on the ark [A:164-165]. Jimmy Hansen calls the Bushmaster-Schultz drinking contest the greatest event since the flood dried [A:19]. A Pattenite reader dates the Floodtide Catastrophes, sudden mountain formation, and Noah's flotation to about 2800 BC in Zabotski's Pristine History of the World, comparing this with Fundamentaler chronology [MTM B9:278]. Zabotski says mountains rose beneath the ark and insists that his own approaching flood will be the original, earlier floods merely practice [MTM B9:281] [MTM B9:287].

A:164-165; A:19; MTM B9:278; MTM B9:281; MTM B9:287

Floodtide CatastrophesCatastrophes dated to about 2800 BC in Zabotski's Pristine History of the World, according to a Pattenite reader who finds its chronology nearly identical to that of the Fundamentalers. The same cluster includes the instantaneous rise of the Alpine-Himalayan System and the flotation of Noah's barge. Zabotski calls the agreement possibly accidental [MTM B9:278].

MTM B9:278

Flores SeaOne of the seas in the catalogue of waters sailed by the Argo and Melchisedech Duffey, listed between the Java and Bali seas [MTM B13:406].

MTM B13:406

FloridaState where Finnegan, Doll, and X stay in lake country, fish, and drink at a shady bait house [D:180-182]. They drive to Orlando, Kissimee, Pine Castle, Apopka, and sometimes Daytona [D:183]. Finnegan later reports that the leftfooted killer has been asking for him in Winter Garden [D:193]. In Le Marin's sea story, Florida is where he comes ashore after hiding for three days aboard the seized Sarcophagus [D:245].

D:180-182; D:183; D:193; D:245

FlourWheat and rye flour form the Danish-bread Christ-head in Duffey's art collection; the narrative associates such loaves with Corpus Christi Day in Denmark [MTM B3:103]. Flour is also among the provisions Finnegan unloads from Papapaleologus's panniers at Anastasia Grandmother's house [D:126].

MTM B3:103; D:126

Flower GrowingOne of the popular arts listed among the lively practices degraded by the deformed counterparts that emerge after the Devil's release [MTM B6:207].

MTM B6:207

FlowersThe underground sunshine of New Orleans bursts through gaps in the pavement like exploding red, yellow, and purple flowers named Philos, Eros, and Agape. Hot purple Agape is the theme flower of the hundred-and-twenty-month late summer shared by Duffey and Letitia [MTM B7:211]. Earlier, the chubby young woman at St. Malachy's takes a red rose; she is subsequently identified as Letitia Koch [MTM B3:88-91].

MTM B7:211; MTM B3:88-91

Flute (Magic)The Magic Flute, one of the celebrated objects in the catalogue of the Argo's discoveries, alongside the Ring of the Nebelungs and the Philosopher's Stone [MTM B13:421-422].

MTM B13:421-422

Flute (Recorder)Old-style recorder flute Duffey builds from walnut and Philippine mahogany, with brass stop-keys and filigree, while helping establish the Pelican Press [MTM B6:190]. Letitia prefers it to his banjo because he cannot sing while playing it [MTM B7:226]. After her death, he plays the flute through a difficult hour of paperwork [MTM B8:254]. He also performs on recorder and banjo during the intermission of Seven Roads at the Ursuline Academy [MTM B12:366].

MTM B6:190; MTM B7:226; MTM B8:254; MTM B12:366

Flute bandsMusical ensembles named among the popular arts whose style and vitality are degraded in the massive trashing of the arts [MTM B6:207]. Duffey had hoped to form a flute band as an occasional alternative to his neighborhood string band [MTM B6:190].

MTM B6:207; MTM B6:190

Fly FishingOne of the popular arts included among the lively practices being degraded in the trashing of the arts [MTM B6:207].

MTM B6:207

Flying muleMule Duffey transports by summoned giant hands at the Pont du Sable Traffic Trestle on November 13, 1935, after Morris Poor and Rollo McSorley challenge him [MTM B4:127] [MTM B4:130-132]. The largest of three mules moves thirty feet across a half-street to a traffic island. Witnesses and newspaper photographs offer varying accounts, though the narrator affirms that giant hands performed the feat [MTM B4:131-133]. The initial claim that this is Duffey's last public magic is immediately corrected by recalling his puppet shows with Letitia [MTM B4:133].

MTM B4:127; MTM B4:130-132; MTM B4:131-133; MTM B4:133

Flying RingsApparatus used with the turning pole in Hans Schultz's agility training. His physical education also includes twice-daily runs on the mile-long track through his father John William's nursery at St. Gallen [A:208].

A:208

Flying SerpentName of the Argo when Willy Jones sails it in the Moluccas, according to the ship's history told by the talking oak [MTM B13:404-405].

MTM B13:404-405

Flying SteinmetzOne of Absalom Stein's self-named mixed drinks at the Bay Hotel picnic. He prepares the assortment with Gilbeys gin and ice, though no separate recipe for the Flying Steinmetz is supplied [A:29-30].

A:29-30

Foetus (Quick)One of the "quick foetuses" cast into the Moloch Furnace during the festival at Babylonia Bagascia. It speaks from the furnace, identifies itself as Little Hugh of Lincoln, and is met with laughter [MB:566]. Foetus is a British spelling of fetus.

MB:566

Fog-Horn SymphonyNinth title in Endymeon Ellenbogen's proposed nine-volume classification of his poetry, which he says remains uncollected and unpublished [A:237].

A:237

FogazzaroFalse name Biloxi Brannagan gives when Finnegan first joins him and Gertrude in their kitchen garden. Finnegan immediately disbelieves it, and Gertrude corrects Biloxi aloud before he supplies Brannagan [D:199].

D:199

Font (Holy Water)The chipped holy-water font on the wall is one of Finnegan's intensely remembered details of his uncertain twelve-year life with Theresa [A:204]. In an earlier exchange, he teases her that the baptismal font cracked when she was baptized; she answers that any of a dozen witches might have cracked it [A:108].

A:204; A:108

Fonts (Printing)The old and damaged printing fonts Stein notices in a supposed newspaper clipping about X. Dotty identifies the obsolete printing as the Pelican Press's own work and concludes that X printed the clipping there before sending it back to entertain them [A:142].

A:142

Foolish ColtsDuffey's comparison for most of the world, which stands in an imagined middle ground although, in his account of Casey's ideological conversion, there is no position between the sides. The discussion concerns Casey's Party commitments and the intended use of the Crock as a Liberal Catholic vehicle for propaganda [A:98].

A:98

Foot-painterProfession of Marie Monaghan's uncle Shoeless Veronese van Rijn. She says he works in watercolors, oils, and charcoal with his feet, travels with carnivals, and may be the world's finest foot-painter [A:28].

A:28

FootballSport in Casey's imagined record books, where he becomes a phenomenal running back while also playing professional baseball [A:156]. Tom "Big Bear" Rogers contributes “The Floating Screen: The Next Important Development in Football” to the Crock [A:41]. Howland has played neither high-school football nor basketball because he never attended high school [A:180]. Football and six-man football appear in the catalogue of threatened popular arts [MTM B6:207]. Zabotski explains his Pristine World by compressing a football game from three hours of clock time to one hour of whistle time, twelve minutes with the ball in play, and roughly three minutes of essential action [MTM B9:279].

A:156; A:41; A:180; MTM B6:207; MTM B9:279

Foraminifera JulepEarlier heading normalized the printed spelling Julip to Julep. See Foraminifera Julip.
Foraminifera JulipDrink Biloxi Brannagan orders from Honeybucket Kincaid in futuristic rural Louisiana, printed as "Foraminifera Julip" [MTM B13:416-418]. Kincaid prepares the drinks using the scene's frequency-based gathering of substances from water, including alcohol; the text supplies no complete recipe [MTM B13:418].

MTM B13:416-418; MTM B13:418

Forca, Freddy Tin-HornOne of the fifty resident regulars at the Old Wooden Ship, listed between Tippio and Sulphur-Bottom Sullivan [D:215-216]. The narrator declines to tell his story but says Tin-Horn describes the kind of sport he is [D:218]. The nickname suggests a pretentious gambler, without establishing his stakes or any particular exploit.

D:215-216; D:218

Ford AlexandrineThe proposed “Ford Alexandrine,” whose next-year model is suggested as a classy chassis for the Casey Machine. The suggestion occurs among advice from the machine’s promoters without an individual speaker being named [CM:508-509].

CM:508-509

ForebearsAncestors. Angela Cosquin's mixed island ancestry includes French, Carib, and English people, with both noblemen and slaves among her forebears [D:259]. During the drinking contest, Bushmaster's supporters praise the bulldog courage of his forebears, prompting Finnegan's pun that some of them are bulldogs [A:23].

D:259; A:23

ForebrainThe seat of ordinary human consciousness in the fictional cranial theory quoted from Carmody Overlark's Studies in the Imagination. The epigraph contrasts modern humans' developed forebrains with Neanderthals' allegedly larger back-brains, assigning the latter unconscious and paranormal powers [D:270-271]. It credits the other people with humanity's imagination and ghostliness while the modern contribution is forebrain consciousness [D:272].

D:270-271; D:272

His attachment to persecuted-minority identity later contributes to his joining the Party [A:157].

Fourth Pleistocene Ice AgeVincent's ice-age reference in his speculation that the universe might have been created ten minutes ago with its apparent past already installed: fossils, sediments, partly run-down atomic clocks, and an earth already partway down the slope from the fourth Pleistocene ice age [A:56]. Henry sees a Francis, alongside Anthony and other saints, aboard the dream ship Navicula Petri [A:44-45]. FundamentalersAdvocates of a short biblical chronology who visit Zabotski and Duffey to discuss their histories. The visitors include Pattenite and Hatch adherents, a follower of the Rev. Patrick O’Connell, and a Cummings-clan member [MTM B9:277] [MTM B9:278] [MTM B9:280]. A Pattenite finds Zabotski’s chronology close to theirs: first life between 20,000 and 10,000 BC, the sixth-day creation of land, animals, and man between 10,000 and 2,800 BC, and the Floodtide Catastrophes about 2,800 BC [MTM B9:278]. Zabotski calls them half correct but insists that their time scale must be understood in relation to the Pristine World; similar dates do not establish agreement about how history works [MTM B9:274] [MTM B9:279] [MTM B9:280]. The Cummings-clan visitor treats the Ark’s survival in High Armenia, guarded by angels, as a test of faith and reports three expeditions searching for it [MTM B9:280]. The visitors finally declare that Duffey and Zabotski are against them because they do not share their teachings [MTM B9:284]. Later news reports nineteen unarmed Fundamentalers killed in a “shootout” with Orthodoxer police [MTM B9:288].

On Padre Island, Don Lewis sees a furtive man and tells of another, Yokipoki, whom he buried on Willy Jones Island; after that experience Lewis himself became furtive [D:43-48]. Having returned under a different name and no longer feeling his own master, he asks whether such singular people are forgotten by God [D:48]. The narrator includes Finnegan among the furtive men and recalls the man who swam out to the Brunhilde [D:41] [D:50]. The swimmer proves to be Manuel, a stowaway and self-described spy. Chapter Eleven of The Devil Is Dead opens with a passage attributed to Galen's Techne Iatrike about Daemons begetting satyrs on women; the narrator then pointedly notes that Galen's teacher was named Satyrus [D:160-161].

Galley SlavePlayful description of Casey Szymansky, who works in the galley while his companions sleep on deck. After midnight, the galley slave comes up and declares the vessel to be the ship named Argo, for that night at least [A:63].

GalvestonTexas port from which Henry Salvatore signs onto cotton boats, cattle boats, tankers, and sulphur boats [A:124]. Mary Virginia Schaeffer is from Galveston [MTM B5:157], and it is included in the birthplaces of the six companions listed after the first five talismanic people [MTM B3:76]. Her family's Red Dog Motor Freight runs from Galveston and Houston toward Morgan City and New Orleans, with other stops in Louisiana and Texas. Joe Smith begins there the triptych of Dotty O'Toole that Finnegan later completes [MTM B6:198]. The Old Wooden Ship Tavern in Galveston is where Gunboat Smith serves as Bulldog-in-Residence before joining the Argo [MTM B13:458].

Galveston IslandSite of one disputed death of Finnegan. Stein says that Finnegan did not die at Saxon X Seaworthy's hand on Galveston Island, although Doll Delancy found a body on West Beach and swore it was his [MB:548]. Archipelago offers Galveston as one possible place where Doppio di Pinne died in Finnegan's stead; the alternative is the Brunhilde's cabin, at Papadiabolous's hands [A:278].

MB:548; A:278

Game wardenRoyal official in Duffey's dream as the Boy King. Summoned to stop men shooting his newly made Birds of Paradise, the warden finds that the fallen birds have become clay pigeons. He nevertheless shoots and kills the men, then threatens to shoot Duffey with his next arrows if called out on another clay-pigeon chase [MTM B2:67].

MTM B2:67

GamesRecreations, deceptions, performances, and contests recur across the cycle. The Rounders' Club advertises games on its Elegant Riverboat Deck, with racquets, whist, poker, and horseshoes [MTM B2:49]. Duffey and his school friends play Kelly pool and rotation in a private house's attic billiard room while escaping a formal dance [MTM B1:32-33]. Charlotte Mullens begins with solitaire, plays two-handed cards with Duffey, and then includes Gloria in three-handed games with kisses for stakes [MTM B3:78]. Charlotte and Gloria, also called the Cavendishes, live by card-sharping and play bridge against Lily Koch and the Girl Countess [MTM B3:95]. Charlotte hears that Sebastian Hilton is rich and fancies himself a gamer, making him an attractive target [MTM B3:94]. Charlotte describes her and Gloria's sexual blackmail schemes while walking with Duffey toward St. Malachy's Church [MTM B3:87]. A compromising photograph of Duffey with Shirley Israel is described as a badger-game entrapment [MTM B4:139-140]. Duffey calls Hilary Hilton and Mary Jean's treatment of Casey a reverse badger game: Casey may have sought death at Hilary's hands but received painful derision [PG:536]. Margaret Stone likens Charlotte's moral peril to Nine Dollar Dog, a game whose outcome becomes unalterable nine plays before its end [MTM B7:217]. The Thunder Colt Game is the climax of the Decatur Street Opera House's bloody performance, accompanied by Thunder Torus music; the colt kills a Finnegan effigy and Margaret Stone [MTM B11:349-351]. In a cosmic contest, Duffey wrestles Morpheus over which will remain as the last dreaming cell, and the narrator calls cosmic wrestling the game of timeless Greek gods [GD:500]. Zabotski compares the Pristine World to the essential action of a football game, stripped of repetition and empty time [MTM B9:279]. A young Saucerite hopes to obtain a chess scholarship to the University of Miami [MB:592]. Game of Hearts is among the titles Dotty gives for the Open Heart Novels [MTM B7:224].

MTM B2:49; MTM B1:32-33; MTM B3:78; MTM B3:95; MTM B3:94; MTM B3:87; MTM B4:139-140; PG:536; MTM B7:217; MTM B11:349-351; GD:500; MTM B9:279; MB:592; MTM B7:224

GannetBird that has remained on the Brunhilde's main stack for days. Papa Devil identifies it as a gannet, and Finnegan reports Manuel's interpretation that someone else will die. Papa replies that Manuel knows of another coming death, but that a bird did not tell him [D:120].

D:120

Gans, JoeAmerican boxer, 1874-1910. During his fighting binge, Finnegan boasts that he went ninety rounds with Joe Gans and challenges local men to a fast twenty rounds [D:191].

D:191

Gaping NothingnessPhrase in X's angry letter to Absalom Stein. After describing the world's coming desolation as its becoming trivial and narrow, X invokes everlasting phoniness and gaping nothingness upon Stein for reading the Teilhard bogus without laughing, and urges him to renounce this prostitution of the mind [A:265-266].

A:265-266

GarAlligator gar, a large freshwater fish. In the Louisiana swamps, Honeybucket Kincaid adjusts voltage and frequency and uses underwater electrodes to summon the nine-pound gar from about a mile around. From perhaps three thousand he selects one for Brannagan's meal, eviscerates it, takes three pounds of tender flank meat requested for grilling, and puts the gar into a high-frequency oven [MTM B13:416-417].

MTM B13:416-417

Gar-fishFrancine's comparison for Finnegan's drinking: she asks whether he still drinks like a gar-fish. He says his friends have stopped asking; she refuses to join that silence [A:247].

A:247

Garbage ScowVessel from which X says he was once dropped, trussed and weighted, during his clandestine adventures [A:138]. Hilary Hilton also boasts of refurbishing three garbage scows and selling them to an Arabian Gulf potentate, transformed into floating palaces [A:255].

A:138; A:255

GardenA place of remembered belonging as well as an ordinary cultivated space. At Archipelago's opening, Finnegan looks up from his beer to find that the Garden has vanished and he is in the World [A:1]. Later he likens the Green Islands to the Garden, but the Malayan boy insists that they are not it and that he must go home [A:88]. The companions sleeping in high grass at the jungle's edge offer a related pastoral image [A:69]. Show Boat, in her letter to Dotty, identifies the Garden's serpent with the many-armed political monster she and Vincent oppose [A:262-263]. In the seventh contingency, Duffey converses wordlessly with the invisible God in an afternoon garden, where an offered solution still carries a possible personal disaster [MTM B10:301]. Other gardens have concrete settings. Loy Larkin complains that the garden she planted in November is all weeds [A:27]. Young Duffey escapes the slant-faced boys through the squash and corn rows at his aunt's house [MTM B1:12-13]. He envisages his old stable yard as a beer garden, courtyard cafe, and open-air market [MTM B2:47]. Henri sends him to New Orleans to grow cucumbers for the Greater Glory in an asphalt garden [MTM B5:184]. The priest at St. Malachy's has a rose garden [MTM B3:87]. Duffey and Brannagan meet in the latter's private beer garden in Biloxi [MTM B13:408-409]. Joseph invites Finnegan to drink gin in a garden at Freetown [D:93]. Don Barnaby describes Madame Le Mourcheor's small interior garden expanding, after his joy pill, into a boundless world of changing people, marriage, and family [D:249-250].

A:1; A:88; A:69; A:262-263; MTM B10:301; A:27; MTM B1:12-13; MTM B2:47; MTM B5:184; MTM B3:87; MTM B13:408-409; D:93; D:249-250

Garfield, CharlotteAdult confidence woman who continues to look like a nine-year-old girl, moving between a child's manner and an experienced woman's voice. Duffey meets her on the night train from Omaha to Chicago in 1925. Calling herself Charlotte Mullens, she plays cards with him and Gloria, with kisses as stakes [MTM B3:77-78]. She claims to be thirty-eight, older than her father and older than her mother, and rejects Gloria's suggestion that Duffey is a father image: he is her sweetheart. Gloria's role shifts from mother to sister; Charlotte identifies the third member of their party, Manolo, as her son [MTM B3:80-81]. She later explains that she recruits pliable flesh-and-blood people, usually actors, and makes them compliant figures of her own aura [MTM B3:83]. Charlotte is a strong psychic who reads Duffey's mind and communicates with him out of physical presence [MTM B3:81] [MTM B3:83-84]. She enlists his help to find Aga Gonof's hidden stash, claiming a small share through her former husband's dealings and proposing to take the remainder as interest. Duffey obtains the key pattern; Charlotte has the key made. In a shared experience she calls a psychosomatic trance, Duffey seizes the coded location and she arranges the information into the bank and deposit-box numbers. She says she has used such trances in mentalist acts [MTM B3:84-86]. She promises to find Duffey's elusive 'moth' in return, directs him to St. Malachy's, and knows the identity of the woman he will marry, Letitia Koch [MTM B3:86-88] [MTM B3:91]. While walking to the church for confession, she describes blackmail schemes conducted with Gloria and exploiting her own childish appearance [MTM B3:87-88]. At the Colony Club, where the troupe is known as the Cavendishes, Charlotte announces that she has stolen and reburied the loot and is now a millionaire. A mental alarm has compromised the disposable name Mullens [MTM B3:93]. The troupe also earns its living through cardsharping [MTM B3:95]. Gloria and Manolo are murdered at their hotel, echoing their deaths in Duffey's trance. Letitia says Charlotte escaped to her prepared hiding place; Charlotte had named St. Angela Orba Orphanage, where two sisters know she is an adult [MTM B3:85-86] [MTM B3:97]. As Charlotte Garfield she later attends the Royal Rogues' and Graceful Swindlers' convention at New Orleans's Royal Orleans Hotel [MTM B7:216]. She now claims to be about two hundred years old, admits her earlier age was a lie, and says her Mendacious Midget Doll bears her true age. Margaret Stone calls her Midge and Baby Face while warning that her chosen game may already have decided her fate [MTM B7:217]. Calling herself Charlotte Carrollton, she advertises for a new professional family under the name Darnley. Separately from recruiting actors, she claims she can bear full-grown nineteen-year-old sons, but declines to explain how. She says she changes families every three or four years, proposes a Patriarch and Angelic Child confidence scheme with Duffey, and eventually engages the Darnleys [MTM B8:259-261]. She remains an old associate of Duffey, criticizes Casey's exploitation of vulnerable people, and says she herself has a foot in several worlds [MTM B12:379-380]. Charlotte Garfield and her son Michael attend Hilary Hilton's party at Randal's [MTM B12:380] [MTM B12:383].

GargoylesA recurrent grotesque image associated with Finnegan: his face is a comic mask with a bugle nose [A:6], and he calls himself a gargoyle while Anastasia recalls a story about one with a good heart [D:39]. During his pursuit of Seaworthy he perches six stories above the street like a living gargoyle [D:162]. The four senior gargoyles he observes are Seaworthy, Gerecke, Wirt, and Orestes Gonof [D:163]. Duffey also includes Gargoyles among the Teras variants whose blood he puts in unusually large amounts into his creations [MTM B5:169-170]. A Chesterton epigraph imagines monsters as gargoyles belonging to a definite cathedral, whose architecture and consecration the writer affirms [MTM B5:177].

A:6; D:39; D:162; D:163; MTM B5:169-170; MTM B5:177

GarlicDe Polis puts garlic into the Brunhilde's stew as Anastasia jokes that prayer and garlic can change the world's nature [D:68]. Theresa Piccone reports cooking three days of specialties at Monica Stranahan's house and leaving a lingering garlic smell. Monica compares garlic to sin and adapts the Gospel warning of woe to whoever brings it [A:48]. The Old Wooden Ship also stands at the end of a garlic block [D:215].

D:68; A:48; D:215

Garlic blockPungent neighborhood description for the block whose last building is the Old Wooden Ship [D:215]. The tavern is explicitly placed in Galveston in More Than Melchisedech [MTM B13:458].

D:215; MTM B13:458

Garment, SeamlessThe Seamless Garment of Christ, listed among the Argo Masters' findings alongside such relics and treasures as Roland's Horn and the Holy Shroud [MTM B13:422].

MTM B13:422

GarnetsStones singled out by the Royal Pop lecturer, with spars and other imperfect crystals, as especially good at recording events in every direction. Hard prismatic crystals are said to focus more particularly on the direction ordinarily called the future [MTM B11:330].

MTM B11:330

Garrard, Ouida (Cotton-Picker)Cotton Picker, a Cajun woman among the resident regulars of the Old Wooden Ship [D:216], the tavern later explicitly located in Galveston [MTM B13:458]. She goes around with Catherine Cadensus, Vivian Gilligan, and Mercedes Morrero, a quartet the narrator calls exceptionally pretty. She enjoys strangers taking her dancing and riding and makes them feel welcome [D:224].

D:216; MTM B13:458; D:224

GasFuel for the burners under Duffey's enormous soup crock [A:133] [MTM B6:195]. At his St. Louis horse-barn business he has gas lighting with replaceable mantles, a gas cook stove, and plans for a gas heater to supply hot water [MTM B2:40-42]. Gas lighting is cut off at night in the boys' school rooms, so his after-curfew store operates by candles or kerosene [MTM B1:26]. Hydrogen lifts Duffey's balloon [MTM B2:63]. Charley Murray proposes compressed-gas or kerosene lights, but Duffey favors electric lighting after reading of fatal explosions on other balloons [MTM B2:64-65]. After the candle-lit dinner aloft, he extinguishes the candles and knocks Murray's cigar overboard before opening a gate valve to release hydrogen and descend [MTM B2:66]. Separately, Finnegan jokes that a jury trial for his disturbance would have sent him to the gas chamber [A:264].

A:133; MTM B6:195; MTM B2:40-42; MTM B1:26; MTM B2:63; MTM B2:64-65; MTM B2:66; A:264

Gas ChamberThe punishment Finnegan imagines he would have received if he had asked for a jury trial after being arrested for disturbing the peace. He writes that the judge would have imposed ten years if empowered to do so, then escalates the joke to the gas chamber [A:264].

A:264

Gascinade RiverSpelling used in Mary Louise's remark that Bagby's supposedly unwritten letters are as fishy as the Gascinade River [MTM B7:219]. It apparently points to Missouri's Gasconade River, though whether the variant spelling is deliberate is uncertain.

MTM B7:219

GasolineFuel in the Dirty Five's improvised lanterns, beer bottles fitted with tightly twisted rag wicks [A:39]. Duffey also equips his balloon with a gasoline engine and propeller, but these affect its speed by only about five miles an hour [MTM B2:64].

A:39; MTM B2:64

Gate of HellEarlier singular heading referred to the plural portae inferi in the cited banner. See Gates of Hell.
Gate ValveValve Duffey opens to release hydrogen and bring his balloon down after the dinner party aloft. Before opening it he blows out the candles and knocks Charley Murray's cigar overboard [MTM B2:66].

MTM B2:66

Gates of HellThe gates of hell, portae inferi, in the banner Portae inferi non prevalebunt on Navicula Petri in Henry Salvatore's dream. It forms a sequence with Tu es Petrus and tibi dabo claves regni [A:44], echoing Matthew 16:18-19 and the promise that the gates of hell will not prevail against the Church.

A:44

Gates of Labor / Media / Pentecostals / Roarers / Teilhardians / Gays / Hot Brains / LevelersConstituencies assigned new Princes, Gates, or Stones in the attempt to give the Ekklesia a sufficiently broad base to survive. The list includes Labor, Media, Pentecostals, Roarers, Teilhardians, Gays, Hot Brains, and Levelers. Media groups receive thirteen Stones and Labor sixteen. Instrumentalists have separate representatives, including five Gates for electric guitarists [MB:561-562].

MB:561-562

Gates, ThePopular title, alongside Stones, for the Princes of the Ekklesia, explained through Cardines, hinges or swingers [MB:561]. Six hundred sixty-six attend the Last Conclave in Babylonia Bagascia, with thirteen Princes absent [MB:566]. Under Hackenschmidt's armed coercion, six hundred sixty vote for the Straw-Man and six for Joseph Cardinal Hedayat; the six dissenting votes are then counted for the effigy [MB:567]. Before the conclave, several Gates break open the decapitated Paul the Eleventh's skull and take his brains to fry with onions and eat [MB:562-563].

MB:561; MB:566; MB:567; MB:562-563

Gautier (Goat-man)An old French goat-herder whom Finnegan meets in New Jersey's back country. He lives with about forty goats in barns, shacks, caves, and summer camps, mowing grass for their winter feed [A:194-195]. He came from southern France in 1908 with six goats, was driven out of New York with them, and after decades of travel now remains in Jersey. His name Gautier is derisively pronounced Goat-Ear because of his goats and hairy ears; he prefers goat-man [A:196]. He is a self-sufficient, one-man Gypsy camp with three carts, each drawn by four goats, tools including a loom and wheel, and skill in making nets, seines, lines, and traps. He eats and trades goat cheese, makes berry jelly and wine, corn beer and potato whisky [A:196-197], and eats boiled wheat with milk and honey, acorns, and dried goat meat chopped with fat and honey for storage [A:197]. His syrinx and bagpipes account for much of the supposed ghost music of the swamps. He sometimes occupies Harlow House and may himself account for its ghost, though whether the house is truly haunted remains uncertain. The claim that ghosts can be seen without fear is made about goats [A:197]. At Harlow House he reads French books aloud to the goats, including Balzac's Contes Drolatiques, Stendhal, Daudet's Tartarin, Lesage's Gil Blas, and Dumas's Count of Monte Cristo. After they sleep, he reads Old American Blood and Thunder romances privately [A:198-199]. Finnegan first gains the goats' friendship by helping Luin, the one youngster unable to join the others climbing a fallen sycamore. The seven youngest have weekday names: Bownee, Luin, Mairt, Keadin, Ordin, Haoine, and Sahirn [A:194-195]. Finnegan's fancy that Gautier resembles an aged Pan remains a fancy [A:194]. He finds the goat-man a spoofer and a little wild, enjoys staying about a week, but refuses the offered inheritance and leaves [A:199-200].

A:194-195; A:196; A:196-197; A:197; A:198-199; A:194; A:199-200

Gawk, GoldenX's mocking image of intellectual idol-worship in his letter rebuking Stein for taking Teilhard seriously. He tells Stein to renounce the adoration of the golden gawk [A:266]. The phrase may recall the golden calf of Exodus 32, but that particular allusion is not explicit.

A:266

GayetyGaiety in Finnegan's “Antipodal Ode to Loy Larkin”: he praises the joy she has drawn from life alongside the southern roil and rant [A:32].

A:32

GaysOne of the constituencies represented by Gates in the expanded Ekklesia before the Last Conclave at Babylonia Bagascia [MB:562] [MB:566].

GazelleOne of the animals furnishing the Boy King Melchisedech with what is called silk but is identified as milk in actuality, along with the camel, ass, ewe, cow, and India buffalo. This belongs to the more genuine childhood behind his temporal lives [MTM B1:17-18].

MTM B1:17-18

GdanskBaltic port near the mouth of the Vistula, where the disguised Kasmir Gorshok joins Duffey and Brannagan aboard the Argo. They initially fail to recognize him; his identification reveals Casey Szymansky, a true Argo Master [MTM B13:424-426].

Gedanken von LeibernGedanken von Leibern, the work credited to Ignace Wolff beneath the epigraph to Chapter Five, The Unaccountable Corpse, of The Devil is Dead. The passage makes bodies the exception to non-contradiction and denies sufficient reason for their existence [D:67].

Gedanken von LiebernEarlier heading reversed letters in the source’s title Gedanken von Leibern. See Gedanken von Leibern.
GeldingCastrated male horse. While planning his sea-stallion paintings, Finnegan imagines a stallion’s lunging gallop as a breaker and declares a sea gelding impossible [D:60].

D:60

GemsJewels in several literal and figurative settings. Ignatius Ti's account of Amoy's former life as a thieving bird includes a swallowed blue diamond, star sapphires, and opals [A:80-81]. Hilary Hilton says he has traded Finnegan diamonds [A:255], while Duffey says Finnegan and Joseph distribute diamonds to Finnegan's friends [MTM B10:303]. Primary documents are compared to treasures of gold and gems brought into daylight [MTM B6:185]. The Royal Pop lecturer wears a turban with a sparkling gem or eye [MTM B11:324]; he says two dozen cheap gems inside the Decatur Street Opera House preserve its complete history [MTM B11:328].
