Gene poolIn conversation with Gertrude Brannagan about Eva, Duffey says that every few centuries another of her people is released from cold storage to contribute to the gene pool. He predicts no disturbance until their proportion reaches about one in ten thousand and qualifies their supposed unfallen state as a popular legend they themselves believe [MTM B13:410].

General JudgmentThe final judgment of humanity. In the theological discussion surrounding the Casey Machine, a soggy sinner asks whether everyone will know all human thoughts and deeds after the Particular or General Judgment. His pastor says everyone will know, but is unsure at which judgment full knowledge arrives; he distinguishes the saved person’s joy from the damned person’s suffering [CM:504].

CM:504

GenesisFirst book of the Bible. In the discussion of Casey and evil, the narrator invokes Genesis for the human heart’s evil from youth, an allusion to Genesis 8:21 [A:154]. Creation and the Flood also shape the Fundamentalers’ chronology when they compare it with Zabotski’s Pristine History [MTM B9:278-280].

A:154; MTM B9:278-280

Genesis 14:18The verse about Melchisedech, king of Salem, bringing out bread and wine supplies the epigraph to Book Two, “Late Boyhood of a Magus” [MTM B2:38]. It links Duffey’s name to the biblical king and priest and introduces the bread-and-wine imagery associated with him.

MTM B2:38

Genesis 6:4The verse about giants, divine sons, human daughters, and ancient men of renown is the epigraph to Chapter Fourteen, Company of Fifty, of The Devil is Dead. Finnegan immediately answers with the mighty men of the present and asks why his remembered short, stooped earth-people have been remembered as giants [D:212].

Geni in the BottleImage in Trinali’s wine-making poem. After describing wine as a divine birth and resurrection, she identifies the Geni in the Bottle with a God imprisoned by the dry desert people who hate that God [A:231].

GeniusIntellectual or creative power in several registers. Letitia’s question about the block’s confounded geniuses points to Casey, whose genius is then directly affirmed [MTM B4:115] [MTM B4:118]. His television projections depend on both electronic genius and psychic magnitude [MTM B12:380]. Brannagan calls Finnegan an impelled genius [MTM B13:453], and Enniscorthy Sweeny is called a near-genius [MTM B13:467]. The Balbo dynasty retains its genius even as its members become mad [MB:558]. Duffey tells the cured stutterer that removing his frustration turns an evil genius into a good or at least complacent one [MTM B13:431]. The postscript’s argument about Havelock Ellis leads to the assertion that all humanity consists of glowing geniuses [PS:477].

Gentleman burglarOne of the former occupations X attributes to Papadiabolous II, Gregory McColum Papadiabolous, who also uses the name Noonan. Before police work he was a gentleman burglar, contrabandist, swindler, and forger; X says that training later proved useful [D:285-286].

Gentleman RounderMagazine for which Absalom Stein has agreed to write reviews after returning from the Devildom. His daughter Becky describes its contempt for ordinary people and worries over his new sense of superiority [MTM B12:355]. John Rattigan calls time on the boys' school sales with 'Time, gentlemen,' and Lily Koch uses the corresponding address to ladies and gentlemen [MTM B1:27] [MTM B1:29]. Duffey advertises a quality gentlemen's bar and club; eight shabby drinking gentlemen soon occupy a loafers' bench [MTM B2:41] [MTM B2:44]. Bagby's tall tale fills the former horse-barn flophouse with five hundred and fifty men sleeping on hooks [MTM B2:44-45]. Finnegan remembers Buffalo's droll gentlemen and ladies [A:191]. In the Louisiana swamps, Duffey and Brannagan meet three hospitable gentlemen: Leonard Archive, Oliver Greenflag, and Harry A. Honeybucket Kincaid [MTM B13:417].

Gerecke, WilliamOne of Saxon Seaworthy's two cronies, with Peter Wirt, in the Brunhilde's ruling circle [D:30]. Finnegan senses in him the same disturbing power associated with Seaworthy, Papa Devil, and the other peculiar people [D:50]. After the deaths of both Papadiabolouses, X names Gerecke among the four remaining rulers [D:155]. GermanLanguage and background associated with Hans Schultz and his German father John William, who teaches him German and Latin [A:208]. Hans receives a German letter from his father [A:39]; Casey learns German and Polish from his own father [A:156] [A:159]. X travels as the supposed West German Karl Metz and is later said to be one-quarter German through his mother's family [MTM B12:369] [MTM B12:371-372]. German lunches belong to Duffey and his school friends' outings [MTM B1:25]. The Bavarian Club has Germanish blonde entertainers, including Helen Platner [MTM B2:58], and German women attend St. Malachy's in Chicago [MTM B3:88]. Duffey's stolen medal stock includes what he calls the German Blue Max [MTM B4:115-116]. Hilary Hilton trades German clay [A:255]. Hackenschmidt addresses the conclave in a bright German-silver voice [MB:567].

German clayCommodity Hilary Hilton includes in his wide-ranging trade, alongside such goods as uncased Swiss movements, tropical birds, and private libraries [A:255].

Germanies, TheDesignation for German lands: Conrad Stone Hackenschmidt comes from Weinsburg in the Germanies [MB:566], while Duffey includes Conrad the Second of the Germanies among the kings whose conclaves he remembers attending [MTM B5:166].

MB:566; MTM B5:166

GhostAn apparition, double, surviving presence, or figure of estrangement. Finnegan feels like a defective ghost searching for his misplaced soul [A:56]; he later calls X his antipodal ghost [D:209]. Private Gregory identifies ghosts with devils in the psychiatric ward's storytelling [A:84-87]. Gautier's pipes account for ghost music in the swamps, and he may himself be the supposed ghost of Harlow House; the claim of seeing ghosts concerns his goats [A:197]. Archipelago's fantastical account of Black Papua includes a nightly ghost life and a waterfall that disappears after the morning rain [A:36-37]. Mary Louise Byrne is apparition-like, and Beth Keegan's living-statue quality prompts the observation that such stories are ghost stories [MTM B2:55] [MTM B2:57]. Teresa describes Finnegan's ghostly visits and inhabiting of people [MTM B6:188]; accounts of his reported deaths leave his survival disputed [MB:548-549]. Mary Virginia encounters Duffey as a ghost after his death in the crash year, while young Teresa sees him in an alternate ending and suggests he can be a young ghost [MTM B12:359-361] [MTM B13:472-473]. Other uses retain their narrative qualifications. Le Marin tells a disputed story of the deserted Sarcophagus and his own disappearance [D:243-246]. Soldiers unable to silence the Sea-Bell and Martyr-Bell near San Simeon call them ghost bells [MB:560] [MB:576]. The apparent supernatural clientele of the Ghost Bar is immediately retracted in favor of Anthony Ghost's coffee shop, though Finnegan's painting remains [MTM B10:292-293]. The epigraph credited to Carmody Overlark connects ghostliness with the other people's inherited mental powers [D:270-272]. In the postscript, Lafferty calls his continuing work A Ghost Story and links the phrase to everyone's capacity to split into ghostly aspects; high spirits can make such multiplicity visible [PS:475] [PS:477-478].

Ghost BarName used in the initially supernatural description of the Ghost Coffee Shop in New Orleans. Ghosts supposedly meet before and after dawn to exchange haunting stories, with a Finnegan painting of their gathering on the wall. The narrator then retracts the whole account except the painting and substitutes the account of Anthony Ghost's ordinary clientele [MTM B10:292-293].

MTM B10:292-293

Ghost Coffee Shop, TheNew Orleans coffee shop run by Anthony Ghost, whose father came from the Netherlands. Its morning customers include dock workers, seamen, wandering Quarter people, night people compared to ghosts, and schoolchildren. Ursuline Academy day students come for breakfast after early mass at the Cathedral. Duffey, a customer for thirty years, talks there with Crissie Cristofero, Therese Doucet, and Cleo Mahoney about Seven Roads; Rebeka Stein sometimes joins the girls [MTM B10:293]. The preceding account of literal ghosts is retracted, but the large Finnegan painting of their gathering remains [MTM B10:292].

MTM B10:293; MTM B10:292

Ghost, AnthonyProprietor of the Ghost Coffee Shop in New Orleans, whose father came from the Netherlands. His customers include dock workers, seamen, night people and schoolchildren; Duffey has been coming there for thirty years [MTM B10:293]. During the discussion of Seven Roads and the potholes that lead into alternate futures, Anthony tells Duffey that he will step into a pothole if one is nearby [MTM B10:294].

MTM B10:293; MTM B10:294

GhostlinessThe books' recurring uncertainty about apparitions, doubles, bodily identity, and the division between living and dead. The postscript calls Lafferty's continuing work A Ghost Story because people can split into aspects without knowing which is the self and which the ghost [PS:475]. It treats visible multiplicity as common but commonly suppressed in memory, illustrating the idea with Fingal's nine black-cloaked fetches accompanying his white-cloaked self and an alleged beheaded double of Charles I [PS:477-478]. These are the postscript's accounts. Mary Virginia calls ghosts the essence of ambiguity while addressing Duffey, whom she says has been dead for months; he fades from her view and withdraws from the crash year [MTM B12:359-361]. The psychiatric-ward stories distinguish several explanations. Private Gregory identifies ghosts with devils and calls possession hypnotism by an immortal will, with great men serving as inhabited shells [A:84-85]. Howell locates the horror in the familiar dead returning and says Irish wake stories temper it with humor. Gregory attributes early fears of revenants to anti-Christian stories of the risen Christ [A:85]. Ignatius Ti explains midnight as a temporary opening in the veil through which the dead may return; he describes fear of corpses and drunken medical pranksters, then tells of a wife who unknowingly sleeps beside her murdered husband's ghost. After his departure, the narrator allows loose ghosts into the ward and the boys' thoughts [A:85-87]. Finnegan's ghostliness includes his sense of being a defective ghost seeking a soul [A:56] and of looking out from a stranger's body [A:92]. Vincent calls Theresa a literal ghost and compares her with Finnegan [A:112]. Teresa later writes that Finnegan inhabits Vincent and herself, that a visitation frightened Stein, and that person and ghost can coexist. She claims the same talent and identifies herself as Anemotrephes in a detached experience rather than a dream [MTM B6:188]. Dotty calls Finnegan her ghost-lover, explicitly distinguishes this from Teresa's intimacy with him, and says Teresa and Finnegan were never lovers [MTM B6:188-189]. Stein's accounts question the repeated reports of Finnegan's death [MTM B6:187] [MB:548-549]. Sally and Duffey see a young painter as a possible younger ghost or fetch of him [MTM B11:333]. After Anastasia's death, Finnegan says he too is dead; he later calls X his antipodal ghost [D:156] [D:209]. Dopey leaves a presence Finnegan senses in his bunk [D:64] [D:78]. Papadiabolous II offers the possibility that Dopey was Finnegan's fetch and was absorbed into him; he describes himself as the close double of another [D:121-122]. The apparent return of the buried Papa Devil terrifies Seaworthy [D:84], but X's later account distinguishes two Papadiabolouses [D:285-286]. Finnegan's dream encounters with the Oreads and an old Teras belong to the same uncertain border of person, kindred, and apparition [D:137-140]. Le Marin's tale of the deserted Sarcophagus instead explains the disappearing crew through doubles, piracy, and murder, and is challenged as a recycled Mary Celeste story [D:243-246]. Duffey's alternate ending places him beyond ordinary sight until five-year-old Teresa Piccone recognizes a ghost who has either died or not yet been born. She also reports talking to Vincent, dead before her birth. She proposes keeping in touch by playing ghost, suggests that Duffey can be young again, and offers to give him a future birth [MTM B13:472-473]. Mary Louise Byrne's resemblance to an apparition and Beth Keegan's living-statue effect offer other personal forms of ghostliness [MTM B2:55-57]. Newton Prescott describes himself as Casey's orange-gloved ghostly splinter, subject to shifting years and retained as Casey's eyes and ears. The apartment viewers glimpse his hands, while the rental lady sees and speaks with him; he connects her ability to the Casey Machine [CM:515-516]. The Argo's mechanical crew are expressly place tokens or materialized residues of absent sailors, rather than wraiths or effigies [MTM B13:415]. Places and events also carry uncertain ghostliness. Archipelago gives Black Papua a nightly life among the dead [A:37]. Gautier makes the swamp's ghost music; the haunting of Harlow House remains uncertain, and apparent ghost-seeing belongs to his goats [A:197]. Chosky Bottoms is a movable spook-place [D:274]. The supernatural description of New Orleans ghosts arriving along Ste. Ann, Dumaine, St. Philip, Ursulines, Decatur, Chartres, Bourbon, Frenchman, and Elysian Field is retracted in favor of Anthony Ghost's coffee shop and ordinary night people; the Finnegan painting survives the retraction [MTM B10:292-293]. The Royal Pop upheaval dislodges evil spirits and uncreations [MTM B11:314], while Duffey and Stein discuss phenomena that unhappen and become unremembered [MTM B11:339-340]. The Thinking Machine proposes guarding blind fireplaces against blind spirits [MTM B13:455-456]. Casey's school notebook identifies human attackers behind one alleged poltergeist encounter without treating that explanation as disproof of all poltergeists [A:164]. Corporeal remains keep these questions concrete. The Devil is Dead announces people unwilling to stay dead [D:6]. Its first remembered encounter stands across from the graveyard, while Finnegan later recalls first meeting Seaworthy inside it and helping put Papa Devil over an older burial [D:10] [D:75-76]. The later graveyard rendezvous with X and Doll locates the grave marked I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch [D:275-277]. X takes custody of Duffey's ashes, expecting to return them to him alive [MTM B13:442]. Demetrio Glauch reports a Crock advertisement selling dead bodies as emptied temples [PG:546]; John Mogul describes his own killing business as the work of a knacker and euthanasiast [MB:572-573]. These uses of bodies accompany the ghost theme without themselves proving an apparition.

Ghostly ThingUnlocated phrase in the working glossary, associated there with a paean sung by Sergeant Murphy's subjects. Its source and proposed connection with the Holy Ghost remain unverified.
Giant HandsThe hands of Duffey's giants, which can be visible although their owners are invisible. As a boy he commands a giant hand to pull a church bell rope, and three companions see it [MTM B1:15]. His giants break rocks and release springs and rivers; their hands also make exceptionally intricate conjuring props [MTM B1:18] [MTM B1:21]. Moving a mountain is a hypothetical possibility when Morris Poor challenges him [MTM B4:129]. Giant hands then lift a mule across a traffic island, seen by some witnesses and sensed by all. The photographs differ: one shows the airborne mule without hands, another shows hands with possible double-exposure blurs [MTM B4:131-132]. In Duffey's dream the hands arrive severed at the forearms, bloodied, powerless, and manacled; they then resolve into a little boy's mittens joined by a drawstring [MTM B2:68]. A picture of Severed Giant Hands hangs above the doorway to the Rounders' Club's Elegant Riverboat Deck. Before his own creations, Duffey feels comparably deprived of creative power [MTM B5:156].

MTM B1:15; MTM B1:18; MTM B1:21; MTM B4:129; MTM B4:131-132; MTM B2:68; MTM B5:156

Giant(s)Duffey commands visible and invisible giants to perform miracles, including breaking rocks, releasing water, ringing a bell, and lifting a mule [MTM B1:5] [MTM B1:15] [MTM B1:18] [MTM B4:131-132]. His ebony or faber-giants help manufacture difficult props; more external art giants guide him toward works by others that surpass excellence [MTM B1:21] [MTM B2:54]. Dandy Dan Dillard seems to rout the giants during Duffey's apparent beating, but Duffey discovers that he has won the fight unmarked and that Dan is the injured fighter [MTM B2:51]. Four black demiurgic giants carry Casey's head-only person in Duffey's television projection from an Adam Scanlon painting; the head is explicitly not shown as severed [MTM B12:381]. Other uses differ in kind. Genesis 6:4 supplies the giants epigraph [D:212]; Patrick Stranahan laments the Church's closed age of giants [A:110]. Papa is called a giant [D:110], while the Majesty is an evil, illusory giant whose mind Duffey enters [MTM B8:241] [MTM B8:243]. A little boy's account makes the Wiper-Person a cloud-high giant who erases clouds and memories [CM:513]. Henry's mythological identities include the Giant of the Beanstalk [A:39]; Marie is the Golden Giantess [D:33]. Giant creatures include the spider in Hans's climbing dream [A:61], squid in Trinali's fanciful account of driftwood [A:233], and the stag in Finnegan's transport into ancestral memory [D:213]. Finnegan's island-creation story invokes great sea turtles [A:35], and San Simeon's legends include the giant huracan bird [MB:557-558].

MTM B1:5; MTM B1:15; MTM B1:18; MTM B4:131-132; MTM B1:21; MTM B2:54; MTM B2:51; MTM B12:381; D:212; A:110; D:110; MTM B8:241; MTM B8:243; CM:513; A:39; D:33; A:61; A:233; D:213; A:35; MB:557-558

Giwa, JohnJohn Giwa of Anecho, the thirteenth double or shadow-man and the replacement for dead Cardinal Doki of Douala. He flies to Marseille, cuts twelve fingers and thumbs from John Mogul's hands, skewers Mogul's tongue, then travels through Miami and parachutes onto Mooring Rock to join the other twelve conclave members. The narrator calls him violent and holy. He says their inner revelation assures them that at least one member is a true cardinal, enough for the conclave's legitimacy [MB:596]. He blesses the risen land as Babylonia Sancta and asks the dead Melchisedech to speak living words. X calls the vote and crowns Finnegan; Giwa greets him with “Reign in grace, Pope Finnegan the First” [MB:597]. When the impersonator of Cardinal Mercy is revealed as a woman, Giwa demands an explanation from X [MB:598].

MB:596; MB:597; MB:598

Glauch, DemetrioWriter and contributor to the Crock under Duffey; a wartime issue includes his ballad [A:41] [MTM B4:138]. Casey names him among Duffey's prospects for the Catholic Center Party of America [A:42]. He denounces the Curley Q and the establishments of Fleshpot Row on Randolph Street as a stifling bawdy house and leaves. Duffey's reluctance to leave with him creates lasting disappointment between them [MTM B4:125-127]. He is present when Morris Poor challenges Duffey's magic and later attends Hilary Hilton's party [MTM B4:128] [MTM B12:383]. Glauch signs the opening assessment of Casey in “Promontory Goats,” dated All Souls Day, Chicago, 1984 [PG:518-519]. In a later commentary he reports that Casey's own supporters or associates have stolen the body, recalling a Crock advertisement for corpses [PG:546].

A:41; MTM B4:138; A:42; MTM B4:125-127; MTM B4:128; MTM B12:383; PG:518-519; PG:546

Globigerina glacéFantastical salad ordered by Duffey during the Argo Masters' visit to Honeybucket Kincaid's swamp establishment. He also orders chlamydomonas with kelp syrup, pond-scum bread, sea-lice soup, and a Hashed-Ectocarpus Collins [MTM B13:417]. The name borrows Globigerina, a real genus of foraminifera. Kincaid's electrical equipment selects and prepares the fish in this meal, but the text does not specify how the salad is made [MTM B13:417].

MTM B13:417

Glotglutz, OttoNightclub comedian nicknamed Glotzie and described as a sick comedian. Hiram III's unexpected answering quip reduces him to tears, while shocked onlookers cry “Shame! Shame!” [MB:564].

MB:564

GodThe characters’ accounts of God range from comic claims to questions about creation, salvation, and the fate of particular people. In Ward Fourteen, Green says that God sustains the universe from moment to moment, identifies himself as God, and demonstrates his power by dimming the lights; Gregory points out that a compressor has just been switched on [A:76]. Sulem says that God has forgotten to give Finnegan a tujuan, or direction in life [A:60]. Askandan, by contrast, assures Finnegan that he has a soul and that God is in him [A:258].

Patrick Stranahan says their faith forbids them to regard anyone as doomed [A:102]. Henry answers the practical problem of rebuilding the world by saying that God gave them each other [A:126]. The account of Finnegan and Theresa’s uncertain twelve years together ends in gratitude for the richness of that life [A:204]. Don Lewis asks whether God knows the singulars who seem to have been forgotten [D:48].

The seventh contingency brings Duffey into a garden with the Invisible God, who affirms the uniqueness of every person [MTM B10:301] [MTM B12:389]. Later, God comes aboard the Argo and tells Duffey’s bones that death has not released him from his work as pilot and master [MTM B13:443].

Other references include the discussion of holy wealth and holy poverty [MTM B4:125], Theresa’s blessing of the wine [A:108], and Seaworthy’s comic threat of divine punishment for bad beer [D:12]. X’s explanation of “Bogovitch” as “son of God” describes a euphemism on a gravestone, not a literal statement of the buried Devil’s divine parentage [D:277-278].

A:76; A:60; A:258; A:102; A:126; A:204; D:48; MTM B10:301; MTM B12:389; MTM B13:443; MTM B4:125; A:108; D:12; D:277-278

God's spy (Zophiel)Unverified heading in the working glossary for a supposed speculation by Duffey about a divine spy or faculty called Zophiel. No supporting passage has been located in the three core books.
Goldbeater, ClementName credited with an Enniscorthy Chronicle passage used as the epigraph to Chapter Ten, “Down with the Dead Men,” in The Devil Is Dead. Its children play at being the Other Kind of People while remaining indistinguishable from ordinary people, introducing the chapter's uncertainty over identity [D:143].

D:143

Goldchild, HarryWealthy benefactor who had the Golden Children's Home and Haven Orphanage built and endowed several decades before the Zabotski episode. The narrator calls him a bloated plutocrat [MTM B9:280].

MTM B9:280

Golden Children's Home and Haven OrphanageOrphanage behind Zabotski's building site, founded and endowed decades earlier by Harry Goldchild and distinguished by a golden roof [MTM B9:271] [MTM B9:280]. His expanding contraption encroaches on its grounds, and the state inspector orders that part removed [MTM B9:274]. Widow Waldo serves the orphans, who assemble green-clay animals capable of moving, though the early ones fall apart [MTM B9:275]. Children carry these animals into the contraption; Waldo, children, and animals depart with Zabotski during the flood, and his craft subsequently reaches his lot on Lake Borgne [MTM B9:284] [MTM B9:287].

MTM B9:271; MTM B9:280; MTM B9:274; MTM B9:275; MTM B9:284; MTM B9:287

Golden Ogress, The (Marie Courtois)Finnegan's name for Marie Courtois, Seaworthy's seagoing secretary, whom he first remembers as the Golden Ogress in an apparent dream while she collects his details for the ship's register [D:32]. She is also the Golden Giantess, a formidable red-gold-haired woman whose strength and beauty are described in primordial terms. Anastasia, her roommate, alternates rivalry and quarrelling with friendship; she calls Marie “la giganta dorada” when Marie rows with exceptional power [D:33] [D:37] [D:57]. In an ocean dream of uncertain bodily reality, Marie identifies herself as both Demeter and Persephone, annually returning from Hell. She argues with Finnegan about immortality, boasts of blood on her hands, and encloses him in her hair in an ambiguously presented seduction [D:91-92]. Finnegan later recognizes her as Don Lewis's murderer; she revels in the killing, and the narration attributes her ability to do it to her extraordinary strength [D:112-113].

D:32; D:33; D:37; D:57; D:91-92; D:112-113

Goldfarb's AlleySuppertime family television comedy playing at Randal's during Hilary Hilton's gathering for Duffey and his old friends. Duffey superimposes an animated version of Adam Scanlon's painting: four black giants carry Casey as a screaming head-only person, explicitly not a severed head [MTM B12:380-381]. Viewers initially mistake the violence for the show's usual comedy, then react with terror or rush into the streets to rescue their cult hero. Even the comedy's pictured characters flee the screen [MTM B12:381].

MTM B12:380-381; MTM B12:381

Golgi bodiesCellular organelles associated with processing and sorting proteins and lipids. A passage attributed to the Eighteenth Book of Strange Encounters includes secretion of Golgi bodies around the lipid vesicule among the alleged tests proving Duffey more than four thousand years old, although his body's material is said to be only fifty-five years old [MTM B8:250]. The real biological term is incorporated into the fictional report's extravagant catalogue of age measurements.

MTM B8:250

Gompertz function analogiesOne of the alleged age measurements in the Eighteenth Book of Strange Encounters report that Duffey is more than four thousand years old. It appears beside Howship's lacunar frequency and numerous other technical-sounding measurements [MTM B8:250]. The phrase borrows Gompertz's name from mathematical work on human mortality, but the fictional report gives no procedure or explanation of its supposed analogies.

MTM B8:250

Gonof, AgaFather of Orestes Gonof. Charlotte says he owns boats carrying liquor from Canada to Chicago, Detroit, and Cleveland, and that one of her husbands dealt with him. He has deposited the stash she seeks; she claims five percent belongs to her and proposes taking the rest as interest. Duffey says it did not rightfully belong to either her or the depositor, who is about to leave confinement [MTM B3:83-84]. Duffey mentally reconstructs the safety-deposit key, and Charlotte goes to have it made [MTM B3:84].

MTM B3:83-84; MTM B3:84

Gonof, Orestes (Captain Gonof)Captain of the Brunhilde and a member of Seaworthy's inner circle, though he can seem an almost forgotten figure [D:30] [D:100]. He takes part in the pursuit of Don Lewis in Tangier, but Don thinks he is not following seriously [D:108]. His reaction on approaching a Greek island is said to reveal his origin [D:115]. After both the true and false Papadiabolous have died, he joins Seaworthy, Gerecke, and Wirt in the ruling four. X calls him exceptionally shrewd and evil; Finnegan says Gonof means thief and is not Greek [D:155]. At the later meeting watched by Finnegan, he is the largest and most menacing of the four senior gargoyles [D:163].

D:30; D:100; D:108; D:115; D:155; D:163

Good Guy's, TheNew Orleans jazz club visited by Duffey, Bagby, Mary Louise, and Salvation Sally. Duffey ranks its music alongside the Rounders' Club's. Its band plays Monumental Jazz, prompting his reflections on classical jazz's aging and diminished inventiveness. Bagby takes a horn and plays the Gadarene Swine Song, and the band joins in [MTM B7:220].

MTM B7:220

Gordon, Harold (Shrimp Boat)Harold “Shrimp Boat” Gordon, a regular at the Old Wooden Ship in Galveston [D:215] [MTM B13:458]. He, Tom, and Barney are commercial fishermen who seldom fish: after assessing sea, sky, and weather, they often decide to stay at the Ship and drink [D:220].

D:215; MTM B13:458; D:220

GorgiosThe Sergeant's term for non-Romanies or outsiders, humorously defined as everyone outside the Dirty Five. He says the group taught the Jojos Polish, which the Jojos thought was English and the Gorgios mistook for a Malayan dialect [A:73].

A:73

GospelThe Christian good news. Henry Salvatore says that the poor need the Gospel preached to them and condemns mouths unable to name Holy Poverty [A:125]. Margaret Stone's urgent street preaching concerns the Resurrection and Real Presence, including people on Dauphin Street at midnight [A:144]. Duffey examines a palimpsest containing a first-century copy, or possible original, of the Fourth Gospel, with notes in pagona shorthand; the child-hero then calls it the original [MTM B11:327]. The Fourth Gospel is John, conventionally dated in its final form to about AD 90-100. Tony Apostolo imagines an angel bringing a Fifth Gospel as a hypothetical news story he would already have covered, not an actual new gospel or angelic visitation [PG:525].

A:125; A:144; MTM B11:327; PG:525

GothicA word used across architectural, typographical, literary, and historical imagery. The Crock's title is printed in black Gothic [A:41]. Gautier calls Balzac's Les Contes Drolatiques Gothic when defending his readings to the goats [A:198]. Finnegan climbs a Gothic hotel and appears as its living gargoyle; Gertrude Brannagan's ample, curly, parapetted appearance becomes Living Gothic [D:162] [D:200]. Countess Margaret mentions, then rejects, the theory that her people are a fragment of a migrating Gothic nation [MTM B8:255]. Duffey's ordeal unfolds under a Gothic sky that he recognizes as a Finnegan sky [MTM B12:393]. An unlabelled speaker in “Promontory Goats” remembers Justinian's skull amid an empire disappearing into Gothic fog [PG:545]. Historically, Gothic names a medieval architectural style prominent from the twelfth through sixteenth centuries and a later literary tradition of terror and the uncanny flourishing in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

A:41; A:198; D:162; D:200; MTM B8:255; MTM B12:393; PG:545

GothsGermanic people associated with the invasions of Roman territories in late antiquity. In X's account of the Devil's Crimean imprisonment, the Goths supposedly call the peninsula Cherson [MTM B6:204]. Countess Margaret also mentions and rejects the idea that her people broke off from a migrating Gothic nation [MTM B8:255].

MTM B6:204; MTM B8:255

GourdContainer from which the Sergeant and a Malayan boy drink jungle juice during his noon-dream of leaving the psychiatric ward and revisiting old companions [A:88] [A:90].

A:88; A:90

GovernessKatie Noonan's occupation in a landed Polish household. X says that Irish governesses commonly taught English to such families and were valued for lower wages, Catholic instruction, and manners. Katie worked in Gregory's home, left some months before the birth of Ifreann Columkill, and returned several weeks afterward [D:279].

D:279

GovernorIn Sulem’s explanation, the liver is the governor of the body and one proposed location of the tujuan, the direction assigned to a life; he distinguishes this from the semangat or soul [A:60]. The governor of San Simeon’s northern province receives Mad King Gaetano VI’s prohibition of bell-ringing and sends forces against the newly sounding Sea-Bell [MB:560].

A:60; MB:560

GoyimTerm for Gentiles or non-Jews. Stein welcomes the appearance of noble noses among the goyim [A:127]. Thadal, one of the Three Slant-Faced Men identified as crooked kings, is called King of the Nations or of the Goyim [MTM B7:227].

A:127; MTM B7:227

GraceDivine favor or a state opposed to damnation, with other uses as charm and delight. Finnegan’s return to drink at Freetown on January 26 is a fall from grace, accompanied by his joke about falling from a woman named Grace [D:93]. Casey says his own fall from grace preceded his doubt [A:153]. Grace and pleasure belong to Finnegan and Theresa’s other life or dream [A:204]; Elena later asks whether he is dangerously fallen from grace [A:274]. Niccolo distinguishes killing a victim in a possible state of grace from killing to secure damnation [A:280]. Duffey says he has walked in grace three days out of four throughout his life [MTM B12:390]. Margaret Stone invokes grace for the unwilling souls of the masked hecklers [MTM B7:232]; later, her promise that none of her acquaintances will be lost raises the disputed question of the Devil’s salvation [MTM B13:447]. In separate uses, Lily Koch calls part of New Orleans’s architectural mixture Place de Grace French [MTM B7:215], and Grace Plunkett is named with Jerome among Duffey’s university friends [MTM B3:99].

D:93; A:153; A:204; A:274; A:280; MTM B12:390; MTM B7:232; MTM B13:447; MTM B7:215; MTM B3:99

GradualLiturgical text heard at Vincent and Theresa’s wedding Mass. Vincent finds its images of a fruitful wife and children like olive plants comical and points them out to Theresa, called Show Boat [A:113].

A:113

GraduateDuffey promises to return next year when Maurine Stranahan graduates; she is then finishing eleventh grade [A:100]. In the narrator’s recurring vision, graduate students watch a composite great mathematician demonstrate changes to the universe [PG:542].

A:100; PG:542

Grail, HolyThe Sancgreal, an object of medieval Arthurian romance whose literary tradition begins in the late twelfth century. In the Argo’s legendary quest history, the Masters recover the Holy Grail that had been stolen from Glastonbury [MTM B13:422].

MTM B13:422

GrainMillet and rice stolen by Amoy in Ignatius Ti’s account of the bird’s earlier life [A:80], and weevily grain that Askandanakandrian claims special skill in rehabilitating [A:257]. Beth interprets Duffey’s lost years as seven sheaves of grain [MTM B2:69]. Poisonous fruit and grain form an image of the dangerously pleasurable harvests of his New Orleans golden age [MTM B7:210]. X recommends taking his information on Infiltrates with a grain of salt [A:137], while Casey’s notebook praises the taller grain of the Great Lakes region in his imaginative comparison with the Mediterranean [A:166].

A:80; A:257; MTM B2:69; MTM B7:210; A:137; A:166

Grand BanksFishing grounds off Newfoundland, used in the narrator’s description of Casey as fishy as the Grand Banks themselves [PG:544].

PG:544

Grand CanaryGran Canaria, one of the Canary Islands, where the Brunhilde party stays two days [D:96]. Finnegan reads reports of upheavals following the ship’s recent ports of call, and Don Lewis tells him that they have been setting those fires [D:98-99]. At a luxurious dinner Papa Devil completes his resemblance to Count von Baummenbauch by inserting a monocle; the glittering company includes Don Lewis already marked for death [D:99-100]. Archipelago recalls Finnegan drinking brandy there and learning about mermaids from one of them [A:188].

D:96; D:98-99; D:99-100; A:188

Grand ConcourseApproach feeding the newly present Decatur Street in the Royal Pop People’s altered New Orleans. A thousand horse carriages pass through it on their way to the opera without crowding [MTM B11:346].

MTM B11:346

Grand MannerEarlier glossary label for Marie Courtois’s sumptuous dress on the Mexican shore. The source describes her as dressed in the “high manner,” drawing the crowd’s admiration [D:57].

D:57

Grandes, LosSeaworthy and his associates Wirt and Gerecke, the powerful conspirators aboard the Brunhilde [D:109]. They go ashore with two seamen at a port whose identity is uncertain [D:67]. Anastasia watches Chris McAbney fill his pipe while he waits for them [D:68]. Don Lewis fears that they may arrange his murder through local men; he also lists Captain Gonof separately among possible killers [D:106] [D:109].

D:109; D:67; D:68; D:106

GrandfatherAncestry is literal, invented and unstable. Sulem makes the small protective amulet called the Grandfather of Finnegan [A:59-61]. Elena Angelino says her great-grandfather was a bear, a claim supported by the Professor but doubted by Hans [A:218]. X considers a manifestation of the Devil his own grandfather and the great-grandfather of Finnegan and Anastasia [D:279]; he also describes family names passing between generations, even from grandson to grandfather [D:278]. In Cuba, he speaks in the manner of his German maternal grandfather [MTM B12:372]. Philip Stranahan mistakes the older and younger appearances of Duffey for grandfather and grandson; Duffey says they are one [MTM B13:473]. San Simeon’s dynastic cycle requires the prince’s grandfather, the previous Mad King Emeritus, to die when the generations advance, but Gaetano’s failure to return delays the succession [MB:559]. Finnegan drunkenly styles himself grandfather of all the saltshakers [D:189].

A:59-61; A:218; D:279; D:278; MTM B12:372; MTM B13:473; MB:559; D:189

Grandfather of FinneganVery small protective amulet carved by Sulem, who believes Finnegan lacks the direction or tujuan needed to guide his life and hopes to trick the ruin awaiting him. It resembles a lizard and a toad, with steady eyes and loathsome integrity. Finnegan baptizes it Heliogabalus and wears it on a chain with his Miraculous Medal. The narrator says it stays with him to the end and is then mistaken for an object of another cult [A:59-61].

A:59-61

GrandsonIn X’s account of the Gregorovitch family’s confusing names, a father may even be named for his grandson [D:278].

D:278

GraniteRecurring image for Saxon Seaworthy’s aged, hard face: old granite, temporarily ashen at Papa Devil’s appearance, tired by the campfire, then relaxed and lit like old cliffs [D:11] [D:15] [D:22] [D:43] [D:48]. Finnegan later calls him a granite-faced fox [D:158] [D:165]. The old teras in Finnegan’s dream also has a gloomy granite face [D:140]. In Trinali’s poem, granite mountains are remnants of a statue’s fingers from an older world [A:227].

D:11; D:15; D:22; D:43; D:48; D:158; D:165; D:140; A:227

Grape CuttingsIn Ignacio’s account of Joseph of Maintz’s journey to the moon, grape cuttings accompany wheat, bread, wine, books and an altar stone so that the priest can continue celebrating Mass [A:271].

A:271

GrapesFruit grown on Naxos [D:125]. Trinali’s wine-making poem specifies a quart of water for every quart of grapes [A:231]. Duffey wishes Charlotte Garfield sons like clusters of green grapes around an old arbor [MTM B8:260].

D:125; A:231; MTM B8:260

GrapevinesAmong the authentic possessions of Melchisedech’s ancient life as the Boy King, set against the less substantial childhoods of his modern life [MTM B1:17].

MTM B1:17

GrassGautier cuts wild grass for his goats’ winter fodder; at their swamp camp Finnegan catches fish among grass roots standing in water [A:194-195]. The Dirty Five and Sammy sleep in high grass after riding the white horses [A:68-69], and Papapaleologus grazes below Finnegan and Anastasia on Naxos [D:132]. The word also appears in the Crock article title “Moles at the Grass Roots” [A:41] and in the comparison of Finnegan’s attack on the Pirate Hotel to a tiger entering a grass-hut village [D:231]. Grass greens Duffey’s remembered ancient country [MTM B1:6]; reed grass feeds the great beasts at Zabotski Flats [MTM B12:362]. The Argo appears to sail through a sea of grass along a weed-grown Louisiana canal [MTM B13:416]. Blood-of-Martyrs Grass reappears on the rising Mooring-Stone after its supposed extinction [MB:595].

A:194-195; A:68-69; D:132; A:41; D:231; MTM B1:6; MTM B12:362; MTM B13:416; MB:595

“Grass Roots (Moles at the)”“Moles at the Grass Roots,” an article in the Crock described as written in Duffey’s style [A:41].

A:41

GrasshoppersAn ancient grasshopper and its virus illustrate the Royal Pop History speaker’s claim that recorded stone patinas can reconstruct the past in minute detail. The speaker says the virus can be analyzed and prescribed for, though medication cannot yet be sent back to the insect [MTM B11:325].

MTM B11:325

Gratz, EframEfram Gate Gratz, one of the Princes of the Crowd at the Last Conclave. He voices their total animosity toward the Ekklesia, saying they have come to bury Peter and intend to kill him, desecrate his grave and prevent a recurrence of the institution [MB:561].

MB:561

GraveBurial places recur as sites of confused identity and return. The Promantia distinguishes an unnamed man buried twice in two graves from another who died twice [D:6]. Finnegan offers to deepen Seaworthy’s grave and helps bury Papa Devil atop an older body [D:75-76] [D:153]. The headstone later reads I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch [D:277]; the grave holds Ifreann Noonan Columkill and Gregory McIfreann [D:284]. X explains that Seaworthy killed Papadiabolous I while reopening his father’s grave for valuable information [D:288]. He calls the sought document a key, plans to recover it [D:290], and Doll drops her Diabolique verses through the split that has persisted since the second burial [D:293]. Finnegan plans to paint Anastasia among the dead in a common grave [D:61], and later buries Don Lewis in a shallow sandy grave [D:111]. Gregory describes possession as hypnotism from beyond the grave [A:84]. A grave without a stone appears among the closing obliterative verses of the Great Day [GD:501].

D:6; D:75-76; D:153; D:277; D:284; D:288; D:290; D:293; D:61; D:111; A:84; GD:501

Grave RegisterBurial register that X believes incomplete for earlier years while searching for the Devil’s grave. Despite inspecting more than two hundred graves, he needs Finnegan to lead him to the neglected marker [D:276].

D:276

GraveyardThe burial ground across the boulevard from the bar where Finnegan sits with Seaworthy [D:10]. Finnegan recalls meeting him there at night during Papa Devil’s burial [D:75-76]. He later returns to the club and crosses to meet Doll and X in the graveyard, where he identifies the Devil’s grave [D:275-277]. X’s remark that doubles do not grow even on graveyard yews belongs to his earlier explanation of the apparent resurrection [D:154]. Trinali calls her driftwood beach the Elephants’ Graveyard [A:232] and makes it the setting of To Trinali in the Old Wood Graveyard on the Dead Sea [A:235]. At the Great Day newspaper office, a staff member suggests that their undated publication might be a graveyard-shift paper [GD:487].

D:10; D:75-76; D:275-277; D:154; A:232; A:235; GD:487

GravityFigurative attraction and weight: Henri Salvatore is the center of gravity of any room he enters [MTM B5:161]; Duffey’s immense but light-moving creations seem to have come from other gravities and worlds [MTM B5:156-157]; and a Texas town draws the wandering Finnegan into its vortex [A:201].

MTM B5:161; MTM B5:156-157; A:201

GrayA recurring color: gray in Brannagan’s sandy hair [D:199], Doll’s eyes [D:173], Mary Virginia’s hair [MTM B11:318], the Naxos raider’s derby [D:147], and the St. Louis squirrels of Duffey’s childhood [MTM B1:17]. X’s nested containers include a gray box [A:136]. Bagby’s mental St. Louis consists of black, white and gray sketches [MTM B2:62]; Count Finnegan’s Ghost Bar painting uses ghost grays [MTM B10:292]; and the terrible sky above the fallen Duffey is gray-orange [MTM B12:393]. The Argo’s moral landscape distinguishes good gray from bad gray [MTM B13:437]. Hans’s meditation on Marie’s green eyes rejects the claim that vair denotes gray [A:24].

D:199; D:173; MTM B11:318; D:147; MTM B1:17; A:136; MTM B2:62; MTM B10:292; MTM B12:393; MTM B13:437; A:24

Gray BoxContainer inside the black box X brings to Duffey; inside it is a brown box. The nested boxes have been stolen from Casey and belong to the Crock [A:136].

A:136

Great Day Contingency, TheThe first of seven possible futures singled out in Book X from an indefinite number of contingencies. It abolishes boundaries and thereby persons. Duffey first imagined it as a joke, but the world’s misplaced faith makes his invention a trap for its inventor. Its theme is the clock stopped at “twelf” and the snake swallowing itself [MTM B10:298-299]. The seven alternatives are not all mutually exclusive. The Great Day is distinct from the fifth, the Thunder Colt Complex or Decatur Street Opera House Presentation [MTM B10:300-301].

The appended story “Great Day in the Morning” develops the same premise. Melchisedech, spelled Duffy in that story, finds his bitterly comic article being fulfilled as an emancipation from walls, clothes, skins, minds, and personal distinction. He calls for laughter to undo the disaster, but Mary Virginia and Salvation Sally reject it as incompatible with the new condition [GD:492-495]. The inhabitants merge into fleshy spheres while the sun remains suspended in its dawning [GD:496] [GD:498-499]. Duffy and Morpheus finally contract into a single-celled creature swallowing itself. Morpheus calls this a repeated beginning; the narrator points to an inaccessible hint of another outcome in Duffy’s old article and still finds persons and verses left to dispose of [GD:500-501].

MTM B10:298-299; MTM B10:300-301; GD:492-495; GD:496; GD:498-499; GD:500-501

“Great Day Rime”Verses of the Great Day that seem to hang everywhere in the air, both tongueless and soundless. Their nameless day interrupts the ordinary weekly sequence in Duffey’s thoughts as he reaches the Pelican Press [GD:490].

GD:490

Great Delta Insurance Company Building, TheBuilding whose tower clock is mutilated at the onset of the Great Day. Three young men saw both clock hands down to stubs; one falls and dies while descending. Duffey interprets the handless clock as a foretold sign of the turning-over and stopped time, while resisting the conclusion that the Great Thing has arrived [GD:483].

GD:483

Great Devil HimselfThe ultimate Devil, whose relation to the Devil-Released-From-Prison remains disputed. Stein sometimes regards the released devil as a minor decoy permitting the Devil Himself to work unnoticed, but on other days believes they are the same [MTM B10:291]. Margaret Stone says the devil she has met is covered by her promise of salvation but is not the Great Devil Himself, whom she has not known; Duffey counters that prevailing opinion identifies him as the Great Devil [MTM B13:447].

MTM B10:291; MTM B13:447

Great Horse Carriages of the PastCatalogue evoked by the Royal Pop History speaker from the memories of a Decatur Street flagstone: Acme Top and Acme Open, Southern Beauty, Fulton Road Cart, Livery Special, Farmers’ Canopy-Top Surrey, Johnson’s Jump-Seat Buggy, Imperial Carriage, Dempster’s Three-Spring Handy Wagon, Drexel’s Eight-Horse Dray, Pontiac’s Special Milk Wagon, Hallock’s Grocery Cart, Sears Famous and Road Runner [MTM B11:329]. The nostalgic display is undercut by the Countess’s admission that the new people are stealing human memories and claiming them as their own [MTM B11:329].

MTM B11:329

Great LakesThe American Mediterranean in item XXXIX of Casey’s school notebook. He imagines their surrounding regions as more abundant counterparts of Africa, Greece, Spain, Illyria and Italy, with Chicago at the center [A:166].

A:166

Great Mogul DiamondFamous Indian diamond discovered in the seventeenth century. It is among the prizes found in the Argo’s legendary history [MTM B13:422].

MTM B13:422

Great Pot ItselfThe thousand-gallon, glass-lined pot supplied by Zabotski for Duffey’s free soup project. Blessed by a priest from St. Katherine’s, it is to boil forever, receiving meat, fish and vegetables from people or secretly from God. Duffey fears that a lack of true Holy Poverty leaves nobody willing to receive its slumgullion, imperiling the project of rebuilding the world [MTM B6:194-195].

MTM B6:194-195

Great Ship ItselfThe larger Argo of earlier times. One opinion holds that the present, smaller Argo is only its ship’s boat or pinnacle, although the present vessel retains the great ship’s relics and identifications [MTM B13:403].

MTM B13:403

Great X-Capo, TheX’s former stage name as a magician and escape artist. He recalls being billed by this name on the circuits while boasting that he can open small locks with mittens on [A:137]. He later brings his old magician’s cloak to the graveyard meeting [D:276].

A:137; D:276

Greater Archipelago (The)The Land of the Animated Marvels, also called the Archipelago: a scattered recuperative island for the Argo whose people live chiefly in Chicago, St. Louis and New Orleans. They provide provisions, healing and virtues, and some are themselves Argo Masters. Its relation to the ship in time and space remains imperfectly understood [MTM B13:448].

MTM B13:448

Greater Chicago Phone DirectoryDirectory Casey brings uninvited onto the Castle Theatre stage during Goat Boy. Reading seven names from it in an ecstatic voice creates an overwhelming audience response and wins his bet, demonstrating his power to spellbind crowds [PG:543].

PG:543

Greater NeustriaStein’s name for the thousand-year domain of Christendom into which he imagines Hitler raiding backward from the future. His Notes on the Finnegan Cycle link this Neustria or Latter Neustria with the Devil’s imprisonment from 946 to 1946 [MTM B6:185]. The name adapts historical Neustria, the western Frankish kingdom of the Merovingian period, to a much broader fictional chronology.

MTM B6:185

Greatheart, MonaArtist among Duffey’s Chicago friends, listed with Cassius Greatheart in the golden-age circle of 1925-1935 and its later electrum phase to about 1946 [MTM B3:98]. She repeatedly models the visiting Monster Giulio in clay [MTM B3:106]. Duffey includes her among the women he loves [MTM B4:111], and compromising photographs later show him playing the funny lover with her [MTM B4:139].

MTM B3:98; MTM B3:106; MTM B4:111; MTM B4:139

Greb, HarryAmerican boxer (1894-1926). During his fighting binge, Finnegan boasts that he has beaten Harry Greb and therefore can beat the local challengers [D:191].

D:191

GreeceRegion in which the Brunhilde’s voyage brings Finnegan into the familiar world of his companions. At Zakinthos, Seaworthy and Gonof’s Greek origins emerge; at Naxos, the party reaches Anastasia’s home and the island associated with Ariadne [D:115]. Ancient and modern Greece mingle in Finnegan and Anastasia’s moonlit conversation, including their extravagant story of a bird flying behind the moon [D:132].

On Naxos, Finnegan confesses to a Greek Capuchin who speaks Italian [D:118-119]. After Anastasia’s death, an Orthodox priest says that he gave her the last rites [D:147-148]. Greece also appears among the countries where Ifreann lived, according to X’s reconstruction of his life [D:280]. See also Greek.

D:115; D:132; D:118-119; D:147-148; D:280

Greece (Ancient)Ancient cultural world invoked both playfully and polemically. Finnegan’s Naxos conversation leads to the narrator’s joke that the Greeks invented the moon [D:132], and Cosmopolis is called a Greek idea as the ship enters Greek waters [D:115]. Cyrus Roundhead, in his campaign to erase human history, claims that Greece consisted of Hellas and five concentric rings and that Macedonians invented heroic Greece and an imaginary Athens; John the Greek challenges him from personal memory [MTM B11:337].

D:132; D:115; MTM B11:337

GreekLanguage and cultural inheritance invoked in several distinct settings. Hans’s father demands Greek instruction for the fourth-grade pupils, but the priest replies that he does not know the language [A:209]. Hans himself puzzles over Greek words for the color of Marie’s eyes [A:24].

Finnegan’s Romaic is inadequate for confession on Naxos. The Greek Capuchin reproaches him for knowing too little Greek and argues that Italians should have retained it as their language [D:118-119]. Finnegan later has trouble following the Orthodox priest’s remarks after Anastasia’s death [D:147-148]. X explains Anastasia’s use of adelphos through what he calls its Old Greek sense of cousin as well as brother [D:279].

Other uses include the Greek Cross among the devices on Henry’s dream ship [A:44], the Greek name of a successor to Casey’s Crock [A:168], Teresa’s remarks about Greek performers at the Star and Garter [MTM B6:188], the qualified suggestion of Greek ancestry in Margaret Stone’s portrait [MTM B11:310], and Morpheus among the Greek gods in “Great Day in the Morning” [GD:500]. See also Greece.

A:209; A:24; D:118-119; D:147-148; D:279; A:44; A:168; MTM B6:188; MTM B11:310; GD:500

Greek AnthologyCollection of Greek epigrams transmitted through successive compilations, notably the Palatine manuscript of the tenth century and Maximus Planudes’s related anthology around 1300. Endymeon Ellenbogen boasts that he has translated the Greek Anthology among his other works [A:237].

A:237

Greek CrossOne of the symbolic devices on the Navicula Petri in Henry’s dream, alongside the Lamb, Fish and Six-Pointed Star [A:44].

A:44

Greek IslandNaxos, where Finnegan and Anastasia eat outdoors at Anastasia Grandmother’s mountain farm, discussing the island’s blue haze and the changing colors of skies [D:125] [D:127].

D:125; D:127

Greek, John theOwner of John the Greek’s Famous French Restaurant. At the Royal Pop History sessions in New Orleans, he challenges Cyrus Roundhead’s denial of Athens by saying that he lived there until he was thirteen [MTM B11:336-337]. His remembered life directly resists the attempt to abolish human history.

MTM B11:336-337

Greely Pack SaddlesPack saddles named by one drinker as the explanation for the padded leather straps in Duffey’s old horse barn. He says the former livery proprietor rented these superior saddles with horses and mules for excursions into the hills and woods. Another drinker gives a different explanation for the straps [MTM B2:45].

MTM B2:45

GreenColor used for eyes, complexions, landscapes, money, and changing life. Hans’s meditation on Marie’s green eyes connects Greek color terms, Romany, French, sacred images, and witches [A:24]. Anastasia has a sea-green touch in her complexion [D:20], and Finnegan also teases her about turning green with seasickness [D:28]. Sebastian Hilton’s complexion is pale greenish [MTM B1:22].

Finnegan describes islands as green and fiber-colored in his account of their creation [A:35]. Trinali speaks of the Green Castles and the Green Death in her stories of driftwood [A:233], and of the Green Groves of Gomorrah in a poem [A:235].

Green also belongs to Seaworthy’s money [D:18], Hillary Hilton’s stock of paint [A:250], the Green Mule drink [MTM B4:132], and the stain of money in a young admirer’s ideal of the rich beach bum [MTM B5:173]. Widow Waldo describes the children’s green-clay animals [MTM B9:275]. A Royal Pop Historian uses “green dust of life” in an account of making history [MTM B11:324]. The green bay tree appears on the Pope’s shield in the closing verses of “How Many Miles to Babylon” [MB:598]. See also Green (Private).

A:24; D:20; D:28; MTM B1:22; A:35; A:233; A:235; D:18; A:250; MTM B4:132; MTM B5:173; MTM B9:275; MTM B11:324; MB:598

Green (Private)Talkative soldier in Ward Fourteen. In the Sergeant’s assessment, Green is mistaken on fewer than six points, which nevertheless hold together logically [A:75-76]. He says the contingent universe depends on God’s moment-by-moment attention and identifies himself as God. When the lights dim as promised, Gregory points out that a ward-boy has started the compressor; Green replies that he created both and can use them [A:76-77]. He prompts Gregory’s account of his troubles [A:78] and has left the ward by the later scene [A:88].

A:75-76; A:76-77; A:78; A:88

Green Bay TreeHeraldic tree on Pope Finnegan’s shield in the novel’s verse attributed to Nostradamus [MB:598]. The wording recalls Psalm37:35 in the King James Bible, where a flourishing green bay tree pictures the wicked in power; that possible scriptural echo sits uneasily beside the poem’s joyful welcome of Finnegan.

MB:598

Green CastlesUnderwater places beneath the Continental Shelf visited by Trinali’s stogy log, which she nevertheless judges uninspired. This is the first log she describes, before the more promising convoluted piece [A:232-233].

A:232-233

Green DeathThe death into which Trinali says a convoluted piece of driftwood descended before returning as a talkative, reminiscent ghost. In her fanciful account, the log has learned from its sea encounters and will become a leering lamp under her tools [A:233].

A:233

Green Eye ShadeJohn Rattigan’s trademark at the boys’ boarding-school sales. He wears it even though their candlelit or kerosene-lit room is too dim to require one, and removes it last when undressing for bed [MTM B1:26-27]. Lily Koch instead uses snap-on celluloid cuffs or gauntlets as her merchant’s trademark [MTM B1:29].

MTM B1:26-27; MTM B1:29

“Green Islands”Title of Chapter Two of Archipelago. Finnegan recounts a creation legend in which a woven mat falls into the sea, turtles tear it into pieces, and these root themselves as green and fiber-colored islands, with Guinea at the stitched center [A:35]. Later, a Malayan boy tells the Sergeant that he has been in the Green Islands long enough and must go home; this visit proves to be part of the Sergeant’s noonday dream in the ward [A:88-90].

A:35; A:88-90

Green LadiesDrinks Margaret Stone says everyone in the New Orleans Quarter has been drinking all week: like peppermint schnapps, except that absinthe replaces the schnapps. Mary Virginia asks about them while questioning Margaret’s account of the city’s extraordinary overnight changes [MTM B11:309].

MTM B11:309

Green Mule, TheRollo McSorley’s name for the potent new drink Shirley Israel serves at Duffey’s party [MTM B4:129-130]. In his facetious Daily News account, titled “I was kicked by a flying mule,” he blames the Green Mule for his condition and admits losing his bet and failing to beat the man he challenged. The narrative instead shows Sebastian Hilton knocking down Rollo and Morris Poor while Duffey moves the actual mule through the air [MTM B4:131-132].

MTM B4:129-130; MTM B4:131-132

Green TreeBar visited by Hans Schultz, Vincent, Finnegan, Tom Shire, Freddy Castle and the newly arrived Casey while Hans prepares for his beer-drinking contest with Joe Bushmaster [A:17-18].

A:17-18

Green-clay animalsAnimals the children of the Golden Childrens Home and Haven Orphanage prepare for Zabotski’s vessel. Early examples fall apart after running about [MTM B9:275]. The children carry later ones aboard while they kick and move weakly [MTM B9:284]. Duffey suggests baking them to hold their heads and legs together, but the children say that would kill them: they come from green-clay eggs and can still be breathed into. Before the voyage, their hooting and bellowing become a great rhapsody of living animal sounds [MTM B9:285].

MTM B9:275; MTM B9:284; MTM B9:285

Greenberry WineOne of the drinks Aunt Gertrude has in her lavishly hospitable household, alongside huckleberry wine and perry, during Finnegan’s stay with the Brannagans [D:208].

D:208

GreeneryVegetation ranging from everyday shade to transformed landscapes. It cuts the glare outside the bar Finnegan and his friends call Sloppy Joe’s [D:235]; appears in bales beside Duffey’s premises as vanished buildings give way to something newly forming [MTM B11:313-314]; and grows tall and lush on Zabotski Flats [MTM B12:362]. Hans’s unwritten aerie poem has golden-touched greenery [A:210], while the speaker of Duffey’s The Alien Awakens seeks greenery beyond the smouldering plain as an escape from horror [D:196-197].

D:235; MTM B11:313-314; MTM B12:362; A:210; D:196-197

Greenflag, OliverOne of the three hospitable men who receive Duffey and Biloxi Brannagan in the Louisiana water country, with Leonard Archive and Harry A. “Honeybucket” Kincaid [MTM B13:417]. Honeybucket operates their frequency apparatus, and Leonard explains its ability to gather organisms and materials from water [MTM B13:417-418]. Greenflag acknowledges that Puff Fish present a moral problem and individual vileness, but doubts that access can be prevented once frequency modulation and braiding are understood. He compares the signals to dippers that can draw any desired thing from water, land or sky [MTM B13:418-419].

MTM B13:417; MTM B13:417-418; MTM B13:418-419

Gregorian chantThe reported reference to Gregorian chant in Don Barnaby’s garden vision has not been located. The cited passage describes changing identities, sleep, travel and the effects of Madame Le Mourcheor’s pill, without the alleged list of musical and theological figures [D:250-252].

D:250-252

Gregorio (Nicholas Cardinal)Cardinal of Messina, named among the thirteen men targeted by John Mogul’s assassination contracts. His double is Arnoldo Rugutini of New York City [MB:571] [MB:578-579].

MB:571; MB:578-579

GregorovitchPatronym given to Katie Noonan’s son Columkill from Gregory, the man who adopts him. X gives the son’s fuller name as Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch Papadiabolous Chortovitch, dates his birth near Krakow to 1830, and argues that his natural father was the Devil [D:278-279].

D:278-279

Gregory (adopter of Columkill)Man in the landed Polish household where Katie Noonan serves as governess. He adopts her son Columkill, who receives the patronym Gregorovitch. X calls Gregory kind and acknowledges, but rejects, the possibility that he was also the boy’s natural father [D:279].

D:279

Gregory (Private)Large, handsome soldier in Ward Fourteen, with a purplish, pumpkin-shaped skull. He says that he never ages and must periodically change identity [A:77] [A:84]. His account stretches through centuries at sea and earlier irregular service to more than a hundred continuous years as a U.S. Army sergeant. Lost papers during the Indian War and Civil War let him reduce his recorded age [A:77]. In 1907, he says, he went AWOL, presented himself as twenty, cultivated political patrons and obtained a Military Academy appointment. He became an Army History specialist, archivist and teacher, remaining an officer for nearly forty years. When an army doctor proposed studying his failure to age, he escaped again [A:78]. As a young Australian private, he was detained after his fingerprints matched those of the vanished American colonel. His unpublished study of subversion within military intelligence also angered the people it exposed [A:79]. He describes possession as the hypnotic action of immortal wills and says influential men may be shells inhabited by devils [A:84-85]. Claiming personal recollection of Roman times, he explains how enemies of early Christianity made the resurrected Christ a frightening figure for children; these are anti-Christian stories about Christ, rather than stories about the Antichrist [A:85]. He remains in the ward after the Sergeant leaves, fearing confinement forever [A:90]. Finnegan later identifies him with Papadiabolis the Devil, while Dotty’s unmailed letter calls him one of the Papadiabouloi without specifying which [A:278] [MTM B6:188-189].

A:77; A:84; A:78; A:79; A:84-85; A:85; A:90; A:278; MTM B6:188-189

Gregory HallResidential hall at St. Bonaventure’s whose boys dominate the school paper, The Towers. Its high towers appear on the masthead; the rival manuscript Chambers answers them with drawings of chamber pots [A:167].

A:167

Gregory McColum Papadiabolous IISee Papadiabolous (II) (Gregory McColum Papadiabolous, Papadiabolous II, Papa Devil, Papa D, Noonan). X gives Gregory McColum as the Irish brother’s name [D:285].

D:285

Gregory McIfreann Papadiabolous ISee Papadiabolous (I) (Gregory McIfreann Papadiabolous, Papadiabolous I). X gives Gregory McIfreann as the Asiatic brother’s name [D:285].

D:285

Gregory van GhiSee Van Ghi. Gregory van Ghi is the artist’s name Finnegan has printed on his cards in New York [A:191].

A:191

Gregory, JohnName either Papadiabolous brother may use. X explains that Gregory McIfreann and Gregory McColum both adopt forms of John as a working first name, including Ivan, Sean, Jan, Ian, Jean, Giovanni, Juan, Johannes and Giannes. This practice complicates his effort to disentangle their identities [D:285].

D:285

Gremium MatrisLatin for the mother’s lap or bosom. In an ocean dream whose bodily reality Finnegan cannot determine, Marie Courtois identifies herself with Demeter and Persephone [D:91]. She lays Finnegan’s head in her lap, binds him there with her hair, and equates the gremium matris with both her lap and the Earth. Her discourse connects this grouping with the Pietà; the maternal image carries a threatening element through the binding and her pleasure in bloodshed [D:92].

D:91; D:92

Grenade manUnnamed older enemy waiting on the shore above the fissured cave to complete an earlier attempt to murder the reawakened Count Finnegan. He has known Finnegan for more than thirty years; two riflemen offshore and an old enemy shark also wait for the Count [MB:554-555]. The man throws three grenades, then a depth charge, and slips into the water after it. The riflemen shoot at a man, or men, flung up by the explosion, while the narrative leaves open Finnegan’s possible escape beneath the shark and launch. The scene is on the Mariano Coast near Havana [MB:556-557].

MB:554-555; MB:556-557

GrenadinesCaribbean island group. In Angela’s account of her father’s forged shipwreck-treasure maps, the Grenadines are one of seven false or shoal passages through the Antilles where he imagines wrecks would accumulate [D:260].

D:260

Grenouilles, soupe auxFrog soup, eaten in Duffey’s vividly appropriated memory of Colmar in Alsace just before his thirteenth birthday. He orders in polished French at the Rotisserie Schillinger and also eats Tournedos au Poivre Vert. The scene was stolen from Sebastian Hilton’s mind, but its detailed flavors become part of Duffey’s own memory [MTM B1:35].

MTM B1:35

Gretchen SislerSee Sisler, Gretchen. She introduces herself to Duffey by this name when he gives her a gold coin [MTM B2:39].

MTM B2:39

GrimaldiOne of the early human types invoked in the novel’s accounts of the “other people.” Harrington’s review reports the suggestion that the supposed Neanderthal returnees might instead be Grimaldi [D:242]. Overlark’s epigraph includes Grimaldi among the types said to possess the enlarged back-brain [D:272].

D:242; D:272

Grimm's LawThe Germanic consonant shift formulated by Jacob Grimm in 1822, describing systematic changes from Proto-Indo-European stops to their Proto-Germanic counterparts. In item XIII of his school notebook, Casey applies the name to a compressed list of correspondences: Latin K or hard C with German or English H, F with B, P with F, and Greek G with Russian ZH or German or English K [A:163]. These are Casey’s notebook formulations; the historical law describes changes from the languages’ common ancestor.

A:163

GrindstonesHousehold tools bearing such iron-lettered names as Schofields and Auto Ball Bearing. Their names belong to the store of noticed objects and words the young Duffey appropriates, often from other people’s minds [MTM B1:17].

MTM B1:17

Grip MachineStrength-testing device at the Fun House out on the Lake. In her Third Epistle to the Kids in St. Louis, Margaret Stone says she can grip only thirty-seven pounds, compared with Dotty Yekouris’s hundred and ninety. She contrasts her physically weak hands with the extraordinary gifts and an hour’s daily care of the world entrusted to them [MTM B5:178].

MTM B5:178

Grisly (Most)Howell’s description of the dead man as the familiar become horrible. A corpse returning to life is, for him, the supreme ghost-story terror, requiring humor to make it bearable, as in Irish wake stories [A:85].

A:85

Groben, HieromeArtist in Duffey’s Chicago circle, named among the golden-age friends [MTM B3:98]. He makes Doré-like engravings of the visiting Monster Giulio [MTM B3:106] and supplies four woodcuts to The Crock [A:41]. He is present when Morris Poor challenges Duffey’s powers [MTM B4:128], and later appears as Groben of Chicago among the artists associated with Duffey’s rebuilding of the world [MTM B6:198].

MTM B3:98; MTM B3:106; A:41; MTM B4:128; MTM B6:198

Groll's TrollsName for people whom Eva regards as the inferior rivals of her own people in running waterfront establishments. She claims that her people served better food and drink, played better music, and told better stories; she nevertheless calls all the groups cousins [MTM B13:408].

MTM B13:408

GrouseBirds among the small creatures along the mile-long track through the nursery where Hans Schultz runs morning and evening [A:208].

A:208

GrovesThe Boy King’s groves of figs, dates, olives, apricots, and pomegranates belong to the childhood presented as more real than Melchisedech’s American childhood [MTM B1:17]. Trinali’s poem asks what became of the “Green Groves of Gomorrah” and imagines their trees surviving, salted and fire-marked, in the Elephants’ Graveyard [A:235].

MTM B1:17; A:235

GrubbyThe Professor calls the pursuit of What rather than Why the “grubby thing” confused with learning [A:220]. Duffey thinks of Hugo Stone as Absalom Stein’s “grubby pupa form” [MTM B5:160]. Zabotski calls sycamore fruit “grubby and trashy” while comparing Bryan Blackstone to the tree [MTM B9:270].

A:220; MTM B5:160; MTM B9:270

Grundy CountyCounty in Illinois where Hillary Hilton buys a bridge while Finnegan accompanies him on his salvage business. Hilton plans to cut it up for a profit [A:253-254]. The identification follows the Chicago setting of this episode [A:246] [A:249].

A:253-254; A:246; A:249

GuadeloupeBasse-Terre is an island within the Guadeloupe archipelago, rather than an alternative name for the entire archipelago. Basse-Terre in the Antilles is the earthly “Paradise” shared by Finnegan, Charles Le Marin, Don Barnaby, and Johnny Duckwalk [D:233] [D:235-237]. The narrator distinguishes it from Basseterre on St. Kitts, presents a French-speaking island society and a volcano named Soufriere, and describes their rum drinking, hammocks, swimming, fishing, poker, and seafaring stories. The haven remains vulnerable to the “snakes” that eventually drive them out [D:235-237]. In a separate account of treasure maps, Barnaby lists the Guadelupe passage among seven true passages through the Antilles [D:260].

D:233; D:235-237; D:260

Guadeloupe, Antilles (aka Basse-Terre)Earlier heading that treated Guadeloupe and Basse-Terre as interchangeable names. See Guadeloupe.
GuaiacumOne of the substances Duffey suggests when asked to identify the odor of the clipping announcing X’s death. Dotty identifies the smell as rosin and recognizes that X printed the clipping himself [A:142].

A:142

GuancheMember of the indigenous people of Tenerife in the Canary Islands. The waiter serving brandy on Grand Canary is described as “a Guanche from before the time of Spain” [D:99-101].

D:99-101

Guardian (Perpetual)The “Perpetual Guardian Payments” obtained for the responsible group maintaining every Casey Machine site as a shrine. They are intended to provide Perpetual Care and continue indefinitely [CM:513].

CM:513

GuardiansKeepers and defenders in several contexts. George Duckhunter says his group is paid as “high priced guardians,” though he no longer clearly remembers the arrangement [CM:504]. X describes Devil worshippers guarding the Devil’s Crimean prison [MTM B6:204]. Zabotski affirms that angels guard the Ark and other things inaccessible to human guardians [MTM B9:280-281]. The armed Orthodoxers who threaten him are ironically called “guardians of pure science” [MTM B9:286]. A letter to Stein assigns the remaining defense against Principalities and Powers to jokers after the “proper defenders” have fallen asleep [A:266]. Finnegan kills two guards during his attack on the Pirate Hotel [D:231]; John Mogul also employs guards [MB:573].

CM:504; MTM B6:204; MTM B9:280-281; MTM B9:286; A:266; D:231; MB:573

GuebwillerTown in France, named among the places whose prehistoric paintings Finnegan discusses with Duffey. Finnegan maintains that apparent birds and butterflies are speech-and-song balloons in the original complex language; Duffey objects that the Neanderthal painters had neither speech nor writing [MTM B6:193].

MTM B6:193

Guest SpeakerThe advertised speaker at the New Catholic Press Guild meeting, called “The Most Important Person in the World” and later “The Majesty.” Duffey recognizes the Devil behind the grand claims and theatrical presentation [MTM B8:239-241].

MTM B8:239-241

GuiltFinnegan considers guilt as one possible explanation of Seaworthy’s dream corpse, then concludes that the corpse was literally a corpse [D:74]. Seaworthy describes himself as guilty of “shattering drunkenness” [D:11]. The verse opening “Biloxi Brannagan” mourns the “guiltless slain” [D:196]. Vincent’s theory of a recently created world includes memories of “debts and guilts” for events that never happened [A:57]. Duffey rejects photographic blackmail because he has confessed his actual sins and been absolved [MTM B4:140]. “Oh Let the Devil Go” describes guilt as “an over-flow” in its vision of the Devil’s suffering [PG:521].

D:74; D:11; D:196; A:57; MTM B4:140; PG:521

GuinessThe spelling Guiness appears in the supplied text. See Guinness.
GuinnessGuinness, the Irish beer associated with St. James’s Gate Brewery in Dublin, which Arthur Guinness leased in 1759. One of the four brews Patrick Stranahan includes in his compact rule of life, alongside an American, a Danish, and a Bohemian brew [A:110]. The text spells the name “Guiness.”

A:110

GuitarSalvation Sally carries a hymn-strumming guitar with a collecting cup attached [A:8]. Dotty doubts that Stein’s tuning can remove its twang and imagines Sally and Mary Virginia leaving only blond hairs and a piece of guitar string after a quarrel [A:147]. The instrument is later said to share Sally’s Australian accent [MTM B7:214]. The narrator contrasts the supposed gloom of guitar music with the banjo [MTM B2:52]. In Elena O’Higgins’s account, Casey replaces a sacred organ score with music for kazoo, peewee guitar, and musical saw [PG:525]. Electric guitarists have five Gates of their own in the enlarged Ekklesia [MB:562].

A:8; A:147; MTM B7:214; MTM B2:52; PG:525; MB:562

Guiterrez, Sammy (Captain)Tagalog captain called Sammy, met on Luzon [A:63], a friend of the Dirty Five who appears thirteen although about twenty-three. He calls the men “hairy old men” [A:66]. He admires Absalom Stein and teaches at the reopened school where Stein is also teaching. With Finnegan distracting the shoe-shine boys on a mouth organ, Sammy borrows their box without permission, earns four pesos from four shines, returns the box, and buys more whisky [A:67-68]. He joins the men’s walk to the field of white horses, an expedition numbered among the Argonauts’ heroic labors [A:68]. The episode continues on the next page: Sammy hums little songs and is the first of the six men to fall asleep in the grass [A:69].

A:63; A:66; A:67-68; A:68; A:69

GulfUsed for several waters and their adjoining regions. Anastasia places mermaids in the Persian Gulf in her account of their former range [D:35]. Hillary Hilton boasts of selling refitted garbage scows to an Arabian Gulf potentate [A:255]. A projected account of Zabotski’s house places it on Lake Borgne where it opens into the Gulf of Mexico [MTM B9:288].

The Gulf also enters the characters’ ordinary surroundings: Gertrude is described as a gulf-state lady, and her home with Brannagan is full of gulf winds [D:200-201]. Gulf southerlies are among the winds in the account of ballooning from St. Louis [MTM B2:65]. The Stranahans plan annual expeditions after gulf marlin [A:103].

D:35; A:255; MTM B9:288; D:200-201; MTM B2:65; A:103

Gulf Coast LadyGertrude Brannagan is described as a “gulf-state lady,” full-built, dark, and pretty, whose presence makes Finnegan feel safe. Her age is given as forty-five, with fifteen years allowed in either direction [D:200].

D:200

Gulf of MexicoThe editor’s note locates Zabotski’s enormous house on the coast of Lake Borgne where the lake opens into the Gulf of Mexico [MTM B9:288].

MTM B9:288

Gulf of OmanPoint of departure in the verse about the Dutchman who still sails from the Gulf of Oman carrying a cargo to Cutch [A:172].

A:172

Gullab CoastCoast named by Don Barnaby among the places where Madame Le Mourcheor’s Juju Joy Pills are not made. He says that they come from New Orleans [D:249]. The supplied page spells the name “Gullab”; its geographical identification remains uncertain.

D:249

Gullah CoastEarlier glossary spelling of Gullab Coast. See Gullab Coast [D:249].

D:249

Gulls of Ship IslandBirds that join the sandpipers of Horn Island in making a glad noise as the Argo enters Biloxi to dock [MTM B13:408].

MTM B13:408

Gum ArabicListed with formaldehyde in Casey’s purported recipe for Bakelite, item XVI in the notebook extracts [A:163].

A:163

Gumbo-headCasey’s self-description in his contrast between “feet of clay” and a “gumbo-head.” He immediately insists that he is almost the cleverest of the group and explains his apparent stupidity as the effect of having seen the odds against their endeavors [A:155-156].

A:155-156

Gums (Lesser)The unnamed lesser gum among Askandanakandrian’s seven sovereign substances for rehabilitating nervous merchandise. He also includes the gum among the four he would choose if forced to reduce his supply [A:257].

A:257

GunFirearms appear as weapons, contraband, and occasions for grim jokes. Manuel describes a force running guns and men in his country, which he says lies south of Mexico [D:56]. The Naxos attack includes rifles, BARs, machine guns, and the larger weapon aboard the Brunhilde [D:143] [D:146].

Sebastian “Shot Gun” Schaeffer’s nickname actually comes from a drink he invented. He is mistaken for a killer, and George “Basin Street” Becaud later frightens him by claiming that his bass case holds an enormous shotgun [D:222-223].

The young discoverer of Perverse Logic fires at Casey Gorshok, but the Argo men have already withdrawn from that time and place [MTM B13:428-429]. Air-guns and blow-guns occur among the proposed murder devices in John Mogul’s contest [MB:580]. The Stranahan family’s “Rod and Gun Club” is Maurine’s nickname for its hunters and fishermen [A:103].

D:56; D:143; D:146; D:222-223; MTM B13:428-429; MB:580; A:103

Gun casesCases in the Stranahan Club Room, which also contains a simulated fireplace serving as a sandbagged pistol range [A:103].

A:103

Gur'yevGuryev, now Atyrau in Kazakhstan. Town described as standing at the east mouth of the Ural River in Tartary. After Duffey’s killing, his bones and smoking ashes appear in an unbusy street there. X and Kasmir Gorshok independently arrive at the same place and identify both as Duffey’s remains [MTM B13:442].

MTM B13:442

GusherA newspaper reporter calls the expected heavy rain a “gusher” while asking whether it will float Zabotski’s construction down Dumaine Street to Lake Borgne [MTM B9:289]. The Laughing Prince’s poisoned spring is also a gusher, defying hydraulic laws [MTM B13:441]. The proposed murder by swarming animals describes a victim’s viscera gushing out [MB:580-581].

MTM B9:289; MTM B13:441; MB:580-581

Gusty JoyA quality attributed in the earlier glossary to the Boy King Melchisedech; the phrase and its cited occurrence remain unlocated.
GutsMargaret Stone reports that the Sardinian Red Fisters threaten to wear her guts as scarves [MTM B7:225]. In How Many Miles to Babylon?, the entrails of Paul XI are used to strangle Hiram III and are then eaten in a further spectacle [MB:564-565].

MTM B7:225; MB:564-565

GutterIn Seaworthy’s dream, he tries dumping the corpse into a gutter but is forced to retrieve it [D:73].
