Vincent’s story of two bums in a gutter mocks the refusal to try a good idea because it has been tried before [A:57]. Wooden crossings over mud gutters are among the details of other children’s lives appropriated by Melchisedech [MTM B1:16].

D:73; A:57; MTM B1:16

H Sound (Latin)The sound that Casey’s notebook says corresponds in German or English to Latin K or hard C. Casey includes the correspondence in his summary of Grimm’s law [A:163].

A:163

HabibForm of address exchanged by Finnegan and an unnamed boy in Tangier. The boy is one of the runners who keep Finnegan informed and directs him to the bottom of the tell, where Don Lewis lies dead [D:104] [D:109].

D:104; D:109

HabitationThe nursery track where Hans runs is the summer habitation of rabbits, coneys, ground squirrels, bull snakes, and many other small creatures [A:208]. X says that he has neither habitation nor name and expects to die without papers on his body [A:138].

A:208; A:138

HabonimLanding place of the Argo where the hilly “Plains of Megiddo” begin. The ship brings the figure identified as Peleus, Kasmir Gorshok, Prince Casimir, and Casey Szymansky, now manifested as the Antichrist, to rule from there for his appointed period [MTM B13:462].

MTM B13:462

Hackenschmidt of Weinsburg, Conrad StoneConrad Stone Hackenschmidt of Weinsburg in the Germanies leads the final Conclave of the Ekklesia in Babylonia Bagascia [MB:566]. With a Browning Automatic Rifle supplied by Monsignor X, he orders each prince to vote Ego eligo effigiem for the Straw-Man. He shoots Stockton Stone Crocker for voting for Joseph Cardinal Hedayat; six dissenting votes are ultimately recounted for the effigy [MB:567]. He orders X to burn the effigy and then the six bodies, announces the dissolution of their princely offices, and demands the destruction of all bells [MB:568]. He declares the thirteen absent princes dead, commissions Track and Total to kill them, and tries unsuccessfully to dispose of X [MB:568-569].

MB:566; MB:567; MB:568; MB:568-569

HacksawTools used by three young men to cut both hands of the Great Delta Insurance Company tower clock down to stubs. One falls to his death while climbing down afterward [GD:483].

GD:483

HadriaticusLatin form associated with the Adriatic Sea. John Schultz, writing to Marie as a former Orpheus, recalls the Argo crossing the Hadriaticus westward from Illyria. Sometimes it had no far shore; sometimes the western shore was not Italy [MTM B6:186].

MTM B6:186

HaggadaThe narrator cites the Haggada for the claim that the forbidden fruit was wormy, adding that St. Augustine seems to refer to the same detail. The worm in the fruit becomes the figure for the disquiet that breaks up the companions’ earthly paradise, beginning with Johnny Duckwalk’s decision to confess his theft and accept imprisonment [D:264].

D:264

HairDuffey has sorrel hair, a color shared by his kit-fox totem; Mary Louise Byrne’s hair is still redder [MTM B1:6] [MTM B1:19] [MTM B2:40] [MTM B2:55]. Among the churchgoers whom Duffey watches is a chubby young woman with blonde hair beneath a black veil [MTM B3:88]. Dotty has chestnut hair [A:106]. Brannagan’s hair is sandy with a token touch of patriarchal gray [MTM B13:409]; Mary Virginia has gray hairs in the halo framing her face [MTM B11:318]. Patrick Stranahan has abundant body hair and exceptionally hairy eyebrows; it is his face that resembles blue emery paper [A:102]. The hairs on the giant spider’s toes are thicker than most trees [A:62].

MTM B1:6; MTM B1:19; MTM B2:40; MTM B2:55; MTM B3:88; A:106; MTM B13:409; MTM B11:318; A:102; A:62

Haiti hoodoo joy pillsOne of the varieties of joy pill listed by Don Barnaby, alongside High Harry, Deep Romany, Dead Frenchman, and Black Rooster. He distinguishes these from Madame Le Mourcheor’s Old Original Juju Joy Pills, whose efficacy he praises [D:248-249].

D:248-249

Hal ClementAuthor of Left of Africa, listed as the first book in Manuscript Press’s “Lost Manuscripts” series. In the publisher’s afterword to Archipelago, Rick Norwood says he obtained publication rights to an unpublished Hal Clement manuscript [A:285-286].

A:285-286

Half-mapsArtificially aged portions of treasure maps made by Angela Cosquin’s father. Confidence men sell matching halves to distant victims, then collect further payments while bringing the owners together [D:261].

D:261

Half-MasterDesignation of X aboard the Argo. After Duffey’s death, Brannagan and Casey Gorshok continue their work as Argo Masters with “the Half-Master X”; Duffey subsequently resumes his duties in skeletal form [MTM B13:443].

MTM B13:443

Hallahan, LarryLarry and Olivia Hallahan belong to the “slippery people” of the Duffeys’ Chicago circle [MTM B3:100]. They remain at supper with Duffey after Demetrio Glauch leaves in disgust [MTM B4:127]. The Hallahans later belong to the salon group that wants to retain Duffey and exploit his magic [MTM B4:137].

MTM B3:100; MTM B4:127; MTM B4:137

Hallahan, OliviaOne of the “slippery people” of the Duffeys’ Chicago circle, named with Larry Hallahan [MTM B3:100]. Olivia joins the women who hiss at Demetrio Glauch like she-adders when he leaves their supper; she remains to finish the meal with Duffey and the others [MTM B4:127].

MTM B3:100; MTM B4:127

Hallock's Grocery CartHorse-drawn vehicle named in the Royal Pop lecturer’s account of the memories preserved by a flagstone in Decatur Street [MTM B11:328-329].

MTM B11:328-329

HallwaysLong corridors in the house of Lily Koch’s kindred through which she leads the eight young people away from the formal dance to the attic billiard room [MTM B1:31-33].

MTM B1:31-33

Halo (Smokey)The “unreality fringe” or smoky halo surrounding Duffey’s magnificent animations at the Rounders’ Club, including Hans, Marie, Henri, Dotty, Mary Virginia, and Absalom. The narration insists that these people are real despite the fringe [MTM B5:158].

MTM B5:158

Ham (Inspired)The theatrical exuberance of the mice Duffey summons to act in his puppet shows. The narrator calls their acting “inspired ham”; the living mice speak their roles and perform beside Letitia’s inanimate puppets [MTM B4:134].

MTM B4:134

HammerA young man uses a hammer to smash the glass of Melchisedech Duffy’s watch with exaggerated gentleness [GD:481]. Small drop-hammers also form part of Zabotski’s brass-smelting equipment [MTM B6:192].

GD:481; MTM B6:192

Hammerschmidt's Gym (St. Louis)St. Louis gymnasium where Bagby brings the young Duffey to work out before boxing managers and promoters. They arrange his preliminary bout against Dandy Dan Dillard [MTM B2:50]. The episode belongs to the summer of 1915, when Duffey is approaching sixteen in this account of his youth [MTM B2:38] [MTM B2:49].

MTM B2:50; MTM B2:38; MTM B2:49

HammockThe four companions keep hammocks near their favorite bar at Basse-Terre, in a secluded spot where they spend weeks together [D:236]. Finnegan twice hears another man’s voice from Don Barnaby’s hammock while Barnaby continues sleeping. One asks him to repay fifty dollars owed to Anastasia; the other says that he has been dead in the sand for three years and begs to be released [D:238] [D:256].

D:236; D:238; D:256

Hammonton, New JerseyHome of Phoebe Anne Ankerson, as recorded on the tag inside the suitcase stolen by Finnegan. The tag gives Hammonton as the return address after her visit to Minnie MacMasters [D:172].

D:172

HamperDoll Delaney brings a hamper of food, drink, ice, and red roses to her graveyard meeting with Finnegan and X on the day of the Indianapolis race [D:276]. X asks for devil’s food cake, but Doll corrects him: it is gingerbread [D:277]. The picnic also includes wine, sandwiches, coffee, and cakes; they return the remnants and papers to the hamper [D:284].

D:276; D:277; D:284

Hand (Invisible Giant)The hand summoned by eight-year-old Melchisedech to help ring the church bell when he is too light to move it alone. The giant is invisible, but its hand is visible to the other boys [MTM B1:14-15].

MTM B1:14-15

Hand (Right/Left)The intended reference for this heading has not been established.
Hand-washing moneyMoney Duffey receives when his “false kindred” rid themselves of responsibility for him. He still has some during boarding school, along with profits from his ventures with Rattigan [MTM B1:24]. At the end of school, a further hundred dollars is described as the final act of the hand-washing ceremony [MTM B2:38].

MTM B1:24; MTM B2:38

Handbook of TreasonsWork credited to Miles O’Connel in the collection of documents inserted into Book Five. Its quoted passage identifies the “spiritual army of evil in high stations” with the devils of the word-mills and says that some of those stations are within the Church [MTM B5:175-176].

MTM B5:175-176

Hands (Severed Giant)Image in Duffey’s dream of a spreading chasm. His summoned giants’ hands arrive severed at the forearms, powerless and manacled; they then become a little boy’s mittens joined by their drawstring [MTM B2:68]. A painting of the Severed Giant Hands hangs above the doorway to the Elegant Riverboat Deck at the Rounders’ Club. In its presence, Duffey feels deprived of creative power by the independence and superiority of his own creations [MTM B5:156].

MTM B2:68; MTM B5:156

Handsomeness (Fevered)Description of Don Lewis at the party’s formal dinner on Grand Canary. The narrator says he already bears the mark of death and will be the featured figure in the next act of the masque [D:100].

D:100

Hannigan (or Hanlon or O'Hanlon)Possible surnames of Casey’s farm-boy schoolmate whom he now calls Hinnegan. Casey admits that knowing Finnegan has caused him to reconstruct the boy’s name and memory so that they rhyme [A:162].

A:162

HansSee Schultz, John G.
HanschenName used for Hans Schultz by Marie Monaghan. Salvation Sally asks what Marie calls him and adopts “Hanschen” in saying goodnight [A:9].

A:9

Harbor expressHidden route to the wharfs used by Count Finnegan and his companion in the role of Herman Hercules to evade their pursuers. The crawl-way passes through cellars, connecting tunnels, storm sewers, electrical conduits, heat ducts, and thieves’ catacombs [MB:587]. The next page leaves the companion’s precise identity, including his possible role as Cardinal Erculo in his double’s disguise, uncertain [MB:588].

MB:587; MB:588

Harbor HouseTavern where Hans Schultz and Joe Bushmaster compete in beer drinking under Dominion Rules [A:15] [A:19]. After Hans wins, the company buys a round for everyone in the house [A:23].

A:15; A:19; A:23

Hard C sound (Latin)Casey’s notebook says that a Latin K or hard C becomes H in German or English, as part of its summary of Grimm’s law [A:163].

A:163

Hard StuffThe earlier glossary associates this phrase with Teresa Piccone’s comments on Finnegan’s drinking, but the passage has not been located.
Harlow HouseAn old house on an abandoned farm in the New Jersey Barrens, where Gautier the goat-man often stays with his goats. The house may be haunted, but Gautier knows no ghost there except himself. His syrinx and bagpipe playing accounts for much of the ghost music in the surrounding wasteland. Finnegan knows the house through Gautier’s descriptions and never sees it himself [A:196-197].

A:196-197

Harmonica (Pocket)Instrument Finnegan plays during the graveyard meeting with X and Doll. His tunes comment on X’s narrative: “Arise, ye Saints, Arise,” Browne’s Prelude, “Oh what was your name in the States?,” “A policeman’s life is not a happy one,” and “Wake the town and tell the people” [D:284-285] [D:287].

D:284-285; D:287

HarpiesMargaret Stone calls Duffey’s visiting women “harpies” in her parody of the Gadarene Swine Song: “The harpies came from Illinois.” Her verses follow Mary Catherine Carruthers’s departure and the news that no more visitors from the North are expected for the moment [MTM B8:262].

MTM B8:262

Harrington, Charles O.A.Named reviewer in the epigraph to chapter sixteen, “Liar’s Paradise.” His review in Science for Today attacks Royce Rollins’s The Return of the Neanderthal, subtitled The Alien Within, while outlining its theory of surviving Neanderthals and hidden bloodlines. He dismisses Rollins as a crank but warns that similarly outlandish notions have founded cults [D:240-242].

D:240-242

Harrison County, IowaOne of the three Iowa counties offered as the birthplace of Melchisedech in the account of one of his childhoods, alongside Shelby and Pottawattamie. Seven towns or townships dispute the honor [MTM B1:7].

MTM B1:7

Hart, CharlesOne of Duffey’s “pretended uncles.” When Mary Ellen Hart worries about the jars of blood Duffey keeps, Charles says he used to keep blood too, since it attracts weasels, and insists that there is no harm in the boy [MTM B1:18].

MTM B1:18

Hart, Mary EllenOne of Duffey’s “pretended kindred,” called Aunt Mary Ellen Hart. She says his first talisman came from a box of crackerjacks, that it has grown since then, and that he makes others like it. She also tells Charles that the boy keeps jars of blood [MTM B1:18].

MTM B1:18

Harvest (The)Salvation Sally announces that “The harvest is at hand” while preaching the Second Coming [A:8]. Mary Lightfoot applies the image to the end of the world, when the “blow-mouths” will be separated from the good and burned; Countess Margaret recalls the enemy who sowed them [MTM B4:130].

A:8; MTM B4:130

Harvesters' DinnerAbundant meal served to Duffey’s party at the Colony Club in Chicago. Charlotte says that either her sister or one of Duffey’s ladies has ordered it. Roasting ears are central, followed by beef, potatoes, bread, cabbage, kale, sauerkraut, cheeses, sausages, and hot biscuits; the food keeps arriving [MTM B3:93-94]. Sebastian joins the table, and the meal belongs to the gathering of Duffey, the Koch sisters, and the Mullens/Cavendish party [MTM B3:93-95].

MTM B3:93-94; MTM B3:93-95

HashA kilo of hash is given to every person in Babylonia Bagascia among the offerings and entertainments preceding the final Conclave. The narrator calls the custom “Hash and Circuses” [MB:566].

MB:566

Hash-BashersOne of the constituencies given special Stones in the enlarged Ekklesia, alongside Trippers, Dippers, Mushroomers, old-time Drunkards, and Fundamentalist Drunkards [MB:562].

MB:562

Hashed-Ectocarpus CollinsCocktail ordered by Duffey from Honeybucket Kincaid during the Argo’s visit to a future Louisiana swamp settlement. Honeybucket gathers its ingredients from the water by manipulating electrical frequencies [MTM B13:416-418].

MTM B13:416-418

HasteJoseph needs a partner who will not spoil a diamond deal through haste or nervousness. He warns Finnegan that realizing the value of a consignment may take years [D:94].

D:94

HatDuffey associates a flat straw hat with banjo playing [MTM B2:52]. Beth Keegan puts on her extraordinary beauty as casually as a funny hat [MTM B2:57]. Casey wears a shako for his planned appearance as the Leader [MTM B4:117]. His later appearance as the initially unrecognized Kasmir Gorshok includes a black hat and ear locks [MTM B13:425-426].

MTM B2:52; MTM B2:57; MTM B4:117; MTM B13:425-426

Hat (Pearl-gray derby)The small pearl-gray derby worn by the black crewman of the Seabach. It is too small for him. He wears it into battle on Naxos and dies laughing [D:135] [D:147].

D:135; D:147

Hat (Wool-Hat)The customer who kills Betty’s father Hochstapler with the swindler’s own barkers’ mallet or gavel during a dispute over less than three hundred dollars. He claims he meant only to hit him and receives a sentence of a year and a day [A:217].

A:217

Hatch followerOne of the Fundamentalers who questions Zabotski, asking whether his reference to the present year as 200,000 AD was a joke. Zabotski responds that the date is a riddle and challenges the certainty of ordinary chronology [MTM B9:281].

MTM B9:281

HatchetSmall hatchets are laid beside every diner’s plate on Zabotski’s ark for cutting tough rhinoceros and behemoth steaks [MTM B12:364]. Duffey attends the meal with Zabotski, Wife Waldo, and the children [MTM B12:363-364].

MTM B12:364; MTM B12:363-364

Haussa boy, JosephHaussa diamond smuggler whom Finnegan befriends in Freetown. He is described as coming from Nigeria or the Gold Coast, with experience as a caravan boy and seaman. They drink palm wine called barn, then gin [D:93]. Joseph speaks English, Arabic, Ful, French, and Afrikaans and intends to learn proper Dutch for his trade. He recruits Finnegan as a trustworthy partner for foreign marketing [D:94]. He warns him about his evil shipmates, then supplies a heavy leather sack of diamonds; Finnegan markets from this and two later sacks and sends drafts to Freetown [D:95]. Duffey later says that their partnership continues and supplies Finnegan’s friends with diamonds [MTM B10:303].

D:93; D:94; D:95; MTM B10:303

HavanaDestination of Duffey’s first journey in search of Finnegan’s reported death. From Havana he intends to investigate the nearby Marianao Coast. His companion is the detective Carmelo Mendoza, subsequently exposed as Mr. X using another disguise [MTM B12:367] [MTM B12:369-371].

MTM B12:367; MTM B12:369-371

Haven (Golden Childrens Home and Haven Orphanage)Orphanage behind Zabotski’s property. The children enjoy his growing construction, but Widow Waldo brings the state inspector’s demand that he remove the part encroaching on its grounds [MTM B9:271] [MTM B9:274]. Its golden roof and the endowment from Harry Goldchild are described by the narrator [MTM B9:280]. The children bring their animate green-clay animals aboard the construction [MTM B9:284].

MTM B9:271; MTM B9:274; MTM B9:280; MTM B9:284

Haven (in the Shoals)The refuge in the hewn cave of the Mooring Stone, among the Belling Shoals or Ringing Rocks. Finnegan, Gilberto Levine and O’Brien, and Herman Hercules leave the Argo there to join thirteen supposed doubles of murdered princes. Finnegan says that one of the thirteen is a surviving holy man rather than a shadow, so the line will remain unbroken before Armageddon [MTM B13:453].

MTM B13:453

Hawk (bird)Anastasia says that hawks nest just out of sight in the sky and appear suddenly when they swoop down. She gives this teasing answer when Finnegan asks where the expected boat, the Hawk, will come from [D:131].

D:131

Hawk (boat/ship)Papa Devil’s small boat, called Shouakh and spelled Seabach. Finnegan says the name means hawk; Papa says that the boat is not fast but appears suddenly [D:122]. He hopes to use it in the Naxos operation but fears a counter-ambush by their clever antagonist [D:123]. Anastasia must signal the arriving boat from a narrow glen after moonset, while Finnegan remains uncertain where it will come from [D:127] [D:131]. It appears as the Hawk upon the Sea in his sonnet [D:134]. The vessel arrives from Anatolia, and the account of the battle says that the smaller boat is sinking after its attack [D:135] [D:146].

D:122; D:123; D:127; D:131; D:134; D:135; D:146

Hay fieldAccording to X’s family history, Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch Papadiabolous Chortovitch was born in a hay field near Krakow, perhaps nearer Skawine, in the year of Restored Salvation 1830 [D:278].

D:278

Hayden, Mary Irene (Schultz)Hans Schultz’s mother, Mary Irene Hayden, married to John William Schultz; Hans is their only child, born at St. Gallen, Wisconsin [A:207]. She has known Professor Kirol for years and views his influence with some doubt. She tells Hans that she first heard “phoney” from the Professor, applied to himself, and calls him a noble but compromised example of the old kind [A:211].

A:207; A:211

Haydens (Family)One of the family names in the older relative’s list of Duffey’s kin. The list belongs to the disputed account of his childhood between five and twelve; Duffey says the supposed relatives may instead belong to his twin [MTM B1:7].

MTM B1:7

HayloftPlace where Howland chants his jingle about five gophers while he and Finnegan lie up for the night during their journey toward Chicago [A:179].

A:179

Hazh-KhazhLanguage in which Zabotski believes the instructions for his great construction are written. Duffey points out that Hazh-Khazh has never been deciphered; Zabotski says he must decipher it as he builds [MTM B9:272].

MTM B9:272

HeadDuffey’s television projection shows Casey as a horrifying head-only person carried by four black giants; the narration explicitly says the head is not shown as severed [MTM B12:381]. In How Many Miles to Babylon?, the severed head of Paul XI is displayed on a pike at the Spanish Stairs and continues speaking under torture [MB:562].

MTM B12:381; MB:562

Head (Casey's Projected)Image of Casey as a livid, grimacing, cursing head-only person, carried by four black giants over the television picture of Goldfarb’s Alley. Duffey animates it from a painting Adam Scanlon made of Casey without Casey’s knowledge. The eyes are sewn open, preventing the image from refusing to see [MTM B12:381].

MTM B12:381

Head (Papa Devil's)Papa Devil’s visible head is compared to a great purple pumpkin. Finnegan cannot draw it convincingly because it is the living face of someone else; he reconstructs the wearer’s true face and paints that instead [D:62]. The painting anticipates the face he recognizes on the dead Papa Devil after the Naxos battle [D:86] [D:146]. X’s later account distinguishes this man as Papadiabolous II [D:285].

D:62; D:86; D:146; D:285

Head (Putiphar's Wife's)Portrait commission from Adrian Shapiro for his wife Mercedes, recast in the narration as Putiphar and his wife. Mercedes’s advances make Finnegan play Joseph: he leaves with his coat but abandons his paints and soon takes to the road again [A:193].

A:193

Healeys (Family)One of the family names in the older relative’s account of Duffey’s many kin during his disputed childhood. Duffey suggests that the relative is remembering his twin instead [MTM B1:7].

MTM B1:7

Hearn, Lafcadio (1850--1904)Writer invoked in Casey’s hostile review of The Bark: he dismisses its New Orleans sketches as work of a kind Lafcadio Hearn had done better in the previous century [A:131]. Hearn (1850-1904) is also known for his writing about Japan, including Kwaidan: Stories and Studies of Strange Things (1904).

A:131

HeavenHeaven is described by Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni as continuing, explosive growth rather than a static state; his tapestry analogy places Heaven, Hell, and Purgatory within the same universe, whose true face human beings cannot yet see [A:211] [A:213-214]. When Duffey loses his wealth, the narrator jokes that the camel and needle’s-eye problem has been solved: Duffey had wondered how he would get to Heaven without imagining that he might cease to be rich [MTM B4:109].

A:211; A:213-214; MTM B4:109

Heavenly Twins (newspapers)Bagby’s nickname for the St. Louis Post Dispatch and the St. Louis Globe, to which he sends flamboyant battle statements publicizing his boxing [MTM B2:50].

MTM B2:50

Heavyweight championshipBeer-drinking title at stake in the proposed Harbor House contest between Hans and Joe Bushmaster; Finnegan calls it the world heavyweight championship [A:17].

A:17

Hebdomadal namesThe set of names Gautier gives his seven youngest goat kids: Bownee, Luin, Mairt, Keadin, Ordin, Haoine, and Sahirn. The narrator calls these “hebdomadal names”; Luin is subsequently glossed as Monday [A:194-195].

A:194-195

Hebert, EmilyEarlier heading supplied the surname Hebert, which the family passage does not establish. See Emily (Henry Salvatore's aunt).
Hebert, JulienOne of Henry Francis Salvatore’s nearby Hebert uncles in the Morgan City family account [A:122-123].

A:122-123

Hebert, Mary GenevieveMother of Henry Francis Salvatore, whose father is Lawrence Salvatore. Their large family belongs to the Morgan City, Louisiana account of Henry’s upbringing [A:122-123].

A:122-123

Hebert, NicoleOne of Henry Francis Salvatore’s nearby Hebert uncles in the Morgan City family account [A:122-123].

A:122-123

HebrewOne of the scripts in which the Argo’s name is painted when it brings the Peter-Bell to the mooring rock, alongside Latin, Greek, and Chaldee [MB:577]. Duffey proposes playing Hebrew melodies on his recorder-flute for the Ursuline play [MTM B9:266]. Book Six also opens with a passage about Melchisedech attributed in the novel to “Paul. Hebrews.” [MTM B6:185].

MB:577; MTM B9:266; MTM B6:185

HebronOne of the possible locations of the burning bush in Finnegan’s poem: he will climb Sinai and see whether the bush is “at Hebron or Hest,” and whether it is burning [A:171].

A:171

Heckel, Charley horseRegular at the Old Wooden Ship bar [D:215]. With Russ and Bob, Charley horse Heckel steers promising big spenders toward the bar; the narrator groups these three with Smokehouse and Bill Dugan as five men cut from the same side of the animal [D:220].

D:215; D:220

Hedayat, Joseph CardinalCardinal of Antioch and the primary of Count Finnegan, his double. In the Resurrection of Count Finnegan painting, their older forms are identical even though their contemporary appearances differ; Mr. X knows Joseph, and the widely traveled Joseph later visits the picture at Duffey’s Art Bijou [MB:552-553]. Hilary Hilton calls Hedayat the likeliest next Pope and reports a prediction that Finnegan will assume the crown under Hedayat’s identity, then be known as Peter the Second [MTM B12:378-379]. At the final Conclave, Hackenschmidt declares the prophecies about Hedayat void and commissions Track and Total to kill the thirteen absent princes; Hedayat heads X’s list of the targets [MB:568-571]. He is the last of the thirteen primaries reported killed, impaled upside down in the event called “Last Gate Swings” [MB:589]. This death appears in the Deaths of the Cardinals series attributed to Count Finnegan aboard the Argo; the narrative also raises the possibility of the accomplished amateur painter Hedayat’s participation [MTM B13:452-453].

MB:552-553; MTM B12:378-379; MB:568-571; MB:589; MTM B13:452-453

Hedges (Thorn)Thorn hedges in the Delectable Place. Duffey wants to cut through them; Patrick Plunket explains that they lie outside the direct route and have to be deliberately sought out by going the long way around. Duffey nevertheless favors the indirect route, while Plunket warns that its danger is real [MTM B12:391].

MTM B12:391

Heine, Heinrich (1797--1856)German poet and writer whose Buch der Lieder (1827) brought lasting fame to his lyric poetry. Born in Düsseldorf in 1797, he moved to Paris in 1831 amid censorship of his work and died there in 1856. His writing joins Romantic lyricism to political criticism and satire. In Archipelago, Heine’s ballads strongly shape Hans’s “Chinese period,” mingling Rhineland sadness with Chinese imagery [A:223].

A:223

Hercules, HermanListed as the double of Martino Cardinal Erculo of Milan [MB:579]. In his conversation with Finnegan, he calls Erculo his primary, recalls his career as a wrestler, and describes himself as one of the long-timers [MB:584-585]. The narration later suggests that the man speaking as Hercules is Erculo in disguise, then leaves the masqueraders’ exact identities unresolved [MB:588].

MB:579; MB:584-585; MB:588

Hidden Hand in the Various Military IntelligencesShort title of Private Gregory’s unpublished Cycles of Subversion: The Hidden Hand in the Various Military Intelligences, found among his old papers. Gregory says the work has angered the people it exposes and that they have hunted him down [A:78-79].

A:78-79

Hidden Years (Duffey's)The seven dark or lost years following Duffey’s disappearance from St. Louis. Later Duffey either cannot or will not explain them. A codicil of the circular log says he boarded the disguised Argo below Eads Bridge and traveled for seven nonconsecutive years, with land adventures not counted in that span [MTM B2:71]. Another account describes intervals removed from time, containing past, present, and future [MTM B10:298]. He collected the Seven Christs during these years [MTM B3:103], and gave Gabriel Szymansky the talisman intended for Casey before Casey’s conception or birth [MTM B4:120]. Bagby sent Duffey weekly letters even during this mysterious absence [MTM B4:145].

MTM B2:71; MTM B10:298; MTM B3:103; MTM B4:120; MTM B4:145

Hidden Years (Hans')Gap of four, five, or six years, depending on the recension, after Hans’s Bohemian spring and summer. He acquired unexplained resources that thereafter let him obtain needed money from a distance, but did not tell this part of his life to Finnegan. His Army enlistment followed in the spring of either 1941 or 1942 [A:240-241].

A:240-241

Higgenbotham, HoraceMarie Monaghan’s supposed Uncle Horace, invoked in Hans’s imagined exchange with her. When Hans disputes attribution of the Lotus Eaters’ perpetual afternoon to Horace, Marie specifies “my uncle Horace Higgenbotham” [A:16].

A:16

High MasterRank held by Count Finnegan as an accredited Astronaut of the Argo; it licenses his effigy’s presence among the ship’s absent Masters [MTM B13:449].

MTM B13:449

High Order of the Dirty FiveName given to the Dirty Five fellowship of which Henry Salvatore is a member [A:124].

A:124

High Period (Trinali's)Trinali Peterson’s name for her newly mature artistic phase. She says her style matured within the preceding eleven days and calls herself in her High Period [A:232]. She later dies from lilac dye, though the account leaves the manner of ingestion uncertain [A:239-240].

A:232; A:239-240

High Rider (of this Horse)Title in the signs advertising the Leader’s appearance beside the equestrian statue in Henry Horner Park: the horse’s High Rider will become Leader of the World and perhaps an Angel out of Heaven. Casey arrives in elaborate regalia, but Letitia intercepts him before he can mount the white horse [MTM B4:116-117].

MTM B4:116-117

High-school danceJunior-year dance to which Maurine Stranahan wants Finnegan to take her. When he doubts he will be admitted, she proposes telling the sister that he is a junior from St. Philomena’s; she also wants permission to tell the other girls they are engaged [A:100-101].

A:100-101

Hildebrand, SaintHildebrand, Pope Gregory VII (1073-1085), appears among the seamen aboard the Navicula Petri in Henry’s dream [A:44-45]. A leading reformer of the medieval Church, he opposed simony and enforced clerical celibacy. His resistance to lay investiture brought him into conflict with Henry IV, whom he excommunicated in 1076. Henry sought and received absolution at Canossa in 1077, but the conflict resumed. After Henry’s occupation of Rome and the violent intervention of Gregory’s Norman allies, Gregory withdrew to Salerno, where he died in 1085. His reported last words were “I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile.” He was later canonized.

A:44-45

HildegardeLiquor bottle named by Finnegan and his companions during their Basse-Terre beach storytelling. Their daily bottles receive women’s names: Hildegarde follows Agatha, Bathildes, Clotilda, Delphina, Etheldreda, Faustina, and Georgina [D:243]. She is half gone after Le Marin’s story and one-quarter full after Don Barnaby’s [D:248] [D:252]. When Finnegan’s story ends she is empty, and the four open Idabel for a final gulp before sleeping [D:256].

D:243; D:248; D:252; D:256

Hildegarde KattWife of Tommy Katt, the tough policeman. At the Old Wooden Ship, she tells Finnegan that her husband is the cop with the little moustache named Tommy, prompting Finnegan and Le Marin to pretend that Tommy is the moustache’s name [D:229-230].

D:229-230

Hill boyThe kind of island boy distinguished from Hans’s friend Sulem, who is specifically a shore boy rather than a hill boy [A:59].

A:59

Hill-billiesThe narrator’s term for inhabitants of New Jersey’s wild back country, described as more remote than people in Tennessee or Arkansas. Finnegan meets Gautier the goat-man in this landscape [A:193-194].

A:193-194

Hilton, AdrianBanker and older brother of Sebastian Hilton, one of the moneyed members of Duffey’s Chicago circle [MTM B3:100] [MTM B4:123]. In the Depression debate, he argues that vested interests deliberately caused the crisis through the March 1933 bank moratorium. He alleges that objecting bankers were murdered and names his father as one; Rollo McSorley claims the father was killed by a jealous husband, and the two men fight until Duffey and others separate them [MTM B4:123-124].

MTM B3:100; MTM B4:123; MTM B4:123-124

Hilton, HilaryWealthy businessman, Sebastian Hilton’s nephew and Mary Catherine Carruthers’s employer; his wife is Mary Jean [MTM B12:377-378]. Having known Casey since childhood, he identifies him as the Antichrist and says he seeks others’ sacrifice rather than money. He believes Casey fears measuring himself against Finnegan or Bishop Salvatore, and reports investigators’ findings that Finnegan is alive and awakening [MTM B12:378]. Hilary arranges a party for Duffey and about a hundred friends to tempt the uninvited Casey to appear, and watches Duffey’s televised projection of Casey’s head [MTM B12:379-381]. He buys the Resurrection of Count Finnegan from Duffey for $20,000 and leaves it in the Walk-In Art Bijou, where he returns to contemplate it [MB:553].

MTM B12:377-378; MTM B12:378; MTM B12:379-381; MB:553

Hilton, SebastianDuffey’s wealthy boarding-school friend, younger and slighter than he, pale and greenish in complexion but a fast, ruthless boxer, runner, and schemer. Duffey recognizes his intellectual superiority; Sebastian excels at the school subjects and understands the talismans more fully than Duffey himself [MTM B1:22-25]. He has traveled in France and Italy and claims an affair with a young countess; Duffey’s mental exploration confirms that a twelve-year-old countess exists [MTM B1:31]. Duffey gives him a talisman to pass to someone else, and Sebastian predicts it will work only partly [MTM B1:35]. He recognizes the three slant-faced pursuers and warns that his association with Duffey lets them triangulate on both targets [MTM B1:36]. He later drives ambulances in France and Italy; Duffey may have borrowed those experiences from his mind [MTM B2:72]. Sebastian attends the Colony Club dinner and belongs to the Chicago golden-age circle; Adrian is his older brother, and Hilary his nephew [MTM B3:94] [MTM B3:98-100] [MTM B12:378]. Duffey predicts his early death despite the family’s assurances of good health [MTM B3:102]. On his final New Orleans visit Sebastian anticipates their next meeting in the Kingdom. He marries Countess Margaret a month after returning to Chicago and is killed one month later [MTM B7:216].

MTM B1:22-25; MTM B1:31; MTM B1:35; MTM B1:36; MTM B2:72; MTM B3:94; MTM B3:98-100; MTM B12:378; MTM B3:102; MTM B7:216

HindEnglish venturer among the treasure ships on Angela Cosquin’s father’s master map. Angela describes this map as the source of commissioned treasure maps and forged supporting documents for confidence men [D:261].

D:261

HindiLanguage of Seaworthy’s dream in which he pushes an unaccountable corpse through an Indian city and cannot get rid of it. The people return it with the words “Ye tumhara hi kasur hai,” rendered in his account as “It’s your own fault” [D:72-73].

D:72-73

Hindi names (gems)Names of gems that Amoy knows only in Arabic or Hindi, beyond Ignatius Ti’s ability to translate. In Ti’s expansive account of Amoy’s former life as a red-winged blackbird, the stolen gems are brought to his jewel-thief master [A:80-81].

A:80-81

Hindrance (Aral)The Malay boy’s gloss for Aral, one of the names of the canoe from which he and the Sergeant dive. The boy also calls it Bumi, “of the world,” and Aragh, “the direction”; the Sergeant consequently recognizes it as the Ship Argo [A:89].

A:89

HinneganCasey’s farm-boy school roommate, who teaches him the musical saw and joins him in compiling a book of formulas [A:162-163]. Their room is supervised by the perennial senior Buttercup Butler. Casey tells Finnegan that the boy’s real name may have been Hannigan, Hanlon, or O’Hanlon; since knowing Finnegan, he has reconstructed the roommate as Hinnegan to rhyme with him [A:162].

A:162-163; A:162

Hiram (King of Tyre)King of Tyre, conventionally placed in the tenth century BC. The biblical account associates him with Solomon’s building projects and maritime expeditions to Ophir. In Hans’s reverie about the far southern land, the men of Solomon and Hiram have spent three years on the trip to Ophir, yet Hans imagines his own destination farther away still [A:16].

A:16

Hiram HuntAttributed author of The Death of the Species, the Chapter Nineteen epigraph. It describes humanity as a tense union of two inherited elements, compares their balance to bow and string, and warns that a victory of either element would destroy the whole [D:283-284].

D:283-284

Hiram III (King of St. Kobarid)Ruler of St. Kobarid in the Julian Alps, called the last king because he refuses the World Consensus General’s order to abolish his nation [MB:563-564]. At the Voltaire Festival in Babylonia Bagascia, fifty senior youths strangle him with the entrails of Paul the Eleventh. The killing takes two and a half or three hours, after which his body is surrendered to dismemberers and souvenir seekers [MB:564-565].

MB:563-564; MB:564-565

Hiram WalkerLiquor in Finnegan’s heavily stocked shoulder-bag when he leaves the Texas bars on foot during his search for the old Moonlight Cavalry [A:202].

A:202

Hitler, Adolf (1889--1945)Austrian-born Nazi leader and dictator of Germany from 1933 to 1945. His regime invaded Poland in 1939, beginning the Second World War in Europe, and carried out the Holocaust and other mass murders. Hitler died by suicide in Berlin in 1945. In Absalom Stein’s Notes on the Finnegan Cycle, Hitler is fantastically described as a raider from the future into Greater Neustria [MTM B6:185]. Tony Apostolo also jokes that even a living Hitler would be an unoriginal news story, claiming seven previous reporter encounters with seven Hitlers [PG:525].

MTM B6:185; PG:525

HoaxDuffey wonders whether the Royal Pop People’s demand for hospitality is a “howling hoax” [MTM B11:312]. Casey later claims that his childhood Leader-and-white-horse episode was only a hoax, but the narrator rejects that explanation: Letitia saw that he meant it seriously [MTM B4:118].

MTM B11:312; MTM B4:118

HoboYoung man with whom Finnegan says he talked all night beside a fire in the north woods. At dawn the man appeared about forty years older; Finnegan fled, then heard his terrible wailing after he saw his aged reflection in a pool [D:14].

D:14

Hochfelsen, Margaret (Countess)See Countess Margaret, The (Margaret Hochfelsen).
Hochheimer, HomerMarie Monaghan’s supposed Uncle Homer in her conversation inside Hans’s mind. She says his color-blindness led him to mistake a purple cow for a black one and sell it cheaply to a butcher, who then made a million pounds from it [A:24].

A:24

HochstaplerNickname given by the Professor and others to Betty’s father, glossed in the novel as a high-class swindler. A victim called a wool-hat kills him with his own barker’s mallet or gavel over less than three hundred dollars, claiming he meant only to hit him; the killer receives a year and a day [A:217].

A:217

Hochstapler, BettyCarnival acrobat and balancer, sixteen when Hans is fourteen, described as an unbreakable blonde doll. She first enjoys humiliating Hans but wants him as her sweetheart and prospective husband. Hans, embarrassed and feeling too young, encourages Angelo Angelino to marry her instead [A:216-217]. She admires her swindler father Hochstapler and is troubled by her inability to discover crookedness in Hans; even before marrying Angelo she has family connections with the Angelinos [A:217].

A:216-217; A:217

Hock shopDuffey’s pawnshop, part of the same establishment as his Walk-In Art Bijou, other businesses, and living quarters in New Orleans [MTM B11:311].

MTM B11:311

Hodson's Superior Horse WhipOne of the whips named by the Royal Pop lecturer in his account of memories preserved by an old Decatur Street flagstone. The list evokes the sounds of horse traffic and its drivers [MTM B11:328-329].

MTM B11:328-329

Hoe-down dancingOne of the everyday lively arts listed among those massively debased after the Devil’s release. The narrator places it beside cotillion dancing in the long inventory of threatened activities [MTM B6:207].

MTM B6:207

Hogan's AlleyPlace invoked in the description of the shabby Seabach: the boat looks as though drunken Irish carpenters from Hogan’s alley cobbled it together, and the narrator adds that parts of it actually were [D:135].

D:135

HogarthWilliam Hogarth (1697-1764), painter and engraver known for narrative series satirizing contemporary life, including A Harlot’s Progress and A Rake’s Progress. Patrick Stranahan names him with Watteau and Durer as one of the few acceptable sources of pictures in his restrictive rule of culture [A:109].

A:109

Hokey-pokey pushcartCart from which an Italian man sells small cakes. Duffey gives the man his first talisman when he is no more than three years old; the memory resurfaces when Mr. X comes to New Orleans [MTM B1:18] [MTM B6:200].

MTM B1:18; MTM B6:200

Hold him! (command)Order shouted by the hammer-carrying young man to his two larger companions. They pinion Melchisedech Duffy while the first man carefully smashes his watch glass [GD:481].

GD:481

Holland GinDrink Joseph contrasts with the palm wine he and Finnegan share in Freetown. He says Finnegan would be drinking whisky or Holland gin with his shipmates in the hotel bar if he were not a fellow low-lifer [D:93].

D:93

Holland, CyrilOne of the people of a scientific bent in Duffey’s Chicago golden-age circle, listed beside Catherine Quick [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

Hollow cliffsPart of the densely packed Black Papua landscape, threaded with dozens of miles of sponge-like caves and described with extravagant numbers of lizards and birds [A:36-37].

A:36-37

HollyScent to which the lingering odor of the burned Elephant Ear bush is compared. After Letitia’s death, Duffey speaks with the flaming bush and grudgingly accepts its explanation; the fire then subsides, leaving an odor “something like holly” [MTM B8:253].

MTM B8:253

Holy Apostle the tipplerApostle invoked by Show Boat in her letter to Dotty as Sanctus Apostolus Potator Incognitus. She reports Papa’s supposed old Italian legend of an apostle who finishes leftover wine, yet remains a successful evangelist; Papa cannot remember whether he was Thomas, Bartholomew, or Jude [A:262].

A:262

Holy ArgoSacred designation of the Argo. Count Finnegan predicts that the Holy Argo will carry Antichrist to the Plains of Megiddo while the unbroken line still has a reigning representative. Duffey, Brannagan, and Gorshok then seek means of preventing Antichrist from coming aboard [MTM B13:453-454]. Duffey also calls it the Holy Ship when recalling the high gestes preceding his shore leave and present lifetime [MTM B12:370] [MTM B12:387].

MTM B13:453-454; MTM B12:370; MTM B12:387

Holy GhostThe Holy Ghost appears in Duffey’s bitter joke to Becky Stein that even the Holy Ghost has bad days, after she attacks the changed funeral Mass [MTM B12:354]. At the Mooring Rock Conclave, the narrator credits the Holy Ghost with revealing that Paul the Eleventh secretly appointed Finnegan a Cardinal [MB:598]. John Giwa also says the Holy Ghost would confirm the election made by even a lone surviving Cardinal [MB:596].

MTM B12:354; MB:598; MB:596

Holy Grail (Sancgreal)The Sancgreal, said to have been stolen from Glastonbury and recovered among the treasures of the Argo voyages [MTM B13:422].

MTM B13:422

Holy MissalBook carried by Joseph of Maintz in the spherical chamber of his moon-launching device, alongside Scripture and other works, in Ignacio’s story of the Benedictine priest’s lunar voyage [A:271].

A:271

Holy PovertySpiritual poverty distinguished from squalor or deprivation. The narrator says it sacrifices good things, including money, rather than treating wealth itself as evil; both Holy Poverty and Holy Wealth are acknowledged [MTM B4:125]. Duffey tells Finnegan and Zabotski that the Devil can defame poverty and substitute degradation for it but cannot give true Holy Poverty. He links giving to willing receivers and to asking in good faith [MTM B6:194]. The Big Pot’s first six customers come from curiosity, and none is described as poor enough to belong to Holy Poverty [MTM B6:195].

MTM B4:125; MTM B6:194; MTM B6:195

Holy SlumgullionDuffey’s name for the food offered from the Big Pot. The plan is to keep it boiling indefinitely for poor people; its first six diners take soup from curiosity rather than poverty. Duffey worries that the pot might stay full because no one asks for its Holy Slumgullion [MTM B6:194-195].

MTM B6:194-195

Holy Water FontSmall chipped font on the bedroom wall in Finnegan’s intensely detailed memory of the twelve years he lived with Theresa. The account leaves the time and ontological status of that shared life uncertain [A:204].

A:204

Holy WealthWealth acknowledged by the narrator as capable of holiness, alongside Holy Poverty. In the passage defending the joy of money, Holy Poverty is meaningful because it sacrifices good things, and the narrator distinguishes both holy states from their unholy counterparts [MTM B4:125].

MTM B4:125

Home TownFinnegan’s native New Orleans, whose mixed speech still cannot fully account for his peculiar dialect [A:6]. In his later disordered wanderings, he reaches the wheel-shaped city where he was born but cannot find his friends or control his movements through it [A:200].

A:6; A:200

HomerTraditional name attached to the ancient Greek Iliad and Odyssey, conventionally dated to the late eighth or early seventh century BC. Homer’s identity and biography are uncertain; blindness belongs to the ancient tradition about him. The poems developed through oral performance, although their transition into written texts remains disputed. The Iliad centers on Achilles’ anger during the Trojan War, and the Odyssey on Odysseus’s return home. In the novel, Teresa claims that even Homer considered the Argonauts unaccountably ancient, insisting that her companions belong to fact older than Greek myth [MTM B7:233-234].

MTM B7:233-234

Homer HooseDumaine Street neighbor of Zabotski. Zabotski’s building lies between Duffey’s and Hoose’s; Hoose in turn lies between Zabotski and Bryan Blackstone. Zabotski says Hoose has not looked out his back window for a long time and is unaware of the giant contraption under construction [MTM B9:268-271].

MTM B9:268-271

HomicideCharge for which Patrick Stranahan says he defended the seaman Doppio di Pinne in St. Louis [A:111]. Finnegan believes Don Barnaby has fled to his island refuge because of homicide [D:249]. In X’s account, Ifreann killed a man at fifteen and escaped the Krakow region after this punishable murder of his sixteenth year [D:280].

A:111; D:249; D:280

HondoTexas town on Finnegan’s wandering route: after Uvalde on Monday, he passes through Sabinal, D’Hannis, and Hondo on Tuesday, then returns to D’Hannis seeking his old outfit, the Moonlight Cavalry [A:202].

A:202

HoneySeventy pounds brought back by Finnegan and Dotty after raiding four bee trees on a country frolic, then dumped into the Big Pot, appreciably changing the soup’s taste [A:134].

A:134

Honey TreeImagined setting in Hans’s hypnosis act with Mabel the bear: he tells her she has robbed a honey tree and is covered with bees, prompting a genuine fear reaction [A:219]. Honey-tree raiding also appears among the everyday arts the narrator says were debased after the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207].

A:219; MTM B6:207

HoneybucketSee Kincaid, Harry A. (Honeybucket).
HonoluluCity associated with Niku Kazuko, double of Cardinal Runosake of Kobe. The list first calls him probably of Honolulu; the later account calls him of Honolulu without qualification [MB:579] [MB:592].

Ifreann Noonan Columkill GregorovitchThe elder Papadiabolous in Mr. X’s account, whose grave bears the initials I.N.C.G.P. and the euphemistic surname Bogovitch. X says he was born near Krakow in 1830 to Katie Noonan, an Irish governess, and to the Devil, allegedly named as father in St. Elmo parish records; Gregory adopted him, accounting for Gregorovitch; X considers but rejects Gregory’s possible biological paternity [D:277-279]. X calls Ifreann Irish for "Devil," although its ordinary meaning is "hell." His story describes a large, brutal child with exceptional mentality but no intelligence, who killed cats, tried to kill children, and fled after killing a man at fifteen. X places his later travels in Austria, Russia, Greece, Smyrna, London, Ireland, Milano, Sicily, and America, and makes him a forty-year-old participant in the Paris Commune and disciple of Kropotkin [D:280-281]. At seventy he allegedly fathered two simultaneous sons by different mothers: Gregory McIfreann, Papadiabolous I, in Smyrna, and Gregory McColum, Papadiabolous II, in Cork, on opposite sides of the century’s boundary [D:285-286]. He died at a hundred in 1930. His son Gregory McIfreann was later buried above him, in the grave Finnegan helped Seaworthy deepen [D:288]. His full family name in X’s account is Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch Papadiabolous Chortovitch [D:278]. X also says he called himself a citizen of Krakow [D:280]. In The Flame Is Green, Ifreann Chortovitch is Dana Coscuin’s great antagonist and Catherine Dembinska’s feared acquaintance from childhood. Catherine repeats the 1830 birth and demonic paternity, reporting that he looked twelve at birth and murdered children; another witness says he looked twelve at two. Reports of his death are accompanied by a were-cat explanation of repeated lives (The Flame Is Green, PDF pp. 189, 210-211, 248). Huge, purple-complexioned, imposing and potentially handsome, he deals in bodies rather than love, threatens Catherine and says he can trace her. His heartiness and vitality exert a disturbing attraction. In one of his Paris houses, an orgy projects the men’s private hells; Charley Oceaan breaks the illusions, and the four companions drink Ifreann into stupor. Catherine and Charley remove documents afterward (The Flame Is Green, PDF pp. 187-190, 203-209). Following Catherine’s murder and the discovery of Ifreann’s signed message, Dana tracks his animal stench and staggering stride, then runs him through with a rapier and takes him for dead (The Flame Is Green, PDF pp. 254-257). In Half a Sky, attacks on Dana’s companions follow their Amsterdam meeting, casting doubt on Ifreann’s death. He reappears to claim the Porte d’Enfer estate and Dana’s rock house, while witnesses debate his bodily and ghostly manifestations. Dana suspects that his four flunkies are zombie-like projections; O’Boyle is one of these agents. Ifreann later explains that he lay wounded for three days and delirious in a Krakow pest-house for six months, projecting that delirium onto Dana. He boasts of having fulfilled his earlier promises of violence and means to kill Dana while he is out of grace (Half a Sky, PDF pp. 22-23, 38-40, 53-58, 62-64, 84-86). He shoots Dana’s thumb during the cliff ambush with O’Boyle (Half a Sky, PDF pp. 90-93). Hidden aboard the Catherine, he corrupts food and thoughts, induces sleep, starts fires and levitates objects; one man is killed. Lured by putrid pork and drugged rum, he becomes a monstrous glutton. Dana stabs him, the company throws him overboard, and he changes through marine forms before swimming away as a man. He returns weakened in Santiago, then recovers enough to assault Dana with visions of a destroyed world (Half a Sky, PDF pp. 111-112, 120-122, 127-132). Kemper’s broader theory of the Devil Unchained asks whether Ifreann is their own projection; Dana rejects this (Half a Sky, PDF pp. 134-136). Ifreann commands the ironclad Brami Piekielne, glossed as Gates of Hell. Dana damages it off the Horn and escapes; Dana uses Kemper’s dead-man sight, while Ifreann has only his own night-eyes. The Lord of the Flies is Ifreann’s uncle (Half a Sky, PDF pp. 143-144, 146, 150-153, 160). Ifreann torments Dana with the claim that the child’s bones in his chest are Catherine’s son by Ifreann’s violation of her after death; Dana’s inspection finds no confirming demonic bone (Half a Sky, PDF pp. 191-193). In the final collision of their ships, the Catherine and Gates of Hell explode, and Dana and Jack Galopade pursue Ifreann into the sea. His final death is not narrated (Half a Sky, PDF pp. 197, 202-204).
