Ignace WolffName to which The Devil Is Dead attributes an epigraph from Gedanken von Leibern. It says that bodies thwart non-contradiction, negate the principle of sufficient reason, and have no sufficient reason [D:67].

D:67

IgnacioLawyer who helps Finnegan in the Spanish-speaking town where Finnegan is unsure of his surroundings. He says the authorities know of Finnegan’s activities and remain friendly, recounts Joseph of Maintz’s moon-rocket story, and discusses the possibility of going to St. Kitts [A:269-272]. Elena calls him after Finnegan’s fight, and he has already contacted Finnegan’s friends [A:273]. Letters from Ignacio and Elena tell Dotty Yekouris that Finnegan is "coming apart" [MTM B8:237].

A:269-272; A:273; MTM B8:237

Ignatius Cardinal TiCardinal of Manila and one of the thirteen Princes of the Ekklesia in Flight targeted by John Mogul. The list of doubles pairs him with Bolo Manolo [MB:579]. He is among the eleven surviving princes who enter Mogul’s contest [MB:580]; his death is reported before the verse commanding that the next victim be flayed [MB:583]. His epitaph is "My chalice indeed you shall drink" [MB:589]. A later passage instead calls Lloyd Cardigan-Pembroke, the pig butcher of Tywyn, the double of the dead Cardinal Ti [MB:594].

MB:579; MB:580; MB:583; MB:589; MB:594

Illo tempore---Part of Mr. X’s opening "In illo tempore" for the story of the Devil’s grave. The phrase functions as a Latin once-upon-a-time formula: X also begins in French and then resumes "Once upon a time" in English [D:284-285].

D:284-285

Illumination (Interior)Interior understanding that Duffey says is needed to interpret the Argo’s log, whose record extends nine thousand years backward and sixty-seven years forward [MTM B13:411].

MTM B13:411

IllyriaAncient region of the Balkan Peninsula along the Adriatic. Gabrielovitch places Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, in Illyria and explains argosy through Ragosy, a fleet from Ragusa [A:127]. John Schultz’s letter associates the Argo’s westward voyages with Illyria and the Adriatic, allowing variant routes [MTM B6:186]. Finnegan’s travel poem wonders whether Illyrian fleets were lost in Illyrian fogs [A:172].

A:127; MTM B6:186; A:172

IllyrianAdjective for the fleets and fogs in Finnegan’s travel poem: he wonders whether all the Illyrian fleets were lost in Illyrian fogs [A:172].

A:172

ImazuOne of the names Mr. X gives during a telephone call involving the "Y" code book. The passage does not identify its bearer or explain its significance [D:184].

D:184

ImmortalityPrivate Gregory calls the will immortal while explaining possession as hypnotism from beyond the grave [A:84]. Marie Courtois claims that the recurring earthly return of beings like herself, Demeter and her own Persephone, is the only immortality; Finnegan answers that she is wrong, although the proof is not there [D:91].

A:84; D:91

Imperial BarPossible name of the Basse-Terre establishment the companions call Sloppy Joe’s; Finnegan is unsure whether its real name is the Imperial or the Royal [D:235]. Its proprietor is Joseph Chastaigne, and Angela Cosquin works there [D:266].

D:235; D:266

Imperial CarriageOne of the vehicles named by the turbaned Pop Historian as he evokes the memories supposedly held by a Decatur Street flagstone [MTM B11:329].

MTM B11:329

Imperial QuartBeer measure described in Archipelago as thirty-nine ounces, with a "jolt at the end." Finnegan, Vincent, Freddy, and Tom progress to it after steins [A:14]. In a separate contest, Joe Bushmaster downs his sixth imperial quart in one gulp, winning even Hans Schultz’s admiration [A:22].

A:14; A:22

In Absentia, O Absentia!Label for Giovanni, Finnegan’s place among the Seven Pillars of Righteousness on the Bark masthead drawing that Finnegan supplies [A:121-122].

A:121-122

In hoc signo vincetLatin motto on a pennant of the Navicula Petri in Henry Salvatore’s dream [A:44]. Its vincet means "he will conquer"; it recalls the traditional In hoc signo vinces, "In this sign you will conquer," associated with Constantine’s vision before the battle of 312.

A:44

In PettoItalian for "in secret," literally "in the breast." Paul XI names Finnegan a cardinal in petto after Finnegan paints his portrait, a week before the pope is murdered [MB:598]. The unreliable Mr. X also claims that a deceased pope made Finnegan a Papal Count in petto [MTM B12:367].

MB:598; MTM B12:367

IncarnationThe Creator’s visit to his own creation, discussed in an epigraph attributed to G. K. Chesterton’s The Everlasting Man [MTM B5:176]. A different idea, reincarnation, appears in Marie Courtois’s claim that she returns every year as both Demeter and her own Persephone [D:91].

MTM B5:176; D:91

IncendiarismDeliberate fire-setting. In Charles O. A. Harrington’s hostile review of Royce Rollins’s The Return of the Neanderthal, Rollins is accused of attributing revolutionary movements, incendiarism, and massacres to alien beings within humanity [D:240-242].

D:240-242

IncenseThe mesquite coals of the Padre Island fish fry give off a weedy smell with a touch of incense [D:34]. Incense bushes belong to the Boy King Melchisedech’s remembered domain [MTM B1:17]. Incense is burned during the offerings at the opening of the Princes’ Conclave in Babylonia Bagascia [MB:565-566].

D:34; MTM B1:17; MB:565-566

IncubusEvil spirit said to lie upon sleepers. Planning the Sinbad panels, Finnegan says that William Gerecke, his Old Man of the Sea, "looks like an incubus" [D:62].

D:62

Indelecio, JohnJohn "Little Alcohol" Indelecio, a regular at the Old Wooden Ship, is the climbing and high-window specialist in a burglary partnership with John "Big Alcohol" Jereboam. The pair undertake jobs only when deeply in debt to Lazarus Reilly [D:215] [D:218].

D:215; D:218

IndiaRecurring setting of Seaworthy’s dreams, which he calls the land of his unconscious. He describes a gray, colorless dream of an unidentified Indian city where he cannot dispose of a male corpse and a cart wheel repeatedly comes off. He also claims that a Hindu sect regards India as Purgatory and its members as already dead [D:72-73]. Finnegan recalls and interprets this conversation while swimming underwater; he decides the corpse is literal and the Indian setting may stand for a Western one [D:71] [D:74]. The Boy King has milk from India buffalo [MTM B1:17-18], and the hybrid Kasmir-Stein is described as a remote jewel of India [MTM B5:183].

D:72-73; D:71; D:74; MTM B1:17-18; MTM B5:183

Indian ScalperA figure of the sensational American adventure literature preserved in the Harlow House library, including the listed Buffalo Hunter and Indian Scalper. These are among the old goat-man’s favorite books [A:197-198].

A:197-198

Indian WarUnspecified conflict during which Private Gregory says his papers were lost. He says losses during this war and the Civil War each allowed him to subtract decades from his recorded age, concealing his failure to age during a long U.S. Army career [A:77].

A:77

Indian-coloredDescription of the cigar-store Christ from St. Kitts among Duffey’s collected Christ images. A Black island artist uses the cigar-store Indian convention, including a hand shaped to hold cigars, but gives the bare-headed figure Christ’s face [MTM B3:103].

MTM B3:103

Indianapolis raceThe Indianapolis 500 automobile race, first held in 1911. Finnegan brings a portable radio to follow the race during his graveyard meeting with Doll Delaney and Mr. X; they choose the day because other cemetery visitors will make them less conspicuous [D:276].

D:276

Indians (Cigar Store)Four life-size wooden figures carved by Finnegan during his approximately three-week stay with Casey in Chicago, combining authenticity, humor, and burlesque. He sells them for a hundred dollars each; Hillary Hilton later keeps one for his love of Finnegan and will not sell it [A:183]. In Not to Mention Camels, a slightly larger-than-life Finnegan cigar-store Indian is described as "woodenly vital" and holds cigars that prove real. The same novel reports a disputed claim that Gregory van Ghi was Finnegan’s disciple, while noting that van Ghi was older. It also gives Count Finnegan a role in shaping the Narrow Corner: Anastasia recounts its prophetic frightfulness, and he projects it back through his visualization.

A:183

IndiesThe Indies are a projected destination in Finnegan’s travel poem [A:173], and Ignacio describes St. Kitts as an unusually interesting island among them [A:272]. Teresa quotes a prophecy that Duffey’s Argo will carry Count Finnegan to an obscure place in the Indies to be elected and crowned [MTM B12:388]. A painting of the risen Count associates his altered flesh with the uncoffined dead of poor people in the West Indies [MB:551].

A:173; A:272; MTM B12:388; MB:551

IndigestionUnverified association with Peter Wirt. The cited passage calls him a man with "the mind of a wolverine," but gives him no digestive complaint [D:163].

D:163

IndulgenceFinnegan’s distant appearance is compared to Dionysus before he became "puffy with indulgence" [A:6]. Seaworthy says that all their sort indulge in amnesia, and Finnegan thinks this is an indulgence he should abandon [D:11-12]. Lily Koch jokes that she envies people whose lifestyles permit them to indulge in murder [MTM B3:97].

A:6; D:11-12; MTM B3:97

IndultEcclesiastical permission for an exception to Church law. The phrase "at the drop of an indult" describes how readily Duffey, the Bark’s theology reviewer, could name the hundred leading theologians [MTM B6:208].

MTM B6:208

Industrial-Agricultural countryThe underlying landscape in Tartary over which a false desert is sometimes superimposed. Duffey notices incorrectly made rocks and plants, suspicious skeletal remains, and fierce heat that does not move the sand or vegetation [MTM B13:439].

MTM B13:439

Ineffable NameGod’s name understood as unutterable or not to be spoken. No specific occurrence or identifiable allusion has been located in the three novels.
InertiaAn unlocated label originally attached to the Great Day’s transformations. The cited episode shows apparently absent coffee cups collapsing, but does not discuss inertia [GD:485].

GD:485

Infidels (New)The New Infidels have ruled Tartary for several generations when the Argo is sent to investigate the Laughing Prince. Tartary is no longer even an official name [MTM B13:438].

MTM B13:438

InfiltratesPlotters or diabolists said to penetrate the People, the State, and the Church, recorded on index cards in the brown box Mr. X steals from Casey [MTM B6:203]. Casey says Duffey has indexed several thousand in laymen’s groups and would have them "up by the thumbs" if he could [A:42-43]. X supplements the file but warns that his information, like all information on the Infiltrates, should be taken with a grain of salt [A:136-137]. Duffey later keeps the file in his walk-in safe [A:143]. In a separate episode Manuel plans to infiltrate the apparatus that turns men into devils [D:56].

MTM B6:203; A:42-43; A:136-137; A:143; D:56

InformationMr. X collects secret information, supplements the Infiltrates file, and warns that it requires skepticism [MTM B6:200] [A:137]. He withholds accusations for which he lacks independent corroboration and says his supposed Devil informant knows only disconnected glimpses of the future [A:139-140]. Duffey’s later account again warns that X cannot be depended upon [MB:549]. X also displays knowledge of Mogul’s assassination contracts [MB:570-571]. Marie Courtois obtains Finnegan’s details for the ship’s register; Anastasia tells him Marie needs more information [D:21] [D:32]. The Naxos raiders rely on inadequate maps and a girl’s childhood memories [D:136], while X later questions Finnegan unsuccessfully about intelligence he might have gathered aboard the Brunhilde [D:188]. Angela Cosquin’s maps suggest she has obtained the locations of Finnegan’s hidden treasure from his mind [D:263]. The narrator gives supposedly exact coordinates for Paradise [D:234]. X says a document buried with the elder Devil contains dangerously valuable information, motivating Seaworthy’s grave-opening and X’s own proposed search [D:288] [D:290].

MTM B6:200; A:137; A:139-140; MB:549; MB:570-571; D:21; D:32; D:136; D:188; D:263; D:234; D:288; D:290

Infra-red cookers (Directional)A proposed assassination device among the submissions to John Mogul’s murder contest. The fictional proposal imagines a directional cooker heating a victim’s internal organs without leaving an external mark [MB:581].

MB:581

Infra-red raysPart of the extravagant description of Teresa Piccone as a blue-light phenomenon: looking too long at her supposedly gives the viewer welders’ eye-burns [MTM B5:163].

MTM B5:163

IngrahamOne of the aliases Mr. X assigns to Gregory McColum Papadiabolous, the Irish-born Papadiabolous II, also called Noonan and described as a son of Ifreann [D:285].

D:285

Inhabited World (Oikoumene)An unlocated term originally associated with the Argo’s voyages. The cited passage says that the ship knows all the world’s seas and islands, but does not name the Oikoumene or say that it sails beyond the inhabited world [MTM B13:405].

MTM B13:405

InkDuffey uses squid ink kept in a bowl for official writing and uses it to answer the Royal Pop People’s invitation [MTM B11:312-313]. Finnegan draws Manuel in ink on the back of a poster during the visit to Demetrio’s bar [D:58].

MTM B11:312-313; D:58

InklingCasey’s impression that rich men might practice a secret higher religion, prompted by seeing them enter the monsignor’s study after Benediction. The meeting is actually for a fundraising drive, and Casey never finds the imagined higher religion [A:158-159].

A:158-159

InnCasey drinks in a College Inn instead of attending a lecture during his irregular college years, 1938-1942 [A:167]. After swimming from Naxos to Paros, Finnegan sits at an inn for three days before Mr. X arrives [D:151-152]. Costerman’s Whalers’ Inn is among the waterfront establishments Duffey remembers [MTM B13:407].

A:167; D:151-152; MTM B13:407

“Interior Garden, The” (story)Don Barnaby’s account of the courtyard at Madame Le Mourcheor’s establishment after he takes one of her joy pills. The apparently small garden expands to contain whole worlds; he experiences a marriage and children whose names and appearances continually change while their identities persist [D:249-250].

D:249-250

Investigator, ThePublication started by Absalom Stein, Melchisedech Duffey, and Gabrielovitch. It is printed at the Pelican Press but is separate from The Bark; the three men’s outside incomes help make it independent. Duffey writes for both journals [A:143].

A:143

IolcusAncient Thessalian city associated with Jason. Rosemary Riorden addresses the amnesiac Sergeant as Aeson’s son and tells him that he will never return in the flesh to Iolcus [A:89]. Gabrielovitch later identifies Ragusa in Illyria as the original Iolcus, within the novel’s shifting account of the Argosy and its voyagers [A:127].

A:89; A:127

Ionian SeaSea between southeastern Italy and western Greece; included among the many seas sailed by the Argo and remembered by Melchisedech Duffey [MTM B13:406].

MTM B13:406

IowaMidwestern American state associated with one of Duffey’s three competing childhoods. An older relative places him with cousins in Iowa towns and on farms from ages five to twelve. Harrison, Shelby, and Pottawattamie are alternative counties of origin, while Minden, Underwood, Beebee Town, Neola, Crescent, Avoca, and Union Township dispute his birthplace [MTM B1:7]. The Iowa memories include the Lake Manawa encounter in which he holds a threatening man underwater by mental force, the substituted fat altar boy at the bell rope, and the farm episode with the sorrel kit fox [MTM B1:8-9] [MTM B1:14-15] [MTM B1:19-20]. Iowa’s red squirrels, apple trees, and wheat and cornfields contrast with his other childhood landscapes and the more convincing memories of the Boy King [MTM B1:17]. Neola, Iowa, was also R. A. Lafferty’s birthplace [D:295].

MTM B1:7; MTM B1:8-9; MTM B1:14-15; MTM B1:19-20; MTM B1:17; D:295

IrelandA source of family identity, names, and stories, often treated with irony. Patrick Stranahan belongs to the “Little-Irish Rich” of St. Louis [A:102]. It is Captain Guiterrez, speaking to Vincent, who calls Irish claims of Milesian antiquity “toy history” [A:66]. Finnegan bears an Irish nickname [D:122], while his family history combines the Solli and McCracken names and his sister locates their childhood in the Irish Channel [A:173-175]. When Doll disputes his knowledge of Ireland, he claims a day and a half in Bantry unloading cargo [D:192].

X’s account makes Katie Noonan the Irish mother of Ifreann and places the birth of Gregory McColum, Papadiabolous II, in Cork [D:279] [D:285]. On the Cuban journey, Duffey’s seaman’s papers identify him as “Mike Duffey,” a citizen of the Irish Free State [MTM B12:369]. In the Argo’s legendary history, St. Brandon sails her from Ireland to America [MTM B13:404].

A:102; A:66; D:122; A:173-175; D:192; D:279; D:285; MTM B12:369; MTM B13:404

IrishIrish identities, manners, and speech recur throughout the novels. Duffey acquires Lace Curtain Irish elegance from Charley Murray and recalls the memorable-face saying when he meets Bagby [MTM B1:26] [MTM B2:43]. A teacher calls Duffey a flaming Irishman, Stein calls him a filthy Irishman, and Patrick Plunket calls him a snake-bit and lame-brained Irishman [MTM B4:135] [GD:493] [MTM B12:391-392]. His Mike Duffey papers identify him as an Irish Free State citizen; in Cuba, he can pass for any Irishman [MTM B12:369] [MTM B12:372]. Irish women attend St. Malachy’s; Irish and Italian guests attend the Stranahan-Piccone wedding; Duffey’s company dines at Girardeau’s Irish Restaurant [MTM B3:88] [MTM B5:183] [MTM B11:315] [MTM B11:318]. Plunket is called an Irish saint, magician, and medical doctor [MTM B12:389]. Patrick Stranahan is lace-curtain and grand-piano Irish rich, and Marie Monaghan belongs to old Irish Monaghan, Larkin, and Murphey families [A:102] [A:7]. Vincent credits the Irish with the bottle; Finnegan’s mixed speech includes waterfront Irish, and Howell discusses Irish wakes’ mixture of horror and humor [A:5-6] [A:85]. A Naxos boy calls Finnegan an Italian with an Irish name. Papadiabolous II identifies Seabach as an Irish nickname, and X identifies that dead double with the Irish policeman called Noonan or Flaherty [D:145] [D:122] [D:154]. X says Ifreann’s mother was the Irish governess Katie Noonan and attributes Irish accents in parts of Poland, Brazil, Italy, and Spain to such governesses and nuns [D:278-279]. He glosses Ifreann as Devil, although the Irish word means hell. X’s own Cork identity is Gregory McColum [D:285]. Finnegan drunkenly claims a brief visit to Bantry, Mary Catherine brings out Irish whisky, and Patti places the Solli family in New Orleans’ Irish Channel rather than the Quarter [D:192] [A:249] [A:175].

MTM B1:26; MTM B2:43; MTM B4:135; GD:493; MTM B12:391-392; MTM B12:369; MTM B12:372; MTM B3:88; MTM B5:183; MTM B11:315; MTM B11:318; MTM B12:389; A:102; A:7; A:5-6; A:85; D:145; D:122; D:154; D:278-279; D:285; D:192; A:249; A:175

Irish ChannelNew Orleans neighborhood in which Patti Solli says her family grew up, contradicting Finnegan’s account of being raised in the heart of the Quarter [A:175].

A:175

Irish saint and magician (Patrick Plunket)Patrick Plunket, called a great Irish saint, magician, and medical doctor, serves as Duffey’s mentor in the seventh contingency. This is a dying vision, still short of death and finality [MTM B12:389]. Plunket insists that the landscape Duffey mistakes for artistic animation is real, identifies the Invisible Mountain as an interior ascent in intensity, and explains that they are in the Presence and walking with Permanence Itself [MTM B12:390-391].

MTM B12:389; MTM B12:390-391

Iron CurtainName for the political division between Soviet-dominated eastern Europe and the West after World War II. In the discussion of imitations of Casey’s Crock, a Tucalul is said to exist behind the iron curtain [A:168].

A:168

Iron LadderSky-hung ladder in Hans Schultz’s exhilarating climbing dream. It rises thousands of feet through clouds and past golden eagles toward the sun; the ascent brings a sense of perfection and achievement, and the dream associates Hans with Apollo [A:61-62].

A:61-62

Iron MeadowsPlaces inhabited by Aspects in an epigraph attributed to Bascom Bagby’s Letters After I Am Dead. It says that some aspects of the Argo Legend dwell in one such meadow, unknown to both God and Duffey [MTM B5:177].

MTM B5:177

Iscamyl AcetateIscamyl Acetate is the novel’s printed form, apparently referring to isoamyl acetate or banana oil. See Isoamyl acetate.
Isle of BlissThe paradise Finnegan’s unwritten verse says he found, almost on Naxos Isle. The poem joins this remembered bliss to the hope of walking there again and to the presence or absence of dead friends [D:117-118].

D:117-118

Isles of Greece, theOpening refrain of the verse attributed to the Unwritten poems of Finnegan, the epigraph to the Anastasia Demetriades chapter of The Devil Is Dead. It celebrates Anastasia and a briefly attained peace, then locates an Isle of Bliss almost on Naxos and imagines returning there; its closing lines remember friends, including the dead [D:117-118].

D:117-118

Isoamyl acetateCasey Szymansky’s high-school notebook identifies a substance printed as Iscamyl Acetate as Banana Oil [A:162-163]. It apparently refers to isoamyl acetate, a compound also known as banana oil.

A:162-163

Israel, ShirleyMember of the Chicago circle around the McSorleys, Calumets, and Hallahans. Her near-north-side salon is rumored to outdo the Duffeys’ in wit and information, and the group wants to retain Duffey because of his magic [MTM B4:137]. A compromising photograph of Duffey with Shirley forms part of the blackmail portfolio; the narrator calls the scene an entrapment and a badger-game trick [MTM B4:139-140]. Shirley disparages Duffey’s bars as old-fashioned, hisses at Demetrio Glauch, and serves drinks fortified with an additive. Rollo’s later report of the Green Mule appears to refer to these drinks [MTM B4:126-127] [MTM B4:129] [MTM B4:132].

MTM B4:137; MTM B4:139-140; MTM B4:126-127; MTM B4:129; MTM B4:132

ItaliansItalian people and identities recur in Duffey’s and Finnegan’s stories. Duffey gives his first talisman to an Italian confectioner; Piccone of the Star and Garter offers work to Mary Louise and Beth; Italian women, including a girl whose beauty elevates Duffey’s soul, attend St. Malachy’s [MTM B1:18] [MTM B2:58] [MTM B3:88]. Sebastian Hilton has traveled in Italy and is fancifully said to order parts for his better world from there [MTM B1:22] [MTM B1:25]. Duffey claims ambulance service in Italy with Hemingway, though his war memories may be borrowed, and witnesses place him there with the Argo [MTM B2:72]. Teresa Piccone’s Italian features and her enormous Italian meals are described; the cooking episode jokes that Italian vegetables are imported even in Italy and compares O’Conner’s and Peterson’s Italian restaurants [MTM B5:171] [MTM B7:230]. Irish and Italian guests attend the Stranahan-Piccone wedding. Margaret Stone is described as Italian and Jewish, with possible Greek and Pre-Adamite elements [MTM B5:183] [MTM B11:310]. Finnegan identifies his ancestry as Italian, speaks Italian with Palermo idlers, thinks the finger-count game Italian, and is called an Italian with an Irish name [D:93] [D:114] [D:104] [D:145]. A Greek Capuchin speaks Italian and chides Solli for inadequate Greek, arguing from southern Italy’s Greek ancestry [D:118-119]. Manuel plans to inform the Pope in Rome, while X attributes Irish-accented English in parts of Italy to Irish nuns and governesses [D:150-151] [D:279].

MTM B1:18; MTM B2:58; MTM B3:88; MTM B1:22; MTM B1:25; MTM B2:72; MTM B5:171; MTM B7:230; MTM B5:183; MTM B11:310; D:93; D:114; D:104; D:145; D:118-119; D:150-151; D:279

ItalyCountry associated with several competing memories and fictional journeys. Sebastian Hilton travels there and is fancifully said to obtain parts for his better world from Italy [MTM B1:22] [MTM B1:25]. Duffey claims Italian ambulance service with Hemingway, though these memories may be borrowed; witnesses also place him there with the Argo [MTM B2:72]. Teresa’s cooking episode jokes about imported Italian vegetables, and Babylonia Bagascia, the site of the Last Conclave, is placed in Italy [MTM B7:230] [MB:570]. The Ionian Sea lies between Italy and Greece and appears in the Argo’s itinerary [MTM B13:406]. Finnegan claims Italian ancestry and speaks Italian in Palermo; the Naxos Capuchin explains southern Italy through Greek ancestry [D:93] [D:114] [D:118-119]. X recounts Ifreann’s life in Milano and Sicily, offers an Irish-governess explanation for Irish-accented English in parts of Italy, and has himself belonged to the Party there under another name [D:279-280] [A:137-138]. Patti contradicts Finnegan’s account of Italian art schooling: she says his only visit was two days in Naples between ships the previous year [A:175].

MTM B1:22; MTM B1:25; MTM B2:72; MTM B7:230; MB:570; MTM B13:406; D:93; D:114; D:118-119; D:279-280; A:137-138; A:175

Jackass FlatsName of one of the precipitous places remembered in Don Lewis’s account of being lost with Santee and Casper on Willy Jones Island, after the killing of the small man called Yokipoki. Despite knowing many named valleys, they cannot identify the valley they have entered [D:44-46].

D:44-46

Jacko (young)Youthful persona in Shakes Pearson’s unfinished first-person limerick about making chewing tobacco from old sacks, boots, and boot-jacks. Shakes is Marie Monaghan’s uncle [A:25-26].

A:25-26

Jacksonville Drover, The (whip)Whip named alongside the Cowles Buggy Whip by the turbaned speaker at a Royal Pop History gathering. It belongs to his catalogue of precisely remembered objects from the former world [MTM B11:329].

MTM B11:329

Jake (Leg) LewisResident regular of the Old Wooden Ship and, with Tommy (Cow Town) Borger, a salt-water cowboy who works aboard cattle boats. He wears cowboy gear, including boots, spurs, chaps, and gauntlets, though these cowboys use no horses and live through long gaps between voyages [D:216] [D:222].

D:216; D:222

Janeway, Celeste LynneEarlier heading inverted Janeway as though it were her surname. See Lynne, Janeway Celeste.
Jangle chainLong hanging chain associated with a zoot suit, typically looping from the waistband to a trouser pocket. The Armenian merchant Askandan, also called Asking Dan, promises to find one for Casey after selling him a zoot suit, pointed shoes, and a monstrous hat on credit [A:258] [A:260-261].

A:258; A:260-261

Januarius O'HigginsLiterary friend named with Elena O’Higgins among Duffey’s Chicago company of the golden years [MTM B3:98]. In Josephine McSorley’s report on the Casey Machine, Januarius calls Casey a hypocrite and predicts that Casey will secretly buy one of the machines himself [CM:506-507].

MTM B3:98; CM:506-507

JanuaryMonth of Hans Schultz’s birth on January 2, 1915 [A:207] [MTM B3:76]. Finnegan stops drinking at New Year’s in Port of Spain and resumes on January 26 at Freetown, the date he describes as his fall from grace [D:85] [D:93].

A:207; MTM B3:76; D:85; D:93

JapanCountry identified with Xavier Cardinal Runosake of Kobe, whom X names among the thirteen contracted assassination targets [MB:571].

MB:571

Japan SeaSea between Japan and mainland Asia, also called the Sea of Japan or East Sea. It is included among the many seas sailed by the Argo and remembered by Duffey [MTM B13:406].

MTM B13:406

Japanese soldierRagged little man who seems to be a Japanese soldier in Don Lewis’s account of October 1, 1944, on Pulau Petir or Willy Jones Island. The pursuing Americans are Charles Santee, Robert Casper, and Timothy Lorrigan; Don Lewis says he was one of them while withholding a firm identification. The small man beckons, twice evades capture by apparent disappearance, is wounded by Santee, and is finally killed by Santee and Casper [D:44-45]. Lewis later calls him Yokipoki, probably not his real name [D:46].

D:44-45; D:46

JargonTerm in Finnegan’s letter to Dotty contrasting the unkindness expressed in jazz with that expressed in jargon. The letter attacks the moral and emotional character of several musical forms [A:263].

A:263

JarsGautier carries dried goat meat mixed with melted fat and honey in jars or skin bags [A:197]. Duffey stocks his new establishment with five-gallon jars of pigs’ feet, spiced Polish sausage, and apple butter [MTM B2:41]. As a child, Duffey also keeps jars of blood; Charles Hart says he used to do the same and remarks that blood attracts weasels [MTM B1:18].

A:197; MTM B2:41; MTM B1:18

JascoyneGreat fish encountered by St. Brandon in the Argo’s legendary history. The ship is said to have been called Land of Behest when he sailed her from Ireland to America [MTM B13:404].

MTM B13:404

JasonLeader of the Argonauts in the quest for the Golden Fleece, identified with Finnegan, John A. Solli, under the spelling Iason [A:39]. Solli’s birth year is 1919 [MTM B3:76]. In the classical tradition Jason is Aeson’s son, deprived of his inheritance by Pelias; the one-sandal prophecy leads Pelias to send him after the Fleece. Hera supports his voyage. In Apollonius’s Argonautica, Jason becomes leader with Heracles’ endorsement. He is Hypsipyle’s lover on Lemnos, but Heracles must spur the company to resume its journey; Apollodorus records their children. The voyagers undergo island mysteries, defeat the Earthborn with Heracles, and mistakenly fight their former hosts at night, when Jason kills Cyzicus. Heracles is later left behind in Mysia. Jason joins the fighting against the Bebrycians; the sons of Boreas drive off Phineus’s Harpies, and Phineus advises the passage of the Clashing Rocks. Tiphys steers, Euphemus releases the dove, and Athena helps the ship through. In Colchis, Medea’s divinely induced love and magical aid enable Jason to yoke the fire-breathing bulls, plough the field, sow the dragon’s teeth, and defeat the earthborn warriors. She subdues the Fleece’s guardian, and they escape together. In Apollonius, Jason kills Apsyrtus in a plot devised with Medea, and Circe purifies the pair. Their marriage among the Phaeacians prevents Medea’s surrender. In Libya Jason receives the goddesses’ riddle and Peleus interprets it, leading to the company’s portage of the ship. Medea defeats Talos, and Jason interprets Euphemus’s dream of the clod that becomes Thera. Apollodorus continues the story after the return: Medea contrives Pelias’s death, Acastus expels the couple, and Jason’s later marriage at Corinth provokes Medea’s revenge. His story combines leadership and resourcefulness with dependence on companions, divine aid, and Medea.

A:39; MTM B3:76

JavaPlace from which Anne broadcasts for the Japanese to Allied troops during the war [A:46]. Brannagan later tells Finnegan that he has lived in Java’s interior [D:203].

A:46; D:203

Java SeaOne of the seas sailed by the Argo, whose name recalls Duffey’s own voyages [MTM B13:406].

MTM B13:406

Jaw bonesRemains invoked in Hans’s comic argument that forks predate fingers: he claims that old jaw bones, brain pans, and pelvises are found, whereas equally old fingers are not [A:5].

A:5

JazzMusic that Finnegan dislikes, particularly in New Orleans; he objects to printing a jazz magazine and later tells Dotty that jazz can express more unkindness than jargon [A:115] [A:117-118] [A:263]. The Crock’s record reviews favor Chicago-style jazz, while Pelican Press plans its jazz paper for Fridays [A:41] [A:118]. Bulo Belonki is associated with the Jazz Sheet, and Howland’s Club Royal has an orchestra playing old classic jazz [A:126] [A:246]. At Good Guy’s, Monumental Jazz prompts Duffey’s reflection that classical jazz is growing old and playing its own funeral [MTM B7:220].

A:115; A:117-118; A:263; A:41; A:118; A:126; A:246; MTM B7:220

Jazz MagazineFriday publication printed by the Pelican Press to help finance The Bark [A:118] [MTM B7:212]. Several successive suitors of Dotty Yekouris are connected with the magazine, and she calls each of them Benny B. Flat [MTM B7:212-213].

A:118; MTM B7:212; MTM B7:212-213

Jazz SheetPelican Press publication associated with Bulo Belonki [A:126]. After Letitia becomes editor of The Bark, she gives the Jazz Sheet and the other publications printed for money less attention [MTM B8:238].

A:126; MTM B8:238

JazzersJokers around Duffey’s Big Pot who fish conspicuously human bones from it and paint a sign calling it Cannibal Duffey’s Irish Restaurant. The three are medical students, and there are strong grounds for suspecting that they put the bones in themselves; the episode is taken in good humor [MTM B6:197].

MTM B6:197

Jean, MaryEarlier heading treated Jean as a surname; the novel uses Mary Jean and leaves her premarital surname unspecified. See Mary Jean.
JeannieOne of the women living at the Old Wooden Ship called salt-water widows, most of whom are married to seamen [D:221].

D:221

JebbiesInformal name for Jesuits in Finnegan’s story of painting a devil. An unnamed anticlerical friend uses it when Father Le Faye, S.J., arrives; Le Faye then exorcises the picture and orders it burned [D:254-255].

D:254-255

Jebel Shammar sectSupposed sect whose three knife-flashing assassins threaten Margaret Stone for preaching the Real Presence at night, claiming nighttime presence belongs to their jealous Djinn. Margaret doubts the sect exists and suspects the men, who attend Tulane, are merely joking [MTM B7:225].

MTM B7:225

JebusBiblical name for Jerusalem, identified with it in Judges 19:10. Cyrus Roundhead’s false history instead treats Jebus as one of several separate ruined cities near the site of an imaginary Jerusalem; he calls it a Jewish city [MTM B11:337].

MTM B11:337

Jereboam (John, Big Alcohol)John (Big Alcohol) Jereboam, an Old Wooden Ship regular and burglary partner of John (Little Alcohol) Indelecio. While Little Alcohol climbs to high windows, Big Alcohol handles the drill, saw, chisel, and pry-bar. They work mainly when heavily indebted to Lazarus Reilly [D:215] [D:218].

D:215; D:218

Jerome (Saint)Church Father and Doctor of the Church, born about 347 and dead in 419 or 420, known for biblical translation and revision underlying the Latin Vulgate, scriptural commentaries, and ascetic writings. His scholarship and spiritual teaching became influential in Western Christianity. In Ignacio’s story of Joseph of Maintz’s lunar journey, Joseph takes Jerome’s writings in his projectile [A:271]. Finnegan, answering Le Marin, names Jerome and John Chrysostom as possible authorities for an insular Paradise, while observing that they did not locate it in the Caribbean [D:234].

A:271; D:234

JerseyNew Jersey. Gautier the goat-man, after years of roaming the Atlantic states, remains there throughout the year [A:196]. Trinali asks Hans to take him to two Jersey locations for driftwood and cypress knees [A:229]. Phoebe Anne Ankerson’s suitcase tag gives her home as Hammonton, New Jersey [D:172].

A:196; A:229; D:172

Jersey ShoreNew Jersey’s coastal region. After abandoning his Manhattan career as Gregory van Ghi, Finnegan takes a taxi to the Jersey Shore, buys socks and a small hand grip, and sets out on the road again [A:191-193].

A:191-193

JerusalemCity discussed in sharply different accounts. A Book Eight epigraph attributed to Josephus says that Melchizedech, its righteous priest-king and first temple builder, changed its name from Salem to Jerusalem [MTM B8:237]. Cyrus Roundhead’s false history denies that Jerusalem ever existed: he calls the name a failed Turkish real-estate promotion near supposedly separate ruins named Jebus, Solyma, Hiero-Solyma, Aelia Capitolina, Uris Lem, and El Quds [MTM B11:337].

MTM B8:237; MTM B11:337

JesusSalvation Sally announces the Second Coming to Hans and Marie [A:8]. Sister Mary Sabina invokes Jesus, Mary, and Joseph when the young Duffey begins reorganizing her class [MTM B1:12]. A contrasting use occurs in Letitia’s scrapbook: a speaker rejects the Historical Christ, claims to see an a-Historical Christ in outcasts and criminals, and denies him in the man next door [MTM B8:251-252]. See also Jesus Christ.

A:8; MTM B1:12; MTM B8:251-252

Jesus BarabbasThe Barabbas released in place of Jesus in the Gospel trial narrative; Jesus Barabbas is a manuscript variant of his name in Matthew 27:16-17. John Schultz’s letter to Marie contrasts this revolutionary with Christ, whom he calls a defender and maker of the law, and says the Jesus People follow Barabbas [MTM B6:186].

MTM B6:186

Jesus ChristChrist is evoked in Duffey’s explanation of the pelican as a symbol of his blood, when the friends debate a name for their magazine [A:121]. Sister Mary Sabina invokes Jesus, Mary, and Joseph as the young Duffey takes charge of his class [MTM B1:12]. In a letter to Marie, John Schultz contrasts Jesus Christ with Jesus Barabbas as part of his argument about dark companions and doubles [MTM B6:186]. See also Jesus.

A:121; MTM B1:12; MTM B6:186

Jesus PeoplePeople whom John Schultz accuses, in a letter to Marie, of following the revolutionary Jesus Barabbas while presenting themselves as followers of Christ. The contrast introduces his discussion of dark followers and correspondences [MTM B6:186]. The name probably alludes to the Jesus People movement, which combined evangelical Christianity with elements of the American counterculture in the late 1960s and 1970s.

MTM B6:186

JewJewish identity appears in the verse accompanying a letter signed S. and, more substantially, in the portrayal of Absalom Stein [A:119]. Casey’s hostile Crock editorial calls Stein, writing as Hugo Stone, a Communist Jew and an antisemite; Stein later describes himself as a neo-Jew [A:128-131]. Kasmir Gorshok’s mixed disguise includes a black hat and ear locks like an old Jew [MTM B13:425-426]. On the Great Day, Duffey answers Stein’s Irish insult with a Jewish one; the exchange briefly seems to preserve their former friendship before Duffey discovers Stein’s lost intelligence [GD:493].

A:119; A:128-131; MTM B13:425-426; GD:493

Jew breadBread supplied by Absalom Stein among the Argo’s sea stores, alongside sea biscuit from Hans and Marie Schultz and Purgatorial Loaf from Bagby. The passage explains that some of the ship’s indispensable stores are intangible [MTM B13:446].

MTM B13:446

Jewel thievesJewel thieves in Karachi who, in Ignatius Ti’s freely translated account of Amoy’s former lives, employ Amoy while he is a red-winged blackbird to steal gems from shops [A:80].

A:80

JewelryMercedes wears gold jangles at her neck, ears, fingers, wrists, and ankles [D:224]. Finnegan buys small pieces of jewelry for Anastasia in Tangier [D:103-104]. Asking Dan classes furs and jewelry as pseudo-nervous merchandise, sold by peddlers who pretend it is stolen [A:257]. Seen through Duffey’s eyes, Absalom Stein gives the impression of wearing splendid jewelry although he wears none [MTM B5:160].

D:224; D:103-104; A:257; MTM B5:160

JewelsIn Ignatius Ti’s story of Amoy’s life as a bird, Amoy steals and swallows a blue diamond as large as an almond, star sapphires, and lesser opals [A:80]. In Finnegan’s dream of following the Oreads, trees look like jewels on a mountain that is translucent like ice [D:138].

A:80; D:138

Jewess (Nefarious)Rollo McSorley’s disparaging description of the woman who served the Green Mule drink in his account of the party; the preceding scene identifies the drink-maker as Shirley Israel [MTM B4:129] [MTM B4:132].

MTM B4:129; MTM B4:132

JewishThe novels apply Jewish identifications and associations in several distinct ways. Duffey’s Boston Irish voice includes a touch of stage Yiddish [A:97]. Casey’s hostile article calls Absalom Stein, also Hugo Stone, a Communist Jew [A:128-129]. Margaret Stone is described as Italian and Jewish [A:143-144]; her account of the Stone family lists twenty male first cousins and disputes Duffey’s identification of Hugo with Absalom [MTM B4:112].

A:97; A:128-129; A:143-144; MTM B4:112

Jewish mother (unnamed)An alleged reference to Absalom Stein’s unnamed mother that has not been located in the cited passages.
Jewishness (Lurid)The narration, following Duffey’s view of the enlarged and overwhelming Absalom Stein in St. Louis, describes his wealthy and lurid Jewishness as a theatrical type last comparably expressed on the Elizabethan stage [MTM B5:160].

MTM B5:160

JewryJewish people collectively. In Mr. X’s account of the Devil’s release in Crimea, Jewish leaders are among several groups he claims were disproportionately represented; Catholic clergy and the liberal intelligentsia are also singled out [MTM B6:204-205]. The narration dates the release to the last Saturday of May 1946, while also questioning whether it had occurred in 1846 [MTM B5:184].

MTM B6:204-205; MTM B5:184

Jews of AfricaJoseph’s name for the Haussa people in his account of their mercantile background. He says his father was a merchant and identifies his own trade as diamond smuggling [D:94].

D:94

Jill of HeartsCard identifying the dead young girl on a sofa in the first chamber of Elroy Redheart’s four-chambered heart artwork. The card is daggered to the wall; the girl’s removed red chocolate heart lies among the candy beside her [MTM B7:221].

MTM B7:221

Jim HoganOne of the theatrical people in Duffey’s Chicago circle, listed with Rosemary Hogan [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

JingleShort verse or song. In Marie’s story, her uncle Shakes Pearson enters a chewing-tobacco jingle contest requiring a limerick [A:25]. Howland chants a five-stanza gopher jingle to a hoe-down tune while he and Finnegan lie in a hayloft on their journey toward Chicago [A:179].

A:25; A:179

Joan of ArcFrench saint and national heroine (1412-1431), born to a peasant family. Her reported visions led her to support Charles VII and the French campaign against the English during the Hundred Years’ War. Condemned for heresy, she was burned at Rouen at nineteen; the condemnation was later annulled, and she was canonized in 1920. Hilary Hilton names her, alongside Caesar, Napoleon, Cleopatra, the Queen of Sheba, and Marie Antoinette, among the exalted predecessors claimed by would-be reincarnations when he attacks Casey’s claims of soul trading [PG:531].

PG:531

Job enrichmentThe newspaper assistant’s term for a new arrangement in which everyone is equally an editor, titles are abandoned, and employees do whatever work they feel like doing or none at all. He explains it to the protesting Duffey after the paper and building have lost their names [GD:487].

GD:487

Jockey (Racing mules)One of the past occupations claimed by Herman Hercules, who describes himself as Cardinal Erculo’s exact double and says his jobs have kept him near crowds and spectacles [MB:585-586].

MB:585-586

JoeA name occurring in several unrelated contexts: the Polish phrase “Jak sie masz, Joe” taught to islanders by the Dirty Five [A:73]; cabdriver Joe Sorrell [D:21]; Brunhilde crewman Joe Cross [D:30]; boxer Joe Gans, whom Finnegan extravagantly claims to have fought for ninety rounds [D:191]; and Joseph Chastaigne, called Sloppy Joe, whose bar Finnegan and his friends nickname Sloppy Joe’s [D:235] [D:266].

A:73; D:21; D:30; D:191; D:235; D:266

John (Apostle)One of the twelve apostles, traditionally associated with the Fourth Gospel. A layer of the Pop People’s parchment is identified as a first-century copy, perhaps the original, of that Gospel; the hoyden asserts that its writer belonged to their group [MTM B11:327].

MTM B11:327

John of the Cross, SaintSee St. John of the Cross.
John the GreekOwner of John the Greek’s Famous French Restaurant. During a Pop-History meeting at Duffey’s establishment in New Orleans, he challenges Cyrus Roundhead’s claim that Athens never existed: John came from Athens and lived there until he was thirteen. Roundhead answers that the Macedonians invented Athens and its culture [MTM B11:336-337].

MTM B11:336-337

Johnson's Jump-Seat Buggy, theA horse-drawn vehicle in the turbaned Pop speaker’s catalogue of carriages remembered by a flagstone in Decatur Street. It appears with the Acme Top, Acme Open, Fulton Road Cart, and other vehicles during the meeting hosted by Duffey [MTM B11:329]. A jump seat is a folding or movable auxiliary seat.

MTM B11:329

Joint accountBank account shared by Mike Melchiades and his wife. He tells Duffey that he withdrew its entire balance, a little over three hundred dollars, immediately after she left, and refused her request to withdraw twenty dollars [MTM B4:142-143].

MTM B4:142-143

JokerA practical joker. Finnegan markets his dog-housebreaking preparation to pranksters in Buffalo [A:189-190]. Ignatius Ti describes medicos posing as corpses to frighten ward boys; Ti’s friend is the ward boy who retaliates against such a prank [A:85-87]. Mr. X calls both himself and Stein born jokers [A:265-266]. Van Ghi tells Finnegan, after the painting of a devil, that he has drawn the Joker instead of the Queen [D:255]. Duffey calls Bagby a joker even in death when his weekly letters continue arriving [MTM B8:237].

A:189-190; A:85-87; A:265-266; D:255; MTM B8:237

Joker-campFinnegan’s term for the place where he says he was held for a while and then evicted, during his postwar confusion about his identity and home [A:93]. The term is not formally explained; his earlier hospitalization for amnesia suggests a psychiatric setting [A:73].

A:93; A:73

JokersPranksters, especially the medicos who impersonate corpses and grab new ward boys in Ignatius Ti’s hospital story [A:85-86]. Finnegan also calls his former place of confinement a joker-camp [A:93].

A:85-86; A:93

JonahBiblical figure swallowed by a great fish for three days and nights. Doctor Saul Rafelson deliberately reverses this image in his notes on Duffey: the world spending three days in Jonah’s belly illustrates a topological inversion in which a person contains the world [MTM B4:146-147].

MTM B4:146-147

Jones (Willy) IslandAlso called Pulau Petir. In Don Lewis’s account, three American soldiers disappear there on October 1, 1944; he claims to be one of them without saying which [D:44]. The episode includes the shooting of the apparent Japanese soldier called Yokipoki and his burial in mud by Lewis [D:45-46]. Lewis sets his further story of the Big House on the same island: its inhabitants live indefinitely by making broth from visitors’ organs [D:48]. A later reference to a furtive man buried in the island’s mud recalls the earlier burial [D:50].

D:44; D:45-46; D:48; D:50

Jones, WillyMariner who sailed the Argo under the name Flying Serpent in the Moluccas, according to the ship’s talking-oak history [MTM B13:404-405]. Willy Jones Island bears the same name, but the island passage does not identify its namesake [D:44].

MTM B13:404-405; D:44

JosephSeveral distinct people share this name.

Joseph the Haussa is the traveler and diamond smuggler Finnegan meets in Freetown on January 26. He recruits Finnegan to market stones abroad [D:93-95].

The biblical Joseph is alluded to when Finnegan declines to interpret Seaworthy’s dream, saying, “I am not Joseph” [D:73]. Saint Joseph is invoked with Jesus and Mary by Sister Mary Sabina [MTM B1:12]. A Joseph Salvatore is also listed among Henry’s brothers [A:122].

D:93-95; D:73; MTM B1:12; A:122

Joseph of MaintzHoly Benedictine priest in Ignacio’s story, which he attributes to Archbishop Turpin of Rheims. In the eighth century Joseph makes a great copper-and-iron tube, lines it with glass, loads it with powder and a chamber, and shoots himself to the moon to escape the world’s temptations. He takes a Missal, Scriptures, Augustine, Jerome, Pliny’s Natural History, bread, wine, an altar stone, grape cuttings, and wheat. His monthly bonfires supposedly show that he lives there for ninety years [A:271].

A:271

JosephusJewish historian Flavius Josephus (c.37-c.100 CE). The Book Eight epigraph quotes his account of Melchizedek as the Righteous King, a Canaanite prince who first served as priest of God, built a temple, and renamed Salem Jerusalem [MTM B8:237]. The passage corresponds to The Jewish War, 6.10.1; the epigraph labels its source Jerusalem and Rome.

MTM B8:237

Joss (Pinkish)Finnegan compares Loy Larkin’s hair to a pinkish joss fitting her like a tipsy crown in his “Antipodal Ode” [A:32]. A joss is an image of a Chinese deity; the poem does not specify an incense stick or explain the comparison further.

A:32

JournalA Journal is one of the preliminary ideas, with an Institute and a Pot, proposed by those to whom Henry Salvatore delegates rebuilding the world, including Duffey [MTM B6:195]. Newton Prescott writes a private journal as therapy for his compulsion to forget, with instructions to burn it afterward [CM:503].

MTM B6:195; CM:503

JourneyCasey’s school notebook records the maxim “Happiness is a journey, not a destination” [A:162-163]. Duffey’s excursion into the Fifth Contingency is also described as a visit to the bright devildom, from which he fears he has brought destructive changes back to ordinary life [MTM B12:354-355].

A:162-163; MTM B12:354-355

JoyFinnegan’s poem to Loy Larkin recalls “urchin joy” [A:32]. At Vincent’s wedding, the narrative says Mass should be heard with joy and recalls Theresa’s smile at prayer and after communion [A:113]. In More Than Melchisedech, joy in money is called primordial and not wholly evil; the discussion connects sacred wealth, the gold-lined chalice, and the sacrifice of good things in holy poverty [MTM B4:124-125]. Duffey’s “joyful labor” at the end of Book Twelve is the making of new Animated Marvels from dung, blood, discarded objects, and lightning [MTM B12:394]. Don Barnaby recounts the lives and pleasures he experienced after taking Madame Le Mourcheor’s Juju Joy Pill [D:248-251]. Doll wishes Finnegan and X “a joyous death” before turning to her own work of saving the world [D:292]. “Promontory Goats” describes the damned’s “joyous gloating” over one another’s torture, even while enduring torture themselves [PG:533].

A:32; A:113; MTM B4:124-125; MTM B12:394; D:248-251; D:292; PG:533

Joy PillsPills discussed in Don Barnaby’s fantastic account of curing a hangover. He distinguishes Haiti hoodoo, High Harry from Jamaica, Deep Romany, Dead Frenchman, and Black Rooster varieties [D:248]. Madame Le Mourcheor’s Old Original Juju Joy Pills, made in New Orleans, supposedly give him years of life, marriage, family, and travel within an apparently boundless garden, although fewer than fifteen minutes pass outside it [D:249-251].

D:248; D:249-251

Joy Pills (Madame Le Mourcheor's Old Original)See Joy Pills. Don Barnaby names Madame Le Mourcheor’s Old Original Juju Joy Pills as the exceptional variety made in New Orleans [D:249].

D:249

Joyce, David / DinahDavid and Dinah Joyce are listed among the college and university people in Duffey’s Chicago circle [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

JudasJudas Iscariot, the apostle who betrayed Jesus. His name appears in Vincent’s exclamation “Judas priest” [A:11] and in Bagby’s label Judas Priests for clergy he regards as unorthodox [MTM B2:62-63]. In the Argo’s fantastic history, Saint Brandon carries the traitor Judas aboard the Land of Behest [MTM B13:404]; Casey later says the ship ferries him across a narrow strait for one night each year [MTM B13:426]. Casey also links the Judas Prophecy, without explaining it, to the prediction that Antichrist will sail on the Argo [MTM B13:454].

A:11; MTM B2:62-63; MTM B13:404; MTM B13:426; MTM B13:454

Judas PriestismOne of the Enemy’s seven contemporary heads named by Bascom Bagby, together with Dialectic Materialism, Artistic Degradation, Secular Liberalism, Panaceic Pentecostalism, Murderous Molochism, and Atheistic Communism [MTM B5:169].

MTM B5:169

Judas PriestsBagby’s term for clergy whom he believes have lost orthodoxy [MTM B2:62-63]. George Koran, a Picayune reporter, tells Duffey that eight such priests respond with snickers when he exclaims “Judas Priest!” at the New Catholic Press Guild’s meeting [MTM B8:239-240].

MTM B2:62-63; MTM B8:239-240

Judas ProphecyA prophecy that Casey tentatively connects with the prediction that Antichrist will sail on the Argo to Megiddo. The three Argo Masters discuss how to prevent the foretold passenger from boarding, but the Judas Prophecy itself is not explained [MTM B13:454].

MTM B13:454

Judas TraitorThe traitor Judas, carried by Saint Brandon aboard the Land of Behest, a former name of the Argo, in the ship’s account of Brandon’s voyage from Ireland to America [MTM B13:404].

MTM B13:404

Jude (Saint)Saint Jude, one of the apostles. Dotty jokingly calls him the patron of printers and little magazines and the only apostle who was a printer; Finnegan answers that he is the advocate of impossible causes [A:115]. He is one of three possible identities, with Thomas and Bartholomew, for Papa Piccone’s tippler apostle in the Italian legend retold by Show Boat [A:262]. Finding his tomb is included among the Argo’s discoveries [MTM B13:422].

A:115; A:262; MTM B13:422

“Judgement Day”Title of the Crock’s serious review section [A:41]. The narration also says that no one, including Duffey, will fully understand his seven hidden years until the afternoon of judgment day [MTM B2:73].

A:41; MTM B2:73

Judges (Drinking Contest)Tom Shire and Freddy Castle, officials in the Hans Schultz versus Joe Bushmaster beer-drinking contest. Bushmaster proposes them because both sides trust them [A:15]. Stein instructs them to distinguish actual spillage from condensation on the glasses [A:20].

A:15; A:20

JugThe tippling jug accompanies Li Po Tai in the poem of the Chinese sage and fisher maid [A:222]. Maurine says Papa Piccone will provide three barrels of wine and a bunch of jugs for the wedding reception [A:105]. The future is imagined as emerging from a jug of smoky glass or rock crystal whose curvature distorts the forms seen inside it [MTM B10:297].

A:222; A:105; MTM B10:297

JugglingOne of the popular arts included in the narrative’s account of the deliberate degradation of everyday arts by deformed counterparts after the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207-208]. Duffey also juggles names and numbers while alternating between sleep and waking before his encounter with Charlotte Mullens in a strange wasteland [MTM B3:85].

MTM B6:207-208; MTM B3:85

JuiceUsed for drink, vitality, and animating power. Vincent imagines Finnegan created with a hangover from jungle juice that was never drunk [A:57]. Torpedo Juice is one of the Anopheles Network’s comic products [A:46], and Hans is powerful when “the juice” is in him [A:68]. The young Duffey calls the lightning in his talisman sticks “fire and juice” [MTM B1:11]. The word returns in the mingled fluids released when the thunder colt destroys the Finnegan effigy [MTM B11:351].

A:57; A:46; A:68; MTM B1:11; MTM B11:351

Juju Joy FabriqueDon Barnaby’s term for the manufacture of joy pills. He likens Madame Le Mourcheor’s reforms to spring entering its musty halls: she supposedly discards tainted additives and returns to special sawdust, honey, and black-cat urine [D:248-249].

D:248-249

Juju Joy Pills (Madame Le Mourcheor's Old Original)See Joy Pills. Don Barnaby names Madame Le Mourcheor’s Old Original Juju Joy Pills as the exceptional variety made in New Orleans [D:249].

D:249

Julep SteinEarlier heading reversed the drink’s name and changed its printed spelling. See Stein Julip.
Julien HebertOne of Henry Salvatore’s maternal uncles, listed with the other Hebert uncles in the account of Henry’s family [A:122-123].

A:122-123

JulietteA romantic comparison applied to Theresa Piccone, described as half Juliette and half urchin as Patrick Stranahan considers Vincent’s approaching marriage [A:104]. The likely allusion is to Juliet Capulet of Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet, although the novel does not identify the play here.

A:104

Jumps (Three big)Judley Peacock's explanation, quoted in Tony Apostolo's Chicago Tribune report, of how the mule reached the traffic island: one jump over the fence and two more to the island. Stein regards the kabouters as immaterial persons, while acknowledging the alternative description as crankinesses [PG:537-538].

KandiPlace named among the destinations of eternal summer in Finnegan's verse, alongside Roi, Rangoon, Kuri, and Cai [A:171].

Critics of Duffey's chronology claim that he was still at school in Omaha or Kansas City when he supposedly ran his St. Louis business, but Mary Louise and Bagby defend those business years [MTM B2:71]. Kansas City is also among the cities he revisits after returning in 1923 [MTM B2:73].

Kapteyn's StarOne of the stars used in Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni's astronomical instruction. Kasimir, PrincePrince Casimir of Poland, identified in Duffey's account as an earlier manifestation of Casey Szymansky and as Saint Casimir. Duffey describes his aid to the poor, a vow of chastity frustrating King Casimir IV's succession plans, and an apparent death at twenty-three that is really a withdrawal from the world [PG:536]. The historical saint lived from 1458 to 1484 and died at twenty-five, so Duffey's age and designation of the period as the High Middle Ages belong to the novel's account. In a prophecy read aloud by Teresa, Prince Casimir is the second of three listed cargoes that a ghostly Duffey will carry on the Argo; he will be landed near Armageddon to reign temporarily as Anti-Christ. Duffey says he has no knowledge of these predicted acts [MTM B12:388].

Keegan, BethElizabeth Keegan, later Beth Erlenbaum, Mary Louise Byrne's close friend and the teasing handmaid she introduces to Duffey. Beth kisses him at their first meeting and says she will keep him. Small, black-haired, and ivory-skinned, with tiny feet and waist and lavish curves, she strikes him as an impossible living ivory statue, cold and strong to the touch. Her costume, voice, and walk are theatrical performances, and her laughter exposes the joke without ending his infatuation or confusion [MTM B2:56-57]. She attends college with Mary Louise and joins Duffey's youthful St. Louis outings [MTM B2:58]. Her mock love-making draws on plays and comic magazines; the narrative likens her to Etruscan and Cretan statuary [MTM B2:60]. After Duffey's return, she is married, has two daughters, and writes and performs comic skits at the Star and Garter. She is godmother to Piccone's infant daughter. The narrator calls Beth ordinary, but says Duffey never realizes this [MTM B2:74]. Later she and her husband join Duffey and the Bagbys at Rounders'; she describes his Animated Marvels as brighter, more colorful versions of him multiplied ten or eleven times [MTM B5:154-155].

Duffey says the Argo's keel was laid at Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, and that her hull was built of oak from the Dinaric Alps, including pieces of a talking oak. The surrounding account explicitly claims symbolic rather than ordinary historical accuracy [MTM B13:412].

Among the murder-contest proposals in 'More Than Melchisedech,' fictional directional infra-red cookers would destroy a victim's kidneys or other organs without an outer mark [MB:581].

An early account describes him as killed in Finnegan's place [D:51], but his body is not found; later accounts leave his disappearance, possible killing, and possible absorption into Finnegan unresolved [D:64] [D:121-122]. These passages do not establish him as one of Don Lewis's pursuers.

Kincaid, Harry A. (Honeybucket)Old Wooden Ship patron, called Harold A. (Honeybucket) Kincaid in its roster and Harry A. Kincaid in his anecdote. He seeks to sell seventy-five billion dollars of stock for electrically harvesting plankton as livestock feed; the narrator reveals that he has never tried it and knows nothing of plankton's appearance. His one real camel remains behind the Ship after a failed amusement ride [D:216] [D:218-219]. In futuristic Louisiana, Harry joins Leonard Archive and Oliver Greenflag in entertaining Duffey and Brannagan. Their frequency technology gathers food, drink, chemicals, and creatures from the water; Honeybucket operates the dials and electrodes for gar and Blooper Fish, makes Foraminifera Julips, and summons three twenty-one-year-old women in a rowboat [MTM B13:417-419]. Archive credits laziness for their discoveries, while Greenflag calls Puff Fish a moral problem. Duffey destroys the Puff Fish frequency himself; Honeybucket thinks the equipment can be repaired, then cannot recall what the missing frequency attracted [MTM B13:420-421].

KingRoyal title recurring in several forms. Duffey is the magical Boy King, with a childhood lasting thousands of years, and the King of Salem [MTM B1:15] [MTM B1:17] [MTM B5:166]. His later recollections repeat both the ancient kingship and his disguised kingship in Iowa [MTM B13:464] [MTM B13:469]. Genesis supplies the priest-king of Salem, and Hebrews the titles King of Justice and King of Peace [MTM B2:38] [MTM B6:185]. Other kings include the Balbo Mad Kings Gaetano I-VI of San Simeon, whose expected successor Gaetano VII becomes a churchman instead [MB:558-559]; King Casimir IV, father of the prince identified with Casey in Duffey's commentary [PG:536]; the former royal owner of Duffey's Spanish ash receptacle [MTM B1:6] [MTM B13:442]; King Richard of England, said to have recaptured the Argo, and the other English king for whom Robert of Namur sailed it [MTM B13:404]. Amraphel of Shinar, Arioch of Ellasar, and Thadal of the Nations follow Chodorlahomor of Elam [MTM B7:227-228]. Henri Salvatore's letter says that all are kings in the Kingdom and invokes the holy Leper King [MTM B5:179-180].

MTM B1:15; MTM B1:17; MTM B5:166; MTM B13:464; MTM B13:469; MTM B2:38; MTM B6:185; MB:558-559; PG:536; MTM B1:6; MTM B13:442; MTM B13:404; MTM B7:227-228; MTM B5:179-180

King's CrossDistrict on Finnegan and Vincent's pub-visiting route, followed by Darlinghurst and the descent to Down-Town [A:2].

King's ShipOne name, alongside Gold Ship and Shimmering Ship, for what the narrator calls an almost universal boys' dream. Such dreams are presented as simultaneous happenings with a basis in reality [MTM B13:436].

KingdomsDuffey tells Casey that those trying to corrupt the Crock have offered him the world's riches and all its kingdoms, likening their offer to Satan's [A:39-40]. The claim occurs while Charley Murray questions how much Duffey has been drinking.

Kipling, Rudyard (1865--1936)British journalist, poet, and novelist (1865-1936), author of The Jungle Book (1894), Kim (1901), and 'If-' (1910), and winner of the 1907 Nobel Prize in Literature. August Koch invokes Kipling's devil asking 'Is it art?' while discussing Duffey's Seven Christs [MTM B3:103]. The allusion is to 'The Conundrum of the Workshops' (1890), with its recurring devil's challenge to human creation.

MTM B3:103

KiriwinansIsland people who, in Archipelago's account, help build the Papuans' lodges. The narrator says that they understand their dependence on the Papuans' vast unconscious and would vanish if the Papuans ceased to sustain them there [A:37].

A:37

Kirol Cardinal GabrailovitchCardinal of Zagreb, the second of the thirteen Princes in Hiding killed in John Mogul's campaign [MB:578]. His double is Mihail Majic of Trieste, who later reaches Mooring-Stone after a fifty-mile swim [MB:579] [MB:595]. Finnegan's series depicting the deaths of thirteen cardinals includes the 'Hanging of Cardinal Gabrailovitch' [MTM B13:452].

MB:578; MB:579; MB:595; MTM B13:452

Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni, ProfessorProfessor and carnival operator, described as the smartest man in the world and the last man who knew everything. The narrative places his birth about 1860 in Bavaria but immediately allows a different place or time; in spring 1930 he is about seventy, give or take a decade [A:211]. He knew Hans Schultz’s parents before their marriage and separately paid for their passages to America. Irene calls him a phoney of an older, nobler school and reports his maxim that dignity belongs to middling minds [A:211-212]. Hans leaves home with him in a truck resembling a medicine-show wagon, and they travel to Wisconsin Rapids to join the carnival. He teaches rapid calculation and prodigious memory as tools he calls Cerebral Athleticism, insisting that they are not thought itself. He condemns chosen dullness and urges a Sabbath for the mind, calling humanity morning dew but also manna [A:212]. His teachings include the trees of knowledge, an expanding Heaven, the Tree of Language and a literal Babel account, and rapid astronomical calculations. He says a properly equipped learner requires at least a month to learn a language [A:213]. He describes material and spiritual reality as aspects of one universe, the visible cosmos as the reverse of Heaven’s tapestry, and re-entrant time as an approach to eternity [A:212-215]. Admitting that he is a charlatan, he says he has returned to the Church and that the Father’s House has room even for charlatans [A:215]. He rents and leases carnival equipment and performs as a mind-reader, memory expert, hypnotist, magician, and answer man. He retains strength but has lost much agility and endurance [A:215-216]. He claims to have known Elena Angelino’s great-grandparents and insists that her great-grandfather was a bear [A:218]. His teaching distinguishes learning that asks why from information that asks what. By the spring of 1935 or 1936, when Hans leaves, he is visibly slowing down [A:220]. His carnival circle includes Betty Hochstapler, Angelo Angelino, and the performing bear Mabel [A:216-219].

A:211; A:211-212; A:212; A:213; A:212-215; A:215; A:215-216; A:218; A:220; A:216-219

KissimeeKissimmee, the central Florida city, spelled 'Kissimee' in the novel. Finnegan, Doll Delancy, and X include it among their evening drives through the citrus and scrub, along with Orlando, Pine Castle, Apopka, and sometimes Daytona [D:183].

D:183

Kit (how-to-build-it kit)Zabotski's construction instructions, copied from an ancient rock-drawing whose language he believes is Hazh-Khazh. He deciphers the writing while building, initially unsure whether the result is a barn or castle [MTM B9:272]. The accompanying scenario specifies six younger people in three married couples; Widow Waldo insists the contraption is a ship, castle, anti-time machine, and shoe [MTM B9:275]. In the separate 'Great Day' account, kits supply an unspecified substitute for vehicle wheels [GD:489].

MTM B9:272; MTM B9:275; GD:489

Kit (love-as-catch-word kit)Phrase in the verse fragment 'Nor used the love-as-catch-word kit / A multitude of sins to cover.' The glossary's proposed location, A:9, does not match the available text; the primary-source location remains unverified.
Kit-foxA small North American fox and Duffey's totem animal. When Duffey is about eleven, a sorrel-haired, grinning fox resembling him warns him of the three slant-faced boys. It attacks one low while Duffey bowls him over, enabling escape from the ambush; Duffey is badly knifed and nearly bleeds to death. The narrator calls the fox providential [MTM B1:19-20].

MTM B1:19-20

Kithara (nine-stringed)Nine-stringed instrument played by Shinar in the Brimstone Combo, in Trinali's poem about the old saloon near Iniquity Square [A:235].

A:235

Kithara ShinarEarlier heading joined the instrument to the name of its player, Shinar. See Kithara (nine-stringed).
Kitty (card game)Earlier heading confused the collection of tips after a musical performance with a card game. See Kitty (tip collection).
Kitty (tip collection)Collection for tips after Falo and Nauti's music at their café: they say they will pass the kitty after playing. The same scene also includes card play, but 'kitty' here refers to the collection [A:65].

A:65

Kiunker (Georgia)Printed variant of the car’s name. See Klunker (car).
Klunker (car)The older second car with a Georgia license plate, acquired so that X, Doll, and Finnegan can escape in two directions if necessary [D:184]. Finnegan leaves in it before dawn after X’s briefing, followed half an hour later by a leftfooted killer and his companion [D:193]. The book calls it both Klunker and Kiunker. After his pursuers repeatedly shoot at him, Finnegan drives it into a ditch and fires back, then continues in the damaged car. In the next town he parks it at the police station to delay pursuit before finding refuge with Brannagan and Gertrude [D:197-199].

D:184; D:193; D:197-199

KnackerA dealer in animal carcasses or worn-out livestock. John Mogul applies the word to his business of killing unwanted people, likening their disposal to rendering carcasses into useful materials [MB:573].

MB:573

KneesThe word links several images. Casey recites a line attributed to Belloc about hacking horses at the knees [A:160]. Trinali seeks cypress knees as craft materials, and Hans later sees her as made of driftwood with cypress knees [A:229] [A:234]. Endymeon Ellenbogen complains figuratively that wolves have eaten his legs up to the knees while describing his failure to make money from popular songs [A:237].

A:160; A:229; A:234; A:237

KnifeWeapon appearing in several episodes. Casey's school notebook calls chiv a Romany word for knife [A:162] [A:164]. Ignatius Ti tells of a ward attendant using a flip-knife to frighten a medico pretending to be dead, then of a woman who unknowingly sleeps with the ghost of her knife-murdered husband [A:86-87]. A clipping apparently reporting X's death mentions an old knife blade in the shoulder; Dotty calls the report an antic [A:141]. Finnegan says that a hostile bistro crowd cut a Z in his cheek with switchblades [A:263-264]. The three slant-faced boys carry knives and nearly kill young Duffey; their later counterparts strip the flesh from his bones in the unreal desert scene, causing a death explicitly described as real [MTM B1:12] [MTM B1:19-20] [MTM B13:441-442]. George Koran reports a knife-brandishing guard at the New Catholic Press Guild meeting [MTM B8:239-240]. A knife hilt protrudes between the shoulders of the dead man identified as Cardinal Runosake at Mogul's door [MB:574].

A:162; A:164; A:86-87; A:141; A:263-264; MTM B1:12; MTM B1:19-20; MTM B13:441-442; MTM B8:239-240; MB:574

Knights of ColumbusCatholic fraternal organization founded in 1882. During his would-be appearance as the world-conquering Leader, Casey wears his father's Knights of Columbus Fourth Degree sword with his other regalia [MTM B4:117].

MTM B4:117

Knistjanses (Swede)Old Wooden Ship regular listed as Swede Knistjanses [D:215]. He belongs to the five men called Swedes although none is Swedish: collectively they are Norse, Danish, Icelandic, German, and from the Orkneys. The text does not assign those origins individually [D:217].

D:215; D:217

Knobs (stone)Stone features called merlons on a small Gothic-style hotel. Finnegan, likened to a living gargoyle, perches on one after climbing six stories up the ornamented exterior [D:162].

D:162

Knockers (olive)Playful name for children in Vincent and Show Boat's response to their wedding Mass's Gradual, which compares children around the table to young olive plants [A:113].

A:113

Knowledge (false)The pseudodendron of false knowledge and the crooked way, the one forbidden tree in Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni's account to Hans. He contrasts it with the many trees of fruitful knowledge [A:211-212].

A:211-212

Knowledge (of achievement and arriving)One form of fruitful knowledge in Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni's teaching to Hans about the many trees of knowledge: achievement and arriving [A:211-212].

A:211-212

Knowledge (of awakening and growing)One form of fruitful knowledge in Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni's teaching to Hans about the many trees of knowledge: awakening and growing [A:211-212].

A:211-212

Knowledge (of expanding and seeing)One form of fruitful knowledge in Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni's teaching to Hans about the many trees of knowledge: expanding and seeing [A:211-212].

A:211-212

Knowledge (of love and realization)One form of fruitful knowledge in Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni's teaching to Hans about the many trees of knowledge: love and realization [A:211-212].

A:211-212

Knowledge (Tree of)Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni tells Hans that all the trees were trees of knowledge: love and realization, achievement and arriving, awakening and growing, expanding and seeing and unfolding. Only the pseudodendron of false knowledge and the crooked way was forbidden. His image leads into continuing growth from caterpillars through butterflies to stars [A:211-213].

A:211-213

KobeJapanese port city associated with Xavier Cardinal Runosake, one of Mogul's thirteen contracted targets [MB:571]. Mogul learns that Runosake has just escaped a Buddhist compound in Kobe; shortly afterward a dying man identified as the cardinal appears at Mogul's Marseille door, and the targets remaining number twelve [MB:572-574].

MB:571; MB:572-574

Koch, AugustFather of Lily and Letitia Koch and husband of Elinore. A neat, imposing, muscular man of integrity and financial competence, he favors the European custom of dowry; Duffey limits the provision for his own marriage to a quarter of August's intended amount, drawing only interest for twenty-five years [MTM B3:101]. August separately offers a million-dollar dowry for a suitable husband for Lily and asks Duffey to help find one [MTM B3:102]. He gives Duffey an additional Christ artwork to stand with the Seven Christs and owns an Argo-named yacht on Lake Michigan [MTM B3:103-104]. Around the beginning of the fourth quarter of 1929 he stores more than twenty tons of gold, valued in the narrative at about twelve million dollars, at the Duffeys' place [MTM B4:110].

MTM B3:101; MTM B3:102; MTM B3:103-104; MTM B4:110

Koch, ElinoreWife of August Koch and mother of Lily and Letitia, one of the family circle in Duffey's Chicago golden age [MTM B3:98]. Duffey falls in love with his mother-in-law at first sight when she welcomes him with outstretched arms and an enormous kiss, a gesture shared by all three Koch women. The narrator praises her style and calls such affection good luck [MTM B3:101]. Duffey continues to love all three Koch ladies [MTM B4:110].

MTM B3:98; MTM B3:101; MTM B4:110

Koch, LetitiaWife of Melchisedech Duffey, younger sister of Lily Koch, and daughter of August and Elinore. Duffey's rib-shaped talisman, entrusted to Lily in childhood, is associated with Letitia's formation and their eventual meeting [MTM B1:30] [MTM B3:90-91] [MTM B3:101]. Initially described as chubby, with smiling eyes and a dazzling soul, she has cascades of hair between blonde, scarlet, and walnut, a ruddy complexion, a high-comedy expression, and eyes between sea-green and Melchisedech blue. She is taller than Duffey and helps move their belongings into their Chicago home above the bookstore; their marriage opens the golden age beginning in 1925 [MTM B3:91-92] [MTM B3:98]. Her beautiful, haunting voice is used in radio advertisements, and she intercepts Casey's appearance as the world-conquering Leader [MTM B4:114] [MTM B4:117]. Duffey says she can read his mind. During the portfolio blackmail, she goes away on a purportedly necessary trip, returning without examining or expressing interest in the pictures [MTM B4:140] [MTM B4:144-145]. In New Orleans the narrator describes her as transfigured into proto-legendary beauty [MTM B7:211]. After Dotty's disappearance she edits The Bark, supports it from private funds, and attends the New Catholic Press Guild meeting with Duffey and Mary Virginia [MTM B8:238-239]. Her death is sudden; at Margaret Stone's insistence her eyes remain open, seeming to follow everyone at the old-fashioned wake in her home [MTM B8:253-254].

MTM B1:30; MTM B3:90-91; MTM B3:101; MTM B3:91-92; MTM B3:98; MTM B4:114; MTM B4:117; MTM B4:140; MTM B4:144-145; MTM B7:211; MTM B8:238-239; MTM B8:253-254

Koch, LilyLily Koch, Letitia's sister and August and Elinore's daughter, is Letitia's partner in Koch's Galleries [MTM B3:92] [MTM B3:98]. As a schoolgirl merchant at St. Mary Major's, she combines boarding and day attendance, with wealthy kindred across the road. She holds private Wednesday sales and public Saturday sales, obtains whisky through Duffey, and sells art, including Sebastian Hilton's hundred-dollar statuette [MTM B1:28-29]. Her merchant trademark is a pair of celluloid cuffs or gauntlets. She and Duffey communicate within her mind, and she kisses him after recognizing his talisman as magi-made. Already 'finished' herself and expecting no children, she undertakes to use it for Letitia [MTM B1:29-30]. Years later the rib-shaped talisman is still displayed in the gallery as effectively priceless; Lily brings Duffey and Letitia together [MTM B3:90-91]. August says she and Sebastian had been engaged 'in a sort of way' [MTM B3:102]. She belongs to the Chicago golden-age circle [MTM B3:98]. After Letitia's death she flies to New Orleans and stays several weeks [MTM B8:254] [MTM B8:256]. She proposes to Duffey, says her old million-dollar dowry has tripled, and explains that Letitia asked her to care for him. By an unexplained calculation she declares it his four-thousandth birthday and arranges the enormous cake and party [MTM B8:257].

MTM B3:92; MTM B3:98; MTM B1:28-29; MTM B1:29-30; MTM B3:90-91; MTM B3:102; MTM B8:254; MTM B8:256; MTM B8:257

Koch's GalleriesChicago art galleries run by Lily Koch and her sister Letitia, who keeps her half-interest after marrying Duffey [MTM B3:92]. The galleries stand two blocks from the Duffeys' establishment, down its prosperous street rather than the poorer street on its other side [MTM B3:100].

MTM B3:92; MTM B3:100

Kofeinik (Rose Ivanova's)Rose Ivanova's restaurant in an unnamed, bustling trucking town encountered during Duffey's Tartary expedition. Its sign claims that truck drivers' presence proves it is the best. Duffey emerges from the Laughing Prince's desert scenes, eats a hearty meal, and drinks eleven glasses of water. Nobody in the town has heard of the Prince. As Duffey leaves for the newspaper office, the town vanishes and the desert returns [MTM B13:438-440].

MTM B13:438-440

KopolatryUnexplained mystical term in Marie Courtois's conversation with Finnegan on a jungle-crowded beach, although they should be aboard the Brunhilde in mid-Atlantic. With his head in her lap and her hair wound around him, she discusses kopolatry beside the gremium matris, identified with the Earth and her lap. Earth worship or fertility symbolism is a possible contextual reading; the word's precise meaning and derivation remain uncertain [D:92].

D:92

Koran, GeorgeReporter for the New Orleans Picayune whom Duffey meets at the New Catholic Press Guild address by 'The Majesty,' the released Devil [MTM B8:240]. He lists the speaker's enormous itinerary among financiers, publishers, politicians, labor leaders, historians, and a Student Repudiation Congress [MTM B8:243]. The next day's engagements include an early communion breakfast in Oklahoma City, Waco Baptists, Dallas, Cow Town, San Antonio, and Houston [MTM B8:244].

MTM B8:240; MTM B8:243; MTM B8:244

Korsakoff, Sergei (1854--1900)Russian psychiatrist Sergei Korsakoff, also transliterated Sergey Korsakov (1854-1900), whose studies of alcoholic polyneuritis and memory disturbance gave his name to Korsakoff's syndrome.
