MehitabelThe alley cat in Don Marquis’s archy and mehitabel. Anastasia Demetriades insists to Finnegan that she is a lady, “even if of the Mehitabel variety,” while disparaging her cabinmate Marie Courtois [D:33].

D:33

Meinkmueller's French RestaurantSt. Louis restaurant styled French where Duffey and Bagby celebrate his business success with zwiebelsuppe, rinderbraten, walnuts, brandy, and cigars [MTM B2:47]. Duffey later takes Mary Louise Byrne and Beth Keegan there with such companions as Charley Murray, Edward Ranwick, or Philip Manford [MTM B2:58]. Before his seven hidden years, the company gathers there and is joined by Monica Drexel and Monica Murray, who somehow know he is leaving [MTM B2:69].

MTM B2:47; MTM B2:58; MTM B2:69

Melchiades, MikePoor Chicago double of Duffey, found in McFadden’s North End Tavern, about forty, with short sandy-orange hair, tired fire-blue eyes, and hands continually weaving and clapping [MTM B4:141]. His voice resembles Duffey’s. Both men describe themselves as half shaded over; Mike calls Duffey a devil and insists that he himself is the tornado of which Duffey is a spinoff. He says witnesses attribute a devil’s misconduct to him, and his wife believes them [MTM B4:142]. After she leaves, he withdraws their joint savings of just over three hundred dollars, refuses her twenty dollars despite her tears, and admits this action was wrong. He asks Duffey to send her home if he sees her. Duffey suspects that Mike’s tornado claim may indeed be true, at least sometimes [MTM B4:143].

MTM B4:141; MTM B4:142; MTM B4:143

MelchisedechBiblical king of Salem and priest of God Most High who blesses Abraham; Hebrews 7 treats his continuing priesthood as a figure for Christ’s. Casey says Duffey took Melchisedech as his confirmation name at forty [A:42]. Teresa calls Duffey the original Melchisedech [MTM B7:234], and the magus later remembers himself as Melchisedech Himself, King of Salem, sometimes named Duffey in latter-day contexts [MTM B13:402]. In Cleo Mahoney’s Seven Roads, Duffey plays this priest, whom she describes as having neither father nor end [MTM B9:265]. Duffey also signs a letter to Stein as the fifty-ninth king of the dynasty and says he remembers having fifty-eight predecessors [PS:478].

A:42; MTM B7:234; MTM B13:402; MTM B9:265; PS:478

Melchisedech DuffeySee Duffey, Melchisedech.
Melchisedech Duffey ProprietorClosing wording of the red-lettered sign Duffey paints on a horse-stall board for his new St. Louis establishment. It advertises ten thousand reduced-price items, food and lodging, drinks, grooming, baths, entertainment, and a gentlemen’s bar and club [MTM B2:41].

MTM B2:41

Melchisedech Paradoxes, TheParadoxes of Duffey’s being that the Invisible God compares with Zeno’s during Duffey’s seventh contingency, a dying vision of walking in a garden. God immediately adds that every person is equally unique and surrounded by wonderful paradoxes [MTM B12:389].

Melchisedech PrimeName for Duffey considered apart from the experiences he appropriates from others. The narrator distinguishes a slightly bovine element in the tangled, largely sister-derived St. Louis childhood from what belonged to Melchisedech Prime [MTM B1:16].

Melchisedech-in-St.-LouisDuffey in his early St. Louis years of flourishing enterprises, the owner of a “multitudinous, golden-touch world.” The narrator says this world ended after most of two years [MTM B2:66], as dreams announce his departure for seven hidden years [MTM B2:68-69].

MTM B2:66; MTM B2:68-69

MeleagerVincent Stranahan’s ancient counterpart [A:39]. Rosemary includes Meleager among the Sergeant’s legendary companions in the Sydney episode [A:89], and Teresa explicitly identifies Vincent with him [MTM B7:234]. In Apollonius’s Argonautica 1.190-201, Meleager is the young son of Oeneus from Calydon, accompanied by his uncles Laocoon and Iphiclus. The poet says that with another year’s growth only Heracles would have surpassed him. During the mistaken night battle with the Doliones, he kills Itomeneus and Artaceus (1.1046-1048). At Colchis he rises with the other volunteers willing to face Aeetes’ trial if Jason cannot undertake it, although his beard has not yet begun to grow (3.504-522). The poem describes other episodes collectively: the Argonauts seek initiation at the island of Electra (1.910-921), fight the Earthborn giants (1.989-1011), guard and celebrate Jason and Medea’s wedding (4.1121-1169), and carry their ship across Libya for twelve days and nights (4.1380-1392). These passages give Meleager no separate exploit. In Apollodorus’s Library 1.8.2-3, his mother Althaea saves the burning brand on which his life depends. He kills the Calydonian boar and gives its hide to Atalanta, who first wounded it. When Althaea’s brothers take the prize from her, he kills them; his mother burns the brand in grief, causing his death. Apollodorus also records a different account in which he dies fighting the Curetes.

A:39; A:89; MTM B7:234

Melk (Crissie verse)Short form of Melchisedech used in a Crissie verse quoted by Cleo Mahoney while explaining the seventh possible outcome of Seven Roads [MTM B10:296].

Melk (Nickname for Melchisedech Duffey)Earlier heading generalized a short form attested in the quoted Crissie verse. See Melk (Crissie verse).
Melky (Nickname used by associates for Duffey)Familiar form of Duffey’s name used by Charley Murray [MTM B1:21], Evelyn London [MTM B2:40], Mary Louise Byrne [MTM B2:56] [MTM B7:218], Beth Keegan [MTM B2:59], Lily Koch [MTM B3:90], and Absalom Stein [MTM B9:266]. Duffey’s aunt also uses it during his childhood [MTM B1:13].

MTM B1:21; MTM B2:40; MTM B2:56; MTM B7:218; MTM B2:59; MTM B3:90; MTM B9:266; MTM B1:13

Melville, Herman (1819--1891)American novelist and poet, author of Moby-Dick (1851). Finnegan invokes him while accusing Hans of telling phony cannibal stories, calling Melville the last person who could tell one with a clean heart and then conceding that he too was somewhat phony [A:58]. Melville’s literary standing revived in the twentieth century.

A:58

Members of the Famous Steeplechase Club (Patrons of Rounders' Club)Status promised to patrons of Duffey’s Rounders’ Club by its sign: customers automatically become members of the Famous Steeplechase Club [MTM B2:49].

MTM B2:49

Memories (Duffey's/Bagby's 'exterior state' letters)Bagby’s weekly letters to Duffey, written with intelligence and compassion on lined tablet paper. They sustained Duffey during the seven hidden years and the Chicago crisis, seeming part of his introspection while remaining external objects [MTM B4:145]. They appear on his table every Monday before ordinary delivery, bearing almost familiar but otherwhere stamps and postmarks. Bagby calls them letters of another context outside daily time; their unconscious-to-unconscious origin is suggested rather than established [MTM B7:218-219]. They continue for many years after his funeral, despite Duffey’s initial explanation that Bagby had arranged advance mailing [MTM B8:237].

MTM B4:145; MTM B7:218-219; MTM B8:237

MemrharStop on the Brunhilde’s northward coastal itinerary after Dakar and St. Louis and before Port Etienne [D:96].

D:96

Mendacious Midget DollCharlotte’s doll, which she says displays her real age, now about two hundred years, more effectively than the Dorian Gray picture in Duffey’s art bijou. She mentions it when Margaret Stone taunts her about something that reveals her true age [MTM B7:217].

MTM B7:217

Mendacious Midget Doll (Margaret Stone's nickname for Charlotte Garfield)Earlier heading that mistook Charlotte’s doll for a nickname applied to Charlotte. See Mendacious Midget Doll.
MendelGregor Mendel (1822-1884), the researcher whose plant experiments founded genetics. During his Transport, Finnegan asks whether Mendel and other authorities could be wrong, since an angry primordial appears again after a thousand generations [D:214].

Mendoza, CarmeloPrivate detective and disguise of Mr. X, accompanying Duffey’s investigation of Finnegan’s possible death. He first asks what Finnegan was a count of; Duffey supplies the possibility “Count of nothing” [MTM B12:367]. Small, lively, pale-haired and pale-eyed, with Austrian-sounding rolled r’s, he looks happy and wistful. Teresa Stranahan recommends him as a superb companion versed in high trickery, though only a so-so detective. He obtains seaman’s papers naming Duffey as Mike Duffey of the Irish Free State and himself as Karl Metz of West Germany; they sail as working seamen for six days and nights [MTM B12:369]. He asks Duffey for the life history behind his surface life [MTM B12:370]. Horace Pie’s “Mr. Eggs” clue exposes him as X, the dealer of doubtful information [MTM B12:371]. He asks about Duffey’s gold-coining power and joins Duffey and Pie in offering coins to witnesses along the Marianao coast [MTM B12:372].

MTM B12:367; MTM B12:369; MTM B12:370; MTM B12:371; MTM B12:372

Merchant Marine papersDocuments Finnegan says are in order when discussing work with Duffey. They would let him ship out of New Orleans; he also considers returning to river barges or tending bar with Dotty, who has saved for a place of her own [A:99].

MercuriusMercury, the Roman counterpart of Hermes. The narrator lists Mercurius, Don Vincent de Ollos, and Austin as identities of Vincent Stranahan [A:39]. Meredith, GeorgeEnglish novelist and poet (1828-1909) whose verse supplies the epigraph to “Promontory Goats”: “You with shelly horns, rams! / And promontory goats!” [PG:517]. The lines come from “Phoebus with Admetus.”

Merhione, Sister MaryTopless nun interviewed at her bar in a clipping in Letitia’s scrapbook. She says the work lets her feel the human heart and sells fifty-cent reprints of her article “Topless Before God” from Paralplegic Church Today [MTM B8:251-252].

Merlin the wizardWizard invoked in the description of Seaworthy’s striking appearance at dinner: the narrator says Seaworthy could have been Merlin if wizardry paid as well as his own line of work [D:100].

Mermaid's hairNaxos’s least-known export in Brannagan’s account, sold from there in shops on Siros, Tinos, and Kea but not on Naxos itself [D:207]. Finnegan recalls handling the short-cropped black hair with lavender lights, which gave off blue sparks when its owner combed it [D:208].

MermaidsSea people described chiefly through Anastasia Demetriades’s account. She calls them close-cropped, boyish, island Greek in feature, and air-breathing even when fishtailed [D:34]. She says they live in island caves rather than underwater palaces, dismisses Norse blond mermaids as sea-cows, and traces their decline after the high Middle Ages [D:35]. She belongs to a Naxian mermaid family that has produced no fishtail for six generations; she estimates that most surviving mermaids now have two feet [D:36]. Archipelago separately says that Finnegan drank on the Grand Canary and learned about mermaids from one of them [A:188].

D:34; D:35; D:36; A:188

MeropenWord that Casey’s notebook entry XXII says the Romanies use for both life and death, without confusion because of its manner of use [A:164].

Merry de Val, CardinalCardinal named among the thirteen men whose executions or murders appear in the “Deaths of the Cardinals” paintings attributed to Finnegan on the bulkheads of the Argo’s Bread and Wine Room [MTM B13:452].

MesseneGreek place invoked in the comparison of Anastasia’s head to Diana Artemis. The narrator describes the image seen by Pausanias in its sanctuary of Asclepius as painted marble with a natural expression; a separate cypress-wood image belongs to Delos [D:133].

MessinaSicilian place on the Brunhilde’s route after Palermo and before Zakinthos [D:114-115]. The Capuchin speaks of it as the home of Finnegan’s people and says Sicilian Naxos was sixty miles away [D:119]. In “More than One,” Nicholas Cardinal Gregorio is identified as of Messina [MB:571].

Messina'sOne of Margaret Stone’s dawn-coffee haunts in New Orleans, along with Anthony Ghost’s. She says the Sardinian Red Fisters who threaten to kill her are always there and spare her to hear the next morning’s shaggy-duck joke [MTM B7:225].

MetanephrioTerm in “lobation of Metanephrio,” one of the purported age tests in the quoted Eighteenth Book of Strange Encounters. Its editors claim this and numerous other measurements establish Duffey as more than four thousand years old [MTM B8:250].

MetanoiaGreek term for a change of mind or heart, repentance or regret. In “The Great Day,” Duffey remembers a prophecy that the metanoia would arrive grotesquely and not wholly holy, while refusing to accept the handless clock as the promised turning [GD:483].

Metoula manualsSmall German-language manuals among the language-learning books on Duffey’s shelves, named in the account of Casey’s ambition to learn every language [A:159].

Metz, KarlWest German identity on the seaman’s papers used by Carmelo Mendoza, who proves to be Mr. X, while sailing with Duffey to Cuba to investigate Finnegan [MTM B12:369]. Horace Pie’s recognition of him as Mr. Eggs leads Duffey to recognize the disguise [MTM B12:371].

Mexican-Prisoner-Story DealersOne class of confidence men for whom Angela Cosquin’s father makes maps and half-maps [D:260-261].

MexicoEscape destination Vincent proposes to Finnegan while frightened of marrying Theresa [A:112]. Manuel denies that Mexico is his country, saying he comes from farther south [D:56]. Later, finding Spanish everywhere, the confused Finnegan wonders whether New Orleans has been ceded to Mexico [A:269]; the supposed New Orleans is actually Havana [A:276].

Mexico CityOne corner, with New Orleans, Havana, and Tegucigalpa, of an imperfect square used to give San Simeon’s rough position. The intersection of its diagonals lies just off San Simeon’s north shore [MB:558].

MB:558

MiamiUniversity destination hoped for by the eleven-year-old Saucerite, who says he will attend the University of Miami next season if he obtains a chess scholarship [MB:592].

MiceLive performers in Duffey and Letitia’s puppet shows, summoned from walls and floor spaces, dressed by Letitia in tiny token costumes, and able to speak or relay voices in an explicitly magical performance [MTM B4:134-135]. At the new Hubbard school, seven exhausted mice arrive after Duffey prays; a zoology teacher identifies them as Central American. Paper oxygen masks revive them before the show [MTM B4:136]. Duffey also pours a living mouse from his hands [MTM B5:170]. In the Argo voyage, Ralph Rolfe says mice ate his writing paper [MTM B13:427-428]. In Duffey’s altered childhood encounter, Philip Stranahan describes young Teresa Piccone carrying pet mice in her pockets [MTM B13:471].

MichaelName claimed for Duffey by an older relative or pretended relative; Duffey replies that she probably remembers his twin [MTM B1:7]. In “The Great Day,” Michael instead names the speaking statue of Saint Michael, whom Duffey addresses as Mike [GD:496].

Michael, HaroldIntended recipient of a little sack of marbles in Phoebe Anne Ankerson’s stolen suitcase. The label says they belonged to Aaron, who has outgrown them, and include some agates [D:172].

Michael, Saint (talking statue)Speaking stone statue in the former entry of Saint Michael’s during the Great Day. As people unstructure the church, he tells Duffey that its living water has gone and no Mass or even morning remains [GD:496]. With one eye gouged out, broken toes, and a dull stone sword, he wishes for a blade-sharpener so he can fight the destroyers. Duffey leaves him crying stone tears [GD:497].

MichaelangeloMichaelangelo is the spelling used in the supplied text and earlier heading. See Michelangelo.
Michaels, Mary AnnePupil at Saint Mary Major’s who threatens to demand that her mother take her home rather than endure the formal dance arrangements [MTM B1:32-33]. She joins the four boys and four girls who follow Lily Koch to the attic billiard room, where they eat, play pool, and dance informally; she becomes especially friendly with Charley Murray [MTM B1:33].

MTM B1:32-33; MTM B1:33

MichelangeloMichelangelo Buonarroti (1475-1564), Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet. Stein claims that the artist’s own nose was flattened in youth and that his resulting de-emphasis of noses shaped conventional depictions, unlike the noble noses of archangels in earlier imagery [A:127]. His works include David, the Pietà, and the Sistine Chapel ceiling; he also worked on Saint Peter’s Basilica and its dome.

A:127

Middle AgesPeriod repeatedly invoked in the company’s arguments, legends, and disputed histories. Patrick Stranahan dismisses Dante as a rimester, Petrarch as a sonnet writer, and famous Renaissance artists as craftsmen who should have stayed anonymous like their medieval betters [A:111]. Lawrence Salvatore tells Henry that he can bring back the sixteenth century but not the thirteenth [A:125]. Ignacio tells of Joseph of Maintz, a Benedictine priest in the eighth century, launching himself to the moon with a Missal, Scripture, Augustine, Jerome, and Pliny, in a story supposedly chronicled by Turpin of Rheims [A:271]. Henry’s unsent letter says Otto I imprisoned the Devil at Aachen in 946 and transferred him to the Euxine Chersonese later that year [MTM B5:180]. X gives the date as 946 or 947, describes delivery through Mohammedans to Devil worshippers, says the peninsula had already been called the Prison for over a thousand years, and compares the captive Devil with enchanted or imprisoned Barbarossa, Alaric, Brian Boru, the Cid, and Arthur [MTM B6:204-205]. Zabotski conjectures that a thousand-year Dark Age may be a delirious invention of a boy chronicler during the plague of 1348 [MTM B9:281-282]. Duffey’s account gives Casey two medieval forms: compassionate ninth-century sorcerer Kasmir Gorshok, who makes artificial people to shelter body lice, and Prince or Saint Casimir, defender of the poor, who defies Casimir IV through chastity and supposedly dies at twenty-three, actually withdrawing from the world [PG:535-536]. Henry is identified as the Emperor Henry of Neustria [MTM B5:183], while Duffey proposes his medieval recorder-flute as an instrument suitable to a patriarch [MTM B9:266].

Mogul, JohnHead of Track and Total, usually called the Mogul although John Mogul is his actual name. X confronts him at his Marseille apartment over contracts to kill thirteen genuine Cardinals in flight or hiding, and Mogul describes his control over the separate contracts and his preference for dispassionate killers [MB:571-573] [MB:579]. He subsequently tracks their doubles as well [MB:578-579]. He extends six digits on one hand and five on the other to count eleven surviving targets [MB:578]. Later John Giwa, Cardinal Doki’s double, breaks in on him in Marseille, severs twelve digits from his hands, skewers his tongue, and carries the severed fingers and thumbs to the conclave in the underground room of Mooring Rock, where they writhe as if swearing vengeance [MB:596-597].

Mohammed (c. 570--632 AD)Arab prophet and founder of Islam, regarded by Muslims as the final prophet. The revelations received by him were collected as the Qur’an, the central source of Muslim faith and practice. In Lawrence Salvatore’s argument with Henry, Mohammed’s time is recalled as an occasion when people thought the world would be lost; Henry answers that half was lost [A:125].

Molasses World (Zabotski's term)Zabotski’s name for the slow everyday world, also called the “Everyday-or-Molasses World.” He says that it occupies the same space as the Pristine World, but in a different way [MTM B9:277] [MTM B9:279]. Duffey compares the apparent distance of the past with a distorting medium in which people themselves are immersed; Zabotski identifies that medium as molasses [MTM B9:272] [MTM B9:273]. The contrast concerns the content of experience as well as its duration: Zabotski says that he can live overflowing years in the Pristine World during a day or two here [MTM B9:279]. Duffey subsequently reports such a journey himself, spending three or five years there and returning in two days [MTM B9:284]. See Pristine World.

Monaghan, Marie SchultzAustralian wife of Hans Schultz, named Marie Anna Monaghan at their secret marriage in Sydney’s Annunciation Church on February 15, 1943. Hans lacked army permission, so the guests were her relatives rather than their friends; they honeymooned on an uncle’s farm [A:31]. Chubby, roguish, tart-talking, red-haired, freckled, and green-eyed, she habitually brushes her hair back with her hand. Hans admires her classical proportions and calls her “at least eternal” in a poem [A:6] [A:24-25]. Her claim to 156 years in Sydney refers to the Monaghan family [A:7]. Theresa tells Vincent that a letter from Marie has disclosed a secret, apparently the marriage [A:49]. Hans and Marie settle in St. Louis, with Mary Catherine staying in their apartment [A:97]. Dotty’s affectionately exasperated letter blames Marie for funding Salvation Sally’s journey to America [A:147-148]. At the Rounders’ gathering Marie disputes Duffey’s claim to have made them, arguing that he collected their forgotten souls and gave them setting and sparkle; he disagrees [MTM B5:158-159]. The list of his twelve talismanic creations calls her Mary Monaghan Schultz [MTM B5:161]. She insists she has recently been on the Argo, explaining her refreshed waking [MTM B12:387]; Hans and Marie supply the ship with sea biscuit [MTM B13:446].

Monday (Day)Recurring publication and correspondence day: the first Answer arrives on Monday morning, with issues scheduled for Monday, Wednesday, and Friday [MTM B4:113]; Bagby’s unexplained letters appear on Duffey’s table every Monday and continue after his death [MTM B7:219] [MTM B8:237]; the Pelican Press publishes the Seamen’s Paper on Mondays [GD:490]. Duffey also returns from the Fifth Contingency to a Monday he has already lived [MTM B12:356].

Monday (Luin) (Goat)Luin, or Monday, is one of the goat-man’s seven youngest kids, named for the days of the week. Unable to make the leap into the old sycamore’s crotch, she receives a boost from Finnegan, winning him the friendship of all seven [A:194-195].

Money (Medium)Finnegan’s source of money puzzles Mary Catherine; X claims in his letter to Absalom that he knows it and is deeply involved, but postpones the story [A:248] [A:266]. Hilary Hilton reports a pact requiring four schoolboys to make a million dollars by thirty or kill themselves [A:254]. When Askandan says he would not cross Finnegan’s enemy for a million dollars, Finnegan claims a slightly larger sum, but the narrator questions his truthfulness [A:258]. His stolen suitcase is called the world’s most valuable, without a stated amount [A:188]. Duffey funds the perpetual soup crock with $15 collected from the gang, $45 from Zabotski, and $40 from panhandling [A:133]. At Basse-Terre the narrator calls money necessary for Paradise, especially for the undeserving, as the four friends recline in hammocks [D:236]. Duffey’s facility for making money is the first of his talents to diminish and the least missed [MTM B4:109]. Casey inherits money from his father’s estate [MTM B4:119]. The Depression weakens the joy of money, though the narrator says that joy is not entirely evil [MTM B4:124].

A:248; A:266; A:254; A:258; A:188; A:133; D:236; MTM B4:109; MTM B4:119; MTM B4:124

Monica (Charley Murray's girlfriend)Monica Drexel is sometimes Charley Murray’s girlfriend and joins the farewell company at Meinkmuellers with his sister Monica Murray, whom she resembles. Duffey initially gives a talisman to the wrong Monica; the other recognizes it as intended for her, but the passage does not name which receives it [MTM B2:69]. A girl named only Monica accompanies Charley to the balloon dinner [MTM B2:65]. The later list of talismanic creations identifies Vincent as the son of Monica Murray Stranahan, making Monica Murray the likelier intended recipient [MTM B5:161].

Monroney, MoiraOne of the three red-haired girls the Sergeant meets at Sydney’s Plaza Hotel with Rosemary Riorden and Minnie McGinty. They drink and become friendly with his party [A:88].

Monster GiulioGiulio Solli, a Teras and father of John Solli, or Finnegan [MTM B3:107] [MTM B5:161]. He is the first customer at Duffey’s St. Louis establishment: dark, powerful, unusually put together, with very wide feet and rough rivermans-blue clothing. A riverboat, ocean-ship, and dock worker, he asks for food, a bath, and lodging, pays a silver dollar, and bathes in a horse trough [MTM B2:41-43]. Duffey gives him a talisman for an unborn son; Bagby then identifies him with the Gadarene Swine and sings of his pursuit and threatened drowning, while Duffey calls him good [MTM B2:47-48]. Later Giulio says he applied the talisman to his wife’s belly and placed it in his son’s hands at birth [MTM B3:107]. Among Duffey’s Chicago friends [MTM B3:99], he is modeled by Mona Greatheart and engraved in Doré-like style by Groben. Countess Margaret says a relative of his inhabited her childhood castle and imagines one in every Transylvanian castle cellar; she distinguishes Teras from Troll [MTM B3:106-107]. Duffey says Giulio has been dead at least ten years, but Bagby reports a recent meeting and says Teras councils include both living and dead [MTM B5:165].

MTM B3:107; MTM B5:161; MTM B2:41-43; MTM B2:47-48; MTM B3:99; MTM B3:106-107; MTM B5:165

MonstersOverlapping names, images, and rival accounts of unusual beings, rather than a single settled classification. The Devil Is Dead invites the reader to arrange its devils, monsters, corpses, and revenants, while Papa Devil calls the plot the old game of monsters and men [D:6] [D:120]. Finnegan calls himself a gargoyle, and the narrator later depicts him as a living gargoyle perched on a hotel; Anastasia identifies both herself and Finnegan as teras or drakon, with her Oread sisters sharing the condition [D:39] [D:139] [D:162]. His resemblance to the Cliff People includes great noses, chinlessness, a shambling gait, and sudden strength and speed [A:59]. Anastasia’s grandmother claims the other blood for herself and partly for her granddaughter, while Brannagan says he and Finnegan carry it in varying recensions, containing the conflict within themselves [D:128] [D:209-210]. In confession Finnegan fears the old animal and Devil’s kindred within him; the priest acknowledges another kindred but assumes salvation includes it [D:119-120]. Other accounts are more hostile. An epigraph credited to Saint Brendon describes unredeemable, long-lived creatures, usually evil but sometimes indifferent or helpful, and always untrustworthy [D:130]. Another, credited to Galen, makes Tityroi or Satyroi the animal-like, human-looking offspring of Daemons and women, with destructive passions and differing fertility in successive generations [D:160-161]. The Asimov epigraph suggests a groomed Neanderthal could pass unnoticed [D:9]. A hostile review of Royce Rollins’s The Return of the Neanderthal reports his theory of surviving elites and hidden ancestry erupting into destructive primordials, with apparitions, doubles, and second sight as ordinary powers of that species [D:240-241]. The epigraph credited to Carmody Overlark links pumpkin heads, bulbous noses, a basal brain bulge, unusual imagination, and ghostliness; these are the book’s attributed speculations [D:270-272]. Finnegan’s Transport gives the older people their own grievance: displaced by newcomers, some hid in the conquerors’ blood and reemerge for vengeance [D:213-214]. He finally declares himself renegade against their destructive purpose, while Doll disputes his and X’s claim that ordinary people cannot save themselves [D:292]. X himself remains unsure that alien flesh exists, though he speaks of a race crossing the races [D:156]. Giulio Solli, the Monster Forgotten, is Finnegan’s father; Stein’s account questions how much of the son’s experience is filial memory supplied through X [MTM B6:187]. Duffey’s first St. Louis customer, Giulio is dark, powerful, oddly assembled, wide-footed, and dressed in rivermans-blue, working on riverboats, ocean ships, and docks [MTM B2:41-43]. He receives a talisman for an unborn son and later describes giving it to his “dago son”; he explicitly confirms that he is a Teras [MTM B2:47] [MTM B3:107]. Bagby reports Giulio’s participation in councils attended by living and dead despite Duffey’s statement that he has long been dead [MTM B5:165]. Finnegan’s parentage is explicit at their later meeting [MTM B5:174]. Papa Devil’s huge purple appearance and noiseless movement are repeatedly emphasized [D:30] [D:70]. Seaworthy calls him the very Devil [D:83], but X distinguishes the original alien conspirator from the Irish policeman Noonan or Flaherty who impersonated him; both have died by the Naxos aftermath [D:146] [D:154-155]. Private Gregory, the purple pumpkin-headed storyteller who looks ghostly in the ward, is identified by Finnegan as Papadiabolous, without specifying which member of the family [A:84-85] [A:278]. Marie Courtois is Finnegan’s Golden Ogress and a primordial figure of immense strength [D:32] [D:37]. Anastasia proposes painting Marie as an ogress; Marie assents, but Finn actually paints the women as Sindbad’s wives and proposes Papa Devil for the man-eating ogre [D:62]. The Loosed Devil meets Duffey to demand his creative service, while speaking of a client and leaving his precise rank uncertain [MTM B10:302-304]. Henry’s unsent letter dates the Devil’s imprisonment to 946; X’s account gives 946 or 947, a Crimean prison, and a recent postwar release, describing the prisoner as misshapen, slant-faced, and printing distorted letters [MTM B5:180] [MTM B6:204-206]. The preaching figure attacks order through defamation, hatred, crooked lines, excess words, and the intended negation of creation [MTM B8:242]. Countess Margaret claims that her horse-sized family wolves frighten the Devil [MTM B8:256]. In Episodes of the Argo, a song accuses him of choosing evil, wasting innocents, and poisoning springs, yet asks to suffer in his place; the accompanying sermon calls him the troll beneath the bridge, and another fragment says he knows the past fully but the future only in fragments [PG:521] [PG:523] [PG:526]. Margaret Stone claims her promise against final loss covers the devil she knows, but she and Duffey disagree whether he is the Great Devil [MTM B13:447]. Show Boat’s letter reports Casey’s financial debt to Seven Devils and his refusal to let them inhabit him again [A:262]. Duffey’s invisible giants can perform physical work, including ringing a massive bell with a visible hand; his talismans create or activate persons, with Finnegan called his greatest masterpiece [MTM B1:5] [MTM B1:15] [MTM B1:18] [MTM B5:182]. Four dark giants of demiurgic appearance also hold Casey’s head in the terrifying televised animation Duffey makes from Scanlon’s painting [MTM B12:381]. Uncreations and broken effigies hiss at Duffey after losing their houses and bodies [MTM B11:314]; the Pop historians later attack pseudo-people, human remnants, morphic dragons, and papier-mâché fire lizards, while Mary Virginia questions the victims’ supposed unreality [MTM B11:338]. Morpheus argues that sleep and waking are illusions, says the cosmos is a single cell’s dwindling dream, and wrestles Duffey for the remaining identity [GD:499-500]. Related prodigies include the still-speaking and weeping head of Paul XI, the Cap-Stone, which is silenced when his brains are removed [MB:562-563], and the devil in Finnegan’s painting, exorcised before its destruction in his story of studying under Van Ghi [D:255].

Ignacio tells of Joseph of Maintz shooting himself to the moon and living there for ninety years, lighting a bonfire at each full moon to show that he is alive [A:271]. Moonlight Cavalry (Finnegan's old outfit)Finnegan’s former army outfit. When he seeks it in D’Hannis, locals say it has not been there for seven or eight years and none of its boys has returned; some now live in San Antonio. He had maneuvered in this neighborhood during his early army days [A:202].

Moonraker (Ship on Master Map)One of the ships represented on the Master Map associated with Angela Cosquin’s father and its treasure-fraud history [D:261].

Mooring Rock, the (Location)Mooring rock in the shoals north of San Simeon, initially described as six hundred by three hundred yards. Its rock-hewn fresh-water well, high natural palisade, and imported soil support hidden gardens and about fifty permanent residents, while several hundred visitors, including millionaires and fisher folk, share its secret. Two tramp steamers call there [MB:575-576]. Count Finnegan brings the Martyr-Bell, and the Argo later brings the Peter-Bell [MB:575] [MB:577-578]. A hewn room reached from the well-shaft becomes the site of the conclave [MB:577] [MB:596]. The later upheaval describes Mooring Rock as three square kilometers, a changed scale, and raises it a hundred meters above the surrounding land; Giwa blesses it as Mooring-Stone and renames Oceanic Babylon Holy Babylon [MB:597]. In the earlier narrative, Count Finnegan names its surroundings the Belling Shoals and Ringing Rocks; its cave receives thirteen apparent doubles of dead princes. He says one will actually be a dead holy man still alive, preserving the line until the last battle [MTM B13:453].

MB:575-576; MB:575; MB:577-578; MB:577; MB:596; MB:597; MTM B13:453

Mooring Stone, the (Location)Name used for Mooring Rock, including in Giwa’s blessing. See Mooring Rock, the (Location).
Moral Sanctions Committee for the Removal of Eye-Sores and Abominations, TheCommittee that confronts Zabotski about his growing contraption. A woman claims that eight years earlier he promised to act against the eyesore “on the morrow”; he corrects her that he promised not to act. Members then remember both yesterday and eight years ago as the time of their previous complaint, which Zabotski explains through Pristine History and their slower historical context [MTM B9:276-277].

MorphēGreek morphē, form or shape. Morpheus claims that it and his own name are really the same word, arguing that shape is known only in sleep and that a waking world would be formless [GD:499].

MorpheusSleep god who confronts Duffey during the Great Day. He calls sleep and waking illusions, connects his name with morphē, or shape, and maintains that shape exists only in sleep [GD:499]. He says the cosmos began as a single cell’s dream and is shrinking back into it. He and Duffey wrestle for the illusion of being the remaining cell, finally becoming a creature swallowing itself; Morpheus calls this another beginning [GD:500-501].

Mosca, Count (Character)Count Mosca of Stendhal’s The Charterhouse of Parma, called Count Mosco in Archipelago. The older goats enjoy the intrigues of him, Gina Pietranera, and Fabrizio while the goat-man reads aloud; the younger goats fall asleep [A:198].

MoscovyMuscovy or Russia, named Third Rome in Henry Salvatore’s dream of the Navicula Petri. It appears among the ship’s shattered and fallen masts, with Albion and Gaul; other masts still totter [A:45].

A:45

MosesBiblical leader commissioned to bring the Israelites out of Egypt and given the tablets of the law on Mount Sinai (Exodus 3:10-12; 31:18). Margaret Stone invokes Luke 16:31, saying that those who disbelieve Moses and the Prophets will not believe one risen from the dead, as part of her urgent street preaching [A:144].

A:144

Moth wingsWings Duffey listens for after returning from his lost years. He asks Beth whether moth wings can be heard across three or four hundred miles [MTM B2:74-75]. In Omaha the summons acquires direction and draws him to Chicago, where the moth proves to be Letitia Koch [MTM B3:77] [MTM B3:90-91].

MTM B2:74-75; MTM B3:77; MTM B3:90-91

MothsImages surrounding Duffey’s call to and recognition of Letitia Koch. A moth call draws him from Omaha to Chicago [MTM B3:77]; Charlotte takes him to St. Malachy’s, where he meets the woman without recognizing her [MTM B3:87-89]. At the Koch shop he names the evoking, seeking, and joyful moths as Tinea evocata, Tinea indagatio, and Tinea letitia. Lily instead calls Letitia a butterfly transformed into Psyche herself [MTM B3:90-91].

MTM B3:77; MTM B3:87-89; MTM B3:90-91

Mottled Tree (Synonym for Sycamore)Sycamore owned by Bryan Blackstone, whom Zabotski compares to its mottled trunk and trashy fruit. Zabotski curses the tree to die by tomorrow, explaining that he can command a tree’s death but not a man’s [MTM B9:270]. When Duffey returns, it is gone: Bandicoot says it died and was cut down long ago, revealing the years that have slipped through Duffey’s apparent overnight interval [MTM B9:276].

Mountain-Building for Fun and Profit (History topic)Topic on the program of the Society for Creative History or Royal Pop Historians, among the titles Margaret Stone recites when announcing her intention to attend [MTM B11:307].

MouseYoung living mouse Duffey pours from his hands onto the table after offering to produce a dinosaur and other creatures. Papa Piccone accepts the mouse proposal, and the company laughs; Patrick Stranahan asks whether Duffey calls that a dinosaur [MTM B5:170].

Mrs. George Brubaker's house (Location)The Brubaker house in Newark, outside which Finnegan and Doll leave George Brubaker’s stolen car. Doll has used Mrs. George Brubaker’s identity when questioned en route; Finnegan leaves a note warning George about unlocked cars and signs it Roving Magistrate Number Sixteen [D:169].

Mt. Ararat (Mountain/Location)Mountain in eastern Turkey traditionally associated with Noah’s Ark, although Genesis 8:4 names the mountains of Ararat rather than a single peak. Askandan claims it as the secluded center of the other blood in his own Armenia [A:258]. In the Fundamentalers’ discussion Duffey argues that wooden remains in its snow are old castles rather than vessels; a questioner invokes angelic guards as evidence for the Ark, while Zabotski says angels guard whatever becomes remote from human sight [MTM B9:281].

Muck of Animation (Duffey's term for creative material)Duffey’s name for the dung he molds into new Animated Marvels while half-buried in a storm-struck dungheap. He uses his own blood as integument, selects broken glass and metal as talismans, and welcomes lightning as the power for infusing the forms [MTM B12:394].

MTM B12:394

Muk Muk Sea (Location)Sea in Turkestan from which Hugh de Turenne says most Black Sea Sturgeon actually come. He uses the claim to explain the surviving commercial label while insisting that the Black Sea itself never existed [MTM B11:336].

MTM B11:336

Mullens, Charlotte (Alias/Persona)Persona of Charlotte Garfield, the confidence woman who appears as a nine-year-old on Duffey’s train to Chicago, plays cards, and drinks whisky with him and her supposed mother Gloria [MTM B3:78-79]. She claims to be thirty-eight and calls Gloria her sister and Manolo her son, but later explains that she makes compliant figures from pliable people, often actors [MTM B3:80-83]. She and Duffey communicate psychically: he finds the key and location of Aga Gonof’s hidden funds, she enters his experience as a psychosomatic trance, and she helps him find Letitia, his moth [MTM B3:84-87]. Gloria and Manolo die in the trance and are later found tortured and murdered in the hotel; Letitia says Charlotte escaped with the millions [MTM B3:85-86] [MTM B3:97]. Charlotte later attends the confidence-men’s convention in New Orleans as Garfield, still looking nine and wearing cowgirl attire. Her Mendacious Midget Doll reveals an age near two hundred, and she admits lying about her age [MTM B7:216-217]. Later she uses Carrollton and advertises for a new family willing to take the name Darnley [MTM B8:259].

MTM B3:78-79; MTM B3:80-83; MTM B3:84-87; MTM B3:85-86; MTM B3:97; MTM B7:216-217; MTM B8:259

Mullens, Gloria (Traveler/Con artist)Charlotte Mullens’s companion on the Chicago train, posing as her mother. She shares food, cards, and whisky with Duffey and tells a story of destitution after her husband’s death [MTM B3:78-79]. Charlotte calls her a sister, then explains that she shapes pliable people into family roles [MTM B3:80-83]. Gloria assists Charlotte’s compromising-and-blackmailing confidence game [MTM B3:87]. She and Manolo are killed in Duffey’s trance and later found tortured with crushed skulls in the Chicago hotel; Letitia says the killers sought information they did not possess and Charlotte had already escaped [MTM B3:85-86] [MTM B3:97].

MTM B3:78-79; MTM B3:80-83; MTM B3:87; MTM B3:85-86; MTM B3:97

Mullens, Manolo (Son of Charlotte Mullens/Garfield)Companion of Charlotte and Gloria Mullens, introduced by Charlotte as her son and accompanying them and Duffey to a Chicago hotel [MTM B3:80-81]. Charlotte later says she forms such family figures from pliable flesh-and-blood people [MTM B3:83]. She orders Manolo and Gloria to divert the attacking stevedore in Duffey’s trance, where they die; the pair are later reported tortured and murdered in the hotel [MTM B3:85-86] [MTM B3:97].

MTM B3:80-81; MTM B3:83; MTM B3:85-86; MTM B3:97

Munster, PeggyArtist named among Duffey’s associates in building and inventing worlds and scenes [MTM B6:198]. Duffey recognizes landscapes associated with her work while entering the mind of “The Majesty” [MTM B8:241]. She is not identified here with Peggy Conner, who appears with Mike Conner among the golfers [MTM B3:99].

Murphy, MargaretAustralian stewardess, also called Margie, who meets Finnegan and Vincent with Loy Larkin in Sydney [A:2] [A:5-6]. She looks like a little girl dressed as an adult [A:5]. Loy’s February 11, 1943 letter plans a picnic and says Margie loves Finnegan too; Margaret adds her own signature, spelled Murphey [A:27].

Murray, CharleySt. Louis friend of Duffey, about two years his senior, met at boarding school. A collector of magic sets and trick books, Charley asks Duffey to build props and accidentally discovers his real magic and giant helpers. He has already attended school with Sebastian Hilton [MTM B1:21-22]. He climbs the school walls in terror after their outings and performs tricks during the boys’ clandestine sales; Mary Anne Michaels becomes friendly with him at the informal attic gathering [MTM B1:25-26] [MTM B1:33]. Later a St. Louis University day student, he performs at Rounders’ and buys half the club, enabling Duffey’s travels [MTM B2:53]. He manages it at the 1946 gathering [MTM B5:162]. Duffey gives him a talisman to pass to his sister’s unborn child; Vincent is identified as Monica Murray Stranahan’s son and one of the talismanic creations [MTM B1:35] [MTM B4:120] [MTM B5:161]. By Duffey’s late St. Louis visit Charley has died and left his half-interest to nephew Vincent [MTM B12:385].

MTM B1:21-22; MTM B1:25-26; MTM B1:33; MTM B2:53; MTM B5:162; MTM B1:35; MTM B4:120; MTM B5:161; MTM B12:385

Murray, Monica StranahanSister of Charley Murray, wife of Patrick Stranahan, and mother of Vincent [MTM B5:161-163]. She comes to Rounders’ with Charley, Patrick, and Papa Piccone; Duffey remembers the serenity she gave him and still feels it [MTM B5:162-163]. Earlier, two look-alike Monicas, Murray and Drexel, attend Duffey’s farewell; he gives a talisman to the wrong one before the other claims it, without identifying either woman in that exchange [MTM B2:69]. Other passages make Vincent a talismanic creation and Charley the intermediary for his sister’s unborn child [MTM B4:120] [MTM B5:161]. She outlives Patrick and Charley and is present at Duffey’s late St. Louis visit [MTM B12:385].

MurryVariant spelling of Monica Stranahan’s maiden name in Vincent’s birth account [A:94]. See Murray, Monica Stranahan.

A:94

Mutant CoyotesUnverified creature reference. The cited Transport passage concerns primordials hidden in human blood and their recurrent war, but mentions no coyotes [D:214].

D:214

N (code name for Gregory Noonan McColum)X’s code designation for Gregory McColum, the Irish twin of Papadiabolous I and the man known as Noonan or Papadiabolous II. According to X, he entered police work at twenty-five and worked undercover for decades: he was N as his colleague was X [D:285-287]. He impersonated his dead twin and was killed by Seaworthy on Naxos, where Seaworthy failed to recognize the dead man as his recent companion [D:289].

D:285-287; D:289

Name forgettingRecurrent loss of names and identity in Finnegan’s story. The soldier detained while the Dirty Five are boarding for home cannot say which of their surnames is his: all seem part of him, and he hopes to identify himself by joining the others and seeing who is missing [A:71-72]. The narrative later explicitly recalls Finnegan’s weeks in the Green Islands without his name or personality [D:50]. He also forgets helping Seaworthy bury a still-moving corpse; his drinking to oblivion follows, rather than explains, the burial [D:75].

A:71-72; D:50; D:75

NattkarletOne of the first three Crocks, Casey Szymansky’s clandestine college magazines, alongside the Night Charley and the Nocnik. They begin during his college years, 1938-1942, with a precedent in the schoolboy Chambers and its chamber-pot mastheads [A:167]. Casey starts a Crock at each of his seven colleges but usually loses control within two or three weeks; the narrator distinguishes his humorous work from the more salacious successors [A:168].

A:167; A:168

Natural MethodPart of the mock advertising slogan for Uncle Joe Tompkinson’s Torpedo Juice, promising an explosive personality by the Natural Method. The imaginary sponsor is heard on Stein’s G.I. radio station, the Anopheles Network [A:46].

A:46

NautiGirl who, with Falo, builds an American-style cabaret shack in the Luzon jungle after the war has ended. Vincent and Finnegan become its first customers [A:63-64]. Nauti calls Finnegan a tao-bunduk, an older mountain creature rather than a man; quotes a peso a bottle for the whisky; and offers to teach him Tagalog [A:64]. She plays harp and expects her uncle in Batangas to bring a piano, which she will play. The four play Robber Cassino with a damaged pack supplemented by paper substitutes, and Falo wins [A:65].

A:63-64; A:64; A:65

Navajo potteryOne of the many goods Hillary Hilton says he can sell in his distressed-merchandise business, listed alongside marked money [A:255].

A:255

Navicula Petri (Peter Ship)The “little ship of Peter,” the name of Henry Salvatore’s dream boat. It resembles a galleon but is something more. Its pennants include the source’s “Ih hoc signo vincet,” the Dirty Five’s “Ubicumque fuerit corpus illic congregabuntur et aquilas,” and the Petrine sequence “Tu es Petrus,” “Portae inferi non prevalebunt,” and “tibi dabo claves regni.” Finnegan’s left-handed “Nisi esses sollicitus-” is scratched out and replaced by “If you can’t be careful, be good.” Devices include a Lamb, Greek Cross, Fish, six-pointed star, Woman, Serpent, and Crescent Moon [A:44]. The crew comprises the Apostles; Stephen, Paul and the Baptist; Linus, Clement and Cletus; Barbara and Catherine; Gregory and Constantine; Jerome and Augustine; Francis and Anthony; Thomas and Patrick; Hildebrand and Adrian the Dutchman; the French and Spanish Theresas; Joan and Xavier. Half toy and half more-than-real ship, it is storm-tossed, with broken masts associated with Albion, Moscovy as Third Rome, and Gaul [A:45]. Henry recognizes the Argo, its quest sanctified through the millennia, and recognizes his vocation in saving it [A:46]. His later proposal to name the magazine Bark recalls this dream; Finnegan supports the name and clairvoyantly draws its damaged ship for the masthead [A:121].

A:44; A:45; A:46; A:121

NaxosIsland of the Cyclades in the Greek Aegean, the ancestral home in Anastasia’s account of her mermaid family [D:35-36]. The Brunhilde reaches it on March 14, Passion Sunday; the narrative calls it the home of Ariadne and white wine [D:115]. It describes a mountainous island twelve miles square, producing figs, olives, lemons, grapes, honey, white wine and emery, with the Demetriades farm and Anastasia Grandmother up the mountain road [D:125]. Finnegan is said elsewhere to have touched eternity there [A:188]. After the shooting at the landing, he finds Papadiabolous, Joe Cross and five unfamiliar men in olive shirts dead in the street, while another man remains dead aboard the sinking smaller boat. Anastasia has been shot and recovered from the water [D:146-147]. X later explains that Seaworthy killed Noonan, Papadiabolous II, there without recognizing the impersonator [D:289].

D:35-36; D:115; D:125; A:188; D:146-147; D:289

Neanderthal Conspiracy / Teras SpeciesInterlocking accounts of an older, partly concealed people, their survival within humanity, and a struggle over humanity’s future. These are delivered through competing characters, visions, narration and attributed writings, rather than one consistently settled taxonomy. Duffey says his creations contain unusually large amounts of Teras blood, naming Gargoyles, Neanderthals, Boogers, Vagaries and Variants [MTM B5:170]. Giulio Solli identifies himself as a Teras; Finnegan is his son [MTM B3:107] [MTM B5:174]. The Brunhilde company is described as the other human race, and Finnegan wonders whether he belongs to it. His accompanying pumpkin-head vision shows their crew extinguishing the lights inside other people [D:50]. Later the narration makes him a member of both human races [D:114]. He confesses a felt kinship with old animals and the Devil; the priest replies that salvation extends to that other kindred [D:119]. Anastasia Grandmother claims the other blood for herself and a little for her granddaughter [D:128]. In Finnegan’s mountain dreams, the Oreads call him a teras or drakon and deny him ascent; he resists, then detects their own kinship. Anastasia confirms that she, Finnegan and her Oread sisters are of this kind, while insisting that some must help people [D:138-139]. A hostile review of Royce Rollins’s The Return of the Neanderthal: The Alien Within presents its author as a crank. His thesis claims that Neanderthals survived their apparent replacement fifty thousand years ago, either isolated or hidden in the human bloodstream; authentic primordials might reappear through prodigious siring, and their return would destroy their successors. The account associates them with ghosts, fetches and second sight [D:240-241]. An epigraph attributed to Carmody Overlark proposes a larger brain with a reduced forebrain and enlarged back-brain, connecting this arrangement with unconscious and ghostly powers. Its physiognomy includes bulbous noses, pumpkin heads and a basal bulge; modern examples are said to include criminals or exceptional seers, poets, humorists and inventors [D:270-272]. These are the novel’s attributed theories. In a Transport, Finnegan experiences the grievances of the people before the people: dispossession, persecution and a contemplated revenge against the later arrivals, themselves called aliens. The older people have survived as the Aliens Within, leaving those of double blood to wonder whether they must protect humanity from their own kind [D:213-214]. Brannagan and Finnegan discuss multiple recensions of that blood and the conflict within themselves [D:209-210]. Finnegan recognizes his paradise companions Le Marin, the Duke, Barnaby and Duckwalk as people of double blood [D:237]. An epigraph attributed to Hiram Hunt proposes interbreeding, cannibal absorption and tension between the older stock and a mutation, warning that destroying either element destroys both [D:283-284]. X offers a different genealogical emphasis, connecting his family and the twin Papa Devils with a purported Devil-father and a secret counter-subversive history [D:278-281] [D:285-289]. Papa calls the struggle the game of monsters and men, or Policia y Ladrones, a partially related-species conflict whose dialogue is written in blood [D:120-121]. He compares the conspirators’ concealment with the Devil’s success in persuading people that he does not exist [D:87]. Finnegan calls himself a gargoyle, later sits as a living hotel gargoyle, and observes Seaworthy’s gathering as a coven [D:39] [D:162-163]. Great noses recur: Brannagan suggests Finnegan’s conceals his chinlessness [D:202], and an unnamed stranger’s nose exceeds his [D:177]. Eventually Finnegan declares himself renegade against those who would roast and eat the human world and so destroy themselves. X still distrusts ordinary humans; Doll objects to both old gargoyles’ dismissal of them [D:290-292].

Neo-CentristLabel in Stein’s proposed title for the magazine that becomes the Bark [A:121]. Casey later attacks the journal in the Crock as a self-described neo-Centrist, anti-Communist Catholic publication without ecclesiastical sanction, while mockingly questioning whether the term means anything [A:128].

A:121; A:128

Neo-Centrist Review of Evolvate Socio-Geopolitical Motifs in a Disintegrating WorldAbsalom Stein’s proposed title for the journal eventually called the Bark, with the subtitle Thesis and Antithesis. Several colleagues object to its length. Henry proposes Bark from his dream of a little boat, and Finnegan’s supporting vote settles the choice [A:121].

A:121

Neo-JewAbsalom Stein’s self-description. He imagines a group of neo-Jews but says he may be its only member; Duffey asks whether this would mean becoming Christian [A:131]. Stein insists that his grandfather left the Temple, whereas he himself has never personally entered or left it: the Church would have to come to him there, and his genes will not let him join it. The narrator says he remains the only one of exactly his kind [A:132].

A:131; A:132

Neo-NeanderthalsPeople exemplified by Eva, whom the narration explicitly calls a Neo-Neanderthal. It attributes their verbal dexterity, easy command of languages and ability to read words from minds to their unusually shaped heads and the resulting emphasis in their brains. Eva hopes to buy Kate’s Neanderthal Bar in Biloxi as a gathering place for her kind [MTM B13:407].

MTM B13:407

Nervous fishAskandan’s expression for fish requiring rehabilitation as merchandise. His discussion concerns spoiled food, including turning fish, and he claims that his seven chemical sovereigns can rescue everything from nervous fish to nervous furniture [A:256-257].

A:256-257

Nervous furnitureThe inanimate end of Askandan’s range of nervous merchandise: he says his seven sovereigns will serve for rescuing nervous fish through nervous furniture, whether the goods are organic or inorganic [A:257].

A:257

Nervous manThe narrator’s punning description of Askandan: although both he and Hillary Hilton speak of distressed and nervous merchandise, Askandan is more a nervous man and Hilton more a distressed one [A:256].

A:256

Nervous merchandiseAskandanakandrian’s term for troubled stock, organic or inorganic, which he claims to rehabilitate with seven sovereigns: an acid, lye, formaldehyde, ammonia, a secret kaoline affiliate, amyl acetate and an unnamed lesser gum. He says they can rescue fish or furniture; forced to keep only four, he would choose acid, base, clay and gum. Soft fruits, wilted lettuce, turning meat and fish, and rancid oils need processing; furs and jewelry belong to a pseudo-nervous category and may be sold through peddlers pretending they are stolen. He also boasts of his ability to handle weevily grain [A:257]. Both he and Hilton use nervous and distressed for their merchandise [A:256].

A:257; A:256

Nesbitt, Little DottyRegular at the Old Wooden Ship [D:215]. She is one of four Dottys frequently confused because of their overlapping marital histories. Little Dotty and Dotty Danvers have been married to two brothers in Sugarland, Texas, one previously married to Dotty Hulme; Danvers also married a man with the same name as Little Dotty’s first husband [D:220-221].

Nests for birds'-nest soupEdible nests made from swiftlet saliva. Hans gives a fanciful account while the soldiers pass the Talaud Islands en route to Luzon: he claims these barren islands are the sole source, and that the birds build nests from regurgitated fish and limestone for Chinese soup [A:62-63].

A:62-63

NeustriaName of the western Frankish kingdom in the Merovingian period, broadly the part of modern France west of the Meuse and north of the Loire. In Absalom Stein’s Notes on the Finnegan Cycle, Neustria or Latter Neustria instead names the thousand-year empire of Christendom from 946 to 1946. Stein describes Hitler as a man of or from the future raiding backwards into that thousand-year province, Greater Neustria [MTM B6:185].

MTM B6:185

Never-Break Dog Whip, TheOne of the whips named by the turbaned speaker at the Royal Pop Historians’ gathering, as he imagines the memories stored in an old Decatur Street flagstone [MTM B11:329].

MTM B11:329

NevisCaribbean island invoked in Angela Cosquin’s story of her father’s forged shipwreck-treasure maps. She includes the pass between Basseterre and Nevis among seven supposed false or shoal passages of the Antilles where wrecks accumulated, or logically ought to have accumulated [D:260].

D:260

New Catholic Press GuildNew, already powerful organization described by the narrator as somewhat suspect. Duffey, Letitia and Mary Virginia attend its paradoxically secret yet heavily advertised meeting. Two-thirds of its members also belong to the older Catholic Press Association; the other third, the narrator says, have come out from under rocks. Its supposedly supremely important guest speaker is the figure Duffey recognizes as Old Clootie [MTM B8:239].

New Day DawnerThe only drink offered at the Stumble-Bum on the Great Day. After Duffey unsuccessfully orders a sazerac, salty dog and old fashioned, the barkeep insists that everyone drinks the New Day Dawner. Duffey leaves [GD:498].

GD:498

New HeavenAdam Scanlon’s phrase for the High Renaissance sky in his symbolic seascape, set over an Old Abyss: a sea he assigns to the Low Middle Ages after the Empire’s death. He also claims to have suggested the absence of the Argo, a meaning even Hans has not understood [A:234]. The phrase recalls the new heaven of Revelation 21:1, though Adam does not cite the verse.

A:234

New JerseyState reached through the tunnel on Finnegan and Doll Delancy’s flight from New York; he offers to release and pay her there if she wants to stop driving for him [D:167]. In another wandering, he crosses to the Jersey Shore, then meets the goat-man in the state’s remote back country, described as bogs, Barrens, low mountains and beaches [A:193-194]. The goat-man’s stories include the possibly haunted Harlow House on an abandoned farm; Finnegan never sees it himself [A:197]. Trinali asks Hans to take her to two places in Jersey for driftwood and cypress knees [A:229].

D:167; A:193-194; A:197; A:229

New Men, Valley of theName asserted by the older people in Finnegan’s Transport: they were a Valley, and its name was Valley of the New Men, despite their later classification as the old people. The grievance is that they have now been denied every valley [D:213].

D:213

New OrleansLouisiana city central to the company’s lives and publishing work. Giovanni (John) A. Solli, Finnegan, is born there on June 1, 1919, to Giulio Solli and Mary McCracken [A:173]. His sister says the family came from Irish Channel, despite his stories of a Quarter childhood; his only art teachers, she says, were school sisters and drunken painters in Pirates’ Alley [A:175]. His extraordinary dialect combines New Orleans OI sounds, waterfront Irish, Little Italy speech, Cajun French and more peculiar ingredients [A:6]. His familiarity with oyster bars there contributes to his seafood expertise [D:40]. Dotty comes from New Orleans for the St. Louis wedding [A:95]. After it, Finnegan, Henry, Duffey, Dotty and Mary Schaeffer drive south, check into the Jung Hotel, and begin the print-shop project [A:114-116]. The Pelican Press and its magazine occupy the Quarter [A:142]. During a later disordered return, Finnegan experiences his birthplace as a city built like a wheel [A:200]. Still later, he believes he is in New Orleans although everything has become Spanish-speaking, he cannot find his old haunts, and a man tells him the boat to New Orleans has already left [A:269-270]. New Orleans friends send mail that reaches him at Palermo [D:114-115], and Don Barnaby places Madame Le Mourcheor’s Juju Joy Pill manufacture in the city [D:249].

A:173; A:175; A:6; D:40; A:95; A:114-116; A:142; A:200; A:269-270; D:114-115; D:249

New South WalesAustralian state associated with Marie Monaghan’s country childhood, compared with Hans’s Wisconsin childhood as they talk through the night [A:9-10]. Loy Larkin’s letter to John Solli, also signed by Margaret Murphey, is headed Cambeltown, New South Wales, February 11, 1943 [A:27].

A:9-10; A:27

New SplendorCoffee-powder brand poured into the urn at the newly fashionable breakfast place. Duffey has never heard of New Splendor and is uncertain whether he likes it, though he finds many of its new tastes pleasant; it echoes the establishment’s commands to be splendid [MTM B11:316].

MTM B11:316

New TestamentChristian scriptural collection read straight through by Absalom Stein. He calls it important enough to rank with Marx and Freud, but rough-hewn and more primitive than the Old Testament despite the sophisticated world into which Christ was born. He remains interested but full of reservations [A:69-70].

A:69-70

New WorldThe American side of the contrast in Anastasia’s account of mermaids. Her taxonomy allows no New World varieties: even giant Mississippi catfish, despite human-looking eyes, fall short of mermaids. She also denies true mermaids in the Atlantic, distinguishing them from northern sea-cows [D:35].

D:35

New Year'sHoliday spent by the Brunhilde at Port of Spain, where the ship stays eight or nine days over Christmas and New Year’s. Finnegan stops drinking on New Year’s and lasts until January 26 at Freetown, Sierra Leone, almost completing his first dry January [D:85].

D:85

New Year's EveThe night the soldiers truck into Manila after supper and begin boarding the homeward ship just after midnight [A:70]. The ensuing identity crisis leaves one of the Dirty Five behind in hospital [A:71-73].

A:70; A:71-73

New YorkCity from which Finnegan flees with the stolen suitcase and Doll Delancy. Doll says she has no friends there, and he puts her at the wheel of an appropriated car headed through the tunnel to New Jersey [D:166-167]. Loy mentions a Duffey’s in New York [A:2]. Finnegan later establishes himself in Manhattan as Gregory van Ghi, lodging at the Waldorf with McGregor, renting a Village studio and an uptown showroom [A:191]. Hans meets James Fitzjames and Trinali Peterson there and rents a three-room apartment with their help [A:225-227].

D:166-167; A:2; A:191; A:225-227

New Young Royal Pop girlsDuffey’s name for the young Pop women, including the hoyden and young countess, who dispute the reality and history of his city. They insist that a real place needs mountains and thunder, and that mountains are recent. Mary Virginia recognizes them as performers in that evening’s Horse Opera, whose advertised spectacle celebrates the destruction of an old human stronghold [MTM B11:333].

MTM B11:333

Niccolo Crotolus (Nick the Rattle, The Sidewinder)Old left-footed professional killer, a large shapeless man whose pocketful of loose objects rattles as he walks [A:278-279]. The narrator offers a possible link between Crotolus, Nick the Rattle, and the Sidewinder; Niccolo instead claims Crotolo is his family name, meaning castanet, inherited from Zingaro dancers and musicians. He compares himself with his namesake the Florentine political thinker and debates ignoring his employer’s repeatedly reversed telegrams because a canceled job pays only half [A:279]. His police contact, whose bribe would also be halved if the job were canceled, encourages him to disregard the latest delay [A:279]. The employer specifies the piccola vendetta, killing the victim while possibly in grace rather than ensuring damnation; Niccolo has become fond of Finnegan and believes him ready [A:280]. Dotty finds Niccolo’s car, slashes its tires, tracks him to the beach, and shoots first [A:281-282]. Gut-shot but still able to fire left-handed, he uses a weapon described as greater than a carbine and less than a rifle. In three exchanges Dotty fires three shots and Niccolo fires six, hitting both Finnegan and Dotty each time; none of the nine shots misses [A:282]. The last page closes the narrative without establishing Niccolo’s death or resolving the three wounded characters’ fates [A:283].

A:278-279; A:279; A:280; A:281-282; A:282; A:283

Nick the RattleNickname of Niccolo Crotolus, associated with the loose objects rattling in his pockets and his lumbering movements. The narrator also connects the name with the Sidewinder; Niccolo gives a different explanation of his family name [A:278-279]. See Niccolo Crotolus.

A:278-279

NicoletteHeroine evoked in Hans’s reflection on Marie Monaghan’s green eyes. He remembers a fragment about Nicolette’s eyes of vair and yellow hair, insists vair was green, and rejects scholars’ gray interpretation [A:24]. The name and eye description recall the medieval romance Aucassin and Nicolette; the color is Hans’s reading, not an uncontested translation.

A:24

Nie dobrzePolish reply glossed in the dialogue as “not real well.” The amnesiac soldier says it when officers test whether his knowledge of Polish will identify him; he explains that all the Dirty Five enjoyed exchanging dialects [A:73].

A:73

Nietzsche, Friedrich (1844--1900)German philosopher and cultural critic (1844-1900), known for challenges to inherited religion and morality, the will to power, the Übermensch, and the death of God. His major works include Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883-1885) and Beyond Good and Evil (1886); his thought influenced existentialist and postmodern philosophy. In the novel, Nietzsche is among the sources mixed into the inflammatory journal The Answer, whose blend of insight and foolishness alarms Duffey [MTM B4:114].

MTM B4:114

Night CharleyOne of the first three clandestine Crock magazines Casey starts during his college years, 1938-1942, alongside Nattkarlet and Nocnik [A:167]. Its later circulated form is called definitely salacious, a departure from Casey’s own humor and intentions [A:168].

A:167; A:168

Night club comedyOne of the lively arts the narration says are deliberately degraded after the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207]. In the later My Heart Leaps Up world, Otto Glotglutz is called a sick night-club comedian; Hiram III’s retort reduces him to tears and scandalizes the audience [MB:564].

MTM B6:207; MB:564

Night thoughtsFearful nocturnal thoughts in Finnegan’s sonnet on the Naxos mountain, alongside a Hawk on the sea and Oreads on the summit. Anastasia is still beside him: when he asks for pencil and paper to preserve the sonnet, she tells him to sleep [D:134]. The expression also recalls Edward Young’s The Complaint: or, Night-Thoughts on Life, Death, & Immortality, published in parts in 1742-1745, though a deliberate allusion is not explicit.

D:134

Night Watch, TheRembrandt’s 1642 painting of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq’s militia company. In Finnegan’s story about painting a devil, Van Ghi says the same minor demonic figure recurs in the background of The Night Watch and other works. This is the alleged old repeater whose painted likeness the Jesuit orders burned [D:255].

D:255

Nights, the (Arabian Nights)The Thousand and One Nights, or Alf Laylah wa-Laylah, a developing collection of tales drawing on Middle Eastern and Asian storytelling traditions and recorded in Arabic during the Middle Ages. The introduction to The Devil Is Dead says old Burton urged his subscribers to keep their copies locked away, comparing the present book’s hazards with those literary precipices [D:7]. During Finnegan’s winning week at the Little Oyster, Anastasia is described as a girl straight out of the Arabian Nights [D:20].

D:7; D:20

Nimrod Flesh PlantRare vegetation growing abundantly on Zabotski Flats. The apparently grass-eating lions and leopards are actually grazing on the Nimrod Flesh Plant [MTM B12:362].

MTM B12:362

Nine Dollar DogGame Margaret Stone uses as an analogy when Charlotte Garfield asks whether she can beat the rap at the end. Margaret says its outcome is fixed nine plays before the finish, with no subsequent chance to change it and no warning that those last plays have begun. Charlotte nevertheless chose the game [MTM B7:217].

MTM B7:217

Nine Man Free-Style Midget Wrestler MeleeWrestling event at the old Decatur Street Arena in New Orleans in which Finnegan recalls seeing Herman Hercules. Hercules says it was before he became champion [MB:585].

MB:585

Nine Mile DepthNamed ocean depth in which the Argo Masters deliberately hide the Sword and Scabbard of Saint Sécaire. They first weld sword and sheath together with molten fillers, bury them a hundred meters into mud and lime ooze, and charge the sea’s creatures to leave them lost. After four hundred years, Cyril and Cyrus Dimbeau recover them during bathysphere coring, contrary to the Masters’ wishes: the object is an anti-prize and danger to the world [MTM B13:422].

MTM B13:422

NinevehAncient Assyrian city, a substantial settlement by about 3000 BC and sacked in 612 BC. In Jonah 3 its people repent after Jonah’s warning. Seaworthy invokes that repentance to condemn the Texas beer served to him and Finnegan, saying that Nineveh did penance for less [D:12].

D:12

Nisi esses sollicitusUnfinished Latin clause, roughly “if you were not anxious,” written in Finnegan’s looping left-handed script on a pennant of Henry’s dream ship Navicula Petri. The Latin is scratched out and replaced in English by “If you can’t be careful, be good” [A:44].

A:44

NoahBiblical builder of the ark, obedient to God’s command to preserve his household and animal life through the Flood, and recipient of the subsequent covenant. Casey tells Hinnegan that knowledge of the Milesians before the Flood would require Noah to have taken two Irishmen aboard along with the other animals [A:164]. In Not to Mention Camels, Noah Zontik, called the Umbrella, is Pilgrim Dusmano’s professional protector, a good but crafty man whose work includes shielding the guilty and thwarting their pursuers. God commissions him as Pilgrim’s powerful friend and surety, responsible for following even if Pilgrim goes to hell; Noah regards Pilgrim as his millstone and finds the assignment strangely familiar. He comes to love his difficult charge, suspecting that someone has ordered even that love (Not to Mention Camels, PDF pp. 36-38). He confronts Pilgrim about Hut’s murder (Not to Mention Camels, PDF pp. 48-49). A Lord Temporal and Spiritual, he nevertheless joins Pilgrim’s cult while regarding Pilgrim as utterly wrong and the enterprise as madness. He believes his commission predates the world; he protects Evenhand as well, seeking to save both men’s lives and souls, and vows to follow when Pilgrim says that both protections must fail (Not to Mention Camels, PDF pp. 100-103). In the novel’s discussions of derivative worlds, Noah initially regards Pilgrim as a projection of one shallow person; he later revises this to many people and doubts Pilgrim’s account of other worlds, while remaining committed to his commission (Not to Mention Camels, PDF pp. 31-32) (Not to Mention Camels, PDF pp. 122-123). He challenges the militia’s warrant when they come for Pilgrim, and is taken with the others (Not to Mention Camels, PDF pp. 134-136). After Pilgrim is torn apart by horses, Noah volunteers to follow his charge and is killed in the same fashion (Not to Mention Camels, PDF pp. 139-141). The later offer of a powerful friend beyond death belongs to another protector, Og Scath, addressing Polder Dossman, rather than to Noah addressing Pilgrim (Not to Mention Camels, PDF pp. 244-245).

A:164

NocnikPolish for “chamber pot”; one of the first three Crocks, with Nattkarlet and Night Charley, begun during Casey’s college years, 1938-1942. These are clandestine student magazines; the narrator distinguishes Casey’s high country humor from the later publications’ obscenity [A:167-168].

A:167-168

Nolan, FisherTheatrical member of Duffey’s Chicago circle, listed together with the other Nolan among the theatrical people [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

Nolan, JohnTheatrical member of Duffey’s Chicago circle, listed together with the other Nolan among the theatrical people [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

Non-peopleCategory Papa Devil, the impersonating Noonan, applies to himself, Anastasia and Finnegan. When Finnegan objects that people do not literally have ghostly doubles, Papa suggests that non-people may, and includes all three of them. He connects Dopey’s duality with Finnegan to their strange blood, while admitting uncertainty about its closeness [D:120-121].

D:120-121

Non-RomaniesThe Gorgios, described as the disorganized part of the world outside the Dirty Five [A:73].

A:73

NookonosUnexplained term in the demiurge Teilhard’s blessing of the Unfaithful Assembled. It occurs with peduncle, neo-anthropocentrism and corpusculization in a scene where Teilhard, flanked by McLuhan and McGonigal, appears transfigured on the altar and the congregation proposes three tents [GD:497].

GD:497

Noon-day devilsDevils encountered during Finnegan’s sickness and delirium in the Texas chaparral, especially after his Southern Comfort and Old Crow have run out. Speaking a little Latin and much Greek, they tempt him with stones and a cactus kingdom; he says he cannot change the stones and already possesses the kingdom for as long as he wishes [A:204-205].

A:204-205

Noonan, Gregory McColum PapadiabolousSee Papadiabolous (II) (Gregory McColum Papadiabolous, Papadiabolous II, Papa Devil, Papa D, Noonan). Gregory McColum is the Irish cop Noonan who takes his murdered brother’s place [D:285-289].

D:285-289

Noonan, Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch PapadiabolousSee Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch. This is the elder Ifreann, father of Papadiabolous I and II, whose grave is marked I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch [D:277-281] [D:285-288].

D:277-281; D:285-288

Noonan, KatieIrish governess employed by the Gregory family in Poland, mother of the elder Ifreann and thus grandmother of the two Papadiabolous brothers. X calls her a good, placid girl, says she left the household months before the birth and returned weeks afterward, and recounts the claim that the Devil fathered her child. Her heart breaks over her son’s monstrosity [D:278-280]. X says she used Ifreann affectionately and glosses it as Devil [D:279]. Catherine Dembinska gives a different naming account in The Flame Is Green: Katie insists that the Devil be recorded as father on the certificate for her son, born in a hayfield between Skawine and Krakow in 1830. Asked for a name, she exclaims “Och Ifreann,” glossed there as “Aw hell!”, and the words become his name. Catherine maintains that he has no Polish blood and recalls childhood testimony about his murders. Dana declines certainty about Ifreann’s half-Irish ancestry and jokes that Catherine’s telling sounds Irish (The Flame Is Green, PDF pp. 210-211).

D:278-280; D:279

NoosphereThe sphere of collective human thought. In Teilhard de Chardin’s account, its formation links increasing complexity with heightened consciousness and a collective human organism, within a spiritual understanding of evolution and its ultimate convergence. The Majesty’s spoken address uses noosphere and socialization as fashionable garnish. Its targets are Pharisees, Legalists, Rigidists, members of the Curia and hierarchies; the word noosphere is not itself listed as a target [MTM B8:243].

MTM B8:243

Norman ShipmanBookish or literary member of Duffey’s Chicago circle [MTM B3:98].

MTM B3:98

NorseOne of the five men collectively called the Swedes is Norse; the others are a Dane, an Icelander, a German and a man from Orkney, so none is Swedish [D:217]. In Anastasia’s account of sea-women, the Norse netted blond, mammalian, vertically tailed sea-cows in the tenth century [D:35]. An unnamed Norse hero’s longing for towering oceans requiring constant uphill sailing supplies a comparison for Finnegan’s dissatisfaction [D:18].

D:217; D:35; D:18

NorthDirection recurring in Finnegan’s journeys and the company’s comparisons. Finnegan is usually already in the North when autumn brings the urge to migrate [D:10], and in an early wandering walks north through meadows with Howland [A:178]. Australian air and sunset are contrasted with those of the North [A:30]; Hans invokes differing motion north and south of the equator in his own explanation [A:4]. Casey notes that Venice lies farther north than Vladivostock [A:163]. The buffalo herd has drifted north for summer, leaving old bulls behind [A:206]; Hans’s St. Gallen is placed in Wisconsin’s Northern Wilderness [A:207]. The Paradise of the later voyage is assigned latitude sixteen degrees north [D:234].

D:10; A:178; A:30; A:4; A:163; A:206; A:207; D:234

North African littoralNorth African coastal route followed by the Brunhilde after Tangier, then onward to Sicily and Greece [D:114]. Earlier, after Lanzarote in the Canaries, the ship calls at Ifni, Agadir, Magadar, Safti, Mazagan, Casablanca and Rabat before reaching Tangier [D:101].

D:114; D:101

North American BursarDuffey’s claimed office in the Argo Balloon Club, according to Bagby’s account: he collects three thousand dollars each from twenty-three sportsmen, pays six thousand for an old balloon, and is left holding the remaining funds because the supposed Geneva headquarters has never existed [MTM B2:63].

MTM B2:63

North CoastPoorest region of the independent nation of San Simeon, a rough coast of rocks, dry swamps and dangerous shoals near the Campeche Banks [MB:559]. There the forbidden Sea Bell of Saint Peter the Martyr sounds, summoning the Hidden Church; difficult terrain and water make the gathering hard for the police to stop [MB:560].

MB:559; MB:560

Northern PlatoonPlatoon said to have been swallowed by quicksand in the Chosky Bottoms, one of the area’s old stories. The conversation does not place Finnegan in that unit or identify its war [D:274].

D:274

Northern ValkyrieFinnegan’s epithet for Nada Patkaniowska, the tall, golden-haired, three-hundred-pound dowager who carries him on her shoulder. He calls her Brynhilde in rounded, spherical form, remembers voyaging on her when she was the Ship, and wonders whether she is also the Argo [A:192-193].

A:192-193

NorthwesternOne of the seven colleges Casey attends between autumn 1938 and spring 1942; Notre Dame is another institution in the list. He starts one or more of the Crocks at each of the seven [A:167-168].

A:167-168

Norwegian Seamen's ClubOne of the special clubs on the upper floors of the Plaza building visited by Finnegan and his companions in Sydney [A:3].

A:3

Nose, Finnegan'sFinnegan’s conspicuous banana nose appears from his first look in the bar mirror and recurs in the prewar Dotty scene [A:1] [A:174]. Other descriptions call it a bugle nose [A:6] [D:23-24]; its prominence helps support his oversized digger hat [A:13]. Stein’s ears are compared with it [A:29]. Vincent introduces the nose as Finnegan when meeting Nauti [A:64]. Dotty uses banana-nosed brat and little banana-nose [A:93] [A:95], while the narrator calls him a banana-nosed river-rat [A:169].
