Finnegan accuses his dead father of giving him the nose despite lacking one like it himself [A:245], and Hilton uses bugle-nose [A:250]. Dopey’s letter identifies him as the bugle-nosed dago with the Irish moniker [D:51]. Finnegan tells Anastasia his gargoyle nose is real and will not come off [D:39]. Doll reports a pursuer’s description of him as a hooked-nosed ape [D:173]. X says he is saved by a nose when kidnappers expecting Finnegan’s unmistakable feature are about to seize another man with an even bigger nose [D:177-178]. A railroad man later breaks it in a fight [D:192].

A:1; A:174; A:6; D:23-24; A:13; A:29; A:64; A:93; A:95; A:169; A:245; A:250; D:51; D:39; D:173; D:177-178; D:192

Nostradamus (Michel de Nostredame) (1503--1566)Michel de Nostredame, French physician and astrologer, 1503-1566, known for the enigmatic quatrains of Les Prophéties, first published in 1555. In “The Great Day,” Duffey interprets the tower clock whose hands have been sawn off as a murky Nostradamus prediction of the turning-over, though he resists accepting that the Great Thing has arrived [GD:483]. More Than Melchisedech concludes by attributing to Nostradamus a prediction made 430 years earlier that fits Pope Finnegan: the Pope of Bells and Bay, with a Green Bay Tree, staff, paint-box, rose and conspicuous holy nose. This is the narrative’s attribution, not an authenticated historical quatrain [MB:598-599].

GD:483; MB:598-599

Nostrodomo-type propheciesProphecies Mr. X exchanges with Jesuit experts: he hears theirs and returns some of his own. The narrator’s form Nostrodomo-type appears to evoke Nostradamus [A:137].

A:137

Notary PublicThe office Papa Devil says he is seeking ashore on the Mexican side. Finnegan recognizes that he needs more than a notary and supplies un falsario, a forger; Papa and Manuel then dismiss Finnegan and the two girls so they can conduct the business [D:57].

D:57

Noted with InterestHeading Gabby uses on the bulletin board for a clipping asserting that people with large noses are passionate. His own prominent nose makes the interest personal [A:127].

A:127

Nothing peopleCyrus Roundhead’s name for the people cleared from a building during the Royal Pop Historians’ murderous expedition. He claims both people and building are unreal, and threatens Mary Virginia with replacement among the victims if she will not finish them. Their resistance makes her question the alleged lack of reality and the destruction of people whose only fault seems to be unimportance [MTM B11:337-338].

MTM B11:337-338

Notre Dame (1)One of the seven colleges Casey attends between autumn 1938 and spring 1942. He begins one or more of the Crocks at each college [A:167-168].

A:167-168

Notre Dame (2)Paris cathedral whose principal medieval construction extended from 1163 to 1345. Van Ghi says that the old repeater devil represented in Finnegan’s painting also appears on Notre Dame in stone, among many appearances in artworks [D:255].

D:255

NovemberMonth in which the Brunhilde sails, on Friday November 7 in an unspecified year [D:27]. The narrator later notes that Finnegan has associated closely with Anastasia since early November, although his Romaic is still insufficient for confession [D:118].

D:27; D:118

Nueve y unoSpanish for “nine and one.” Finnegan answers Elena’s list of possible troubles with this phrase, expanding it as nine yesses and a no: he accepts the troubles but says he drinks because drinking is good, and excessively because of his own evil streak [A:274].

A:274

NumbersBiblical book named as the source of the chapter-seventeen epigraph in The Devil Is Dead. The excerpt brings together the giants descended from Enac, the people’s fear, and the assurance that their enemies can be overcome [D:258].

D:258

Nursery Plant catalogSource of the extravagant adjectives applied to Dotty, including floriferous, succulent, hardy and disease-resistant. Even the plant catalogue’s vocabulary, the narrator says, cannot adequately describe her [MTM B7:213].

MTM B7:213

O quam beata Civitas!“O how blessed a city!” Latin exclamation in Finnegan’s “Antipodal Ode to Loy Larkin,” following his description of Loy’s pinkish hair as a tipsy crown lending grace to Sydney Town [A:32].

A:32

O'Boyle, Crystal (the untraditional glass goblet lady)Artist called the untraditional glass goblet lady, one of the artists whose work Duffey sells as part of the company’s project of rebuilding the world through art [MTM B6:198-199].

MTM B6:198-199

O'Brien, FrancisOne of Duffey’s ladies who comes to his Rounders’ Club in St. Louis and kisses him goodbye on his farewell evening. His departure is announced as a seven-year assignment [MTM B2:69-70].

MTM B2:69-70

O'Brien, Gilberto Levine yGilberto Levine y O’Brien of Rio, the double or shadow of Carlos Cardinal Artemis of Santa Cruz [MB:579]. He sails toward Mooring-Stone aboard the Argo with Count Finnegan and Herman Hercules after their primaries have died [MB:589-590]. Finnegan asks to inspect the marks Gilberto made to identify his skin. Gilberto fears that their nearly identical appearance may conceal forgery, yet refuses inspection and prefers to leave the matter doubtful [MB:590-591]. Artemis had been flayed, and the narrative explicitly leaves uncertain which skin belonged to which man. Finnegan’s secret painting on the inside of the Cardinal’s skin could now be with Gilberto or on John Mogul’s trophy [MB:591].

MB:579; MB:589-590; MB:590-591; MB:591

O'Brien's Polynesian Palace (bar)Waterfront establishment in Duffey’s catalogue of remembered places. Eva seems to follow his thoughts, then asks about buying Kate’s Neanderthal Bar [MTM B13:407].

MTM B13:407

O'Connel, MilesAttributed author of Handbook of Treasons, quoted on the devils of the word-mills as a spiritual army of evil in high stations, sometimes within the Church itself [MTM B5:175-176].

MTM B5:175-176

O'Conner, GabriellaYoung grade-school girl, one of Duffey’s ladies who comes to the Rounders’ Club in St. Louis and kisses him goodbye during his farewell evening [MTM B2:70].

MTM B2:70

O'Dwyer, EdithSchoolgirl acquaintance of Duffey, one of four girls joining him, Charley Murray, Sebastian and Rattigan at the formal dance. Lily Koch leads all eight to the soundproof attic billiard room, where they eat, play pool and dance informally. Edith talks with Duffey while Lily teases that he is really her boy [MTM B1:32-33].

MTM B1:32-33

O'GniveName credited beneath the epigraph about being strangers at home and exiles in Erin, introducing Chapter Two, section 9 of Archipelago [A:55].

A:55

O'Higgins, ElenaJournalist in Duffey’s North Chicago literary circle during its golden age of 1925-1935 [MTM B3:98]. She proposes a feature on Giulio for the Chicago Herald and Examiner [MTM B3:106]. Present when Morris Poor challenges Duffey’s powers, she calls a photographer for the mule demonstration [MTM B4:128] [MTM B4:130]. Her November 14 report is modest and attempts factual description: witnesses agree the mule traveled thirty feet through the air, though their explanations differ. The photograph accompanying her piece shows the airborne mule without giant hands [MTM B4:132]. She later attends the party at Randal’s where Duffey projects Casey’s grotesque head on television [MTM B12:380-381] [MTM B12:383]. In her surviving commentary on Casey, she condemns his Crock advertisement offering consecrated hosts for experiments, describes the fragment of sacred organ music she salvaged before he burned the larger work, and deplores his replacement scoring for kazoo, peewee guitar and musical saw [PG:524-525].

MTM B3:98; MTM B3:106; MTM B4:128; MTM B4:130; MTM B4:132; MTM B12:380-381; MTM B12:383; PG:524-525

O'Higgins, JanuariusBookish or literary member of Duffey’s Chicago golden-age circle [MTM B3:98]. Josephine McSorely’s Underground Eagle report places him at the Casey Machine discussion: he calls Casey a hypocrite and predicts he will buy a machine through a middleman despite his disavowals. Casey’s curse and Evelyn Apostolo’s embrace of hell follow Januarius’s challenge [CM:507]. The account’s narrator claims to possess the only remembered copy of that newspaper issue and subsequently names Januarius among the opportunistic promoters who helped develop the machine’s market [CM:507-508].

MTM B3:98; CM:507; CM:507-508

O'Hoolihan, Hallohan J.Papa Piccone’s stock comic impersonation of Patrick Stranahan at the Star and Garter. Patrick imitates Piccone with hands, voice and motion, but does not know that Piccone’s reciprocal imitation has put him onstage for years as Hallohan J. O’Hoolihan. When Show Boat calls Patrick by that name, he understands only half the joke [A:104].

A:104

Oatmeal, John BentlyPotter named among the artists whose work Duffey sells during the New Orleans rebuilding project. The narrator says the Renaissance of Pottery began with him, and includes these artists’ ideas among contributions to the company’s Rebuilding Thesis [MTM B6:198-199].

MTM B6:198-199

Octavian, Cecil (of England)English double or shadow-man of Paul Cardinal Brokenbolt of Freemantle, Australia [MB:579]. After his primary’s death, he travels along the Mexican coast in a tramp steamer with Niku Kazuko and Daniel Jean Boulle; they pose as archaeologists to elude killers and acquire the company of the stone Pyramid Lord [MB:592-594]. He is among the thirteen assembled in the underground Room of the Conclave at Mooring-Rock for the conclave that elects Finnegan the First [MB:596-597].

MB:579; MB:592-594; MB:596-597

Octopus Joe's (bar)Waterfront establishment in Duffey’s catalogue of remembered places. Eva seems to follow his thoughts, then asks about buying Kate’s Neanderthal Bar [MTM B13:407].

MTM B13:407

Oh Boy birdUnidentified jungle bird whose call sounds like Donald Duck saying “Oh Boy.” It is heard as Casey and Henry descend to the bivouac after swimming; the narrator says they never learned its proper name [A:44].

A:44

OI soundsSounds the narrator says occur more often in some New Orleans blocks than in Brooklyn. They are one ingredient in Finnegan’s extraordinary composite dialect, together with waterfront Irish, Little Italy speech, Cajun French, mud-cat language and an element peculiar to himself. His voice sounds almost magical at a distance but grotesque when understood [A:6].

A:6

Old American Blood and ThunderAmerican adventure books remaining in the looted library at Harlow House, as described by Gautier the goat-man: Old Wild West, Train Robber, Buffalo Hunter, Indian Scalper, Bank Robber and Brigand, the “blue-jowled romances” he loves [A:198]. He reads these silently after the goats are asleep; the French books are the ones he reads aloud to them on winter nights [A:199].

A:198; A:199

Old ClootieFamiliar name Duffey uses for his adversary, calling the Majesty Clootie during the latter’s address [MTM B8:243]. In the closed place associated with the Sixth Contingency, the adversary first claims to be the Devil’s agent, then reveals himself as the Majesty. Duffey’s use of Clootie disconcerts him because the name suits a minor devil, not His Majesty. The passage nevertheless leaves open whether this is the Devil himself or a lesser devil using the claim as a tactic [MTM B10:302-304].

MTM B8:243; MTM B10:302-304

Old CountryFrance, the homeland of Gautier the goat-man, who came from southern France in 1908 with six goats [A:196]. His surviving French books include Balzac’s Contes Drolatiques, Stendhal, Tartarin of Tarascon, Gil Blas and The Count of Monte Cristo. He reads them aloud to the goats on winter nights, recalling the speech of their shared Old Country [A:198-199].

A:196; A:198-199

Old CrowBrand of bourbon whiskey drunk by Finnegan. An inch remains in his bottle when he wakes in a foul dump after his “shipwreck” [A:177]. He carries more, with Southern Comfort and other liquors, in his shoulder-bag while walking in Texas [A:202]. The noon-day devils trouble him particularly after the Southern Comfort and Old Crow are gone [A:205].

A:177; A:202; A:205

Old Dogs Lying in the SunPomodorus’s epigram, quoted by Newton Prescott: “Old dogs, lying in the sun, are one form of history.” Prescott places it beside residual magnetism and the idea that the earth retains impressions of its history [CM:510].

CM:510

Old FrenchLanguage in which Gautier says the pun about cutting capers works better. Finnegan’s joke combines dancing or tricks with castrating a goat; Gautier then discusses Italian capra and capro and Spanish goat-related words [A:199].

A:199

Old Kind of PeoplePeople whom the Royal Pop Historians regard as obsolete. Margaret Stone reports their term “People of the Old Kind” and their claim that such people will not understand Pop History [MTM B11:308]. The townspeople’s description of Zabotski as almost the last of his kind appears just before this [MTM B11:307].

MTM B11:308; MTM B11:307

Old Man of the SeaFigure from the Sindbad adventures whom Finnegan intends William Gerecke to represent in the Brunhilde murals, because Gerecke looks like an incubus [D:62].

D:62

Old Original Juju Joy PillsNew Orleans pills described in Don Barnaby’s extravagant account of a cure for a terrible hangover. His general recipe is sawdust, honey and cat urine; Madame Le Mourcheor’s special version uses Arabian frankincense wood, honey from bees near Megapolis in Arcady, and a black cat with glanders. He attributes the result to simpler, purer ingredients [D:248-249]. One pill makes an interior garden expand to contain the world and other worlds. He marries a wife whose appearance changes and acquires children whose names, appearances and number vary while their identities persist [D:250]. Sleep transports him between places and periods, and he later encounters Sour John in this boundless garden. John rejects the offered pill, says only fifteen minutes have passed, and returns him to his bunk under a strap until sailing [D:251-252]. Three years later Barnaby has not returned to his family, though he vows to do so and bring back the secrets, alive or dead [D:252].

D:248-249; D:250; D:251-252; D:252

Old Pop PotterMan cited by Finnegan in the conversation about Chosky Bottoms. His saying places the spook country in the next valley or among the people next door, illustrating how neighbors become the subjects of ghost stories [D:274].

D:274

Old Stone ShipWaterfront establishment run by Eva Ewaglouwshkoul’s father in her ancient world. After forty thousand years in the ice, Eva asks Duffey to take her to Biloxi, where she plans to acquire a saloon or hotel and wait for a seaman of her own blood. Her father’s Old Stone Ship supplies a precedent for that plan; the text does not place his establishment in Biloxi [MTM B13:401].

MTM B13:401

Old TestamentBiblical setting Cleo Mahoney assigns to the Melchisedech of her play, a role she asks Duffey to take. She identifies the character as “Melchisedech of the Old Testament” while insisting that Duffey is particularly suited to portray him [MTM B9:265].

MTM B9:265

Old Wooden ShipTavern in Galveston, Texas, an unpainted, pungent building whose four stories, numerous doors, loose shutters and swaying creak make it resemble a ship. Lazarus Reilly’s company includes some fifty regulars, among whom Finnegan and Le Marin wait while murderers lurk outside [D:214-216]. Francis Paradise’s account helps draw Le Marin toward the Paradise voyage [D:233]. Much later, following Father Brown’s advice to use an English bulldog against the Man of Mystery, Melchisedech recruits Gunboat Smith, the tavern’s Bulldog-in-Residence, for the Argo [MTM B13:458].

D:214-216; D:233; MTM B13:458

Olga SanchezEmployee of Duffey’s Rounders’ Club in St. Louis, noted for her “torchy shoulders” [MTM B2:49]. On first hearing “The King Shall Ride,” immediately Duffey’s favorite tune, she carries him on her shoulders; afterward either Olga or Lucille repeats the celebration [MTM B2:52]. At his farewell Olga carries him through the rooms and into the street [MTM B2:70]. When he returns after the hidden years, she welcomes him lovingly; she has married the club’s beautiful Mexican high chef [MTM B2:74]. Duffey still counts her among the women he loves [MTM B4:110], and she caresses him when the Animations arrive at Rounders’ [MTM B5:159].

MTM B2:49; MTM B2:52; MTM B2:70; MTM B2:74; MTM B4:110; MTM B5:159

Oliver Oscar OmygoshBurlesque figure Papa Piccone claims to have created for the Star and Garter. Piccone calls him a hopeless botch: a wrong-colored putty nose, swollen red eyes, an unshapely real rump, size fifteen shoes, falls and a stuttering “O-O-O.” A man identifying himself with the character complains backstage; the supposed putty nose bleeds when Piccone strikes it [MTM B5:167-168]. Piccone says the 1939 St. Louis telephone book lists Oscar Oliver Omygosh. Bascom Bagby, rather than Piccone, supplies the nearby O-O-O What Fun Novelty Store and describes the man’s real glandular troubles, dizzy spells, pain, melancholy, stumbling and tears. Bagby denies that Piccone made him; Piccone insists that he did, accidentally [MTM B5:168].

MTM B5:167-168; MTM B5:168

Ongoing Quest AdventureCleo Mahoney’s interpretation of the fourth contingency: repeated successful quests become addictive. Their goodness acquires something poisonous through endless success, provoking revenge and the death of some questers. Momentum keeps them from admitting death even when shown their bones and ashes; they retreat a little into the past and live again, leaving the problem unsolved [MTM B10:295]. Cleo calls the pursuit of excellence a broken record, but Rebeka Stein enthusiastically disagrees [MTM B10:296].

MTM B10:295; MTM B10:296

OnreeCajun pronunciation of Henri, distinguished from the English pronunciation of Henry, in the discussion of Henri Salvatore’s name [MTM B6:195].

MTM B6:195

Orba, St. Angela (Orphanage)Chicago orphanage named by Charlotte Garfield during Duffey’s psychosomatic trance. She says two sisters there know who she is, while the others mistake her for a little girl; she wants commitment papers and love, and proposes that Duffey adopt her. She subsequently insists that the experience was a trance rather than a dream [MTM B3:86].

MTM B3:86

OreibatesOne of the three Oreads Finnegan meets in his dreams on the mountain at Naxos, with Anemotrephes and Akroreia. They call Anastasia their sister. Finnegan sees the mark of the polypus on Oreibates’s wrist, though the girls deny having such marks [D:137]. When he recognizes their kinship with the teras, Oreibates laments their condition and says they try to climb toward the light. The three push him off the mountain; Anastasia subsequently confirms their kinship with herself and Finnegan [D:139].

D:137; D:139

Original Argo crew (aka Animated Marvels)Earlier heading called this the original crew, contrary to Teresa’s explicit statement that it was not the first. See Argo Company (Teresa's account).
OrpheusThracian singer and Argonaut identified with John G. Hans in the Argo books [A:38] [A:89] [A:207]. Trinali’s poem asks whether Hans has forgotten that identity [A:227]. Hans himself writes to Marie that he was Orpheus and is traveling again on the Argo [MTM B6:186]. Teresa identifies Hans as Orpheus and later Faust, and Marie as Eurydice, while giving Eurydice a deliberately different journey to Australia [MTM B7:234]. In Apollonius’s Argonautica, Book 1, Orpheus is Calliope’s son, whose music moves trees and rocks; Jason accepts him on Cheiron’s advice. His cosmogonic song settles a quarrel, his lyre sets the departing rowers’ rhythm, and he sings to Artemis. He directs the visit for secret initiation on Electra’s island and, after Cyzicus’s death, orders an armed dance whose noise covers the people’s lament during the rites of Rhea. In Book 2 his lyre accompanies the celebration of Polydeuces after the Bebrycian fighting; he directs worship of Apollo at dawn and dedicates a lyre at Sthenelus’s tomb. In Book 4 his playing overcomes the Sirens, although Butes leaps into the sea and requires Aphrodite’s rescue. He provides wedding music for Jason and Medea, appeals to the Libyan nymphs for water, and recommends the propitiatory offering of Apollo’s tripod. In Ovid’s Metamorphoses, Books 10-11, his attempt to bring Eurydice back from the dead fails when he looks behind him. Maenads later kill him; his severed head and lyre continue their lament as they travel down the Hebrus to Lesbos. His shade is reunited with Eurydice.

A:38; A:89; A:207; A:227; MTM B6:186; MTM B7:234

OrthodoxerA member of the party that defends the established scientific chronology and account of origins against Zabotski. Armed Orthodoxers accuse him of rejecting their time scale, associating with Fundamentalers, and substituting false history for the accepted account. Their badges proclaim “Darwin or Death,” “Herbert Spencer Forever,” and “Huxley the Bulldog forever!” [MTM B9:286]. Earlier, they burn a “Clear Bright Flame of Science” on Zabotski’s lawn; Duffey’s account associates such burnings with punishments ranging from horse-whipping to hanging, drawing, and quartering [MTM B9:284]. The armed party threatens to shoot Zabotski, who obscures their sight with darkness or clouds and climbs aboard his contraption [MTM B9:286]. Later news reports that Orthodoxer police have killed nineteen unarmed Fundamentalers in a “shootout” [MTM B9:288]. See also Vigilante Orthodoxers.

MTM B9:286; MTM B9:284; MTM B9:288

Ostwald, Howard StoneOne of the Big Stones, Princes of the Ekklesia, at the last Conclave in Babylonia Bagascia. Responding to Efram Gate Gratz’s attack on Peter and his grave, Ostwald says they intended the building to fall when they removed the capstone. He wants every building to fall because buildings divide people [MB:561].

MB:561

Otto I (of the Germanies)Otto I, Holy Roman Emperor, born in 912 and dead in 973. In Henri Salvatore’s longer, unsent letter, Otto quietly bolts the door on the Devil at Aachen in 946; the Devil is then transferred to a firmer prison at the Euxine Chersonese in the Crimea [MTM B5:180].

MTM B5:180

Ouspensky, P.D.Pyotr Demianovich Ouspensky (1878-1947), Russian philosophical and esoteric writer, author of Tertium Organum. The Book Eleven epigraph credits him with questions about the real becoming phenomenal, creation and uncreation [MTM B11:306]. The passage occurs in Tertium Organum, Chapter XXII, within Ouspensky’s quotation of Max Müller; the novel prints the title as Tertium Organus. Duffey later wonders how Ouspensky would account for the grotesque transformation of the world [MTM B11:341]. Jon Nelson’s essay “1974 From the Thunder Colt’s Mouth” argues for extensive Ouspensky influence on Not to Mention Camels and reads the Thunder Colt episode as a parody of Tertium Organum.

MTM B11:306; MTM B11:341

Overlark, CarmodyAuthor to whom The Devil Is Dead attributes the epigraph from Studies in the Imagination. Its speculative account links Neanderthal brains, the unconscious, ghostliness and imaginative power, then extends its back-brain type to Grimaldi, Aurignacian and related early humans [D:270-272]. In Fourth Mansions, Overlark is Special Assistant to the Secretary of State. According to Michael Fountain, the former Charles became Carmody about two years earlier for numerological reasons; he had been a wealthy party contributor and brilliant amateur. Foley notices his resemblance to the historical Khar-ibn-Mod and the ancient mask of Kir-ha-Mod; Bagley treats his archaic ears as a repeater sign. The identity explanations differ: Bagley proposes recurring men, O’Claire a recurring shape of mind, and Oriel a replacement of the former Charles (PDF pp. 4, 23-25, 30-31, 44-46, 64-66, 127-129). The Harvesters prompt Foley’s investigation. Overlark resists their mental attack and can enter dreams about himself (PDF pp. 8-10, 123). Confronting Foley, he claims his group lives repeatedly by choice in a nonaging state, seeks heightened experience, allows no interference and descends from ancient sea-born gods. He calls his tribe the Intelligentsia. Foley considers him mad and rejects a straightforward account of literal reincarnation, suspecting a wraith working through a borrowed human body. Overlark is formidable, direct and cruel, enjoying secrets, fear and his subordinates’ suffering, yet betrays fear himself (PDF pp. 147-160). His slight body has remarkable musculature, fine fishlike skin and strange eyes and complexion. Foley watches him submerge his head and upper body in brackish water for about fifteen minutes; the water and fish display impossible behavior, and he emerges refreshed. Overlark claims a sea origin, admits eating live rats and appears to be testing Foley as a recruit. He threatens confinement on grounds of madness or a fabricated murder charge; Foley is subsequently taken to an institution (PDF pp. 149, 155-161).

D:270-272

P.F.C. Timothy LorriganBoston private first class, one of the three Americans in Don Lewis’s story who disappear on October 1, 1944, on Pulau Petir, called Willy Jones Island. The others are Sergeant Charles Santee of Orange, Texas, and Corporal Robert Casper of Gobey, Tennessee [D:44]. Lorrigan lags behind when the others go to kill a little man apparently taken for a Japanese soldier. Don Lewis slips into the first person while describing this reluctance, then refuses to confirm which soldier he was [D:45]. He later calls the little man Yokipoki, explicitly warning that this probably was not his real name [D:46].

D:44; D:45; D:46

Padre IslandDesolate island off the Texas coast where most of the Brunhilde company go ashore for a beach party and fish fry. Their preceding ports include Freeport, Palacios, Port O’Conner, Aransas Pass and Corpus. They dig a pit, burn mesquite to aromatic coals, and swim in the Gulf [D:34]. Supper includes barbecued and fried pork, boiled and fried shrimp, red snapper and pompano. Papa Devil compounds drinks until Anastasia takes over; DePolis dislikes the beach cooking, while Joe Cross, Anastasia and Finnegan contribute their expertise [D:40]. Don Lewis tells his campfire story afterward [D:43].

D:34; D:40; D:43

PalFriend or companion; an English word borrowed from Romani words for brother or comrade. Casey lists pal among words of Romani origin, but the knife gloss in his sentence belongs to chiv [A:164].

A:164

PalaciosPort visited by the Brunhilde during its coastwise passage through Texas ports, before the company’s Padre Island beach party [D:34].

D:34

Panebianco, Marie CaterinaMarie Caterina Panebianco, mother of Theresa Antoinette Piccone, called Show Boat. Theresa’s father is Gaetano Piccone, proprietor of the Star and Garter [A:94].

A:94

Panther callsOne of the animal calls Giulio made for his son Finnegan during trips to the Cajun swamps. He whittled them from tupelo-gum wood, along with alligator, devil-fish, swamp-boa, hairy-man and white-shark calls. Finnegan recalls never knowing what he might summon from the water or trees [MTM B5:174].

MTM B5:174

Papa (Loy Larkin's Father)Loy Larkin’s father. In her letter from Cambeltown, New South Wales, dated February 11, 1943, Loy says he neglected the garden she planted in November but killed the fatted calf for his returning prodigal daughter the day before [A:27].

A:27

Papa Papadiabolous (Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch Papadiabolous Chortovitch)See Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch. This is the elder Ifreann, father of Papadiabolous I and II, whose grave is marked I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch [D:277-281] [D:285-288].

D:277-281; D:285-288

Papa-DFamiliar shortening of Papa Devil’s name, used by the bargirl when his appearance startles Seaworthy and Finnegan [D:15], and by Finnegan himself as Papa D [D:30]. The man accompanying the Brunhilde is the impersonating Papadiabolous II, Gregory McColum, whom X later identifies as the Irish cop Noonan [D:285] [D:287-289].

D:15; D:30; D:285; D:287-289

Papadiabolous (I) (Gregory McIfreann Papadiabolous, Papadiabolous I)The Asiatic Papadiabolous, Gregory McIfreann, whom X describes as a son of the elder Ifreann and the quasi-twin of Gregory McColum, Papadiabolous II. In X’s account the brothers were conceived together and born on the same night at the turn of the century, in Smyrna and Cork, to different mothers. Gregory McIfreann uses Sanditen, Chrysostom, Protagoras and Hochstruwelpieter-Goltz; both brothers use forms of John and may be called John Gregory [D:285].

X portrays him as a purposeful evil revolutionary with extraordinary physical and diabolical power, trained in the conspiracy. He names Seaworthy, Genof, Wirt, Gerecke, Wedekind, Askadrian, Sanditen and Sorensen among his associates, some reputedly his half-brothers. While the father lives, the son is crown prince [D:285-286]. After the father’s burial in 1930, he heads an unstable regency until Seaworthy is selected to murder him. X reconstructs a shooting during the opening of their father’s grave, while admitting uncertainty about several details [D:288].

Finnegan remembers Seaworthy striking the still-moving body with a shovel, then helping him deepen the old grave and bury the new corpse above earlier remains [D:75-76]. X identifies the grave marked I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch as the father’s [D:277-278]. He says Papadiabolous II takes his murdered brother’s place the following morning, creating Seaworthy’s apparent encounter with a man returned from death [D:288-289].

D:285; D:285-286; D:288; D:75-76; D:277-278; D:288-289

Papadiabolous (II) (Gregory McColum Papadiabolous, Papadiabolous II, Papa Devil, Papa D, Noonan)Gregory McColum Papadiabolous, the Irish quasi-twin, born in Cork at the turn of the century. X says he and the Smyrna-born Gregory McIfreann share their father, the elder Ifreann, but have different mothers and were conceived together and born on the same night. Both use forms of John; II’s other names include Noonan, Flaherty, Christy, Clarenden, Cobbett, Malory, Ingraham and Arbuthnot [D:285]. Identical in build, coloring and skull shape, the brothers differ in their fleshed faces. X calls II comparatively good despite youthful work as gentleman burglar, contrabandist, swindler and forger. Excluded from the family’s revolutionary training, he enters police work at twenty-five and becomes the undercover N, keeping track of his kin [D:286-287]. His extraordinary mimicry and access to police stations around the world serve his hatred of the gang [D:154-155]. After Seaworthy kills I while opening their father’s grave, II assumes his brother’s place the next morning and deceives the associates for months [D:288-289]. His club appearance terrifies Seaworthy and Finnegan [D:15]; Anastasia notices that Papa has become nicer [D:24]. In the impersonation he is a huge, heavy man with a high purplish complexion, expensive purple shirts and a reddish fringe around a bald pate. His red-eyed glare supports his claim to authority aboard the Brunhilde [D:22-23]. He carries the unconscious Finnegan aboard and appears unaffected by seasickness [D:28-29]. At Padre Island he mixes drinks and becomes unusually gay and florid [D:40]; the narrator says he never sleeps [D:51]. He often sights his rifle on distant men and cultivates a reputation as a great shot, though seldom firing [D:54]. He obtains forged papers for Manuel [D:57] [D:59]. Joe Cross suspects him of killing Doppio di Pinne, whose screams end after Papa enters the cabin and whose body cannot be found [D:64]. When Finnegan confronts him about the buried predecessor and the mimicry, Papa evades him and suggests that Dopey may instead have been Finnegan’s double [D:87-89]. He says Don Lewis contacted him at a distance without recognizing the substitution, and describes his own small Hawk boat, Seabach [D:120] [D:122]. Killed on Naxos, he lies shot repeatedly and bludgeoned, with pockets emptied or cut out, an unfamiliar olive shirt shredded, and shoes removed. Finnegan recognizes the face beneath the impersonation [D:146]; his sketch lets X identify Noonan [D:154]. According to X, Seaworthy kills II without recognizing him as the man who has been masquerading as I, and the surviving gang continues to think Papa Devil is alive [D:289].

D:285; D:286-287; D:154-155; D:288-289; D:15; D:24; D:22-23; D:28-29; D:40; D:51; D:54; D:57; D:59; D:64; D:87-89; D:120; D:122; D:146; D:154; D:289

PapapaleologusDonkey accompanying Finnegan and Anastasia on Naxos. The narrator jokingly presents him as a lineal descendant of the last Roman emperors of the East [D:125]. He understands Anastasia Grandmother’s Romaic perfectly and carries the supplies up to her house [D:126]; later he grazes in the narrow glen beneath the pair on the mountain [D:132].

D:125; D:126; D:132

ParadiseThe Earthly Paradise found by Finnegan and his three companions, Charles Le Marin, Don Barnaby and Johnny Duckwalk, at Basse-Terre in the Antilles. The narrator gives its coordinates as 61°44′42″ west and 16° north and distinguishes it from the Heavenly Paradise intended by St. Francis [D:234-236]. Its playful requirements include freedom from frost, breeze and bloom, a weekly ship, French-speaking black people and English-speaking Frenchmen, centuries of history, a Lost Dauphin legend, a volcano named Soufriere, discovery by Columbus, those three friends and a little money [D:237]. Their haven eventually fails through its remaining snakes [D:235]. The grave marked I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch belongs to the elder Ifreann, father of Papadiabolous I and II, whose identity X unfolds there; it is not the grave of a single man identifiable as both father and I [D:277-281] [D:285-288].

D:234-236; D:237; D:235; D:277-281; D:285-288

Paradise BirdsClay birds Duffey makes in a just-before-morning dream as the Boy King or Boy Magician. He gives them the color of living gold, releases them, and sees further brilliant colors appear in flight. Rough men shoot them down; the falling clay lets them claim they were only clay pigeons, always in season. The game warden nevertheless kills the men but angrily warns Duffey against another such chase. Beth reads the dream as doubt about his powers and creations [MTM B2:67].

MTM B2:67

ParaisoMexican coastal stop off which the Brunhilde anchors while Finnegan sketches on deck for the planned Sindbad murals in the barroom [D:59]. The later Unaccountable Corpse episode may occur at Paraiso, Campeche or another stop; the narrator explicitly leaves the location uncertain [D:67].

D:59; D:67

Parakeet (Amoy)Amoy, the talking parakeet in the ward. He calls himself a big and beautiful bird, though the narrator denies both claims. Ward boy Ignatius Ti translates his compressed Tagalog-Parakeet into expansive tales of previous lives, including life as a jewel-stealing red-winged blackbird and as a fish [A:79-81]. A sadistic medico poisons him to watch him suffer; though gravely ill, he clings to life. An official order to kill the stinking bird drives him into the trees by day and back to his friends at night. The narrator calls him possibly the best-balanced inhabitant of the ward: his persecution and unpopularity are real, and he tries to remain cheerful [A:81-82].

A:79-81; A:81-82

Parakeet TagalogCompressed language of Amoy the parakeet, called Tagalog-Parakeet by the narrator. Three or four words commonly expand into many paragraphs in Ignatius Ti’s translations [A:79].

A:79

Parallel LivesOne of the fantasy types, together with Successive Lives, listed by Doctor Saul Rafelson in his notes on Duffey. Rafelson also insists that Duffey can make such fantasies happen, considering several possible explanations for his other persons and selves [MTM B4:146].

MTM B4:146

ParamariboPort from which the Sarcophagus sails in Le Marin’s story. He says Castleman infiltrated it before departure, then replaced crewmen with lookalikes at successive ports; the supposedly untouched cargo was partly stolen [D:244].

D:244

ParisCity Patrick Stranahan includes, with Dublin, London and Rome, among the journeys he thinks a Christian man should make for his soul’s sake [A:110]. X later reports seeing Levi van Wei there and relays his interest in obtaining more Finnegan pieces [MTM B6:201].

A:110; MTM B6:201

ParosAegean island Finnegan includes in his account of the original five-island cluster or Pentanesia [A:35]. After the Naxos massacre, Finnegan and Manuel swim there, the distance being guessed at seven miles. They tow their clothes, shoes and Finnegan’s bag of stones on floats, rest on shore, hide until dawn and check that the Brunhilde has not followed. At breakfast in Paros town they divide their $720 equally. Finnegan’s unexplained roll may have been left by Anastasia. Manuel leaves for Rome to tell the Pope of the evil men [D:151].

A:35; D:151

Parousia HimselfChrist of the Second Coming, the third cargo in a prophecy Teresa quotes from an unnamed latter-day prophetic book. It describes ghostly, bony Melchisedech Duffey and a crew of wraiths carrying Count Finnegan to election and coronation in the Indies, Prince Casimir to his reign as Antichrist near Armageddon, and finally the Parousia Himself on the Argo’s last voyage [MTM B12:388].

MTM B12:388

Party of OneDuffey’s expression for solitary membership, used when Absalom Stein calls himself a neo-Jew and wishes he could find others to form a group [A:131]. Earlier, Casey describes Duffey as the sole member of the Catholic Center Party of America and explicitly calls this a party of one [A:42].

A:131; A:42

Party, thePolitical Party joined by Casey Szymansky, whose imagined role in Fortress Christianity as a persecuted minority helps draw him into it [A:157]. Margaret Stone has also belonged to the Party before joining the Church and the Bark circle [A:143].

A:157; A:143

Pascha nostrum immolatus est ChristusLatin words from 1 Corinthians 5:7, rendered by Duffey as “Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us.” He exclaims the fuller phrase beginning Etenim when he and August Koch place the eighth Christ with the seven others in his Priceless Item Room [MTM B3:103].

MTM B3:103

PassagouleEarlier heading omitted two letters from the place name printed in the poem. See Passamagoule.
PassamagoulePlace printed as Passamagoule in the opening poem of the Finnegan chapter, paired with Castres among the speaker’s imagined destinations [A:171].

A:171

Passion SundayDay identified as March 14 when the Brunhilde reaches Naxos [D:115]. Finnegan seeks his Easter Duty confession from a young Greek Capuchin who speaks Italian [D:118]. After confession and Mass he breakfasts with Anastasia and the impersonating Papa Devil at a breakwater cafe [D:120]. In Teresa Piccone Stranahan’s private letter, Stein’s first Finnegan Visitation occurs on the afternoon of Passion Sunday, 1948, and frightens him as an apparent death visitation [MTM B6:188].

D:115; D:118; D:120; MTM B6:188

Paterson, TrinaliEarlier misspelling of the surname. See Trinali Peterson.
Patkaniowska, NadaMagnificent, hilarious dowager who likes to be escorted by Finnegan in his role as the painter van Ghi. Six feet two inches tall, three hundred pounds and abundantly golden-haired, she replaces her boa-constrictor shoulder-piece with Finnegan seated on her right shoulder in her raised arm [A:192]. Noticing that he has grown fat, Finnegan recalls her heavier breathing after carrying him upstairs. He calls her Brynhilde, the Northern Valkyrie, in forma rotunda et globosa, says he voyaged on her as the Ship and wonders whether she is also the Argo [A:193].

A:192; A:193

PatmosIsland used as a landmark in Anastasia’s mermaid history: she places Christian mermaids in the second century on an unnamed small island between Patmos and Lipsos. Their chapel was dedicated to Our Lady of the Dolphins and, she says, still exists in poor condition [D:34-35].

D:34-35

PatriarchMargaret Stone invokes “the Patriarch” who could not find enough righteous people to avert destruction while explaining her urgent street preaching [A:144]. The allusion is to Abraham’s plea for Sodom in Genesis 18:23-33; Margaret’s version begins with seventy, whereas the biblical negotiation begins with fifty and ends with ten. Separately, Cleo Mahoney calls Duffey the “Patriarch Melchisedech” while explaining the seven contingent futures in her play: he cannot end, yet cannot continue in his accustomed way [MTM B10:293].

A:144; MTM B10:293

PatriciaPatricia Solli, also called Patti and Patrish, sister of Giovanni/Finnegan and Giacomo/Jake, daughter of Giulio Solli and Mary McCracken [A:173-174]. An acrobatic dancer of striking, weirdly comic beauty, she shares Finnegan’s sudden, almost inhumanly lithe movements. She is often with him and asks Dotty about his absences. She also identifies Doppio di Pinne as the same brother in another state [A:174]. Her family recollections contradict his: their father was a poor dockworker, literally antediluvian; Finnegan had spent only two days in Italy between ships and had invented van Ghi. She says she partly raised him, though he remained a stranger to her, and insists that he is incapable of wrongdoing despite appearances [A:174-175].

A:173-174; A:174; A:174-175

PatrickSaint Patrick, one of the saints Henry recognizes aboard the dream ship Navicula Petri, near Thomas, Hildebrand and Adrian the Dutchman [A:44-45]. A fifth-century bishop and missionary from Roman Britain, he is honored as Ireland’s patron and apostle. His Confessio recounts capture at about sixteen, six years of slavery and sheep-tending in Ireland, escape, return to his family and a visionary call to return as a missionary. He describes thousands of baptisms, the ordination of clergy and the growth of Christian and monastic life. His other surviving work, the letter against the soldiers of Coroticus, condemns the killing and enslavement of baptized converts. These writings are early firsthand evidence of Irish Christianity. The commonly given dates 432 for his return and 461 for his death are uncertain; his feast is March 17. Later traditions include the shamrock explanation of the Trinity and the banishment of snakes. Tírechán’s Collectanea lists Magonus and Succetus among four names for him; these should not be treated as a securely documented birth name “Magonus Sucatus.”

A:44-45

Patrick J. StranahanSuccessful St. Louis attorney and former magistrate, husband of Monica and father of Philip, Hugh, Timothy Navisius, Vincent, Norma and Maurine. Archipelago spells Monica’s maiden name Murry; More Than Melchisedech uses Murray [A:94] [MTM B5:161]. Patrick is large, hairy, muscular and paunchy, with a blue-emery-paper face, enormously hairy eyebrows and a rumble even when silent. Fey and discerning, he lives in the Cat Castle and is “Little-Irish Rich,” of the lace-curtain and grand-piano kind [A:102]. He is an excellent easy-chair pistol shot and an old lawyer-friend of Papa Piccone; the two imitate one another, Piccone turning Patrick into the stage character Hallohan J. O’Hoolihan. Patrick calls Show Boat “the Urchin” [A:104]. He expounds his compact philosophy of reading, art, travel, drink and religion in late conversation with Piccone, Father McGuigan and Charley Murry [A:109-110]. He is the father of one of Duffey’s Animated Marvels, Vincent, rather than one of that listed twelve himself [MTM B5:161-162]. Patrick is dead by Duffey’s late visit to the Cat Castle [MTM B12:385].

A:94; MTM B5:161; A:102; A:104; A:109-110; MTM B5:161-162; MTM B12:385

PaulSaint Paul, the first-century apostle whose missionary journeys and letters shaped Christianity’s teaching about salvation, grace and the Church. His birth is uncertain, often estimated near the beginning of the century; ancient traditions place his martyrdom at Rome under Nero, approximately AD 64-68. Finnegan says he never saw an Ocean Island [A:35], and Henry recognizes him with Stephen and the Baptist aboard Navicula Petri [A:44-45]. Finnegan’s comparison of Anastasia to Diana humorously recasts Paul’s opposition to Demetrios as criticism of the silversmith’s oversized, pasty statue heads [D:133]. Book Six quotes Hebrews on Melchisedech under the traditional attribution “Paul. Hebrews.” [MTM B6:185]. Hebrews itself is anonymous, and its Pauline authorship is not accepted by the modern scholarly consensus. The Majesty, boasting of his own gibberish, recalls Paul’s contrary teaching that God is not its god [MTM B8:243].

A:35; A:44-45; D:133; MTM B6:185; MTM B8:243

PausaniasPausanias, the Greek traveler and author of the ten-book Description of Greece, approximately AD 115-180. His account of sites, monuments, local history and religious practices preserves eyewitness evidence of ancient Greece. Hans, wondering about Marie’s green eyes, recalls that the statues were still painted when “Pausanes” saw them and asks what color words he might have used [A:24]. In The Devil Is Dead, Finnegan compares Anastasia’s head to the small Diana Artemis that “Pausanius” saw in the sanctuary of Asclepius at Messene [D:133]. The classical passage is Description of Greece 4.31.10, which lists Artemis Bringer of Light among the sanctuary’s statues; the small size, paint and natural expression belong to Lafferty’s description.

A:24; D:133

PausaniusPausanius and Pausanes are the forms used in the novels for the Greek traveler Pausanias. See Pausanias.
Pearson, ShakesMarie Monaghan’s whiskey-shaking poet uncle in her comic family story to Hans. Shakes enters a chewing-tobacco jingle competition, but repeatedly leaves his unfinished limericks for more pop-skull whiskey. Because he writes on bark with oak-ball juice, squirrels eat each attempt [A:25-26]. Marie says he kills himself, leaving Miriam, after whom she says she is named, a note urging her to do something about the squirrels. When Hans asks why they spared that note, Marie says it frightened them away. His further question about Australian squirrels exposes the story’s deliberate absurdity; she says wallabies would require explanation and cannot read [A:26-27].

A:25-26; A:26-27

PeleusThe Argonaut identity of Kasmir W. Szymansky, Casey [A:39] [PG:535]. In his commentary, Duffey remembers Peleus as a good, brave crewman whose heroism remains largely hidden: called the great hero of Thessaly, yet indecisive and buffeted by accidents. In Duffey’s account he accidentally kills his half-brother Phocus and father-in-law Eurytion and is trapped by Acastus of Iolcus and his wife. The heroism concealed in Peleus appears openly in his son Achilles [PG:534-535].

A:39; PG:535; PG:534-535

PelicanDotty’s proposed name for the New Orleans magazine. Duffey explains its liturgical symbolism through the belief that a pelican feeds its young with its own blood, an image of Christ’s blood, and through its place as Louisiana’s symbol. Finnegan backs Henry’s proposal Bark, settling the choice [A:121]. The Holy Pelican also appears on the ornate door of the Pelican Press, bronzed by Finnegan and so vivid that Duffey wants to throw it a fish [MTM B12:359].

A:121; MTM B12:359

Pelican LandCasey’s mocking designation for the Louisiana home of the Pelican Press in his Crock editorial attacking the newly launched Bark: the new magazine comes “From Pelican Land and off the Pelican Press” [A:128]. The surrounding magazine venture is based in New Orleans [A:142].

A:128; A:142

Pelican PressNew Orleans printing and publishing operation associated with the Bark. Its old, worn fonts allow Dotty to identify the press used for Mr. X’s fabricated clipping about his own death: she says he printed it there and added the reverse before leaving [A:141-142]. The independently financed Investigator is also printed there [A:143]. After Dotty disappears, the people at the press keep expecting her return. Letitia becomes editor, loses some of its paying publication accounts and keeps the Bark afloat with private funds [MTM B8:238-239]. In “The Great Day,” Duffey seeks refuge in the old Quarter building he started with Finnegan and Dotty. Its schedule is the seamen’s paper on Monday, union sheet Tuesday, Sporting News Wednesday, jazz paper Friday, and the Bark Thursday or whenever it appears. Mary Virginia Schaeffer, Salvation Sally and Margaret Stone are there when he arrives [GD:490].

A:141-142; A:143; MTM B8:238-239; GD:490

PenelopeNickname Dotty reports in her letter to Marie. Immediately after complaining that Finnegan has not written, she says the boys call her Penelope and that her own suitors keep her spirits up [A:147-148]. The joke likens her waiting to that of Odysseus’s wife in Homer; Archipelago elsewhere identifies Finnegan with Ulysses [A:39].

A:147-148; A:39

PentanesiaFive-island cluster in Finnegan’s account of the original archipelagos. His Aegean list is Andros, Tinos, Paros and Amargos, with Hans supplying the forgotten Naxos; Finnegan insists that five is the magic number [A:35-36]. Later Ignacio calls the Leewards a group of five little islands. Finnegan says every pentanesia has a rogue island, and Ignacio nominates Barbuda as useless, a judgment Finnegan first questions and then accepts [A:272].

A:35-36; A:272

Pentecost MorningThe original Pentecost as invoked by Margaret Stone to justify the urgency of street preaching. She says it was not easy then and contrasts that first urgency with the complacency of people for whom Christianity came two thousand years earlier [A:144].

A:144

Pentecost SundayDay Margaret Stone names for her own recent Pentecost: it came to her one year before the conversation in which she explains her urgent street preaching [A:144]. The preceding account describes her leaving the Party and joining the Church [A:143].

A:144; A:143

People of the BookPhrase in Marie Monaghan’s playful comparison of Arabs and Americans over coffee with Hans. She calls both “Peoples of the Book” despite irreligious intellectuals, then compares their distrust of alcohol, plainsmen, thugs and slum children [A:7].

A:7

People of the NoseComic grouping that includes Gabby Gabrielovitch and Finnegan. Gabby’s nose is likened to the craggy trans-Adriatic coast and a Montenegrin shepherd’s crozier [A:127]; Finnegan’s is introduced as a banana nose [A:1].

A:127; A:1

PesoCurrency in the Philippine episodes. Nauti charges a peso for a bottle of Four Feathers or Five Roses whiskey, and the girls charge a peso for a dozen bananas because they have no change [A:64-65]. The soldiers scrape together two pesos for one bottle of Black Label [A:66]. Sammy Guiterrez then temporarily steals a shoeshine box while Finnegan distracts its owners with music and earns four pesos for four shines; the money buys more whiskey, including a final bottle for two pesos [A:67-68].

A:64-65; A:66; A:67-68

Peter (1)Saint Peter, apostle and a leading figure of the early Church, regarded in Catholic tradition as the first Bishop of Rome and first pope. Christian tradition places his martyrdom in Rome during Nero’s persecution. The inherited glossary associates him with the line “A firster Peter for a rock” in the Paean; that preliminary text is absent from the available Archipelago PDF, so the quotation and its locator remain unverified.
Peter (Salvatore Cousin)Henry Salvatore’s younger cousin, part of the extended family around Morgan City, Louisiana. The nearby relatives comprise thirteen families. Peter follows Henry in everything, along with the older cousins Basil, Sebastian, Fabian and Adrian [A:122-123].

A:122-123

Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca) (1304--1374)Francesco Petrarca, Petrarch (1304-1374), Italian poet, scholar and leading early humanist. His recovery of Cicero’s letters contributed to the revival of classical learning. His Canzoniere, or Rerum vulgarium fragmenta, comprises 366 poems in several forms, especially sonnets, much of it centered on Laura; its intense self-examination and poetic forms strongly influenced European lyric poetry. Endymeon Ellenbogen boasts to Hans that he has translated Petrarch [A:236-237]. When Anastasia tells Finnegan to sleep instead of writing down his sonnet, he asks what would have happened if Laura had refused Petrarch paper and pencil [D:133-134].

A:236-237; D:133-134

Petrof, Lord PeterAlias of Ali ben Taife, the jewel-thief master whom Amoy serves in Karachi in Ignatius Ti’s story [A:80-81].

A:80-81

Petrus, Tu esLatin for “You are Peter,” from Matthew 16:18. It appears on a banner of Navicula Petri, Henry’s dream ship [A:44].

A:44

PhariseesFather McGuigan calls Patrick Stranahan a Pharisee of the Right and says such people are no different from the Sadducees of the Left; Patrick replies that the Sadducees denied the resurrection [A:110]. The Devil’s mouth-spoken address to Duffey attacks Pharisees alongside Legalists, Rigidists and the Reactionary Curia; his accompanying mental address is essentially the same speech [MTM B8:243].

A:110; MTM B8:243

Philip StranahanVincent Stranahan’s older brother, ten years old when Duffey emerges from the Mississippi beneath the Eads Bridge in St. Louis in 1923. Philip is fishing from the pier. He is the eldest of Philip, Hugh, Timothy and Vincent, and has the eyes Duffey remembers in the adult Vincent. In this altered past, however, Philip says the baby Vincent was born on April 5, 1921, and died on April 10. Philip is in fifth grade, Teresa Piccone in first; he invites Duffey to the Cat Castle [MTM B13:470-471]. On Duffey’s return to the pier, Philip protests that it is afternoon when Duffey sings about morning [MTM B13:473].

MTM B13:470-471; MTM B13:473

PhilologyThe study Papa Piccone recommends to policemen and colonels during a dispute over the sign advertising his theater as burlesque. In Show Boat’s letter, Papa is a purist who means the word in its original sense; suggesting that the authorities take a short philology course only worsens the dispute [A:48].

A:48

Phoenecian, oldOld Phoenician, spelled “old Phoenecian” in the text: the language Casey dreams of speaking fluently with an exceptionally odd traveler during the seventh of his twelve hidden worlds [A:159].

A:159

Piccone, Papa (Gaetano)Gaetano Piccone, proprietor of the Star and Garter theater, husband of Marie Caterina Panebianco and father of Theresa, Show Boat [A:94]. Flamboyant and fond of gambling, he likes to display hundred-dollar bills [A:95]. Show Boat’s letter describes his quarrel with authorities over the original meaning of burlesque [A:48]. An old friend and agreeable argumentative opponent of Patrick Stranahan, he can talk until sunrise; each imitates the other, and Papa turns Patrick into Hallohan J. O’Hoolihan onstage [A:104]. For Vincent and Theresa’s wedding he proposes playing accordion in the church aisles instead of hiring an organist, but Maurine says he is kidding. His wine preparations comprise three barrels and a collection of jugs: he intends to avoid the shortage at Cana [A:105]. He joins Charley Murray’s older family party at the Rounders’ Club [MTM B5:162]. He claims to have made a fictional man who became real, named Oliver Oscar Omygosh in his account and Oscar Oliver Omygosh in the ensuing recollection. Bagby remembers the novelty-shop proprietor but rejects Papa’s claim to have created him [MTM B5:167-168]. Papa is dead by Duffey’s late visit to the Cat Castle [MTM B12:385].

A:94; A:95; A:48; A:104; A:105; MTM B5:162; MTM B5:167-168; MTM B12:385

Piccone, Teresa (Theresa Antoinette Piccone, Show Boat, Showboat, Teresa Piccone Stranahan, Margie la Maga, La Maga-La Strega)Theresa Antoinette Piccone, also called Teresa or Show Boat, is born in St. Louis on October 15, 1923, to Gaetano “Papa” Piccone, owner of the Star and Garter, and Marie Caterina Panebianco [A:94]. She is Beth Keegan’s goddaughter [MTM B5:162]. She marries Vincent Stranahan on the last Saturday of May 1946 [A:95] [A:113]. Patrick Stranahan calls her the Urchin [A:104]. Her shifting expressions make her difficult to describe; Duffey encounters her as a person of dazzling presence and great kindness [MTM B5:162-163] [MTM B5:180-181].

She and Finnegan are the two central figures among Duffey’s creations [MTM B5:162]. She later disputes the language of creation: Duffey awakened their ancient selves and brought about their rebirth [MTM B7:233]. She identifies herself as Atalanta, only one part of her identity [MTM B7:234], and describes their talismans as pieces of the Holy Argo [MTM B5:179]. Before the assembled friends, she washes her hands, face, and hair in flame drawn from Duffey’s ashes [MTM B7:232-233].

On a New Orleans visit, she writes and sets an entire issue of the Bark, then produces a Show-Bill with an advertisement for the newly appearing Decatur Street Opera House. She also cooks elaborate Italian meals that her friends find difficult to eat [MTM B7:229-230]. Her street-preaching with Margaret Stone is disrupted by disguised hecklers, who prove to be Finnegan, Vincent, and Stein. Once she recognizes them, she turns the crowd against them [MTM B7:231-232].

Her intimacy with Finnegan crosses ordinary identities and time. He writes to her of a love only the two of them understand [A:146]; she describes his ghostly visits in a private letter [MTM B6:188]. He calls her a witch while she calls herself a magician and clairvoyante [A:108], and later, while studying his portraits, he identifies her with Anastasia [A:278]. In Archipelago, Chiara, Rafaello, and Theresa Anna belong to her uncertain twelve-year life with Finnegan; the text says her children with Vincent at that time have different names [A:204]. More Than Melchisedech later gives the same three names to her younger children with Vincent [MTM B12:385].

She writes to Dotty about Casey, Vincent, and the ordination she has attended [A:262-263]. She recommends Carmelo Mendoza to Duffey as a companion for his journeys [MTM B12:369]. After Duffey deeds her his half of the Rounders’ Club, she runs it with Vincent, who has inherited Charley Murray’s half [MTM B12:385]. She discusses the amnesia surrounding the Argo and recites a prophecy of its final cargoes [MTM B12:386] [MTM B12:388]. Near the end, a five-year-old Teresa recognizes the ghostly Duffey and speaks with him about Vincent’s uncertain life and their possible births [MTM B13:472].

A:94; MTM B5:162; A:95; A:113; A:104; MTM B5:162-163; MTM B5:180-181; MTM B7:233; MTM B7:234; MTM B5:179; MTM B7:232-233; MTM B7:229-230; MTM B7:231-232; A:146; MTM B6:188; A:108; A:278; A:204; MTM B12:385; A:262-263; MTM B12:369; MTM B12:386; MTM B12:388; MTM B13:472

Pig-StickerDuffey’s preferred name for the projected New Orleans magazine, which he considers direct and inclusive of its aims. Henry proposes Bark, and Finnegan’s support settles that choice [A:121].

A:121

PillarThe “Pillar and the Cloud” invoked by Absalom Stein when asking Duffey whether he had been in Egypt, the desert and Babylon with the Jews. Duffey then asks why Stein is a neo-Jew rather than a Christian [A:131]. The biblical background is the Lord’s guidance of Israel by a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night in Exodus 13:21-22.

A:131

Pinne, Doppio di (Dopey the Seaman)Seaman called Dopey, whose identity overlaps Finnegan’s. Patti calls Doppio di Pinne the same brother in another state [A:174]. Joe Cross notes the same size, shape and coloring, especially an alarming resemblance in peripheral vision; Finnegan, who remembers only having Dopey pointed out to him, sees little facial resemblance [D:65]. Dopey occupied Finnegan’s bunk on the Brunhilde. Joe reports that Papadiabolous entered the cabin and shut the door; three screams followed, but Joe found only Papa and a little blood. No body was produced. The account does not establish a locked door or an unambiguous killing [D:63-64]. Finnegan sometimes feels another presence in the bunk [D:64] [D:78]. A letter hidden behind an upper balk reveals Dopey’s bargain, hopes of wealth and power, the intended replacement of Finnegan, impatience that the “bugle nose” is still alive and fear that Dopey himself will die trapped [D:50-51] [D:78]. Papa first suspects that Finnegan killed Dopey or is Dopey with an altered nose [D:89]. Later he calls Dopey a fetch, ghost or absorbed double and admits uncertainty about who, if anyone, killed him. He describes Dopey as of the strange blood, a sometime killer brought by Seaworthy to kill Papadiabolous [D:121-122]. X’s later account links the intended victim to the old Papadiabolous and explains Seaworthy’s mistake of Finnegan for the hired killer [D:153]. While shaving, Finnegan sees Dopey in the mirror: the same coloring but coarser follicles and a different skin texture, dazed and afraid of the razor. Dopey says he is not dead and guesses he is there. After Finnegan smashes the mirror, its fragments still show Dopey with his eyes closed in tortured sleep [D:187-188].

A:174; D:65; D:63-64; D:64; D:78; D:50-51; D:89; D:121-122; D:153; D:187-188

Pirates' AlleyNew Orleans location where, according to Patricia Solli, Finnegan received his art instruction from drunken painters, apart from grade-school teaching by sisters [A:175]. Duffey also sells magazines there and around its studios [A:143]. Mary Virginia mentions the new painters around Pirates’ Alley among the attractions distracting Duffey from the Populist History [MTM B11:310].

A:175; A:143; MTM B11:310

Pirogue, Candy SueOne of three twenty-one-year-old women drawn by Honeybucket Kincaid’s frequency modulation to the dock where Duffey and Biloxi Brannagan are visiting. She arrives in a rowboat with Janeway Celeste Lynne, who introduces her as a cousin, and Etta Mae Mansion [MTM B13:419]. Candy Sue asks for Puff Fish despite finding them disgusting. After Duffey removes their frequency and existence, she can no longer remember their name [MTM B13:420–421].

MTM B13:419; MTM B13:420–421

Plato (427--347 BC)Greek philosopher, approximately 428/427-348/347 BC, a pupil of Socrates, founder of the Academy at Athens and teacher of Aristotle. His dramatic dialogues examine knowledge, ethics and politics; the Republic presents rule by philosophers, and his theory of Forms concerns intelligible, unchanging realities. His portrayal of Socrates is influential but is not a verbatim record of the historical man. Anastasia jokes that she and Finnegan could give Plato lessons: he was not very platonic, whereas they develop their own ideas [D:124]. The fictional Carmody Overlark lists broad-headed Plato among supposed Neanderthals in an epigraph from Studies in the Imagination [D:271].

D:124; D:271

Plaza HotelVast Sydney building described as the city’s center and a place where shimmering people pass pleasurable hours. It contains forty-eight bars, railway and tram stations, shops, arcades and clubs. Finnegan and Vincent arrive with Loy and Margaret, and Hans and Marie join them; Margie is Margaret, not an additional visitor [A:2-3]. During the Sergeant’s strange passage out of the hospital ward and island setting, he returns to Sydney and drinks gin there with Tom Shire and Freddy Castle [A:88].

A:2-3; A:88

Pleistocene Ice Age, fourthStage of geological history in Vincent Stranahan’s Theory of the Uncreated Creation. He asks whether the earth could have been created ten minutes earlier, already descending from a fourth Pleistocene ice age and supplied with fossils, vestiges, carbon balances, atomic clocks and sediments suggesting fifteen hundred million years. This is his thought experiment about created evidence of age [A:56].

A:56

Pliny the Elder (Gaius Plinius Secundus) (23/24--79 AD)Gaius Plinius Secundus, approximately AD 23/24-79, Roman author, naturalist and naval commander. His Natural History is an encyclopedic account of the natural world and human knowledge. His nephew’s account describes him commanding the fleet at Misenum, taking ships to rescue people during the eruption of Vesuvius and dying at Stabiae. In Ignacio’s fanciful history of a cannon-fired lunar journey, Father Joseph Maintz takes Pliny’s Natural History along with the Bible, a missal, Augustine and Jerome [A:271].

A:271

PolandCountry invoked in Casey’s hostile Crock editorial: he accuses the Bark of supporting clerical-reactionary elements and Gabrielovitch of opposing what Casey calls a rational Polish-Russian settlement [A:129-130]. X’s account places the birth of Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch in a hayfield near Krakow [D:278-279]. Duffey’s Argonaut commentary identifies Prince Casimir with Poland [PG:536]. In Duffey’s encounter with Kasmir Gorshok, the stranger’s face resembles a map of Poland with its changing, lopsided outlines [MTM B13:425-426].

A:129-130; D:278-279; PG:536; MTM B13:425-426

PolishLanguage that the Sergeant says the Dirty Five taught the Jojos, who thought they were learning English while the Gorgios took it for Malay [A:73]. Casey is willing to learn Polish from his father, and the account of his hidden worlds says his father knew it [A:156] [A:159]. The adjective also occurs in Casey’s attack on Gabrielovitch’s support of the London Polish government [A:129], X’s account of Katie Noonan as a governess with a landed Polish family [D:279], and the description of Zabotski’s large Polish hands [MTM B11:343].

A:73; A:156; A:159; A:129; D:279; MTM B11:343

Polly Polyglot (Mary Frances Rattigan)Mary Frances Rattigan’s pen name for “Books Abroad” in the Crock during Duffey’s wartime editorship [A:41]. Under that name she supplies translations for the magazine [MTM B4:138].

A:41; MTM B4:138

Pop skull whiskyWhiskey drunk by Shakes Pearson, Marie Monaghan’s uncle in her comic family story. She describes him drinking and continually shaking [A:25].

A:25

Pope, Alexander (1688--1744)Alexander Pope (1688-1744), English poet noted for heroic couplets and satire, including The Rape of the Lock and The Dunciad. An Essay on Criticism treats poetry and critical judgment; An Essay on Man examines humanity, morality and the order of the world. During the account of Casey’s problem of evil, Archipelago quotes the master passion growing “Like Aaron’s serpent” and swallowing the rest [A:154], from An Essay on Man, Epistle II, lines 121-122.

A:154

Popotov, SarkisRussian resident of New Orleans whose account Margaret Stone quotes during the Royal Pop History episode. He has lived in the same place for forty years, but cannot remember the buildings that stood next door before the appearance of Artaguette Park. The park looks unfamiliar, though tourists assure him it will look familiar by the next day [MTM B11:309].

MTM B11:309

Populus tremuloidesAspen name used by X when comparing his trembling with trees and recalling his young wife. He calls Populus tremuloides the aspen of his own land and contrasts it with Populus grandidentata, using American and European labels [A:140-141]. His botanical comparison mixes the names: P. tremuloides and P. grandidentata are both native to North America, while the European or Eurasian aspen is P. tremula.

A:140-141

PorpoiseAnimal in Trinali’s account of driftwood in the Old Wood Graveyard: it has learned to leap like a dolphin and plunge like a porpoise [A:233]. Anastasia compares mermaids to porpoises because they must surface to breathe air [D:34]. The concluding account of bells says creatures from plankton to porpoises enjoy submerged bells and their signals [MB:575].

A:233; D:34; MB:575

Port SaidPort named by Loy Larkin as a location of a Duffey’s Tavern, along with Cork and New York [A:2].

A:2

Portae inferi non prevalebunt“The gates of hell shall not prevail,” words from Matthew 16:18 on one of the banners of Henry’s dream ship Navicula Petri [A:44]. The novel spells the last word prevalebunt; the standard Latin biblical form is praevalebunt.

A:44

PossessionPrivate Gregory’s proposed perfect ghost story: possession as hypnotism from beyond the grave by an immortal will. He identifies ghosts with devils and claims that powerful leaders can become shells inhabited by devils through a bargain for power. In his account, such possessed men do much of the world’s running [A:84-85].

A:84-85

Pot, TheOne college version of Casey Szymansky’s student Crocks, whose related names include Nattkarlet, Night Charley and Nocnik. At successive colleges he loses control of the papers within two or three weeks. The Pot subsequently circulates in a foul form; the account distinguishes this deterioration from Casey’s original, nonfilthy humor [A:167-168].

A:167-168

Potator Incognitus, Sanctus Apostolus“Holy Apostle, Unknown Drinker,” the playful invocation Show Boat uses in her letter to Dotty while defending Finnegan. Papa Piccone has told her an Italian legend of a tippling apostle, either Thomas, Bartholomew or Jude, who finished the abandoned wine yet converted tens of thousands; Papa cannot remember which apostle it was [A:262].

A:262

Power FactorElectrical term in entry XIV of Casey Szymansky’s high-school notebook. He defines it as the cosine of the phase-lag angle between voltage and current in an alternating-current circuit [A:162-163].

A:162-163

PragueCity Vincent proposes visiting with Finnegan while trying to escape his approaching marriage: with his three thousand dollars and mustering-out money, they could sail to Venice and Prague. Finnegan answers with a joke about the sea-coast of Bohemia [A:112].

A:112

PreadamiteSpeculative element in the narrator’s description of Margaret Stone’s ancestry: she is Italian and Jewish, with “possibly a little” Preadamite in her [A:144].

A:144

Prescott, NewtonElectronics repairman and designer who narrates “The Casey Machine.” He writes his journal as therapy for a compulsion to forget the events surrounding the machine [CM:503]. In Josephine McSorely’s account, he credits Casey with the impetus for the device, proposes giving its initially mental operation physical components, and describes using electrical discharges from the dead [CM:506–507]. In the addenda, Prescott doubts that he exists as an independent person and calls himself a minor aspect of Casey. He recalls Casey saying that he gave a splinter of his personality a ghostly body and the name Newton Prescott, to remain his eyes and ears after death [CM:515].

CM:503; CM:506–507; CM:515

PresenceHypnotic stage quality, paired with “the Mystic,” that Hans cannot develop during his apprenticeship with Professor Kirol. Although below the Professor’s class as a performer, Hans genuinely hypnotizes people in cases where the Professor sometimes fakes it; the narrator jokes that the real thing must serve when the counterfeit is beyond one’s ability [A:219].

A:219

Priestism, JudasOne of the seven contemporary heads Bascom Bagby assigns to the old enemy. His full list is Dialectic Materialism, Artistic Degradation, Judas Priestism, Secular Liberalism, Panaceic Pentecostalism, Murderous Molochism and Atheistic Communism [MTM B5:169].

MTM B5:169

Prince CasimirCasey Szymansky’s medieval identity in Duffey’s Argonaut commentary: Prince and Saint Casimir of Poland, defender of the poor who thwarts the mighty and whose apparent death is a withdrawal from the world [PG:536]. Teresa also quotes a prophecy that the ghostly Duffey will carry Prince Casimir aboard the Argo to reign as Antichrist near Armageddon [MTM B12:388]. During the later voyage, the passenger is explicitly revealed as Peleus, Kasmir Gorshok, Prince Casimir, Casey and Antichristus, and is landed at Habonim near the Plains of Megiddo [MTM B13:462]. Duffey, Brannagan and Gunboat then leave this future, admitting they failed to prevent it this time and wondering about another chance [MTM B13:463].

PG:536; MTM B12:388; MTM B13:462; MTM B13:463

Pristine TimeSee Pristine World. This index heading refers to time in the Pristine World, whose chronology Zabotski distinguishes from that of the everyday world [MTM B9:279] [MTM B9:280].

MTM B9:279; MTM B9:280

Pristine WorldThe world that Zabotski visits during absences of a day or two which contain years of experience [MTM B9:269] [MTM B9:271]. He calls it “the real and essential world,” occupying the same space as the Everyday-or-Molasses World without occupying it in the same way. In his account, it excludes duplicated and non-valid persons and situations, while adding much that ordinary history lacks [MTM B9:279]. He compares it to a film of a football game reduced from three hours of clock time to a few minutes containing the game’s complete essence. Its brevity therefore accompanies an abundance of experience: he can live overflowing years there during a day or two in the Molasses World [MTM B9:279]. Zabotski says he remains imperfectly accelerated for it and returns here to rest and see friends [MTM B9:277]. Duffey’s narrative confirms his own visit of three or five years, followed by a return in two days [MTM B9:284]. Zabotski’s Pristine History of the World approaches the Fundamentalers’ chronology by a different method, excluding duplication and non-validity rather than simply adopting their dates [MTM B9:279] [MTM B9:280].

MTM B9:269; MTM B9:271; MTM B9:279; MTM B9:277; MTM B9:284; MTM B9:280

Prosody, LatinSubject of Henry Salvatore’s seminary verse assignment, which ends Deus tam dilexit mundum! His instructor marks him down with the joke that Latin is not Italian enough to have italics and therefore cannot use them [A:149].

A:149

ProtagorasName used by Gregory McIfreann Papadiabolous, the Asiatic brother or Papadiabolous I, in X’s account of the brothers’ aliases [D:285]. It is also the name of Protagoras of Abdera, the Greek Sophist, approximately 490-420 BC.

D:285

Psychosis, Korsakof'sFinnegan’s own name for his condition when the Travelers’ Aid woman questions his confusion and memory loss in a railway station. He calls it “Korsakofs Psychosis,” declines a doctor, and says doctors blame drinking, as they did with his father [A:243-244]. Korsakoff syndrome is a severe memory disorder associated with thiamine deficiency and often chronic alcohol misuse; the novel’s identification remains Finnegan’s self-report.

A:243-244

PulaTagalog word for red or redness. Amoy says it after Ignatius Ti describes an earlier bird incarnation as a crow or blackbird; Ti freely expands the reply into the statement that Amoy was a red-winged blackbird [A:80].

A:80

PurgatoryAfterlife realm appearing in several different voices. The narrator’s fantastic account of Black Papua says its inhabitants die nightly, visit Purgatory and return shaken with instructions from the dead [A:37]. Professor Kirol places Purgatory, Hell and Heaven within the spiritual universe already surrounding us [A:214]. Show Boat wishes Vincent a long afternoon in Purgatory when he challenges her use of “inordinate” in the tale of the tippling apostle [A:262]. Cardinal Salvatore locates the dead Bascom Bagby on Purgatory’s north slope [MTM B12:384]; Bagby’s posthumous letters describe work, strengthened passions and complex relationships outside ordinary time [MTM B8:248-249]. Patrick describes a particularly shabby, dank, mud-colored section where persistent makers compulsively form things over and over [MTM B12:391]. Bagby’s commentary places Casey among the Poor Souls, repairing the exhausted scapegoats that bring them further burdens from the living [PG:546].

A:37; A:214; A:262; MTM B12:384; MTM B8:248-249; MTM B12:391; PG:546

Purple PrinceOne of the adversaries of the Argo Masters, named with the Evil Prince, the Mocking Prince and the Laughing Prince. The narrative calls this group among the most formidable of the Masters’ opponents, while suggesting that the Laughing Prince of Tartary may be the most powerful and trickiest of them [MTM B13:437].

MTM B13:437

PutipharBiblical name the narrator gives Adrian Shapiro, the wealthy, well-connected husband of Mercedes. Finnegan is commissioned to paint Mercedes and sees an opening into a dazzling circle. Her playfulness casts him as a goatish Joseph: he departs with his coat but leaves his paints of many colors, fearing ridicule rather than imprisonment and welcoming an excuse to return to the road [A:193].

A:193

PuttyMaterial whose recipe Casey records in entry XVII of his high-school notebook: chalk and linseed oil [A:162] [A:164].

A:162; A:164

PygmiesPatrick Stranahan’s belittling contrast to giants when he tells Father McGuigan that the Church’s age of giants has ended and an age of pygmies is beginning [A:110]. The inherited glossary also records “They never knew the race of pygmies” from the Paean, concerning the early Argonauts; that preliminary text is absent from the available Archipelago edition, so the quotation remains unverified.

A:110

PythagorasGreek thinker from Samos, approximately 570-490 BC, who established a religious way of life in southern Italy associated with the transmigration of souls and an ordered, harmonious cosmos. Later tradition emphasizes mathematics and the theorem bearing his name, but a proof by Pythagoras himself is not securely attested. In the discussion of Casey’s problem of evil, the narrator attributes to him a catalogue dividing qualities into good and evil, then calls it incomplete [A:154]. This echoes the Pythagorean table of opposites reported by Aristotle, Metaphysics I.5; the novel reverses the traditional positions of odd and even.

A:154

Pythagoras (c. 570--c. 495 BC)Earlier heading supplied an approximate death date differing from the date used in the checked account. See Pythagoras.
Quantum lawThe narrator’s term for the threshold needed to ring an old rope-operated church bell in an Iowa town during one of Duffey’s childhoods: an insufficient pull produces no movement. A fat altar boy normally supplies the necessary weight. When that boy has pneumonia, eight-year-old Duffey, weighing sixty-three pounds, takes his place [MTM B1:14]. Duffey commands an invisible giant to help; the giant’s hand itself is visible to the other boys and successfully pulls the rope [MTM B1:15].

MTM B1:14; MTM B1:15

QuarterNew Orleans neighborhood in which Finnegan and Dotty revisit friends, carouse, talk and visit her former workplace while avoiding the noisier jazz haunts Finnegan dislikes [A:115]. He knows everyone there and claims to have grown up in its heart, while Patti places their home in Irish Channel [A:175]. During his later confusion, it becomes a spinning, gin-soaked city of altered street names and apparently part-animal people, mixing remembered and future places from other cities [A:200-201]. Margaret Stone reports that people in the Quarter have been drinking Green Ladies during the transformations surrounding the Pop History meetings: like peppermint schnapps, but with absinthe replacing the schnapps [MTM B11:309].

A:115; A:175; A:200-201; MTM B11:309

Queen (Virgin Queen)Protective figure in the Tristram-and-Isolde ballad opening the Casey chapter of Archipelago. Isolde dreams of standing before a pit, guarded by the Virgin Queen’s watchful hands [A:151]. Later she recalls them as holy hands and asks to return, yet finally feels drawn toward the pit and Tristram’s distant island despite the storm [A:152].

A:151; A:152

Quest Accomplished motifThe Fourteenth Voyage of the Argo, presented among the alternatives of Duffey’s world, is the “Quest Accomplished” motif: the fleece has been found, the moment of finding endures, and continuing beatitudes promise Final Beatitude [MTM B10:300]. The opening poem of Vincent’s chapter likewise makes the Dirty Five sailors on the ancient Argo in search of golden cargo [A:91].

MTM B10:300; A:91

Questions 382, 383 (Baltimore Catechism)Questions quoted as numbers 382 and 383 in the Casey Machine epigraph. The just rise glorious and immortal; its explanation describes bodies shining like the sun, swift as thought, able to penetrate matter, beautiful and free of pain or change.
