The damned also rise but receive eternal punishment. The following narration applies bodily splendor and penetration of time to the Casey condition [CM:511]. The same basic questions are numbered 418 and 419 in the consulted Baltimore Catechism text.

CM:511

Quick, CatherineOne of Duffey’s Chicago friends of a scientific bent [MTM B3:99] and one of the adult women he loves [MTM B4:111]. She appears among the women with whom photographs show him playing the funny lover in the blackmail portfolio associated with Hugo Stone [MTM B4:139]. In Proud & Glorious, Stein names her among the scientific friends he has consulted about brain-reading and mind-reading [PG:539].

MTM B3:99; MTM B4:111; MTM B4:139; PG:539

Quintessence of IbsenismGeorge Bernard Shaw’s The Quintessence of Ibsenism, read by Casey in high school. His notebook uses it to illustrate his rule to read originals: books about Shaw did not explain Shaw to him, and Shaw’s book did not explain Ibsen, so he had to read each author directly [A:166].

A:166

Quirt, The MilfordWhip in the turbaned Pop History speaker’s nostalgic list. A specially enduring flagstone on Decatur Street remembers its snap and swish along with those of other whips and the traffic of horses, carriages, streetcars and automobiles [MTM B11:329].

MTM B11:329

Quo vadis, filia mea?“Where are you going, my daughter?” The old church-tower bells ask this in the Tristram-and-Isolde ballad, as Isolde fears the storm and the voyage toward the island [A:151-152]. It may echo Peter’s question to Christ, “Lord, where are you going?”, in the apocryphal Acts of Peter 35, where Christ’s answer turns Peter back toward Rome and martyrdom.

A:151-152

R.C.sAbbreviation for Roman Catholics. Salvation Sally guesses Marie and Hans are R.C.s from their flippancy about the Second Coming, though they alone have contributed to her cup. She calls established churches traps and theirs the deepest. Marie speaks the French sentence about Rome's power; Sally answers that she knows that power, adding that she knows Bohemia's heresy too [A:8].

A:8

RabatMoroccan city on the Atlantic coast, called at by the Brunhilde after Casablanca and before Tangier on its northward voyage [D:101].

D:101

Rabbit raisingOne of the small arts and activities the narrator says were trashed during the cultural decline following the Devil's release [MTM B6:207]. The catalogue concludes that these activities have lost their class and style [MTM B6:208].

MTM B6:207; MTM B6:208

RacquetsGame advertised on the sign of Duffey's Rounders' Club in St. Louis, an establishment for gentlemen rounders offering racquets, whist, poker, horseshoes and other amusements [MTM B2:49]. Charley Murray subsequently becomes its half owner [MTM B2:53].

MTM B2:49; MTM B2:53

Rafelson, Doctor SaulChicago analyst whom Duffey and Letitia call Doctor Raffles. He never releases Duffey as cured and considers a cure impossible. He catalogues Duffey's fantasies: Child of God, Child of Gold, Master of Ebony Slaves, Master of Giants, Riding King, Boy King, Miracle Worker, immense age, successive and parallel lives, a many-layered self, the monster within, living shadows, conferring power, making people, the company of elites, conferring talismans and lives, and saving the world by his intervention. Rafelson calls these ordinary fantasies of unhealthy boys' minds; Duffey's extraordinary quality is making them happen. He has seen weaker examples in two other patients [MTM B4:146]. He considers psychic projections, captured real people and independent split images as explanations. Two freestanding images he analyzes have healthy, intelligent, substantial bodies; one donates blood. These images are distinct from Duffey's twelve creations, which Rafelson interprets as aspects of monumental egomania. He acknowledges Duffey's magic and entertains the possibility of a topological inversion placing the world within Duffey. The twelve are contingent: if they attain congruent fulfillment they will always have existed, with a past supplied by preternatural plot construction; otherwise they will never have existed [MTM B4:147]. He warns that three embodied unrealities might murder Duffey and have already tried. He believes Duffey's phenomena bear on overlapping persons, creator and created, shared reality and the meaning of matter, but refuses to pursue the implications because they frighten him [MTM B4:148].

MTM B4:146; MTM B4:147; MTM B4:148

Raft racingOne of the activities the narrator says were trashed during the cultural decline following the Devil's release; it appears among minor arts and recreations said to have lost their class and style [MTM B6:207-208].

MTM B6:207-208

Rag musicMusic played on two victrolas, one cylinder and one disc, in the soundproof attic billiard room at the house of Lily Koch's relatives during the first compulsory school dance. Duffey, Charley Murray, John Rattigan, Sebastian Hilton, Lily, Mary Anne Michaels, Sedalia Schoefeld and Edith O'Dwyer dance there away from the formal gathering [MTM B1:33]. A player piano supplies rag music during Beth Keegan's balloon dinner party; a serving man pumps it, and Beth takes over while the after-dinner wine is served. The Black Midnight Rag accompanies Duffey's descent [MTM B2:65-66].

MTM B1:33; MTM B2:65-66

Ragosa, theEarlier heading altered the source’s printed Ragosy to Ragosa. See Ragosy, the.
Ragosy, theThe source's spelling is Ragosy. Gabby Gabrielovitch tells Stein that the Argosy is really the Ragosy, a fleet out of Ragusa in Illyria, and that Ragusa was the original Iolcus [A:127]. This is Gabby's account of the Argonaut tradition.

A:127

RagusaHistorical Latin name of Dubrovnik. Gabby Gabrielovitch identifies Ragusa as a city of Illyria, the original Iolcus and the home of the fleet he calls the Ragosy, underlying the name Argosy [A:127]. His Iolcus identification belongs to the novel's account of the Argonaut tradition.

A:127

Raleigh, Sir WalterEnglish courtier, explorer and colonial promoter, born in the early 1550s and executed under James I in 1618. Favored by Elizabeth I, he sponsored the Roanoke colonial expeditions and published The Discovery of Guiana in 1596. Dotty recalls the thought that whoever knows only land knows only half the world and is only half a person; she cannot remember whether Raleigh wrote it or Finnegan said it [A:280].

A:280

RamiresElena Musquiz's husband, who recognizes Finnegan after seven years when they find him near D'Hannis following his 105-hour ordeal in the chaparral [A:203]. Elena carries Finnegan to their cart; the couple, traveling to Sunday Mass, bring him to help [A:203] [A:206].

A:203; A:206

RandwickThe novel's spelling of Randwick racecourse in Sydney, now Royal Randwick. Finnegan initially takes Ranwick for a bar. He remarks that the horses run clockwise, or backwards, and Hans offers a comic explanation involving the Coriolis effect [A:3-4]. Finnegan, Vincent, Hans, Marie and the stewardesses Loy and Margaret go there, meet Australian soldiers Tom Shire and Freddy Castle, win bets, drink beer and watch the ponies from the infield. The course is the best the boys have seen, with perhaps twenty thousand spectators [A:2-4].

A:3-4; A:2-4

Rang-Dang-DooValley in Don Lewis's story of three servicemen, Sergeant Santee, Corporal Casper and PFC Lorrigan, who kill an apparent Japanese soldier they call Yokipoki and become lost. Lewis admits being one of the three but withholds which [D:44]. The surrounding maze includes Cotton-Picker Valley, Pepper-Belly Valley, Hound Dog, Horse Collar, Dog-Dirt Draw, Jackass Flats, Little Joker Canyon, Aching Back, Slit Trench, Sore-Head Gulch, Little Fat-Head and Big Fat-Head [D:45-46].

D:44; D:45-46

RangoonFormer English name of Yangon, Myanmar. The poem opening Finnegan's chapter places Rangoon among Roi, Kandi, Kuri and Cai in an imagined region of eternal summer [A:171].

A:171

RanwickRanwick is the spelling used in the novel for the Sydney racecourse. See Randwick.
Ranwick, EdwardArt-school acquaintance in Duffey's St. Louis circle. Duffey's outings with Mary Louise Byrne and Beth Keegan include one of Charley Murray, Edward or Philip Manford, the music-school student. They sometimes ride in Duffey's carriage and sometimes in Manford's Overland automobile. At the Bavarian Club Edward compares the strong blonde hostesses to brewery horses, a likeness the narrator disputes. Edward already has a reputation at art school, but Duffey dismisses his work as skinny art [MTM B2:58].

MTM B2:58

Rasputin, GrigoriRussian religious figure Grigori Rasputin (1869-1916), named among the broad-headed visionaries in the fictional Carmody Overlark's Studies in the Imagination epigraph. The passage speculates about a back-brain type, supposed Neanderthal traits, criminality, religious pathfinding, prophecy, poetry and invention [D:270-272]. Its remark attributed to Santana concerns mystics' ugly faces generally, rather than making an individual judgment about Rasputin [D:271].

D:270-272; D:271

RatFinnegan recognizes rats by their smell when he wakes bloody in a foul dump; the surrounding language of shipwreck and Odysseus is figurative [A:177]. In Don Lewis's story, large rats make the sounds and movements in Yokipoki's grave that Lewis initially takes for the dead soldier's return [D:47]. The river rats at Demetrio's bar are human patrons described by that slang term [D:58].

A:177; D:47; D:58

Rat-leaf palmTwo palms under which X and Finnegan take cover after Finnegan notices the glint of a rifle scope during their graveyard conversation with Doll Delaney [D:291]. They are visiting the grave marked I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch [D:277].

D:291; D:277

Rattigan, JohnChicago boarding-school friend of Duffey, Charley Murray and Sebastian Hilton, about two years older than Duffey, with a witty look and a calculating grin. A resourceful trader, he knows wholesalers and clandestinely sells sundries, candy, fruit, tobacco, gadgets and new and used books [MTM B1:22]. Refused a talisman, he copies Duffey's and tricks him into holding the copy; Duffey thinks he understands only half the process. In another school-year identity he is Delbert Dugan [MTM B1:23-24]. He climbs walls like a monkey and sells a hundred books a week, sharing the business with Duffey [MTM B1:25]. Their merchandise sales run three nights weekly after curfew by candle or kerosene light. Rattigan wears a green eyeshade; Duffey pirates his mind and thinking fingers and eyes to learn money's worth [MTM B1:26]. Though himself thirteen, Rattigan admits only students sixteen or older to his whisky bar, charging ten cents for watered whisky and clearing seven. Curiously modest, he undresses in darkness and removes his eyeshade last [MTM B1:27]. He knows girls but not “girls,” in the narrator's distinction [MTM B1:31], and becomes very friendly with Sedalia Schoefeld at the attic dance [MTM B1:33]. Duffey later remembers him among school friends who knew him as a disguised king [MTM B13:464].

MTM B1:22; MTM B1:23-24; MTM B1:25; MTM B1:26; MTM B1:27; MTM B1:31; MTM B1:33; MTM B13:464

Rattigan, Mary Frances (Polly Polyglot)Translator who contributes to the Crock's “Books Abroad” material under the name Polly Polyglot while Duffey runs the magazine during Casey's army service [A:41] [MTM B4:138]. The narrator calls her one of the quasi-creatures of a talisman that only half worked [MTM B3:99]. As a girl of eight or nine, she visits Duffey's Chicago bookstore and is involved, often with Ethyl Ellenberger, in his funny-uncle wrestling on the old black leather sofa. The narration explicitly questions its harmlessness when he is alone with Mary Frances [MTM B4:111]; compromising photographs of such encounters appear in the later portfolio [MTM B4:139]. She is subsequently listed as Mary Frances Rattigan (Gompers) among the gathering at Pelican Press [MTM B12:383].

A:41; MTM B4:138; MTM B3:99; MTM B4:111; MTM B4:139; MTM B12:383

Rattle-snakesDuring his 105 hours in the chaparral Finnegan may have visited the rattlesnakes' ancestral city; the narration leaves the experience uncertain and allows that he may have seen more than was there [A:203-205]. The following buffalo episode, rather than the rattlesnake city, is located in Frio County [A:205]. The sidewinder, Crotalus cerastes, also supplies a possible explanation learned by Niccolo Crotolus's employers for his nickname Nick the Rattle; he offers a family-name and castanet explanation himself [A:279].

A:203-205; A:205; A:279

Ravel, AlexiTenant in Zabotski's apartment building near Duffey's own place. After Duffey returns from the Fifth Contingency to an ordinary Monday he has already lived, Ravel confronts him about a dream in which Duffey abandoned him to die [MTM B12:354-356]. Duffey recognizes the neglected, unsplendid bit of trash as Ravel in mortal agony and feels ashamed. Ravel rejects the excuse that it was only a dream, spits in disgust and goes back inside [MTM B12:356].

MTM B12:354-356; MTM B12:356

RavennaCity in northeastern Italy. In the poem opening Finnegan's chapter, the speaker reports being told Ravenna is sweet in spring [A:171-172].

A:171-172

Raviola Joe aka Giuseppe GabrielangeloGiuseppe Gabrielangelo, nicknamed Raviola Joe, one of the Company of Fifty associated with Galveston's Old Wooden Ship [D:216]. With Saddle-Sore Sandy and Bay-Rum Johnny he is described as unkempt and uncouth beside the establishment's otherwise high standards [D:224].

D:216; D:224

Razzle DazDuffey's comic strip in the Crock, whose characters include Finnegan, Hans and Show Boat. Marie praises inclusion in it as the summit of splendor but disputes Duffey's account of creating their souls: she says he collects them from old junk stories and provides a new setting and sparkle, while he insists that he made them. Dotty threatens to change the danger awaiting her [MTM B5:159]. Finnegan is John Solli, Hans is John Schultz and Show Boat is Teresa Piccone [MTM B5:161].

MTM B5:159; MTM B5:161

ReadingPennsylvania city on the Pittsburgh bus route from Newark, via Allentown. Finnegan sends Doll Delancy to buy tickets for both Pittsburgh and Baltimore [D:169-170]. She explains that the Pittsburgh bus goes through Reading rather than Philadelphia; they ultimately take the Baltimore bus and get off in Philadelphia [D:170-171].

D:169-170; D:170-171

Real PresenceDoctrine Margaret Stone proclaims on Dauphin Street at midnight, defending the urgency of preaching to people whose only home is the nighttime street [A:144]. She later reports that men claiming to be assassins of the Jebel Shammar sect threaten her unless she stops preaching it at night, when they claim their jealous Djinn is the only Real Presence. Margaret doubts the sect exists: the three men attend Tulane and may be joking [MTM B7:225].

A:144; MTM B7:225

Rebeka SteinAbsalom Stein's daughter, sent to Ursuline Academy at her mother's insistence for a narrower education after her earlier education had become too broad [MTM B9:264-266]. She joins Crissie Cristofero, Therese Doucet and Cleo Mahoney at the Ghost Coffee Shop to discuss Seven Roads with Duffey [MTM B10:293]. Fifteen years old, she has known him all her life. She interprets the play's potholes as appropriately ridiculous, incongruous dream-transformation activators dredged from Cleo's unconscious and warns Duffey where he steps [MTM B10:294]. She calls Crissie a sibyl or pythoness for producing prophetic couplets without understanding them [MTM B10:295]. Against the complaint that the ongoing quest is a broken record, Rebeka insists its repeated excellence cannot be excessive [MTM B10:296]. After the seventh contingency she wishes Crissie understood her own verses, which would make their work easier [MTM B10:297].

MTM B9:264-266; MTM B10:293; MTM B10:294; MTM B10:295; MTM B10:296; MTM B10:297

Red CrowErroneous heading for Old Crow. The bottle with an inch remaining when Finnegan wakes in the dump and the whisky in his Texas shoulder-bag are both explicitly called Old Crow [A:177] [A:202]. See Old Crow.

A:177; A:202

Red DecadeThe narrator's name for the 1930s, when an aggressive ideological element is said to be especially strong in Chicago while extending across cities and persons. It is one deadly head of the old monster. This follows the account of Shirley Israel's salon circle trying to use Duffey and of the trashy campaign that savages him; the narrator also places most university and newspaper people under the red influence [MTM B4:137]. A later passage describes the mass emergence of deformed counterparts to the bright arts after the Devil's release [MTM B6:207].

MTM B4:137; MTM B6:207

Red Dog Motor Freight LineSchaeffer-family trucking business for which Henry Salvatore drives after leaving the sea; through that work he meets Mary Virginia Schaeffer [A:124]. Its routes run from Galveston and Houston to Morgan City and New Orleans and also cover Baton Rouge, Shreveport, Port Arthur, Orange and Beaumont. Mary Virginia transfers to its New Orleans terminal and works both for the company and with Dotty on the Bark and other projects [MTM B6:198].

A:124; MTM B6:198

Red FistersSardinians who, Margaret Stone says, threaten to wear her guts as scarves. Yet she meets them over dawn coffee at Messina's or Anthony Ghost's, tells them a shaggy-duck joke and hears that they let her live to tell the next one despite calling her a Whore of Rome. She finds the silent Slant-Faced Men much more frightening [MTM B7:225].

MTM B7:225

Red FoxOne of the ships on Angela Cosquin's father's master map of fifty or more real or imaginary treasure wrecks. Prospective buyers could select a ship and even alter its location before commissioning a forged treasure map and supporting papers [D:260-261].

D:260-261

Red RidgeWords on axe heads in Duffey's childhood catalogue of iron inscriptions, alongside Hubbard's and Jamestown. He appropriates many such household details from other people's minds and loves the stolen words [MTM B1:17].

MTM B1:17

Red RiverRiver north of the Cajun country in the narrator's deliberately extravagant account: people south of it were already speaking Cajun, driving buggies, raising rice, attending Mass, trapping muskrats and drinking poor wine and beer before Rome was built [A:124].

A:124

Red RoosterErroneous heading for Black Rooster, one of Don Barnaby's named varieties of joy pills, alongside Haiti hoodoo, High Harry, Deep Romany and Dead Frenchman [D:248]. See Black Rooster.

D:248

Red SeaSea in Anastasia Demetriades's account of mermaid history. Mermaids whose ancestral home was the Cyclades had reached the Red Sea by Alexander's time, by an unknown route; later, after their medieval peak, they disappeared from both the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf [D:34-36].

D:34-36

“Red Sky in the Morning”Poem in the collection of Kasmir Szymansky's work, following Demetrio Glauch's introductory assessment. Its speaker rejects rescuing the “nobly lost,” fears the blade and severed head, and accuses God of failing to recognize certain shades of red [PG:519-520]. The preceding discussion of Casey's faults, failures and elective affinities is Glauch's introduction, not an essay by Casey [PG:518-519].

PG:519-520; PG:518-519

Red-headed womenLoy says camel drivers in one port rejected her and Margaret because they considered red-headed women witches; Vincent agrees with the label [A:2]. Loy Larkin and Margaret Murphy are red-headed Sydney companions [A:2] [A:5-6], as are Marie [A:24] and the later picnic companions Virginia and Dorothy [A:29]. In Hans's meditation on Marie's appearance, the narration also describes the Virgin in early Flemish Annunciations as red-headed and green-eyed [A:24].

A:2; A:5-6; A:24; A:29

Redfox, MargeryMember of Duffey's Chicago golden-age circle, listed among its slippery people as Marjory Redfox [MTM B3:100]. Under the spelling Margery, she joins the salon supper but, unlike the other named women, does not hiss at Demetrio when he leaves [MTM B4:127]. She attends Morris Poor's challenge to Duffey's powers and asks where the nearest mule can be found for a demonstration [MTM B4:128-129].

MTM B3:100; MTM B4:127; MTM B4:128-129

Redheart, ElroyArtist of a four-chambered red-heart autobiographical construction in porcelain or ceramic. Duffey has displayed it several times; Hennessy has it when Bagby sees it. Redheart sells some miniature paintings and statuettes out of it when hungry and makes replacements, so it changes somewhat [MTM B7:221]. Its scenes move from rural youth and a dead Jill of Hearts to opulence and war, with a mutilated, bone-thin Jack of Hearts [MTM B7:221-222]. The later Jack and a beautiful, adventurous woman inhabit a more feverish world. Hot artificial colors signify artificial sins, while cheap Hong Kong plastic figures and prismatic reflections deliberately represent cheapness without careless workmanship [MTM B7:223]. The woman finally pins her Queen of Hearts card to her extracted heart; the fourth chamber is vacant and offers an optional noose. Bagby pays Hennessy one thousand dollars and has the work sent directly to St. Louis [MTM B7:224].

ResurrectionReturn from death, literal or figurative in several distinct passages. Finnegan calls Anastasia the resurrection after she washes him, treats his wounds and restores his respectability with an electric shaver [D:16]; he later teases her as Little Miss Resurrection [D:33]. Mr. X, not Saxon X. Seaworthy, tells Finnegan that deaths are easier to explain than resurrections while they discuss the buried Papadiabolous and his apparent return; their conversation identifies the substitute as the Irish policeman Noonan or Flaherty [D:153-154]. Resurrection of Count Finnegan, TheTwelve-by-eight-foot, sea-sounding painting by John Solli (Finnegan), received at Duffey's New Orleans art bijou in the mid-1950s and initially taken for a magnificent joke [MB:550]. A Latin scroll identifies the half-risen figure in the ocean-cave crypt as Papal Count Finnegan. He stands partly in dark-green water and partly in bright-green air, replacing a long strip of fallen flesh and preparing to mend other decay. He looks thirty years older than Finnegan at his reported death, which this account places two or three years before the painting's arrival. His banana nose has become noble, his artist's hands more intricate, his eyes combine humor and torment, and his strength, speed and apparently moving mouth remain recognizable. His flesh shows simultaneous transfiguration and corruption, a sea change of the uncoffined dead; a possible winding sheet hangs in tatters and old traveling clothes await him [MB:551]. The cave-roof fissure also divides the composition from the Annunciation of Joseph Cardinal Hedayat of Antioch in a Syrian or Lebanese scene. The aged Hedayat and Finnegan are identical in appearance despite their younger selves' differences [MB:552]. Duffey sells it to Hilary Hilton for twenty thousand dollars, but Hilton leaves it in the bijou for its possible role in the foretold events [MB:553]. It hangs there at least thirty years [MB:554]. Duffey later uses it as a clue with Carmelo Mendoza; a description attributed to the fictional How Many Miles to Babylon is quoted in the account [MTM B12:367-369].

Return of the Neanderthal, TheFictional book by Royce Rollins, subtitled The Alien Within, presented through Charles O. A. Harrington's hostile review in Science for Today [D:240-242]. Its thesis is that defeated Neanderthals survive both as isolated elites and within human bloodlines, periodically producing primordials bent on destroying humanity. It attributes apparitions, doubles, second sight and related powers to them [D:241]. Rollins nevertheless appeals to returnees of good will to resist their destructive fellows and allows in an appendix that they might be Grimaldi or another ancient people rather than Neanderthals [D:242].

Revision and/or correction of historyThe Royal Pop Historians' project in Duffey's Fifth Contingency [MTM B12:354]: alter people, places and remembered history while presenting the imposed result as what always existed. Margaret describes vanished buildings replaced by apparently ancient parks whose former sites people can no longer recall [MTM B11:307-310]. The lecturers claim that all history is present now and available for reconstruction and revision [MTM B11:324-325]. Hugh de Turenne announces the Black Sea's destruction to expunge Himself's imprisonment and weaken Colchis, the Argo and the Fleece; he and Cyrus Roundhead deny that the sea, Athens, Rome or Jerusalem ever existed. Their historical sessions alternate with violent hunts for human remnants [MTM B11:336-337].

Roundhead, CyrusRoyal Pop Historian in New Orleans, introduced as a forthcoming speaker and later wearing a monocle with additional lenses. After Hugh de Turenne announces the Black Sea's destruction, Roundhead offers pseudo-explanations that the sea and the cities Rome, Athens, and Jerusalem never existed. [MTM B11:327] [MTM B11:336-337] He directs hunts against supposed unreal people and the deflation of their buildings, insisting that the important must eliminate the unimportant. [MTM B11:338] At Girardeau's dinner he describes the selective recording and destruction of humanity, distinguishes the splendid people's minds and persons from their temporary bodies, and denounces human guilt, introspection, and lack of kinetic intuition. [MTM B11:344-346] At the Decatur Street Opera House he participates in the elimination of human remnants; afterward, from the loge, he envies the depth, intensity, and legacy his own species lacks. They organize the Royal Pop History meeting and reject human identity; Roundhead regards their similar bodies as temporary dwellings for an essentially different species. [MTM B11:307] [MTM B11:315] [MTM B11:345-346] The Countess and Child Hero belong to this company, as do Cyrus Roundhead and apparently Hugh de Turenne, described as a genuine member of its inner historians. [MTM B11:334] [MTM B11:336] Their revision of history extends to erasing places, memories, and human populations, with recent recruits joining extermination hunts. Rule of St. BenedictBenedict of Nursia's monastic rule, composed after 529, with a prologue and seventy-three chapters governing communal life under an abbot: prayer, reading, manual work, silence, meals, and the reception of new members. It became central to Western monasticism, with observance standardized across the Carolingian empire in the early ninth century, and remains a guide for Benedictine communities. At St. Bonaventure's boarding school it is supplied, alongside a Dictionary, Bible, Missal, and Atlas, in the six-boy chambers of St. Martin's Hall where Casey lives. [A:161-162]

Its linguistic entry says a Greek G is likely to become Russian ZH and labels this part of Grimm's law. [A:162-163] Separately, Patrick Stranahan calls the old Russian novelists supreme while objecting that reading them consumes days of a limited life. [A:109]

Sabbath of the mindProfessor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni's name for the mental respite necessary for thought. He tells Hans not to become absorbed in the world's furniture, but to remember humanity's position always at the beginning: fragile as morning dew, yet also manna, a contingent species whose hoped-for realization has a purpose. His precocious proposals make her pray aloud that there might not be another smart child that year; she nevertheless lets him divide the class into mixed groups of four under responsible leaders. She asks Jesus, Mary, and Joseph to remember at her last agony how cheerfully she bore such trials. [MTM B1:11-12]

SabinalTown in Uvalde County, Texas, on Finnegan's itinerary before his strange interval in the chaparral. He is in Uvalde on Monday, then Sabinal, D'Hannis, and Hondo on Tuesday, returning to D'Hannis to look for his old cavalry outfit. [A:202]

SaftiName printed in the Brunhilde's coastal itinerary between Magadar and Mazagan, before Casablanca, Rabat, and Tangier; apparently Safi, the Moroccan Atlantic port. [D:101]

SahirnOne of Gautier's seven youngest goats, a group of three twin pairs and a single kid born to four sisters. Sahirn ends the hebdomadal list Bownee, Luin, Mairt, Keadin, Ordin, Haoine, and Sahirn, apparently representing Saturday (compare Irish Dé Sathairn). [A:194-195] The goat-man is named Gautier, though neighbors mock him as Goat-Ear. [A:196]

SalemCity of the biblical Melchisedech, priest of God Most High; Hebrews interprets his name as righteous king and his kingship of Salem as kingship of peace. The Genesis 14:18 epigraph to Book Two recalls his offering of bread and wine. [MTM B2:38] Lily Koch playfully invokes the “Royal Malarky of Salem” in her metaphor about Duffey and Letitia. [MTM B3:96] Absalom Stein alternates between regarding Duffey as the ancient King of Salem himself and regarding him as a man who shares that patron saint's memories through unusual accord. [MTM B10:291]

SalinaIsland off Sicily named with Filicudi in the narrator's fanciful history of mermaids, who are said to have lived there in the Middle Ages. [D:35]

Sally, Salvation (Sally)Australian street preacher first met by Hans Schultz and Marie Monaghan in a harbor coffee house during the Sydney furlough. She preaches the Second Coming, strums hymns on her guitar, and collects donations in a cup suspended from it. She accepts coffee but rejects brandy, distrusts churches, and claims the gift of tongues. Her appearance and voice are odd and her speech full of catchphrases, yet the narrator calls her electric and authentic. She accepts Marie's offer of a room after insisting on love rather than charity; the three make lasting commitments to one another. Years later Hans finds that an ordinary-looking letter cannot convey her extraordinary Australian voice. [A:7-9] [A:31]

Marie pays her passage to America, and Sally joins the New Orleans undertaking to rebuild the world. [A:147] [MTM B6:198] Dotty's letter calls her a crow and bushwhacker and jokingly complains that Margaret failed to drown her; it is Dotty who calls Marie a filthy Irishman for sending Sally. Mary Virginia insists on keeping her, and Sally has given her remaining money to people less fortunate. [A:147] Her later portrait includes an aggressive bony face and a pewter heart; she cites Chesterfield for leaving good reading for good company. [MTM B7:218]

In the Fifth Contingency she joins the Royal Pop extermination hunts with Margaret and Mary Virginia, reporting that she and the Child Hero have cleared a building's third floor. [MTM B11:336-338] In “The Great Day” she is at the Pelican Press, drinking tea without a cup and sharing the new nakedness. She rejects Duffey's proposal that laughter might save the world, declares salvation outside time impossible, and repeatedly urges him to remove his clothes. [GD:490-492] [GD:496]

A:7-9; A:31; A:147; MTM B6:198; MTM B7:218; MTM B11:336-338; GD:490-492; GD:496

Salvatore, Henry Francis (Henri)Member of the Dirty Five, born in Morgan City, Louisiana, on December 8, 1920, to Lawrence Salvatore and Mary Genevieve Hebert [A:122]. Before the army he works at sea and drives trucks, including for the Schaeffer family’s Red Dog Motor Freight Line, where he meets Mary Virginia. He joins the army on his twenty-first birthday [A:124]. Mary Virginia had been his betrothed; he gives her up for God [MTM B7:214].

After the war he enters seminary and sets his friends to work rebuilding the world. His dream of an endangered boat inspires the journal The Bark, which he names; Finnegan draws its masthead [A:121] [A:124–126]. He is one of its seven founding trustees and directors. After seminary he serves a parish deep in the swamps [MTM B7:214].

Later, as Henri Cardinal Salvatore of New Orleans, he joins the gathering in St. Louis during Duffey’s last days [MTM B12:384–387].

A:122; A:124; MTM B7:214; A:121; A:124–126; MTM B12:384–387

[MTM B2:52] Olga still works there when he returns after seven years away, greeting him as her love, boy, and prince while noticing that he is not quite all back. SantanaName cited in the epigraph attributed to Carmody Overlark's Studies in the Imagination. Santana is credited with wondering why mystics of beautiful, singing thought were facially ugly; the allusion's personal identity remains unverified. [D:271-272]

Santee, CharlesAmerican sergeant from Orange, Texas, one of the three soldiers in Don Lewis's account of a patrol that disappears on October 1, 1944, on Pulau Petir, also called Willy Jones Island. The other two are Corporal Robert Casper and PFC Timothy Lorrigan. Don Lewis claims to have been one of them but withholds which one. [D:44] Santee shoots and wounds the elusive little man called Yokipoki; he and Casper later go ahead and kill him while Lorrigan hangs back. The soldiers lose their way among the island's valleys; after a quarrel Santee and Casper sleep on separate heights while Don Lewis stays below. [D:45-46] Their eventual fates remain uncertain: Don Lewis reports hearing both that the other two were killed and that they returned separately with incredible stories. [D:48]

Santo Spirito!Italian invocation meaning “Holy Spirit!” It punctuates the narrative's loving evocation of Theresa making bread by hand in the house of her impossible twelve-year life with Finnegan. [A:204]

Sao LuisSão Luís, a Brazilian coastal city, named between Belem and Camocim among the Brunhilde's ports before its Atlantic crossing. [D:86]

SarcophagusCoffin-shaped ship in Charles Le Marin's account of a supposed mysterious derelict. He claims to have been one of the seamen who disappeared and were never seen again. [D:243-244] In his story Castleman infiltrates the ship before it leaves Paramaribo, then replaces successive crewmen in port with lookalike dock rats. Le Marin says that he too was replaced and never knew what happened to himself, but subsequently narrates the takeover from among the infiltrators. [D:244] Castleman arrives in the Tercel Hawk, transfers the captain and loyal crew to it, and has them bound, weighted, and drowned. Le Marin hides, then swims ashore in Florida three days later. Castleman reports the Sarcophagus found inexplicably deserted, concealing his theft of its cargo. Whether the switch of Le Marin was ever completed remains doubtful, even to Castleman. Johnny Duckwalk challenges the tale as a version of the Mary Celeste story. [D:245-246]

SardiniaIsland from which the Red Fisters in Margaret Stone's New Orleans account come. She says they threaten to wear her guts as scarves, but also share dawn coffee with her at Messina's or Anthony Ghost's and claim to spare her in order to hear the next morning's shaggy-duck joke. She fears the humorless Slant-Faced Men more. [MTM B7:225]

SatanDevil invoked by Duffey as a comparison in his letter to Casey: people trying to take over the Crock offer him wealth, distribution, and the world's kingdoms, as Satan once offered riches. These offers would make the journal an organ of the infiltrates. [A:39-40] In Show Boat's later letter to Dotty, Casey says that the Seven Devils have found him swept and garnished and want to return. [A:95] Bagby's funeral is also on a Saturday; Duffey and Letitia return to New Orleans on the following Monday. [MTM B8:237]

SatyrusHistorical medical teacher of Galen. After an epigraph attributed to Galen describes the daemon-begotten Tityroi or Satyroi, the narrator asks where Satyrus obtained his name and where Galen obtained his information. The juxtaposition invites a connection between the teacher and the mythical race without asserting that Satyrus was nonhuman. [D:160-161]

Saucerite (from the Big Triangle)An eleven-year-old visitor from the Big Triangle who joins the Argo shortly before the Mooring-Stone conclave. He attends Gaetano Polytech in Balbo City, takes human classmates to his undersea nest in his saucer, and hopes to obtain a chess scholarship to the University of Miami. Herman Hercules calls him “little owl-eyes.” The visitor says that he is real although fingers can pass through him. He calls Earth the “World of the Covenant” and thinks that its inhabitants probably carry “super-seed,” while finding their attainments uneven. He intends to report on the conclave for a small press network [MB:591-592].

Scanlon, AdamPainter associated with Hans Schultz, James Fitzjames, Trinali Peterson, and Francis Schraffenberger. At the driftwood shore he paints seascapes and explains a High Renaissance sky above a sea of the Low Middle Ages, with the Argo suggested by its absence. He likes to talk to an audience while painting. His friends compare him to Leonardo, and Finnegan later calls him an accomplished professional of comparable ability [A:230] [A:233-234] [A:236]. The narrative places Scanlon and Finnegan among the two greatest American artists [MTM B6:199]. Duffey uses Scanlon's painting of Casey, made without Casey's knowledge, for the terrifying televised apparition of Casey's head; Scanlon disliked Casey but was Finnegan's friend [MTM B12:381].

Schaeffer familyOwners of the Red Dog Motor Freight Line, for which Henry Salvatore drives when he meets Mary Virginia Schaeffer [A:124]. The line connects Galveston and Houston with Morgan City and New Orleans, also covering Baton Rouge, Shreveport, Port Arthur, Orange, and Beaumont. Mary Virginia transfers to its New Orleans terminal while working with Dotty on the Bark [MTM B6:198].

A:124; MTM B6:198

Schaeffer, Mary VirginiaMary Virginia Schaeffer, also called Mary Schaeffer or Mary V., is Henry Salvatore’s former fiancée. Archipelago calls her Henry’s girl from Morgan City, Louisiana, and one of the sweetest persons in the world [A:97]; More Than Melchisedech also identifies her with Galveston [MTM B5:157]. Dotty calls her the Saccharine Kid, partly affectionately and partly jealously. Henry gives her up for God while doubting that God is good enough for her; the narrator calls her a bonus beyond price and a valuable working ornament [MTM B7:214]. She attends the St. Louis gathering for Vincent and Teresa’s wedding in May 1946 [MTM B5:171]. She drives with Mary Catherine, Finnegan, Henry, and Duffey through the Illinois towns [A:98], then takes Finnegan, Henry, Duffey, and Dotty to New Orleans in her Ford after the wedding [A:114]. Finnegan includes her among the friends of his ordinary life [D:90]. Her family owns Red Dog Motor Freight, serving Galveston, Houston, Morgan City, New Orleans, Baton Rouge, Shreveport, Port Arthur, Orange, and Beaumont. More Than Melchisedech describes her transferring herself to the New Orleans terminal and working both for the firm and with Dotty on the Bark [MTM B6:198]; Archipelago says she leaves her father’s firm to work with Dotty [A:143]. She helps run the Bark, although she is not one of its designated Seven Pillars of Righteousness [MTM B7:214-215]. One of Duffey’s Animated Marvels, she is the gentle figure who recognizes him at Rounders’ Club [MTM B5:156-157]. Teresa identifies her ancient self as Laonome and describes Duffey as the awakener, rather than the maker, of the old Argo company [MTM B7:233-234]. Mary Virginia remembers fragments and says she hates her ancient name, printed as Laonone in her reply [MTM B7:235]. Stein alternatively proposes that she and the others helped make Duffey what he is, while admitting that on other days he believes Duffey made them [MTM B10:304]. She plays the piano while the group develops the song about Bagby’s liver [MTM B7:226]. Duffey asks her to record The Majesty’s speech so that its recorded, remembered, and inward versions can be compared [MTM B8:241]. After Letitia’s death she says the Glorious Mysteries of the rosary with neighbors and people from the Seaman’s Paper, Jazz Sheet, and Sporting News [MTM B8:253]. Her own reflections in her Duffey Book suggest that he comes from one of the discarded worlds [MTM B10:291-292]. She worries about his wandering, warns that he may not return from a doomsday walk, and recognizes him as a magus [MTM B10:304-305]. In the Royal Pop History episode, her beauty has deepened over decades, while her kindness has acquired a vacant quality. She reports the Dominicans’ warning that the world will end that week [MTM B11:310]. She jokes that she once created more history herself [MTM B11:307]. Seeing broken things that resemble forgotten friends, she questions their destruction; the young Pop countess calls her “the Mary Virginia” and warns that such questions could make her a target. Gray hairs appear in the halo around her face [MTM B11:318]. She nevertheless joins Margaret Stone and Salvation Sally in the exterminating hunts [MTM B11:336-337]. While destroying a half-grown boy, she asks why unimportant people must be destroyed [MTM B11:338]. Later she carries a child she has killed, horrified that its body remains flesh and blood. She refuses to surrender it as trash; Margaret takes it and secretly arranges its burial [MTM B11:342] [MTM B11:344]. When Duffey visits a year ahead of his own time, she greets him at the Pelican Press with affection, exasperation, and a gently burning look. The narrator calls her open, intelligent, kind, and complex [MTM B12:359]. She tells him he has been dead for months and asks why he has not found peace. When he withdraws from that future, she is again demanding his overdue review column [MTM B12:361]. In “Great Day in the Morning,” she joins the Pelican people’s experiments in living without ordinary containment. Laughter collapses her unsupported coffee and burns her [GD:490-491]. She hands Duffey the old Bark containing his Great Day article, treating his satire as fulfilled prediction and calling laughter a blasphemy [GD:492]. The narrator finds her alone sufficiently well formed to go unclothed. She proposes abandoning print for wordless song, faith-painting, and other Great Day communication [GD:494], and looks forward to everyone shedding their skin [GD:495].

Schultz, CeciliaOne of Hans and Marie Schultz's daughters-in-law. She is listed among those probably present during the continuing farewell conversation with Duffey, whose setting shifts among Rounders' Club, Cabramatta Castle, and other St. Louis houses [MTM B12:385].

MTM B12:385

Schultz, John G. (Hans, Who was Orpheus, Aquinas in a T Shirt, John Schultz y Hayden, John Gottfried Schultz, Dutchman, Hanschen, Milwaukee Seidel)John Gottfried Schultz, called Hans, is one of the Dirty Five and their Orpheus [A:38]. He is the only child of John William Schultz and Mary Irene Hayden, born January 2, 1915, at St. Gallen, Wisconsin, in the lake country beyond Rhinelander near Eagle River. Called John until half grown, he remembers his childhood country as a place of splendid sunlight. His father, a nurseryman and the strongest man in St. Gallen, teaches him German, Latin, horticulture, physical strength, and morality. Hans does not rebel against this last education, though his morality is less fierce than his father’s. He attends St. Joseph’s by pony or on foot. His father quarrels with the nuns and Father Baumgartner, demanding Greek, Aquinas, and Albert in the fourth grade [A:207-209]. At fourteen, according to the narrator, Hans leaves for his Wanderjahr with his father’s old friend, Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni. The departure is placed in early spring 1930, a date that does not fit the stated age and birth date. The Professor is presented as the last man who knew everything before knowledge multiplied beyond one mind [A:210-211]. They travel in a truck like an old medicine-show wagon. Kirol teaches rapid calculation and prodigious memory as cerebral athleticism, distinct from thought; he discusses the trees of knowledge, the Tree of Language, and his literal belief in Babel [A:212-213]. Hans learns to calculate the right ascension of likely requested stars, including Alpha Centauri, Procyon, CC624, Kapteyn’s Star, Rigel, Vega, and Betelgeuse. Kirol describes the visible universe as the reverse of Heaven’s tapestry and insists that they are already within eternity [A:214]. Hans spends five or six years with the carnival, traveling several continents, learning fortune-telling or dukkerin and Deep Romany, reading minds, answering unasked questions, and taking the platform to answer any question in the world. He is the sorcerer’s apprentice, still fifty years behind his master. His strongman feats include lifting a horse in a harness, supporting the Donkey Walk across his stomach, and bending coins, horseshoes, and bars [A:218-219]. He is a genuine hypnotist, though without Kirol’s commanding theatrical presence, and performs with Betty Hochstapler and Mabel the bear. Betty’s swindler father had been killed by a wool-hat with his own little mallet [A:217] [A:219]. Hans leaves in the spring of 1935 or 1936, fearing that he will inherit the carnival apparatus, and goes to Bohemia as a way of life rather than a country [A:220-221]. With several thousand dollars saved, he joins a New York circle of young artists in a period both joyful and sad. He gives the scholarly panhandler James Fitzjames money for Jaufre and Brunissende, buys Les Cents Novelles Nouvelles for himself, and shares bagels and beer with him. Fitzjames calls him Dutchman; they then collect Trinali Peterson uptown [A:224-226]. Hans rents a three-room apartment for forty-five dollars a month. To Trinali, ten unencumbered dollars would make him rich [A:227] [A:229]. At Lupido’s he meets Endymeon Ellenbogen, formerly Elmer Eggleton Ellenbogen, who praises him as a good listener [A:236-237]. After Trinali’s death, Hans questions whether the companions were real even in their sudden youth. This Bohemia probably lasts only one spring and summer; it is followed by four, five, or six hidden years, depending on the recension, in which he acquires resources that later allow him to obtain money from a distance [A:240-241]. He enters the Army in the spring of 1941 or 1942 [A:241], serving in the same battery as Vincent, Casey, Henry, and Finnegan [MTM B5:171]. In Sydney he wins the Dominion Rules beer-drinking contest against Joe Bushmaster at the Harbor House. Jimmy Hansen bills him as the Milwaukee Seidel, opposite Bushmaster’s Lion of the South; Absalom Stein presides [A:15] [A:19-23]. Hans attributes his prospects to a pure heart and crafty mind [A:17]. He marries Marie Anna Monaghan at the Annunciation Church in Sydney on February 15, 1943, without Army permission [A:31]. He is reduced from staff sergeant to basic for the marriage, but remains exuberantly happy. In New Guinea he climbs to the cliff people, eats with them, and learns their speech. Finnegan dismisses such reports as liars’ tales; the narrator both calls Hans a liar in those days and affirms the encounters [A:58]. The shore boy Sulem teaches him to distinguish tujuan, life’s direction or orders, from semangat, the soul, and says Finnegan has the latter but lacks the former [A:59-60]. Hans hears Marie’s talk in his mind as well as in her presence [A:16] [A:25]. He writes her a love poem; she protests that it makes her old and answers with stories about her uncle Shakes Pearson. Shakes is a figure in her story, not another listener at their table [A:25-26]. Hans’s unpublished ballad of Li Tai Po belongs to his Chinese period, in which Heine is a strong influence. The simultaneous flute-playing and singing is Li Tai Po’s feat inside that ballad [A:221-223]. Salvation Sally joins Hans and Marie at the coffee house, and the three make lasting commitments to one another. She learns the familiar name Hanschen. Years later Hans marvels at hearing her distinctive speech through a letter whose written words look ordinary [A:8-9]. Henry calls Hans a scholar [A:43]. After the war, Hans and Marie settle in St. Louis, where Hans pursues building business during the wedding gathering of May 1946 [A:97] [MTM B5:171]. Hans becomes one of the original Seven Pillars of Righteousness, the Bark’s trustees and directors. Finnegan labels his masthead portrait Aquinas in a T Shirt [A:121-122] [MTM B7:214]. In a hostile Crock article, Casey calls him Acquinas in a T shirt, remembers his dinner jacket and highball, and reports that the contractor has put his own money and other people’s money, without their knowledge, into the project. These are Casey’s allegations [A:128-129]. Hans hoped to make enough money in three or five years and then turn to other pursuits, but becomes trapped by his success, with his wealth in heavy equipment, developing property, and futuristic paper. Finnegan answers his letters; Marie does not understand his discontent or envy of Finnegan [A:146]. Later the narrator says Hans cannot keep himself divested of money, but has restored a consensus of conscience in one field of business [MTM B8:247]. Finnegan’s absence takes a savor from Hans’s life, more strongly felt than Vincent’s corresponding loss [A:187]. Hans’s early history is largely drawn from his talks with Finnegan during a week on a construction job, probably in summer 1950; their conversations also return to the carnival and the talent of his New York friends [A:207] [A:220] [A:236]. In Duffey’s view Hans is one of his Animated Marvels: a huge, loud, vividly colored holy ox like Aquinas, a mythological thunderhead [MTM B5:158-161]. The narrator calls him big-brained and big-hearted, apparently open yet hard to know [MTM B5:182]. Marie disputes Duffey’s claim of creation, saying that he collects them and supplies their settings; Duffey insists that he makes them [MTM B5:159]. Hans describes the Argonauts as exiles on a mundane shore, awaiting their return to the Argo. In a letter to Marie he remembers sailing as Orpheus, and Teresa identifies him both as Orpheus and as a later manifestation of Faust [MTM B5:178] [MTM B6:186] [MTM B7:234]. Stein reports that Hans experienced a rapport with one of the Brunhilde incidents, without identifying that incident [MTM B6:188]. At Duffey’s last St. Louis gathering, Hans and Marie’s Cabramatta Castle is one of several possible settings for the continuing conversation. Their daughter-in-law Cecilia is probably among those present [MTM B12:385]. Hans believes he has lately sailed on the Argo; Marie says she knows she has. Duffey counts Hans among the five good friends who have helped rebuild the world [MTM B12:387-388]. Hans and Marie supply the ship with sea biscuit [MTM B13:446]. The inherited heading’s form John Schultz y Hayden has not been located in the supplied texts.

Schultz, John WilliamFather of Hans Schultz, a nurseryman in St. Gallen, WI [A:208]; strongest man there; provided Hans intensive education in German, Latin, horticulture, physical culture (dynamic tension, cable exercisers, bar bells, kettle drums, turning pole, flying rings, mile run) [A:208]; quarreled with nuns and Father Baumgartner at St. Joseph's school over the curriculum, advocating for Greek and Aquinas in 4th grade ("'This that you teach, it is little stuff. It is for children,' John William said." "'Well, John is only nine years old.'" "'They should know these things already. Some of them they should know before they are born.'") [A:208-209]. John William had himself traveled with Professor Kirol and wanted Hans to do the same. Schultz, Marie MonaghanMarie Anna Monaghan, Australian wife of Hans Schultz. She describes the Monaghans as an old Irish family established in Sydney for 156 years; to Hans's friends she appears chubby, roguish, tart-talking, and given to brushing her hair from her eyes with the back of her hand [A:6-7]. She and Hans marry secretly at Sydney's Annunciation Church on 15 February 1943 because he lacks army permission; they later settle in St. Louis [A:31] [A:97]. Hans calls her queenly and imagines her speaking in his mind; she calls him Hanschen [A:9] [A:16]. One of Duffey's Animated Marvels, she disputes his account of creating them: he collects them and gives them their settings, she says, while he insists that he makes them [MTM B5:159]. Teresa addresses her with the former Argo company [MTM B7:233]. Marie says she has recently been aboard the ship and wakes refreshed because of it; she and Hans supply its sea biscuit [MTM B12:387] [MTM B13:446].

Seaworthy, Saxon X. (Sindbad, The Old Fox)Eccentric millionaire and owner of the Brunhilde, whom Finnegan first encounters in the narrative as a shabby, unshaven man with the shakes, claiming to be a true eccentric [D:9]. They are sitting outside a bar across from a graveyard; neither initially remembers how he arrived there. Seaworthy has a scar or tattoo inside his left wrist and says that Finnegan has the same mark below the skin. Much older than Finnegan, he has a deeply lined, granite-like face whose apparent dullness has a bottomless depth. He speaks of their shared amnesia as a characteristic of changelings, then remembers his name [D:10-12]. He gives Finnegan a hundred dollars, which Finnegan understands as payment for some service, though he does not know whether past or future. When Papa Devil enters the club, Seaworthy suddenly looks so old that the bargirl says he has aged forty years in three seconds; he quickly regains his composure. He later gives Finnegan another hundred dollars and promises their voyage once unexpected business is settled [D:13-17]. Finnegan also perceives a killer's mark on him, distinct from the wrist mark [D:16-17]. Seaworthy proposes a voyage around the world, and Finnegan and Anastasia are entered on the papers of his diesel yacht Brunhilde [D:11] [D:21]. He is associated with Papa Devil, William Gerecke, and Peter Wirt; Anastasia says that these men control the captain and crew [D:24] [D:30] [D:40]. He conducts mysterious business in coastal ports. According to Anastasia, he owns many ships, undertakes illegitimate work, and profits from transporting people as cargo [D:34] [D:55]. His Greek origin, initially suggested by her remark that his X does not stand for Xavier, is explicitly confirmed by the narrator [D:55] [D:115]. He commissions Finnegan to paint the ship's barroom with the voyages of Sindbad. The narrator identifies Seaworthy with Sindbad and stresses the murkiness behind the supposedly upstanding adventurer [D:59]. Seaworthy recounts a gray, Hindi-speaking dream set in India, where he cannot dispose of an unaccountable corpse that eventually asks who will bury him. The narrator confirms that he has dreamed it for three nights and already understands it [D:72-73] [D:77]. It prompts Finnegan to remember their actual first meeting in the graveyard: Seaworthy was burying a man who stirred again, and silenced him with a shovel blow that broke his skull. Finnegan helped deepen the grave, broke into an older burial, and handled its bones; Seaworthy stood over him with the shovel raised but did not strike. They buried the new corpse above the old one [D:74-76]. Finnegan later confirms that the newly buried man was Papadiabolous. Seaworthy is certain that he killed him, yet cannot account for his apparent return to life. Finnegan knows that the man now accompanying them is a different Papadiabolous, a distinction Seaworthy does not understand [D:82] [D:84-85]. X's later account identifies Seaworthy as a halfbrother of the two Papadiabolous brothers and a leader of the mutiny against Papadiabolous I. X reconstructs the killing as a scheme to open their father's grave for valuable information: Seaworthy shot Papadiabolous I with a small-caliber weapon during the digging, before Finnegan's intervention. X acknowledges uncertainty about parts of this reconstruction [D:286-289]. He also attributes the killing of Papadiabolous II on Naxos to Seaworthy, who still failed to understand the substitution. In X's account Seaworthy is a materialist who keeps Finnegan as a witness to the first killing and a reassurance of his own sanity. X lures him back to the grave with forged notes in Papadiabolous's handwriting and predicts that he will die in the trap that night; this is a prediction, disputed by Finnegan [D:289-291]. Years after the voyage, Finnegan tracks the old fox to a gathering in another island city. Seaworthy now has pherea, neck protuberances described as a sign of aging in his species. Finnegan attacks with both Seaworthy's throat and the group's treasury as his targets, but kills Gerecke instead, hearing Seaworthy laugh as he escapes [D:162-165]. The description of Seaworthy as smarter than the Devil belongs here to the narrator; Finnegan later makes the same comparison to X, while X calls Seaworthy smart and able to feign incapacity [D:165] [D:288-290]. Archipelago reports his oath to have Finnegan killed while expressly warning of improbabilities and incompatible versions in these travel accounts [A:187]. When Finnegan later draws his face, he thinks of Seaworthy as an enemy who will have him killed, then asks whether even this prevents their friendship [A:278]. For comparison, Lafferty's Sindbad, The Thirteenth Voyage develops competing claims to the Sindbad identity. Master Mariner and Master Spy Essindibad Copperbottom, a citizen of Kentauron Mikron, calls himself the original Sindbad; his rival John Scarlatti Thunderson concedes that Essindibad possessed the identity by birth and inheritance before John replaced him through trickery. Essindibad says that his thirteen voyages, including the present one, were diplomatic or espionage adventures on seven planets, whose coded logs accidentally reached Earth as fantastic stories. His wife is Grand-Dame Of-The-Seven-Musics Goodlife Tumblehome, whom he says accompanied four previous voyages, dying and returning on two of them. He instructed spies for the Kentauron Foreign Office, including the later Citizen Heifritz. His present mission begins with a commission to find the reborn Harun and bring him back to Kentauron (Sindbad, The Thirteenth Voyage, PDF viewer pp. 6-7, 10-14, 28-29, 74). John, from Chicago's North Side, uses open-ended analytics to build an Almost-Anything machine and travels to the Baghdad he calls the Arabian Middle Ages, adopting the espionage name Ali ben Raad. Buried alive beside his apparently dead bride Blue Moon, he discovers that she is a mechanical woman who can be revived by winding her mechanism; she subsequently explains that she is a spirit inhabiting it. He describes this as an improved version of Sindbad's Fourth Voyage. He also creates an alternative Kentauron past for himself, including a prior marriage to Grand-Dame Tumblehome, which Essindibad does not remember. Blue Moon invokes a purported Arabian proverb making Sea-Weed growing at the body's shouka, or bifurcation, the proof of the true Sindbad. She removes Essindibad's Sea-Weed and implants it on John, who then claims the identity (Sindbad, The Thirteenth Voyage, PDF viewer pp. 7, 61-74). The competing accounts make this criterion unstable. Essindibad calls John false; Scheherazade inspects John's genuine Sea-Weed but calls it an implant and him a forgery. Blue Moon insists that the transplant makes John genuine and that Essindibad cannot regrow it. Scheherazade says that she originally wrote voyages of Slattery the Sailor, named for Joe Slattery of Galveston, and that oral storytellers changed the name to Sindbad. It is Essindibad, commenting on John's account, who says that John's drivel reflects facts upon which Scheherazade builds stories (Sindbad, The Thirteenth Voyage, PDF viewer pp. 78, 82-86). Caliph Al-Amin commissions Essindibad to inspect and protect hell's iron doors, invoking the Sea-Weed criterion although Essindibad has already lost his growth. A hostile False Ship subsequently tests him, declares him false, and identifies the approaching John as true. Essindibad and his wife survive their captivity aboard that ship; Scheherazade, John, and Blue Moon help defeat their captors, and the party inspects the doors before returning to Baghdad. Mamun's later denunciation of a false Sindbad attacks Al-Amin's commissioned traveler, Essindibad, rather than naming John (Sindbad, The Thirteenth Voyage, PDF viewer pp. 90-110, 118-119). Finally, Essindibad's wife imprisons him in a bottle. His closing journal reports Sea-Weed growing on him again, which he takes as proof that he has regained the identity and John has lost it. His opening account claims a happy retirement on Kentauron, but the closing journal leaves his escape precarious: corrosive fish food is making a hole in the bottle, and he may escape or die. The renewed Sea-Weed does not by itself establish a completed happy ending (Sindbad, The Thirteenth Voyage, PDF viewer pp. 6-7, 149-155).

Serpent (2)Snakes occur as creatures, figures of speech, and images in Finnegan's travels. The Chosky Bottoms are said to harbor eighteen-foot bull snakes [D:274]; the killers closing on Don Lewis in Tangier are compared to snakes entering a burrow [D:106]; and small snakes inhabit the Naxos ruins [D:68]. The narrative's earthly Paradise still has snakes, which eventually drive Finnegan and his companions out [D:235]. Finnegan's sonnet imagines an ancient sacred snake biting the world [D:133]. The Flying Serpent is a name of the Argo when Willy Jones sails her in the Moluccas [MTM B13:405].

Seven Lost YearsThe seven years of Duffey's disappearance from St. Louis, lived aboard the Argo in nonconsecutive time. Intervening land adventures do not count toward either the seven years or the years of his life [MTM B2:71]. The Sea of the Seven Lost Years has scattered channels and shores, some apparently inland; Duffey continues to encounter stray days from it [MTM B13:406]. He can reenter it from shores corresponding to different ages of his life, becoming young again on leaving shore [MTM B13:445]. Within their own context these are the Seven Golden Years [MTM B10:300]. Duffey collects seven representations of Christ during the lost years and sends them back to himself [MTM B3:103-104]. The talisman given to Gabriel Szymansky for his future son belongs to the hidden years; the Wisconsin, Morgan City, New Orleans, Galveston, Chicago, and Australian gifts are placed in those years or possibly earlier [MTM B4:120-121].

Shaw, George Bernard (1856--1950)Irish playwright, critic, and Fabian pamphleteer, author of Pygmalion, Man and Superman, and Saint Joan; recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature for 1925, awarded in 1926. Marie's “Shaw” is a joke about her uncle Shamus McGregor [A:28]. Casey's notebook uses Shaw and The Quintessence of Ibsenism to argue for reading original works instead of accounts of them [A:166]. Shaw is among the writers contributing to the ideological mixture in The Answer [MTM B4:114]. The Postscript names him among famous people whom Havelock Ellis regarded as no more innately able than obscure people [PS:476].

Sheehan, ElmoOne of the “slippery people” in the Duffeys' Chicago circle [MTM B3:100]. He defends Chicago-hot jazz as “our kind of worthlessness” and is among the Fleshpot Row company from which Duffey eventually withdraws [MTM B4:126-127]. He accompanies Rollo McSorley among the portfolio man's supporters during the attempt to blackmail Duffey into admitting their group to the Crock [MTM B4:140].

MTM B3:100; MTM B4:126-127; MTM B4:140

ShelenoThe Romany term glossed as “Gypsy green” in Hans's reflections on the color of Marie Monaghan's eyes. It is compared with Greek and French color words as he wonders whether her green eyes have classical precedents [A:24].

A:24

Shenandoah SagaOne of Endymeon Ellenbogen's three published novels, issued through a subsidy press at his expense [A:237].

A:237

Shire, TomAustralian soldier whom Finnegan, Vincent, and Hans befriend in Sydney in 1943. Initially large and fair, he and Freddy Castle are said to be unmistakably Australian. Tom explains Australian knife-and-fork habits [A:4-5]. He and Freddy disguise Finnegan and Vincent in winter tunics and digger hats to enter a wet canteen; Tom gives Vincent a disastrous haircut and inspires the anti-Yank affidavit Finnegan signs [A:11] [A:13]. Tom and Freddy are the trusted judges of the Schultz-Bushmaster drinking contest and join the later pub crawl [A:15] [A:20] [A:23]. When the Sergeant revisits Sydney and meets them at the Plaza Hotel, Tom is small and dark instead of large and fair, although otherwise unchanged [A:88]. Finnegan includes him among the familiar people of his normal life and later sketches his face [D:90] [A:278].

A:4-5; A:11; A:13; A:15; A:20; A:23; A:88; D:90; A:278

Shirley IsraelOne of the “slippery people” in the Duffeys' Chicago circle [MTM B3:100]. She promotes Fleshpot Row and joins the hissing when Demetrio Glauch, then Duffey, leave in disgust [MTM B4:126-127]. Her increasingly potent mixed drink inflames the party that challenges Duffey to move a mule by magic [MTM B4:129-130]. Her salon is reputed to rival the Duffeys', and her circle wants to exploit Duffey's magic [MTM B4:137]. A compromising photograph of her with Duffey is used in the blackmail attempt against him; the narrative calls the encounter an entrapment or badger-game trick [MTM B4:139-140].

MTM B3:100; MTM B4:126-127; MTM B4:129-130; MTM B4:137; MTM B4:139-140

Show-BillWeekly show-business paper printed by the Pelican Press on Friday mornings. The Star and Garter in St. Louis advertises in it until the theatre closes. Teresa produces an issue herself containing an advertisement for the Decatur Street Opera House, whose existence Dotty initially denies [MTM B7:230].

MTM B7:230

Shrake, Jessica (Princess of Porcelain)Earlier heading that misspelled the artist’s surname. See Shrike, Jessica (Princess of Porcelain).
Shrike, Jessica (Princess of Porcelain)Artist listed among those whose work Duffey sells in New Orleans, called “that princess of porcelain” [MTM B6:198-199].

Silas WhitericeSee Whiterice, Silas.
SindbadVoyager of the Nights with whom Saxon X. Seaworthy is identified. Finnegan paints scenes of Sindbad's voyages in the Brunhilde barroom; the narration hints at a darker Sindbad behind the familiar story [D:53] [D:59]. Anastasia becomes the dead wife of the fourth voyage and Marie Courtois the wife of the seventh, who expects a happy ending. Marie says Seaworthy has traveled, traded, and suffered shipwrecks on a still greater scale [D:61-62]. The talking oak aboard the Argo says that Abd-Aliah of the Sea sold the ship to Sindbad of El-Basrah [MTM B13:404].

D:53; D:59; D:61-62; MTM B13:404

Sindbad LoungeDrinking bar aboard the Argo, decorated to suggest sunlit underwater space filled with fish and golden sands. Its oceanic paintings were made by Count Finnegan when the ship was called the Brunhilde, long after Sindbad's ownership [MTM B13:404].

MTM B13:404

SingularsParticular beings considered individually. Don Lewis applies the term to furtive men like himself and asks whether they have been forgotten “behind God's back”: “Does God have knowledge of singulars?” [D:48].

D:48

Sinhor DedosRio alias of Amoy's master Ali hen Taife, also called Lord Peter Petrof and Count von Vinger. Ignatius Ti's story glosses it as “Mr. Fingers.” The master takes the gems Amoy steals and finally cuts the bird's throat to recover a blue diamond it cannot disgorge [A:81].

A:81

SirnukaPeople among whom men bear children, according to Biloxi Brannagan’s account. He claims to have witnessed the births; Finnegan gives this story little credit [D:206-207].

SirosIsland where, according to Brannagan, small shops sell mermaids' hair brought from Naxos; he names Tinos and Kea as other outlets [D:207].

Sisler, GretchenA sturdy girl, almost nine, who recognizes Duffey's magic in St. Louis and calls herself his fan. She suggests that he make a gold coin rather than sparks, takes the five-dollar piece he produces, and says her mother has just lost her restaurant job. She promises to ensure that they meet again [MTM B2:39]. She later kisses him goodbye with the other visitors at Rounders' Club [MTM B2:70]. In the Chicago years he still loves her and visits St. Louis, while she writes to remind him that she is no longer so young [MTM B4:110].

MTM B2:39; MTM B2:70; MTM B4:110

Sisler, LucilleMother of Gretchen Sisler. After losing a restaurant job, she goes to work at Duffey's Rounders' Club in St. Louis. Though only twenty-eight, she is jokingly called his mother-in-law because Gretchen claims him as hers [MTM B2:39] [MTM B2:49]. Gretchen arranges Lucille's work and dates with Duffey, but the encounters end with Duffey and the daughter together on the family sofa [MTM B3:78]. Lucille and Olga Sanchez take turns carrying Duffey on their shoulders when “The King Shall Ride” is played, and both are his devoted partisans [MTM B2:52].

MTM B2:39; MTM B2:49; MTM B3:78; MTM B2:52

Sister Mary MerhioneA nun interviewed in the topless bar where she works, in a clipping preserved in the scrapbook Duffey reads. She defends her work in a “gentle and forgiving voice” and sells reprints of her article “Topless Before God” from Paralplegic Church Today [MTM B8:252].

Sister Mary SabinaSee Sabina, Sister Mary.
Sister MarysUnverified nickname. The earlier glossary attributes Sister Marys to Marie Monaghan as a name for Hans Schultz’s eyes; the cited passage does not establish that usage.
Situation BitPhrase attributed to the preliminary “Paean” of Archipelago in the earlier glossary. The required preliminary page is absent from the supplied copy; both the wording and the proposed connection with situational ethics remain unverified.
SjahrirName attached to the brown stone statues which, in Brannagan's account, are people petrified by Seti darts and the preparations in which they are dipped [D:206].

SkawinePlace near Krakow, Poland, mentioned in X's account of Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch Papadiabolous Chortovitch's birth in 1830. X places the birth in a hayfield near Krakow, possibly nearer Skawine [D:278].

Skinny ArtDuffey's dismissive description of Edward Ranwick's work. Ranwick has already gained a reputation at art school, but his art leaves Duffey unimpressed [MTM B2:58].

Skinny CountessDescription Charlotte Garfield uses for Sebastian Hilton’s companion at the Colony Club, naming her as one of the psychics present [MTM B3:93]. See Countess Margaret, The (Margaret Hochfelsen).

SkyllaGreek word used by Anastasia as an insult for Marie Courtois. Anastasia tells Finnegan that she cannot say directly what Marie really is, but that the Greek word is skylla [D:33]. The modern Greek skýla means a female dog and is also an insult for a woman.

SlaintheIrish toast meaning “health,” used by Finnegan when drinking with Casey and Henry after their return through the jungle to the bivouac. He then takes another drink as Solli the Italian and says “salute” [A:44].

A:44

Slant faced boys (Three)Recurring enemies of Duffey, first seen when he is about six. Two years older and larger than he is, they have slack mouths, slanted faces, and knives. They come to the house with the Prisoner John Window intending to kill him, and return to wait for him inside it [MTM B1:12-13]. Duffey later supposes that they caused the house fire by overturning a lamp [MTM B1:14]. At about eleven he escapes their ambush in a timothy field with help from his kit-fox, but is badly knifed and nearly bleeds to death [MTM B1:19-20]. He sees them again on his school roof after they nearly kill Sebastian Hilton [MTM B1:36]. Mary Louise says they are Bagby's principal brawling opponents [MTM B2:62]. Bagby later says that he and Duffey have each killed one, yet three, or many groups of three, remain. Dotty Yekouris reports their appearance in Flame Man, White Avenger, and Captain Justice [MTM B7:225]. Flame Man supplies their names, Amraphel, Arioch, and Thadal; the narrative identifies them as three crooked kings and followers of Chodorlahomor [MTM B7:227-228]. Duffey reports seeing them kill Sebastian and carve the Devil's tetragrammaton on his chest in a detached experience, but his subsequent inspection finds that Sebastian died of plague and that the corresponding marks are sores, not knife cuts [MTM B7:226]. When they threaten Margaret Stone and her singing companions with switchblades at the Majesty's assembly, Quarter rowdies remove the winders from their backs and they collapse with racing gears and stuttering sprockets [MTM B8:244]. Duffey later sees them as the Laughing Prince's bully boys in the desert sequence [MTM B13:440].

MTM B1:12-13; MTM B1:14; MTM B1:19-20; MTM B1:36; MTM B2:62; MTM B7:225; MTM B7:227-228; MTM B7:226; MTM B8:244; MTM B13:440

Slant-Faced Men (SFM)See Slant faced boys (Three).
Slavic language pressPress described in Casey's polemic against The Bark. Casey accuses Gabrielovitch of filling it with comments favorable to Draja Mihailovitch and attacks on Tito and the “major Slavic ally” [A:129].

A:129

Slick, ShermanSherman Slick, one of the friends of scientific bent in Duffey and Letitia’s North Chicago circle. The roster lists him immediately before Silas and Maud Whiterice [MTM B3:99].

Slit TrenchOne of the named valleys in Don Lewis's account of the wartime pursuit involving PFC Lorrigan, Sergeant Santee, and Casper. They know these valleys but become lost in a different, unrecognized one [D:45-46].

Sloe ginLiqueur made with sloes, the fruit of the blackthorn. In his high-school notebook Casey says that drinking it marks one as an adolescent; he and Hinnegan have moved on to whisky and hot water [A:165].

Sloppy Joe'sFinnegan and his three companions' joking name for the Imperial Bar, or Royal, at Basse-Terre in their Terrestrial Paradise. The establishment is clean and even fastidious; the friends are Charles Le Marin, Don Barnaby, and Johnny Duckwalk [D:235-236].

SlurryUnverified name. The earlier glossary proposes that Slurry is a misprint for Lucille Sisler, Gretchen’s mother. No passage establishes that identification.
Smith, GunboatEnglish bulldog whom Duffey trusts to detect the familiar turning strange. Following Father Brown's advice, Duffey brings him from the Old Wooden Ship Tavern in Galveston, where he is Bulldog-in-Residence, to help protect the Argo from the Man of Mystery. Gunboat and Kasmir Gorshok growl at one another [MTM B13:458]. After their failure to stop the future unfolding around the Antichrist, Gunboat speaks about returning and trying again. Rebuked by Brannagan for talking, he gives a final growl and fades out after Brannagan [MTM B13:463].

Smith, JoeVagabond painter who begins the Dotty O'Toole triptych in Galveston; Finnegan later finishes it. Smith's work has a disturbing excellence, but he never completes anything, and leaves more than a dozen unfinished masterpieces with art dealer Duffey [MTM B6:198].

MTM B6:198

SmokehouseRegular at the Old Wooden Ship tavern, grouped with Russ, Bill “Buffalo Chips” Dugan, Bob, and Charleyhorse Heckel [D:215] [D:220]. Smokehouse and Bill work at the same garage. Because the proprietor confuses them, one quits and they thereafter work alternate days under one job and split the pay. This halves their earnings but doubles their time off [D:220].

SmoochKissing sound in Beth Keegan's playful “telephone operator's kiss”: “Smooch, smooch, smooch, your three minutes are up, please” [MTM B2:60].

SmyrnaOne of the places where Ifreann Gregorovitch lives in X's account [D:280]. X also identifies it as the birthplace of Gregory McIfreann Papadiabolous I, the Asiatic of the two sons he calls twins [D:285].

D:280; D:285

SocratesAthenian philosopher, conventionally dated about 469-399 BC, remembered for examining ethical questions through conversation and exposing unrecognized ignorance. He left no writings; Plato, Xenophon, and Aristophanes provide differing portraits of him. Tried on charges involving impiety and corruption of the young, he was executed by drinking hemlock. His life and death became enduring models of philosophical inquiry. In Archipelago, Captain Sammy compares the serious, dedicated, kindly Absalom Stein with his idea of Socrates, while Casey rejects Sammy's admiration for Stein [A:67].

A:67

Socrates (470--399 BC)Earlier heading gave an approximate birth year as an exact date. See Socrates.
Solli y Gordonasco, SignorName Gertrude Brannagan uses when calling Finnegan to a telephone call. After he takes it, the caller sounds like a man speaking from a badly ventilated grave. Finnegan recognizes X [D:208].

D:208

Solli, Giulio (The Monster Forgotten, Monster Giulio)Giulio Solli, father of Giovanni (John) A. Solli, or Finnegan, Giacomo (Jake), and Patricia (Patti); his wife is Mary McCracken [A:173]. Dark, powerful, and carelessly put together, he is the monster who becomes Duffey's first customer. He works on riverboats, ocean ships, and docks [MTM B2:41-43]. Bagby knows him as a troubled visitor who appears about once a year. Giulio asks Duffey for something to help an unborn son and receives a talisman; Bagby associates him with the Gadarene Swine and their song [MTM B2:47-48]. Giulio says a poor man's devil afflicts him and returns with seven worse devils whenever expelled [MTM B3:106]. The Countess identifies him as a Teras, and he agrees. He reports holding the talisman to his wife's belly and placing it in his Italian son's hands at birth [MTM B3:107]. The account of Duffey's talismans says Giulio alone understood from the beginning to apply it at conception and during gestation, then give it to the special son at birth [MTM B4:120-121]. Finnegan is explicitly identified as Monster Giulio's son [MTM B5:161]. Finnegan recalls swamp journeys with him and the extraordinary animal calls he whittled from tupelo-gum: calls for panthers, alligators, devil-fish, swamp-boas, hairy men, and white sharks [MTM B5:174]. Patricia derides Giulio as a poor dock worker and literally antediluvian, reporting that someone called him the Monster Forgotten [A:174-175]. Years after Giulio's death, Finnegan sees him shabby and sad at a railway station and takes him to a beer place. He reproaches his father's work, drinking, poverty, and marriage, then tells him how difficult things became after his death. Giulio silently cries and leaves. Finnegan at last understands that his father loved them and did all he could, while the family derided and possibly killed him [A:244-245]. In The Devil Is Dead, Finnegan reflects that Giulio belonged to a monstrous apparatus and died as the Monster Forgotten [D:229].

Solli, JakeGiacomo Solli, Finnegan's brother, who has become Jake, a smooth-talking Irishman driving taxis and steering tourists. The narrative says he cares little for his Italian brother except to borrow money and make jokes about him [A:174].

A:174

Solli, John A.See Finnegan (John A. Solli).
Solli, Patricia aka Patti, Patrish (Patrish)Sister of Finnegan and Giacomo (Jake) Solli [A:173]. An acrobatic dancer with striking, weird, comical beauty, she moves with sudden strength like Finnegan's and is often with him. Her intimacy with Doppio di Pinne unsettles Dotty; Patti calls him her brother too and says he is the same person as Finnegan [A:174]. Her accounts of their childhood contradict Finnegan's. She calls their father a poor dock worker and literally antediluvian [A:174]. Only a year older than Finnegan, she says she partly raised him but always felt him a stranger or changeling. She defends him as incapable of wrongdoing and says they came from Irish Channel, despite his claim to a Quarter upbringing [A:175]. Finnegan includes his sister Patty among those friendly to him in his normal life [D:90].
