SolomonBiblical king of Israel, traditionally placed in the tenth century BC, noted for wisdom and wealth and for building the Temple in Jerusalem. First Kings also connects his later conduct with the coming division of his kingdom. In Archipelago, the men of Solomon and Hiram take three years on the journey to Ophir [A:16]. Duffey claims to have sat with Solomon in Kings' conclaves [MTM B5:166]. Bagby invokes Solomon when asking how to choose between good jazz and good conversation [MTM B7:220].

A:16; MTM B5:166; MTM B7:220

Son of the DevilX's translation of Chortovitch. He says that this name has been softened on the Devil's gravestone to Bogovitch, which he translates as “son of God” [D:277-278].

“Sonnets and Succotash”One of the nine projected volumes under which Endymeon Ellenbogen has classified his poetry. He says the poetry remains uncollected and unpublished [A:237].

Sore-Head GulchOne of the named valleys in Don Lewis's account of the wartime pursuit involving PFC Lorrigan, Sergeant Santee, and Casper. They know these valleys but become lost in a different, unrecognized one [D:45-46].

SorensenOne of Papadiabolous I's revolutionary associates in X's account. X says that several members of this group are rumored to be Papadiabolous's half-brothers, without specifying which ones [D:286].

Sorrell, JoeCab driver who takes Finnegan and Anastasia to the dock where the Brunhilde is berthed [D:21]. He joins them for a drink aboard [D:22]. Papa Devil orders all three off the ship, and Sorrell drives them away [D:23].

SoufriereName required for a volcano in the narrator's list of conditions for a Terrestrial Paradise: among its history, climate, ships, and friends, the place must have “a volcano named Soufriere” [D:237]. Soule, Jacob (Deutero-Finnegan, Finnegan Image)Young painter whom Stein calls Deutero-Finnegan. He resembles Finnegan slightly, leaves pictures on consignment with Duffey, and paints work resembling Finnegan's orange period. During the Fifth Contingency he momentarily seems to be Finnegan himself and speaks of Dotty, who disappeared before Soule arrived [MTM B11:343]. Named Jacob Soule, he joins Duffey's party at Girardeau's [MTM B11:344]. Though accepted as splendid and noetic, he voluntarily puts his hands into the testing ashes outside the Opera House. They burn with a yellow, then orange flame; he refuses the Marshal's invitation to withdraw and insists on being human even if he must die for it [MTM B11:347-348]. The thunder colt kills him in the arena, where Margaret Stone remarks on the orange color of his blood before the colt kills her too [MTM B11:351]. After Duffey returns, Soule is dead in the ordinary setting as well, one of at least two deaths brought back from the splendid Devildom [MTM B12:355].

Sour JohnSee Sourwine, John (Sour John).
Sourwine, John (Sour John)John Sourwine, called Sour John, is one of the resident regulars at the Old Wooden Ship [D:215-216], celebrated for his storytelling [D:221]. In Don Barnaby's account of the Juju Joy Pill, Barnaby considers Sour John the world's unhappiest man and tries to share his new happiness with him [D:251]. Sour John refuses the pill, preferring a hangover to Barnaby's condition. He takes Barnaby to the ship, straps him into his bunk, and stays until the ship sails [D:252].

D:215-216; D:221; D:251; D:252

Southern ComfortWhiskey liqueur among the bottles in Finnegan's shoulder-bag when he leaves D'Hannis on foot [A:202]. The noon-day devils appear particularly after it and his Old Crow have run out [A:205].

Spanish StairsThe Spanish Steps in Rome. In My-Heart-Disconsolate, the severed head of the Cap-Stone Paul the Eleventh is displayed there on a pike before the Last Conclave; it continues to speak while being mutilated by its tormentors [MB:561-562].

SpartanThe narrative's description of the life led by the group around the Pelican Press. Gabrielovitch does not adopt their Spartan life: because The Bark pays nothing and he likes money, he takes paying work elsewhere [A:126].

Speaking Oak of DodonaSource of the piece of wood Finnegan tells a fellow traveler he stole from the prow of a ship he once sailed. Asked whether the wood bears writing, he answers, “Not all the time,” and identifies it as part of the Speaking Oak of Dodona [A:244].

Special DoveProdigious dove with a wingspan exceeding ten feet. Its cote survives aboard the Argo among the relics and identifying objects of the Great Ship [MTM B13:403-404].

SphereCasey's high-school notebook gives the volume of a sphere as its diameter cubed, multiplied by pi and divided by six: V = πd³/6. Casey adds that he was the only one who knew it that day [A:163].

Its red eyes resemble locomotive headlights and its movement shakes the web with thunder [A:61]. Hans attacks with a Roman sword, which seems oddly late for a creature associated in the narration with an older Greek or Hindu myth [A:62].

Spider's webWeb Hans climbs in a dream to reach a giant spider in a cave shaft. Its threads are cables eight inches thick; before he reaches the web's center, the bottom of the shaft has dwindled to a point and disappeared [A:61].

A:61

SpinkOne word in X's coded telephone sequence, between Vlissinger and Tineo. The recipient evidently has trouble with the codebook, and X says Y has one [D:184].

Splendid AnimationsName for Duffey's living, talismanic creations, including Finnegan, Hans, Henry, Vincent, Casey, Dotty, Marie Monaghan, Mary Virginia, Teresa Piccone, Absalom Stein, Mr. X, and Mary Catherine Carruthers [MTM B5:161-162] [MTM B8:261]. Mary Catherine has seemed the least of them, despite her closeness to Duffey [MTM B8:261]. The Fourth Contingency says that all have sailed, are sailing, and will continue to sail on the Argo, even when they believe themselves engaged elsewhere [MTM B10:300]. Patrick Plunket challenges Duffey's account of making them, saying he only woke them [MTM B12:391]. The Countess Margaret is separately described as an Animation of someone whose identity remains unclear [MTM B7:215].

MTM B5:161-162; MTM B8:261; MTM B10:300; MTM B12:391; MTM B7:215

Splendid PeopleName claimed by the supposedly new, noetic species in Duffey's Fifth Contingency. Cyrus Roundhead declares that they are the splendid, final persons and denies that they were ever human [MTM B11:345] [MTM B11:350]. Their presentation at the Decatur Street Opera House includes the slaughter of human victims [MTM B11:349-351]. Duffey returns from his time among these people with a jaundiced view of his city [MTM B12:355-356].

MTM B11:345; MTM B11:350; MTM B11:349-351; MTM B12:355-356

Splitting ImageTerm from popular lore invoked by Dr. Saul Rafelson for living images that may have split off from Duffey into independent existence. He treats this as one possibility alongside psychic projections or real people drawn into Duffey's orbit [MTM B4:146]. Rafelson says he has examined two flesh-and-blood images, and distinguishes the twelve young people Duffey believes he made from his “shadows” [MTM B4:147].

SponsorOne of the godparent terms used when the narrative asks whether Duffey's relation to talismanic Casey is more than ordinary sponsorship. It compares that relation with non-species sponsors such as fairy godmothers, without settling whether these are equivalent to a sorcerer's relation to his creatures [MTM B4:119]. Duffey had given Casey's father a talisman before Casey's conception or birth [MTM B4:120].

MTM B4:119; MTM B4:120

Spook placeA haunted or uncanny place, the sense Finnegan reports Old Pop Potter giving to Chosky Bottoms. Such a place is always just over the next ridge or in the next river valley: home to the man-killing panther, swamp ghost, masked riders, giant coons and fish, Bloody Mulligans, eighteen-foot bull snakes, and the story of the Northern Platoon lost in quicksand [D:274].

D:274

Sporting NewsWednesday sporting paper printed on the Pelican Press, one of the paying jobs supporting The Bark [A:118] [MTM B7:212]. Bello Belonki is associated with it in More Than Melchisedech [MTM B7:213]. Archipelago instead names Berny Cacciatore in connection with the sporting news sheet [A:126].

A:118; MTM B7:212; MTM B7:213; A:126

Sporting News SheetDescription of the Pelican Press sporting paper. See Sporting News.
SportsNewspaper department that Jimmy Hansen says should cover the Bushmaster-Schultz drinking contest. A novice crime reporter, he explains that Sports is almost always unavailable so early in the day [A:18].

A:18

Square mileMeasure illustrating the extraordinary density of Black Papua. Casey invents the phrase "Coefficient of Scenic Density," and the narration describes a square mile with over fifty waterfalls, eighteen hundred feet of elevation change, pools less than ten yards across and three times as deep, and dozens of miles of caves. Its deliberately extravagant abundance includes a thousand kinds of lizards, a million kinds of birds, and three dozen families speaking three languages, with a fourth tribe possibly still undiscovered [A:36].

A:36

SquidAnimal used by Margaret Stone to characterize Stein, whom the narration calls neither fish nor flesh: she says he is some sort of squid [A:132]. Squids also appear in the shore song Finnegan sings to Elena; she understands their curling as relaxing for the night [A:276].

A:132; A:276

SquirrelsIn Marie Monaghan's story of Shakes Pearson, squirrels repeatedly eat his poems, written on bark with oak-ball juice; his last note asks Miriam to do something about them [A:25-26]. Asked whether Australia has squirrels, Marie answers, "Not that I know of," and admits that calling them wallabies would have complicated her story [A:27]. At the dump Finnegan briefly guesses that the unseen small animals might be squirrels, before recognizing rats by their smell [A:177]. Duffey's childhood narration describes coal-black squirrels in the Council Bluffs park, claiming that they occur nowhere else, and contrasts Iowa's red squirrels and St. Louis's gray ones with Boston, where people supposedly do not know what a squirrel is [MTM B1:9] [MTM B1:17].

A:25-26; A:27; A:177; MTM B1:9; MTM B1:17

St. Angela Orba OrphanageChicago refuge Charlotte Garfield uses when she needs to go to ground. She says that all but two of the sisters think she is a little girl; the two who know what she is provide commitment papers and love [MTM B3:86].

MTM B3:86

St. AnthonyAnthony the Abbot (251-356), an Egyptian ascetic. The narration compares the beautiful, treacherous temptations of this saint with the amazons, female gladiators, Cretan girl bullfighters, and circus acrobats in Casey Szymansky's second imaginary world, adding that they might even be the same girls [A:157].

A:157

St. AugustineNorth African bishop and Latin Church Father (354-430). Casey invokes the "early Augustine" when challenging Finnegan's attempt to dissociate himself from his sins; the quoted belief that another kind of being sinned within him is a former belief, not Augustine's mature doctrine of original sin [A:154]. Patrick Stranahan recommends reading Augustine once in youth for background [A:109]. In Ignacio's story, Joseph of Maintz carries Augustine's writings in his moon-bound chamber alongside Scripture, the Missal, Jerome, and Pliny [A:271]. The narrator of The Devil Is Dead, rather than Papa Devil, says Augustine seems to refer to the worm in the forbidden fruit [D:264]. Notes near the end of More Than Melchisedech attribute to him the statement that eddying thoughts have no part in the saints' vision of the world [MTM B13:469]. The Confessions (397-400) recount his life and conversion in a sustained address to God. The City of God (413-426) interprets human history through the conflicting loves of God and self. His treatment of original sin, grace, free will and the Church profoundly influenced Western theology. He adapted Neoplatonic philosophy to Christian thought and is venerated as a Doctor of the Church. The former belief invoked by Casey comes from Confessions V.10.18, where Augustine rejects his earlier excuse for sin. The later note appears to echo Summa theologiae I.10.3, which cites Augustine on the saints’ unchanging vision of the Word; the supplied novel reads “world.”

A:154; A:109; A:271; D:264; MTM B13:469

St. BarthelemyName in Angela's list of seven false or shoal passages through the Antilles, places where wrecks piled up or should have piled up [D:260].

D:260

St. Benedict of Nursia (c.480--547)Author of the Rule of St. Benedict, one of the books on the shelves of Casey’s room at St. Bonaventure’s [A:162]. Benedict (c.480-547) came from Norcia in Umbria. After living as a hermit at Subiaco, he organized monastic communities and settled at Monte Cassino in 529. His Rule joined common prayer, sacred reading, manual work, obedience and care for others in a disciplined communal life. Its moderation and capacity for local adaptation helped it spread; it became the prevailing monastic rule in much of medieval Western Europe. Benedictine monasteries subsequently supported learning, manuscript copying, agriculture, hospitality and missionary work. Benedict is venerated as the Father of Western Monasticism, though he did not found a centralized Benedictine order. Paul VI proclaimed him patron of Europe in 1964.

A:162

St. Bonaventure'sBoarding school forty miles from Casey Szymansky's home, where he attended high school [A:161]. Its Towers, dominated by boys from Gregory Hall, inspired a rival manuscript paper called the Chambers among the St. Martin's boys; Casey later traced the idea for the Crock to those school papers [A:167].

A:161; A:167

St. BrandonIrish voyager saint, generally known as Brendan (traditionally c. 484-c. 577). The Devil Is Dead attributes an epigraph about unredeemable creatures and long sublunar lives to "Saint Brendon, Trachtas" [D:130]. The Argo's history says he sailed her as the Land of Behest from Ireland to America, encountered the great fish Jascoyne, and carried Judas [MTM B13:404]. Brannagan declares that he was and still is St. Brandon of Ireland [MTM B13:413].

D:130; MTM B13:404; MTM B13:413

St. ChristopherName Ignacio gives for St. Kitts. He calls it a landfall of Cristobal Colon and one of five little Leeward Islands, while Finnegan has his own imagined paradise in mind [A:272]. Finnegan later considers going to St. Kitts but admits that the name is loosely applied, at least by himself, to several islands [D:273-274]. See also St. Kitts (St. Christopher).

A:272; D:273-274

St. Christopher (3rd century? AD)Ignacio identifies the island of St. Kitts as St. Christopher [A:272]. The saint’s story supplies background to that name, rather than a biography narrated in the novel. Christopher is a legendary martyr and patron of travelers. In the Golden Legend, the giant Reprobus seeks the greatest lord: first a king, then the Devil whom the king fears, and finally Christ, whose cross frightens the Devil. A hermit teaches him the faith and proposes that he serve Christ by carrying travelers across a dangerous river. One child becomes so heavy during the crossing that Christopher fears drowning. The child reveals himself as Christ and explains that the giant has carried the world and its creator. The name Christopher means Christ-bearer. The legend continues with his preaching, conversions, miraculous survival of tortures and eventual beheading. Accounts place his martyrdom under different rulers, including Decius or Maximinus; the narrative is not secure historical biography. In Western art he commonly carries the Christ Child across water with a staff. His commemoration was removed from the general Roman calendar in 1969, but he remained in the Roman Martyrology and continued to be venerated. Travelers’ medals and prayers reflect that continuing devotion.

A:272

St. Cristina's ChurchChicago parish where, according to Elena O'Higgins, a substitute for Casey Szymansky's destroyed sacred organ music is performed on kazoo, peewee guitar, and musical saw. She calls it a parish working to be the city's trendiest [PG:525].

PG:525

St. ElmoParish that X calls the nearest to Krakow. He claims to have inspected a record there listing "The Devil" as the father of Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch [D:279].

D:279

St. Francis de SalesCatholic writer (1567-1622) and bishop of Geneva from 1602. Finnegan reads his description of Paradise while Le Marin reads over his shoulder and claims to know the place [D:233]. The narration observes that the saint intended Heavenly Paradise, while the two men understood it as terrestrial; Finnegan reaches the wrong Basseterre and thus Paradise by accident [D:235]. A passage on chastity, beginning with its comparison to a lily among virtues, is also attributed to him [MTM B1:27].

D:233; D:235; MTM B1:27

St. Gallen, WisconsinWisconsin birthplace of John Gottfried Schultz (Hans), born January 2, 1915, to John William Schultz and Mary Irene Hayden. Hans remembers it as a place of splendid sunlight and larger summer [A:207]. His father operated a nursery there, and Hans attended St. Joseph's school [A:208].

A:207; A:208

St. Henry IIFinnegan is shriven on the feast of “St. Henry Emperor” in preparation for possible death, and thereafter drinks only a little wine [A:277]. Henry II (c.973-1024) became king of Germany in 1002 and was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 1014. He strengthened royal authority through the Church, founded and endowed the diocese of Bamberg in 1007, and supported monastic and ecclesiastical reform. His use of bishops as royal officers complicates an unqualified portrayal of him as a defender of ecclesiastical independence. His marriage to Cunigunde was childless; their supposed mutual vow of chastity belongs to disputed later tradition. Pope Eugene III canonized Henry in 1146, and Cunigunde was canonized in 1200. His feast falls on July 15 in the older Roman calendar, as retained in the 1962 missal, and on July 13 in the modern calendar. Catholic devotion presents the couple as examples of holiness within royal and married life.

A:277

St. Henry II (972--1024)Earlier heading gave a disputed birth year as exact; the checked account uses c.973. See St. Henry II.
St. John ChrysostomChurch Father (c. 347-407). Finnegan suggests to Le Marin that Chrysostom, or failing him Jerome, might support the idea of Terrestrial Paradise as an island surrounded by four rivers, although such authorities looked in the Near East [D:234].

D:234

St. John of the CrossSpanish Carmelite mystic and poet (1542-1591), born Juan de Yepes. Finnegan reads him alongside Father Farrell’s books on the Summa during his late Havana days of Mass, beach walks, sketching and books, recognizing the fleece itself in his reading [A:277]. A chapter epigraph attributed to Wimbish A. McDearmott’s Panegyrica calls John de Yepes an exemplary scientist of Divinity whose direct experimental method is mysticism [D:176]. John helped Teresa of Avila reform the Carmelites and suffered opposition and imprisonment. His works include The Ascent of Mount Carmel, The Dark Night, The Spiritual Canticle and The Living Flame of Love, exploring purification, detachment and union with God through poetry and prose commentary. He was canonized in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926. In Heaven, Duffey identifies John and Teresa with sixteenth-century Spanish elements in what he thinks is mystical symbolism; Plunket insists that the place is real [MTM B12:390].

A:277; D:176; MTM B12:390

St. Joseph'sSchool in St. Gallen, Wisconsin, attended by Hans Schultz, who rode a pony or walked or ran there. His father John William quarreled with the nuns and Father Baumgartner because he thought the teaching too easy for his son [A:208].

A:208

St. JudeSaint whom Dotty Yekouris jokingly claims as patron of printers and little magazines and the only apostle who was a printer. When Finnegan calls him the advocate of impossible causes, she answers, "Same thing" [A:115]. Finding his tomb appears among the Argo Masters' discoveries [MTM B13:422]. Christian tradition identifies Jude Thaddaeus, one of the Twelve, with the Thaddaeus named in Matthew and Mark and Judas son of James in Luke and Acts. The New Testament letter attributed to Jude warns against corrupt teachers and urges fidelity. Traditions of his later preaching range through Judea, Samaria, Syria and Mesopotamia, often linking him with Simon the Zealot; accounts of his martyrdom differ, placing it around AD65 in Persia or Syria. He is invoked as patron of desperate or impossible causes. One devotional explanation associates his former neglect with confusion between his name and Judas Iscariot’s; this is a tradition, not an established account of the patronage’s origin. Devotional literature also recounts Bridget of Sweden’s vision directing her to invoke him. His attributes include a club or axe, an image of Christ associated with the Edessa legend, and a flame representing Pentecost. Modern shrines have helped spread this devotion.

A:115; MTM B13:422

St. Katherine'sChurch from which Duffey obtains a priest to bless his continuously boiling crock of barley soup at the Pelican in New Orleans [A:133]. During the later New Orleans episode, Mary Virginia mentions two Dominicans giving a hellfire mission at "Ste. Katherine's" and predicting that their world will end that week [MTM B11:310].

A:133; MTM B11:310

St. Kitts (St. Christopher)Island name associated in Finnegan's mind with an intended paradise. Ignacio identifies St. Kitts as St. Christopher, a landfall of Columbus in the Leewards, which Ignacio therefore calls a holy island [A:272]. Finnegan later considers going there, while admitting that he loosely applies the name to several islands [D:273-274]. Duffey owns a cigar-store Christ from St. Kitts, adapted by an island artist from the cigar-store Indian form, with fingers shaped to hold cigars [MTM B3:103].

A:272; D:273-274; MTM B3:103

St. KobaridSmall kingdom in the Julian Alps, ruled by Hiram III and described as the last nation not yet abolished. Winter snow delays armed abolition there [MB:563]. Hiram is killed at the Voltaire Festival in Babylonia Bagascia, garroted by a youth team using Paul the Eleventh's entrails [MB:564].

MB:563; MB:564

St. LouisBirthplace of Vincent Stranahan, on April 5, 1921, and Theresa Antoinette Piccone, on October 15, 1923. Her father owns the Star and Garter [A:94]. Their wedding, planned for the last Saturday of May 1946, brings the Dirty Five and their friends together in the city [A:95]. Hans and Marie have decided to live there [A:97]; Patrick Stranahan and his family occupy the Cat Castle [A:102].

St. Louis also belongs to one of Duffey’s competing childhoods, whose memories may have been taken from a sister-person. Pecans and gray squirrels are among its remembered details [MTM B1:16-17]. As a young man he buys a former livery stable on Walnut Street and begins his business [MTM B2:40-41]. The account of these early business years is disputed within the narrative; a later account has him leave from below the Eads Bridge aboard the disguised Argo for the Seven Lost Years [MTM B2:71].

At the later reunion Duffey still has business interests, partners, a sister, and a share of the Rounders’ Club in the city [MTM B5:152]. Patrick has defended Doppio di Pinne there for homicide [A:111], and Bagby reports a recent visit by Giulio [MTM B5:164]. Bagby’s own funeral takes place in St. Louis, after which his weekly letters continue to arrive in New Orleans [MTM B8:237].

A:94; A:95; A:97; A:102; MTM B1:16-17; MTM B2:40-41; MTM B2:71; MTM B5:152; A:111; MTM B5:164; MTM B8:237

St. Louis GlobeOne of the two St. Louis newspapers Bagby calls the "Heavenly Twins," to which he sends his flamboyant boxing battle statements [MTM B2:50]. Cyrus and Edith Summerfield are society commentators in both this newspaper and its counterpart [MTM B2:65].

MTM B2:50; MTM B2:65

St. Louis IX (1214--1270)Louis IX (1214-1270), king of France from 1226, is the namesake of St. Louis, Missouri. That city is the place where Melchisedech recalls boarding the disguised Argo below Eads Bridge [MTM B13:406]; the king’s life is historical background to the place-name. Louis strengthened royal justice and arbitration, restrained abuses by officials, and helped develop the royal court into specialized institutions, including the Parlement. His 1254 reforms prohibited bribery and regulated punishment, while his moral legislation restricted blasphemy, gambling and interest-bearing loans. He founded or supported hospitals, religious houses and the college of Robert de Sorbon. The Sainte-Chapelle housed the Crown of Thorns and other Passion relics he acquired. Biographical tradition remembers him hearing grievances beneath an oak at Vincennes, feeding the poor and washing their feet; Joinville describes his daily attendance at a Requiem Mass and a sung Mass. Louis led the Seventh Crusade in 1248, was captured in Egypt in 1250, and remained in the eastern Mediterranean after his release until 1254. His second expedition, the Eighth Crusade, ended with his death from illness near Tunis in 1270. Catholic devotion presents him as a model of Christian kingship, but an unqualified portrait of benevolent rule overlooks his coercive religious policies, including the requirement that Jews wear a distinguishing badge. Boniface VIII canonized him in 1297; his feast is August 25.

MTM B13:406

St. Louis MurraysFamily to which Charley Murray belongs. His membership explains why he has money during his school years with Duffey and the other boys [MTM B1:24].

MTM B1:24

St. Louis Post DispatchOne of the two St. Louis newspapers Bagby calls the "Heavenly Twins," to which he sends his flamboyant boxing battle statements [MTM B2:50]. Cyrus and Edith Summerfield are society commentators in both this newspaper and its counterpart [MTM B2:65].

MTM B2:50; MTM B2:65

St. Louis UniversityUniversity where Duffey takes courses from the Jesuits in the summer of 1915 [MTM B2:49]. Charley Murray attends as a day student; although he shares none of Duffey's classes, they see much of each other [MTM B2:53].

MTM B2:49; MTM B2:53

St. LuciaName in Angela Cosquin's list of seven true passages through the Antilles, spelled "Ste. Lucia" in her account of her father's treasure maps [D:260].

D:260

St. Malachy's Church (1)Little stone church two blocks north of Duffey's Chicago hotel, which he visits with Charlotte. Its south front has three spread-winged archangels and each of its east and west sides has nine large angels; to Duffey the stone seems alive with wings [MTM B3:87]. Letitia says she has already arranged most of their wedding there, scheduled for the day after tomorrow [MTM B3:92]. They visit the church during their preparations [MTM B3:96], and their marriage is subsequently recorded [MTM B3:98].

MTM B3:87; MTM B3:92; MTM B3:96; MTM B3:98

St. Malachy's Church (2)St. Louis church where Bascom Bagby attends Mass, traveling across town because he believes it comes nearest to preserving the true faith amid the clergy's loss of orthodoxy [MTM B2:63].

St. MarcOne of two treasure ships near Angela Cosquin's island, represented on her father's maps as lying one atop the other with the San gre del Cristo. Angela calls the story a fabrication, but the narrator says both ships are real, within three hundred yards of her, and extraordinarily full of gold. She dives to the wrecks and later uses them to safeguard her own money [D:262].

D:262

St. Martin'sHall at St. Bonaventure's boarding school where Casey lives in six-boy chambers, each furnished with beds, lockers, desks, and a communal table [A:161]. The hall's boys produce the manuscript Chambers in rivalry with Gregory Hall's Towers; Audifax O'Hanlon draws chamber pots on its mastheads. These school papers underlie Casey's later Crock ventures [A:167].

St. Mary Major'sGirls' boarding and day school where Lily Koch is both a boarder with a private room and, when she wishes, a day student living with wealthy kindred across the road. She holds private Wednesday-night sales in her schoolroom and public Saturday sales at their mansion [MTM B1:28]. Twenty-five girls from the school are to be escorted by twenty-five boys from Duffey's school to a compulsory dance at the mansion [MTM B1:31].

MTM B1:28; MTM B1:31

St. MarysChurch where Hans and Marie stop for Mass as morning light begins, after talking through the night and walking in the rain during their Sydney stay [A:10].

A:10

St. MichaelSaint whom Papa Devil names with God as responsible for worrying about whether the Devil can be killed [D:87]. On the Great Day, Duffey talks with the damaged stone statue of St. Michael at the church in New Orleans. Duffey asks where an oasis can be found; Michael replies that the living water has left this place. One of the statue's eyes has been gouged out [GD:496].

D:87; GD:496

St. Michael'sNew Orleans church Duffey visits at dawn on the Great Day. People are "unstructuring" it through faith, and most of the building has fallen. Duffey speaks with the stone St. Michael in the former entry; the statue says the living water has gone and no oasis remains. Its eye has been gouged out, perhaps by an ordinary hammer and chisel, perhaps by their faith equivalents [GD:496].

GD:496

St. PaulNew Testament apostle whom Finnegan says never saw an Ocean Island [A:35]. The narration of The Devil Is Dead comically recasts his quarrel with Demetrios over Diana as a dispute over the silversmith's poor workmanship [D:133]. Trinali compares the basket in which Lupido lowers food to her with Paul's basket escape; Hans prompts her to explain that Lupido and Paul were not contemporaries [A:229]. Passages attributed to Paul's Philippians 4:4-9 and Ephesians 6:12-13 are among the original documents inserted into Duffey's story [MTM B5:175]. The Devil contrasts Paul's God with himself as the god of gibberish [MTM B8:243]. The Argo's history names Paul among those she has carried [MTM B13:404].

A:35; D:133; A:229; MTM B5:175; MTM B8:243; MTM B13:404

St. PetersburgCity where X says Papadiabolous I was present on November 7, 1917, aged about eighteen and serving his practical revolutionary apprenticeship [D:286].

D:286

St. PhilomenaThe name occurs through St. Philomena's, the school Maurine would claim Finnegan attended to get him admitted to a high-school dance [A:101]. Philomena is venerated as a young virgin martyr, but her dates and biography are not established by ancient testimony. Her nineteenth-century devotion followed the discovery of remains in Rome’s Catacomb of Priscilla in 1802. Reordering the tomb’s three inscribed tiles produced the name Filumena. The identification of the remains, the possible reuse of the tiles, and the supposed evidence of martyrdom have all been disputed; the vessel found in the tomb cannot simply be described as proven martyr’s blood. In the later devotional narrative associated with Sister Maria Luisa di Gesù’s claimed revelations, Philomena is a Greek king’s daughter who vows virginity, rejects Diocletian, survives scourging, arrows and attempted drowning through heavenly aid, and is finally beheaded at thirteen. These are elements of her legend. The relics were taken to Mugnano in 1805. Reported cures, including Pauline Jaricot’s in 1835, spread the devotion, and Gregory XVI authorized a local liturgical cult in 1837. August 11 became her traditional feast day. A 1961 liturgical decree removed her feast from calendars; this did not forbid private devotion. Devotees continue to invoke her as a wonder-worker and patron of children, young people and the sick.

A:101

St. Philomena (c.291--304)Earlier heading supplied life dates that are not established by ancient testimony. See St. Philomena.
St. Philomena'sSchool named in Maurine Stranahan's proposed excuse for bringing Finnegan to her junior-year high-school dance. Maurine invites him and says that, if challenged by the sister, she will present him as a junior from St. Philomena's and explain his age by calling him 'retarded.' She also wants to tell the other girls that they are engaged [A:100] [A:101].

A:100; A:101

St. SécaireSaint named in the Sword and Scabbard of Saint Sécaire, an anti-prize the Argo Masters deliberately lost three times. At its final concealment they sealed sword and scabbard with molten metals and brimstone, buried them deep in the Nine Mile Depth, and charged the ocean's creatures to keep them lost. Four hundred years later, Cyril and Cyrus Dimbeau recover them in a bathysphere on the morning Duffey and Brannagan go to sea [MTM B13:422].

MTM B13:422

St. StephenSaint named in Casey’s crown decoration. See Crown of St. Stephen; for the Hungarian ruler, see King Stephen of Hungary.
St. VincentName in Angela Cosquin's list of seven true passages through the Antilles [D:260]. The voyage poem opening Finnegan's chapter imagines sliding a sloop through a pass at "St. Vince," followed by shining at the Ritz and sleeping on the sand at St. Kitts [A:172].

D:260; A:172

St. ZermattoPlace Finnegan names, with Chamonix and Guebwiller, in a dispute over prehistoric rock paintings. He says shapes interpreted as birds and butterflies are actually elaborate speech balloons in an original complex language, and includes himself among the Neanderthal artists. Duffey disputes their capacity for speech and writing [MTM B6:193].

Staghorn ChristOne of Duffey's seven exceptional Christ figures, from Mesa Negra. The narration dates the hard-stone carving nine thousand years before Christ's birth and identifies its figure, impaled on a giant stag's antlers in a crucified posture, as Christ [MTM B3:104].

Star and Garter, TheSt. Louis burlesque theater owned and run by Gaetano "Papa" Piccone, father of Show Boat [A:94]. His stock character Hallohan J. O'Hoolihan caricatures Patrick Stranahan [A:104]. Duffey devotes an evening a week to the theater during his St. Louis period [MTM B2:50]; he and friends take Mary Louise Byrne and Beth Keegan there, and the two women sometimes join the skits [MTM B2:58]. Beth later works there, writing skits and playing comic roles [MTM B2:74]. Two of its acrobats attend Duffey's farewell at the Rounders' Club [MTM B2:70]. Piccone recounts creating at least one new character weekly for over thirty years, including Oliver Oscar Omygosh, whom he claims to have brought into actual existence, though Bagby disputes the claim [MTM B5:167-168].

A:94; A:104; MTM B2:50; MTM B2:58; MTM B2:74; MTM B2:70; MTM B5:167-168

Star BarrelInscription on churns among the household "iron words" in Duffey's childhood memories. Some of these memories come from observation and some from other minds; the passage does not single out Star Barrel as one kind or the other [MTM B1:17].

Star of the Ninth FusiliersOne of the numerous decorations Casey wears in his scarlet Leader regalia when Letitia intercepts him before he can mount the white horse [MTM B4:117].

MTM B4:117

States (the States)The United States. Finnegan compares clockwise Australian horse racing with the counterclockwise racing he knows "in the States" [A:3]. A bargirl contrasts beer from the states with the Texas beer she serves [D:12]. At Palermo, Finnegan receives his first mail since leaving the States, including letters from New Orleans, St. Louis, and Chicago [D:114-115]. When he is hunted in Basse-Terre, he begins considering a return [D:267].

A:3; D:12; D:114-115; D:267

Station HospitalMilitary hospital to which the amnesiac Sergeant is returned after the Captain's interrogation breaks him. The Sergeant threatens to remember the Captain's name and find him even in Hell; after being taken back to the hospital and sleeping, he feels better [A:74].

Ste. GenevieveIsland associated with the Martyr-Bell. The narrative says English raiders on the Lord Cramner killed thirty-nine Christians there in 1594 for refusing to abjure their faith. After the ship wrecked nearby, islanders recovered bronze cannon and cast the bell, which rang for four hundred years when enemies approached [MB:576]. Islanders later intercept Count Finnegan and instruct him to take it south to the mooring rock, where it is to summon good people rather than warn enemies away [MB:576-577].

Stein the RedName applied to Absalom Stein in the narration of Casey's compulsory "Reaffirmation of American Values" course after his stockade term and reduction in rank [A:50].

Stein ZombieOne of Absalom Stein's gin drinks at the Bay Hotel picnic. Finnegan jokes that its name is descriptive of its great originator [A:29-30].

Stein, AbsalomAmerican Special Service sergeant, publisher, and member of the Argo company, also called A. Stein, Kephos, and Ab-Salom. He comes from Chicago; his identification with Hugo Stone is disputed within the books [A:19] [MTM B5:158] [MTM B9:266] [MTM B7:234]. Duffey remembers Hugo Stone as a boy who visited his Chicago bookstore and insists that Hugo became Absalom. Margaret Stone disputes this, saying that Hugo was a joke name used by several of her cousins and that Absalom’s branch always used Stein. She names twenty Stone boys in four families: David, Hershel, Jacob, Samuel, Max, Nathan, Avram, Yosef, Stuart, Isaac, Myron, Efram, Barnard, Sidney, Joel, Robert, Milton, another David, another Nathan, and another Robert. She says that Absalom was their second cousin and lived six miles north; Myron and Efram, twins, most often played Hugo. Casey denies knowing Absalom before their army service in New Guinea about 1943, although Duffey remembers Casey’s clashes and two lost fistfights with Hugo [MTM B4:111-113]. The Dirty Five know Stein as a sergeant who lectures in service clubs and writes for army publications. He appoints himself master of ceremonies for Hans’s beer-drinking contest and quickly masters its Dominion Rules [A:19-20]. At the seaside picnic he mixes the Flying Steinmetz, Steinheim Stinger, Stein Zombie, Stein Collins, Ein-Stein, Stein Julip, and Dr. Stein’s Barnacle Remover [A:29-30]. He establishes the Anopheles Network, a small army radio station, and provides entertainment for the troops; Casey writes squibs for it despite hating him [A:46]. Sammy, who teaches alongside him, calls him serious, dedicated, and kind, comparing him to his idea of Socrates [A:67]. Casey identifies Stein with the former Hugo Stone whom the Crock’s warning letter calls an infiltrator [A:40]. When Casey challenges his lectures, Colonel Laycheck admits writing Stein’s speeches and threatens Casey with punishment [A:47]. Stein subsequently teaches the rehabilitation course Casey must attend [A:50]. The Dirty Five and their Australian allies try to overthrow Stein and his patrons by exploiting his apparent love for Tommy Trouncer in the role of Tania. Tommy beats him, and Casey puts him to bed and treats his injuries before reviving the scheme. The resulting raid temporarily lowers Stein’s standing and brings down Laycheck and the three majors [A:51-54]. A later account from Hans reverses the apparent deception: Stein knew Tommy’s identity, helped invent the joke, and saw how to turn it against the officers, though he underestimated Tommy’s blows [A:55]. Duffey says that Stein was born into the Party and is showing signs of leaving it; this reverses Casey’s movement in the opposite direction [A:98]. At the Pelican Press, Stein appears at the typewriter with a publisher’s placard. His arrival helps precipitate Finnegan’s departure, although Stein understands and wishes to help him [A:120]. He is one of the Bark’s seven founding directors and the Seven Pillars of Righteousness, appearing on Finnegan’s masthead as ‘Absalom to Omega. Oh, the big O’ [A:121] [MTM B7:214-215]. His one-shot Bite burlesques the Bark with vinegar and kindness [MTM B6:198]. He later joins Duffey and Gabrielovitch in starting the independent Investigator and writes for both publications [A:143] [MTM B11:315]. He is a large, owl-faced young man with horn-rimmed glasses and a cigar [A:120]. At the St. Louis gathering Duffey finds him overwhelming, larger than life, and apparently splendidly jeweled although he wears no jewelry; the estimate of size is explicitly Duffey’s [MTM B5:160]. Stein wishes for a more imposing nose and expounds the importance of noble noses [A:127]. His big hands, brains, heart, and gall support an elegant war of interlocking promotions: he remains loyal to the ordered arts and restores form where it has been abandoned [MTM B8:246]. Margaret Stone is his kindred [A:143]. His daughter Rebeka, or Becky, attends Ursuline at his wife’s suggestion, so that her education may become narrower rather than excessively broad. Rebeka takes part in Seven Roads and has known Duffey throughout her fifteen years [MTM B9:266] [MTM B10:294]. After Duffey returns from the Fifth Contingency, Becky grieves for Aunt Margaret, killed by a horse; the narration explains that Margaret is a sort of aunt to her [MTM B12:354]. The novels keep several accounts of Stein’s origins in play. Duffey regards him as one of the high twelve talismanic creations but admits past uncertainty about this [MTM B5:158-160]. Teresa identifies him as Ab-Salom, Father of Peace, a chandler and provisioner on the Euxine who joined the Argo to protect his investments. In her account Duffey awakens the old company into new bodies rather than creating it from nothing [MTM B7:233-234]. When X denies that Stein could know Rosemary Riorden’s words, Stein answers that to some extent he was that sergeant and that members of the old company partake of one another, though amnesia seals the connection [A:127-128]. Stein’s Notes in a Motley Notebook alternates between accepting Duffey’s ancient identity and explaining it as unusual accord with a patron saint. It similarly alternates between treating the released Devil as the Devil himself and as a decoy [MTM B10:291]. In another passage Stein reverses the creation story, imagining that he and the others made Duffey, their beloved moth-eaten magus, before admitting that on other days he believes Duffey made or awakened them [MTM B10:304]. The narrator later allows Duffey some creative role while placing the Marvels among an ancient, interdependent company of Argo Masters; Stein’s precise function in their mutual life remains a question. He supplies the ship with Jew bread [MTM B13:446]. His attributed writings include Notes on the Finnegan Cycle [MTM B6:185], Notes on the Argo Legend and Further Notes on the Finnegan Cycle [MTM B6:187-188], Notes in a Motley Notebook [MTM B10:291] [MTM B10:304], Notes on the Argo Cycle [MTM B11:330-331], and Notes on the Argo Legend [MTM B11:341]. His account of Finnegan distinguishes reports, apparent deaths, and uncertain identities, and admits uncertainty about the relation of the Argo Legend to the Finnegan Cycle [MTM B6:187-188]. Stein calls himself a neo-Jew, perhaps the only one, and refuses Duffey’s suggestion that a gentile could join him [A:131]. Mary Virginia reports his maxim that everything can be described in two words [MTM B11:308]. In the Pop History episode he tries to remember people threatened with oblivion, believing that his recollection might save them, but cannot yet recover their faces [MTM B11:315-316]. He investigates courthouse records, tax rolls, and directories, and questions the supposed antiquity of a newly appeared park [MTM B11:320] [MTM B11:331]. He insists on scientific methods without submitting to accepted scientific content, and questions whether the strange events are happening at all [MTM B11:339]. His teasing account of the Morning People has a demiurge put them to sleep on a mountain, then accidentally awaken them with the reserved tone of thunder; the child hero recognizes elements of it as true [MTM B11:334]. Stein withdraws with Duffey and Zabotski to examine the events from his apartment [MTM B11:335]. Later he tells Cyrus Roundhead that he mostly likes the Pop Historians’ effect but has reservations [MTM B11:344]. After the return from the Fifth Contingency, Becky worries that her father now regards the truly aware as a separate, superior species and is writing for Gentleman Rounder [MTM B12:355]. In the future year Duffey visits, Stein appears splendid and noetic, afflicted with the overweening superbity Becky identified. He roars with laughter on seeing Duffey, who is treated there as a ghost [MTM B12:360-361]. When Duffey returns to his own present and asks what was so funny, Stein is taken aback; Duffey then gives a laugh rivaled only by Stein’s [MTM B12:362]. In the Great Day episode, Duffey first greets him as an old friend of kindred intelligence, then discovers that he is clothed only in smoke and a cigar and has lost his brains. Stein declares brains useful only during the transition and now a handicap; faith and freedom are what matter. His growing cigar, made of faith-tobacco, is to replace his name. The narrator describes his later obesity and his old habit of straight-faced kidding, while leaving him a distant possibility of hope [GD:493-494]. Accounts of the soul trade differ. Stein says that he exchanged an old soul, Hugo Stone the Chicago red, for an old soul of Casey’s, leaving Casey with his later muddled one; Casey is now red and Stein ironically white as dirty Gary snow [MTM B5:169]. Hans’s letter to Marie says that Casey compassionately agreed to go to Hell for Stein and that Stein acquired Casey’s brains and talents while Casey diminished [MTM B6:186]. Stein’s own later commentary says that they exchanged kabouters, interior goblins or fixations, which made each privy to the other’s secrets without greatly changing their relative quantities of goodness and sleaze. He recognizes compassion in Casey’s desire to suffer for another, professes affection for him, and offers to use his access to powerful people to help [PG:537-538]. X’s letter, rather than Stein’s own declaration, tells him that he has seen the burning bush, must wander forty years in the desert, and must remain intelligent and serene [A:265-266]. After a separate letter in which Duffey calls himself the fifty-ninth King of Salem, Stein wonders about his own dynastic number and the possibility of rapport with previous or future bearers of a dynastic identity [PS:478-479].

Stein, Rebeka (Becky)Absalom Stein's daughter, sent to Ursuline at her mother's suggestion for a narrower education [MTM B9:266]. A fifteen-year-old Jew who has known Duffey all her life, she joins the schoolgirls at the Ghost Coffee Shop and discusses the potholes as symbolic activators in Seven Roads [MTM B10:293-294]. She plays the Countess in the expanded Fifth Road and read Duffey's lines at the rehearsal he missed [MTM B12:352]. She welcomes his name "Thunder Colt" for the play's animal [MTM B12:353]. Margaret Stone's death by a reportedly rabid horse devastates her; she satirizes the changed funeral Mass in a verse of her own [MTM B12:354].

Stone, HowardSee Ostwald, Howard Stone.
Stone, HugoContested identity associated with Absalom Stein. Duffey recalls a camera-carrying boy who frequented his Chicago bookstore, addressed him as "Duffey, baby," and later became Stein; Margaret says Hugo was a joke name used by several Stone cousins, most often the twins Myron and Efram [MTM B4:111-112]. Duffey insists that he made Hugo, while Casey denies knowing Stein before their army service despite having twice lost fights with Hugo in the bookstore [MTM B4:112-113]. Duffey later attributes compromising photographs of himself with young girls to Hugo; his blackmailer calls Hugo a clever kinsman who accumulated useful material [MTM B4:139]. During the war, a letter from Duffey warns Casey about a torpedo formerly called Hugo Stone, whom Casey identifies as Stein [A:40]. Casey's later editorial accuses Stein, under that name, of being a card-carrying Communist [A:129].

MTM B4:111-112; MTM B4:112-113; MTM B4:139; A:40; A:129

Stone, MargaretChicago member of the Bark circle and kinswoman of Absalom Stein, formerly in the Party and subsequently a Catholic. The narration attributes that conversion's possibility to intricate ethnic reasons and describes her as small, intense, Italian and Jewish, perhaps partly Preadamite, with a large musical voice and no complacence [A:143-144]. She preaches the Real Presence on Dauphin Street at midnight, driven by the urgency of her own recent Pentecost and the fear that she may be responsible for finding the one further soul who will save the world [A:144]. X calls her "Margaret the bonfire" in a letter to Stein [A:266]. Duffey knew her as a young bookstore visitor; she was a cousin, not the sister she sometimes claimed to be, of Hugo Stone [MTM B3:99]. Her sharp hearing produces the puzzling report that Bagby asked what his own letter said, though the narration raises the possibility of a misunderstanding [MTM B7:219]. She sings a Gadarene Swine verse about Duffey [MTM B10:305]. In the Fifth Contingency she attends the Pop History sessions with Mary Virginia and Sally, and the women join the hunts against old humans [MTM B11:336]. The Thunder Colt kills her after she jokes about the blood of Deutero-Finnegan; her laugh is all it cannot reach [MTM B11:351]. In the returned world Becky mourns her death by a reportedly rabid horse [MTM B12:354]. In the separate Great Day account she is at the Pelican Press and pushes down a wall, killing a child in the street while crying for freedom [GD:490] [GD:493].

Stranahan, Patrick J.Successful St. Louis lawyer, former magistrate, husband of Monica, and father of Philip, Hugh, Timothy, Vincent, Norma, and Maurine [A:94] [A:102]. He is a large, hairy, rumbling man with a busy stomach, wrestler's shoulders, a blue-emery-paper face, and heavy eyebrows. His wealth is described as lace-curtain and grand-piano Irish richness; the Cat Castle, his large three-story home, was left to him by the elderly Cat Woman, a legal client [A:102]. Called fey, he sees Finnegan as living several lives and perhaps being alien, on a dark road but capable of a happy death [A:102]. He and Papa Piccone imitate one another; Piccone's stage caricature is Hallohan J. O'Hoolihan, which Patrick does not fully recognize as himself. The two friends drink and argue through long evenings [A:104]. Patrick advocates a deliberately limited cultural education, a philosophy short enough for one sheet, select travel and food and drink, and denounces what he sees as the passing of the Church's giants [A:109-110]. He tells Finnegan that Doppio di Pinne, whom he defended for homicide, is the same man despite little physical resemblance and incompatible locations [A:111]. Duffey recalls having given Patrick a gift [MTM B5:154]. At the Rounders' gathering with Monica and Piccone [MTM B5:162], Patrick describes creation as reciprocal: he accepts Duffey's part in making Vincent and others but says he himself consciously helped create Duffey. Father McGuigan objects to the language, while Duffey insists that his own magical creations are literal [MTM B5:165-166].

A:94; A:102; A:104; A:109-110; A:111; MTM B5:154; MTM B5:162; MTM B5:165-166

Stranahan, PhilipOldest of the four Stranahan brothers, whose poker-playing friends visit the family house [A:104]. In the 1923 shore scene Duffey meets him fishing below the Eads Bridge; Philip says he is ten and that Vincent died five days after his birth in April 1921, contradicting Duffey's memories of Vincent's adulthood. He identifies Teresa Piccone as a comical first-grader and invites Duffey to the Cat Castle [MTM B13:470-471]. After Duffey reappears as a young man, Philip mistakes him for the earlier visitor's grandson, about fifty years younger. Duffey then sees a touch of unreality in Philip and boasts that his own ghost is more solid [MTM B13:473].

Suitcase (the chrysus)Heavy, shabby suitcase, also called the chrysus or thesaurus, which Finnegan seizes after killing William Gerecke in his attempt on Seaworthy [D:165]. It contains 36,000 pieces of paper, each 2.5 by 6.125 inches, bundled in hundreds, arranged three bundles lengthwise and six across, and stacked twenty bundles high; it weighs eighty pounds. Finnegan guesses it is the world's most valuable suitcase [D:166]. Doll retrieves it from a locker and checks it through to Baltimore, though they leave the bus at Philadelphia [D:171]. She later tells X that it contains a million dollars [D:174]. X takes the claim check from her bag, retrieves the suitcase, and plants a similar one containing 36,000 newspaper pieces as a decoy [D:178]. Brannagan compares its great value with that of his own sea-bag, then fears Gertrude will spread word that it contains over half a million dollars [D:204-205]. Archipelago also alludes to Finnegan's theft of the world's most valuable suitcase [A:188].

SulemShore boy and friend of Hans Schultz in the Green Islands who carves heavy black wood. He proposes that Hans rough out a hundred carvings daily with power tools, with his uncles finishing them and girls selling them. Hans rejects the mass-production scheme, but permits rasps, files, and saws [A:59]. Sulem explains tujuan as a person's direction or orders for life and semangat as the soul. He says that tai leaves reveal a person's aura, and that Finnegan lacks both aura and tujuan, though everyone has a semangat [A:60]. To protect Finnegan from ruin he carves a small Grandfather amulet, saying that he and his uncles must dream its appearance. The result resembles a lizard and toad; Finnegan baptizes it Heliogabalus and wears it with his Miraculous Medal [A:60-61].

Sweeny, EnniscorthyMusical friend of the Duffeys during their Chicago golden age, named with Mary Sweeny among their composers, players, and stagers. [MTM B3:99] An editorial interruption before an alternate conclusion calls him ruddy-faced and a near-genius. It quotes his comparison of an event to a box whose past, present, alternative present, and future are different, equally valid views: accepting one must not cancel another. [MTM B13:467]

He is the protagonist of “The Three Armageddons of Enniscorthy Sweeny,” the second part of Apocalypses, which gives his dates as 1894-1984. Widely recognized even by strangers, he has a famously difficult-to-describe, ruddy, peeling face and a Midwestern Irish voice. His apparent age and size resist ordinary comparison, and his handling of time makes his records impossible to arrange securely in sequence. The same box-and-event passage appears in this portrait. Within the novel's alternative twentieth century, Doctor Henry Devonian's November 1910 formulae make Sweeny the unique answer to the Particular Equation, the individual on whom the era's reality depends (Apocalypses, PDF pp. 199, 201, 203-205, 219-221, 233, 236-243).

His portrait balances genius against “spacious bungler.” A genuine genius on the flute and exceptionally gifted on other instruments, he reaches near-genius or occasional unquestionable genius in cartooning, drama, opera, film, art, and competitive sport despite supposedly lacking the necessary killer instinct. He is also an excellent craftsman and stone carver. His journalism is often vivid but defective: he sometimes omits results rather than impose an outcome, and insists on recording everything because things have not truly happened until written down. His many businesses flourish under his animating presence and sell brilliantly, but buyers discover shambles once that presence departs; he nevertheless has ready money from childhood. His apparent failures as a prophet are entangled with conflicting versions of events and his disregard for ordinary sequence (Apocalypses, PDF pp. 205-219, 372).

His works include the Tyrrhene Triptych, comprising Armageddon I, II, and III; the play The Great Depression; essays such as “On the Construction of the World”; the novel Secret Agents Six; and the late farce My Name is Sweeny and I'm in Trouble, in which a younger actor plays the Sweeny who represents Everyman. Sweeny calls his catastrophic works scapegoats intended to carry horrors away from the world. Their effects are dangerous nonetheless: the narrative reports suicides after performances of Armageddon III and the spread of enormous horror-for-its-own-sake cults. Whether his fictions produce the wars or might prevent them remains disputed, even as their influence and his involvement become overwhelming (Apocalypses, PDF pp. 214-216, 265, 320-324, 340-341, 356, 375-378).

His wife is Mary Margaret McGronsky Sweeny. He brings about her extraordinary beauty and then her preeminence as an opera singer before he wins her, after five dangerous years; their subsequent marriage lasts in almost perfect amity for another sixty-five years. Other early episodes show the extent and instability of his influence. His mother's dated account records President Harold Standpipe crediting the seven-year-old Ennis with his rise to office. A boyhood wish is fulfilled when Sweeny knocks out the reigning heavyweight champion amid startling changes of apparent size and injury. At twelve he preaches at St. Malachy's, performs poltergeistic feats, and makes the clock run backward through a day before the retreat master removes him from the pulpit (Apocalypses, PDF pp. 207-211, 221-231).

Alistar Grogg, Wimbish McDearmott, and Elton Quartermas infer from the Devonian equations that killing Sweeny might prevent catastrophe. Grogg dies before his first intended attack but continues the pursuit as a ghost. Sweeny hires six detectives to protect him from these three and from the opposing Friends-of-the-Catastrophes, code-named Marshals Mosco, Tosco, and Rosco, who insist that he continue producing his desolating visions. He regards the mathematicians as friends trying to save the world and the marshals as friendly enemies. The protectors and threats eventually live with him, thirteen persons in the Royal Assassins-and-Detectives Club, also called by Mary Margaret the Old Mens' Menagerie (Apocalypses, PDF pp. 233-245, 319-324, 338, 357-358).

Detective Branagan counters Grogg's psychic infestation by bringing his bones into Sweeny's home, the safe center of the psychic storm, and making a portable locket containing bone shavings, spirit essence, and charms. Sweeny's gift for illusion also diverts an assassination onto Ellis Swinton. The thirteen Drayman's Alley murders over forty years all substitute victims for Sweeny; each dead face acquires his likeness, although Flanagan cannot establish who makes the resemblance permanent. An invisible spiked collar initially tortures Sweeny when he resists the marshals. Later it is put on another person during repair, and Sweeny feigns its effects while the unknown substitute suffers (Apocalypses, PDF pp. 322-323, 334-340, 345-346, 350-357).

Near the end, one explicitly possibly subjective account gives nearly a thousand consecutive days of maximum length, prolonging 1983 and echoing Sweeny's “The Three-Year-Long Year.” He withdraws into a hollow tree, calling himself the scapegoat and an impediment to the final resolution. Comfortable there and spending much time in prayer and prophetic gestures, he resists Mary Margaret's appeals to come down. He has long engraved 1984 on his own tombstone and predicts death when Achilles catches the rabbit in his version of Zeno's paradox. When Ultimate Armageddon arrives and 1984 is finally allowed to begin, people burn his tree: seven dark spirits sink into the ground, and a golden spirit flies away whistling music from his old Prohibition, A Farce. This is the recorded end of the “old and almost forgotten prestidigitator” (Apocalypses, PDF pp. 372-383).

Sword and Scabbard of Saint SécaireDangerous anti-prize that the Argo Masters repeatedly hide. They weld sword and scabbard together with iron, lead, brimstone, and babbet metal, then bury them a hundred meters into the ooze of Nine Mile Depth, where they remain four hundred years until Cyril and Cyrus Dimbeau recover them by bathysphere [MTM B13:422]. Duffey warns that drawing the sword an inch will put two-thirds of humanity into a fatal sleep unless it is resheathed, while drawing it completely will end the world. The scientists experiment and ten assistants fall asleep [MTM B13:423]. Brannagan reseals the sword with the molten flux; Duffey drops it back to its old hiding place, and Brannagan covers the party with the Forgetfulness Mesh [MTM B13:424].

Szymansky, GabrielChicago pawnbroker and antique dealer, husband of Miriam Lessing and father of Kasmir W. (Casey) Szymansky [A:153-154]. His rich-street antique shop and poor-street pawnshop stand back to back, connected beneath an alley; he is wealthy but his stinginess leads Casey to suppose the family poor [A:160]. Szymansky, Kasmir W. (Casey)Kasmir W. Szymansky, called Casey, born in Chicago on October 7, 1921, the only child of Gabriel Szymansky, a pawnbroker and antique dealer, and Miriam Lessing [A:153-154]. One of the Dirty Five, he is identified with Peleus among the Argonauts and with the ninth-century scholar and necromancer Kasmir Gorshok, Casey the Crock [A:38-39].

Archipelago presents his life as he tells it to Finnegan, adjusted by Finnegan’s knowledge of him [A:153]. The problem of evil is his overriding concern [A:154]. His twelve childhood dream worlds concern sports, erotic adventures, fortress religion, literature, exploration, a secret higher ethic, languages, art, revolution, worldly success, sadistic fantasies, and revenge. He recounts these dreams to Finnegan; they are imagined lives and ambitions, not twelve separately established universes [A:156-161]. His invented athlete is named Casey Syman [A:156-157].

Duffey tells Casey that he helped form him through a talisman given to Gabriel before Casey’s birth. Casey remembers holding the object from birth until six months old and confirms that it is solid gold [MTM B5:151]. For other roles and related accounts, see Crock (4) (Casey the), Prince Casimir, Zodiac, Casey of the, and Casey Machine.

Talisman

Object through which Duffey helps form or awaken a person. One recipient describes a talisman as a flat, engraved gold stick about an inch wide and eight inches long, bearing the designated person’s being, encounters and destiny. The narrator says that a child usually absorbs it after holding it for days. Duffey bestows twelve primary talismans, though not every talisman belongs to that group [MTM B4:120]. His childhood talisman sticks receive lightning during his contest with the clouds [MTM B1:10-11].

At about three years old he gives his first talisman to an Italian confectioner with a pushcart, to bring about the first member of the Duffey Nation [MTM B1:18-19]. Other gifts go to Charley Murray and Sebastian Hilton [MTM B1:35], to Giulio Solli for an unborn son [MTM B2:47], and to Gabriel Szymansky for Casey. Charley’s is intended for his sister’s child [MTM B4:120]. Casey remembers holding his own from birth until six months old and confirms that it is solid gold [MTM B5:151]. A separate, rib-shaped talisman passes through Lily Koch to her sister Letitia, Duffey’s future wife; Letitia is explicitly additional to the twelve primary creations [MTM B1:29-30] [MTM B3:90-93].

John Rattigan, refused a talisman, makes a convincing copy and tricks Duffey into holding it. Duffey warns that, if it works, it will work wrongly [MTM B1:23-24]. Dr. Rafelson calls Duffey’s claims fantasies but also acknowledges evidence that his creations may become persons with real histories [MTM B4:146-147]. The account of how these objects work therefore includes disagreements among Duffey, his recipients and his interpreters.

TetteraglotsPlural form of the word Angela Cosquin uses for her father, whom she calls a tetteraglot from childhood, a speaker of four languages. She links this to his expertise in archaic spelling and handwriting when fabricating old treasure maps [D:260].

Texas beerOnly cold drink available when Finnegan and Seaworthy enter the newly opened bar after sitting across from the graveyard. Seaworthy condemns the beer in mock-biblical language, saying they asked for a drink in Christ's name and were given this [D:10] [D:12].

D:10; D:12

ThadalKing of the Nations or Goyim, one of the Three Slant-Faced Men whose names Duffey discovers in the Flame Man comic strip. With Amraphel and Arioch he is called a crooked king and an anti-magus without magic [MTM B7:227]. The narration identifies the three as followers of Chodorlahomor of Elam or Susiana, a connection not given in the strip [MTM B7:228].

MTM B7:227; MTM B7:228

Thalassocratic AdventurePhrase for the wartime military and sea campaign that the narration leaves outside its account. Its little iron insects have been eating up bird-shaped New Guinea before the company moves four hundred miles beyond the Vogelkop to a small Dutch island [A:50].

A:50

ThanatosName Stein gives Finnegan's sought-for fleece, contrasting thanatos with mallion in his account of Finnegan's repeated search for death without finding it [MTM B6:187-188].

MTM B6:187-188

Thatcher, Hugh (the Yellow Kid)Artist known as the Yellow Kid whose work Duffey sells during the New Orleans rebuilding project, among the local and distant artists contributing to that effort [MTM B6:198-199].

MTM B6:198-199

The Analyst and the Essence of ManTheme connecting analysis of Duffey with the difficulty of locating a person's essence. An unnamed analyst concludes that Duffey was physically, mentally, and psychically a girl for several childhood years; Duffey pays and leaves, while the surrounding narration describes his appropriation of other minds [MTM B1:16]. Doctor Saul Rafelson accepts that Duffey's fantasies become external realities, examines two of his independent images, and recognizes his sorcery and possible world-inversion; he ultimately refuses to follow the implications further because he is frightened [MTM B4:146-148]. Finnegan tells Duffey of a powerful analyst who dissects a person and finds no centralized essence, only an empty jug and its wrappings. Yet the scattered parts glow, suggesting essence diffused through them; the analyst dies before investigating further. The narration applies this to Finnegan's essence, which cannot be bottled in one place [MTM B5:181-182].

MTM B1:16; MTM B4:146-148; MTM B5:181-182

The AnswerNewsletter sent to about three hundred prominent Chicago citizens near the end of 1931, issued on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. It covers economics, ethics, government, education, religion, and militarism with a startling, quippy style [MTM B4:113]. Its mixture of Augustine, Aquinas, Pope Benedict, Nietzsche, Shaw, the Webbs, Machiavelli, and both Roosevelts alarms Duffey, who finds much of it intelligent but fears its appeal to followers. The second issue expands from four to sixteen pages and proclaims that the Leader has been found [MTM B4:114]. Friday's issue announces the Appearance in Henry Horner Park [MTM B4:116]. Ten-year-old Casey secretly prints it on Duffey's press. Letitia intercepts the costumed Leader, prevents Casey's promised ascent to power, and takes him to enjoy the park festivities without his regalia. The paper does not reappear; Casey later calls it a hoax, but Letitia knew his intention was serious [MTM B4:117-118].

MTM B4:113; MTM B4:114; MTM B4:116; MTM B4:117-118

The AppearanceRally announced by The Answer for seven o'clock on Friday evening at Henry Horner Park, where the Leader is to mount a decorated white horse. About a hundred thousand people and three bands assemble, but Letitia intercepts the Leader, ten-year-old Casey Szymansky, and makes him remove his costume and medals before they join the crowd [MTM B4:116-118].

MTM B4:116-118

The ArgosyName Gabrielovitch connects with the Ragosy, a fleet from Ragusa in Illyria. He identifies Ragusa as the original Iolcus, adding a philological claim to the company's Argo legend; Stein agrees about sailing from Illyria, provoking X to challenge his access to that memory [A:127].

A:127

The AssemblyGloss of Ekklesia, also rendered the Crowd, the roughly two-thousand-year-old institution whose termination is declared at the Last Conclave in Babylonia Bagascia. Its princes assemble with the intention of dismantling its structure [MB:561].

MB:561

The Back-Door of HistoryWork attributed to Arpad Arutinov as the source of the epigraph to Chapter Two, Mermaid and Ogress, in The Devil Is Dead. The passage rejects rigid distinctions between persons and species, describes bloodlines and ghost and flesh mingling, imagines devils whose removal would kill their hosts, and presents the children of Ahriman as returning ancient monsters or mutations [D:26]. These claims frame the chapter's interest in mixed and hidden identities.

D:26

The Baltimore CatechismCatechism quoted in Newton Prescott's journal in “The Casey Machine,” in a passage numbered 382-383 that contrasts the glorious immortal bodies of the just with the punishment of the damned. Its account of bodily radiance, swiftness, beauty, freedom from pain and ability to penetrate matter prompts Prescott's speculation that such powers are already available in a single splendid moment [CM:503] [CM:511].

CM:503; CM:511

The Broadway Oyster HouseSt. Louis seafood restaurant where Duffey meets the big-nosed John Solli, Finnegan, who orders one hundred oysters and shares them with Duffey and other diners. The meal evokes Fingal or Finn McCool eating a hundred enormous oysters. Finnegan shows Duffey his paintings and scrimshaw, identifies himself as Van Ghi and Count Finnegan, and explains that a first-class beach bum needs the aura of a fortune. The conversation reveals his parentage as the son of the Monster Giulio and his plan to wander for seven years before being buried on the Marianao Coast of Cuba [MTM B5:172-174].

MTM B5:172-174

The Cadillac BarBar visited on the Mexican side by Finnegan, Anastasia, and Marie Courtois. The narration describes it as dingy outside and rich within, with mostly Texan customers and white-jacketed bar-boys amid chrome and crystal. The three drink and mellow there [D:57-58].

D:57-58

The Colossal NoisearamaEntertainment event in the Babylonia Bagascia sequence where Hiram III and several sheriffs capture part of the amplification system. Hiram yodels loudly during a solemn Rock Movement, breaking up the performance and becoming marked for death [MB:564].

MB:564

The Comedy Music BoxMorgenstein's entertainment venue on Randolph Street in Chicago, where Duffey, Letitia, and Lily attend an extravaganza after supper. On leaving, they buy a midnight newspaper and learn that Gloria and Manolo Mullens have been tortured and murdered, while Charlotte is missing [MTM B3:97].

MTM B3:97

The IndiamanEnglish venturer named by Angela Cosquin among the supposedly treasure-laden sunken ships in her father's map lore, alongside the Golden Mastiff, Hind, and Crane [D:261].

D:261

Thompson, FrancisEnglish poet addressed by Casey Szymansky in the poem titled “To Francis Thompson” [PG:523].

PG:523

Thorndyke, DoctorCode name for one of the detectives consulted by Argo Masters; advised always noticing the frame of a problem or picture closely and suggested the answer might lie within the frame's material itself, requiring minute examination of the ship plank by plank [MTM B13:456].

MTM B13:456

Three Apparitions (Teilhard, McLuhan and McGonigal)Satirical transfiguration at St. Michael's during the Great Day: the demiurge Teilhard appears on the altar with McLuhan at his right and McGonigal at his left, all transfigured with light. They bless the Unfaithful Assembled with a sequence of technical-sounding terms [GD:497].

GD:497

Three monkey-like wraith-like creaturesSeamen seen on the Argo's ice-sheeted rigging; wraiths or of lighter flesh, they climbed the frozen cliffs "like ascending lightning" carrying ice axes, cheerful and ready for assignment [MTM B13:398].

MTM B13:398

Three young toughsThree large, drunken young men who accost Melchisedech Duffy before dawn on the Great Day. Two pinion him while the first grips his wrist, carefully smashes the watch glass and removes every shard, then breaks off its minute hand. He says the Great Day no longer requires such precision in time [GD:481-482].

GD:481-482

Thrombocyte-shaped remnantsOne of the elaborate bodily tests cited by The Eighteenth Book of Strange Encounters for its claim that the New Orleans art dealer Melchisedech Duffey is more than four thousand years old [MTM B8:250].

MTM B8:250

Thunder Colt Complex, TheName for the fifth of the seven possible contingencies confronting Duffey, also called the Decatur Street Opera House Presentation of the World. Its ending of humanity accompanies the beginning of another species [MTM B10:300-301].

MTM B10:300-301

Thunder Colt Game, TheClimactic performance at the Decatur Street Opera House, called the Thunder Colt Game in the text and orchestrated to Thunder Torus music. A human is thrust alive into the great egg and eaten by the still-unconscious colt; lightning then breaks the egg and awakens it. Its ensuing rampage kills Deutero-Finnegan, also called the Finnegan effigy, and Margaret Stone [MTM B11:350-351].

MTM B11:350-351

Thunder Colt Games, TheEarlier heading changed the source’s singular Game to Games. See Thunder Colt Game, The.
Thunder Colt, The actualTotem animal of the Royal Pop Persons, whose awakening Cyrus Roundhead presents as a symbol of their own. It devours a human inside its egg, then hatches when lightning strikes during the Thunder Colt Game at the Decatur Street Opera House [MTM B11:350]. It kills Deutero-Finnegan, the Finnegan effigy, and Margaret Stone [MTM B11:351].

MTM B11:350; MTM B11:351

Thunder Harps, TheA self-designation used by the Pop Countess for the Royal Pop Persons [MTM B11:316].

MTM B11:316

Thunder Torus musicMusic accompanying the Thunder Colt Game at the Decatur Street Opera House. Its stark music picks up tempo as the colt hatches and runs riot [MTM B11:350], then crashes to an end after Margaret Stone is killed [MTM B11:351].

MTM B11:350; MTM B11:351

Thurneysen, RudolfSwiss scholar Rudolf Thurneysen (1857-1940), author of Die irische Helden- und Königsage. Absalom Stein recommends the work while considering Finnegan's possible identities as Fingal and Cú Chulainn [MTM B6:187-188].

MTM B6:187-188

ThursdayDay on which Duffey initially supposes Bagby wrote and mailed the letter received after his Saturday funeral. More letters subsequently arrive, unsettling that explanation [MTM B8:237]. Thursday is also the usual publication day of the Bark, though it appears on Thursday or whenever and sometimes skips a week [GD:490].

MTM B8:237; GD:490

Ti, IgnatiusChristian Chinese ward boy whose family has lived in the islands for centuries. He translates the parakeet Amoy's stories [A:79]. Ti explains midnight as the hour when souls cross and returning ghosts can slip through a hole in the veil. He warns against turning one's back on corpses and describes medicos pretending to be dead to frighten ward boys [A:85-86]. His predecessor countered such tricks with a blow to the throat and a displayed knife, remarking that even a pig has its throat cut. Ti also tells of a murdered husband whose ghost returns to bed with his wife before she learns of his death [A:86-87]. More Than Melchisedech names Ignatius Cardinal Ti of Manila among the Princes in Hiding targeted by John Mogul and lists Bolo Manolo as his double [MB:578-579]. A later passage instead calls Lloyd Cardigan-Pembroke the double of the dead Cardinal Ti [MB:594]. The identity of the ward boy with the cardinal is not established in these passages.

A:79; A:85-86; A:86-87; MB:578-579; MB:594

Tibeau, George (Tippio)George Tibeau, called Tippio, a regular at the Old Wooden Ship bar [D:215]. In a tavern tale he repeatedly tries to fool a fortune-telling penny scale, but after changing clothes with a bum loses the money needed to leave town [D:217-218].

D:215; D:217-218

Tide-water (blood type)Narratorial hyperbole in the discussion of Cajun identity: after listing supposed racial classifications and blood types, the narration says many Cajuns have tide-water instead of blood and no heads at all [A:123].

A:123

Tiger (Papa Devil)Tiger imagery attached to Papa Devil on Naxos: he says he was once a tiger and intends to regrow his lost stripes after dark [D:122]. When his corpse is found shot, bludgeoned, stripped of its shoes, with pockets turned out or cut away and its olive shirt shredded, the narration says he briefly regained his stripes before death [D:146]. Finnegan's later feral condition is distinguished from Papa's tiger, resembling instead another cat, an ape, or a climbing grotesquerie [D:162]. X identifies the Papa Finnegan knew as Papadiabolous II, Gregory McColum, the Irish undercover policeman [D:285] [D:287].

D:122; D:146; D:162; D:285; D:287

TiggerEarlier heading used Tigger, a form not found in the cited passages. See Tiger (Papa Devil).
Timeless (scent)Scent worn by the Pop Countess, whose youthful appearance leaves her actual age uncertain [MTM B11:316-317].

MTM B11:316-317

Tin-Horn Forca, FreddyRegular at the Old Wooden Ship bar [D:215]. The narrator declines to tell his story, saying that he is called Tin-Horn because that is the kind of sport he is [D:218].

D:215; D:218

Tinder, RitaArtist whose work Duffey sells during the New Orleans rebuilding project, among the local and distant artists contributing to it [MTM B6:198-199].

MTM B6:198-199

TinosAegean island named in Finnegan's account of a primordial five-island group. His creation story makes the Aegean islands fragments of an electrum cup [A:35]. Brannagan says mermaids' hair from Naxos can be bought in shops on Siros, Tinos, and Kea, although an ancient reluctance prevents its sale on Naxos itself [D:207].

A:35; D:207

Tippio, George TibeauSee Tibeau, George (Tippio).
Tito, Josip Broz (1892--1980)Yugoslav communist leader Josip Broz Tito (1892-1980), who led the Partisans during World War II and later became president of Yugoslavia. His break with the Soviet Union in 1948 was followed by a leading role in founding the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961. In Casey's polemic against Gabby, Tito is called their noble ally, while Gabby is accused of attacking him and supporting Draja Mihailovitch [A:129].

A:129

TitoistsFollowers of the Yugoslav communist leader Tito. The narration states that the Titoists shot at Gabrielovitch, Gabby, during the group's years of publishing and political conflict [A:132].

A:132

TityroiBeings described as Satyrs in the chapter-eleven epigraph, which the novel attributes to Galen’s Techne Iatrike. In that account, Daemons beget them on human women; only the first generation is fertile, so the race requires repeated Daemonic renewal [D:160-161].

D:160-161

Tmutarakan, Principality ofPrincipality in X's account of the Devil's imprisonment. X calls it an advance host of the Khanate of the Golden Horde and says it shared the Crimean peninsula with the Kingdom of Kiev when the Devil was imprisoned in 946 or 947 [MTM B6:204].

MTM B6:204

To Karkik KarikiOne of the continuations or imitations of Casey's clandestine student Crock magazines. The narration says that its Greek name is accompanied by repeated references to an attributed ancient Greek trait, unlike the humor Casey himself intended [A:167-168].

A:167-168

To WeighMeaning Finnegan assigns to the common root of the Greek and English uses of talent, adding tolerant to the same etymological family. He makes the remark during Askandan's challenge about the parable of the talents and how Finnegan will answer the Master for their use [A:258].

A:258
