Toast, Mary ReginaOne of the confidence and gamine friends in Duffey's Chicago circle during its golden age [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

Togetherness (concept)Ideal Casey mocks as the seculars' only god and urges Christian men to keep in perspective. The narration recalls this saying when he is irritated that the others have read his mail before him [A:38].

A:38

TolerantWord Finnegan connects etymologically with talent and the meaning to weigh, in his conversation with Askandan about the parable of the talents [A:258].

A:258

TomRegular at the Old Wooden Ship bar [D:215].

D:215

Tom Collins (drink)Drink Duffey jokingly says Dives should have requested from Lazarus instead of water, together with the alternative of a cool Mint Julip. Duffey claims that this was the failed test of the parable, during his New Orleans discussion with Finnegan about jazz and salvation [A:117]. The underlying story is the rich man and Lazarus in Luke 16:19-31.

A:117

Tommy (moustache)Name jokingly attached to the moustache of Hildegarde Katt's husband. When she identifies him as the cop with the little moustache named Tommy, Finnegan treats Tommy as the moustache's name and persists in the joke after she corrects him [D:229]. The next page names the man Tommy Katt and calls him the toughest cop in town [D:230].

D:229; D:230

Tommy TrouncerSee Trouncer, Tommy [A:51-53].

A:51-53

Tompkinson, ChristopherAuthor of "The Mythology of Liberalism," an article published in the Crock magazine [A:41].

A:41

Tone-Control ArtistPainter in Jimmy Fitzjames's account of artistic categories, ranked above a Primitive, who in turn outranks an Orthoclast. Jimmy says the Tone-Controller considers colors as musical equivalents and orchestrates hues into vibrations perceptible only to the more intense observers [A:230-231].

A:230-231

Tone-Control paintingPainting described by Jimmy Fitzjames as arranging colors according to their musical equivalents. He claims that ambient vibrations are its whole effect, so it can be enjoyed with one's back turned and its visual aspect ignored [A:230-231].

A:230-231

Tongues, gift ofAbility Salvation Sally claims during her Sydney conversation with Marie Monaghan and Hans. After Marie quotes French verse about Rome and Bohemia, Sally invokes her gift of tongues and answers its religious challenge [A:8].

A:8

Tooth's (beer)Beer named with Toohey's and K. B. Lager in Finnegan and Vincent's opening pub sequence in Sydney, after Finnegan finds the Garden replaced by the World [A:1-2].

A:1-2

Top SergeantRank Show Boat says Finnegan held in his army outfit, in a letter to Dotty defending him and calling him the outfit's best man [A:262].

A:262

Top-PeterTitle paired with Cap-Stone of the Ekklesia. At the Final Conclave, Conrad Stone Hackenschmidt forces the election of the Straw-Man to this role [MB:567], then orders Monsignor X to burn the effigy [MB:568].

MB:567; MB:568

Tornabuoni, MariaItalian girl from New Orleans seeking stripping work at the Star and Garter in St. Louis. Show Boat describes her in a letter to Vincent, says the penniless girl is staying with the Piccones and taking small parts, and jokes that her Renaissance name suits her Renaissance figure [A:48-49].

A:48-49

Torpedo (person)Duffey's term in his warning letter for the smooth-talking, jug-eared man assigned to target Casey, who once used the name Hugo Stone. Henry asks Casey whether Stein is this torpedo, and Casey confirms that he is [A:40].

A:40

Torre del MarifiSpanish treasure ship among the real or imaginary wrecks on the master map made by Angela Cosquin's father. Angela lists it with Estrella del Mar, Virgen la mas Benigna, and Casa del Oro, comparing the names to a litany of the Blessed Virgin [D:260-261].

D:260-261

TrachtasWork named in the Chapter Nine epigraph and attributed there to Saint Brendon. The passage describes unredeemable species denied eternal life but given long sublunar lives as flesh, returning ghosts, or continuing legend; some are helpful, yet none are to be trusted [D:130].

D:130

Track and TotalContract-killing firm hired after the Final Conclave to hunt and kill the thirteen Princes in Hiding [MB:569]. Its chief, John Mogul, also tracks their doubles and organizes a lavishly rewarded contest for colorful murder suggestions [MB:578-579].

MB:569; MB:578-579

Traffic Trestle, Pont du SableChicago bridge Duffey visits before dawn on the morning he wakes knowing he has lost his golden touch. A heavy truck has knocked out an underpinning during the night, weakening the structure [MTM B4:109].

MTM B4:109

Tramp steamingPopular art of travel included in the narration's catalogue of pursuits stripped of style and class during the great trashing of the arts [MTM B6:207].

MTM B6:207

TramsSydney transport vehicles whose brightness belongs to the fresh morning of the opening creation conceit; the narration says trams were made on the fifth day [A:2]. Finnegan and Vincent later take a tram following Tom and Freddy's elaborate directions to meet them near their barracks [A:10].

A:2; A:10

Transport (of Finnegan)Visionary state that comes over Finnegan as he speaks of shadowy history and identifies with a primordial people. His speech asks how earth's earlier inhabitants became aliens and monsters, describes their ancient life among animals, and claims that defeated people hid within the victors' bloodstream, periodically returning to war [D:212-214]. The transport fades into vague rhapsody and leaves him weak; he returns to awareness with Le Marin in the Old Wooden Ship [D:214].

D:212-214; D:214

TransylvaniaRegion in Countess Margaret Hochfelsen's extravagant invitation to Duffey. She claims nineteen long-lived generations of her family still live there, that its extent reaches Colchis, and that wolves larger than horses serve her family and frighten the Devil. She asks Duffey to marry her and share centuries of life there; he repeatedly challenges her geography and tall tales [MTM B8:255-256].

MTM B8:255-256

Trashman's Girl-a-RamaEstablishment where Duffey, Dotty, Mary Virginia Schaeffer, Margaret Stone, Bagby, and their companions gather in the Slant-Faced Men discussion. Dotty's line about Bagby's liver becomes a song, with Mary Virginia at the piano, Duffey on a house banjo, and the unofficial Pelican Glee Club joining in [MTM B7:225-227]. The narrator says more songs have been born there than anywhere else on the block [MTM B7:226].

MTM B7:225-227; MTM B7:226

Traveler's AidRailroad-station assistance desk, printed Travelers’ Aid, where a confused Finnegan asks a woman to read his ticket and tell him his destination. It is only an old race-track ticket showing that he was in Hot Springs seven weeks earlier [A:243]. When she asks what is wrong, Finnegan answers Korsakofs Psychosis and refuses her offer to take him to a doctor [A:244].

A:243; A:244

Traveler's SaloonSaloon visited by Duffey and his school friends Rattigan, Murray, and Hilton. Traveler serves sensible twelve- and thirteen-year-old boys small glasses of whisky for five cents; Rattigan also buys a quart twice a week to resell in mixtures to schoolmates [MTM B1:25]. The boarding-school episode deliberately blends several possible cities rather than fixing one location [MTM B1:24-25].

MTM B1:25; MTM B1:24-25

Trevino (family name)One of the surnames within the Angelino clan, alongside Obermeyer, Viskochil, Borg, and Larrigan. The narration describes a family mostly Italian, then German, with Bohemian, Mexican, and Irish Tinker ancestry and cousins around the world [A:218].

A:218

TriflesUsed by a complaining magus for the seemingly trivial payments received for losing major magical powers [MTM B1:5].

MTM B1:5

Trinali CocktailMixture of Trinali's old wine and Hans's new wine, which Trinali calls a dialectic and a synthesis. She elaborates its interplay as water and vinegar, sun and bacteria, then invokes old wine in new bottles and new wine in old bottles as a scriptural contradiction [A:231].

A:231

Trinali PetersonYoung poet and maker of dolls and novelties in Hans Schultz’s New York Bohemian circle, during the spring and summer after he leaves the carnival in 1935 or 1936 [A:220-221] [A:240]. Hans meets James Fitzjames among the secondhand bookstores; they walk uptown and pick up Trinali [A:224-225]. Her mother named her Mary Jane. She adopts the Gypsy name Trinali and writes hundreds of pages about herself: “Ode to Trinali,” “Trinali at Sundown,” “To Trinali in a Red Dress,” “To Trinali at Dawn on March 4th,” and the taxi-composed “Ode to Trinali on the Way to the Village” [A:226]. She is slight, immature in figure, and just short of beauty, with rusty black hair she insists is red. Her electricity has been cut off; she obtains bread, wine, and candle ends from Lupido, steals longer candles, and makes figures from bottles, corks, and raffia [A:228]. She also makes lamps and toys, dyes corks in the dishpan used for dishes, and works with driftwood and cypress knees. She admits that her creations tend to look alike [A:229]. Hans sees her metaphorically as driftwood with cypress knees, rough, sea-stained, and remarkably convoluted [A:234]. She mixes old and new wine into the Trinali Cocktail and writes about wine as a bottled god [A:231-232]. At twenty she calls “To Trinali in a Rainstorm” her greatest ode and says her style has matured in the preceding eleven days. She romanticizes dying young but denies having a plan, imagining future works called “To Trinali on the Brink” or “To Trinali with Clarity” [A:232]. She dies from the luminescent lilac dye used on corks, either through the unwashed dishpan or, in Adam Scanlon’s account, from coloring added to wine. She is buried on September 1 with “To Trinali in Her Coffin with Her Red Hair Loose About Her.” The nondenominational service seems chilly and inadequate to Hans and Fitzjames [A:239-240].

A:220-221; A:240; A:224-225; A:226; A:228; A:229; A:234; A:231-232; A:232; A:239-240

Triple CrownPapal crown, or at least a double of it, that Monsignor X brings to the conclave inside Mooring-Rock [MB:596]. After twelve members vote for John Finnegan Solli and Finnegan abstains, X places it on his head and John Giwa hails him as Pope Finnegan the First [MB:597].

MB:596; MB:597

Triple OBagby's nickname for Oscar Oliver Omygosh, a painful, melancholy novelty-shop owner near the Star and Garter. Papa Piccone claims that this man materialized from a badly made burlesque character of his own invention. Bagby remembers the man but disputes that Piccone created him; Piccone insists he did [MTM B5:168].

MTM B5:168

Triple-decade vastPhrase denoting thirty years, attributed to the “Paean” in the earlier glossary. The earlier glossary cites the opening “Paean” of Archipelago, page ix. That preliminary page is absent from the supplied copy, so the reading remains unverified.
Triple-stallTommy Trouncer's boast that he can pull a double-stall or triple-stall and keep Stein on a loose hook during the Tania deception. He makes it before the tryst that ends with his beating Stein and ruining the conspirators' plan [A:53].

A:53

Triumphant (state/concept)Word attributed to the “Paean” in the earlier glossary. The earlier glossary cites the opening “Paean” of Archipelago, page ix. That preliminary page is absent from the supplied copy, so the reading remains unverified.
TrobriandsIslands skirted with the d'Entrecasteau group on the boys' voyage from the south back to their New Guinea bay, by way of the China Straits [A:36].

A:36

TrollCreature type the Countess Margaret distinguishes from Giulio Solli: she says he is a Teras rather than a Troll, and Giulio confirms her classification [MTM B3:107].

MTM B3:107

Troop Movement OfficeOffice to which Hans and the other boys on Australian furlough report on Thursday, February 18, 1943, before being sent back to New Guinea [A:31]. Henry had stayed behind and was not part of the furlough party [A:38].

A:31; A:38

Trouncer, TommyTow-headed Australian lance corporal with a double voice and a talent for impersonation. Dressed as Tania, he auditions for Stein's Coconut Grove show and becomes the object of Stein's infatuation [A:51]. Tommy calls himself the best in the world as Casey enlists him and another Australian in the Dirty Five's scheme to discredit Stein and his superiors [A:52]. After starring in the show, Tommy loses his temper during a tryst and beats Stein against trees and into a slough, disrupting the encounter, though he says Stein still has not recognized the deception [A:53]. Hans’s later account says Stein knew who Tommy was and had devised the gag himself, though he had not expected Tommy to hit so hard [A:55].

A:51; A:52; A:53; A:55

Trout (river fish)The earlier glossary associates trout with Hans Schultz's St. Gallen childhood and the St. Croix River, but this association remains unverified in the supplied text. Its former citation, A:225, concerns Hans's New York companions.
Troyat, MartinName replacing Sebastian Hilton for a year or so in the composite account of Duffey's boarding-school quartet, while John Rattigan similarly becomes Delbert Dugan. The narration says the changes preserve the group of four; Sebastian reappears in the final school year after an interval in Europe [MTM B1:24].

MTM B1:24

TshowaxWitch Casey says he conjured at five, the summer before he started school, by reciting a formula from a story at midnight. He says she still visits when she comes to Chicago [PG:524].

PG:524

Tuba mirum spargans sonamTuba mirum spargans sonam is the printed variant in Archipelago; the standard liturgical line is Tuba mirum spargens sonum. See Tuba mirum spargens sonum.
Tuba mirum spargens sonumThe Dies irae line normally given as Tuba mirum spargens sonum, about the trumpet spreading its wondrous sound. The novel prints Tuba mirum spargans sonam. In Duffey’s joke about jazz and salvation, Finnegan may rise from his coffin when the funeral sequence reaches this line and urge the player to blow that horn, though Duffey advises against waiting until death [A:117-118].

A:117-118

TucalulClandestine Crock imitation said by the narration to circulate behind the Iron Curtain, in the account of Casey's student magazines and their later continuations [A:167-168].

A:167-168

Tufa stoneStone used for the freestanding, life-sized Black Christ from Bahr El Ghazal in the Sudan, one of Duffey's Seven Christs. The figure holds a cattle herder's crooked rod [MTM B3:104].

MTM B3:104

tujuanSulem's term for a person's direction or allotted life, distinct from the soul, which he calls semangat. He describes it as orders written on cuscus-skin vellum, rolled small and placed somewhere within the body. Chewing tai leaves allows him to see an aura and understand the tujuan, but he says Finnegan has neither. Sulem thinks this lack leaves Finnegan vulnerable to ruin and makes a grandfather for him as possible protection [A:60].

A:60

Tupelo-gum treeType of wood from which Giulio Solli whittled intricate animal calls (panther, alligator, etc.) for his son Finnegan [MTM B5:174].

MTM B5:174

TurbanHeadwear of the laughing Christ from Turkish Anatolia, one of Duffey's Seven Christs. The figure is carved from reused monumental marble [MTM B3:104].

MTM B3:104

TurkestanDistant location in the narrator's exaggeration of Tom Shire and Freddy Castle's unmistakably Australian appearance. Even a femur found in Turkestan thirty thousand years later, the narrator suggests, would still be recognized as Australian [A:5].

A:5

Turpin of Rheims, ArchbishopArchbishop in the Charlemagne legends, invoked as the last prelate and general comparable to Henri Salvatore [MTM B5:183]. The legendary figure grew around a historical archbishop of Reims, traditionally dated to about 800 at death; the chronicle once credited to him is a later work now known as the Pseudo-Turpin.

MTM B5:183

Tuthill, Tim and GaleMembers of the ecclesial/vineyard/churchy circle associated with Duffey in Chicago during the Golden Age [MTM B3:99].

MTM B3:99

Twain, Mark (Samuel Langhorne Clemens) (1835--1910)American author and humorist Samuel Langhorne Clemens (1835-1910), known as Mark Twain, author of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884, with U.S. publication in 1885). The Argo's fantastic history lists him among its passengers [MTM B13:404]. Rick Norwood's publisher's note in the supplied Archipelago edition also mentions Twain's unfinished Tom Sawyer and the Indians [A:285].

MTM B13:404; A:285

Tweed, JohnStudent d'Alesandro calls his most brilliant, who has become world-famous by the time d'Alesandro asks him about a classroom joke involving Casey's altered equations. Tweed calls it a pair of mathematical puns in a kind of dialect and doubts they can be put into words [PG:526].

PG:526

Twicherby, MajorOne of the three livid majors, with Meyerhofer and Terwilliger, present when Colonel Laycheck threatens Casey over his challenges to Stein's lectures. None is a line officer [A:47].

A:47

Two Lives, Finnegan of theNarrative designation for Finnegan as a story and character out of the Taine. Meeting Dotty at the St. Louis train station, he feels like a stranger inside his own body, watching and feeling through the confused Finnegan person he inhabits, whose identity he is not ready to accept as his own [A:92].

A:92

Two-headed eagleLiving eagle conjured from sparks by Kasmir Gorshok. One head supplies half a coin, and the other supplies Kasmir's name; the completed coin bears the eagle on one side and a Crock or Pot on the other. The narration calls it an eagle of Poland, and Kasmir releases it to restore the endangered creatures' number to nine [MTM B13:426].

MTM B13:426

TywynTown in Gwynedd, Wales, home of Lloyd Cardigan-Pembroke. The list of cardinal doubles pairs him with David Cardinal Lloyd Spencer [MB:579]. The later account calls him a pig butcher of Tywyn but then identifies him as the double of the dead Cardinal Ti, an unresolved inconsistency [MB:594].

MB:579; MB:594

U.S. ArmyMilitary organization that brings the Dirty Five together in the same battery: Vincent Stranahan, John Schultz or Hans, Kasmir Szymansky or Casey, Henri Salvatore, and John Solli or Finnegan [MTM B5:171]. Casey joins in April 1942 and asks Duffey to run the Crock during his service [MTM B4:138]. He insists that he first knew Absalom Stein in New Guinea around 1943, although Duffey remembers their earlier Chicago connection [MTM B4:112]. Private Gregory claims over a century of continuous service as a sergeant before changing identity in 1907, with missing records from the Indian Wars and Civil War. He then obtains an appointment to the U.S. Military Academy [A:77-78]. Don Lewis says he was one of three American soldiers who disappeared on Willy Jones Island: Sergeant Charles Santee, Corporal Robert Casper, or PFC Timothy Lorrigan. He refuses to say which [D:44].

MTM B5:171; MTM B4:138; MTM B4:112; A:77-78; D:44

U.S. MailPostal service that delivers the first issue of the Answer to prominent Chicago citizens, including Duffey, on a Monday morning. The newsletter is scheduled for Monday, Wednesday, and Friday publication [MTM B4:113].

MTM B4:113

UkalegonName paired with Melchisedech in Book Five's epigraph, attributed to Edwin Arlington Robinson's “Two Men.” The following commentary says Skalsky considers Ukalegon a woman and, in every way, Melchisedech's negation [MTM B5:149]. The classical Ucalegon is a Trojan elder in the Iliad; in the Aeneid, his house catches fire during Troy's destruction.

MTM B5:149

UlyssesGreek mythological wanderer, also called Odysseus, whose identity the narrator associates with Finnegan, alongside Dionysus, Terras, and Arracht [A:39]. Finnegan waking battered and shoeless is likened to Odysseus washed ashore, beginning another day as Ulysses [A:177]. Hans imagines the Australian south as farther than Ulysses traveled [A:16]; Finnegan's difficult annual visits to Dotty are likewise treated as Ulysses keeping appointments [A:145]. A related Ulyssean wanderer is Roadstrum in Lafferty's Space Chantey, whose relationship to Finnegan is a literary comparison. His hornet spacecraft takes him through Odyssey-like episodes: the pleasure-induced lassitude of Lotophage, giants on Lamos explicitly called Laestrygons, man-eating shepherds on Polyphemia, the witch Aeaea's transformation of him and his companions into animals, and the deadly song of Sireneca. On Sireneca a crewman recalls the old remedy of waxed ears and a captain bound to the mast. Their fall into the Vortex brings extreme aging and death, reversed by a device installed by Hondstarfer; a later underworld episode brings them before Tiresias on Hellpepper Planet. Roadstrum returns after twenty years to Big Tulsa on World, his son Little Tele-Max, and his wife Penny. Tele-Max recalls the older story of shooting an arrow through twelve holes and killing the suitors. Roadstrum then kills Penny's suitors, but this homecoming parodies marital fidelity: Penny and the suitors have partied through his absence, and she later recounts her intimacies with them. Roadstrum's forked tongue gives him persuasive, deceptive eloquence, recalling Ulysses' cunning speech. His eventual rejection of a peaceful ending and departure with a new crew extend the wandering pattern (Space Chantey, PDF viewer pp. 8-15, 30-35, 80-92, 126-132, 161-165, 176-188, 217-222, 225-238).

A:39; A:177; A:16; A:145

Un-Duffeying a DuffeyCasey Szymansky's phrase in the Crock for undoing what he considers Duffey's harm and influence. Casey declares it harder than unsaying a lie or proverbially unscrambling an egg [A:130].

A:130

Unaccountable CorpseCorpse Saxon Seaworthy dreams he is trying to dispose of in an unidentified Indian city, in a gray dream where its face repeatedly disappears [D:72-73]. Seaworthy asks Finnegan whether he has ever tried to dispose of an unaccountable corpse. Finnegan later understands the dream as connected to the actual corpse he helped Seaworthy bury when they first met: Seaworthy had struck its reviving body with a shovel in a graveyard [D:74-75].

D:72-73; D:74-75

Uncle Joe Tompkinson's Torpedo JuicePseudo-sponsor of Absalom Stein's Anopheles Network G.I. radio station, advertised as providing “Explosive Personality by the Natural Method” [A:46].

A:46

Uncollectable Art CollectionNarrator's name for Duffey's imaginary collection of living works of art. Charlotte Mullens asleep in her beauty would be one of its supreme pieces, alongside the ivory figurine Beth Keegan and others yet to appear [MTM B3:89]. Beth is elsewhere described as a laughing, living ivory statue, fashioned by herself and friends, with Duffey perhaps her final creator [MTM B2:57] [MTM B2:60].

MTM B3:89; MTM B2:57; MTM B2:60

Uncreated CreationVincent Stranahan's theory that creation might have occurred only ten minutes ago with its apparent past already built in: red shift, momentum, partly spent life, expanded matter, fossils, vestiges, an earth halfway down from the fourth Pleistocene ice age, carbon balances, partly run-down atomic clocks, sediments indicating fifteen hundred million years, and insects and tumbleweeds at their present development [A:56]. Human memories and dreams would likewise have been supplied without the remembered events ever occurring. Vincent calls it Stranahan's Theory of the Uncreated Creation and hints at a further Shadow and Substance motif he refuses to explain [A:57].

A:56; A:57

Underground EagleNewspaper in which Josephine McSorely publishes her account of the Casey Machine's origin, beginning “Oh salving hatred, Oh revivifying derision, Oh nourishing slander!” [CM:506].

CM:506

Underthing peopleNarrative term for the other human race Finnegan senses in Seaworthy, the Devil, Gerecke, Peter Wirt, Marie, and even Anastasia: peculiar people with old black blood and disturbing strength. He wonders whether he belongs among them while still doubting their existence [D:50].

D:50

UnderwoodOne of seven Iowa locations claiming to be Duffey's birthplace during one of his possible childhoods, with Minden, Beebee Town, Neola, Crescent, Avoca, and Union Township [MTM B1:7].

MTM B1:7

Union SheetTuesday newspaper printed by Dotty and Duffey's Pelican Press [MTM B7:212]. Its half-dozen associated men are always seen in committees [MTM B7:213]. Letitia pays it less attention after becoming editor of the Bark [MTM B8:238].

MTM B7:212; MTM B7:213; MTM B8:238

Union TownshipOne of seven Iowa locations (along with Minden, Underwood, Beebee Town, Neola, Crescent, Avoca) suggested as a possible birthplace for Melchisedech Duffey during one of his contested childhoods, though not properly a city itself [MTM B1:7].

MTM B1:7

United StatesNation containing the American settings of The Devil Is Dead. Finnegan first meets Seaworthy in a Texas seaport, later returning to the same town's Old Wooden Ship and its Company of Fifty [D:10-12] [D:215] [D:225]. More Than Melchisedech identifies the Old Wooden Ship Tavern as being in Galveston, Texas [MTM B13:458]. The Brunhilde calls at Freeport, Palacios, Port O'Conner, Aransas Pass, Corpus, Port Isabel, and Brownsville, and anchors off Padre Island [D:34] [D:55]. Demetrio recalls travels to Alice, Eagle Pass, Uvalde, Beeville, San Angelo, Weiniar, and Port Isabel [D:58]. Finnegan and Doll escape New York through Newark and Philadelphia to Baltimore; Pittsburgh is an alternative bus destination for which they buy tickets [D:167-172]. Their southern journey reaches the Florida lake country and Orlando [D:180] [D:190]. Finnegan later stays in Biloxi and is warned away from New Orleans [D:201] [D:209-210]. During another interval he visits friends in New Orleans, St. Louis, and Chicago [D:272].

D:10-12; D:215; D:225; MTM B13:458; D:34; D:55; D:58; D:167-172; D:180; D:190; D:201; D:209-210; D:272

United States Five Dollar Gold PiecesCoins Duffey produces while rubbing his hands together: seven appear before Patrick Stranahan and the others at the 1946 gathering. Patrick identifies them as United States five-dollar gold pieces minted about ten years earlier and suggests Duffey could have been carrying them [MTM B5:167] [MTM B5:171]. As a boy, Duffey also produces one for Gretchen Sisler in an unnamed city [MTM B2:38-39].

MTM B5:167; MTM B5:171; MTM B2:38-39

Unities of AristotleDramatic conventions of action, time, and place later associated with Aristotle. The narrator invokes the Unities of Aristotle and Heroics of Plutarch as accidental constraints of the mainstream world, from which Finnegan's shadow life after death is free [D:161].

D:161

Universal rule (re:rogue islands)Finnegan's assertion that every pentanesia, or five-island group, has a rogue island. Ignacio answers that he had not known it was a universal rule but agrees that Barbuda is good for nothing [A:272]. The earlier creation story presents five as the original number of islands in each archipelago, with the Aegean as an example [A:35].

A:272; A:35

University of ChicagoOne of several colleges and universities (including Notre Dame, DePaul, Northwestern, Marquette) attended intermittently by Kasmir Szymansky (Casey) [MTM B4:119].

MTM B4:119

Unreality FringeSmoky halo surrounding Duffey's magnificent animations, called the unreality fringe in the language of sorcerers. The narrator twice insists that these people are nevertheless real [MTM B5:158].

MTM B5:158

Urals, wine of theWine mixed with goats' milk in the drink Finnegan shares with Askandanakandrian while receiving his advice about distressed merchandise and life [A:256].

A:256

“Urbe et Orbe”Section of the Crock containing the month's notes on Chicago and the world [A:41]. Its title plays on the papal blessing Urbi et Orbi, “to the city and to the world.”

A:41

Urchin (1)Patrick Stranahan's habitual nickname for his future daughter-in-law Show Boat. The narrator describes her as half Juliette and half urchin [A:104]. X also calls her the Urchin in his letter listing people who must pass through the passion [A:266-267].

A:104; A:266-267

Urchin (2)Name Finnegan uses for Anastasia Demetriades when she asks if she is beautiful. She asks whether she is a beautiful urchin, and he agrees [D:38]. Later she reminds him that he calls her both an urchin and a tramp [D:70].

D:38; D:70

Urchin disguiseNarrative name for the body Duffey wears while concealing his person and powers as the Boy King, whose powers include invisibility [MTM B1:18].

MTM B1:18

UrsineBear-like strain or quality; Elena Angelino, who handled trained bears for the carnival, insisted her great-grandfather was a bear (a belief the Professor shared), contrasted with the wilder Romany strain also present in the Angelino family [A:218].

A:218

Ursuline AcademyNew Orleans girls' school whose students prepare the Seven Roads sign as an advertisement and prop for their play [MTM B9:264]. The students include painter Crissie Cristofero, playwright Cleo Mahoney, and casting director Therese Doucet; some day girls breakfast at the Ghost Coffee Shop after early Mass at the Cathedral [MTM B10:293]. The academy's auditorium hosts Seven Roads, with Duffey acting himself and performing magic and music during the interval [MTM B12:366].

MTM B9:264; MTM B10:293; MTM B12:366

UvaldeTexas town Finnegan visits on a Monday during his chaparral wandering, before Sabinal, D'Hannis, and Hondo. He remembers earlier army maneuvers in the neighborhood [A:202]. Uvalde also appears in Demetrio's list of youthful travels [D:58].

A:202; D:58

VagariesOne of the kinds Duffey names with Gargoyles, Neanderthals, Boogers, and Variants when discussing the Teras element in his creations. He says everyone has some variant blood, but he has put more than usual into his creations [MTM B5:170].

MTM B5:170

VairIn Hans Schultz’s reflections on Marie’s green eyes, the color of Nicolette’s eyes in a remembered French song, contrasted with Romany sheleno. Hans imagines vair degenerating into vert with the French soul and rejects its interpretation as gray [A:24]. This is the passage’s poetic philology: historically vair derives from Latin varius and can describe gray-blue eyes, while vert derives separately from viridis.

A:24

Valley of the New MenThe valley-name claimed by Finnegan for his ancestral people, the “people before the people,” in his account of their prehistoric life and displacement. He insists that theirs is the Valley of the New Men, “not of the old” [D:212-213].

D:212-213

Valleys (Pepper-Belly, etc.)The named valleys and draws on Willy Jones Island, also called Pulau Petir, in Don Lewis’s account of the pursuit of Yokipoki. Santee and Casper kill the little man; the three soldiers then discover they are lost, and Don Lewis later buries him [D:44-46]. Their familiar landscape includes Cotton-Picker Valley, Pepper-Belly Valley, Hound Dog, Horse Collar, Dog-Dirt Draw, Rang-Dang-Doo, Jackass Flats, Little Joker Canyon, Aching Back, Slit Trench, Sore-Head Gulch, Little Fat-Head, and Big Fat-Head. Jackass Flats is described, despite its name, as exceptionally precipitous. They know these valleys but cannot identify the one they have entered [D:45-46].

D:44-46; D:45-46

Van Dusen, Augustus S.F.X.Name used by one of the experts consulted by Duffey, Biloxi Brannagan and Kasmir Gorshok to prevent the Antichrist from boarding the Argo. The experts include fictional persons and actual persons under fictional names; Van Dusen is also called the Thinking Machine [MTM B13:454–455]. He warns that fireplaces can provide entrances overlooked in a locked-room problem, and recommends stationing a firedrake at each fireplace, guarding the other entrances and checking that the intruder has no ally already aboard [MTM B13:455–456].

MTM B13:454–455; MTM B13:455–456

Van GhiGregory van Ghi is an artist’s identity explicitly used by Finnegan, although Finnegan also tells a conflicting story of studying under a great master Van Ghi in Florence. Patricia says that Van Ghi is a name her brother invented [A:175]. Dotty recognizes the signed Van Ghi paintings in Finnegan’s possession as his own work and does not dispute his claim that their painter is the greatest traditionalist-modernist-experimentalist [A:176]. In New York he has Gregory van Ghi cards printed, rents a Village studio, and successfully sells his Orange Period paintings; the narrator calls Finnegan the man underneath the constructed persona [A:191-192]. He tells Duffey outright that he is Van Ghi when consigning paintings to him, and later speaks of knowing Scanlon “when I was Van Ghi” [MTM B5:173] [A:236].

In the Florence account, Van Ghi teaches him the painter’s trade. After Finnegan paints a devil, Father LeFaye calls the master an old mountebank. Van Ghi identifies the depicted devil as an old repeater appearing in The Night Watch, Bruegel’s paintings, Giotto’s Betrayal, the “Burial” of Count Ortega, El Grecos, Notre Dame stonework, Etruscan vases, and Aztec statuettes. He agrees that the picture should be burned and advises painting without inspiration [D:252-255]. The supplied edition prints Van GM repeatedly on D:255.

A:175; A:176; A:191-192; MTM B5:173; A:236; D:252-255

Van Gogh, Vincent (1853--1890)Dutch Post-Impressionist painter (1853-1890), known for expressive color and dynamic brushwork. His paintings include The Starry Night and Sunflowers. Commercial success was limited during his lifetime, though critical interest was growing by 1890; his work later influenced Fauvism and Expressionism. The specific allusion to him in the Argo novels remains unidentified.
Vanadium steelA merciless streak in the narrator’s metaphorical alloy of Betty Hochstapler’s heart, alongside brass, extremely resilient phosphor bronze, and a warmer metal that often glows cherry red [A:216].

A:216

Vance, PhiloCode name of one of the experts consulted by Duffey, Biloxi Brannagan and Kasmir Gorshok about keeping the Antichrist off the Argo. The experts include fictional detectives and actual persons using fictional names [MTM B13:454–455]. After invoking music, African violets and games, Vance reduces his advice to “Get a dog.” Father Brown recommends an English bulldog, and Duffey brings Gunboat Smith aboard [MTM B13:457–458].

MTM B13:454–455; MTM B13:457–458

VanityPatrick Stranahan’s assessment of scholarship beyond the little Latin and Law he considers sufficient [A:109].

A:109

Vast cavernsThe spaces in the Papuans’ “bottomless unconscious” in the novel’s mythic account of them as the Well of the World. Other peoples and lands are entities maintained in these caverns of their under-persons; the Kiriwinans and other neighboring peoples are said to understand that their existence depends on the Papuans [A:37].

A:37

VaudevilleTheatrical entertainment among the forms in which Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni works. As a mind-reader, memory and information expert, and hypnotist, he has appeared in circuses, music halls, and vaudeville theatres around the world; he is also a nightclub magician and, chiefly, an answer man [A:215-216].

A:215-216

Vecchia zimarra senti“Old coat, listen,” the opening of Colline’s Act IV aria in Puccini’s La Bohème. Finnegan sings it during the gathering around a charcoal-filled trencher outside the Australian hotel, which has forbidden a bonfire [A:31].

A:31

VegaOne of the stars whose movements Hans learns to calculate under Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni [A:214]. The earlier glossary also connected Vega with the Paean’s comparison of stellar heights; that reference remains unverified because the Paean is absent from the available source copy.

A:214

VeilThe partition between the living and the dead in Ignatius Ti’s account: a hole opens at midnight as souls cross, allowing nimble old dead to return. The narrative subsequently describes loose ghosts entering the psycho ward through that hole [A:86-87].

A:86-87

Velikovsky, Immanuel (1895--1979)Russian-born American author and independent scholar (1895-1979), whose Worlds in Collision (1950) proposed catastrophic celestial events in human history. The popular book met strong scientific rejection. A hostile review of Royce Rollins’s The Return of the Neanderthal invokes Velikovsky disparagingly [D:240]. Duffey later names him with Braden, Cayce, and Otto while wondering about possible events becoming real through human insistence [MTM B11:340].

D:240; MTM B11:340

VellumCuscus-skin writing material in Sulem’s account of the tujuan, a person’s divinely given directions for life. The writing is rolled as small as a pebble and placed inside the body, variously located in the brain, liver, or diaphragm [A:60].

A:60

Vendetta, grandeThe “great revenge” in Niccolo Crotolus’s account of assassination: killing someone almost certainly outside a state of grace. He says it cost several times more than the piccola, since the advertised outcome included damnation, and claims that his family delivered what it was paid for [A:280].

A:280

Vendetta, piccolaThe “little revenge” in Niccolo Crotolus’s account of assassination: killing someone probably or possibly in a state of grace, sometimes after allowing a chance to attain it. It ensures death, not necessarily damnation. Crotolus says his employer has specified only the piccola for Finnegan, whom he has grown fond of following [A:279-280].

A:279-280

VeniceItalian city to which Vincent Stranahan proposes sailing with Finnegan, along with Prague, while considering flight before his wedding. His three thousand dollars are in addition to his mustering-out money [A:112].

A:112

VentriloquistPerformer at the Star and Garter whose act Theresa “Show Boat” Piccone joins. She operates his figures and also brings men, usually soldiers, from the audience to sit on her lap while she supplies their voices [A:49].

A:49

Vernal ecstasyPhrase attributed to Absalom Stein by an Australian informant describing his attraction to the perfumed Tommy Trouncer in the guise of Tania. Stein is said to want to make Tommy a good woman and live with her in a better, cleaner world [A:52].

A:52

Verne, JulesFrench novelist (1828-1905) and a pioneer of science fiction. Marie Monaghan uses his name as a nickname for her purported Dutch uncle, the barefoot carnival painter Shoeless Veronese van Rijn [A:28].

A:28

Veronese van Rijn, ShoelessMarie Monaghan’s purported Dutch uncle, nicknamed Jules Verne, a carnival foot-painter who works in watercolors, oils, and charcoal and goes barefoot. Hans questions the pronunciation involved in the Shoeless/Jules nickname [A:28].

A:28

vertFrench for green. Hans’s reflection on Marie’s eyes treats it as a degeneration of the older poetic vair [A:24]. The words actually have separate Latin origins: vert from viridis, vair from varius.

A:24

VestigeThe narrator’s description of the buffalo with whom Finnegan feels an affinity in their ancestral capital. They are said to be older than the earth’s other cattle, as his own strain is older than its proper people [A:206].

A:206

VetturaItalian for a carriage or automobile. Finnegan uses it, with faeton, drozhe, and carrozza, to praise Mr. X’s extraordinary multicolored vehicle [D:179].

D:179

VicesThe unspecified activities in which Henry Salvatore is said to have dabbled, from Copenhagen to Aruba, during his seafaring life as a rake before his trucking work and army service [A:124].

A:124

Vickers, Little EvaResident of the Old Wooden Ship, named in its roster of regulars and among the women called “salt water widows” [D:216] [D:221].

D:216; D:221

Vienna (Wien)City on the Danube, called Wien in the text, where Duffey and Brannagan join a group debating whether it is better to do right for the wrong reason or wrong for the right reason. Casey leaves the discussion to look at buildings and pastry shops [MTM B13:432].

MTM B13:432

Vigilante OrthodoxersThe armed Orthodoxers who confront Zabotski and threaten to shoot him for rejecting their chronology and account of origins. He covers their sight with darkness or clouds and reaches his contraption [MTM B9:286]. See Orthodoxer.

MTM B9:286

Vincent J. Stranahan (Vincent, Austin, Meleager)One of the Dirty Five, born in St. Louis on 5 April 1921 to Patrick J. and Monica (Murry) Stranahan; More Than Melchisedech spells his mother’s maiden name Murray [A:94] [MTM B5:161]. The opening presents Vincent as born in the World beside Finnegan, who is of the other world; the later roll of the five nevertheless associates them all with Wonder and identifies Vincent with Meleager, Mercurius, Don Vincent de Ollos, and Austin [A:2] [A:39]. The narrator describes his crooked eyebrows and mobile mouth, and Hans remembers his recitations of “Corrymeela” and “Downfall of the Gael” [A:5] [A:9]. He belongs to a sporting family of amateur boxers and footballers [A:103]. He marries Theresa “Show Boat” Piccone after the war; More Than Melchisedech places their wedding on the Saturday of the last week of May 1946 [A:113] [MTM B5:171].

Finnegan names him among friends of his normal life and later recalls long visits with him [D:90] [D:273]. Vincent and Teresa visit New Orleans with two children. With Finnegan and Absalom Stein, he becomes one of the three disguised “hyenas” heckling Showboat during her street mission with Margaret Stone; the women turn the crowd against the hecklers [MTM B7:229] [MTM B7:231-232].

A:94; MTM B5:161; A:2; A:39; A:5; A:9; A:103; A:113; MTM B5:171; D:90; D:273; MTM B7:229; MTM B7:231-232

Vinobianco, DominicOne of Casey Szymansky’s roommates at St. Bonaventure’s boarding school, with Johnny Carruthers, Hinnegan, Germany Metzger, and a senior assigned to their room. Dominic comes from Elgin [A:161-162].

A:161-162

VioletResident of the Old Wooden Ship tavern and boarding house, named among its “salt water widows,” women married to seamen [D:216] [D:221].

D:216; D:221

Virgen la mas Benigna“Virgin most Benign,” one of the Spanish ship names on the master treasure map described by Angela Cosquin. Her father supplies aged maps and supporting papers for confidence schemes; customers can choose a purported sunken treasure ship and even relocate it on the map [D:261].

D:261

Virgil (70--19 BC)Publius Vergilius Maro (70-19 BC), Roman poet of the age of Augustus, author of the pastoral Eclogues, the agricultural Georgics, and the Aeneid. Ancient biographical tradition describes his education in rhetoric and philosophy. The Aeneid follows the Trojan Aeneas toward Italy, connecting the Homeric past with Rome’s destiny and Augustus. Its treatment of duty, piety, and empire includes both Roman glory and the suffering involved in achieving it. A school text since antiquity, it became a central work of later European literature; Dante made Virgil his guide through Hell and Purgatory. Patrick Stranahan invokes the Georgics as his standard of poetry, declaring that there has been no real poetry since [A:109].

A:109

VirginThe Blessed Virgin, invoked in Hans Schultz’s reflections on Marie’s green eyes. The passage describes her as red-haired and green-eyed in early Flemish Annunciations, then turns to witches and Lilith in its fanciful genealogy of green-eyed women [A:24].

A:24

VirginiaOne of the red-haired town girls at the Bay Hotel picnic in Australia, with Dorothy, Tom Shire, Freddy Castle, and members of the Dirty Five. Casey declines to attend because Stein is there [A:29].

A:29

Virginia Dare White and RedWhite and red wines in Finnegan’s heavy shoulder bag when, after being refused further service in the bars around D’Hannis, he sets out into the Texas chaparral. The list gives three or four bottles of each [A:202].

A:202

Virtual miracleWhat Duffey says is required, with prayer and fasting, to bring mice to the new, mouse-free Gurdon S. Hubbard Elementary School. After the doors are opened and he concentrates or prays, seven exhausted mice arrive and perform in the puppet show; a teacher identifies them as Central American mice [MTM B4:135-136].

MTM B4:135-136

VirtueA quality Casey’s hostile Crock editorial says the Bark finds in Chiang’s refusal to cooperate with the “futuristic elements” in his country [A:128-130]. Elsewhere the narrator discusses Duffey’s retained but increasingly scruffy virtue, distinguishing his continuing honesty and courage from the complications of his affections [MTM B3:77] [MTM B4:109-110].

A:128-130; MTM B3:77; MTM B4:109-110

ViskochilOne of the surnames of the extended Angelino carnival clan, with Obermeyer, Borg, Trevino, and Larrigan. The narrator describes the clan collectively as largely Italian and German, with Bohemian, Mexican, and Irish Tinker ancestry; the passage does not assign an ethnicity to each surname [A:218].

A:218

VocationA calling that Henry Salvatore recognizes in his dream of the endangered Navicula Petri, which he understands to be the sanctified form of the Argo. Before waking he knows that the vocation has come to him whether he accepts it or not [A:44-46]. Later, lying in a pasture, he offers to give things up if God will take them in exchange [A:69]. Finnegan compares his unwanted artistic gift to Henry’s vocation: it frightens him, and he says that he has not accepted it and will try to escape it [A:99].

A:44-46; A:69; A:99

VogelkopThe Bird’s Head peninsula at the western end of New Guinea. The soldiers leave it behind on their transfer to a Dutch island four hundred miles farther on [A:50].

A:50

Voice rolesThe intelligible speaking parts of the live mice in the Duffeys’ puppet shows. The narrator leaves open whether the mice themselves speak, which would be first-degree magic, or whether Melchisedech’s or Letitia’s voices speak through them, second- or third-degree magic. Their correctly timed actions are called first-degree magic [MTM B4:134].

MTM B4:134

Voila!French “there it is” or “there you are,” used by Trinali Peterson as she announces the Trinali Cocktail. She mixes her old wine with Hans’s new wine and invokes a dialectical synthesis achieved by putting old and new wines into the scripturally wrong bottles [A:231].

A:231

Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet) (1694--1778)François-Marie Arouet (1694-1778), French Enlightenment writer, historian, and philosopher, known for Candide (1759), religious toleration, and campaigns against injustice and fanaticism.

In More Than Melchisedech, a grotesque fictional Voltaire is kept in a senile stasis and awakened for a festival celebrating his three-hundredth birthday. The authorities call him the Father of Reason and stage the killing of Hiram III with the entrails of Paul XI as the fulfillment of a wish they attribute to him. He watches delightedly before being allowed to sleep again [MB:563-565].

MB:563-565

Volvox colonialA preparation of colonial green algae that Biloxi Brannagan requests as the fruit course of his meal. His other choices include desmid salad with ulothrix, spirogyra bread, hydrodictyon soup, and a Foraminifera Julip [MTM B13:418].

MTM B13:418

VolvoxaAquatic material that Honeybucket Kincaid gathers with ectocarpus by manipulating frequencies while preparing Duffey and Brannagan’s food and drinks. The narrative says the two can arrive together and then be separated [MTM B13:418].

MTM B13:418

VomitingSedalia Schoefeld’s proposed trick for escaping the formal dance: she says she can vomit at will and will pretend to be ill. Lily Koch first asks to be splashed so that she too can leave, then leads the group to the attic billiard room instead [MTM B1:33].

MTM B1:33

Von Vinger, CountyAn alias of Ali ben Taife, also called Lord Peter Petrof and Sinhor Dedos or Mr. Fingers. In Ignatius Ti’s account, he employs Amoy as a jewel-stealing red-winged blackbird, then cuts the bird’s throat to recover a blue diamond it will not regurgitate [A:80-81].

A:80-81

Voyages of Sindbad the SailorThe subject of the Brunhilde barroom panels Finnegan paints for Saxon Seaworthy, whom the narrative identifies with a morally dubious Sindbad [D:59]. Anastasia requests the dead wife of the fourth voyage; Marie claims the happy-ever-after wife of the seventh. Finnegan paints those roles and proposes Papa Devil as a man-eating ogre and Gerecke as the Old Man of the Sea [D:60-62]. His difficulty portraying Papa Devil leads him to recognize that the apparent face is not the Devil’s own [D:62].

D:59; D:60-62; D:62

VulgateThe Latin Bible translation Henry Salvatore prefers to the French. During his dream of the storm-tossed Navicula Petri, a Latin account of the storm is followed by French, prompting him to tell the dream that he has already recognized the passage [A:44-45].

A:44-45

WaldoEarlier heading omitted Waldo’s surname, Waldorf. See Waldorf, Waldo.
Waldo, Wife of ZabotskiZabotski’s wife, still called the Widow Waldo, resident with him in the extraordinary house on Pristine Cove, Lake Borgne. The magazine account describes them as gracious hosts surrounded by children, strange animals, and an atmosphere of “top speed without hurry” [MTM B9:267]. Formerly Miss America, she married the promoted strongman Waldo Waldorf; after his murder by a jealous rival she devoted herself to orphans. She cooks for Duffey and Zabotski during construction and insists that many children accompany the vessel [MTM B9:275]. She relays the state inspector’s order to remove the part encroaching on the Golden Childrens Home and Haven Orphanage grounds [MTM B9:274]. She feeds the visiting Fundamentalers, joking that there is almost no limit to the food she can take from the orphans’ mouths [MTM B9:280].

Duffey visits her and Zabotski in their floating boat palace, already shared with many children and animals [MTM B10:290]. During a later dinner she says Zabotski has announced their departure daily for nine years, urges him to rest his injured tongue, and explains their large steak meals [MTM B12:363].

MTM B9:267; MTM B9:275; MTM B9:274; MTM B9:280; MTM B10:290; MTM B12:363

Waldorf, WaldoWaldo Waldorf, deceased husband of the Widow Waldo. He was Mr. Body Beautiful of the West North Central States, including Illinois; their marriage was a publicity stunt devised by promoters. His killing by a jealous rival preceded his widow’s dedication to orphans [MTM B9:275].

MTM B9:275

Walnut StreetDowntown St. Louis street where Duffey buys the empty horse barn that becomes his establishment [MTM B2:40]. Bagby’s cabinet shop occupies the adjoining building; Bagby says both were made from the walnut grove felled before the street was laid out and named [MTM B2:46].

MTM B2:40; MTM B2:46

Wandering JewHowell’s comparison for Private Gregory’s account of never aging and periodically changing identity. Howell calls “The Wandering Jew, are there Others?” his six-hundred-and-twenty-third subject of conversation, out of the thousand he claims to have catalogued [A:77].

A:77

Ward FourteenThe hospital ward occupied by the Sergeant, Private Gregory, Howell, George Buckram, Martin Benning, and Green. The Sergeant considers it a possible test of whether its inmates differ from other people, wonders about their kinship with “gooney birds,” and concludes that they are confined through misunderstanding [A:75].

A:75

Warneke, FannyOne of the arty friends in the Duffeys’ North Chicago golden age of 1925-1935 [MTM B3:98].

MTM B3:98

Washington UniversityOne of the institutions at which Duffey takes courses in the summer of 1915, alongside St. Louis University, Concordia, a pharmacy school, and a music school. He calculates twenty-eight hours of activity per day before sleep, already knowing tricks with time [MTM B2:49].

MTM B2:49

Watson (Dr. John H. Watson)Earlier heading identified an unspecified Watson with Sherlock Holmes’s companion without supporting evidence. See Watson (unidentified allusion).
Watson (unidentified allusion)A surname in Duffey’s list of unconventional scientific investigators, with O’Connell, Field, and Spraggett, during the discussion of strange events and possible changes of human species [MTM B11:339]. Lyall Watson, author of Supernature, is a plausible identification, but the passage supplies no first name; it does not establish Sherlock Holmes’s companion.

MTM B11:339

WatteauOne of the painters Patrick Stranahan names with Durer and Hogarth in his account of sufficient culture. He says one minor original and a dozen good copies are all an honest man can afford [A:109].

A:109

Waves of the FutureAbsalom Stein’s expression for forces from the future breaking backward into the past. His Notes on the Finnegan Cycle treats Hitler as one such raider and argues that the future’s evil and cheapness should encourage resistance [MTM B6:185].

MTM B6:185

“Way Back in the Hills”Tune Finnegan plays on his mouth organ to occupy the shoe-shine boys while Captain Sammy borrows their box for a money-making trick. It follows “A-Rang-Dang-Doo” and precedes “The Wreck of the Old Ninety-Seven” and “The Wabash Cannon Ball” [A:67].

A:67

Weaver, RufusOne of the musical friends in the Duffeys’ North Chicago golden age. The group collectively includes operatic, ragtime, Chicago-hots, and string-band composers, players, and stagers; Weaver’s individual specialty is not given [MTM B3:98-99].

MTM B3:98-99

Webbs, TheProbably Sidney and Beatrice Webb, the Fabian social thinkers. The Webbs appear with Nietzsche, Shaw, Machiavelli, and both Roosevelts among the sources mixed into the Answer, a journal that Duffey reads with mingled admiration and alarm [MTM B4:114].

MTM B4:114

WedekindOne of the associates of Papadiabolous I named by X, alongside Seaworthy, Genof, Wirt, Gerecke, Askadrian, Sanditen, and Sorensen. X says several of this group were rumored to be Papadiabolous’s illegitimate half-brothers, without specifying which [D:286].

D:286

WeinarEarlier heading altered the printed place-name; identification with Weimar remains unestablished. See Weiniar.
WeiniarA place Demetrio includes in the travels of his youth, with Alice, Eagle Pass, Uvalde, Beeville, San Angelo, and Port Isabel. The supplied text actually prints Weiniar [D:58].

D:58

Weinsberg-Valeni, Kirol vonSee Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni, Professor.
Welch, Art (Two Shot)Art “Two Shot” Welch, resident of the Old Wooden Ship and a card sharp and trickster paired with Art “One Shot” Yodel. The narrator says the pair are repeatedly outwitted by better sharpers [D:216] [D:221]. The earlier resident list calls his partner Ant “One Shot” Yoder [D:216].

D:216; D:221

Well of the WorldThe narrator’s name for the Papuans in the novel’s mythic cosmology. Their bottomless unconscious contains the other peoples and lands, which survive only while maintained in its caverns. The Kiriwinans and neighboring peoples are said to understand this dependence, while more distant peoples do not [A:37].

A:37

Wellington (Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of)Arthur Wellesley, first Duke of Wellington, included by the narrator among people said to have seven hidden or dark years in their lives. The list provides a precedent for Duffey’s missing years and also names Caesar, Diocletian, Boëthus, Carl the Great, Lincoln, Sam Houston, George Barrow, and Hans Schultz [MTM B2:72].

MTM B2:72

WestThe direction Finnegan travels after leaving the goat-people. He walks chiefly in the hours before dawn and later remembers the summer as continually foggy, though the narrator allows that the fog may not have been physical [A:200].

A:200

West BeachPlace on Galveston Island where Doll Delancy finds a body she swears is Finnegan’s. Stein reports her identification while doubting that Finnegan died at Seaworthy’s hand [MB:548].

MB:548

West KansasThe comparison used to convey Black Papua’s densely crowded landscape: an equal square mile of West Kansas is imagined as open enough to count fence posts a mile away, with nothing larger between [A:37].

A:37

WhammoIgnatius Ti’s word for the delayed impact of his ghost story. He defends its quiet climax by saying that the after-effect hits the listener “Whammo” [A:87].

A:87

Where Three Men Stand Together Are Kingdoms Less By ThreeThe line Hans quotes during his solemn three-way handshake with Henry and Finnegan after the group’s drinking excursion in Luzon. The narrative likens the gesture to the formation of a mystic trio within the Dirty Five; the group later sleeps in the pasture near the two white horses [A:68-69].

A:68-69

“Whistle Stop Jump”One of the tunes in the Rounders’ String Band’s St. Louis repertoire, remembered among its sweet old songs. Duffey plays banjo in the group and associates that instrument with the flat straw hat [MTM B2:52].

MTM B2:52

White AvengerOne of three comic strips in which Dotty says the Slant-Faced Men have appeared, with Flame Man and Captain Justice. She would find them funny if she did not know they were real [MTM B7:225].

MTM B7:225

White Horse(s)The two horses in a Luzon field to which Hans leads the drinking party after a brief fight with other soldiers and a walk through the jungle. He runs down the larger white horse, catches it by the mane, and rides it through low branches in the darkness. The narrator counts this capture among the Argonauts’ appointed heroic labors [A:68].

A:68

White wineOne of the drinks Patrick Stranahan considers sufficient for a settled life, with one red wine, one whisky, one brandy, one rum, and four brews [A:110]. The narrator also says white wine is made on Naxos [D:125]. Finnegan and Anastasia bring wine among their provisions for Anastasia Grandmother, although that list does not specify its color [D:126].

A:110; D:125; D:126

Whiteduck, DorcasOne of the artists or makers Duffey associates with during the New Orleans rebuilding project. The group is described as building or inventing worlds, moments, situations, or scenes; Whiteduck’s individual medium is not specified [MTM B6:198].

MTM B6:198

Whiterice, MaudOne of the friends of scientific bent in the Duffeys’ North Chicago golden age, listed with Silas Whiterice [MTM B3:98-99]. She and Silas attend Duffey’s later Chicago reunion, where her name is spelled Maude [MTM B12:383]. Their joint commentary discusses the strange encyclopedia entry identifying Casey Szymansky as the Antichrist; they call it a hoax while affirming the accuracy of its birth details [PG:528-529].

MTM B3:98-99; MTM B12:383; PG:528-529

Whiterice, ShermanEarlier heading combined Sherman Slick’s given name with the surname of the following Silas and Maud Whiterice. See Slick, Sherman.
Whiterice, SilasOne of the friends of scientific bent in the Duffeys’ North Chicago golden age, listed with Maud Whiterice [MTM B3:98-99]. Both attend Duffey’s later Chicago reunion [MTM B12:383]. Their joint commentary describes a variant encyclopedia entry naming Casey Szymansky as the Antichrist; they call the insertion a hoax but affirm its account of his birth [PG:528-529].

MTM B3:98-99; MTM B12:383; PG:528-529

WhitesOne of the family names given by an older relative or pretended relative who disputes Duffey’s lack of kindred in the account of his possible Iowa childhood. Duffey questions whether she is remembering his twin instead [MTM B1:7].

MTM B1:7

“Who Is Iason, but Who Is Also of the Other People”Subtitle attached to “Finnegan” in the heading of Chapter Seven [A:171].

A:171

“Who Is Meleager”Part of the Chapter Four heading, “Stranahan, Who Is Meleager” [A:91].

A:91

Widow WaldoSee Waldo, Wife of Zabotski [MTM B9:267] [MTM B9:275].

MTM B9:267; MTM B9:275

Widow wooingOne of the minor arts of everyday life that the narrator says lost style and was trashed during the cultural decline after the Devil’s release [MTM B6:207-208].

MTM B6:207-208

Wild Beasts Devouring Entrails in the Holy PlacesAn “old saying” in the narrative that supplies the theme for a second grotesque presentation at the Voltaire Festival. After Hiram III’s murder, fifty members of the Consenting Adults’ World Congress eat the entrails of Paul XI in a large holy place, struggling with their toughness and gamey taste [MB:565].

MB:565

Wild onion huntingOne of the minor arts whose cultural destruction is lamented after the Devil’s release. It appears in the narrator’s catalogue and is repeated in Duffey’s protest that hardly a joy has survived [MTM B6:208-209].

MTM B6:208-209

Wild TurkeyBirds among the creatures along the mile-long track through John William Schultz’s nursery at St. Gallen. Hans runs the meander every morning and evening during his physical education [A:208].

A:208

William Count of PoitouNamed in item V of Casey Szymansky’s school notebook as the figure to whom poetry in the mother tongue can be traced. Casey tentatively attributes this statement to Belloc, or to another writer he read around the same time [A:163].

A:163

Willy Jones IslandIsland also called Pulau Petir where, in Don Lewis’s account, he and two other American soldiers disappear on 1 October 1944. Santee and Casper kill Yokipoki; Don Lewis buries him, is subsequently taken into a peculiar custody, and returns under another name, no longer his own man [D:44-48]. He also tells the island’s story of the Big House, whose inhabitants live on broth made from murdered visitors’ organs [D:48-49]. The narrative connects Yokipoki’s burial with Don Lewis’s becoming a furtive man [D:50].

D:44-48; D:48-49; D:50

Windward PassageOne of the seven true passages through the Antilles in Angela Cosquin’s account of her father’s forged shipwreck maps. She contrasts these with seven false or shoal passages: Jardines Banks, Cabo Rojo, Vieques, St. Barthelemy, the Basseterre-Nevis pass, the Basse-Terre-Marie Galante pass, and the Grenadines. This is Angela’s explanation of where her father placed plausible wrecks on his maps. [D:260]

D:260

Wine makingA traditional craft included in the narrator’s catalogue of activities condemned or “trashed” during cultural decline. [MTM B6:207-208] Trinali Peterson mixes her old wine with Hans’s new wine to make the “Trinali Cocktail.” Her accompanying poem gives a grape, water, and sugar recipe with optional brandy and six months’ gestation, mentions a thirteen-day potato wine, and presents winemaking as the birth and imprisonment of a god. [A:231]

MTM B6:207-208; A:231

Wine of the UralsWine associated with the drink Finnegan shares with Askandan after Hillary Hilton leaves. The passage says that Finnegan imbibes knowledge and “a drink made of goats’ milk and a wine of the Urals”; it does not establish that the wine itself is made from milk. [A:256]

A:256

Winter GardenPlace where, according to Finnegan, the leftfooted killer had been asking for him the previous day. Finnegan reports this while X briefs him on the continuing pursuit. [D:193]

D:193

Wiper, The (giant)A “cloud-high giant” described to Newton Prescott by a little boy. The Wiper uses a rag to erase part of a cloud and, with it, part of something in people’s heads. Prescott accepts the boy’s intuitive account of this personification of forgetting and subsequently notices drawings of the Wiper on walls and sidewalks. [CM:503] [CM:513-514]

CM:503; CM:513-514

Wirt, PeterOne of Saxon Seaworthy’s two cronies aboard the Brunhilde, with William Gerecke, sharing the mystery surrounding Seaworthy and the Devil. [D:30] Anastasia includes him among the powerful men who own the captain and crew; Finnegan senses a strong, earthy power in him at the beach gathering. [D:40] [D:50] Wirt goes ashore with Seaworthy and Gerecke and later waits with them aboard the ship at Naxos, an experienced combatant rather than a nonentity. [D:57] [D:136] X names him among the four rulers after the two Papadiabolouses die. [D:155] At the subsequent meeting he has the “mind of a wolverine.” [D:163] Papadiabolous I’s associates include Wirt; several of that group are rumored to be illegitimate half brothers, without identifying which ones. [D:286]

D:30; D:40; D:50; D:57; D:136; D:155; D:163; D:286

WisconsinThe state of Hans Schultz’s childhood. During Hans and Marie’s exchange of childhood memories, the narrator observes that Wisconsin and New South Wales are very much alike in summer. [A:10] Hans’s birthplace, St. Gallen, is described as Northern Wilderness lake country beyond Rhinelander and near Eagle River. He remembers its splendid sunlight and calls it the land of the larger summer. [A:207]

A:10; A:207

Wisconsin RapidsTown reached by Hans Schultz and Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni after an eighty-mile drive from St. Gallen in a truck resembling an old medicine-show wagon. The Professor lectures Hans on the journey; they meet the rest of the carnival at Wisconsin Rapids. [A:212] [A:215]

A:212; A:215

Wisdom of FinneganThe source Hans names for the reversed maxim “If you can’t be careful, be good.” He is correcting Salvation Sally, who has offered the conventional wording; Marie Monaghan is also present. [A:9]

A:9

Wolf huntingOne of the traditional activities included in the narrator’s catalogue of pursuits condemned or “trashed” during cultural decline. [MTM B6:207-208]

MTM B6:207-208

Wolff, IgnaceName credited with the epigraph to Chapter Five, “The Unaccountable Corpse,” from a work styled Gedanken von Leibern (Thoughts on Bodies). The epigraph says that bodies thwart non-contradiction and negate the principle of sufficient reason: “There is not sufficient reason for bodies.” [D:67]

D:67

Wooden Ship (Old Wooden Ship)A Sydney pub visited by Finnegan, Vincent, Hans, Casey, Tom, and Freddy, after the Commodore and before the Green Tree, during the preparations for Hans’s drinking contest. Marie joins them later at the Harbor House. [A:17-19] The Old Wooden Ship in The Devil Is Dead is a four-story, unpainted, pungent tavern at the end of a garlic block, with raked shells for a sidewalk, many doors and stairs, loose shutters, and a ship-like creaking sway. Finnegan and Le Marin frequent it alongside its Company of Fifty resident regulars. Proprietor Lazarus Reilly supplies accommodation, credit, and loans and refuses nobody lest an applicant be an angel in disguise; barmaid Soft-Talk Susie Kutz is called an “angel unaware.” [D:215-216] [D:225] A camel lives in the weed patch behind it. [D:219] Finnegan’s journey to Paradise begins there after his reading of St. Francis de Sales. [D:233] More Than Melchisedech explicitly locates the Old Wooden Ship Tavern, where Gunboat Smith is Bulldog-in-Residence, in Galveston, Texas. [MTM B13:458]

A:17-19; D:215-216; D:225; D:219; D:233; MTM B13:458

Wordless Repartee Between Melchisedech Duffey and the Invisible God, TheThe seventh of Duffey’s possible contingencies: a silent exchange with the invisible God in a garden one afternoon. Everything and a solution to all problems are promised. A failure would have to be sought out through stubbornness and confusion; its disaster might affect only Duffey, or return him to a beginning. The text leaves unclear whether he can choose between the contingencies. [MTM B10:301]

MTM B10:301

Wordsworthian Intimations of a BeginningThe beginning of a life pattern Finnegan wishes to escape after his death: “Wordsworthian Intimations of a Beginning, Baconian Turgidity in the Middle, and Bierceian Irony at the End.” [D:237] The opening phrase alludes to William Wordsworth’s “Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood.”

D:237

WorkmanThe workman in “Great Day in the Morning” who rebukes Melchisedech Duffy for asking what has happened to vehicle wheels, calling him a “roundskin” and “roundheel.” Nearby, workmen and owners are replacing wheels with an indistinct device from kits. [GD:489]

GD:489

World (1) (the World)The World into which Finnegan looks with new-made eyes after the Garden disappears, doubting he will find a place there. Vincent, in this opening account, was born in it and belongs there. [A:1-2] Later the Dirty Five, including Vincent, are described as belonging in their fleeting moments to the Wonder rather than the World; the difference between these accounts is left standing. [A:39] Vincent argues that the world might have been created ten minutes ago with its fossils and vestiges already in place, and later declares that the present world exists for an elite of one, himself. These are Vincent’s arguments, not settled narration. [A:56] [A:58]

A:1-2; A:39; A:56; A:58

World (2)One of the names X gives for the ship on which Finnegan sailed, alongside Delay and Argo. X’s report is an account of the ship’s uncertain identity, not a verified registry name. [A:187]

A:187

World ConsensusThe authority whose order to abolish St. Kobarid is defied by King Hiram III, leaving it the world’s last unabolished nation in the fictional account. The passage does not specify what kind of organization the World Consensus is. [MB:563]

MB:563

World Labor Czar (Poot Plambert)Title of Poot Plambert, voted the World’s Most Beloved Man of the Year. King Hiram III refuses to contribute to the worldwide cash benefice for him. [MB:564]

MB:564

World of Record, TheDotty Yekouris’s name for the place where people wake, sleep, and wake again while their rich other life of the Argo Voyages continues in reserved places. Her statement insists that the voyages are ongoing rather than merely events of many centuries ago. [MTM B5:180]

MTM B5:180

World-Wide Argonauts Argo Balloon ClubClub of rich sportsmen which Duffey joins or, in another version, founds. Its entrance fee is $3,000. Bagby later claims Duffey collected that sum from each of twenty-three members as North American Bursar; the Geneva headquarters to which he was supposed to remit it never existed. Duffey spends $6,000 on a large custom silk balloon using hydrogen and sandbag ballast. [MTM B2:63-64] He first calls it The Argo Twelve, then changes the name to The Argo Twelve and Half after a powerful misty visitor tells him that Argo Twelve is already active and that his balloon may serve as its pinnace. [MTM B2:64]

MTM B2:63-64; MTM B2:64

Wright, PeterName on anvils among the household and trade words young Duffey encounters during his mind-piracy. [MTM B1:17]

MTM B1:17

XMr. X, the former magician and escape artist called the Great X-Capo, is an elusive associate of Finnegan and Duffey [A:137] [D:152]. More Than Melchisedech introduces him as an ally or counter-ally, a shabby, wistful clown of a north Italian type, apparently about Duffey’s age [MTM B6:200]. Duffey tells him that he is one of the people Duffey made [MTM B1:6]. The narrator of Archipelago says that almost all his information is true, but that he cannot evaluate it and is drawn to the excitement of the game. His convictions change: he has joined the Party sincerely, yet makes peace with the Church at Easter, becomes agnostic by midsummer, and atheist by fall [A:138]. In Archipelago he calls Duffey at three in the morning, disguising his voice with a rosin-impregnated handkerchief or by talking through his hat. He then arrives with nested black, gray, and brown boxes, the last containing the Crock’s intelligence files, which he has stolen from Casey [A:135-136]. He says Casey has ceased properly using the information. X has memorized and annotated it, and spends about two hours writing more cards. He boasts that he opens such locks with mittens on. He visits congressmen and Justice Department agents at midnight, receives tips from Dutch importers and Bucharest rivermen, exchanges Nostrodomo-type prophecies with Jesuit experts, and has been a Party member under different names in France and Italy [A:137-138]. More Than Melchisedech gives another account of this first New Orleans visit: Letitia opens the door to the shy visitor and embraces him, while Duffey is slow to understand who is expected [MTM B6:200]. X brings both the nested boxes and a canister containing Duffey’s own ashes. His old red-box trick becomes the occasion for a real intervention by Duffey [MTM B6:201-203]. Most of the index cards were written by Duffey, with others by X and further contributors. X has added an orange-red card, apparently three times the others’ size yet fitting the box, for the newly released Devil. He claims to have witnessed the release in the Crimea under one of his assumed identities [MTM B6:203-205]. X says that the glassy eye, or oculum vitreum, sometimes reveals that a powerful man receiving his secret information is himself in the Conspiracy. He carries a dagger blade in his shoulder and a pellet in his neck, and recounts escaping after being bound, weighted, and dropped from a garbage scow [A:138]. He calls pursuing the Conspiracy a courageous instance of flogging a dead horse, and credits the Devil with inventing that discouraging phrase. His account of a nocturnal visitor who might have been the Devil remains uncertain; he admits it could have been a hoax. In another sense and another life, he says, he did know the Devil and dug him up [A:139-140]. He has a wife in Milano whom he loves but has not seen for years. Danger and intervening circumstances first delay his return; then fear of her irony and his renewed shyness keep him away [A:140-141]. He sends his New Orleans friends a false clipping describing his own murder, including the identifying blade and pellet. Dotty recognizes both his rosin and the Pelican Press’s worn type, and he later returns sheepishly [A:141-142]. In Paros he admits the trick to Finnegan, whom he knows in both his lives, and proposes pooling their knowledge of Papadiabolous. He acknowledges that he missed the burial but says he may tell the story later as an eyewitness [D:151-153]. He joins Finnegan and Doll Delancy during their night out in Baltimore, seeming a comical little drunk, though Finnegan realizes he is sober [D:172-174]. He helps them leave as pursuers mistake another large-nosed man for Finnegan. X has lifted the suitcase claim check from Doll’s bag, retrieved the chrysus, and substituted a similar suitcase containing thirty-six thousand pieces of cut newspaper [D:177-178]. The original case contains thirty-six thousand pieces of currency [D:166] [D:185]. He buys an eight-toned car with a D.C. plate, the hurtling rainbow or Celestial Omnibus. He explains its conspicuousness through a sequence of butterfly and klunker counter-plans, but admits Doll is right: he chose it because he liked it, and the explanation is rationale [D:177] [D:179-180]. He divides the money among three bags, giving Finnegan the heaviest and Doll the smallest [D:180]. In Florida he makes frequent long-distance calls and speaks a coded sequence beginning with Xochilmileo. That passage does not clearly establish the word as his own alias [D:183-184]. Doll proposes their eventual separation in three vehicles; X arranges signals, briefing, and a rendezvous a year, a day, and some odd weeks later beside Ifreann’s grave. He warns that he will select, arrange, and fictionalize details when telling their story [D:185-186]. After Finnegan’s crisis he gives the lengthy briefing, then leaves in the Celestial Omnibus [D:193]. Later he calls Finnegan in Biloxi with a disguised voice, warning him to leave and avoid his old haunts [D:208-209]. At the graveyard rendezvous X still needs Finnegan to locate the grave. He explains its I.N.C.G.P. Bogovitch inscription as a softened form of Chortovitch, distinguishing the elder Ifreann Noonan Columkill Gregorovitch Papadiabolous Chortovitch from his sons [D:275-278]. X believes that the Devil who fathered Ifreann was also his own grandfather and Finnegan’s and Anastasia’s great-grandfather. He admits the alternative that Gregory, Ifreann’s adoptive father, was his biological father, though he rejects it [D:279]. His account distinguishes the quasi-twins born to different mothers: Papadiabolous I, Gregory McIfreann, and Papadiabolous II, Gregory McColum, the undercover policeman he knew as Noonan or N. X is unsure even whom he himself now serves [D:285-287]. X says the elder Ifreann was buried in 1930, that Seaworthy killed Papadiabolous I while reopening that father’s grave, and that II assumed his brother’s place; several details are explicitly conjectural [D:288-289]. He has forged taunting notes in Papadiabolous’s handwriting to bring Seaworthy back. He intends to reopen the grave for a key document and trap Seaworthy there, while warning that Finnegan may not survive his own encounter [D:289-291]. X regards ordinary people as incapable sheep and expects resistance to come from a minority of the older race. Doll challenges this contempt and insists that people can act to save themselves [D:290] [D:292]. In Duffey’s later travels X appears as Carmelo Mendoza and Karl Metz, with Mr. Eggs as another form of his name. Horace Pie recognizes him before Duffey does; X supplies information about Finnegan’s submerged resting place near Cuba’s Marianao coast [MTM B12:371]. With Kasmir Gorshok he finds and identifies Duffey’s remains in Gur’yev. He keeps the ashes, anticipating a chance to return them to Duffey alive, while the bones are carried aboard the Argo. He is explicitly its Half-Master [MTM B13:442-443]. As Monsignor X he serves the Final Conclave in How Many Miles to Babylon, including putting the straw effigy and six bodies into the stove [MB:566] [MB:568]. When Hackenschmidt orders his death, X produces a submachine gun and leaves. He declares that he will sometimes work for the former princes, sometimes for the thirteen absent princes, and sometimes for their contracted killers, Track and Total: nothing less than a triple agent would suit him. He also promises to ornament the story across its disordered tenses. Here his vaudeville name is printed Great Ex-Capo [MB:569].
