X-Capo, The GreatSee Great X-Capo, The [A:137] [D:276].

A:137; D:276

Xavier (St. Xavier)St. Francis Xavier (1506-1552), the Jesuit missionary to India, the Indonesian archipelago, and Japan. Finnegan hails him as apostle to the greater Archipelagos and imagines his recognition of a miracle: after the world’s end was reached, there was still an ocean full of islands. [A:35] Xavier also appears among the saints on Henry’s dream-ship Navicula Petri. [A:45]

A:35; A:45

XenoiThe word the talking oak translates as “Strangers” when X asks to join the Argo. X claims that Attic ephebic inscriptions use X for Xenoi, answering the oak’s demand that every passenger be found in Scripture or Inscription. The oak’s translation reinforces its claim not to know him. The speaking piece of oak is in the ship’s wheel. [MTM B13:434-435]

MTM B13:434-435

XochilmileoWord X uses at the beginning of a coded telephone exchange. It is followed by Vinschoten, Vlissinger, Spink, Tineo, Abo, Imazu, Ligueria, Sheboygan, Absecon, Xariia, Oquawka, and Neffs, and by a question about the listener’s code book. The passage does not establish that “Xochilmileo” is X’s own alias or explain its meaning. [D:184]

D:184

Yalta ConferenceThe historical conference of Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin at Yalta in the Crimea, February 4-11, 1945. In X’s fictional account, notables had visited the neighborhood for years to consult the imprisoned Devil and learn when he would be released; X further claims that the conference itself depended on daily or hourly consultations with him. [MTM B6:204]

MTM B6:204

YanksColloquial name for Americans, used variously in jokes, rivalry, and mistaken expectations. Tom Shire and Freddy Castle pretend that Finnegan and Vincent need disguises to enter an Australian wet canteen. Sergeant Bushmaster actually greets the “Yanks” hospitably, although he later taunts their drinking capacity and suggests goats’ milk. [A:11-15] Finnegan is induced to sign an anti-Yank affidavit conceding Australian superiority at beer drinking, calling Americans wet behind the ears, and adding explicit obscenities. [A:13] Bushmaster calls Hans a “red-eyed Yankee” during their drinking contest. [A:22] Marie thinks of Americans and Arabs as similarly close “Peoples of the Book”; this is her comparison. [A:7] In Cuba, Ignacio is surprised that Finnegan is a Yankee because he lacks Ignacio’s expected New England traits. Visiting American tourists speak pidgin Spanish to Finnegan as though he were a barefoot Latino. [A:273]

A:11-15; A:13; A:22; A:7; A:273

Yekouris (family name)Family name of Dorothy Mary (“Dotty”) Yekouris. [A:95] In The Devil Is Dead, Finnegan includes her among the friends of his normal life while talking to another self across a table. Despite knowing these people, he feels a barrier between himself and humankind. [D:90]

A:95; D:90

Yekouris, Dorothy (Dotty)Dorothy Mary Yekouris, usually Dotty, a New Orleans printer’s daughter raised in the trade who also takes up bartending when printing does not provide a living. She comes to St. Louis for Vincent and Show Boat’s wedding in the last week of May 1946, staying with Show Boat. She and Finnegan love each other, but his wandering and conviction of irretrievable loss keep them apart; the narrator says no sharp word will pass between them. [A:95] [A:106] [MTM B5:171] She has attended bartenders’ school and is particularly angered when Casey’s hostile editorial questions her ability to distinguish drinks. [A:129] [A:131] More Than Melchisedech also makes her a member of the Poison Pen Society. [MTM B5:183] Dotty and Duffey establish The Bark at the Pelican Press in New Orleans. She is one of its original seven trustees and directors, the Seven Pillars of Righteousness; Finnegan’s masthead calls her “The Beautiful Barmaid.” She, Duffey, Stein, and Mary Virginia do the actual work of running the paper. [A:121-122] [MTM B6:198] [MTM B7:214-215] Dotty’s immense journalistic talent is acknowledged by both Stein and Duffey; under her editorship the paper outdoes its diabolical rivals in liveliness, intelligence, printing, writers, and features. The press also issues seamen’s, union, sporting, and jazz papers to support its work. [MTM B7:212-213] Her many suitors include men associated with these papers, but the narrator says she loves only Finnegan. Called a “beautiful bonus forever,” she is extravagantly described through a borrowed nursery catalogue’s flower and fruit adjectives, ending “hardy and disease-resistant.” She is the New Orleans native whom Stein calls a gracious French lady who turns out to be Lithuanian. It is Dotty who calls Mary Virginia the “Saccharine Kid,” partly affectionately and partly jealously. [MTM B7:212-214] Dotty belongs among Duffey’s Animated Marvels. During the argument over whether Duffey created or merely collected these people, she warns him that changing them would be at his peril: they like themselves and him as they are. [MTM B5:159] She is credited with Pelican Pellets, including a limerick about Duffey’s inventions, and with a statement that the Argo Voyages continue as their rich other life beyond the “World of Record.” The wedding gathering identifies her among the people of the Argo Legend and the original crew. [MTM B5:171] [MTM B5:177] [MTM B5:180] [MTM B5:183] Her New Orleans circle includes Duffey, Mary Virginia, Margaret Stone, Salvation Sally, Stein, Zabotski, and X. She jokes that X should be given milk and put out as an unaffordable pet, then welcomes him; later she firmly refuses to publish his list of those present at the Devil’s release. [A:136] [MTM B6:195-198] [MTM B6:206] [MTM B7:212-215] In Archipelago, a Havana lawyer’s letter prompts Dotty’s voyage to Finnegan; she mentions earlier letters and money from Finnegan himself. After arrival, Ignacio maps Finnegan’s walks and explains the danger. Dotty buys a pistol, tracks the left-footed Nick the Rattle, disables his car, and shoots him. Nick returns fire on her and Finnegan; the book leaves the three exchanging unfailing shots, with both lovers repeatedly wounded. [A:277] [A:280-282] More Than Melchisedech instead emphasizes letters from Ignacio and Elena and says Finnegan did not write to her directly. Dotty leaves, does not return, and no solid news follows. X reports both lovers slain near Havana but will not swear that their deaths are final and still feels their presences. These accounts preserve uncertainty about their ultimate fate. [MTM B8:237-238]

A:95; A:106; MTM B5:171; A:129; A:131; MTM B5:183; A:121-122; MTM B6:198; MTM B7:214-215; MTM B7:212-213; MTM B7:212-214; MTM B5:159; MTM B5:177; MTM B5:180; A:136; MTM B6:195-198; MTM B6:206; MTM B7:212-215; A:277; A:280-282; MTM B8:237-238

Yellow SeaSea between mainland China and the Korean Peninsula, included among the many seas sailed by the Argo and remembered by Melchisedech. [MTM B13:406]

MTM B13:406

YenboPlace paired with Lith in the opening poem of the chapter “Finnegan: Who Is Iason, but Who Is Also of the Other People”: “The Desert is burning at Yenbo and Lith.” [A:171]

A:171

YiddishLanguage invoked in several character descriptions and verbal performances. Duffey’s voice is Boston Irish with a touch of stage Yiddish. [A:97] Hans’s mother Irene, recalling Professor Kirol, says that “phoney” is Yiddish rather than English or German and once carried more humor and less shoddiness; this is her etymological claim. [A:211] In the graveyard, X boasts that although his listeners hear his explanation of the Papadiabolous family, watchers reading his lips through binoculars see mouth movements telling humorous Yiddish stories. [D:278]

A:97; A:211; D:278

Yoder, Ant (One Shot)Resident regular at the Old Wooden Ship, listed as Ant (One Shot) Yoder in its Company of Fifty. [D:215-216] The later account calls Art (One Shot) Yodel the partner of Art (Two Shot) Welch: they are unsuccessful card sharps and tricksters, often outwitted by better sharpies. The matching nickname and partner suggest a textual name variant, which should not be silently regularized. [D:221]

D:215-216; D:221

YokipokiName Don Lewis gives, while admitting it is probably not the real one, to the ragged man who seems to be a Japanese soldier on Pulau Petir or Willy Jones Island on October 1, 1944. The patrol consists of Sergeant Charles Santee, Corporal Robert Casper, and PFC Timothy Lorrigan. Lewis initially withholds which soldier he was, but his later correction of “I” to Lorrigan strongly identifies him with the private. [D:44-46] The little man repeatedly disappears when encircled and reappears hundreds of yards farther away. Santee wounds him; after a long pursuit, Santee and Casper kill him while Lorrigan hangs back. Lost and quarrelling, the three soldiers separate for the night. [D:44-46] Lewis remains in the valley and uses his short shovel and the dead man’s double-edged butcher knife to dig a grave. He removes Yokipoki’s boots, gags him, binds wrists and ankles, bandages his eyes, covers him with mud, says “Requiem” and “lux perpetua,” and drinks to him as a Christian burial. Later squealing and movement in the grave terrify Lewis, who imagines the dead man cutting his bonds with the buried knife; after an attack on his ankle, he recognizes rats at the corpse. [D:46-47]

D:44-46; D:46-47

Z'drovieCasey Szymansky’s toast when he, Henry, and Finnegan share a drink in their jungle bivouac. Henry answers with “Sante,” and Finnegan with Irish “Slainthe” and Italian “salute.” [A:44] Casey’s spelling resembles Slavic health toasts, particularly Polish na zdrowie; the novel does not explicitly label its language.

A:44

Zabotski (Zab)Zabotski, often Zab, is an experimenter, artist, prophet, historian, and probably wealthy landlord, formerly a chemist. Abrasive and loud, he looks smelly without smelling bad; he carries tenants more generously than his detractors. [MTM B11:306] He supplies the glass-lined thousand-gallon crock for Duffey’s Big Pot and courts the Widow Waldo, who becomes Wife Waldo. [MTM B6:195] [MTM B6:197] [MTM B9:285] He lives on Dumaine Street between Duffey and Homer Hoose before moving with her to his floating home on Lake Borgne. His claim to be gentle coexists with quarrelsome behavior and his neighbors’ complaints. [MTM B9:267-269] He builds an enormous backyard contraption from an ancient illustrated instruction text he thinks is in Hazh-Khazh, initially guessing it is a barn or castle. After talking with the Fundamentalers, he recognizes the ark’s manual and purpose. [MTM B9:272] [MTM B9:284] He calls himself an artist and prophet before a historian and writes Pristine History of the World. His Pristine World occupies the same space as the slow Everyday-or-Molasses World but excludes duplication and invalidity, allowing years of experience within ordinary days. He and Duffey debate these accounts of time, origins, and history with the Fundamentalers; Duffey then makes a Pristine journey himself. [MTM B9:277-284] Zabotski curses Blackstone’s sycamore and predicts Blackstone’s death while denying that he can cause a man’s death. The apparent next morning brings a missing tree and an older Bandicoot, who says it died and was cut down years ago. Blackstone’s later death completes Zabotski’s “five days” against a much longer family chronology. [MTM B9:269-270] [MTM B9:276] [MTM B9:288] In one account at the Decatur Street Opera House, bulls kill him during the Cretan Bull Drama; he gives a last bellow after death and earns the Ugly Ovation. The narrator, rather than Zabotski, says he makes a good show. [MTM B11:349] In the later boat-castle visit, he instead reports surviving an attempted lynching near the Opera House with help from poor neighbors, although his tongue is mangled. He is living with Wife Waldo and fifty-two children. These divergent outcomes remain part of the narrative. [MTM B12:362-364]

MTM B11:306; MTM B6:195; MTM B6:197; MTM B9:285; MTM B9:267-269; MTM B9:272; MTM B9:284; MTM B9:277-284; MTM B9:269-270; MTM B9:276; MTM B9:288; MTM B11:349; MTM B12:362-364

Zabotski FlatsAbout two hundred acres bought by Zabotski on Lake Borgne, where his boat-castle rides at a kedge anchor. Two-thirds are sweet meadows and one-third salt, extraordinarily lush though neighboring land is sparse. Zabotski attributes the transformation to God’s blessing. [MTM B12:362] Lions and leopards eat the abundant Nimrod Flesh Plant; hippopotami and leviathan graze in the salt meadows, whales visit the deeper water, and water buffaloes use both portions. Zebras, asses, cattle, sheep, goats, rabbits, coneys, and smaller game occupy the sweet-water parts. [MTM B12:362-363]

MTM B12:362; MTM B12:362-363

Zabotski Folly (Zabotsky House, Zabotski Happening)The giant, outlandish structure Zabotski builds in his Dumaine Street backyard, intruding onto Duffey’s, Hoose’s, Blackstone’s, and the orphanage’s land. [MTM B9:268-271] He works from ancient rock drawings and writing he thinks is in Hazh-Khazh, at first unable to tell whether he is constructing a barn, castle, or something else. Waldo identifies its overlapping prototypes as ship, castle, anti-time machine, and the old woman’s shoe. Zabotski eventually recognizes the ark’s instruction manual. [MTM B9:272-275] [MTM B9:284] With Wife Waldo, children, and strange animals aboard, it floats away in a sudden flood toward the Shoal Street Viaduct. Zabotski insists this will be the original Flood and says they can travel on water, air, or space; the structure comes to rest at anchor on his Lake Borgne property, near Pristine Cove. [MTM B9:267] [MTM B9:285-287] The magazine House and Home Happenings introduces a projected two-part feature, publishing Duffey’s “myth of origin” and promising the architectural description later. Its rapidity blurs fast photographs and changes a reporter’s experience of elapsed time. [MTM B9:267] [MTM B9:288] At Duffey’s later visit, the ark houses fifty-two unrelated children whom Zabotski praises as exceptionally capable, along with many animals; its surrounding meadows support hippopotami, leviathan, buffaloes, zebras, lions, and leopards. [MTM B12:362-364]

MTM B9:268-271; MTM B9:272-275; MTM B9:284; MTM B9:267; MTM B9:285-287; MTM B9:288; MTM B12:362-364

Zabotsky HouseSee Zabotski Folly (Zabotsky House, Zabotski Happening), the structure introduced in House and Home Happenings Magazine. [MTM B9:267]

MTM B9:267

ZackAustralian slang for a sixpence. The Sydney wet-canteen barman tells Finnegan that a zack, not a supposed beer chit, is all he needs to buy a beer. [A:14]

A:14

ZakinthosGreek stop reached by the Brunhilde after Messina. The narrator places it within Anastasia’s sphere. Finnegan initially feels alien while his companions are at home, then suddenly feels himself one of the oldest and most other people: it is a region where duality is strongest. [D:115]

D:115

ZauberkonzertComposition attributed to Andreyev by the expert codenamed Philo Vance, who says that one answer to the Man of Mystery problem lies in its eighth movement. He then broadens the claim absurdly to the eighth movement of anything, African violets, cribbage, and checkers, finally advising Duffey to get a dog. [MTM B13:457]

MTM B13:457

Zauberlehrling“Sorcerer’s Apprentice,” the carnival nickname Betty tells Hans Schultz he has acquired while studying with Professor Kirol von Weinsberg-Valeni. [A:217] It recalls Goethe’s poem “Der Zauberlehrling,” in which an apprentice’s borrowed magic escapes his control.

A:217

Zeno ParadoxesThe philosophical paradoxes of Zeno of Elea, a fifth-century BC thinker, concerning such problems as plurality, motion, and divisibility. During Duffey’s garden encounter, the Invisible God says, without words, that the Melchisedech Paradoxes are at least as wonderful as Zeno’s and that every person is uniquely surrounded by paradoxes. [MTM B12:389]

MTM B12:389

Zero Growth lobbyOne of the lobbies represented among the new Princes, Gates, and Stones in the attempted broadening of the Ekklesia before its Last Conclave. The passage gives no detailed program for this lobby. [MB:561-562]

MB:561-562

ZiggaratName the hoyden gives the one low mountain supposedly present before the multiplication of mountains. In her mythic account it served as the Mountain of the Commandments, was rolled from country to country, and prefigured Ararat. [MTM B11:333-334]

MTM B11:333-334

Zingaro (Gitano)Italian zingaro and Spanish gitano, terms traditionally rendered “Gypsy.” Niccolo Crotolus uses them for his family’s claimed background as dancers and musicians. He says that Crotolo is their family name and an old word for a castanet; this is his explanation, offered against the narrator’s alternative nickname derivation. [A:278-279]

A:278-279

Zippo the Fire-EaterCarnival fire-eater whose image Hans Schultz says he painted, along with Edgar the Seal and other acts, for carnival advertising. Hans recalls spectators saying the performances were not as good as his pictures. [A:230]

A:230

ZoarThe big African drummer in the Brimstone Combo in Trinali’s poem about the Green Groves of Gomorrah and the saloon at Beelzebub and Hell-Raiser Streets. [A:235] His name recalls the biblical Zoar, the town to which Lot escapes from Sodom in Genesis 19.

A:235

Zodiac, Casey of theIdentity of Casey Szymansky, also Kasmir Gorshok and Casey of the Crock, explicitly recognized as a true Argo Master. [MTM B13:426] Duffey earlier reports Casey’s offer to exchange souls with the Devil and suffer in his place, while Stein claims a lesser trade of old souls between himself and Casey. [MTM B5:169] Hilary Hilton later identifies Casey as Antichrist; Casey himself announces “I am Casey of the Zodiac, the Anti-Christus.” [MTM B12:378] [MTM B12:382] Casey has projected his idealized face and voice over television programs, building his cult. The grotesque head shown at Hilton’s party, however, is projected by Duffey from an Adam Scanlon painting. Casey denounces it as a fraud before finally yielding to Duffey’s demand to meet. [MTM B12:380-382]

MTM B13:426; MTM B5:169; MTM B12:378; MTM B12:382; MTM B12:380-382

Zombie devilThe figure invoked when the narrator calls the Argo’s mechanical crewmen “as robotic as the zombie devil himself, only not cute.” The crewmen are place tokens or materialized residues of Argonauts who have sailed before and will return, including Duffey and Brannagan during their absences. The passage does not name this “zombie devil.” [MTM B13:415]

MTM B13:415

Zoot suitAn exaggerated suit style associated with the 1940s. In Askandan’s sales pitch, the outdated zoot suit he offers a naked Casey is rare and will supposedly fit anyone because nobody can tell whether it fits. In fact it is painfully too small. Finnegan bought it for nine dollars for the prank; Askandan demands sixty-five and then seventy-five dollars before selling it with pointed shoes and a monstrous hat on credit. Casey’s predicament finally makes him laugh. [A:260-261]

A:260-261

ZuqarPlace where “The Sea is on Fire” in the opening poem of Finnegan’s chapter. The adjacent burning-desert line concerns Yenbo and Lith, not Zuqar. [A:171] A plausible geographical referent is Zukur or Zugar, the volcanic island in the southern Red Sea’s Zukur-Hanish group; the poem does not explicitly establish the identification.

A:171
